en: Adhyāya 1 The *Bhāmatī*:
Of Him who is the source, assisted by the pair of indeterminable nesciences (*avidyā*), these— ether, air, fire, water, and earth— are the illusory manifestations (*vivarta*).
We bow to that Brahman—the immortal, consisting of immeasurable bliss and knowledge—from which this universe, both moving and unmoving, high and low, has come into being. //1//
The Vedas are His breath; the five elements are His glance; the moving and unmoving world is His smile; and the great dissolution is His sleep. //2//
We pay homage to the Veda and to Bhava, who is endowed with six limbs, possessed of various imperishable [forms], and eternal. //3//
We pay homage to Mārtaṇḍa, Tilakasvāmin, and Mahāgaṇapati, who are worshipped by the entire world and bestow all spiritual accomplishments. //4//
Salutations to that Vyāsa, the author of the Brahma-sūtras, the second Creator, who is an incarnation of the power of knowledge of the Blessed Lord Hari. (5)
Having bowed to Śaṅkara, the treasury of compassion, whose consciousness is utterly pure, this commentary—clear and profound—is now analyzed as it was composed by him. (6)
Even the speech of those like us, though devoid of the refined composition of a master, purifies like the falling current of the Gaṅgā purifies the water in a street. //7//
Now, that which is free from doubt and devoid of purpose is not an object of inquiry for a discerning person,
just as a jar situated in bright light and in contact with the sense organ and the mind,
or the teeth of a crow.
And thus, the statement "this is Brahman" constitutes the perception of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
For it is said that Brahman is indeed the Self (*ātman*) because of its vastness (*bṛhatva*) and its capacity for expansion (*bṛṃhaṇatva*).

And this [Self] extends from worms and moths up to the divine sages (*devarṣi*), belonging to every living being among those who are the locus of the notion of "I," distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects.
Because [the self] is established through the immediate experience of "I," which is certain and free from error by virtue of its distinction [from the body], it is not an object for inquiry.
Indeed, no one ever doubts in this regard, wondering "Am I or am I not?"; nor does anyone err, thinking "I am certainly not."

Nor is it correct to say that this ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has the body as its substrate, on the grounds of observing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with bodily attributes such as "I am thin," "I am fat," or "I go."

For if that [body] were the object of apprehension, there could be no such synthesis as: "I, who experienced my parents in childhood, am the very same person who now experiences my great-grandchildren in old age.
Indeed, between the bodies of the child and the old man, there is not even a trace of recognition by which their identity might be determined.
Therefore, that which persists while certain things undergo change must be distinct from them, just as a thread is distinct from the flowers [strung upon it].
And likewise, even though the bodies of children and others undergo mutual change, that which persists as the locus of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) is distinct from them.

Furthermore, one who, while in a dream, assumes a divine body and experiences enjoyments appropriate to it, upon waking perceives himself as having a human body and thinks, "I am not a god, I am only a human," even as the divine body is sublated.

Furthermore, even a yogi perceives the uncontradicted locus of the "I" as distinct from the body; moreover, a yogi experiences the self as undivided even upon the dissolution of the body. Thus, the body is not the objective support of the "I"-conception (ahaṅkāra).
For this very reason, the sense organs either are not its objective support, [or they are included within the body].

Even though there is a difference in the sense faculties, because there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) having "I" as its objective support— expressed as "I who saw that very same thing now touch it"—
the distinction of this [self] from the objects is indeed quite evident.

Furthermore, since the two instruments, intellect (*buddhi*) and mind (*manas*), are manifested as the appearance of an agent in the form of "I," it is illogical for them to be the objective supports [of such a recognition].

We consider it logical that expressions such as "I am thin" or "I am blind," even though there is no actual identity [between the self and these attributes], are figurative (*aupacārika*) in some way, like the expression "the beds cry out.

Therefore, it is established that the Self—which is distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects that are the referents of the notion of "this"—is not an object of inquiry because it is clearly known through the experience of "I" and is free from doubt;
furthermore, because it lacks a purpose [for inquiry].

For instance, liberation (*apavarga*), defined here as the cessation of *saṃsāra*, is intended as the goal. And *saṃsāra*, which is caused by the non-experience of the true nature of the self (*ātman*), must be brought to an end through the knowledge of the true nature of the self.
If this [ignorance] is beginningless and persists alongside the beginningless knowledge of the true nature of the self, [then how can it be removed?]
From what could its cessation arise? [It cannot,] because there is no contradiction.
And from what could there be a non-experience of the true nature of the self?
For there is no knowledge of the true nature of the self other than the experience "I am."
Nor can the Self— which is established by the most vivid and universal experience as "I" and is distinct from the body, senses, and so forth— be subverted even by thousands of Upaniṣads,
because that would contradict direct experience;
for not even a thousand scriptures have the power to turn a jar into a cloth.

Therefore, because this contradicts experience, we consider it logical that the Upaniṣads have only figurative meanings; with this intention, having raised the objection, he refutes it with the words: "Of the two objects of the notions of 'you' and 'I'. Here, the portion beginning with "of 'you' and 'I'" and ending with "it is logical that [the self] should be false" constitutes the text of the objection;
the portion beginning with "nevertheless" constitutes the text of the refutation.
Nevertheless, because of the connection with the word "tathāpi" (nevertheless), one should read "yadyapi" (even though) to express the doubt.
While it would have been sufficient to say "of these two [objects] within the scope of our own cognition," the use of the term "yuṣmad" (you/that) is intended to indicate absolute difference.
For the notion of "you" (*tvam*) is the counter-correlative of the notion of "I" (*aham*), whereas the notion of "this" (*idam*) is not.
This is because we frequently observe such usage as: "We are these," "we are those," and "we exist."
The self, whose nature is consciousness, is the subject; the intellect, the sense organs, the body, and external objects, whose natures are insentient, are the objects.
For these bind—that is, they fetter—the conscious self.
The meaning is that they cause [the objects] to be defined by their own respective forms.
Regarding the extreme difference which is the cause for the absence of mutual superimposition, the illustration is "like darkness and light.
For indeed, no one can ever perceive light and darkness—which function through their respective modes of manifestation—as being of the nature of one another.
This is what was stated: "in the impossibility of mutual existence.
Mutual existence means being one another, that is to say, identity.
Regarding the phrase "in the absence of that":
it might be argued that there may be no mutual existence between the two subjects; however—
However, there will be a mutual superimposition (adhyāsa) of their attributes—such as insentience and sentience, or permanence and impermanence.
For it is observed that even when the two substrates (dharmin) are perceived as distinct, there occurs a superimposition of their attributes;

for example, although a crystal gem is perceived as distinct from a flower, because of its extreme transparency it receives the reflection of a hibiscus flower, leading to the illusion of redness, such that one says, "The crystal is red. It is for this reason that the following was said:
—“Of their properties as well”:
the existence of properties within one another’s substratum is their mutual exchange;
that [exchange] is untenable.

This is the intended meaning: for a substance possessing form, due to its extreme transparency, might indeed take on the reflection of another substance possessing form—even one being perceived separately from it;
however, the conscious self (cidātmā), being formless and the subject (viṣayin), cannot possibly receive the reflection of an object (viṣaya).
As they have said:
[The question is: "What kind of reflection-ness belongs to sound, smell, taste, and so forth?

In this context, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be that through the mutual interpenetration of the object and the subject, there occurs a reciprocal exchange consisting of the mutual interpenetration of their attributes as well;
for if those two substrates were perceived with absolute distinction, they would remain non-interpenetrated.
The dharmas of those two are even more unmixed, because they are far removed by the intervention of their respective substrata;
this is what is meant by the word "even more."
"By the opposite of that" means by the opposite of the object;
the word "mithyā" (false) is a term signifying denial.
This is what is meant: superimposition is pervaded by the non-apprehension of difference;
and here, its opposite—the apprehension of difference—is present.
This apprehension of difference, by removing the non-apprehension of difference, also removes the superimposition that is pervaded by it.
The construction is: "Even though it is proper that [the self] should be false, nevertheless...
The underlying intention here is this: this would indeed be so if the reality of the self were manifested in the experience of "I";
however, this is not the case.

For indeed, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*)—which is the one essence of infinite bliss-consciousness (*anantānandacaitanya*), unconditioned by any adjuncts (*upādhi*), indifferent (*udāsīna*), partless, and non-dual—is celebrated in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇas*. Moreover, these texts, through their introductions, intermediate references, and conclusions, repeatedly declare such a reality of the Self; being intent upon that very reality, they cannot even by Indra be made to have a figurative meaning.
For in the case of repetition, there is an intensification of the object’s significance, as in: "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful!"
Not only is it not limited, but it is certainly not figurative.

However, how can the experience of "I" have the reality of the Self as its object, or how can it be free from distortion, when it presents the Self as localized and overwhelmed by a manifold expansion of grief, suffering, and the like?
Nor is it reasonable to claim that because it contradicts perception—the oldest means of knowledge—the Veda, which depends upon it, lacks authority or possesses only a figurative meaning.
Since it is not of human origin, all suspicion of defect has been dispelled from it;

and since its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is self-evident by virtue of its capacity to produce knowledge, it is independent regarding its own effect, which is the resulting cognition. If it is argued that even though it is independent regarding the resulting cognition, it depends upon perception for its own origination, and therefore its invalidity consists in its non-origination due to contradiction with perception—[we reply: no.
Because it is not an adversary to the arising [of perception].

For the conventional knowledge derived from scripture does not undermine the validity of direct perception, such that it would cease to exist due to the absence of its cause; rather, it is the [knowledge of] ultimate reality that does so.
Nor is its producer ultimately real,
for it is observed that the knowledge of reality arises even from conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*) which lack ultimate validity.
Likewise, properties such as shortness and length, though superimposed upon a letter and belonging to something else, serve as causes for the comprehension of reality.
For ordinary people, when they understand from the words "nāga" or "naga" either an elephant or a tree, do not become mistaken.
Nor is it logical for a sentence that is not intended for another purpose to have its primary meaning treated as figurative;
for it has been said: "In a prescriptive injunction, the word does not have a secondary meaning."
Moreover, seniority (*jyeṣṭhatva*) is a cause for being sublated (*bādhyatva*), but not for being a sublater (*bādhakatva*),
since we observe that the older cognition of silver is sublated by the younger cognition of nacre;
for it is impossible for that [younger cognition] to arise as having the nature of sublation unless it first sublates that [older one].
And it has been demonstrated that the status of being an authentic means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not depend [on anything else].
Thus, there is a sūtra of the Great Sage: "In a sequence of earlier and later, the earlier is weaker, as in the case of the original nature (*prakṛti*).
And likewise:
In that case, let it be understood that the subsequent [cognition] possesses superior force over the preceding one,
provided that the cognitions arise independently of one another.
— thus.
Moreover, even those who maintain that the self is the locus of the notion of "I" must not accept its ultimate reality;

for in the cognition, "I am here in this very house, knowing," the all-pervading [self] is perceived as localized. This is like the appearance of a blade of durva grass to one standing on the ground when looking at great trees situated on a high mountain peak.
Nor is it correct to argue that it is the localization of the body that is being experienced, and not that of the self.

For at that time, it does not occur as "I," nor—if it were secondary—does it occur as "one who knows. Furthermore, a word for one thing is used for another through connection with a quality that is being indicated; where there is agreement between the speaker and the listener regarding this, that is secondary (gauṇa).
And that [usage] is preceded by a cognition of difference.

For example, the word *agnihotra* in the statement regarding the regular *agnihotra* is used figuratively—on account of similarity in what is to be accomplished—with respect to the rite belonging to the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*, where the difference is determined by another context, as in the injunction: "He performs the *agnihotra* for a month."
In the case of a boy, the word "lion" [is applied] because a distinction from a [real] lion is established through experience;
however, the primary referent of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) is not experienced as distinct from the body and so forth by having its inner core fully extracted,
such that the word [“I”] would be figurative when applied to the body and other such things.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even when a term is used figuratively due to extreme conventional usage, there is no misconception regarding its figurative nature—as in the case of the word "oil" (*taila*) applied to mustard seeds and the like.

Even there, once the difference between the oil produced from sesame and [other oils] such as mustard is established, the misconception that mustard seeds and so forth are denotable by the word "oil" arises;
however, there is no determination of non-difference between the two objects, namely, sesame oil and mustard oil.

Thus, it is established that being secondary (gauṇatva) is pervaded by the knowledge of the distinction between the secondary and the primary for one who perceives both; therefore, here, the pervading knowledge of such distinction, upon ceasing, also causes the cessation of being secondary.

Nor should it be argued that even when there is a difference between the bodies of a child and an old man, there is an experience of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, based on the recognition of the single Self in the form "I am he."
Indeed, this statement concerns investigators,
not ordinary people;
for even investigators do not transcend common worldly practice at the time of conventional transaction.
For the Blessed Commentator will indeed state immediately thereafter: "And because there is no distinction from cattle and other such beings.
Outsiders also say: "Those who contemplate the scriptures indeed analyze in this way, not those who merely practice.
Therefore, by process of elimination, the worldly person employing the ego-sense directed toward the conscious self in the form "I am here in this house" [is referring to the body].

We consider it logical that one conceives of the self as being limited in extent due to the apprehension of its non-difference from the body and so forth, just as space appears limited by adjuncts such as jars, water-pots, or flower-vessels.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that the self is limited in extent like the body on the grounds of the authority of the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*);
for in that case, it would have to be either of atomic dimension or of the dimension of the body.
If [the self] were of atomic dimension, there would be no such notions as "I am stout" or "I am tall.
If, however, it were of the same dimension as the body, then, by virtue of having parts, it would follow that it is non-eternal, just like the body.
Furthermore, in this view, either the collection of parts would cognize, or each part individually.

If the position were that each part cognizes individually, then because there would be no single-minded consensus among many independent cognizers, the body would be torn asunder by their simultaneous and contradictory movements in various directions.
Or else, it would follow that there is no action at all.
If consciousness were a property of the aggregate, then when one part is severed, a part of the conscious self would also be severed, and thus it would not perceive.
Furthermore, no necessary rule of mutual inseparability is observed among many parts;
whenever a particular part falls apart, then in its absence, the whole would not perceive.
Even though the notion of "I" has consciousness as its object, its erroneous nature remains exactly as it was,
because that notion manifests as a stable entity while consciousnesses themselves are unstable.
By this, [notions] such as "I am fat," "I am blind," and "I am walking" are also explained as being cases of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Thus, when the notion of "I" has been rendered as rotten as a rotten gourd by the sequence of reasoning just described, the venerable Śruti is able, without obstruction, to negate in the Self that nature of being an agent, an enjoyer, and the essence of pleasure, pain, grief, and so forth, which was previously attributed to it by the experience of "I.

Therefore, this is the detailed explanation— by way of its essential nature, its cause, and its result— of that notion of "I," whose falsity is well-known from all philosophical systems, the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, beginning with the words "in one another," and so forth.
Having superimposed mutual identity— one thing upon another substratum such as the self or the body— thinking "I am this body," and so forth;
and the term "this" refers to the object in reality, not merely to its appearance.

Worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) is the transaction of people; it consists of the designation "I am this," as indicated by the word "iti," as well as the process of cognizing through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) the various objects of cognition— whether favorable or unfavorable to the body and so forth— and subsequently engaging in their acquisition, avoidance, and so on.

Having superimposed the attributes of one upon the other substratum—that is, having superimposed the attributes of the body and so forth, such as birth, death, old age, and disease, upon the self as the substratum (which has had the state of being the body superimposed upon it), and likewise having superimposed the attributes of the self, such as consciousness, upon the body and so forth (which have had the state of being the self superimposed upon them)—there arises the worldly usage and designation: "This is mine; [I am subject to] old age, death, sons, cattle, ownership, and so on.
The word "iti" indicates the corresponding activity and so forth that follow from this.

And here, the agent inferred from the two actions of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is the same; thus, by virtue of having a common agent, the expression "having superimposed, there is transaction" (*adhyasya vyavahāraḥ*) is justified. He clarifies that superimposition is the cause of transaction, as indicated by its priority in time, stating: "transaction has false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) as its cause. False knowledge is superimposition.
It is caused by that, meaning that the existence or non-existence of worldly transaction follows the existence or non-existence of that [superimposition].
Thus, having stated the nature and the result—namely, worldly transaction—of superimposition, he states its cause: "through the non-discrimination of one from the other."
The meaning is: "by means of grasping the distinction.
Now, why is it not simply non-distinction (aviveka), in which case there would be no superimposition (adhyāsa)? To this he says: "of the attribute and the substrate, which are absolutely distinct."

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the distinction (*viveka*) between two substrata (*dharmin*) is their non-identity (*atādātmya*), and the distinction between their properties (*dharma*) is their non-confusion (*asaṃkīrṇatā*).
This may be so:

it is logical that for two distinct real entities, there arises the delusion of identity based on the non-apprehension of their difference, just as the delusion of identity with silver arises when the difference of mother-of-pearl from silver is not apprehended.

But here, since there exists no real entity such as the body and so forth other than the *cidātman* (the conscious self) which is ultimately real, how can there be a non-apprehension of the difference from the *cidātman*, and how can there be the delusion of identity? To this he says: "having coupled the real and the unreal. The construction is: "having superimposed [the one] due to the non-apprehension of their distinction."
Truth is the conscious self (cidātman),
and untruth is the intellect, the senses, the body, and so forth;
the meaning is that these two substrates are made into a pair, that is, joined together.

Furthermore, since there can be no ultimate union between that which exists conventionally and that which exists ultimately, the suffix *cvi* is employed here in the sense of "the becoming of something that was not [previously] so.
What is meant is this: because it is impossible to superimpose what has not been cognized, the cognition of the object to be superimposed is required, rather than its actual ontological existence.
This might be so.

Since the superimposition (*samāropa*) of what was previously perceived occurs when there is a cognition of the object to be superimposed (*āropya*), and that cognition is itself dependent upon superimposition, a mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*) is unavoidable; therefore, he says: "Innate" (*naisargika*) means natural (*svābhāvika*); this empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) is beginningless.
Because this empirical usage is beginningless, its cause—superimposition—is likewise so.
It has been stated that [superimposition] is beginningless;

therefore, since each preceding false cognition presents the intellect, the sense organs, the body, and so forth for the sake of each subsequent superimposition, there is no mutual dependence—just as in the case of the seed and the sprout—because of this beginninglessness.
This might be argued.
In the case of a superimposition (*āropa*), it is merely prior cognition that is required,
not the ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*) of that which is being cognized.
However, cognition itself is not possible for something absolutely non-existent, such as the body, sense organs, and so forth, which are like a lotus in the sky.

Indeed, even for the conscious self (*cidātman*), existence consists solely in its being manifest, and not in something distinct from that—neither in inherence in the universal "existence" (*sattāsāmānya*) nor in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*), because that would entail duality.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate another existence or another causal efficiency for existence and causal efficiency themselves, it would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, manifestation alone must be accepted as existence.
Thus, the body and so forth are not non-existent because they are manifest, just like the conscious self.
Or, if they were non-existent, they would not be manifest;
how then could there be a union of the real and the unreal?
And in the absence of that [union], for whom and from what source could there be a non-apprehension of difference?
The objector, harboring the intention, "In the absence of that [distinction], how can there be superimposition (adhyāsa)?", asks: "What is this so-called superimposition?
Here, the word "what" (*ka*) is used in the sense of an objection.

The respondent, while explaining the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as established in common worldly experience, refutes the objection—stating: "It is said: it is an appearance (*avabhāsa*) of what was previously perceived, in the form of a memory, upon another [object].
An "appearance" (*avabhāsa*) is an appearance that has either subsided (*avasanna*) or been disparaged (*avamata*).
Its subsidence or disparagement consists in its being sublated by another cognition.
By this much, it has been stated that [this] is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
This is its detailed explanation, beginning with the words "the appearance of what was previously seen" (*pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsa*).
The appearance of what was previously seen is "the appearance of what was previously seen."

Furthermore, a false cognition does not occur without the pairing of an object of superimposition (*āropya*) and that which is superimposed (*āropa-viṣaya*). Thus, by the mention of "previously seen," it brings forward the unreal thing to be superimposed.
And for that [object], its mere state of having been seen is what is required, not its actual existence as a real entity; this is why the term "seen" is used.
Nevertheless, since a presently occurring seen object or act of seeing is not useful for superimposition, the word "previous" was stated.
And that which was previously perceived, although existing in its own nature, is unreal because it is indefinable as something to be superimposed.
He states the reality that serves as the locus of superimposition with the words "paratra" (elsewhere):
in "elsewhere," such as mother-of-pearl and the like, which is ultimately real.
Thus, by this, the union of truth and falsehood has been stated.
This might be [objected]:
"The definition—that there is an appearance of what was previously seen elsewhere—is not a valid characteristic."
Because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
For there is indeed the appearance of the previously perceived "cowness" (*gotva*) in a healthy cow elsewhere in a black-spotted cow;
and there is also the correct appearance of Devadatta, previously perceived in Pāṭaliputra, elsewhere in Māhiṣmatī.
Furthermore, the term "manifestation" (avabhāsa) is well-established even in the case of a correct cognition, as in the expressions "the manifestation of blue" or "the manifestation of yellow.
Therefore, he says: "having the form of memory" (smṛtirūpa).
That which has a form like that of memory is "memory-like" (*smṛtirūpa*).
And having a non-present object is what constitutes being "memory-like.
Since recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that has a present object is valid, there is no over-extension [of the definition].

Nor is there any lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because dream-cognition, which consists of both memory and error, is likewise of this nature; for even in that case, when a father or other such person who is being remembered is not perceived as being present due to the influence of a sleep-affliction, [the cognition arises].
In each such case, there is a superimposition of that very thing previously perceived as being present in a specific place and time.
This same definition should also be applied to cases such as "the conch is yellow" and "molasses is bitter.
For instance, one perceives yellowness residing in the substance of bile—which is in contact with the clear rays of the eyes issuing outward—as being devoid of bile itself.

Perceiving that the whiteness of the conch is obscured by a defect, and not perceiving the absence of connection between yellowness and the conch, one superimposes the previously observed grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of yellowness and conch-ness— just as in cases such as "the yellow mass of gold" or "the yellow *bilva* fruit"— due to the similarity of the non-apprehension of that non-connection, and says: "The [conch] is yellow."
"Conch-shell," it is said.
By this, the cognition "bitter jaggery" is also explained.

Likewise, when clear mirrors, water, and the like are positioned facing the person who perceives them, the ocular light, though it has struck [the surface], is turned back against its current by the more powerful solar light and becomes conjoined with the face.
One perceives the face;

yet, due to the influence of defects, one fails to perceive its actual location and its non-facing orientation toward the primary object. Instead, one superimposes upon the face the location of the mirror or water-surface previously seen facing oneself, as well as the quality of facing that surface. Thus, even the delusion of a reflection is characterized.

By this, the definition should be applied as appropriate even to such delusions as the double moon, confusion of the directions, a whirling firebrand, a city of Gandharvas, and a snake in a bamboo stalk.
What is meant is this: existence does not consist merely in being manifest, such that the body, sense organs, and so forth would possess reality simply by virtue of being manifest.

For it is not the case that ropes and the like, or crystals and the like, do not appear as possessing qualities such as redness due to the absence of a snake; nor, when they do appear, do they become identical with that [snake] or possess its properties.

If that were so, then one who, having perceived a mass of mirage-rays in the desert and proceeded with the thought, "This is the Mandākinī river flowing nearby, with its garland of high, surging, and lofty waves," would drink that water.
It would merely allay one's thirst.
Therefore, even against one's will, one must not admit that what is manifest yet superimposed possesses real existence.

Nor can it be said that water in the form of a mirage is non-existent in its own nature while being ultimately real in its essence; for how could the body, the senses, and so forth—which are non-existent even in their own nature—be superimposed, given that they do not fall within the scope of direct experience?
This is not correct;
for if non-existent things are not objects of experience, how then do non-existent things such as mirages become objects of experience in their nature as water and so forth?
Nor do they become existent even in their nature as water and so forth by virtue of possessing intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*).

If it should be argued: "Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not something distinct from existence (*bhāva*); rather, existence itself is non-existence insofar as it takes on the nature of another existence, while in its own form it is existence.
As they have said:
"For non-existence is indeed another state of existence, depending on a certain perspective.
Consequently, because it can be described as having the nature of an existent entity, its being an object of experience is logical.
Furthermore, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is absolutely non-existent, devoid of all capacity, and lacks any reality, how could it be an object of experience,
or how could it be superimposed upon the conscious self?

Nor can it be argued that even in the absence of all capacity on the part of the object, consciousness itself— arising through the power of its own internal cognition and possessing a distinct nature established by its own evidence without requiring an external example— is what manifests the non-existent.
Therefore, it is correct that its very power to manifest the non-existent is ignorance (*avidyā*). For what, then, is the object of this power of consciousness to manifest the non-existent?
If you say it is "the non-existent," [we reply:]...
Is this an action to be performed, or is it something to be made known?
It cannot, first of all, be an action to be performed.
Because reality cannot belong to that which is non-existent;
nor is it something to be made known, since no other cognition is perceived.
Furthermore, this would lead to an infinite regress.
If it is argued that the very nature of consciousness itself is the manifestation of the non-existent, then what kind of relationship can there be between the existent and the non-existent?
If it is claimed that the relationship of the existent cognition with the non-existent consists in the fact that the cognition’s determination is dependent upon the non-existent—
Oh, how utterly exhausted is this poor dependent phenomenon, since its investigation proceeds even though it is non-existent! And yet, the cause does not impart anything to it,
because it is impossible for a cause to provide support to that which is non-existent.

If it is argued that the nature of cognition itself is such that it does not manifest without an object, and that this is not dependent upon the object being real, then oh, how great is its partiality for the non-existent! For this cognition—which does not arise from that [object], nor has that as its essence—is nonetheless invariably restricted to a necessary connection with it. Therefore, the body, the sense organs, and so forth, being absolutely non-existent and devoid of reality, cannot possibly be objects of experience.

To this we reply: If that which lacks reality (*nistattva*) is not within the range of experience, then are the rays of light now possessed of reality (*satattva*) in their nature as water, such that they become objects of experience?
They are not possessed of reality.
Because the rays do not exist as that [water] itself;
and the reality of entities is twofold— existence and non-existence— among which the former is intrinsic, while the latter is extrinsic.
As they have said:
"In an entity that is eternally characterized by both existence and non-existence through its own nature and the nature of others,
some aspect is cognized by some people at some time."
Thus, is the cognition appearing as water in mirages an object that has reality as its domain?
If so, it would be correct; consequently, it would neither be erroneous nor subject to sublation.
Certainly, it would not be sublated if one were to perceive these rays of light as having the nature of water when they do not possess the nature of water;
but since one perceives them as having the nature of water, how could one be non-erroneous, or how could [the perception] be non-sublatable? Alas!
The nature of water in mirages, which are essentially the absence of water, is not existent;
for since they are non-different from the absence of water, it is logically impossible for them to have the nature of water.
Nor is it non-existent; for the non-existence of one thing is understood only as being another distinct thing.
By those who maintain that "non-existence is simply another state of being and nothing else, because it cannot be defined as such," it is held that a superimposed form is not a distinct entity;
for that [superimposed form] would have to be either the rays of light themselves, or...
Or, regarding water found in the Ganges and other rivers,
in a previous eon there would have been the cognition "mirage," and not "water."
In the northern case, however, there would be "the water in the Gaṅgā," but not "here.
If the distinction of place is not remembered, there would simply be "water."
Nor can it be said that "it exists here";
nor is it correct to claim that this [object] must be absolutely non-existent, devoid of all intrinsic nature, and a mere falsehood,
because such a thing cannot logically fall within the scope of experience.
This has been stated above;
therefore, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Nor can it be both existent and non-existent, because of their mutual contradiction;
therefore, one must accept that the water superimposed upon the rays of light is indeed indeterminable (anirvācya).
Thus, by this process, the superimposed water is like real water.
Therefore, it is as if previously seen;
but in reality, it is neither water nor was it previously seen.
But [unreality] is that which is indefinable (*anirvācya*).
And thus, the manifold world (*prapañca*) consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, is also indefinable;
it is logical that even though it is unprecedented, it is superimposed upon the other—the conscious Self—as if presented by previous false cognitions.

This is because it possesses the characteristics of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Furthermore, the sublation of the phenomenal world consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, will be established later.

The conscious Self (*cidātmā*), however, is the object of the Vedas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas; its nature is determined by reasoning that is rooted in and non-contradictory to them as being pure, awakened, and liberated. Thus, it is to be defined solely as existing (*sattvena*).
Its existence is simply its own uncontradicted self-luminosity;
and that is the very nature of the conscious self, not some "existence-universal" inherent in it, nor its capacity for causal efficiency— thus all is clear.

And this superimposition (*adhyāsa*), characterized in this manner, is accepted as indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) by all investigators; there is disagreement only regarding its specific nature. To confirm its indeterminability, he says: "Some [regard it] as that," referring to silver, which is an attribute of another thing—that is, an attribute of cognition.
That is to say, [it refers to] the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*).
"Superimposition" (*adhyāsa*) occurs elsewhere, namely, upon the external.
In the Sautrāntika system, at least, the external exists as a real entity (*vastusat*).
In that regard, there is the superimposition of the form of cognition.

Even for the Vijñānavādins, although an external object does not exist as a real entity, nevertheless, an unreal external object is superimposed by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
In this regard, there is the superimposition of the form of cognition.
And the justification is as follows: it is a general rule that whatever form is established by experience must be accepted as being exactly like that;
however, its being otherwise occurs due to the force of a powerful subverting cognition.
Since the sublation "this is not silver" can be accounted for even by the sublation of the "this-ness" alone, it is not appropriate to regard it as having silver as its object;

for if the substrate (dharmin) silver were sublated, both the silver and its attribute (dharma), namely this-ness, would have to be sublated. Therefore, it is better that only this-ness, as its attribute, be sublated.
Nor, however, is silver the locus (*dharmin*);
and thus, since silver is sublated externally, it must by implication reside within internal cognition, whereby the superimposition of the form of cognition onto the external is established.

Some, however, dissatisfied with the theory of the manifestation of the form of cognition (*jñānākārakhyāti*), say: "Wherever there is a superimposition of X upon Y, that error is based on the non-apprehension of the distinction between them."

And they have stated the reason for dissatisfaction: the nature of consciousness as being [the form] of silver and so forth must be established either through direct experience (*anubhava*) or through inference (*anumāna*).
Of these, inference will be refuted later on.
The experience must be either the cognition of silver or a subverting cognition;
it cannot, first of all, be the experience of silver.
For that [silver] makes known the silver which is the locus of the "this-ness," but not something internal;
for in that case, it would have to be "I," because it would be non-different from the cognition of the perceiver.
Erroneous cognition determines its own internal form as being external;
thus, that [external object] is not the domain of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra). Furthermore, you, sir, should consider the subverting cognition regarding its status as a form of consciousness.
Does it distinguish the object standing before one from silver, or does it also demonstrate its nature as a form of cognition?
In this regard, the "Beloved of the Gods" (the fool), whose wisdom is indeed praiseworthy, asserts that the function of the subverting cognition is to demonstrate its nature as a form of cognition.
If it is argued that its nature as a form of cognition follows by implication from the negation of its being present before one, we say no.
Because its non-proximity is denied by the denial of its apprehension, it is not present;
for how could there be an absolute proximity of this [silver] to the cognizer, consisting as it does of the cognizer himself?
Nor is this a negation of the silver.
And it is not the "this-ness" (idantā) that is superimposed, but rather the practical activity regarding silver occasioned by the non-apprehension of the distinction [between the shell and silver].
Nor is it the case that the very silver itself is superimposed upon the mother-of-pearl by the cognition of silver.
For it is not logical that the appearance of silver should have mother-of-pearl as its objective support (*ālambana*),
because that would contradict experience.
Indeed, something cannot be an objective support by virtue of its mere existence.
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
for since all objects are indistinguishable in terms of their existence, it would follow that they must all equally serve as cognitive objects.
Nor [can it be said that they are objects] by virtue of being causes.
Because the sense faculties and so forth are also causes [of cognition],
the meaning of "objective support" (ālambana) is simply the state of appearing;
and yet, in the cognition of silver, the mother-of-pearl does not appear.
Thus, how can there be an object of cognition?
Or, if its appearing is admitted, how is there no contradiction with experience?
Furthermore, since the capacity of the sense organs and so forth to produce correct knowledge has been observed, how could false knowledge arise from them?
If it is argued that those [causes], when accompanied by defects, possess the capacity even for a false cognition, we say no;
for the function of defects is merely to obstruct the capacity to produce the [correct] effect.
Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of a banyan sprout arising even from a scorched *kuṭaja* seed.
Moreover, if cognitions were to deviate from their own objects, there would follow the consequence of a total lack of confidence in all knowledge whatsoever.
Therefore, it must be accepted that all cognition is valid (*samīcīna*).
And thus, [in the case of the cognition] "this is silver,"...
The two cognitions consisting of "this" are of the nature of memory and direct experience.
Therein, "this" is the apprehension of the mere substance present before one;

because of a defect, the specific universal of "mother-of-pearl-ness" residing therein is not apprehended. That mere [substance], having been apprehended, generates a memory of silver through the process of awakening latent impressions (saṃskāra) by virtue of its similarity [to silver].

And although that [cognition] has the nature of apprehending what has already been apprehended, due to the influence of a defect and the loss of the aspect of "having been apprehended," it remains as mere apprehension.

Thus, because of the non-apprehension of the mutual difference— both in terms of essential nature and object— between the recollection of silver and the apprehension of the mere substance present before one,
[the cognition] "this" [arises] through its similarity to a cognition whose object is nearby silver.
"this is silver"— these two, perception and recollection, likewise bring about the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In some cases, however, there is perception in which the mutual difference between the two is not grasped,
as in "the conch is yellow."
For here, as the eye-rays emerge, the yellowness of the bile-substance—which is transparent like glass—is perceived, while the bile itself is not perceived.
The conch-shell, too, by the force of the defect, is perceived in its mere essential form, devoid of its white quality.

Thus, because of the non-apprehension of the non-connection between these two—the quality and the qualified—and because of their similarity [to each other], there arises a linguistic usage of non-difference and a designation of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), just as in the case of the cognition of a mass of molten gold.

Furthermore, because the linguistic usage of non-difference—which is occasioned by the non-apprehension of difference—is sublated, the sublating nature of the discriminative cognition "this is not that" is also established;
and once that is established, the erroneous nature of the preceding cognition is likewise proven as it is commonly recognized in the world.
Therefore, all disputed instances of doubt and delusion are in accordance with reality.
Because it is a cognition, like the cognition of a jar and so forth.
This is what was stated: "where there is the superimposition of that."
The common worldly consensus that a superimposition (adhyāsa) of silver and the like occurs upon a mother-of-pearl shell and the like is not based on the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti);

rather, it is an error caused by the non-apprehension of the distinction between the perceived silver and its recollection— both of which have lost their aspect of being previously perceived— and thus consist merely in what was perceived, namely, the mere substance standing before one as "this" and the cognition thereof.
And the state of being erroneous consists in the designation of mutual coreferentiality between perception and recollection, as well as the practical usage [of the object] as "silver" and so forth.

However, others, dissatisfied even with this, maintain that superimposition occurs where there is the attribution of a contrary property to that very [object] upon which it is superimposed. The underlying intention here is as follows: it is a matter of common experience for everyone that one who seeks silver proceeds toward the object present before them based on the cognition "this is silver," and that there is a designation of coreferentiality [between the two].
This, therefore, cannot possibly arise merely from the non-apprehension of the mutual difference between perception and memory, as well as their respective objects;
for how could the practical activity and verbal designation of a conscious being—which are rooted in actual apprehension—arise from mere non-apprehension?
But was it not said that it does not arise from mere non-apprehension?
However, it is precisely the act of perception and the act of recollection, which have not apprehended their mutual distinction either in terms of their own nature or their objects,

that— by virtue of resembling a correct cognition of silver present before one— give rise to the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Now, is it this similarity to a correct cognition, when being perceived, that is the cause for the engagement in such practical usage?
Or [it is] not being apprehended as mere existence;

or, even when it is apprehended, there is the apprehension that "this similarity of form belongs to these two cognitions, namely the cognition of 'this' and the cognition of 'silver'," or else the apprehension that "there is a non-apprehension of the mutual difference between those two very [cognitions], both in their own nature and in their objects."
In this regard, first of all, the cognition "it is similar to a correct cognition" does not function to initiate practical activity in the same way as a correct cognition itself.
For the cognition "a gavaya is similar to a cow" does not cause one who seeks a cow to act toward a gavaya.
Furthermore, the cognition "there is simply a non-apprehension of the difference between these two" is contradicted [by experience].
For it is not the case that there is "non-apprehension of difference between these two" when there is no apprehension of the two as such;
nor is it the case that there is "non-apprehension of difference between these two" when there is apprehension of "these two.
Therefore, it must be stated that non-apprehension of difference, by its mere existence, is the cause of linguistic usage even while remaining unapprehended.
In this regard, is this [conventional usage] a cause for linguistic convention through the process of generating a superimposition (*āropa*),
or rather, is it so by itself even without generating a superimposition?

We, however, observe that because a conscious linguistic convention cannot logically be preceded by ignorance, it occurs precisely through the process of generating the cognition of a superimposition.
Now, it might be argued that true volitional activity is not preceded by ignorance, but rather by the apprehension and recollection of distinctions that have not been previously known.
This is not so.
For the mere recollection of the meaning of the nominal stem "silver" (rajata) is not sufficient for purposeful action.
Indeed, it is undisputed that the activity of those seeking silver is directed toward the locus of the "this-ness" (idam).
And how could such a person engage with the locus of "this-ness" if they did not desire it?
To desire one thing while doing another is a contradiction.
If one did not know that this object, which is the locus of the "this-ness," was silver, how could one desiring silver desire it?
If you were to say it is because of the non-apprehension of it as being otherwise (i.e., as non-silver), [we reply:]...
And he must be answered thus:
"If it is not grasped as suchness, why would one not remain indifferent?

Thus, this consciousness, being pulled in both directions by grasping and indifference, remains unsettled; yet, through the superimposition of silver upon that which is the locus of the notion "this," it is established precisely in grasping.
Thus, the non-apprehension of difference (bhedāgraha) is the cause for the engagement of a conscious agent through the process of generating a superimposition (*samāropa*).

For instance: having superimposed "silverness" upon the locus of the notion "this" due to the non-apprehension of difference, and having reflected upon the fact that what belongs to that same class is a cause of utility, [the agent acts].

Having inferred that the silver, which is the locus of the "this-ness" (idaṃkāra), belongs to that same class [of silver], one who desires it proceeds toward it; thus the sequence of events is established.
Furthermore, a memory of silver situated elsewhere is not capable of inferring that the locus of the "this-ness" functions as a cause for the utility [of that silver].
Because the reason, namely "silverness," lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).
Indeed, it is the perception of one part that leads to inference, not the perception of many parts;
as they say: "From the perception of one part by one who knows the connection."
In the case of superimposition (*samāropa*), however, there is the perception of a single part [of the object].

Thus it is established: this cognition of silver and so forth, which is the subject of dispute, has as its object the thing standing before one, because it invariably causes a person seeking silver and so forth to act toward that [thing].
Because it invariably induces a person seeking a particular object toward a specific thing;

for whatever knowledge invariably induces one who seeks a certain object toward a certain thing, that knowledge has that thing as its object, just like the well-established cognition of real silver acknowledged by both parties; and this [cognition] is likewise.
Therefore, it is "so" (tathā).

As for what was said—that because it does not appear [in that form], the mother-of-pearl is not the objective support (*ālambana*)—you, being questioned on this point, must explain: is it the nature of the mother-of-pearl (*śuktikātva*) that is not the objective support for the cognition "this is silver," or rather the mere substance standing before one, which is white and lustrous?

If you claim that the "shell-ness" (śuktikatva) is not the objective support (anālambana), that is certainly true; however, for you who assert that the subsequent [cognition] is without an objective support, there is a contradiction with your own experience.
For instance, while experiencing "this is silver," the experiencer points to the object present before him with his finger and so forth.
Moreover, it is observed that defective causes possess the capacity to produce a different effect by obstructing their natural effect;
for example, cane seeds scorched by a forest fire produce plantain stalks, and the digestive fire of one afflicted with *bhasmaka* disorder digests vast quantities of food.
Furthermore, the inference that illusions possess correspondence with reality has its object sublated by perception and is thus a fallacy,
like the inference that fire is not hot. As for what was said— that if false cognition were inconstant, there would be a lack of confidence in all means of valid knowledge— [that too is refuted].

This has been refuted by us in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*, where we demonstrated that intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) consists in being a means of cognition and not in non-deviation; thus it is not elaborated upon here. A mere indication regarding this refutation of the theory of "the loss of memory" (*smṛtipramoṣa*) has been stated;
the full detail, however, is to be understood from the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā*.

This is what has been stated: "But others say that where there is a superimposition of one thing upon another, it is the attribution of contrary properties to that very [thing] which is being described.

The construction is as follows: where there is a superimposition of silver and so forth upon mother-of-pearl and so forth, it is the attribution of contrary properties—that is, the attribution of the property of "silver-ness"—to that very mother-of-pearl and so forth.
Now, let there indeed be these disagreements among the investigators; yet...
To the question, "What follows from this in the present context?", he says: "In every way" (*sarvathāpi*).
The attribution of the properties of one thing to another is falsehood (*anṛtatā*), and that [falsehood] is indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*); this was to be established previously.

Therefore, the meaning is that according to the view of all investigators, the conceptualization of one thing as having the attributes of another necessarily involves the "indefinable" (anirvacanīya); thus, indefinability is a doctrine established by all schools (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*).

The point is that even those who maintain the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti-vādin*) must, though unwillingly, accept this out of regard for the necessity of the rules governing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), verbal designation, and practical activity.
Not only is this falsity established for investigators, [but it is also accepted by others].

Moreover, he says that this is so even for worldly people: "And thus there is experience in the world: 'For mother-of-pearl appears like silver,'" with the implication that it is not [experienced] as "this is silver.
This might be so.
The delusion that one thing has the nature of another is established in common experience;

however, since the delusion of difference in that which is single and non-different has never been observed, how can there be a delusion of difference among individual souls (jīvas) who are non-different from the conscious self (cidātman)? To this, he says: "The single moon appears as if accompanied by a second. He further raises an objection regarding superimposition upon the conscious self: "But how [is this possible]?"
The meaning is this: does the conscious self (cidātman) manifest or not?
If it does not manifest, how can there be superimposition (adhyāsa) upon it of objects and their attributes?
Indeed, the superimposition of silver or its attributes upon a substance that does not appear before one is impossible.
Nor is it logical that this [silver], while appearing, is insentient like a jar and dependent on another for its manifestation;
for it is certainly not the case that the same thing can be both the agent and the object, as that would be a contradiction.
For an object (*karman*) is that which possesses the fruit of an action inhering in another;
however, since the action of knowing does not inhere in another, how can it have an object?
Nor can that very [action] be both itself and other, because of contradiction.
But if one accepts that [the self] inheres in another self, it follows that the self which is the object of knowledge would itself be non-self;
likewise, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress of "that and that.
This might be argued:
The self, although insentient and appearing in all cognitions of objects, is only the agent and not the object,

because it lacks the possession of a fruit of action inhering in another, just like Caitra. For instance, when Caitra reaches a city through an action inhering in Caitra— even though the action inheres in both— the status of being the object belongs to the city alone.
This is because it possesses the fruit of an action inherent in another,
and not because Caitra possesses the fruit of his own action, since the act of going is inherent in Caitra himself.
That is not so, because it contradicts scripture;
for it is heard in scripture: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
And it is logically consistent as well.
For instance: this manifestation of an object, which is the fruit [of cognition], in which both the object and the self are manifested—is it insentient (*jaḍa*) or self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*)?
If it were insentient, then since both the object and the self would also be insentient, what would manifest in what, given their lack of distinction?
Thus, the entire world would necessarily fall into total blindness.
And thus there is a popular proverb:
"Like one blind man clinging to another blind man, there is a fall at every step."
Nor should it be argued that consciousness, while remaining latent, makes known both the object and itself— just as the eye and other sense organs do—
for "making known" means the generation of a cognition,
and a cognition once generated, being insentient (*jaḍa*), cannot escape the aforementioned defect.
In this way, each subsequent cognition would also be insentient, leading to an infinite regress.
Therefore, consciousness must be accepted as having a self-luminous nature that is not dependent on anything else.
Even so, what does this have to do with the object and the self, both of which are by nature insentient?
It follows from this that the consciousness of those two must be non-inert.
But does it follow that because the son is learned, the father must also be learned?
If you argue that this is the very nature of self-luminous consciousness—that it is related to both the object and the self—then [we reply]:
Ah! It is the same in that this is the very nature of even a learned son, namely, to be connected with his father.

If it is argued that the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) is such that its manifestation occurs simultaneously with the manifestation of the object and the self, but not without the manifestation of the object and the self, then are the manifestations of consciousness, the object, and the self distinct from consciousness?
And thus, consciousness is not self-luminous, nor is it the case that consciousness is the illumination of the object and the self.
Now, if the illumination of the object and the self were not distinct from consciousness, [then...]
Those two are consciousness alone.

If this is so, then what is meant by saying "consciousness together with the self and the object" is precisely what is meant by saying "consciousness together with the manifestation of the object and the self."
And thus, the intended meaning is not established;
nor is there even a coexistence with the object for two cognitions whose objects are past and future.
If it is argued that there is coexistence with the object because they produce the cognitions of rejection, acquisition, or indifference regarding that object, we say no.
For it is untenable that the cognitions of rejection and so forth should have that [object] as their object in the same way that the cognition of the object itself does.

If it is argued that the cognitions of rejection and so forth have the object as their object because they produce rejection and so forth, and that the cognition of the object has that [rejection, etc. as its object because it produces the cognitions of rejection and so forth which have the object as their object—[then we reply:]

In that case, is the meaning [of perception] that the conjunction of the self with the body—which possesses effort—is the cause of the body's engagement or withdrawal? Or let it be that the manifestation of the object is the meaning?

If you argue that the conjunction of the body and the self is not the manifestation of the object because of its insentience (*jāḍya*), then surely this [self], though self-luminous, is luminous only within itself, like a firefly.
It has been established, however, that the object is insentient;
moreover, objects are not the very nature of light,
for they are experienced as being discrete, long, and gross.
This light manifests as internal, neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long;

therefore, just as when the moon is being perceived there appears a second moon, we rightly perceive that any object other than this self-luminous light must be indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
Furthermore, no distinction of specific characteristics is experienced in this light itself, even by one who does not know it.
Furthermore, an indefinable difference between objects cannot serve to differentiate a definable manifestation, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor does the mutual difference between objects itself abide within the path of valid cognition; this will be demonstrated further below.

Therefore, this very light— self-luminous, one, immutable, eternal, partless, and the inner self (pratyagātman)— is called "inner" (pratyaṅ) because it turns toward and knows itself as definable, in opposition to the body, senses, and so forth, which are indefinable;
and since it is the self, it is the "inner self" (pratyagātman).
And because it is self-luminous and partless, it is not an object; therefore,
there is a superimposition upon it of the attributes of objects—
the attributes of the body, the senses, and so forth.
How so? "What" (*kim*) is used here as an objection;
the objection is that this superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is improper.
To the question "Why is it improper?", he says: for everyone superimposes one object upon another object situated before them.

This is what is meant: that which has a manifestation dependent on another and which possesses parts appears otherwise when its general aspect is grasped but its specific aspects are not grasped due to defects in the instruments of cognition.

The inner self (*pratyagātman*), however, because its manifestation does not depend on another, does not require causal instruments for its own cognition, whereby it could be corrupted by defects residing in them.
Nor does it possess parts, such that some of its parts would be perceived while others would not.

For it is not possible for that very same thing to be both apprehended and unapprehended by that very same [cognition] at that very same time; thus, there is no superimposition (adhyāsa) under the view of self-luminosity (svayaṃprakāśatā).
Furthermore, even if [the object] were eternally non-manifest, there could be no superimposition because of the absence of "being situated in front" (puro 'vasthitatva) and "immediacy" (aparokṣatva).
Indeed, one does not superimpose silver upon a mother-of-pearl shell when it is not situated in front, thinking, "This is silver."
Therefore, it is established that there is no superimposition (adhyāsa) in the case of either absolute apprehension or absolute non-apprehension.
This might be argued:
since the conscious self (cidātman) is not an object, there can be no superimposition upon it.
But the conscious self (*cidātman*) is itself the object of the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*);
how then can there be no superimposition (*adhyāsa*)? To this he says: "of that which is devoid of the notion of 'you' (*yuṣmat-pratyaya*).
For if the conscious self were an object, there would have to be another subject (*viṣayin*).
And thus, that which is the subject (viṣayin) is the very self consisting of consciousness (cidātman);
but the object (viṣaya) must be admitted as distinct from that, being the sphere of the notion of "you" (yuṣmat-pratyaya).
Therefore, because it would otherwise follow that [the self] is not the Self (anātmatva), and in order to avoid an infinite regress, it must be devoid of the notion of "you."
For this very reason, it must be stated that the Self is not an object;
and thus, there can be no superimposition [upon it]. He answers: It is said—that, to begin with, this [Self] is not absolutely a non-object.
Why? Because it is the object of our cognition (*asmat-pratyaya-viṣayatvāt*).

This is the meaning: although the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is not an object [of ordinary perception] due to its self-luminosity and is partless, nevertheless, through the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*)—namely the intellect (*buddhi*), the mind (*manas*), and the subtle and gross bodies and sense organs—conceived by beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyāvidyā*), [it appears as such].
Although in reality it is unlimited, it appears as if limited; although non-different, as if different; although a non-agent, as if an agent; although a non-enjoyer, as if an enjoyer;

and although not an object, as if it were the object of the "I-notion" (*asmat-pratyaya*). Having attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), it manifests like the sky appearing as if divided and possessed of manifold attributes through the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as jars, water-jars, and flower-vessels.
For in the case of the Self, whose sole essence is consciousness, when the conscious aspect is apprehended, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unapprehended.
Indeed, bliss, eternity, omnipresence, and so forth, do not in reality differ from its conscious nature;
for if they did, they would not be apprehended when that [consciousness] is apprehended.
However, although [the Self] is indeed grasped, because it is not distinguished by means of the imagined difference, it appears as if ungrasped.
Furthermore, the difference of the Self from the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth is not real, such that when the conscious Self is grasped, that difference would also necessarily be grasped;
for since the intellect and so forth are indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), their difference is likewise indeterminable.

Therefore, because the distinction between the self-luminous, undivided conscious Self (cidātman) and the limited [entities] such as the intellect (buddhi) is not grasped, the state of being a living individual (jīvabhāva) arises through superimposition upon that [Self]. And for that [Self], which is essentially "not this, not this" (anidaṃ), its status as the object of the notion of "I" (asmat-pratyaya) is thus established. For instance, the conscious Self appears as the agent and the enjoyer in the notion of "I."
And for that indifferent [Self], neither the power of action nor the power of experience is possible;
and as for that aggregate of effects and instruments such as the intellect, although it possesses the powers of action and experience, it lacks consciousness.
Therefore, the conscious Self alone, when bound by the aggregate of effects and instruments, acquires the powers of action and experience, while being self-luminous.

Nevertheless, due to its intermingling with objects such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, it becomes in some sense the object of the notion "I," and is designated as the *jīva*, the locus of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the living being (*jantu*), and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). Indeed, the *jīva* is not distinct from the conscious Self (*cidātman*).
For thus says the Śruti: "By this living self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).

Therefore, because it is non-different from the conscious Self, the individual soul (jīva), although self-luminous, is made fit for empirical transaction as agent and enjoyer by means of the notion of "I"; thus, it is called the substratum of the notion of "I.
Nor is it correct to argue that there is a circularity—namely, that superimposition exists only when there is objectivity, and objectivity exists only when there is superimposition.

Because it is beginningless like the seed and the sprout, there is no contradiction in the fact that what was made an object of a preceding superimposition and its latent impression (vāsanā) becomes the object of each subsequent superimposition; this has been stated by the Bhāṣya passage: “This worldly transaction is innate.
Therefore, it is well said: “To begin with, this [self] is not absolutely a non-object.”

The meaning is this: although the individual soul (jīva), by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness and self-luminous, is not an object [of cognition], it becomes an object through its conditioned (aupādhika) form.
This might be argued:
we do not refute superimposition on the grounds that it is not an object because its manifestation is independent of anything else.

However, we maintain that the inner self (pratyagātman) is not an object because it does not manifest either by itself or through another. Thus, since the inner self does not manifest in any way whatsoever, how can there be superimposition upon it? To this, he says: "And because the inner self is well-known through its immediacy."
The manifestation (*prathā*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is its being well-known (*prasiddhi*),
because it is immediate (*aparokṣa*). Although there is no manifestation other than that within the inner self, nevertheless, the metaphorical designation of difference (*bhedopacāra*) is employed.

As in the expression "consciousness of the person. This is what is meant: the conscious self must necessarily be admitted as immediately present (aparokṣa); for it has been stated that if it were not manifest, nothing would be manifest, which would result in the blindness of the entire world.
And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined."

Having thus stated the refutation from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), he now states another refutation by way of bold assertion (prauḍhavāda), even while conceding that the conscious self (cidātman) might be imperceptible, saying: "And this [self] does not exist as such" [only] when it is situated before one;
that is, it is indeed directly perceived (aparokṣa).
To the question "Why is this not a restrictive rule?", he says: "Even though it is imperceptible" (*apratyakṣe 'pi*).
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because.
For space (*nabhas*), being a substance, is not perceptible by the external sense faculties due to its lack of color and tangibility.
Nor is it mental,
because the mind, being without assistance, does not function toward external objects;
therefore, it is not perception.
And yet, there, the ignorant and undiscriminating, seeing only what others have shown them, sometimes superimpose a dark hue from the shadow of the earth and sometimes a white brilliance from fire;
they describe it as dark like the petal of a blue lotus or white like a flight of royal swans.
Even there, it is an appearance in the form of memory of a previously perceived form—whether luminous or dark—in the other [space], namely the sky.
Thus, they superimpose that very surface as if it were a great cauldron made of sapphire, turned upside down; this is the meaning.
He concludes: "In this manner," that is, by the method stated, because all objections have been resolved.

The superimposition of non-self entities—such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is not contradictory. Now, since there are indeed thousands of other types of superimpositions, for what purpose has this specific superimposition alone been elucidated through objection and resolution, rather than superimposition in general? To this, he says: "The wise consider this very superimposition, characterized in such a manner, to be ignorance (*avidyā*)."
For it is well known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts that ignorance (avidyā) is the seed of all evils;
and the author will state later that the Vedāntas are directed toward its eradication.

Furthermore, the superimposition of the non-self upon the inner self (pratyagātman) alone is the cause of all evils, and not delusions such as [mistaking] mother-of-pearl for silver; therefore, that [superimposition] alone is ignorance.
Since that very nature [of the self], if unknown, cannot be eradicated, it is precisely that which must be investigated, and not mere superimposition (adhyāsa) alone.
And here, by the phrase “having such a characteristic,” its status as the cause of evil is stated by way of its specific form:

because, through the false attribution (āropa) of the internal organ and other things endowed with hunger and so forth onto the inner self (pratyagātman)—which is itself devoid of hunger and the like—it renders the non-suffering inner self a sufferer.
Therefore, it is a cause of harm.
Furthermore, ordinary people do not conceive of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in this way, such that it would not need to be explained; hence it was said: “the wise conceive [it thus].”

To those who think that this ignorance— bound by dense and deeply rooted latent impressions (vāsanā) from beginningless attachment— is impossible to suppress due to a lack of means, he states the means for its suppression: "And the determination of the true nature of reality through the discrimination of that [ignorance]."
The wise say that knowledge free from doubt is true wisdom (*vidyā*).

Indeed, with respect to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is absolutely distinct from the intellect and other faculties, there occurs a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the nature and attributes of the intellect and so forth, caused by the failure to perceive the difference between the intellect and the rest.

In this context, when the non-apprehension of discrimination (*viveka*) has been removed by that discriminative knowledge (*viveka-vijñāna*) arising from hearing, reflection, and so forth, there occurs the ascertainment of the true nature of reality, which consists in the sublation of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). This means that *vidyā*—which is the very form of the conscious self (*cidātman*)—remains established in its own essential nature.
This may be so.

Even though ignorance (*avidyā*), which is permeated by extremely deep and dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*), has been sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*), it will arise again due to the force of its own latent impressions and will bring about its own appropriate effects, such as further latent impressions; with this in mind, he says:
"In that case, being so"—that is, when there is such a determination of the reality of things.
Wherever there is a superimposition of one thing upon another,
that [substratum] is not connected even in the slightest degree with the defect or quality produced by that [superimposed thing]; thus,
the conscious self is not connected with the defects of the internal organ and so forth, nor with hunger and the like.
The internal organ and the rest are not connected with the quality of the conscious self, such as consciousness, bliss, and so forth.

This is what is meant: the very nature of the practice of discerning reality is such that it removes false cognition, even though that cognition is beginningless and possesses deeply rooted, dense latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
For it is the very nature of cognitions to lean toward reality,
as even the outsiders have said:
"The nature of a thing that is real and free from defects cannot be subverted by erroneous perceptions."
There is no sublation [of the cognition], even in the absence of effort, because cognition has a natural bias toward its own object.
Thus [it is said].

Specifically, however, how could there be a sublation by indefinable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*) of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which has the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*) as its essence and is most intimately internal?
As it has been stated: "Having joined together the real and the unreal..."

"By superimposing [the Self] due to the failure to grasp the distinction, there arises the worldly usage [expressed as] 'I am this' and 'this is mine'"; thus, the usage characterized by verbal designation is explicitly stated therein.
He demonstrates the worldly usage indicated by the word "iti" with the phrase: "This very [superimposition], called ignorance."
This has been explained by the preceding statement.
[The opponent] objects: "But how can the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, have as their object that which is possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
For valid knowledge (*pramā*) is indeed the discernment of reality (*tattva*), which is *vidyā*."
How can the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which are the instruments for achieving that [liberation], have as their object one who possesses ignorance?
