He applies it to the subject of the illustration: "in the same way" (*tadvat iti*).
Furthermore, in the Vedānta texts which are intent upon the injunction for the knowledge of the Self, the determination of the reality of the Self would not be verbal (*śābda*).
For at that time, they were not intent upon the reality of the self,
but rather upon the injunction for the knowledge thereof; and whatever a person is intent upon, that alone is their true purpose.

Nor can the determination of the reality of what is to be known (bodhya-tattva) arise even from those [scriptures] whose primary intent is something else, because cognition depends upon being directed toward that which is to be known,
and because such determination could occur through mere superimposition.
Therefore, it is established that the Vedāntas do not have the injunction of enlightenment as their primary purpose.
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words, "therefore, something must be stated.
The meaning is: that in the absence of which the inquiry into Brahman does not arise, but in the presence of which it certainly does arise.
Thus he says: "It is said—discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities," and so forth.
The eternal is the inner self (*pratyagātman*); the non-eternal are the body, the senses, objects, and so on.
If the discernment regarding that [object] were a definitive certainty, then there would be no need for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*),
since Brahman would already be known.
Now, if discernment were merely knowledge and not a certainty,
then it would follow that this would be a doubt distinct from error.
And thus, one would not cultivate detachment; if one does not cultivate it, how can it be the cause for the desire to know Brahman?
Therefore, it must be explained in this way.
That which abides in the eternal and the non-eternal is the "eternal-non-eternal entity," and its property is the "eternal-non-eternal entity-property";

the discrimination between those two substrates—the eternal and the non-eternal—and their respective properties is "discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal entity" (*nityānityavastuviveka*).
This is what is meant: let it not be that "this is truth, it is eternal."
"This is that which is false and impermanent" is the discrimination between two specific substrates (dharmin);
one indeed determines the discrimination between the mere substrates—namely, the permanent and the impermanent—and their respective attributes.
Permanence is truth; that which possesses this [permanence] is permanent and true.
And thus it is the domain of non-reliance:
impermanence and unreality—whatever possesses these is impermanent and untrue;
and thus it is the domain of non-reliance.

Therefore, while these objects and subjects—the spheres of the notions of "you" and "I"—are being experienced, that which is established as real, eternal, and blissful will become the object of one's reliance;

whereas that which is impermanent and unreal, being enveloped by the threefold suffering, will be abandoned. This very discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal entities arises for one whose internal nature (sattva) has been purified by actions performed in previous lives or in this life, through both experience and logical reasoning.
Indeed, it should not be said that there is no such thing as truth;
for in its absence, even falsehood— which has truth as its basis— would be impossible,
since even for the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins), emptiness itself is the truth.

Then, as this preeminent among men was thus investigating with great precision through both experience and reasoning— from Satyaloka down to Avīci— he beheld himself and the world of living beings revolving in the cycle of birth and death, incessantly tossed by the waves of the ocean of saṃsāra— consisting of moments, muhūrtas, watches, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, years, yugas, sets of four yugas, manvantaras, pralayas, mahāpralayas, mahāsargas, and intermediate creations—
and enveloped by the threefold affliction; and he perceived that within this sphere of saṃsāra, [all things] are impermanent, impure, and of the nature of suffering.
Discernment (prasaṃkhyāna) returns.
Then, from such discernment characterized by the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, there arises for him dispassion toward the enjoyment of objects here and hereafter.
An "object" (artha) is that which is sought after or desired.
"Result" means up to that point;
"detachment" toward it is the mental state of equanimity whose nature is effortlessness (*anābhoga*);
from that arises the perfection of the means, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).
For the mind, intoxicated by the wine of the impurities such as passion, sets the senses toward various high and low objects;

and by fashioning diverse activities that bear the fruits of merit and demerit, it offers the person as a sacrifice into the most terrible fire of saṃsāra, which is thick with the flames of manifold sufferings.

But the mind, whose intoxication from the wine of the passions such as attachment has been shattered by the ripening of dispassion obtained through the practice of higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), is conquered—that is, brought under control—by the person.
This conquest of the mind caused by dispassion is designated as "tranquility" (*śama*) and "the state of mastery" (*vaśīkāra*).
And the mind, once conquered, is led to the fitness for being employed upon the objects of reality (*tattva*).
This very fitness of his is "self-restraint" (dama); just as it is understood that this young bull, being tamed, has been made fit for drawing the plow, the cart, and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), endurance of sense-objects, renunciation thereof, and faith in reality are subsumed.
Therefore, the Śruti says: "Hence, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and possessed of faith, one should see the Self in the very Self; he sees everything in the Self.
This refers to the perfection of these means consisting of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth.
Excellence is the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).
From that, there arises in him the desire for liberation from the bondage of *saṃsāra*; thus he says: "And the state of desiring liberation."

Having heard that knowledge of Brahman—whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—is the cause of liberation, there arises a desire to know that [Brahman], both before and after the desire to know Dharma;
therefore, he says "for in them" (*teṣu hi*) to indicate that the immediate sequence belongs to those [means of knowledge] alone, and not to the desire to know Dharma.
It is not merely a desire to know.
But rather, he says that there is also knowledge—“and to know.
He concludes with “therefore” (*tasmāt*). He explains the word *ataḥ*, which follows in the sequence: the word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
He states the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (hence) as having the form of a reason: "Because [it is] in the Veda itself.
Here, this objection is raised: it is true that the inquiry into Brahman occurs immediately after the attainment of the aforementioned means; however, that very inquiry is untenable.
Because detachment from the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next is impossible;
for a fruit is to be experienced as favorable, since the very definition of a fruit is that which is desired.
Furthermore, detachment cannot arise toward that which is the cause of attachment.
If it is argued that detachment toward pleasure occurs because one perceives its association with suffering,
then alas, my friend, why does attachment not likewise arise toward suffering because of its association with pleasure?
Therefore, when seeking pleasure, one should strive to avoid suffering;
for even if suffering arrives as something unavoidable, by discarding it, one will enjoy only the pleasure.
It is just as, for example, one who desires fish takes up the fish along with their scales and bones.
Having taken as much as can be taken, he returns;
or just as one who seeks grain brings in the grain along with the straw, having taken as much as can be taken, he returns.
Therefore, out of fear of suffering, it is not right to abandon pleasure— whether experienced in this life or the next— that is agreeable to the senses.
For rice is not left unsown because there are deer,
nor are pots left unplaced on the hearth because there are beggars.

Furthermore, visible pleasure— such as that born from contact with sandalwood, women, and the like— might indeed be abandoned by one who is extremely fearful, because it is permeated by the suffering characterized by decay;
however, this does not apply to the pleasure of the hereafter, such as heaven and so forth, because of its imperishability.
For it is heard in scripture: "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal";
likewise, "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible.
Nor is the inference of perishability based on the reason of being produced possible in this case.
This is because its subject matter is sublated by scripture (āgama), just like the inference regarding the purity of a human skull.
Therefore, since the aforementioned requirements for the means [of knowledge] are absent, it follows that there is no inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā).
This being the position reached, the venerable author of the Sūtras says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
The author of the Commentary explains its meaning: "Because the Veda itself...
The underlying intention is this: it is true that deer, beggars, and the like can be avoided by cooks, farmers, and others;
however, suffering—which arises from the convergence of many kinds and many causes—is impossible to avoid.

Ultimately, because there is an invariable rule that all created pleasure is inseparable from the two types of suffering characterized by perishability and dependence on means, even a master craftsman cannot consume food mixed with honey and poison by discarding the poison while keeping the honey.
Furthermore, the scriptural statement beginning with "Just as here, [the results] produced by action... is a teaching establishing perishability, reinforced by the inference of perishability.
The statement beginning with "We have drunk Soma" (apāma somam) is understood to resort to a secondary sense (jaghanyavṛtti) when the primary sense is impossible;
as the authors of the Purāṇas say:
"Immortality is indeed spoken of as a state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings."
And here, by the word "Brahman," the Veda, which is its means of valid cognition, is brought to mind;
and that [Veda], by virtue of its fitness, is referred to by the pronoun "ataḥ" (therefore) in the passage beginning with "tadyatheha karmacitaḥ" and is indicated by the ablative case as the reason.
This might be so.
Just as there is an association with suffering for created happiness such as that of heaven, so it is also for Brahman; therefore, he says: "so also even from the knowledge of Brahman.

By this, the meaning is as follows: from the scripture which establishes the perishability of heaven and the like, and which establishes that the knowledge of Brahman is the supreme human goal, there arises the perfection of the aforementioned means; and from that, the desire to know (jijñāsā) is established.
He states the explanation of the term *brahmajijñāsā*: "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*).

By demonstrating that it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it should be understood that the dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) proposed by the ancient commentators—namely, that "the desire to know for the sake of Brahman" (*brahmaṇe jijñāsā*) is *brahmajijñāsā*—is refuted.

This is because of the rule of Kātyāyana stating, "In a compound denoting purpose (*tādarthya*), the mention of the material cause and its modification must be made," which restricts the dative compound to cases such as "wood for a sacrificial post" (*yūpadāru*) where there is a relationship of material cause and effect; since [Brahman and the desire to know] do not stand in a relationship of material cause and effect...

Because such [compounds] are prohibited in these and similar cases; because in the case of *aśvaghāsa* and so forth, the formation of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is specifically provided for by the rule "aśvaghāsādayaḥ ṣaṣṭhīsamāsā bhaviṣyanti";
and because even in a genitive compound, the actual predominance (*vāstavaprādhānya*) of Brahman is logically established.
This might be so:
when it is said "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇo jijñāsā*), because the word *brahman* has multiple meanings, there arises a doubt—of which Brahman is there the desire to know?
For the word *brahman* exists [in the sense of] the caste of Brahmins (*vipra-jāti*).
For example, "brahmahatyā" (the killing of a Brahmin);
and it exists in the Veda as well, for example, "brahmojjha" (the abandoning of a Brahmin).
And this [identity] exists with respect to the Supreme Self, as in: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed.
He dispels this doubt by stating: "and Brahman has the characteristics that will be described hereafter."

Since, having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), he formulates the definition of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in order to make that known, we understand from this that this is indeed an inquiry into the Supreme Self, and not an inquiry into the caste of a Brahmin (*vipra*) or similar matters;
this is the meaning.
Furthermore, even if the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is accepted, this [genitive] is not a genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Rather, it is by indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and since "subsidiary" (*śeṣa*) means merely a relationship, when it is said "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahma-jijñāsā*), it is effectively said that it is the desire to know that which is related to Brahman.

And thus, all desires to know the nature of Brahman, its means of valid cognition, its logical proofs, its instruments, and its purpose, become included within the desire to know Brahman and are encompassed by the term "the desire to know Brahman."
This is because it is connected with Brahman either directly or through a lineage.
However, if the genitive case were used in the sense of an object (*karman*), then the referent of the word "Brahman" would be the object;
and since that [object] is merely its own nature (*svarūpa*), its means of knowledge and so forth would not be excluded.

And likewise, for those who think that there might be an inquiry into matters not proposed [as the subject] regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, he says in response: "Of Brahman," in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*).
He states the reason for this: "to be desired to be known" (*jijñāsya*).
Knowledge is the necessary concomitant (*anubandha*) for the attainment of the desire.
And the object of knowledge is Brahman; indeed,
knowledge cannot be defined without its object,
nor can the desire to know exist without knowledge.
Thus, because it is connected to practice (*pratipatti*), the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) first requires an object (*karman*) itself,
and not merely a related entity; for even in the absence of a [general] relation, that [object] is determined provided there is an object.
For when one perceives the moon or the sun, there arises no search for a related entity by asking, "To whom does this belong?
However, when the word "knowledge" (jñāna) is uttered, there does arise a search for its object, [asking] "Of what is it the object?
Therefore, because it is required first, Brahman is connected [to the verb] precisely as the object.
But it is not by virtue of mere relationship, because that is inferior;
thus, the meaning is that the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

[Objection: It may be true that an inquiry cannot be defined without an object of inquiry; however, there will be some other object of inquiry for this [inquiry], while Brahman will be connected as a subordinate element. To this, he says: "There being another object of inquiry... [and so forth].
With a hidden intention, he objects: "But even if the genitive case is taken as a residual one (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*)...

The meaning is that even so, since the general relationship is not incompatible with a specific relationship, the determination of *jijñāsā* (the desire to know) remains possible without any obstruction to its status as an object (*karmatā*).
With that same hidden intention, he refutes it: "Even so, [it would follow] that Brahman is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*)."

"By abandoning the connection with the expressed objecthood— which is first required because it is what one desires to know and is fit for the primary relation— one instead connects with a mere related thing which is only somehow required later; thus, the inferior is made primary and the primary is made inferior— this is a very poorly articulated principle of logic."

The designation of "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) and "indirect" (*parokṣa*) is intended to signify "being first" (*prāthamya*) and "not being first," as well as "clarity" (*sphuṭatva*) and "lack of clarity" (*asphuṭatva*).
The proponent reveals his own intention, stating: "It is not useless [to say] 'all that is based on Brahman'";
this has been explained below.
The respondent reveals his own underlying intention: "No, it is the acceptance of [Brahman] as the primary cause";
for Brahman possesses actual primacy.

The remainder, including the term "with demonstration" (sanidarśana), has its meaning not hidden; likewise, the conformity with scripture (śrutyanugama) is not hidden. Having thus established the intended summary, he states the meaning of the term *jijñāsā*: "to know" (*jñātum*).
It might be argued: knowledge is not the object of desire;
rather, it is the attainment or avoidance of pleasure and pain, or the means thereto, that becomes the sphere of desire by way of that [knowledge].
But the knowledge of Brahman is not like this;
for it is certainly not experienced as being "conducive" or as the "cessation of what is adverse," nor is it a means to those two.

Even when that [pleasure] exists, no distinct pleasure is observed, and the persisting suffering does not cease; therefore, the status of knowledge as the primary object [of injunction] cannot be established by the mere word of the author of the Sūtras. To this, he says: "ending in comprehension" (*avagatiparyantam*).

It is not merely knowledge that is intended; rather, that which brings about realization—that is, direct intuition—and culminates in realization, is the object of the desire expressed by the suffix *san*.
Why? Because desire has a result as its object; the implication is that desire ranges over the means to that result until the result is attained.
[Objection: Let it be that knowledge culminates in realization; [but what of it?]
Is this much also desired?

For knowledge that does not have a necessary object as its domain is not accepted even if it culminates in comprehension; therefore, he says: "Brahman is indeed what is intended to be comprehended by means of the instrument of knowledge.
Let there be comprehension whose object is Brahman.

Even so, how is it desired? To this he says: "The realization of Brahman is indeed the human goal. Is it prosperity (*abhyudaya*)? No; rather, it is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Since the realization of Brahman—which is a mass of supreme bliss from which all connection with suffering has vanished—is the very nature of Brahman, that alone is the supreme good and the human goal.
It might be argued:
the realization of Brahman is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
for a human goal is that which is pervaded by human activity.

Furthermore, for this [Brahman], which has the nature of Brahman, origination, modification, conditioning, and attainment are impossible; for if that were the case, its essential nature would be untenable due to impermanence.
And in the absence of origination and so forth, there can be no pervasion by activity.

Therefore, it might be argued that the realization of Brahman is not a human goal (puruṣārtha); to this he replies: "Because it destroys the evils such as ignorance, which are the seeds of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence.
This is true; in the realization of Brahman, whose nature is that of Brahman itself, there can be no such things as origination and so forth.
Nevertheless, due to the power of beginningless, indefinable ignorance (avidyā), the very nature of Brahman—though its manifestation is independent of anything else—appears [as otherwise].
It does not truly manifest; as if its light were dependent on another, though distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, it appears as if non-distinct.
Thus, prior to the eradication of the evils such as ignorance—the seed of transmigratory existence—it is as if unattained, but when that [eradication] occurs, it is as if attained.
Therefore, it is logical that it is called "the goal of man" (puruṣārtha), because it is sought after by the person (puruṣa).
By the inclusion of the phrase "ignorance and so forth" (*avidyādi*), its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are also encompassed.

It should be understood, however, that the cessation of ignorance and the rest results from direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), which is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttibheda*) produced by meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
He concludes: "Therefore, Brahman must be sought after by one who desires liberation and possesses the characteristics previously described."
Indeed, without that knowledge, ignorance—which is the cause of various sufferings along with their latent impressions—is not severed;

and without its cessation, there can be no manifestation for the individual soul (*jīva*) of the direct realization of the nature of Brahman, which is a mass of bliss from which all attachment to suffering has vanished.
Therefore, by one who desires the nature of Brahman as a mass of bliss, that means—knowledge—must be sought.

And since that [knowledge] does not arise from the Vedāntas alone, but rather from the Vedāntas aided by the Brahmamīmāṃsā, one is directed toward the Brahmamīmāṃsā by way of [the desire for knowledge];
however, one is not directed toward the Vedāntas themselves or toward the intention to express their meaning therein.

For in that regard, the injunction to study one's own Veda—which aims at the comprehension of meaningful results—has already been set in motion by the very sūtra "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (Athāto dharmajijñāsā).
Furthermore, since the mention of "dharma" serves as an indicator for the meaning of the Vedas in general, it likewise indicates Brahman, just as it indicates adharma.

And although the investigation of Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*) could indeed be implied by the investigation of the meaning of the Vedas (*vedārthamīmāṃsā*), as is the case with the investigation of dharma (*dharmamīmāṃsā*),
nevertheless, that [Brahman] is not expounded by the former investigation.

Nor does the inquiry into Brahman (brahmamīmāṃsā) follow immediately after mere study; therefore, this aphorism must be commenced both to introduce the inquiry into Brahman and to demonstrate that it follows immediately upon the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, and so forth—thus there is no tautology.
It may be argued as follows:
it has been stated that by this aphorism, the status of the inquiry as a means to the knowledge of Brahman is established.
"That is incorrect, because it cannot withstand critical analysis," he objects with the words: "But as for that Brahman..."
It must be either well-known or unknown from the Vedantas, whose authority is self-evident due to their being of non-human origin.
If it is well-known,
it has been made the object of a determinative cognition arising from the Vedantic statements.
Therefore, it need not be investigated;
for when an action has already been accomplished, an instrument that does not produce any further distinction fails to conform to the logical principle of being an instrument (*sādhana*).
Now, if [Brahman] is not established by the Vedāntas, [then it must be investigated].
In that case, since the Vedāntas do not establish it, that which is entirely unknown cannot possibly be an object of inquiry.
For desire arises toward what has been experienced as pleasant, but not toward what is entirely unexperienced and unprecedented.
Moreover, even if it were desired, it could not be known.
Because there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For it must be stated that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is its means of knowledge, as he will state later: "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).
If it does not bring about that realization, how can it possess validity with respect to it?
Nor does one proceed toward Brahman by means of another instrument of knowledge.

Therefore, the objection is raised that Brahman is not an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), because that which is already well-known cannot be an object of inquiry even if it is capable of being known, while that which is unknown cannot be an object of desire for inquiry, as it is impossible to know.
He refutes this, saying: "It is replied: Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, certainly exists.

The meaning of this is as follows: even prior to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*), for one who has studied the Vedas and has understood the relationship between words and their meanings through the study of the *Nigama*, *Nirukta*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and so forth, [Brahman exists].

From the introductory passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," up to the conclusion, "That thou art," there is an initial comprehension of the nature of Brahman as endowed with eternity and other attributes, even without formal inquiry.

Here, by the word "Brahman" and so forth, which constitute the object of comprehension, he indicates the comprehension itself; for while its existence is established, its specific determination occurs only after inquiry when a doubt arises.
The term "eternal" (nitya) introduces suffering characterized by decay;
"pure" (śuddha) removes even that suffering conditioned by the body and so forth;
and "enlightened" (buddha) reveals the self as bliss, whose luminosity is not dependent on another.
Because bliss and light are non-different.
This might be so:
these qualities, such as purity and so forth, manifest for him when liberation has been attained.

Furthermore, because [the Self] was previously thought to be joined with the suffering of birth, old age, death, and so forth—due to its non-difference from the body and other such things—it was stated: "liberated" (*mukta*).
The meaning is that it is always liberated and always solitary, yet through the power of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), it appears as such due to delusion.
Having thus shown the unconditioned form of Brahman, he describes the form conditioned by ignorance: "all-knowing and endowed with all powers."

By this, its status as the cause of the world has been demonstrated, since the existence or non-existence of its causality follows from the existence or non-existence of its power and knowledge. But from what source is there such an understanding of the nature of Brahman? To this he says: "For of the word 'Brahman'... [hi].

Not only is the realization of Brahman as being of such a nature [the Supreme Reality] attained by examining the sequence of passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), but the word *brahman* itself also confirms this very meaning through the power of its etymological derivation.
He states the derivation: because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh* (to grow great).
For the root *bṛh* (to grow) signifies "increase" (*vṛddhi*) or "surpassing" (*atiśāyana*).
The meaning is that this surpassing, being unrestricted and understood through other words, allows for [the attribution of] qualities such as eternal purity and omniscience to that [Brahman].

Having thus stated the well-known nature of the referent of the word *tat*—namely its purity and so forth—he speaks also regarding the referent of the word *tvam*: "And because it is the Self of all, the existence of Brahman is well-known."
The existence of Brahman is well-known even to every plowman with dusty feet;
why? Because it is one's very self (*ātmatvāt*).
He clarifies this very point with the words: "For everyone... and so forth.
He confirms this very cognition by refuting its non-cognition with the words "not not": the construction is that one does not fail to cognize "I am," but rather one certainly does cognize it.
Now, one might object: "He will cognize 'I am,' yet he should not cognize the Self. To this, he says: "If... [The meaning is: he would not perceive "I am";
for if he did not perceive the individual self (jīvātman), which is the locus of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), he would not perceive it as "I. Thus is the sense.
Now, one might object: "Surely everyone perceives the self as the locus of the ego;

what, then, has this to do with Brahman? To this, he says: "The self is indeed Brahman," because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word for that (*tat*) and the word for you (*tvam*).

Therefore, since the referent of the word *tat*— such as pure Buddhahood and so forth— is established through verbal testimony, and the referent of the word *tvam*, namely the individual self (*jīvātman*), is established through direct perception,

and because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words, the realization of the identity of the referent of *tvam* with Brahman is logically possible from the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*); this is the intended sense.
The objector states the fault based on the first alternative: "If, then, in the world... Here, "the world" refers to the succession of teachers and students.
In that context, if Brahman were already well-known as the Self through such statements as "That thou art," [then the inquiry would be redundant].

While it should have been stated as "the Self as Brahman," the expression "Brahman as the Self" is to be understood through the intention of expressing non-difference. He refutes this: No; why? Because there is disagreement regarding its specific nature.
Thus, by this, it is stated that the seed of doubt arises when there is an absence of both proving and refuting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And the point is that from such doubt, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is established.
The subject (*dharmin*), which is the locus of dispute, must be accepted as being established by the universally recognized tenets (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*).

Otherwise, there would be no conflicting opinions (vipratipatti), either because they would lack a basis or because they would have different bases. For conflicting opinions are indeed contradictory cognitions;
and cognitions do not exist without a basis.
Because it would result in the [cognition] being without an object;
nor are [properties] contradictory when they have different substrata.
For "the cognition is impermanent" and "the self is permanent" do not constitute a case of contradiction between a correct apprehension and a mistaken one.

Therefore, it is an established conclusion in all systems that the purity and other attributes of the referent of the word *tat* (That) are understood from the Vedāntas, while the existence of the referent of the word *tvam* (Thou), namely the individual self (*jīvātman*), is established through worldly experience.
Disagreements arise here only regarding specific distinctions, such as whether these [worldly cognitions] are mere semblances or not.
Therefore, when the substratum (*dharmin*) is established in a general sense but there is disagreement regarding its specific nature, doubt concerning those particulars is appropriate.

In this regard, he first demonstrates the disagreements concerning the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*), beginning with the words "the body alone" and ending with "only the enjoyer, not the agent.

Here, according to the positions that [the self is] the body, the senses, the mind, momentary consciousness, or pure sentience (*caitanya*), the attributes of the referent of the term "that" (*tatpadārtha*), such as eternity and so forth, cannot be connected with the referent of the term "thou."
Because of the absence of fitness [for such a status].
Even in the case of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyapakṣa*), how could that which is devoid of all designations and is not a referent of words (*apadārtha*) be the object of the path to reality?

Furthermore, since even the nature of being an agent and an enjoyer is subject to transformation, there is likewise an inconsistency regarding the permanence and other attributes of that term’s referent.
Even on the view that [the Self] is an enjoyer despite being a non-agent, there is an inconsistency with its eternity and other attributes due to its undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*).

Furthermore, even on the view that it is not an enjoyer, if there is a plurality of selves, then because they would be limited by multiplicity, the consequence of non-eternality and so forth would follow, and because of the loss of non-duality (*advaita*), the inconsistency regarding the referent of the word *tat* remains exactly as before.

Moreover, through the disagreement concerning the referent of the word *tvam*, disagreement regarding the referent of the word *tat* is also demonstrated; for the Lokāyatikas and others who deny the authority of the Vedas consider the cognition of the referent of the word *tat* to be false.

Even those who maintain the authority of the Vedas consider that term [Īśvara] to be either figurative or unintended in its primary sense. Thus, having indicated disagreement regarding the referent of the word *tat* by way of the disagreement concerning the referent of the word *tvam*, he states the disagreement directly regarding the referent of the word *tat*: "Some hold that there exists a Lord distinct from that [individual self], who is omniscient and omnipotent."
The word "that" refers to the individual soul (jīvātman);
it is distinct not only from the body and so forth, but also from other individual souls,
and it rules over the entire world.
For the sake of establishing his sovereignty, it has been stated that he possesses two natural forms, namely, "omniscient" and "all-powerful.

However, because these too are distinct from the individual souls (jīvātman), they cannot be placed in grammatical apposition with the referent of the term *tvam* (the "thou"); thus, he states his own view:
"Others hold that he is the Self, the enjoyer."
The Lord— that referent of the term "That"— is the Self of the individual soul (jīvātman), which is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance;
the meaning is that the individual soul is non-different from that Lord, just as the space within a jar is non-different from the supreme space.
Concluding the discussion on misconceptions, he states the seed of misconception:
"In this way, many... The construction is: "being those who rely upon reasonings and fallacious reasonings, as well as statements and fallacious statements."
Now, one might object: "Granted that there are conflicting views and the doubt caused by them;
nevertheless, for what purpose is the Brahma-mīmāṃsā commenced? To this, he says: "In that regard, without having investigated... and so forth.
And the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); it cannot arise from the lack of knowledge of reality.
Furthermore, he says that when there is nihilism (*nāstikya*) due to the lack of knowledge of reality, there is also the attainment of misfortune (*anartha*).
And "anartham ca" (and [it leads to] misfortune).
He concludes the purport of the Sūtra with "tasmāt" (therefore).
The Vedānta-mīmāṃsā is indeed reasoning (*tarka*);

and it is that for which other reasonings—which do not contradict it—are its auxiliary means, such as those stated in the Adhvara-mīmāṃsā and in Nyāya concerning the purification of the validity of the Veda, perception, and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the Brahma-mīmāṃsā, which has the knowledge of Brahman as its purpose—the means to the supreme *niḥśreyasa*—must be commenced.
It has been stated that Brahman is to be investigated.
But what is the defining characteristic of that Brahman? To this, the venerable author of the Sūtras says:
"That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]. (1.1.2)

Thus, having established the commencement of the inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*) by means of the first aphorism, he begins the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*: "From which [Brahman] proceed the birth and so forth of this [world].
Regarding this aphorism, the author of the Commentary states the introductory transition (*pātanikā*):
It has been stated that Brahman is to be investigated;
but what, then, is the defining characteristic of that Brahman?

In this context, although by the primary proposition concerning the knowledge of the nature of Brahman its ancillaries— such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth— are also implicitly proposed, nevertheless, because the nature [of Brahman] is primary, that alone is first raised and established.
In that regard, whatever is experienced is all limited, impure, non-intelligent, and perishable.
By means of that which is perceived, it is not possible to define the essential nature of Brahman, whose nature is the opposite of that— namely, eternally pure and enlightened;
for no one ever defines the eternal by means of being produced,
nor is it defined by its attributes such as eternity and so forth.
Because that has never been perceived before;
for a definition must be something well-known,
not something entirely unknown.
And thus, even the word does not apply here,
because Brahman— being absolutely unknown— is not a word-meaning (*apadārtha*) and therefore cannot be the meaning of a sentence (*avākyārtha*).
Therefore, the intention of the objection is that Brahman should not be an object of inquiry due to the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Blessed One, the author of the Sūtra, refutes this objection with the words: "From which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this [world].
Let it not be that the world, as it is being experienced, is the definition of Brahman either by way of its attributes or through identity with it.
But by means of its arising, there will be [the perception of motion], just as the movement of the sun is [inferred] from its arrival at another location; this is the intended meaning.
He analyzes the components of the sūtra: "Its beginning is birth, arising" (*janmotpattiḥ ādir asya*).
For the sake of brevity, the author of the Sūtras employed the neuter form "janmādi" (birth,
etc.); to justify this, he states the collective compound as "janmasthitibhaṅgam" (birth, subsistence, and dissolution).
The textual passage beginning with "And from birth" and ending with "the indication of the cause" is explained by its very recitation (nigadavyākhyāta).
This might be so.

Since [theories such as] Primordial Matter (pradhāna), Time, the World-Guardians (lokapāla), Action, Chance, Intrinsic Nature (svabhāva), and Non-existence (abhāva) are all subject to subversion, how can there be any possibility that Brahman—which is omniscient and whose very nature is omnipotent—is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe?
To this, he says:
"Of this world... [and so on].
Here,

by the phrase "of that which has been differentiated by name and form," [the author] precludes the possibility of non-conscious entities such as *pradhāna* being the agent, as well as the agency of an indefinable cause, through the suggestion that it must have a conscious being as its agent;
for whatever is indeed differentiated by name and form is observed to have a conscious agent.
Just like a jar or similar objects,
the world— which is the subject of dispute— is differentiated by name and form;
therefore, it is conceivable that it has an intelligent creator.

For a conscious being, having delineated name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) within the intellect, produces an external jar by means of the name "jar" and the form characterized by its conch-like neck and so forth.

Precisely for this reason, even though the jar is to be produced (*nirvartya*), it possesses the status of an object (*karman*) because it is already established within [the mind] in the form of a mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), as in the expression "he makes a jar.
As they have said: "But that which is established by the intellect is not non-existent."
The point is that it is impossible to conceive of an insentient entity performing an action that has not been inscribed upon the intellect.
This might be argued:
"Sentient beings, the planets, or the world-protectors, having inscribed name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) upon the intellect, will produce the world."
Since it has been stated that [the world] was created by Brahman whose nature has already been described, he says:
"of that which is joined with many agents and enjoyers.
Some are indeed agents.
Just as the charioteer, the officiating priests, and so forth are not the enjoyers,
whereas some indeed are the enjoyers.
Just as in the case of the Śrāddha, the Vaiśvānara-īṣṭi, and other rites, the father, son, and so forth are not the performers;
therefore, both [the agent and the beneficiary] are mentioned.
"Place, time, cause, action, and fruit"—this is a mutual dvandva compound.
The analysis of the compound is: "those [factors] such as place and so forth, which are each specifically determined.
The world has that [collection] as its basis; [the word "tasya"] refers to that.
Some indeed arise in specific locations, such as black antelopes and the like;
some arise at specific times.
For example, the calls of the cuckoo and so forth;
and some have specific causes,
such as the pregnancy of cranes and the like, which is caused by the sound of new clouds and so forth.
Some [actions] have specific prescribed functions, such as officiating at sacrifices and so forth for Brahmins, but not for others;
likewise, some have specific prescribed fruits.
Just as some are happy and some are miserable, so too those who are happy at one time may become miserable at another;

all of this would be impossible if things were accidental— another name for being arbitrary— and if they were inherent, or if they were produced by a creator who was neither omniscient nor omnipotent.
Because it is impossible for those such as the planets and world-protectors, whose power of knowledge is limited, to know or to create it;
this is what was stated:
"of that which has a form whose construction is inconceivable even by the mind."
Thus it is said;
for even the form of a single bodily structure cannot be conceived by the mind at any time, much less that of the creation of the universe.
"How much more so, then, to perform [it]?"—this is the meaning.
He completes the sentence of the Sūtra:
"That is Brahman"—this is the remainder of the sentence.
This might be asked: why, then, are only birth, subsistence, and destruction included here by the mention of "and so forth" (ādi), and not growth, transformation, and decay as well? To this he says:
"of other modifications of being as well, such as growth and the rest."
Regarding the inclusion [of growth] within these three alone:
growth (*vṛddhi*) is, first of all, the accumulation of parts.
Therefore, from a whole consisting of few parts, such as a two-threaded [fabric], a distinct and large cloth is produced; thus, growth is simply birth (*janman*).
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is also threefold—characterized by the property (*dharma*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the state (*avasthā*)—and is simply origination (*utpatti*).
For, the transformation characterized by the property of a substrate such as gold is [the production of] bracelets, crowns, and so forth; that is its origination.
Likewise, for a bracelet and the like, the transformation of characteristics—consisting of the characteristics of being present and so on—is their origination.
Thus, the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) consists of origination (*utpatti*) such as newness, oldness, and so forth;
whereas decay (*apakṣaya*) is the diminution of parts, which is indeed destruction.
Therefore, the meaning is that growth and the like are not mentioned separately because they are included within their respective categories among birth and the others.
Now, even if these [states] such as growth (*vṛddhi*) and so forth are not included within birth (*janman*) and the others,

nevertheless, only origination (*utpatti*), subsistence (*sthiti*), and dissolution (*bhaṅga*) must be adopted. For when that is the case, and the Vedic statement "from which indeed these beings [arise]" (*ayato vā imāni bhūtāni*)— which establishes those [three states]— is brought to mind, Brahman, the root cause of the world, becomes defined.
Otherwise, if one were to take [the sequence] as "is born," "exists," "grows," and so forth, then the etymological statement (nairukta-vākya) explaining those [terms] would come to mind;
however, that statement is not intended to establish the primary cause,

because the modifications of being (bhāvavikāra)— such as birth and the rest— mentioned in that statement are possible even during the period of maintenance (sthiti) subsequent to the great creation (mahāsarga).
To dispel such a doubt, he states that the mention of origination, subsistence, and dissolution as taught in the Vedas is intended; thus he says:
"But of those enumerated by Yāska..."
[Objection: Even so, let only origination be indicated; persistence and destruction are understood as being inseparable from that. To this, he says:
"That which is the origination of Brahman from its cause."

Its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is indicated by three [characteristics]; however, mere origination is common to efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) as well, and thus would not indicate material causality.
This is what was stated:
Regarding the phrase "in that very [context]":
he states the purpose of the previously mentioned qualifications of cause and effect with the words "not as stated."

Thus, by this continuous exposition, the possibility of the nature of Brahman— the subject of the proposition— has been stated by way of its definition. In that regard, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must now be stated,
as the Naiyāyikas have said:
"The thesis, having been conceived, should be established by means of a reason;
there is no protection for it from reasons for that which is destroyed at the very moment of its arising."
And as in the case of "the barren woman is a mother," and so forth;
thus indeed, birth and so on are the grounds for possibility.
For this very reason, others such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others desire the ascertainment of God (Īśvara) through inference and other means based on these [grounds].
Thus, in order to strengthen the reason for this possibility, he says: "This very [point]. He raises an objection:
"Now, here too..."—
having concluded the meaning of the present section with just these words, he offers a friendly rebuttal by restating the point of the section to be discussed next:
"No, [it is] Vedānta."
He demonstrates that [the treatise] has the very purpose of stringing together the flowers of the Vedānta statements— this is shown by the words "Vedānta" [in the title].
The final determination (*adhyavasāna*) resulting from inquiry is the eradication of the two-fold ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanāvidyādvayoccheda*).
For from that [knowledge] indeed comes the cessation [of bondage] and the manifestation of the realization of Brahman.
Therefore, should no other means of knowledge besides the Word (śabda) be sought regarding Brahman?
And if so, whence could there be reflection (manana)?
And from what source does that experience arise as direct realization? To this he says:
"But when the Vedānta texts exist.
It should also be understood that inference which is not in conflict with the Vedānta and which depends upon it [is the means].
Reflection (*manana*) is the discernment [of reality] by means of reasoning (*yukti*) that is not in contradiction with scripture and which depends upon it;
and this reasoning is either presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*).
This might be so.
Since one might ask why it is not the case that Brahman, like Dharma, does not require the assistance of human intellect, he says:
"Not as in the case of the inquiry into Dharma."
"Scripture and so forth" means that the Vedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"Experience" is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti-bheda*), namely the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman.
The fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the manifestation of the true nature of Brahman through the removal of ignorance (*avidyā*).
And that [manifestation] should be understood as a "fruit" in a figurative sense, like a fruit.
Although perception and the other means of knowledge do function within the causal complex even in the inquiry into *dharma*, they do not do so directly.

But regarding the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), he says— “because it culminates in direct experience”— that direct experience and the like are possible, and that the inquiry into Brahman has direct experience as its goal. The direct experience of Brahman, which is the realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman, is the supreme human goal.
"Because it consists of supreme bliss from which all suffering has been wiped away.
Now, one might object: let it be granted that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) has the experience of Brahman as its purpose;
however, that very experience is impossible.
Because Brahman is unfit to be an object [of such cognition], he says:
"And because the knowledge of Brahman has an existent reality as its object.
In the case of the direct realization of difference, the relationship between object and subject is of a conceptual nature.
But knowledge of dharma does not terminate in experience,
because that experience itself is not the human goal,
since the human goal is to be accomplished through the performance of that [dharma].
And since the performance [of an action] is established even without direct experience through verbal knowledge alone, he says:
"For regarding that which is to be done... and so forth.
Nor is this [the Self] capable of being an object of direct perception.
And because it does not exist [as a permanent entity], it is not stable; thus he says:
"dependent on the Puruṣa.
He explains that the dependence on the Puruṣa belongs precisely to worldly and Vedic activities:
"Whether to do or not to do"—this refers to worldly action, which is unstable; he illustrates this with the example:
"as by means of a horse."
He combines the Vedic example with the worldly example, stating:
"Likewise, the Atirātra.
This is stated as an illustration of the phrase "to be done or not to be done."
He provides an example of the phrase "to do otherwise" or "to do differently" with the words "udita" (arisen).
This might be so.
If human autonomy were the case, injunctions and prohibitions would be purposeless, because human engagement and desistance would not be dependent upon them; therefore, he says:
"And here, injunctions and prohibitions would be meaningful."
"One takes" is an injunction;
"one does not take" is a prohibition.
The injunction concerns both the offerings made after sunrise and those made before sunrise.

Thus, prohibitions such as the prohibition against touching a human bone, and injunctions such as the rule for averting that [prohibition] by means of the "slayer of a Brahmin"—injunctions and prohibitions of this kind are meaningful.
Why is this so? To this he says:
"And there are options, general rules, and exceptions."
What is the reason?

Because, since there is a contradiction between grasping and not grasping, and between the offerings made at sunrise and those made before sunrise, and because their combination is impossible and—due to their equal strength—there is no relationship of sublation (bādhyabādhaka-bhāva), an option (vikalpa) must be resorted to out of necessity.
However, in the case of the prohibition against touching human bone and the injunction to avoid it, although they are contradictory, there is no option because they are not of equal strength.
However, there is a sublation of the general rule prohibiting touch by the specific rule concerning the act of wearing.

This is what is meant: it is precisely through injunctions and prohibitions that such a subject matter—one whose nature is to be produced in the future—is presented, whereby a person attains autonomy even in their engagement in activity or cessation from activity, which are dependent upon injunctions and prohibitions.
But regarding an existing entity, this alternative does not apply; thus he says:
"but the entity itself is neither 'thus' nor 'not thus'.
By this, the conceptualization of modes is refuted.
He negates the conceptualization of the possessor [of qualities] with the words "it exists" or "it does not exist.
This might be so.
Even regarding an existing entity, conceptual construction (vikalpa) is observed, as in "Is it a post or a person? Therefore, how could an entity not be conceptually constructed? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "but the conceptualizations":
the human intellect is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
with reference to that, the conceptualizations are doubt and error.
Alternatively, they may have their origin solely in the mind accompanied by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as in a dream;
or they may have their origin in both the senses and the mind accompanied by latent impressions, as in the doubt regarding a post— "Is it a post or a person?"—
or the error "It is indeed a person" with respect to that same post.
Because the word "other" denotes a person who is in fact other than the post,
it does not depend upon either the reality of the person or the reality of the post,
since its production depends solely on the perception of the common property and the substratum.
Therefore, conceptual constructions based on things as they are not do not conceptualize or alter the thing itself; this is the meaning.
Knowledge of reality, however, does not depend upon the intellect, but rather depends upon the thing itself.
Therefore, the determination of the reality of things is logical from that [source], but not from conceptual constructions; thus he says:
"not the true nature of the thing."

Having thus established that the validity of cognitions regarding real entities depends upon those entities themselves, he states that the knowledge of Brahman likewise depends upon the entity itself:
"This being so... Here, an objection is raised:
Now, as for the phrase "what is already established" (*bhūta*):

indeed, a statement whose subject matter is an established fact is observed to be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*), because its object falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the sentence, "There are fruits on the riverbank."
And so it is with the Vedāntas;
therefore, because they possess the nature of describing an existing reality (*bhūtārtha*), they would merely restate an object already perceived by other means of knowledge.
And it has been stated that regarding Brahman, inference—characterized by the world's origin and so forth—is another such means of knowledge.

And thus, it is that very foundational [reality] which must be examined, and not the Vedānta statements, since their truth is dependent upon it; this is the sense of the objection as to how the Sūtras can have the purpose of stringing together the Vedānta statements. He provides the answer:
"No, because [the Self] is not an object of the senses.
But why, then, is the inner self (pratyak) not an object of the senses? To this he says:
"By its very nature."
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self.
For it has been established that the inward-facing self is not an object [of perception] when the sense organs are present.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate more thoroughly below how even inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam anumānam*) does not apply to Brahman;
this has also been established by us in detail in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*.
Nor will it be a mere repetitive restatement (*anuvāda*) simply because its subject matter is already established as real; this too we shall demonstrate below.
Therefore, everything is clear.
Furthermore, the Śruti, in the passage "from which indeed," shows birth;
and in "by which those born live," it shows maintenance, that is, life.

The phrase "yat prayanti" refers to dissolution (laya) into that very [Brahman] itself; and the decisive statement regarding that is "ānandādhyeva. Furthermore, when there is doubt as to whether the subject matter here concerns Pradhāna and so forth, the decisive statement is "ānandādhyeva."

This is what is meant: just as a stream, which has the rope as its material cause (upādāna) conjoined with the ignorance of the rope, exists in the rope and dissolves back into the rope itself, so too the world, which has Brahman as its material cause conjoined with ignorance, exists in Brahman alone and dissolves back into that very same Brahman; this is established.
By demonstrating that Brahman is the cause of the world, it is suggested that Brahman is omniscient.
Strengthening that very point, he says: "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (Sūtra 1.1.3).
In order to introduce another sūtra, he states the connection with the preceding sūtra:
"by demonstrating His being the cause of the world.
Not only is the omniscience of this Blessed One [established] because He is the source of the world, but...
It should also be understood that [the Lord] has the scripture as His source (*śāstrayonitva*).
He establishes that having the scripture as one's source is a proof for omniscience by stating:
"of the great scripture, such as the Ṛgveda."

The *Śāstra*— the Ṛgveda and so forth— is so called because it instructs (*śāsana*) disciples regarding the four castes and the four stages of life, respectively, concerning the procedures for obligatory, occasional, and optional rites (which begin at the *brahmamuhūrta* and conclude at dusk) from conception until the cremation ground, as well as concerning the reality of Brahman; and for this very reason, it is "Great" (*mahat*) due to its vast subject matter.
Its greatness is not only due to its vast subject matter, but also because it is supported by numerous primary and secondary branches; thus he says:
"of that which is augmented by many fields of knowledge."

The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and so forth constitute the ten fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*); by means of these, [the Dharma] is assisted through their respective avenues. By this, the acceptance of the entire community of refined persons (*śiṣṭajana*) has also removed even the suspicion of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

For the great sages (maharṣis) who composed the Purāṇas and other works are cultured authorities (śiṣṭas); by them, the Veda has been accepted as it was explained through various means and its meaning was respectfully practiced. Nor is this [Veda] non-comprehending or of obscure comprehension, such that it would be invalid; thus he says:
Like a lamp, they illuminate all objects;
the meaning is that, making known the entire range of objects in every way, they are neither non-cognizant nor cognizant of things indistinctly.
For this very reason:
"Of one who is almost omniscient" means of one who resembles the omniscient.
For the knowledge of the omniscient has all things as its object, and the teaching of this treatise also has all things as its object; thus there is a similarity.
Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in this way, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"Indeed, for such a one"—
that is, for the Omniscient One, the quality is the state of having all things as his object;
the scripture is endowed with that [quality].
Because this [treatise] also has all things as its object.
He provides a proof for the stated point: "Whatever treatise has an extensive meaning, from whichever distinguished person it [originates]..."
The construction is as follows: "It is possible that there exists a particular person who possesses even greater knowledge than that scripture."

Even today, when treatises concerning correct objects are composed by people such as ourselves, the knowledge derived from the words of us speakers possesses a greater range of objects [than our direct perception].
For those various unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*), though being experienced, cannot be expressed in words.
Indeed, even by Sarasvatī herself, the distinctions between the sweet tastes of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth, could not be described.
The inclusion of the term "in detail" (*vistara*) is intended to show that even a statement in its expanded form does not have an object of cognition equal to that of the speaker's knowledge.
He states the conclusion along with the application (*upanaya*):
"What need is there to say more?"—

the construction is as follows: since the origin of the Veda is from that Great Being who is its source, what need is there to mention the unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence of that Great Being, Brahman?
Regarding the phrase "having many branches":
here,
it begins with "of that which is divided by the distinctions of many branches," and so forth.
The section ending with "saṃbhava" is the application (upanaya);
the section beginning with "tasya" and so forth is [the conclusion].
The conclusion extends up to "and the possession of all powers. Regarding the phrase "without effort," it means with only slight effort.
Just as in the expression "gruel without salt," [the sense is understood].

For that which even the celestial sages (devarṣis) are unable to accomplish despite great exertion, he performs with mere slight effort, as if in play; thus his unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence are declared.
Regarding his authorship of the Veda without exertion, the Śruti says: "Of this Great Being... (asya mahato bhūtasya).

Even those who maintain the eternity of phonemes (varṇa) must nevertheless admit the non-eternity of words (pada), sentences (vākya), and so forth; for a word consists of phonemes possessing a specific sequence,
and a sentence consists of words possessing a specific sequence.

Furthermore, sequence (*anupūrvī*) is a property of the individual manifestation (*vyakti*), not a property of the phonemes (*varṇa*); for since phonemes are eternal and all-pervading, it is impossible for them to have priority or posteriority either in time or in space.

And since the manifestation is non-eternal, how could the status of being a word (*padatā*)—which consists of those very phonemes as grasped by that manifestation—be eternal, even though the phonemes themselves are eternal?
And by the impermanence of words, the impermanence of sentences and so forth is also explained.
Therefore, the imitation of words and so on is like the imitation of a dance;
for just as a dancer performs certain movements of the limbs and so forth, a trainee dancer imitates them exactly as they are performed.

But it does not manifest that very [order]; rather, in whatever sequence the teacher establishes and teaches the letters, words, and so forth of the Vedic texts, the student merely imitates that same [sequence],
and does not utter that very [original] one.

Because individual students are distinct from individual teachers, there is no dispute among those who maintain that phonemes are both eternal and non-eternal regarding the human origin of worldly and Vedic words and sentences;
the disagreement concerns only whether or not there is human independence with respect to Vedic sentences.
As they have said: "The independence of persons must be carefully negated by us.

In this regard, the followers of Jaimini (Jaiminīyas), who do not accept creation and dissolution, declare that the study of the Veda proceeds through an unbroken succession of teachers and pupils like ourselves, which is beginningless. However, those who follow the doctrine of Vyāsa (the Vaiyāsikas) maintain that [the Lord], although possessing all powers and all-knowledge obtained through the conditioning of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyopadhāna*), [acts] in accordance with the creation and dissolution established by Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and so forth.
Even for the eternal Supreme Self, the source of the Vedas, there is no independence regarding them,
because He composes their specific sequence in accordance with each preceding creation;
for just as the causes of benefit and harm, such as sacrifices and the killing of a Brahmin, though being transformations of Brahman, do not change from one creation to another.

For never, in any creation, does the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) become a cause of harm or a cause for the sin of killing a Brahmin; nor does fire moisten, nor do waters burn— just as that [is impossible].
Just as in this creation, the study of the Vedas in its fixed sequence is the cause of worldly prosperity and the supreme good,

whereas otherwise that very same study becomes a cause of harm through its nature as a "thunderbolt of speech," so it is also in other creations; therefore, even though he is omniscient and omnipotent, the Creator is not independent when composing the Vedas, as he does so in accordance with the sequence of each preceding creation.
Even the followers of Jaimini accept that "non-human authorship" (apauruṣeyatva) consists merely in the lack of independence on the part of a person;
and this is the same for us as well, except for our differing dogmatic attachments.
Nor is it reasonable to say that there is no confidence in the intuition of a single person;
for indeed, there is no reason to have confidence even in the intuition of many who are ignorant or wise but possessed of defects of character.
However, confidence is entirely appropriate in the intuition of even a single person who possesses knowledge of reality and has discarded all defects.

Furthermore, the determination of the true nature of the Prajāpatis and divine sages—who existed at the beginning of creation and were endowed with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—is possible; and through their authoritative testimony, there arises conviction regarding that [Brahman] even for those of later times. Thus, it is established that Brahman has the scripture as its source, and that the scripture is not of human origin.
"And validity.
Thus ends the first section. He begins another section:
Alternatively:
by the preceding section, the possibility of defining the nature of Brahman was asserted after dispelling the doubt regarding its impossibility;

now, by removing the suspicion that such a definition might be merely inferential, it is stated that scripture is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman through the presentation of sacred tradition (*āgama*).
The literal meaning, however, is not obscure:
it was stated that Brahman has scripture as its authority merely by way of a proposition;
that [proposition] is now to be established by this sūtra.
Thus the author of the Bhāṣya formulates a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that goes beyond the sūtras, beginning with: "But how [is this]?"—that is, as an objection:

if the Vedāntas were to declare that Brahman is an existent entity to be disregarded because its nature is pure, awakened, and indifferent, they would fail to teach what is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and thus they would result in being purposeless.

Furthermore, because it would have the same object as perception and other means of knowledge by virtue of its being a statement of an existing fact, there would be the undesirable consequence that it lacks authority, like an ordinary worldly sentence.
Indeed, ordinary worldly sentences do not possess intrinsic authority when they communicate an object that is already within the scope of another means of knowledge;
if the Vedāntas were likewise [dependent], their authority—characterized by independence—would be undermined.
Nor is it logical for them to be without a valid means of cognition (apramāṇa),
nor without a purpose,
because there is a rule that they must possess a purpose established by the injunction for the study and recitation of the Veda (svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi).
Therefore, the Vedāntas have the purpose of action (kriyārthatva) precisely by virtue of being intent upon establishing the agents, deities, and so forth required for those various enjoined rituals.
However, if one does not accept this because of their non-proximity [to ritual injunctions], then the Vedāntas must be intent upon proximate actions such as meditation (upāsanā) and the like.

The intended meaning is that in this way, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) and its purposefulness (*prayojanavattva*) are established by virtue of having a domain not already apprehended by perception and other means, and thus being independent (*anapekṣatā*). The citation of the aphorism of the Great Sage (*pāramarṣasūtra*), however, is for the sake of strengthening the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Furthermore, "uselessness" (*ānarthakya*) means the lack of purposefulness (*aprayojanavattva*).
And the failure to produce valid cognition due to dependence [on another source] is because it is a mere restatement (anuvādaka).
Therefore, the section beginning with "ataḥ" and ending with "vā" is the summary statement (grahaṇakavākya).
The commentary on its divisions begins with "na hi" and ends with "upapannā vā."
It might be argued:
even if they do not have action as their purpose, the Vedāntas will nonetheless be intent upon injunctions regarding the nature of Brahman;
and thus, according to the principle "But [it is so] because of being syntactically one with an injunction" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.7).
Thus, the sūtra of the final conclusion (rāddhānta) will be supported;

for indeed, an injunction (vidhi) is not merely that which impels one to act who has not yet acted, since an originative injunction (utpattividhi) has the purpose of making known what was previously unknown.
And because the Vedantas, which make known Brahman as previously unknown, possess that same nature [of being injunctive], he says:
"Nor is there [an injunction] regarding that which is already established. For every injunction is accepted as having for its object only a state of being that is yet to come or is to be produced.
Because those forms— qualification (*adhikāra*), application (*viniyoga*), performance (*prayoga*), and origin (*utpatti*)— are mutually inseparable,
and because they are impossible once [the ritual] is established;
however, the specific purport (*aidaṃparya*) of those sentences differs.

Just as, from such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," one obtains the knowledge of the qualification (*adhikāra*), the application (*viniyoga*), and the performance (*prayoga*),
the sentence "He performs the Agnihotra" is concerned solely with the origin (*utpatti*); yet,
it is not the case that application and the other elements are absent therein.
Even though [the means] exist, they are not intended to be expressed because they have been obtained from another source;
therefore, an injunction can only have cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as its object, and it cannot pertain to an already established entity.
He concludes:
"Therefore" (*tasmāt*):
having stated the reason for dissatisfaction with this [view], he proceeds to another alternative with "now" (*atha*).

This being the case, since the word has no primary intention (*atātparya*) regarding Brahman in the form described above, whatever nature of it is established by other means of knowledge is not contradicted by the word; for that [scriptural passage] is devoted to meditation (*upāsanā*), and meditation is possible through superimposition (*samāropa*).
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words "therefore, not";
he establishes the final position by means of the aphorism.
"It is said" means that he explains this very point with the words "the word 'but'."
He analyzes the proposition of the opposing view with the words "That [is] Brahman. The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), possessing a harsh disposition, asks:
"How? means "in what manner? The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) states the distinction in manner as the reason for his own position:
Because of the pervasive presence (*samanvayāt*).
"Pervasive presence" (*samanvaya*) means correct connection (*samyaganvaya*); it is because of that.
This very point is now being analyzed:
Regarding the phrase "in all the Vedāntas":
desiring to declare that the Vedāntas have the single-minded purpose of Brahman, he cites many passages, beginning with "Being alone."

However, the sentence "from which indeed these beings [are born]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), which was cited previously as the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world, has not been recited here because it has already been recalled.
For according to the grammarians, that by which a sentence begins and that by which it concludes constitutes the very meaning of the sentence.

Just as in the case of the Upāṃśuyāja passage, its purpose is the injunction of the novel rite of the Upāṃśuyāja, established by first mentioning the defect of monotony (*jāmitā*) regarding the two *puroḍāśa* cakes of the *anūc* offerings and concluding with the remedy for that defect.

Thus, here too, because the discourse begins with Brahman in the words "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and concludes with the individual soul being identified as Brahman in the words "That thou art," the purport of the passage is indeed that [Brahman]. In the same way, by examining the sequence of other passages as well, it should be understood that they have Brahman as their ultimate purport.

Furthermore, when it is possible for them to have the observed sense of being directed toward that [the ritual action], it is not reasonable to postulate an unobserved sense of being directed toward something else,
as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It is not only the sense of being directed toward an agent that is unobserved in those [Vedic texts].
And he says that [this view] is untenable:
"Nor is it the case for them...
Having recalled the seed of the prima facie argument—that their lack of authority stems from their being dependent [on other means of knowledge]—he refutes it.
"And even though [the Vedāntas] have the nature of an established entity"—this is the intended meaning:
for it is on the basis of the example of human speech that the dependence of the Vedāntas is suspected due to their having an already-existent object as their referent.
To this, you, being thus questioned, should explain:
Is the dependence of human statements due to their having an already-existent object as their referent, or rather due to their being of human origin?
If it were due to their having an already-existent object, then it would follow that even perception and the other means of knowledge lack authority because they are mutually dependent.
For even those [Vedic statements] have real things as their objects. Now, if a human statement is dependent because it is preceded by human intellect,

then in that case, there is no lack of authority for the Vedāntas— which do not have such [human] antecedents— even though they have real things as their objects, just like perception and the other means of knowledge which arise from specific sense organs, logical marks, and so forth.
If it should be argued: "Only if the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedāntas were established would their authority be established through independence;
however, that very [non-human origin] is not established by virtue of [the Vedāntas] having an existent entity as their object (*bhūtārthatva*);
for an existent entity can be known by a person independently of words through other means of knowledge, and thus its intentional composition is possible."
Since an inference of the Veda’s being of human origin— based on such logical marks as its being composed of sentences— is produced without hindrance,
it follows that its dependence [on other means of knowledge] due to its being of human origin is unavoidable, but not so its dependence due to its having an already-existent object (*bhūtārtha*).

If, however, they have an injunction as their purpose, then because the effect—the *apūrva*—is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge and has never been experienced before, it cannot enter into human cognition either in its own form or through superimposition; consequently, since the Vedāntas intended for that purpose could not have been composed by anyone, they lack human authorship, and their status as an independent authority (*anapekṣa-pramāṇa*) is established. Thus, for the sake of their validity, we maintain that the Vedāntas also must have an injunction as their primary purport.
To this we reply: What, then, is this "effect" (kārya) intended by your venerable self, which is impossible for a person to know?
If you say it is the "unprecedented" (apūrva), alas, from what source does its status as the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth derive?
Because that [injunction] is non-worldly (*alaukika*), it lacks the experience of a connection [with worldly objects];
for, according to worldly convention, only a worldly action is understood as the object (*kārya*) denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers.

Thus, in the statement "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is understood as one characterized by heaven as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

If it is argued that he understands only that effect which is conducive to heaven, and since an action—which is momentary—cannot lead to a heavenly realm in the next world, it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the connection of the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. with the "newly acquired" effect (*apūrva*) as the object to be accomplished is grasped solely from the Veda;

[we reply: alas, then the same consequence of being an "apūrva" effect would follow for sentences concerning the worship of a *caitya* and so forth, due to their connection with words such as "one desiring heaven."
Furthermore, since those [other texts] would also be impossible to compose, they would consequently fall into the status of being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
