Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that when a past thing is taught for the sake of something to be accomplished, it is no longer past?
For by virtue of its connection with that which is to be accomplished, it too would possess the nature of being 'bhavya'. To this, he says:
For it is not the case that an existent thing being taught [is identical to the word]; thus,
the relation is not characterized by identity (tādātmya), but rather is a connection (anvaya) with the effect, characterized by the relationship between purpose and the means of accomplishing it.

The meaning is that, through the verbal root (bhāvārtha) which has that [existence] as its object, those things whose nature is already established (bhūtārtha) possess the character of action (kriyātmatva).
He raises an objection: "Even if they are not action... (akriyātve 'pi).
The sense is that, in this way, the teaching of Brahman—which is non-active, immutable, and eternal—would be untenable. He refutes this:
"This is not a fault."
Regarding the phrase "even though it has action as its purpose":
for an existing thing (*bhūta*) being taught for the sake of action does not thereby become non-existent;
rather, it remains an existing thing that is simply fit for bringing about an action.

And likewise, words whose capacities have been determined to refer to an existent entity (*bhūta*) are seen in some instances to have as their object that existent residing in themselves; having thus died or become cold [to the sphere of action], it is not appropriate in any way to force them toward a state of being centered on action (*kriyā*).
For that which has been observed hundreds of times in its conditioned state does not become unobserved simply because it is not observed in its unconditioned state.

And thus, in common usage, descriptions of forests and the like—which do not have action as their purpose—are frequently encountered even when expressed in the present tense, being conditioned by the verb "to exist" (*asti*).
In this way, even verbal suffixes (kriyāniṣṭhā) terminate merely in a relation;
for example, in response to the question "Whose man? the answer is "The king's.
Likewise, [verbal suffixes] may terminate merely in the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha).
For example, in response to the question "What kind of trees are these?", the answer is "They bear fruit.

For it is not that the questioner wishes to ascertain the existence or non-existence of either the person or the trees; rather, he wishes to know the specific identity of the owner of the person and the specific variety of the trees.

And explaining what was required by the questioner, he [the teacher] spoke only of the difference in owners and the difference in modes for each individual instance, but not of existence itself, because that was not what the questioner desired to understand.

And it has been established that words possess a meaningful linguistic derivation even with respect to an existent (bhūta) object. [The opponent] objects: "Even if an existent object has indeed been taught..."
What purpose could there be for you, whether as the teacher or the listener?
Therefore, even if it is an existing reality, it should only be taught if it possesses a purpose, not if it lacks one;
and Brahman is devoid of purpose.
The sense is that because that indifferent [Self] is devoid of all activity, it cannot be a benefactor. He provides the rebuttal: "It is said... (ucyate).
And likewise, the instruction concerning the reality of the Self, which has not yet been understood, must indeed be purposeful;
the word "and" (ca) also implies this meaning.

This is what is meant: although Brahman is indifferent (udāsīna), nevertheless, knowledge derived from verbal testimony concerning It—which culminates in direct realization—is a true science (vidyā) that, by severing ignorance (avidyā)—the root cause of transmigratory existence and the very opposite of such knowledge—is purposeful.
Furthermore, even those who maintained that all words have as their purport only an action to be accomplished (kārya)—[must concede this].
Even for those [prohibitions], such as "A Brahmin must not be killed" or "Liquor must not be drunk," it is impossible to maintain that they have the nature of being a task (kārya).
For a task, whose boundaries are established by a verbal suffix (kṛti), is pervaded by that suffix; thus, when the suffix is removed, the task ceases to exist.
Just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* [ceases] upon the cessation of the state of being a tree;
for "action" (*kṛti*) is human effort,
and that is defined in dependence upon its object.

And its object, by virtue of having the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), must be a verbal entity (*bhāvārtha*) consisting of a temporal sequence that is conducive to the production of another;
it cannot be a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*).
For the object of an action (*kṛti*) is that which is directly pervaded by the action itself.
Furthermore, for substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), once they are established, there is no state of being pervaded by activity (*kṛti*).
For this very reason, the author of the Śāstra states: "Words denoting action have the sense of *bhāva*; from them, the action (*kriyā*) is to be understood.
Even though words denoting substance and quality involve a reference to an effect during their occasional (*naimittika*) state, [they do not denote the action itself].

Since the apprehension of an effect arises from the connection with *bhāva* (action) even in the case of words denoting substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*), the understanding of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) follows only from those words whose primary meaning is *bhāva*,
and not from words denoting substances or qualities.
Nor [does this apply] in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).
In passages such as "he pours continuously" (*saṃtatam āghārayati*), curds and other substances are the objects of the action;
for even there, the action (kārya) has as its object only the meaning of the verbal roots *hu* (to sacrifice) and *ā-ghṛ* (to pour).
And it is not on this account that—just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma"—there is an injunction for a sacrifice or pouring qualified by curds, continuity, and so forth.
The statements "He performs the Agnihotra" and "He pours the Āghāra libation" are restatements (anuvāda) of that [obligatory nature];
for even here, the task (kārya) concerns only the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha).

Nevertheless, because they are invariably concomitant with the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are also enjoined, even though they are not themselves the objects of the injunction.

For the meaning of the verbal root, being indistinct as a mere operation of an agent, is specified by a particular agent such as a substance; thus, the substance and so forth are its concomitants (*anubandha*).

Consequently, when the meaning of the verbal root is enjoined, it is enjoined together with its concomitants; therefore, although substance and quality are not themselves the objects of the injunction, they become enjoined by virtue of being its concomitants.

And thus, an injunction that has passed on to substances and the like by way of the channel of the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha), fearing excessive complexity (gaurava) and because its own primary object is already established through other means, becomes subordinate to that [object] as a qualifier of the substance and so forth which are its adjuncts; therefore, in every case,
the injunction has the meaning of the verbal root as its sole domain.
By this, the view that in the statement "The cake on eight potsherds belongs to Agni," the injunction concerns the relation [between the deity and the material] is refuted.
Now, it may be argued that the meaning of the root *bhū* (to become) is not what is to be enjoined;
for when the subject (*bhavitṛ*) is already established, that which has already attained its form cannot be an agent with respect to the act of becoming.
Indeed, space does not come into being; nor does it [come into being] when unestablished,
because that which is unestablished cannot be directed toward action.
It is like a flower in the sky;
therefore, the operation of the instigator— the producer— is implied by the operation of the one to be produced, and that [implied] operation is *bhāvanā*.
It is an action, or effort;
and being without an object, it is impossible to apprehend.
Therefore, when there is a requirement for an object (*viṣaya*), the very relationship between the substance and the deity brought to mind by the word *āgneya* is its object.
[Objection: But human effort has as its object an operation (*vyāpāra*); how can it take as its domain a relationship, which is not of the nature of an operation?
For even in the case of "Make a jar," human effort does not directly take the jar—the referent of the noun—as its domain.
Rather, one employs the staff and so forth by means of the hand and so forth;
therefore, one understands the effort directed toward the pot as having the [instrumental] operation as its object,
and not as having the pot as its object in its own right.
However, in this case, the jar exists as the intended object (*uddeśyatayā*), but not as the objective content (*viṣayatayā*);
rather, the objective content is the very operation of the hand and so forth.

For this very reason, even in the case of "the *āgneya* [oblation]," the sacrifice itself—implied by the relationship between the substance and the deity—is the objective content of the action to be enjoined.
What is meant by the statement “it belongs to Agni” (āgneyo bhavati)?
It means that one should bring about [the result] by means of the sacrifice dedicated to Agni (āgneyena yāgena).
For this very reason, it is said: “He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day.”

The statement, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day," is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sixfold set of sacrifices enjoined by such rules as "That which belongs to Agni" (*yad āgneyaḥ*).

For this very reason, the connection with the qualification (*adhikāra*), namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," applies precisely to that which has been both enjoined and restated.
Therefore, it is an absolute rule that everywhere an injunction has as its object only the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) through the channel of human effort (*kṛti*).

And likewise, in such cases as "one should not kill" or "one should not drink," if a task (kārya) were admitted, then its pervader— namely, volitional effort (kṛti)— would necessarily have to be admitted.
And the object [of the injunction] is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), which is pervaded by that [prohibition].

Thus, according to the principle of Prajāpati’s vow, the injunction would have that as its object by way of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), characterized by the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to refrain from killing or drinking.
In this way, it would follow that the absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is rendered obsolete, as it would be like water already poured out.
Furthermore, when a primary meaning is possible, a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not logical.

However, in passages such as "One should not look at [the sun] rising," because of the governing context of "His vow," and since a simple prohibition (prasajya-pratiṣedha) is impossible, it is appropriate to understand the figurative indication of a mental resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding non-looking through the function of exclusion (paryudāsa).
Therefore, [in the case of] "One should not kill,"...
In prohibitions such as "one should not drink," because there is an absence of the meaning of a positive action (bhāvārtha), there is an absence of the effort (kṛti) pervaded by that [action];

and in the absence of that [effort], there is an absence of the effect (kārya) pervaded by it. Thus, he says: "such as 'the Brahmin is not to be killed,'" indicating that there is no rule that every sentence must have a purport consisting of an effect.
Now, one might ask: why is it that cessation itself is not the effect, or rather, why is it not the means to that [effect]? To this, he says:
"And that is not an action."
The word *kriyā* denotes that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*). He analyzes this very point with the words: "of those [words] whose meaning is not action" (*akriyārthānām*).
This might be so:
from hearing the injunctive suffix, an action to be performed (kārya) is indeed understood here;
and that [action] cannot exist without a verbal root-meaning (bhāvārtha).
Furthermore, for one who has already engaged in action out of passion, a state of indifference regarding killing, drinking, and so forth cannot arise spontaneously without a restraining effort;

therefore, that very restraining effort which holds back the mind, speech, and body from being oriented toward activity is the "action" (kriyā) within the scope of prohibitive injunctions. Thus, he says: "Nor can it be imagined that the negative particle (nañ) has as its object an unestablished action apart from the indifference resulting from the cessation of the act of killing."
For what reason is it not possible? To this he says:
"Because of the negative particle (*nañ*) being colored by the meaning of 'killing' which has attained its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
The meaning is this: as a general rule, when an injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*) is perceived as being intent upon killing or drinking, it enjoins those very acts.
Nor can these [non-existences] be enjoined, because they are already obtained through passion (*rāga*).

Furthermore, in this context, a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) is not to be enjoined; for that too, being of the nature of indifference (*audāsīnya*), is already established and thus already obtained.
Nor is there an effort that sustains [the body],

because such an effort is not mentioned in the scripture and would therefore have to be indicated through secondary implication (lakṣaṇā), and it is improper to resort to secondary implication when a direct meaning is possible.
Furthermore, because the distinction of injunctions is merely a restatement of activity already prompted by passion, it cannot be the object of an injunction.
Therefore, having restated the possibility of drinking or killing with the words "whatever one might drink" or "kill," it is negated by "not that";
thus, the absence of such action is made known.
However, it is not the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) that is being enjoined.

Since non-existence (*abhāva*) conforms to the shadow of existence by being defined through its opposite, existence, it appears as established when [existence] is established, and as something to be accomplished when [existence] is to be accomplished; thus, there arises the delusion that the object of the negative particle—the meaning of *nañ*—is itself the effect (*kārya*), because it appears as if it were to be accomplished.
This is what he says:
"And this is the inherent nature of the negative particle (nañ).
Now, one might object: let the negative particle indeed cause the non-existence of that which is related to itself to be understood; [but how can it denote the absence of something else?]
But how can there be a sudden cessation of the mind, speech, and body when they are oriented toward active engagement? To this he says:
"And the cognition of non-existence is the cause for maintaining equanimity."

The intended meaning is this: immediately upon hearing such injunctions as "one who has a fever should eat wholesome food" and "one should not offer a finger to a serpent," the elder person being prompted engages in eating the wholesome food, while [another] is intent on offering a finger to the snake.

Then, having observed the cessation [of activity] from that [object], the child, desiring to acquire proficiency, infers that desire and aversion are the causes of the elder's engagement and withdrawal.
For instance: the elder’s engagement and withdrawal are caused by desire and aversion, because they are independent acts of engagement and withdrawal.
Like my own independent engagement and withdrawal,
his desire and aversion are preceded by the cognition of the state of being a means to what is desired or undesired, which inheres in the same object as the state of being something to be done;
for they are desire and aversion that serve as the causes of engagement and withdrawal.

Like desire and aversion which serve as the causes for my own activity, desire and aversion have never at any time existed in me as being preceded by a cognition of sound, its operation, the intention of a person, the uninterrupted continuity of cultivation across the three periods of time, or a prior latent impression (*pūrva*); rather,
they appear only as being preceded by those aforementioned causes for one who repeatedly reflects upon them within oneself.

Therefore, the causal relationship is established by the following sequence: the independent activity and cessation of the elder, as well as the distinctions of desire and aversion, are preceded by the cognition that [an object] is a means to what is desired or undesired, which inheres in the same locus as the sense of "what ought to be done. Thus, it is proven that the activity and cessation of the elder who is being prompted arise from the cognition that [the action] is a means to the desired or undesired. Furthermore, since this cognition—which did not exist previously—arises immediately after hearing the word, it has the hearing of the word as its cause.

In injunctive statements such as "one should sacrifice" (yajeta), the word itself, by making known the activity that is to be performed as a means to the desired end, makes known both its status as a means to the desired end and its status as something to be performed;
for both of these [properties] cannot be obtained from any other source.
And because that which is not obtainable from any other source constitutes the meaning of a word;
whereas in cases such as "one should kill," where the necessity of performance is obtained from another source.
In cases such as "one should not drink" (*na pibet*),

since the engagement in killing or drinking is obtained through passion (*rāga*), the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and other such forms, occurring in conjunction with the negative particle (*nañ*) after restating that [engagement], make known merely the fact that these two acts are causes of harm, which was not otherwise established.
For the fact that these two are means for achieving what is desired is indeed perceived through direct perception,
since otherwise they could not be objects of desire.

Therefore, the injunction "one shall not kill" is primarily intended to make known that [killing] is a means to achieve what is harmful, by way of restating the sense of duty already established by desire and other such factors.

The statement "one should not drink" and so forth does not, however, have the nature of enjoining something to be done; thus it has been well said that prohibitions are intent upon what is not to be performed.
Furthermore, the cognition that the prohibited acts are means to undesirable ends is itself the cognition of the non-existence of the prohibited act.

Indeed, by means of that [discrimination], this conscious being, although seeing an immediate attractiveness, perceives the absence of engagement upon reflecting on the future consequence; he understands desistance (*nivṛtti*) and turns away.
That is to say, he establishes himself in a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*).
This may be so.
If the cognition of non-existence were the cause for establishing indifference,
it would persist as long as that indifference persists;
yet it does not so persist.
For even a neutral person whose mind is distracted by another object does not possess the cognition of the absence of that [object];
nor is it observed that an effect persists in the absence of its sustaining cause; for indeed, when a pillar collapses, a palace does not remain standing.
Therefore, he says:
"And that [ignorance] subsides by itself, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.
Indeed, this [individual soul] remains intent upon worldly activity only so long as it does not realize its status as the cause of its own misfortune.

Through the realization that [the world] is the cause of what is harmful, one's engagement with it is uprooted along with its very root; like a fire whose fuel is consumed, it subsides of its own accord.
This is what is meant: just as a pillar is the cause for the stability of a palace, the cognition of non-existence (*abhāvabuddhi*) is not the cause for the stability of indifference (*audāsīnya*);
rather, it is the cause for stability by providing protection against adventitious causes of destruction.
Just as armor, as hard as the back of a tortoise, serves as the cause for the preservation of a warrior's life by protecting him from the blows of weapons;
yet it is not the case that the warrior’s life perishes merely upon the removal of the armor, provided no weapon-blows are struck.
He summarizes: "Therefore, it is indeed indifference [consisting in] the cessation of engaged activity.
He specifies this by characterizing it through the cessation of engaged activity, because indifference exists even for one who is unaware of it.

Therefore, by way of a conclusion, he refutes the Jaiminian position—that [the Upanishads] are purposeless because they do not have action as their meaning—by suggesting that it is indeed inconsistent; he does so with the words, "Therefore, [they serve] the purpose of man.

The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions concern those subjects such as narratives which are either useless for the purpose of man because they lack the nature of action, or which are claimed to have action as their purpose.

But they do not have the Upaniṣads as their subject matter; the meaning is that the Upaniṣads themselves culminate in the realization of Brahman, which is the very nature of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, this refers to one who, considering the knowledge of the self taught in the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada-ātmajñāna*) to be not a human goal...
It was stated [earlier] that "without entering into an injunction of what is to be done" [the Veda has no purport];
here, with a hidden intention, he recalls the previously mentioned rebuttal: "That has been answered."
Here, the objector recalls his own stated point:
"But even for one who has heard about Brahman... [he says].
He then reveals the hidden intention of the respondent's resolution:
To this it is replied: "Not for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self.
It is true that the mere knowledge of Brahman is not the cause for the cessation of worldly attributes;
rather, it is [knowledge] culminating in direct realization (sākṣātkāra).

The direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) is a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛttibheda*) born of the mind aided by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by hearing, reflection, and so forth; it has its origin in the mind refined by the study and practice of the science of music (*gāndharvaśāstra*), just like the direct realization of the distinctions between the musical notes such as *ṣaḍja* and others.

And it has been established above that this [realization], while uprooting the entire great illusion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) along with its roots, uproots itself as well, since it is not different from the phenomenal world in its nature as a manifestation.
Therefore, it is established that this case is exactly like the description of the true nature of a rope.
And here, because it is rooted in the authority of the Veda,
it is said to be "produced by the authority of the Veda."
Right here, he states two illustrations according to the distinction between the non-arising of pleasure and the non-arising of pain, beginning with "For it is not [the case] for the wealthy...
He cites a scriptural passage as an example:
Thus it has been said. [The opponent] objects: "When the body has fallen... etc.
He refutes this, saying: "No; because of having a body.
For if having a body were something real, [then the objection would hold].
It would not cease while one is still living; however,
it is caused by false knowledge,
and that can be removed even by one who is living, once the knowledge of reality has arisen.
Furthermore, that which is bodilessness is its very nature (svabhāva), and thus it cannot be removed;
for if its nature were lost, it would follow that the entity itself perishes. Thus he says:
"Bodilessness is eternal."
It might be argued as follows:
embodiment is not caused by false knowledge, but rather by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);
and that [embodiment] does not cease without the cessation of its own causes, namely merit and demerit.
And since that [bondage] ceases only at death, one might raise the objection that there is no bodilessness for one who is still living—
this is what is meant by the phrase "tatkṛta" (caused by that). Here, the word "tat" refers back to the Self.
He refutes this, saying: "No; because of the connection with the body.
To begin with, the self is not able to directly perform dharma and adharma.
For those two [bondage and liberation] are produced by the undertaking of speech, intellect, and body; they do not occur when there is no connection with a body.
But one who seeks to establish a connection with a body through those two clearly incurs the fault of mutual dependence (parasparāśrayatva).
This is what he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the connection with the body":
if it should be argued that while there is indeed mutual dependence,
this is not a fault;
Because it is beginningless, like the seed and the sprout; therefore, he says:
"This conception of beginninglessness is merely a blind tradition."
As for what is thought—that this beginninglessness is not like a succession of the blind;

for it is not the case that from the very same distinction of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) which arises from the specific relation between the self and the body, there arises that same distinction of merit and demerit from that very relation with the body;
rather, this [distinction] arises from a prior relation between the self and the body, which was produced by a prior distinction of merit and demerit.
To the one who argues that the connection between the self and the body arises from another distinction of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma),
he replies:
"Because of the absence of inherence of action."
He raises an objection: "By mere proximity. He replies:
"No.
"Acquisition" (upārjana) means taking possession.
But this [acquisition] does not belong to the self; thus he says:
"But not with regard to the self.
However, for those who hold that the conceit of "self" regarding the body and so forth is not false, [the following applies].
Rather, they consider it to be figurative, like the attribution of the nature of a lion to a young boy;
having set forth that view, he refutes it:
Regarding this, they say:

"prasiddho vastubhedo yasya puruṣasya" means "that person for whom the distinction between entities is well-known. And since this has already been established by us in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*, it is not established here.
Just as, in dim darkness, regarding an object whose specific features are not apprehended, the word and the cognition "this is a man" arise with reference to a post due to doubt;
for in that case, although "manhood" is indeterminate, it is indeed superimposed.
Having thus cited an example of what is superimposed and uncertain in the case of doubt, he now cites an example of what is certain in the case of erroneous cognition:
Or as in the case of mother-of-pearl (*śuktikā*):

when a white, lustrous object stands before one, and there is a commonality between it and silver as mother-of-pearl, why is it that until the certain determination (*viniścaya*) of it being silver occurs, there is not rather a certain determination of it being mother-of-pearl,
or at least a doubt (*saṃśaya*), both of which would be more appropriate?
Because one perceives a subject possessing common properties, because there is no fixed determination regarding perception and non-perception,
and because of the recollection of two particularities— the cause for the awakening of latent impressions— this [doubt] is equal in both cases due to similarity residing in both.
Therefore it was said:
Regarding the term *akasmāt* (accidentally):

by this, it is stated that even when the visible cause is the same, the invisible cause is [also] a factor; the sense is that this [invisible cause] is unique because it is to be inferred from the observation of the effect.
"Of those who discriminate between the Self and the non-Self" means:
of those who are merely learned through proficiency in hearing and reflection;
that is to say, of those in whom the direct realization of reality has not yet arisen.
As it has been said:
"And because there is no distinction from cattle and other [animals].
The remainder of the text has a meaning that is not obscure.
And he cites Śruti and Smṛti regarding the bodiless state of the wise person while living— namely,
"And so it is"— which is easy to understand.
He concludes the subject under discussion with the words:
"Therefore, for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self...

Now, it was indeed stated that if the realization of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman alone is the cause for the cessation of transmigratory attributes, [then what of this objection?]
"Alas! The injunctions for reflection and so forth would be rendered purposeless; therefore, the Vedāntas are solely concerned with the injunction to realize [the Self].
Having restated this position, he refutes it:
Furthermore, as for what was said regarding [the stages] subsequent to hearing:
there is no injunction for reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) either,

because those two, which have direct realization as their fruit established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), are merely restated by means of statements that have the form of injunctions.
This has been stated [in the sūtra]: "Because its purpose is realization" (avagatyarthatvāt).
Realization (avagati) is the direct intuition (sākṣātkāra) of Brahman.

The meaning is that the fact that reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) have that [realization] as their purpose is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Now, why is it not simply an injunction (*vidhi*) for reflection and so forth? To this he says:
"For if [the truth] were already understood... and so on.

It has already been stated above that reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) are not primary rites (*pradhāna-karman*) having as their object an unseen potency (*apūrva*) and resulting in the fruit of immortality;
therefore, it remains that these two are subordinate rites (*guṇa-karman*), like threshing or sprinkling.
However, even that is untenable.

The meaning is that [the Self] lacks the state of having been used or being about to be used for anything else; specifically, this is because it is contradictory for the Upaniṣadic Self to engage in the performance of ritual action.
He concludes the subject under discussion:
"Therefore"—
thus, since the Upaniṣads have as their purport Brahman in its established form,
and since Brahman, the subject matter of the scripture, is distinct from dharma;

Because the scriptures are distinct due to their having different subject matters, the status of "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) as the commencement of the scripture is justified; thus he says:
"And this being so... (*evañca sati*).

Otherwise, however, since it would be merely an inquiry into dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) and not a separate scripture (*śāstrāntara*), there would be no commencement of a distinct treatise; thus he says: "because its purport lies in the injunction for realization" (*pratipattividhiparatva*).
It is not only because of its established nature (*siddharūpatva*) that the identity of Brahman and the Self is different from dharma.
Furthermore, by way of a conclusion, he says "therefore, I am Brahman" (*tasmād ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) because of the contradiction [otherwise].
By the particle *iti*, he refers back to the knowledge.

For injunctions are the means of valid knowledge regarding dharma; and they, being based on the distinctions between the goal, the means, and the procedure, as well as producing dharma which is itself based on those distinctions, do not prevail when there is the identity of Brahman and the Self,
because of contradiction— this is the meaning.
This principle applies not only to the treatise that is the authority for the Dharma, but to all means of valid cognition as well; thus he says:
"And all the other means of valid cognition."
Why?
Because "not indeed" [is said].
For in non-duality (advaita), the relationship of object and subject does not exist.
Nor is there agency, because of the absence of an effect;
nor is there causality, for the same reason.
This has been stated by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [they] have no cognizer.
In this very context, he cites the verses of those who know Brahman:
Moreover, they say:
"The identification with the self (ātma-abhimāna) regarding one's son, wife, and so forth is secondary (gauṇa).
Just as one becomes sorrowful through the sorrow of one's own [son]," and so on.
Just as one is happy through one's own happiness, so too is one happy through that which pertains to one's sons and others; thus, this [notion] is figurative (*gauṇa*),
and not a conceit of identity (*ekatvābhimāna*).

Because the distinction [between the self and the body] is established by experience, the notion "the Vāhīka is a cow" is merely figurative; however, since there is no experience of such a distinction regarding the body, senses, and so forth, the identification with the self (*ātmābhimāna*) in relation to them is not figurative.
However, it is false, like the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl.
Thus, this twofold conceit of self sustains the course of worldly life;
but in its absence, there would be no worldly course.
Nor can there be the experience of the identity of Brahman and the self,
because of the absence of its means, such as hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana).
This is what he says:
"Because of the affliction of the son's body and so forth.

This means that if the secondary self (*gauṇātman*) does not exist, there would be no affliction regarding sons, wives, and the like; that is to say, there would be an absence of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*).
If the false self does not exist, there would be the sublation of the body, senses, and so forth, as well as the sublation of hearing and the other [means of knowledge].
Consequently, it is not merely that the worldly course of life would be cut off;
rather, there is the realization whose nature is awakening in the form: "I am the existent Brahman."
The task—meaning, the direct realization of non-duality (advaita)—how could that even come to be? Why is its impossibility [claimed]? To this, he says:
The state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) belongs to the Self prior to the realization of the Self that is to be sought;

and this is merely an illustration, so it should also be understood as referring to the distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the act of knowing (*pramā*).
This is what is meant: for this very distinction is the cause of the direct realization of non-duality, because it invariably precedes it;
therefore, in its absence, the effect does not arise.
Nor is there another Self to be sought by the knowing subject; thus he says:
"The one who is sought would be the knowing subject itself, free from evil, defects, and the like.
For the illustration of the necklace around the neck has been stated.
This might be the case:
how can the experience of ultimate non-duality arise from what is not a valid means of knowledge? To this he says:
"Just as the notion of the body being the self is imagined to be a valid means of knowledge..."
This worldly means of valid cognition is exactly like that [previously described].
He states its limit: "until the certainty regarding the Self."
The meaning is: "until the direct realization of the nature of Brahman.

This is what is being said: even by those who maintain that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is ultimately real, it must be admitted that the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth is false, because it is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And it must be accepted that this [non-dual reality] is the cause of all means of valid cognition and the bearer of the actual course of worldly life;
this same principle will apply to our realization of non-duality as well.
Furthermore, this realization of non-duality is also a particular modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and is not, in the final analysis, ultimately real.
As for that direct realization which is ontological,
it is not something to be produced,
because it is of the very nature of Brahman.
But as for ignorance, if it were to destroy ignorance or produce it, there would be no inconsistency whatsoever;
and thus says the Śruti:
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge.
Thus,
therefore, everything is clear.

Thus ends the "Tetralogy of Aphorisms" (Catuḥsūtrī). In this way, it has been established that the Vedāntas possess authority with respect to Brahman— which is an already established reality— without reference to a task to be accomplished, and that they themselves lead to the human goal.

Having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the validity of the Vedāntas with respect to the omnipotent cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world was established through the series of sūtras beginning with "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this" and ending with "But that [is so] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*). And that [validity] belongs to Brahman in the ultimate sense.
It has already been established that [the term "Brahman"] refers precisely to Brahman.
Now, a doubt arises here: is that material cause of the world conscious (cetana) or unconscious (acetana)?
And in this regard, since there is a conflict of opinions among various proponents and no specific distinguishing feature is perceived, a doubt occurs.
Regarding this, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the Upaniṣads merely restate what is established by inference—that the primary cause (pradhāna), which is insentient, is the material cause of the world.

The followers of Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that the Upaniṣads restate what is inferred—that the four kinds of atoms, presided over by a sentient Lord who is distinct from the individual soul and the atom, are the material cause of the world.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the view that non-existence (abhāva) is the material cause and other such positions are to be understood.

The knowers of Brahman maintain that the world, as established by scripture, has for its material cause a conscious entity endowed with the power of beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyānādyavidyāśaktimat*).
And the seeds of these conflicting views are [respectively] inference, scriptural statements, and fallacious inferences.
Thus, since there is doubt due to this conflict of opinions, what is the prima facie position?

In that regard, because the unchanging Brahman lacks the powers of knowledge and action, the possibility of possessing all powers and consciousness does not exist in it; however, such a possibility does exist in the Pradhāna.
Indeed, the powers of knowledge and action have their existence inferred from the observation of the effects of knowledge and action;
yet knowledge and action do not exist in the conscious self (*cidātman*),
because it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*) and unitary (*ekatva*).
However, these two are possible within the *pradhāna*, which consists of the three *guṇas* and is subject to transformation.
Even though action and cognition do not exist as manifest functions within the *pradhāna* during its state of equilibrium, they nonetheless exist there in an unmanifest form as potencies.
And thus, it is Pradhāna alone that is omniscient and omnipotent,
and not Brahman;
for its intrinsic consciousness, being obscured, is of no use to us, just as it is to the individual souls (jīvātman).
Nor can there be agency in the consciousness of one's own nature, because that is not an effect;
or, if it were an effect, there would be no omniscience at all times.

However, creation is the transformation of the insentient *pradhāna*— which, though not presided over by a conscious being, proceeds through the sequence of the great principle (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth— caused by the primordial conjunction of *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*, and impelled by the two aims of human life characterized as enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).
And it is observed that even the insentient, without being presided over by a conscious being, acts toward the aim of the *puruṣa*.

Just as insentient milk flows forth for the sake of the growth of the calf, so too the scriptural passages such as "It thought: May I be many, may I procreate" show that even in the insentient, there is an orientation toward its own effects through a metaphorical attribution of sentience, just as one says, "the bank wishes to fall."
Whatever is heard in a context where something predominates is understood as being of that same nature;
since this [scriptural statement] is heard in a context where the figurative predominates, it is therefore understood as figurative.

Moreover, the elders say: "Just as when one sees something written in a place that is mostly excellent, they say, 'This must be excellent,' so too here, in a context where figurative usage predominates—such as 'Those waters thought' and 'That fire thought'—the statement 'It (Pradhāna) thought' should be understood as purely figurative.

Furthermore, by saying, "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms," [the text] declares that the Pradhāna possesses the nature of the living self (jīvātmatva) through its functioning for the sake of the living self.

For just as King Bhadrasena, who acts for the king's interest, is figuratively addressed by the king as "Bhadrasena is my very self," so too the scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (tattvam asi) should be understood as being either figurative or intended to express a state of identification (saṃpatti).

Furthermore, the etymological explanation (nirukta) in the passage "He has gone to his own (svam apīto bhavati)" states that the dissolution (apyaya) of the individual soul (jīva) into its own primary source occurs during the state of deep sleep.

For when the *jīva* is submerged in the small pool of *tamas*, which is the primary constituent, it becomes as if immersed in darkness. As they say: "Sleep is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that has the non-existence of other modifications as its objective support. The meaning is this: sleep is the *vṛtti* of the *jīva* which takes as its object that *tamas* which is the cause—the non-existence—of the other modifications such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth.
Likewise, with reference to the Omniscient One, the Śvetāśvatara mantra also says: "The lord of the lords of the organs of the Sāṅkhyas"—this refers to the Pradhāna (Primordial Matter).
It has been established above that omniscience belongs to the Pradhāna alone.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the Śrutis describe the non-conscious Pradhāna as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world.
In this way, even in the systems of Kaṇāda and others, the scriptural texts may be somehow reconciled;
however, as for the literal meaning, it applies to the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause as well— thus [the phrase] "of Pradhāna also."
The particle *api* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
This might be the case:
if his omniscience results from the perfection of existence (*sattva*), then why does his lack of omniscience not likewise result from the perfection of darkness (*tamas*)? To this he says:
And by that "sentient-being-nature" (sattvadharma), which is knowledge;
for sentience (sattva) is luminous by nature, possesses unsurpassed excellence, and is the seed of omniscience.
Thus they have said: "The seed of omniscience is unsurpassed."
Indeed, whatever possesses a degree of excellence is observed to reach its limit of excellence somewhere, as in the case of the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits; for instance,
magnitude increases in degrees until it reaches its ultimate limit in the infinitely great ether (*vyoman*).
In this way, knowledge also possesses degrees of excellence by virtue of having one, two, or many objects; therefore, it must also reach a point of being unsurpassed in some respect.
And its state of being unsurpassed is precisely this: that everything which is to be known has been known.
This omniscience is possible only when there is an unsurpassed degree of excellence in the sentient being.

This is what is meant: although *rajas* and *tamas* also exist, nevertheless, due to the excellence of the preponderance of the qualities impelled by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, when there is the unsurpassed intensity of *sattva*, the effect known as omniscience arises. Thus, even in the state of *pradhāna*, by either intending or not intending its mere potentiality (*tanmātra*), the *pradhāna* is metaphorically designated as "all-knowing" with respect to the effect of *tamas*.
He states what is excluded by the restriction [expressed] by the two particles *api* (even) and *eva* (only)—namely, "not of the solitary one" (*na kevalasya*).
For a single cause does not produce any effect; rather, it produces many.

The conscious self (cidātman) is one, whereas primordial matter (pradhāna) consists of the three qualities (triguṇa); therefore, it is from that [matter] alone that an effect can arise, and not from the conscious self— this is the meaning.
He states that even for you, the omniscience of the conscious self (cidātman) is accepted on the basis of its mere capacity alone, and not through connection with effects—

this is expressed by the words "by you also" (tvayāpi). He elaborates on this point, namely that it does not belong to the isolated [self] which is neither cause nor effect, by means of the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokana):
"Prior to origination," and furthermore,
"of the Pradhāna"— the word "and" (api ca) has the sense of "moreover."
This being the position reached, it is said:
"On account of seeing [it], it is not that which is devoid of scriptural authority" (īkṣaternāśabdam).
The evidence for the hypothesis that this cause possesses only the general characteristics of the world of names and forms—which is the effect—is the observation of that very effect.
However, there is no inference regarding the conceptualization of that [cause] as either insentient or sentient; this will be explained further below.

Therefore, for the valid knowledge of the distinction between the causes of the manifold world of name and form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), the Blessed One, the Scripture (*āmnāya*) alone, is to be resorted to for meditation.

Thus, since the cause of the world is to be understood solely through the Scripture, when the Scripture—upon reflection on its preceding and succeeding parts—speaks directly [of it], [that is the truth].
That alone is accepted as the seed of the world, and it resides directly within consciousness.
Indeed, in various sections of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), the birth of the world is declared to proceed from a conscious cause by means of statements such as "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for non-conscious entities such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or atoms (*paramāṇu*) to possess the quality of being a thinker. [Objection:
Primordial matter is a thinker by virtue of its *sattva* component.
If it is argued that this is because [sattva] is illuminating, we say no;
for its nature as such is untenable due to its insentience (jāḍya).
What, then, is the distinction of sattva from rajas and tamas?
Purity is sattva; for sattva is indeed clear,
while rajas and tamas are not clear.

And while the designation "illuminator" applies to the clear [mirror] because it receives the reflection of consciousness, it does not apply to the other two, since they lack that capacity due to their lack of clarity.
Although they are equally composed of earth, the jewel possesses the capacity to receive reflections, whereas clods of earth and the like do not.
However, the status of being a seer (īkṣitṛtva) belongs directly to Brahman, because it is determined from scripture that its nature is eternal knowledge.
But [one might object]: for this very reason, it cannot be a seer.
Because the eternal vision, which constitutes the very nature of knowledge, is non-active, Brahman lacks the status of being its instrumental cause (*nimitta*).

And since the status of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*) ceases when there is no activity as its cause, the agency (*kartṛtva*) that is pervaded by and specific to that [causal factor] also ceases.
True; consciousness, which is the intrinsic nature of Brahman, is not an action due to its eternality.

However, for that [Brahman], which is in itself undivided, its non-eternality and its being an agent—which are due to the imagined distinctions arising from the delimitation by the various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of specific objects—is logically established.
Thus, in this manner, Brahman’s agency, characterized by sovereignty over all objects within such an act of seeing, is justified.

And although its true nature is one of indifference—being immutable, eternal, and unchanging—nevertheless, because it appears as if possessed of activity when delimited by beginningless and indefinable ignorance (avidyā), its status as an agent is established.

Others also have argued: even for those who maintain that consciousness is immutable and eternal, such agency with respect to mental modifications must be admitted; for the state of being a knower is perceived as being co-located with consciousness in general.
Indeed, the thirteen internal and external organs, though composed primarily of the quality of *sattva*, are themselves insentient.
By means of that [knowledge], they are able to know either themselves or another;
for indeed, even a thousand blind travelers do not find the path,
whereas if it is known by a single person who possesses sight, [all may follow].

In that case, he alone is the seer of the path, the independent agent, and their leader. Likewise, although the intellect (*buddhisattva*) is itself insentient, if the status of being a knower is attributed to consciousness through the transfer of the reflection of consciousness [into it],
then consciousness alone is the knower and is independent.
The internal and external organs are like a thousand blind men, lacking their own protection;
nor does this consciousness possess any connection with activity;
yet, even in the absence of such connection, it is not a non-knower.
Because even those things possessing activity are insentient and thus lack consciousness,
the conceit of agency is attributed to the power of consciousness (citiśakti) by superimposing upon it the activity residing in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
or else, by superimposing consciousness upon the internal organ, that organ has the conceit of being a knower.
In every respect, according to your view, this knowership is not inherent anywhere;
rather, the ultimate truth is that it is merely conventional.
Furthermore, the claim that knowledge is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the eternal self has been rejected by those who refute the positions of both difference and non-difference.
Furthermore, it will be refuted later on that knowledge is an attribute distinct from the immutable and eternal Self, which is itself devoid of activity.

Therefore, it is established that consciousness, which is in reality unconditioned, becomes the effect known as "knowledge" when it is delimited by the objects of name and form—which are undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) as either identical to or different from [consciousness], and which are intended to be manifested;
and its agent is the Lord, the knower, who is omniscient and omnipotent.
And so says the Śruti: "By austerity Brahman is built up; from that food is born;
from food come vital breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality in ritual acts."
He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving— whose austerity consists of knowledge—
from him this Brahman, as well as name, form, and food, are born.
Thus, by means of austerity and knowledge— that which has as its object the unmanifest name-and-form— it is accumulated and becomes desirous of manifesting that [name-and-form],
just as a weaver or similar craftsman, having first visualized an unmanifest cloth or other object in his mind, desires to produce it.
One who possesses a single attribute is said to be "accumulated" through the production of a second attribute.

And when there is accumulation due to the desire to manifest (*vyācikīrṣā*), from that arises the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—the food to be consumed, common to all transmigrating beings—which is intended to be manifested.

From that indeterminate food which was intended to be manifested, Prāṇa—Hiraṇyagarbha, the thread-soul (*jagatsūtrātman*) of the world, the substratum of the powers of knowledge and action of Brahman—is born as a common [entity].
From the unmanifested [cause], when it desires to manifest, there arises an intermediate effect such as a two-threaded cloth and so forth;
from that, there is born what is called the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*), which consists of the manifestation of volition, doubt, and so on;
and from that mind, which consists of manifestation, there are born space and the other elements denoted by the word "truth" (*satya*).

From those [principles] known as the Truths (satya), the worlds beginning with Bhūr arise in succession; within them, living beings such as humans are born according to the order of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), and from them arise actions consisting of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).
From these actions arises the fruit called "immortal" (amṛta), such as heaven, hell, and so forth.
And because that fruit does not perish as long as its own causes—merit and demerit—exist, it is termed "immortal."
"Up to the point of being the agent of dharma and adharma" means:
he who is omniscient in a general sense and all-knowing in a specific sense.
The austerity and dharma of that Blessed One consist of knowledge, not of physical exertion; therefore, this subsequent Brahma is the supreme effect of that prior Brahma.
Furthermore, from it are born name-and-form and food, such as rice and barley.
Therefore, because the Pradhāna lacks the capacity for seeing while in its state of equilibrium,
and because the Kṣetrajñas, despite possessing consciousness, do not perceive objects at the beginning of creation, and because metaphorical attribution is improper when a primary sense is possible;
Furthermore, it is impossible for one who desires liberation to receive instruction that is not in accordance with reality; such instruction would contradict liberation itself.
Moreover, since fire and the other elements cannot exist in their primary sense [in the context of the body], it is established by reason that they must be understood through figurative application.
Furthermore, in cases of doubt, the context of proximity (*tatprāyapāṭha*) serves as a determinative factor;
however, in this instance, since the primary meaning is established by its inherent naturalness (*autsargikatva*), there is no doubt.
Otherwise, even a Brāhmaṇa who dwells in a region crowded with hundreds of Kirātas would incur the status of being a Kirāta himself.
Brahman alone, accompanied by beginningless and inexpressible ignorance (*avidyā*), is the material cause of the world,
just as mother-of-pearl is the cause of the superimposed silver,
or as rays of light are the cause of [the appearance of] water.
Thus, it is like one moon in relation to a second moon;
however, it is not the insentient *pradhāna*, atoms, or the like,
for those are not mentioned in the scripture (*aśabda*).

Nor is it tenable that either primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or atoms, presided over by an omniscient Lord distinct from them, constitute the material cause of the world; for [the world] is an effect.

Since there is no difference between a cause and its effects, the complete knowledge of all effects through the knowledge of the cause has been established by scripture using the illustration of clay and so forth; and if there were a difference, such knowledge would be impossible.

Furthermore, because of the direct negation of the world as something distinct from Brahman through such passages as "One only, without a second," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "He goes from death to death," the established conclusion is that the world has consciousness alone as its material cause,
just as a snake [is superimposed] upon a rope which is its material cause.
For only if it were established that the world has "Being" (sat) as its material cause could one, having raised the doubt whether that cause is conscious or unconscious, proceed to investigate it.
However, even now, the fact that Being is the material cause remains unestablished; therefore, he says:
"In this regard, that which is denoted by the word 'this'... and so forth.
[This is shown] by the passage ending with "he shows.

Nevertheless, there might be an Ishvara who is distinct from the ultimate Pradhana and the Kshetrajña, as the followers of Hiranyagarbha say; therefore, the Scripture declares: "One only, without a second."
And by saying "May I be many," the non-intelligent cause itself declares its own state of becoming manifold;
by this as well, it is admitted that the effect is non-different from the intelligent cause.

Although there is the creation of the elements beginning with space, nevertheless, because the intended subject is the threefold combination (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of fire, water, and food alone, and because fire comes first among them, fire is mentioned first.
Regarding the point that Brahman alone is the single, non-dual material cause of the world, he cites another scriptural passage:
"Likewise elsewhere":
"Brahman has four quarters, eight hooves, and sixteen parts."
For example: the four parts consisting of the east, west, south, and north are the first foot of Brahman, named *Prakāśavat* (the Luminous).
Half of that is a *śapha*.
Likewise, the earth, the intermediate space, the sky, and the ocean are another four parts; this is the second foot, named *Anantavat* (the Endless).
Likewise, fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning are four digits;
this is the third foot, named "The Luminous.
Breath, the eye, the ear, and speech are four digits.
And that is the fourth foot of Brahman, named "Possessing Abodes.
Thus it is established that Brahman, consisting of sixteen parts—that is, having sixteen limbs—is to be meditated upon.
This may be so.
By the word "īkṣateḥ" (because of seeing), the verbal root itself is expressed by the suffix -ti.
However, since a mere verbal root whose meaning is not intended cannot possibly serve as a means for establishing the conscious being as the material cause, he says:
"īkṣateḥ" is intended as a reference to the meaning of the verbal root.
The subject is [known] by means of the characteristic of the object;
and he says that this characteristic is well-known, using the example "as in the case of 'he sacrifices'."

Having presented the Sāṃkhya's own resolution of their position— namely, that [the Lord] is "all-knowing" (sarvajña) in a general sense and "all-perceiving" (sarvavit) in a specific sense— he proceeds to refute it:
Regarding what was stated as "by means of the property of existence" (sattvadharma), he raises the Sāṃkhya objection once more:
"But has this not already been said? (nanūktam).
He refutes this with the words "that too":
first of all, existence (*sattva*) does not possess a manifest mode of activity (*sāmudācaradvṛtti*).
The inequality of the qualities [cannot be established] because their equilibrium is untenable.
Furthermore, knowledge is not possible in its unmanifest form;
the meaning is that even silver and darkness exist in a subtle form as obstructions to that [knowledge].
Furthermore, the verb *jānāti* denotes a function whose primary locus is consciousness (*caitanya*), and its usage has never been observed in reference to mere unconscious functions; thus he says:
"Moreover, [knowledge] is not without a witness" (*nāsākṣikā*).
If so, how then is the omniscience of yogins caused by the excellence of the quality of purity (*sattva*)? To this he replies:
"But for the yogins," [it is said].
The meaning is that the excellence of the sattva-portion benefits the yogins who possess the eye of consciousness, but not the blind Pradhāna.
But if, setting aside the doctrine of Kapila, one were to adopt that of Hiraṇyagarbha, he says regarding that as well:
"Or else, [the omniscience] has the Witness as its cause.

For even according to them, the omniscience belongs only to a particular Puruṣa who has taken up preeminent *sattva* and is untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its fruition (*vipāka*), or latent impressions (*āśaya*).
But [this is] not [the case] for the non-conscious Pradhāna;
moreover, that too has been refuted by the scriptural texts on non-duality (advaita)—this is the sense.
He restates the seed of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa):
As for what was further stated regarding Brahman as well:

although pure consciousness is eternal, that which is conditioned (upahita) is non-eternal and an effect, just as space is [non-eternal] when delimited by a jar; with this intention, he offers the following rebuttal:
"This much, first of all, is what you have said.
Regarding the statement, "In the case of the sun, whose heat and light are pervasive," this too intends to convey that the effect is a manifestation delimited by its object.
He raises an objection concerning the disparity:
"Now, regarding the phrase 'of the sun' (nanu savituḥ):
do you state this discrepancy with the intention of referring to an actual absence of action, or rather to an absence of the desire to speak of it? If it is the latter,"
By the phrase "it illuminates," let there be no equality [with the object];
however, by the phrase "it shines," there is [equality]. For here, the status of being an object (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed.
And yet, [the author] refutes the objection that independence belongs to the sun because its nature is luminosity by stating: "No;
even in the absence of an object.
The phrase "even in the absence" means "even when not intended [to be present]."
Alternatively, if it is argued that this inequality is stated with the intention of referring to the non-existence of action in a real sense,
that is not so,
because the non-existence of action is unestablished.
He answers [the objection] by stating, "And because the object is intended here," namely, "But when there is a requirement for an object.
The meaning is: those scriptural passages which are justified even when the object is not intended to be expressed, are all the more so justified when the object is indeed intended to be expressed.
Regarding the phrase "by whose grace":
the construction is that it goes without saying that eternal knowledge belongs to that eternally perfected Lord (Īśvara) by virtue of His grace.
As the authors of the Yogaśāstra have stated: "From that [practice], there arises the realization of the inward-facing consciousness as well as the absence of obstacles."
And the commentators on that [text] state: "The Lord, being won over by a particular degree of devotion, bestows grace upon him through knowledge, dispassion, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "like the light of the sun":
having stated that what is eternal is in reality independent of causes by way of its own nature, he states it also by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of one possessing ignorance and so forth":
by the inclusion of "and so forth," desire, karma, and the like are subsumed.
[The phrase] "not of one devoid of the causes that obstruct knowledge" [is used].

The point is that although transmigrating beings possess eternal knowledge in reality, there exist causes for the obstruction of that knowledge due to ignorance; however, for the Lord, who is devoid of ignorance, no such cause for the obstruction of knowledge is possible.
For Him, there exists no effect such as the removal of an obscuration.
The meaning is that [the world] does not return; thus is the intention.
Activity proceeds by the power of knowledge;
however, because the primary cause (pradhāna), being insentient, lacks the power of knowledge, there is no activity of the world [from it]. This is the sense.
He is handless yet grasps;
he is footless yet possesses speed and the power of movement. The rest is clear in its meaning.
This might be so:
let there be the delusion of limitation caused by adjuncts such as a jar in the non-self, which is like space;
however, that [delusion] does not apply to the self, which is established by its own nature as luminosity. To this, he says:
And it is observed that this occurs only while the self exists;
"clinging" (abhiniveśa) is a false conceit (mithyābhimāna).
"By the preceding [view] consisting of mere false cognition":
by this, its beginninglessness is shown.

This might be so:

Brahman alone is what one desires to know, yet that cannot be made understood by Śvetaketu immediately due to its subtlety; therefore, it is the *pradhāna* (the primary cause) associated with it [that is first taught].

Furthermore, regarding the cause of the world, the Śruti provides an etymological explanation for the term "svapiti" (he sleeps), stating that it means "saṃkocati" (it contracts); thus, the Śruti declares the conscious [Self] alone to be the cause of the world.
If the word *sva* denotes the Self (*ātman*), even so, it is untenable for the conscious Puruṣa to possess the unconscious Pradhāna as His own.

If, on the other hand, the word *sva* denotes that which belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*), even so, since the unconscious [Pradhāna] would be "belonging to oneself" only insofar as it serves the purpose of the Puruṣa, it remains untenable for the conscious [Puruṣa] to undergo dissolution [into it].
For a pot, whose nature is clay, does not dissolve even in its own water, but rather in the clay itself which constitutes its very self;
nor does it dissolve in an elephant, which is not of its own nature, but rather in the lime (śukti) which is its own constituent. Thus he says:
Because of [the Lord's] going to sleep [in him]. //9//
"Because of the commonality of the process" (gatisāmānyāt). "Process" (gati) means comprehension. "As in the systems of the logicians" (tārkikasamaya iva).

For it was indeed promised that Brahman is to be investigated.

And that [Brahman] is to be known solely through the scripture; furthermore, it has been demonstrated by reasoning that the scripture is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to Brahman—the omniscient, omnipotent cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world—and not with respect to the primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or other such entities.
Nor is there any portion of the Vedānta that could teach anything contrary to this, as it has been stated on account of the uniformity of the scriptural teaching (*gatisāmānyāt*).
What else remains for which there might be the introduction of a series of sūtras concerning another subject?
What is the occasion [for this]?
The objection is raised with "kim" (what?). He provides the answer:

Although Brahman is, in reality, devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it cannot be taught in that form; therefore, it must be taught by means of its conditioned form.
In that context, in some instances, a specific limiting adjunct is intended, and there are meditations (*upāsana*) upon those adjuncts.
Some are for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), being recited here because they have the mind alone as their means;

In some cases, however, even that which is redundant is intended as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),

as for example here itself with the five sheaths (*kośa*) beginning with *annamaya* and ending with *ānandamaya*. Therefore, it has not yet been determined at this point which [sheath] is intended as the limiting adjunct and which is not.

The meaning is that the commonality of destiny (*gatisāmānya*) has also been stated as if already established, yet it has not actually been proven up to this point; therefore, the subsequent textual context is commenced for the purpose of proving that.
This might be so.

Since the Supreme Self remains non-different even when qualified by various distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), how can there be a difference in meditation, and how can there be a difference in results? To this, he says:
"But [the Self] is indeed one."

The meaning is that even though there is no difference in the underlying form (*rūpa*), there is a difference in meditation due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) or the difference in the conditioned entity (*upahita*), and likewise there is a difference in the fruit;
"sacrifice" (*kratu*) here means volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Now, [an objection]: if the Self is one, immutable, eternal, unsurpassed, and hidden within all beings, [how can there be such differences]?
How is it that there is a gradation [of qualities] in this substratum of the elements, given the scriptural declarations? To this he says:
"Even though the Self is one.
Even though the nature of the Self—its sovereignty, knowledge, and bliss—is indeed without any distinction whatsoever.
Nevertheless, within those various classes of living beings, which are shrouded by beginningless ignorance, [this consciousness] appears in some as if non-existent,
in some as if existent,
and in some as if inferior.
In some places it appears possessed of excellence, and in others as if possessed of extreme excellence;
for what reason is that?
This is due to the varying degrees of intensity and diminution of the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā-tamas*).

Likewise, although the sun, the supreme illuminator, fills the entire sphere of the sky with its very nature of light, it appears as if its light were diminished during the rainy season, yet it manifests as if its light were intensified in autumn; so too is this [the case] here.

[It is taught] as an object of meditation when connected with limiting adjuncts that are required [for worship], and as an object of knowledge when freed from connection with limiting adjuncts. //11//

"Consisting of bliss, because of repetition. First, he formulates the section according to the opinion of a partial exponent (ekadeśin) regarding the Taittirīyaka passage beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).
"Even when there is a fall into a figurative stream, the primary sense is still applicable;
however, when both senses are equally primary, the observation of the majority serves as the differentiator."

Since the suffix *mayaṭ* has an equal primary meaning both in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) and in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), it is logical that the term *ānandamaya*— given its placement within a series of terms such as *annamaya* which denote modifications— must also signify a modification. Nor is it correct to argue that in the case of *prāṇamaya* and the others, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (without denoting a modification) because a modification is impossible there.

For the Self, when delimited by limiting adjuncts such as the vital breath (prāṇa), becomes subject to the modifications of those [adjuncts], just as the space within a jar is subject to the modifications of the jar.
And it is not appropriate for a word to have a reflexive meaning when its primary sense is already established.
"But if there were four sheaths, it would not be called the innermost of all;
moreover, it would be illogical for the individual soul (jīva), which possesses a body and partakes in states such as pleasure, to be Brahman."
Nor is it correct to say that Brahman alone is the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) because it is the innermost of all, and not the individual soul (jīva);

for this scripture does not state that the one consisting of bliss is the innermost of everything, but rather that the sheath consisting of bliss is the innermost of the four sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya).

Nor is it logical to conclude that this alone is the innermost (*sarvāntara*) simply because no other inner entity is heard of; for that which is heard to be inner only in relation to something else becomes inner only with respect to that very thing. Indeed, when it is said that Devadatta is strong, he is not understood to be strong in comparison to lions, tigers, and the like, but rather in relation to other individuals of the same kind.

Thus, even the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is internal only relative to those beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya), but not relative to everything. Furthermore, since the partless Brahman cannot possess limbs such as "beloved" and so forth,
nor can it logically possess a body, the one consisting of bliss must be none other than a transmigrating soul (saṃsārī).

Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is only Brahman as conditioned (upahita) that is intended here as the object of meditation, and not Brahman in its true nature as the object of knowledge.
Furthermore, even if the suffix -maya denotes abundance (prācurya), [the objection remains].
Nevertheless, that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*),
and not Brahman;
for an abundance of bliss occurs only when there is the presence of even a slight trace of its opposite, suffering, and not when such [suffering] is absolutely non-existent.
And there is not even the slightest possibility of the occurrence of a particle of suffering for the Supreme Self, because its sole essence is bliss; thus he says:
"And [it is not so] while it possesses a body."
Furthermore, since that which is bodiless has not even the slightest connection with anything unpleasant, the suffix *mayaṅ*—which signifies abundance—is also not applicable; this is the meaning.
It is replied:
first of all, Brahman, as the tail which is a limb of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), lacks primacy by virtue of being merely a subordinate part.
Rather, the primacy belongs to the Brahman consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) itself, which is the possessor of the limbs.

And thus, it is logical that the repeated mention of the word "bliss" within that context produces the cognition of that [Brahman]; therefore, it is correct that this repetition refers to that very one consisting of bliss.

This is just as the repetition of the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring"—which occurs within the section on the Jyotiṣṭoma—is intended merely to prescribe a specific time.
Moreover, the direct repetition of the Self consisting of bliss is heard in the scripture: "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss.
Having restated the seed of the prima facie argument—namely, that which was said regarding [the sequence] starting from the one consisting of food—he refutes it.
For the vision of the principal Arundhatī does not become a vision of the secondary Arundhatī simply because it is recited in proximity to those various visions of the secondary Arundhatī.
If you argue that, because they are for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*), the preceding visions conform to the final vision and do not contradict it, we reply:
here too, there is no hearing of anything else internal to the *ānandamaya*.

However, because the scripture declares that [the Self] is the innermost of all, beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya), its purpose is equally established in reaching that ultimate conclusion.
Furthermore, the connection with limbs such as "dearness" and its being the body have been resolved by the Commentary;
moreover, it has been demonstrated that even the connection with a trace of suffering resulting from the possession of limbs like dearness is merely adventitious (aupādhika) to the Supreme Self.
And thus, it has been established that the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term *ānandamaya* signifies abundance. // 12 // // 13 // // 14 //

Moreover, because there is a consensus regarding the relationship between the mantra and the brāhmaṇa as the means and the end, Brahman alone is the referent of the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). For in the mantra, the Supreme Brahman is heard to be "another inner self," and that very same entity is recognized in the brāhmaṇa as "another inner self consisting of bliss."

The author of the Sūtras states that the Supreme Brahman alone consists of bliss: "And it is the very one described in the mantra-text that is sung [in the Brāhmaṇa] as consisting of bliss. That is to say, the Supreme Brahman, who is described in the mantra-text, is likewise sung in the Brāhmaṇa as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). //15//

Moreover, with reference to the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), since the scripture declares its status as the creator prior to the origination of the body and other things, and since it declares the non-difference of the beings being created from their creator— the one consisting of bliss— by the words "May I be many," he says that the one consisting of bliss is indeed the Supreme Self.
The Sūtra states: "Not the other, because of impossibility.
Not the other—the individual soul (jīva)—is the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).
Because that [consequence] does not logically follow. //16//
And because of the designation of difference:
"This Self consisting of bliss is indeed the essence, for by obtaining this essence, one becomes blissful.
This state of being the obtainer belongs to the individual self (jīvātman).
Furthermore, since the one consisting of bliss is something to be attained, non-difference is not tenable;
therefore, it is established that the supreme Brahmanhood belongs to the individual self (jīvātman) in its state of difference from the one consisting of bliss.
He objects: "How then?
[meaning: if, having been obtained, it is not to be obtained again, [how can there be attainment?]
