How, then, is the meaning that the Supreme Self is attained by means of the individual self (jīvātman), which is in reality non-different from the Supreme Self? He answers:
"Certainly."
"Even so":

it is true; although there is non-difference in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the relationship between the attainer and the attainable is established by relying on the difference superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
For the individual soul (*jīva*) is shown to be distinct from the Supreme Brahman through ignorance.
But not even from the individual soul (jīva).

Thus, if the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) were the individual soul, no distinction of the soul from itself—even through ignorance—would have been shown; the meaning is that there would be no relationship between the attainer and the object to be attained.
It has been stated above that there is neither difference nor non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Brahman.
This might be argued:

just as the individual self, being distinct from the Supreme Lord, is not the seer, so too the Supreme Lord is not distinct from the individual self who is the seer; thus, if the individual soul is indeterminable, the Supreme Lord must also be indeterminable.
It might be so; however, because [the Lord] exists as a real entity, he says:
"But the Supreme Lord [is distinct] from that which is imagined through ignorance."
For silver superimposed upon a mother-of-pearl shell is not distinct from that shell;
indeed, it cannot be defined either as different from it or as non-different from it.
The mother-of-pearl, however, being ultimately real and definable, is indeed distinct from the indefinable silver.
Right here, he states an example that possesses only partial similarity:
"as in the case of a magician.
Dissatisfied with this, he provides an example of absolute similarity:
Or, as in the case of "the space within a jar" (ghaṭākāśāt); the rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //17// //18//
In order to uphold his own position, he refutes the view of the partialist (ekadeśin), stating:
"But this must be said here.
First, there is this general rule: that from the word "Brahman" in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," Brahman is understood [to be the foundation].
But the pure Brahman is modified [into the form of the Self] by virtue of the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
In that case, since the word "tail" (puccha) is used in conjunction with "consisting of food" (annamaya) and others in the sense of a limb,

and since the word "tail" here also has the sense of a limb, should the word "Brahman" (brahma), which is in grammatical apposition with it, also be interpreted— by abandoning its primary meaning— as somehow referring to a limb?
And should the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) be taken as denoting a modification, given that it is listed among terms like "consisting of food" which mostly denote modifications?
Alternatively, if it is a term for abundant bliss,
let it be explained as referring to Brahman through some secondary function (*vṛtti*) that is not its primary sense;
and by the repetition of the word "bliss," let the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) be indicated (*lakṣya*), just as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is indicated by the word "light" (*jyotis*).
Furthermore, let the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) have the sense of a modification,
and let the word "brahman" retain its own primary meaning as "belonging to a Brahmin," while the repetition of the word "bliss" (ānanda) likewise retains its own primary meaning.

Let those of refined intellect understand that this mere list of questions, written primarily as individual components, is to be explained as referring to the subject-matter (*adhikaraṇa*) as a whole.
In this regard: "The abandonment of the context of the majority of readings and the transgression of the triad of primary [meanings] occur in the former position;
in the latter position, there is the sublation of the context of the majority of readings."

For the word "puccha" (tail) is primary when referring to the tail itself, whereas it is only secondary when referring to a limb consisting of bliss; thus, the transgression of the primary meaning of the word is equal whether one takes it as referring to a limb or as referring to the "support.
Furthermore, the subversion of the reading that favors a limb is equal to the subversion of the reading that favors a modification (*vikāra*).
However, there is an additional [burden] in the transgression of the triad of terms: *brahman*, *ānandamaya*, and *ānanda*.
Therefore, because it violates the three primary [criteria], the former position is less sound;
rather, the latter position alone is logical, as it accords with the three primary [criteria].
Furthermore, if the term *ānandamaya* were to have Brahman as its referent, [it would entail the following]:
It is not tenable that "Brahman is the tail," for it is not logical that the same thing should be both the whole and a part;
moreover, if the word "tail" were intended to mean a substratum, [it would be inappropriate].
This [interpretation] as "establishment" (pratiṣṭhā) is also more appropriate;
for while the inner nature of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is established in relation to the sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya),
the inner nature of Brahman is understood by implication from the one consisting of bliss, and thus it was not explicitly stated by the Śruti.

Thus, just as in the case of the [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya), it is logical for the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) to have limbs such as "dear" (priya) and so forth.

However, regarding the supreme Brahman, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, the connection with limbs such as "dear" and the quality of abundance are established only by incorporating limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
They should be explained by means of the affliction (*kleśa*).
And thus, because it is the Brahman mentioned in the Vedic mantra itself that is designated as "Brahman is the tail, the support" as the primary subject,
the qualification belongs to that [Brahman] alone, not to the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
The summary of the meaning is that even such scriptural passages as "He desired" and so forth have Brahman as their subject;
the rest is easy to understand.
As for the Sūtras, they should be explained as follows.

In the event of a conflict between the Vedas and the Sūtras, the principle "but when there is no [inferior] quality, an improper assumption [of meaning] is not to be made" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.34) dictates that the Sūtras must be interpreted otherwise.
By the term *ānandamaya*, the word *brahman* found in the sentence "Brahman is the tail, the support" is indicated.
What is meant is this: in the passage beginning with "consisting of bliss," the word *brahman* in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support" is indeed used in its primary sense.
As for the fact that the Śruti says "Brahman is the tail" when it ought to have said "the locus is Brahman itself," for what reason?

It is because, due to the previous usage in which the member was the primary sense, that very usage remains present in the mind; and thus, even by that [usage], the definition of being a locus is established.
And it is proclaimed as being based precisely on the words of the mantra. 1.9.5.

That which was spoken of as Brahman by the Vedic mantra beginning with "That which is Truth and Knowledge," is itself proclaimed in the Brāhmaṇa—as the primary subject—with the words, "Brahman is the tail, the support.

For if this [word "Brahman"] were used in the sense of a mere limb, there would be a contradiction between the mantra and the Brāhmaṇa regarding the means and the end: the mantra would have primacy [as the end], while the Brāhmaṇa would have primacy [as the means].
Not the other, because it is not possible. //16//

In this context, instead of the commentary reading "And for this reason [it is] the one consisting of bliss," it should be read as "And for this reason [it is] the Brahman that is the tail, the support.
And because of the designation of difference. (Sūtra 17)

In this regard as well, we have read the two commentaries—"from here [it follows] that [the Self] consists of bliss" and "in the section concerning that which consists of bliss"—respectively in place of "Brahman is the tail, the support" and "in the section concerning the tail that is Brahman.
And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference. (1.8)
And in this [state], he teaches his union with that. (1.9)
Thus, in the commentary on these two Sūtras as well, the reading "brahma pucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā" (Brahman is the tail, the support) should be understood in place of "ānandamaya.
And because its cause is designated [as Brahman]. //14//

If Brahman is merely a limb—the "tail"—of the modification that consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), how could Brahman be said to be the cause of this entire collection of modifications, including that which consists of bliss, according to the scriptural text: "It created all this, whatever there is"?
For it is not logically possible that Brahman, being a modification as a limb of a modification consisting of bliss, should be the cause of everything.

Therefore, it is established that Brahman is not the *ānandamaya*—a modification consisting of parts—as a limb [of itself]; nor is the *ānandamaya* modification, which would be a suitable part for such a Brahman, intended here as the object of meditation. Rather, it is Brahman itself, as the primary subject, which is intended here as the "tail" (*puccha*) to be known. 1.9.9.
"He is the bringer of the end [of transmigratory existence] because he teaches that doctrine.
In the preceding section, the five sheaths were established merely as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) serving as means for the realization of Brahman, from which all distinctions have been discarded;
however, these were not intended to be described in their own right.

It has been determined that Brahman alone is the primary subject, introduced as the object of knowledge in the statement, "Brahman is the tail, the support. Now, however, it is determined that Brahman is introduced as the object of meditation with its intended limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and not the individual soul (jīvātman) known by the term "Āditya," whose excellence is attained through the preeminence of knowledge and ritual action.
In that regard, the forms consisting of the support of the boundaries exist in the transmigrating soul, but not in the Supreme;
therefore, the sun, which is subject to karma, is the one to be worshipped by the transmigrating soul.
Because of the hearing of descriptions such as "having a golden beard," and because of the hearing of specific locations, namely, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye."

And because he rules over those worlds beyond that [world] as well as over the desires of the gods— both on account of this sovereignty and because of scriptural testimony— it is the transmigrating soul alone, consisting of a complex of cause and effect and endowed with form and other qualities, who is to be meditated upon here; not the Supreme Self, for that [Self] is devoid of all forms according to such scriptural passages as "without sound, without touch," and is without any substratum according to such passages as "in his own glory."
Furthermore, he whose boundless sovereignty has been established by such scriptural passages as "He is the Lord of all" can be understood here as an object of worship;
moreover, the absence of all evil is possible in the Person in the Sun,
because the scripture concerns human beings and deities lack the capacity for merit and demerit.

Furthermore, since it is logically untenable for anything else to possess form and so forth, and since the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of cause and effect, is intended as the object of meditation,

the fact that its being the self of all is heard in scripture as consisting of "seeing" and so on must somehow be a praise of the person in the sun alone; thus, the conclusion reached is that the person in the sun alone is the object of meditation, not the Supreme Self.

And in the case of being without a substratum (*anādhāratva*), the reasons are eternality (*nityatva*) and omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*). For an impermanent effect has a cause as its substratum and is thus not without a substratum;

likewise, even that which is eternal but not omnipresent is not without a substratum, since whatever stands below another serves as the substratum for that which is above it. Thus, [the self] is not without a substratum.
Therefore, both have been stated.
This being the case, it is replied: "Because of the teaching of its attributes [as being] within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.20).
"Here, [the Lord] is spoken of by means of His universal selfhood and His freedom from all evil. (Śaṅkara Bhāṣya)
Brahman alone is the cause of all, just as a modification [is the effect] of its material cause, by means of two non-deviating [reasons].
For by the etymological derivation of the name, its arising is said to consist in being the source from which all evil has departed.

And even though the deity Āditya lacks eligibility for ritual action, it is not the case that he is devoid of all evil, given the possibility of evil in the form of merit (*dharma*) acquired in previous lives. Nor is it correct to say that these [deities] possess only merit from previous lives and no evil at all.
Even when there is the manifestation of excellence in knowledge and action, it is possible for latent evils acquired through the beginningless succession of existences to still persist;
nor is it logical to claim that one who identifies with the body is free from all evils simply on the grounds of the authority of scripture,
since the authority of that scripture is equally established by its having Brahman as its subject matter.
Nor is there a lack of a reason for definitive selection (*vinigamanā*), because the absence of all evil is repeatedly heard in scripture in relation to Brahman alone;
and because that very [Brahman] is recognized here as the existing reason for definitive selection.

Moreover, the state of being the self of all (sārvātmya) is logically possible only for Brahman, the cause of the world, because the entire collection of effects is non-different from its cause, and Brahman is the cause of the world.
However, the individual self (jīvātman), which identifies with the body of the Sun, cannot be the cause of the world;
nor is it appropriate for a statement to have the purpose of praise through the figurative indication of excellence when the primary meaning is possible.
Furthermore, its possession of form may be due to the manifestation of a body for the sake of favoring others.
Or rather, because the entire collection of effects is a modification of that [Brahman],
and because a modification is not distinct from that which possesses the modification, it is taught through such a distinction of form,
just as one says, "That is the fragrance."
Nor does a scripture that describes a form created by Brahman through *māyā* become a non-scripture; rather, it is a scripture because it brings that [form] about.
However, where [Brahman] is presented as an object of knowledge stripped of all distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [it is not described as having such a form].
In this regard, the scripture proceeds: "Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable.
Therefore, even the possession of form is logically consistent with the Supreme Self.
By this very [argument], the distinctions of spatial limits and support are also explained.

Moreover, the transmigrating soul who identifies with the body of the sun is mentioned as distinct from the Inner Controller; yet that very same soul must be recognized here through the similarity of the scriptural term "within" (antar) in the phrase "the one within the sun.
Therefore, [the text says]: "those who possess wealth."

"Those who possess wealth" means those who possess power (*vibhūti*). Why, then, does the possession of power apply to being favored by the Supreme Lord? To this he says: "Whatever possesses power... [and so forth].

The meaning is that although [the Supreme Lord] is the self of all, the manifestation of the nature of the Supreme Lord occurs only in those possessed of power (*vibhūtimat*), and not in those devoid of power whose nature as the Supreme Lord is obscured by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā-tamas*). This also includes the lordship over the worlds and desires.
Therefore, the meaning is that his sovereignty is unrestrained by the principle that [otherwise] everything would ultimately serve another's purpose. //20// 1.1.7.21 // 21 // 1.1.8.22.
"Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark.

In the preceding section, because of the observation of attributes unique to Brahman, it was established that the meditation belongs to this very [Brahman] as characterized by its intended limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
It has been established, however, that this does not refer to the individual self (jīvātman) who identifies with the body of the sun; rather,
it is now established that because of the perception of unique attributes, that very [Self] is taught as the object of meditation by being superimposed upon the Udgītha,
and not the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
In this regard, must the statement "He said, 'Space'" be somehow interpreted in accordance with the primary sense of space— so that the questions "What is the support of this world?",

"All these beings," "Greater than which," and "The ultimate resort" are explained accordingly— or, conversely, must the word "space" be explained figuratively as referring to the Supreme Self in order to conform to those [questions]?
Because it is the ground for all leaves and because it is primary, space alone is primary for us;
the certainty is that the others must be explained in accordance with it.

Since, in response to the question "What is the goal of this world? the answer "He said, 'Space'" establishes space as the primary subject by presenting it as the goal, whereas the passages beginning with "All these indeed" are subordinate as qualifiers of that [space]; therefore, according to the principle "But when there is a quality, there is an assumption of something else," even many subordinate elements must be interpreted in accordance with the primary one.
Furthermore, in the subsequent passage, "He said, 'Space,'" space is first understood and is not yet subject to contradiction;

therefore, when that [notion of space] has colored the intellect, whatever else subsequently occurs within that same sentence—being of secondary importance and thus subject to contradiction—must be established in accordance with it.
Nor, because the word "space" is used figuratively for Brahman in some instances, must it necessarily refer to Brahman everywhere.

In the case of "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), the word "Gaṅgā" is taken as referring to the bank due to semantic inconsistency; however, by this same logic, in the case of "the waters in the Gaṅgā" (*yādāṃsi gaṅgāyām*), it would have to be taken as referring to that [bank] as well.
The possibility [of the literal sense] is equal in both instances.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is not used in its primary sense even with respect to Brahman.
Because having multiple meanings is not a fault, and because it is logical that the term is used for Brahman figuratively,
and because in common worldly usage this word is firmly established as referring to the sky.
Furthermore, since the comprehension of Vedic meaning is preceded by that [ordinary usage], its reversal is untenable;
and in accordance with this, the author of the Commentary himself has interpreted passages such as "All indeed... accordingly.
Therefore, it is the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) alone that is taught here as the object of meditation.
It follows, then, that it is not the Supreme Self.
To this prima facie view, it is replied: by the word "ether" (ākāśa), Brahman is to be understood.
Why?
Because of its characteristic mark (*liṅga*).
For it is said: "By virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the meaning is established] through the question and its answer."
Due to the consideration of what precedes and follows, there is a state of being secondary even when [something] is primary.
Even though the word "ether" (ākāśa) has the Pradhāna as its primary meaning, nevertheless, one must answer exactly what was asked.
Indeed, no sane person, when asked about the mango tree, describes the *kovidāra* tree.

Therefore, in this context, since the question, "What is the goal of this world? concerns the goal of the entire manifest expansion of names and forms that is perceived, it is in accordance with that [question] that whatever is the goal of the entire world is designated by the word "ether."
He should be answered as follows:
The elemental ether is not the refuge of the entire world,
because it too is included within the world.
For it is untenable that his understanding was simply that [the ether is] that very [elemental ether].
Nor is it correct to say that because the elemental ether is heard of in the subsequent answer, the question itself must have been about the effect of the elemental ether;

for it is impossible to restrict a primary understanding—which concerns the common worldly ether and has not yet encountered any contradiction—by means of a subsequent answer that encounters contradiction, since the answer must be interpreted in accordance with that primary understanding.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that an answer of established meaning cannot be restricted by a question whose form is a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and whose meaning is unsettled; for even though the ignorance, doubt, and error caused by that [question] may be unsettled, the answer itself remains established with respect to its own object. Otherwise, the answer would either lack a basis or result in a mismatch of referents (vaiyadhikaraṇya).
Moreover, even in the subsequent passage there is much that is inconsistent.
For instance, in the statement, "All these beings, indeed, arise from space alone," the word "all" would have to be explained as having a limited scope in some way.
Likewise, the restrictive particle "eva" (alone) is also inconsistent.
Indeed, water does not have space alone as its cause, but fire as well;
likewise, for food too, space alone is not the cause, but fire and water as well.
However, when there is an intention to state the ultimate cause, the restriction [to Brahman alone] is entirely appropriate.
But the incomparable space exists in the elemental ether;
thus, the dissolution of all elements occurs in Brahman alone.
In this way, Brahman alone is greater than all things.
Thus, Brahman alone is the supreme goal.

This is because the inquiry begins with the words "of all worlds," and because in the subsequent sections there is a reference to the unique attributes of Brahman, and because the movement that was asked about is concluded by summarizing those unique attributes of Brahman as "the supreme goal."

For the sake of favoring the majority of the scriptural passages, let the single term "ether" (ākāśa) alone be inconsistent—just as in the maxim, "one may sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family.
For by this much, a great deal will remain consistent.
Nor is there any predominance of ether in what follows.
However, because the answer pertains to the subject matter of the question, and because what is common to the world is what was asked,
and because the conclusion "the supreme goal" refers to that very same thing, Brahman alone is the primary subject.
And thus, for that purpose, the word "ether" (ākāśa) has the Pradhāna as its primary meaning, and not otherwise.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman alone is the Pradhāna intended here as the object of meditation by the word "ether," and not the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
Moreover,
at the very beginning of this [section], Śālāvatya was addressed with the fault of being limited by the words, "Your Sāman is indeed finite."
Nor is the word "ether" (ākāśa) even when used figuratively slow to be understood;

for since the word "ether" and its synonyms are frequently employed in various places for Brahman, through such constant repetition, this [figurative usage] is also understood as quickly as the primary sense. Thus, the abundance of Vedic usage regarding Brahman is shown for the sake of demonstrating this point.
This has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya;
and in that very context, the subsequent [text] is interpreted in accordance with what was first understood, provided it is possible to do so otherwise.

But where it is not possible [to interpret it in that way], there the first [term] is led [to its meaning] solely in accordance with what follows; thus he says: "Even at the beginning of the sentence" (vākyopakrame 'pi). For this very reason, [the word] *prāṇa* [refers to Brahman].
In the section on the *udgītha*, after the statement, "The deity that is associated with the *prastāva*," it is heard: "Which is that deity? 'It is Prāṇa,' said Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa.
In connection with the meditation on the *udgītha*, the Commentator has stated that the meditation on the *prastāva* is also included under the term *udgītha*.
The *prastāva* is a specific division (*bhakti*) of the Sāman; the deity that is "associated with" (anvāyattā), meaning "followed by" or "inherent in" it, is Prāṇa.
Here, since the word *prāṇa* is seen to refer both to Brahman and to a modification of air (vital breath), a doubt arises: does this term denote Brahman, or does it denote a modification of air?
In that regard, for the very reason of the aforementioned marks of Brahman (*brahmalinga*), it is logical that *prāṇa* is indeed Brahman alone and not a modification of air.
If this is so, then since the matter has already been established by that [preceding section], what is the purpose of beginning a new topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*)?
To this it is replied: "When an object is cognizable solely through scripture, we indeed rely upon scripture alone;
but when it is cognizable through other means of knowledge, its determination follows the force of those [other means]."
Regarding whether Brahman is the cause of all beings,
or whether space is the cause of the elements such as air and so forth, no means of knowledge other than scripture is capable of functioning.
In that regard, by examining the preceding and following passages, whatever meaning the scripture is consistent with— that alone is accepted as its meaning.

If the other [the individual soul] were being abandoned, then here, when the entering and emerging of beings with respect to the *prāṇa* are being stated, there arises the doubt as to whether Brahman is being referred to or a modification of air; regarding this, [there is the passage] beginning: "When a person sleeps, then speech merges into *prāṇa*."

By the force of the Śruti— which, through its demonstration of the entry and exit of the senses that are the essence of all beings, demonstrates the entry and exit of all beings, and has obtained its capacity through the support of other means of knowledge— the entry and exit belong to the vital breath (prāṇa) which is a modification of air alone,
and not to Brahman.

Moreover, in this context, regarding the two Sāma-chant portions, the *udgītha* and the *pratihāra*, other deities than Brahman—namely, the sun and food—are mentioned as being of the nature of an aggregate of cause and effect;
by association with them, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must also be a deity of the very same nature of an aggregate of cause and effect.
This point has also been established in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*.
This has been restated again to reinforce the reasons for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) mentioned previously.
Therefore, it follows that the meaning of the word "prāṇa" here is simply a modification of air.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "The greater authority of a human statement [is established] through its convergence with other means of knowledge."
In a sentence that is not of human origin, what will its connection with that [human author] accomplish?

Indeed, an impersonal (apauruṣeya) word, whose status as a means of valid cognition is established intrinsically, does not depend on another means of knowledge for the production of the cognition of its own object or for its practical application; for that impersonal word, having all suspicion of defect eliminated, is by itself determinative.
Because it is determinative... because it is determinative.

Since the engagement in worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by certainty, there is therefore neither lack of firmness nor firmness regarding that very [object], whether it be in the case of form— as with the visual faculty which does not correspond— or in the case of substance— as with the tactile faculty which does correspond. Thus, let [the notions of] entering and emerging belong merely to the senses, as modifications of the vital air (*prāṇa*).
However, the fact that all beings enter into and emerge from [it] is not understood from that sentence;
or, if it were so understood, then even there the *prāṇa* would be Brahman itself and not a modification of air—
just as in the sentence, "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this *prāṇa* alone," the word *prāṇa* denotes Brahman.
Furthermore, the dissolution and emergence of all beings within this modification of air are not observed through any other means of knowledge.

Nor can the statement regarding the dissolution and emergence of all beings be explained in any way as referring to the sense organs— on the grounds that the statement about the dissolution and emergence of the sense organs is strengthened by corroboration established through other means of knowledge—
for a statement whose status as a valid means of knowledge is self-evident and inherently firm has no need for other means of knowledge.
Nor does this [passage] form a single syntactical unit with that [preceding one];
for it has been stated that if they were a single syntactical unit, then that too would have Brahman as its sole subject.
Furthermore, the entering and emerging of the senses can be reconciled even as a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*).
It is like saying "he chooses one" or "he chooses two";
however, the meaning of the word "all" does not admit of such restriction.
Therefore, one should meditate upon the *prastāva* division as Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Prāṇa."
It is established that [the fruit] is not seen as a modification of air;
likewise, for the worshiper, the attainment of vital breath or the success of ritual action becomes the fruit—
this is by the force of the remainder of the scriptural passage.
The meaning is that proximity is weaker than syntactical connection (*vākya*).
Furthermore, another example has been refuted by the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which explains itself through its own words (*nigada-vyākhyāta*). 1.1.10.24.
*Jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt* (Because of the mention of the feet).

They declare this: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme—that is indeed this light which is within this person.
That light which shines and illuminates beyond this heaven, the world of the sky, on the backs of all, that is, above all things; on the backs of everything, that is, above all things.

To show that this word *viśva* (all), which possesses an unrestricted application, denotes the entire circle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*) by virtue of its being indivisible, he says:
"in the highest [worlds] behind all.
And this is not merely the highest, but rather the supreme of all; thus he says: [the following].
"Supreme" (anuttama) means that there is nothing higher than these.

"This indeed is that— the light within this person"— this is inferred by the mark of bodily heat, which is perceptible to the skin, and by the sound, which is perceptible to the ear when a man covers his ears.
In this regard, the perception of the bodily heat by means of the skin is "vision" (dṛṣṭi),
and the hearing of its sound is "audition" (śruti); and both that vision and audition belong to the light itself.
"Because it is inferred from its characteristic mark.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the word "light" (jyotis) refer to physical fire or to Brahman?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it refers to fire.

Why? Because, regarding the choice between a secondary and a primary sense, the rule of taking the primary sense is the general principle (*autsargika*); because the marks (*liṅga*) of "light" are perceived within the sentence; because there is no restrictive rule from another sentence; and because the meaning [of that other sentence] is not connected [to the present context].
Indeed, it was only due to the onset of a powerful subverting factor that the terms *ākāśa* and *prāṇa* were displaced from their primary meanings and established elsewhere.
In this case, however, there is no subverting factor within the remainder of its own sentence to prevent the word *jyotis* from denoting light in its primary sense;
on the contrary, there is even a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of light, namely, "it shines" (*dīpyate*).
Furthermore, it is heard in its own scriptural context that [the one who knows this] becomes "pleasing to the eye," "possessed of beauty," "learned," and "renowned," which indicates a limited result.
Indeed, a radiance—which is another name for fire—cannot possibly exist in Brahman without heat;
nor can there be a resemblance to the gastric light in Brahman apart from external brilliance.
Furthermore, the perception of heat, sound, and signs, as well as hearing [them], is not possible for Brahman except through its greatness;
nor is the meditation on Brahman, which yields great fruit, suitable for a minor result.
However, by superimposing [the idea of] external fire upon the internal fire, this meditation on fire becomes appropriate as it corresponds to its result.
This, then, is the fiery liṅga;
and for its corroboration, the multiplicity of boundary-supports— which had already been refuted— is introduced here, because there is no reason to refute it at this point.

Furthermore, it is not impossible for the mass of light to possess limits, because that [light] of the sun and so forth consists of parts, and thus limits to its various regions are possible; moreover, it is prescribed as an object of meditation.
However, since Brahman is partless, the meditation upon its parts is untenable.
Furthermore, since there is no possibility of conceiving [the light] as a part when the alternative of [it being Brahman] is available,
it is not reasonable to claim that another scriptural passage establishing Brahman— namely, "All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven"—
establishes that the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to Brahman in the statement, "That light which is beyond this heaven."
Indeed, a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) occurring in one sentence cannot be diverted from its primary meaning merely by the proximity of another sentence.

Furthermore, in another sentence, heaven (*dyauḥ*) is heard as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); it cannot be recognized as the same entity when it is heard in the sense of a boundary (*maryādā*) in the phrase "from heaven" (*divaḥ*).
Moreover, the fact that even the other sentence has Brahman as its referent is yet to be established; it is not proven even now.
How, then, could that sentence—"that which is beyond this"—be capable of being restrained by him [the opponent] through the claim that Brahman is the subject?
Therefore, it follows that *jyotis* is indeed light (*tejas*) and not Brahman.
The mention of darkness (*tamas*) in the context of discussing light is for the purpose of producing a firm understanding regarding another counter-position by means of presenting its opposite.
"It is that which obstructs the functioning of the eye," [meaning] by way of being an obscuration. The objector says:
"Is it not the case that the same applies to the effect as well? To this, the proponent of a partial solution replies:
"Let it be so, then."
That light which is not mixed with water and earth is called "not triplicated" (atrivṛtkṛta).
The objector refutes this, saying: "No."

The meaning is that it (the whole) is not useful for any purpose whatsoever, because in all causal operations (*arthakriyā*), only that which has been divided into three parts is of use. He states the objection of the *ekadeśin* (partialist) with the words "this very [thing]."
The objector refutes this: "No;
because it serves another purpose.

The meaning is that the scriptural statement, "Let me make each one threefold, threefold," which has as its scope the meditations on fire and the other elements, ought not to be restricted [to a mere literal sense].
When the proponent of the partial view has been thus refuted, the opponent, who is a supreme respondent, says:
"In that case, let it be precisely that which is composed of the threefold [elements]; this is the logical position."

Although the scriptural mention of a plurality of substrates can somehow be explained even in the case of Brahman as being based on imagined limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), nevertheless, it is explained that "it is more appropriately explained" because it applies with greater appropriateness to the effected light (*kārya-jyotis*) than it does here [to Brahman].
"Prākṛta" means born from primordial nature (prakṛti), that is to say, an effect.
When this [objection] has been raised, it is said: "A pronoun is used for the sake of referring to something already established; it does not serve to negate a matter yet to be proven."
Depending on conventional usage, that which resides in a preceding sentence is understood as being subordinate.

By the force of that [preceding rule], the signs of fire (tejoliṅga) must also certainly be interpreted as referring to Brahman alone; for while Brahman is indeed the primary meaning, the word "fire" (brahmacchanda) does not apply there.

Generally speaking, there is a rule that [a sentence] restates what is not already established, which even causes an injunctive suffix to deviate from its inherent nature of making known a previously unknown matter—

as in "If the fire of one who has established the sacred fires should burn his house," or "If both sacrificial offerings of one should meet with ruin. However, where that [restatement] is already well-known and cannot be obtained from any other source, [the rule does not apply].
In that context, the statement "but because of the novelty [of the matter]" forcibly removes the well-known meaning of the pronoun *tat*.
For example, in the passage, "That which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni," [the word *tat* refers to something not previously established].

Similarly here, in the phrase "The light which is beyond this heaven," by the force of the word *yat*, the light must necessarily be one that is already well-known, even if it is defined by the limit of heaven.
Nor is there any establishment of that [Brahman] through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since in the preceding sentence the Brahman consisting of the three quarters was established as being connected with heaven, when there is a requirement for something already established, that very same [Brahman] is what is connected [here].

Moreover, when the primary meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is recognized as being that very same thing, it is not logical for the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), which is its qualifier, to become something else merely because of its difference in grammatical form.

Thus, since the signs of light found in that passage would otherwise be inconsistent, they must be understood as referring to Brahman alone; and indeed, they have been so interpreted by the author of the Commentary.
In that context, the phrase "light is a modification of Brahman" indicates that Brahman itself is being characterized by means of its effect, light.

Alternatively, since the word *jyotis* (light) denotes mere luminosity, and since luminosity belongs to Brahman, it is established that *jyotis* refers to Brahman in its primary sense. [The objection] that this would result in "abandoning the subject under discussion" (*prakṛtahāna*) and "introducing what was not under discussion" (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*) is answered as follows: with respect to conventional usage, that which occurs in the preceding sentence is the relevant subject (*prakṛta*), being proximate.
However, that which is not established should be postulated, but it is not the subject under discussion;
therefore it was said:
"it is postulated."
Regarding the "tongs" (saṃdaṃśa) [section], he says:
"Not only...
[meaning] that even for the supreme Brahman, it is like the case of names and so forth being its symbols (pratīka).
For the gastric fire is a modification of the Supreme Self that has entered into the state of the individual soul (jīva);
this is known from the fact that the body is cold when in the state of being a living soul, yet warm while one is alive.
Therefore, the meditation upon that symbol is logical.
The rest of the commentary is explained by its own words (*nigadavyākhyātam*).

"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of meditation] because of the mention of the meters (*chanda*), we say no; because there is a statement regarding the fixing of the mind in that way, for so it is seen [in scripture]. (1.1.10.25)
For this would be so only if it were established that the preceding sentence has Brahman as its referent;
however, it does not have Brahman as its referent,
but rather Gāyatrī as its referent.
With reference to the Gāyatrī, this is heard in scripture: "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here," and "Three-quarters of it are the immortal in heaven.
But is this not already covered by the sūtra, "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks"?
For instance, in that verse beginning "Such is its greatness," Brahman is described as having four quarters.
And that very [Brahman] has its meaning connected by the statement, "This same thing is declared by the Ṛg-verse," which serves as a mark of Brahman.
Likewise, in the passage "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," the status of being "all" is not possible for the Gāyatrī merely as a collection of syllables;
nor is it possible for the Gāyatrī, in its own nature, to possess the essence of the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the vital breaths.
Furthermore, the Gāyatrī does not possess a relationship with the Person in Brahman (brahmapuruṣa).

Therefore, since meditation on Brahman itself is performed by means of the Gāyatrī—and not on the Gāyatrī itself—this [present discussion] need not be commenced, as its purpose has already been covered by the preceding [section].
Nor is this entire collection of sūtras intended merely to recall the logic of the previous case.
To this it is replied: there is indeed a further doubt.
For instance, what is the meaning of "meditation on Brahman by means of the Gāyatrī"?
Does it mean meditation on Brahman as having the Gāyatrī as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)?
Nor does that which is conditioned by those adjuncts— that is, that which is delimited by them— possess the nature of being the Self of all,
because the adjunct itself is a limitation;
for space delimited by a jar does not become undelimited.

Therefore, its being the self of all and so forth is for the purpose of praise; let that praise rather belong to the Gāyatrī itself through some indirect means, based on such scriptural passages as: "Speech indeed is the Gāyatrī; speech indeed sings and protects this entire world."

And thus, beginning with "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and having explained the Gāyatrī itself through its heart and other parts, the conclusion— "This is that four-footed, sixfold Gāyatrī"— is appropriate only with respect to the Gāyatrī; for if [the subject] were Brahman, everything would be inconsistent.
The word "Brahman" in the phrase "That which is indeed that Brahman" refers exclusively to the Vedic meters,
just as in the expression "this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman," the secret doctrine of the Veda is meant.
Therefore, since this refers to the Gāyatrī meter, the conclusion is reached that this does not concern the Supreme Brahman.
This being the case, it is replied:
No. Why?
"Likewise, because of the mention of the fixing of the mind (cetorpaṇa).

By means of the meter called Gāyatrī, this Brahman-text declares the fixing of the mind—that is, the concentration of the intellect—upon Brahman, which conforms to the modification in the form of Gāyatrī. This is what is meant: [the text teaches that one should meditate on Brahman through the medium of the Gāyatrī].
The *gāyatrī* is not a delimiting attribute (*avacchedaka*) of Brahman,
like blueness is of a blue lotus; for if it were, then [the nature of Brahman] would not exist elsewhere, due to the absence of that delimiting attribute.

However, since this Brahman—which is the self of all and the cause of all—is impossible to teach in its own essential nature, it is indicated by means of its modification, the Gāyatrī. This is because, among all modifications, the Gāyatrī is appropriately established as the primary medium due to its pervasion of all meters, its pervasion of the three libations, and its being the mother of the second birth for the twice-born, according to the Śruti; nor is the indicated object not perceived simply because there is no indication elsewhere.
For the form of the neck, which was characterized by the earrings, does not become unperceived when the earrings are later removed;
this is because qualifiers serve solely for the purpose of making that form known and do not function as restrictive delimiters.
Thus, since the word *gāyatrī* has its primary meaning [in this context], it is said that Brahman is characterized by the *gāyatrī*.
Now, he shows that the word *gāyatrī* refers to Brahman itself through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) based on a commonality of number,
by stating "another says":
for just as the *gāyatrī* has four feet consisting of six syllables each, so too [Brahman] is four-footed.
In this way, Brahman also consists of four quarters:
for all beings, both stationary and moving, constitute one quarter of it;
or else, there are three quarters in the divine space.
For thus says the Śruti: "This indeed is that space which is within the person.
That is his state of waking;
for while awake, he indeed perceives external objects.
Likewise: "This indeed is that which is the space within the person"—meaning within the body;
for that is his place of dream.
Likewise: "This indeed is that which is the space within the heart. The meaning is "within the lotus of the heart" (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), for that is his place of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
This very [Brahman] is what was described in the passage, "Three-quarters of it are the immortal in heaven.
Thus, because of the commonality of having four quarters (*catuṣpāt*), Brahman is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*.
According to this view, it is Brahman alone that has been expressed.
It has been stated that [the Gāyatrī] is declared to be Brahman because it has Brahman as its supreme object (brahmaparatvāt).

Regarding the phrase "of six kinds" (ṣaḍvidha): six aspects—namely, the elements (bhūta), earth (pṛthivī), body (śarīra), heart (hṛdaya), speech (vāk), and vital breath (prāṇa)—are heard in scripture as belonging to Brahman known by the name Gāyatrī.

And as for the expression "five Brahman-persons" (pañca brahmapuruṣāḥ), the mention of "Brahman-persons" in reference to the apertures of the heart is possible only if the intended meaning is their connection with Brahman.
The meaning of this is: indeed, there are five apertures—that is, five openings—in this heart.

And because these are guarded by the deities, such as Prāṇa and the others, they are the gateways for attaining heaven; thus they are called "divine apertures" (*devasuṣayaḥ*). For instance, the wind situated in that aperture of the heart which faces the east is Prāṇa;
for by means of it, one travels at the time of departure to the heavenly world.
The meaning is that he alone is the eye and he alone is the sun,
according to the Vedic scripture: "The external vital breath (prāṇa), indeed, is the sun."
Now, that which is its southern cavity is the specific vital air located therein called *vyāna*;
the ear is connected to it, and that is the Moon, according to the Vedic scripture: "The Vaiśyas and the Moon were created by the ear."

Now, that particular wind which is located in the posterior opening of this [body] is the *apāna*; and because of its connection with speech, it is *vāk* (speech), according to the Vedic scripture: "Agni is indeed speech.
Now, that particular wind which is located in the northern opening of this [body] is the *udāna*.
Starting from the soles of the feet and extending upwards to the eyes;
that wind and its support, space, are the deities.
These indeed are the five openings.

The five persons connected with that [Gāyatrī] belong to the Brahman residing in the heart; they do not exist merely within the arrangement of syllables of the Gāyatrī, but rather in the Brahman itself. (Sūtra 27) As it is said:
"As the word 'soka'... [refers to the fire].
When the primary sense of "heaven" (div) is that of a substratum, then the limit (maryādā) must be explained in some way.
For a hawk that is actually on the top of a tree is indeed also beyond it;
for even apart from its front portion, that very same hawk exists beyond the tree by virtue of being situated in its rear portion.

Thus, it is logical that Brahman, residing in the internal celestial region of the heart— which is distinct from the external celestial region— should be situated beyond the external celestial region. However, when the boundary itself is intended as the primary and principal meaning, then its status as a locus must be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
just as in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," where the proximity [to the river] is the basis for the usage.
This is what was stated: "Another says...
For this very reason, it was said: "even beyond heaven. //27// 1.1.11.28.
"Prāṇa [is Brahman] because it follows [the context].
"When there is a conflict of many marks, which mark of the possessor of the mark shall prevail? This point, not previously considered, is now deliberated upon."

Many signs of several entities— the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), the individual soul (jīva), the presiding deity (devatā), and Brahman— converge here; therefore, it is investigated which among these is the true sign and which is a mere semblance of a sign.
Furthermore, this matter has not been investigated in the section [beginning] with "Therefore, the vital breath.
It might be argued:

the attainment of the supreme human goal, the non-association with all sins such as the killing of an embryo, the state of being the conscious self (*prajñātman*), and bliss and so forth, are not possible in the primary vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*).
Likewise, such statements as "He causes one to perform good deeds" and "He is the Lord of the worlds" also apply [to Him].
While the nature of being the conscious self (*prajñātmatva*) might somehow be possible in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is impossible for others [the organs].

Furthermore, although the quality of being a speaker—the state of possessing the activity of the organ of speech—does not exist in its own right within the Supreme Self, [it is attributed to Him through His presiding over them].

Nevertheless, in order to avoid contradicting numerous characteristics of Brahman that cannot be otherwise accounted for, this [passage] must somehow be explained as referring to Brahman itself through the medium of the individual soul (jīva), because of the non-difference of the soul from Brahman.
Thus says the Śruti: "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed..."

"Know that very Brahman to be you"—by saying this, he declares that Brahman is the cause of the organ of speech. Although the maintenance of the body belongs primarily to the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, nevertheless, because the activity of the vital breath is dependent upon the Supreme Self, it belongs to the Supreme Self alone.
And although there is here an indicative mark (liṅga) of the deity Indra, who possesses a physical form, [it does not contradict the conclusion].
For instance, having addressed Pratardana who had gone to Indra’s abode, Indra said,
"Know me alone," and beginning thus,
he uttered the word "prāṇa" with respect to the Self in the passage, "I am prāṇa, the conscious self."
Furthermore, its nature as wisdom-soul (prajñātman) is appropriate, because the deities possess unimpeded power of knowledge;
and due to Indra’s preeminent capacity, he is also the cause of the most beneficial human goal.

Since the scripture has humans as its primary authority, it does not apply to the gods; thus, it is logical that there is no mention of sins such as the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*) in their case.
Furthermore, the world belongs to Indra because he is the guardian of the world (*lokapāla*).
And the nature of bliss and so forth belongs to heaven itself, because heaven is bliss.
Furthermore, Indra’s immortality is established by the Smṛti text: "For the state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called immortality.
Moreover, the praise [of him] as having a physical body, such as "He slew the son of Tvaṣṭṛ," is appropriate only in that context.
Nevertheless, since liberation, the supreme human goal, cannot be attained through anything other than knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, [he must be identified with that].

Because the supreme nectar and agelessness, which consist of the nature of supreme bliss, do not deviate from the nature of Brahman, and because the abundance of internal spiritual connections is impossible in the case of the external Indra;

therefore, for Indra— who is a deity, who has awakened in his own self, and who is in his final body— there remains only the residual store of karma whose fruition has already begun, just as in the case of Vāmadeva.

"If all this is possible for Brahman alone through its enjoyment [of these powers], then by the abandonment of the body, the senses, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the vital breaths (*prāṇa-vāyu*), it is Brahman alone that is understood here by the word 'prāṇa'; thus, since there is no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) [to refute], this [section] need not have been commenced.
To this it is replied: "That which is indeed *prāṇa* is wisdom (*prajñā*), and that which is wisdom is *prāṇa*; for these two dwell together in this body."

Regarding the statement, "dwelling together, they depart together," it is precisely that vital breath (prāṇa) which was previously described as the object of meditation as the conscious self (prajñātman) whose departure along with that conscious self is here stated.
Furthermore, there is no duality in Brahman.
There is neither coexistence nor departure;
therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed air,
and the living being (jīva) is the conscious self (prajñātman).
Through the simultaneous occurrence of both engagement and withdrawal, the identity of these two is figuratively attributed by such passages as "That which is Prāṇa... and so forth.
Furthermore, qualities such as bliss, immortality, sovereignty, and freedom from evil will belong to the Prāṇa insofar as it is Brahman.
Therefore, according to the appropriate application, exactly three are to be meditated upon here.
Nor does this syntactical split (vākyabheda) bring about a fault,
because the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is preceded by the comprehension of the word-meanings,
and because word-meanings possess independence according to the path already described.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that there is a threefold division of meditations due to the difference in the objects of meditation.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: it is true that the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is facilitated by the comprehension of the meanings of the words; yet, it is not the case that words have as their sole purpose the comprehension of word-meanings.
Rather, they are intent upon the comprehension of the single meaning of the sentence;

however, since they are unable to produce that very single sentence-meaning without the comprehension of the word-meanings, they cause those meanings to be understood in the interim for that very purpose.

Therefore, words whose natural inclination is toward the cognition of a single qualified meaning are led—only by the presence of a powerful subverting factor—to the state of having multiple meanings as their intended object.
As they have said: "When a single syntactical unity is possible, a split in the sentence is not desired.

Therefore, just as in the case of the Upāṃśuyāja passage—where there is an introduction regarding the defect of monotony (*jāmitā*) and a conclusion regarding its remedy—it was determined that for the sake of syntactical unity, statements such as "Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a low voice" are not separate injunctions, but rather explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Thus, having begun with "Know me also here in this way," and having stated "I am the breath, the conscious self," and concluding finally with "That very breath is the conscious self, blissful, undecaying, and immortal,"— since a single coherent unity with respect to Brahman is thus understood,
even the indicative marks (liṅgas) of the individual soul (jīva) and the primary vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) must be interpreted in conformity therewith.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

As for the observation of their distinction in the passage, "For these two together," that is a reference to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the inner self (*pratyagātman*), made in order to indicate the inner self itself by means of the distinction between the powers of knowledge and action.

For this very reason, the indicator indicates the non-difference of the indicated—the nature of the inner self—by means of difference, stating: "The vital breath itself is the conscious self. The summary is: "Therefore, because of the conformity with the marks of Brahman which cannot be established otherwise, the marks of the vital breath and the individual soul are explained by the force of the single sentence. (Sūtra 1.1.11.29–31)
"It cannot be a statement about Brahman"—
this means that this entire textual context cannot possibly be a statement about Brahman alone;
rather, according to its proper application, there is something here that is a statement about the individual soul (jīva).
The meaning is that some passages concern the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), while others concern Brahman;
this is because [the former] depend on other vital breaths which are the instruments of cognition (prajñā).
The other vital breaths are the sense organs, for they are established in the principal breath;
the phrase "either the individual soul or the principal breath" is merely an introductory statement.
The point of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that both [are impermanent];
however, Brahman is eternal.
It is not the case that Brahman is [impermanent].
The meaning is not that it is Brahman alone;
[it refers to] "of the ten elements" (bhūtamātrāḥ),
namely the five [objects], sound and so forth.
The five beginning with earth constitute the ten elements (bhūtamātrās).
The five sense organs of cognition and the five objects of the Buddha constitute the ten cognitions (prajñāmātrās).
Having thus explained it according to his own view, he now explains it according to the opinion of the ancient commentators (vṛttikṛts):
Regarding the phrase "Or else" (athavā):

previously, the objection was stated that a split in the sentence would result from a threefold division of meditations—namely, one meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa), another on the individual soul (jīva), and another on Brahman.
However, the view of the ancient commentators (vṛttikṛt) is that there is no such split here, because a single Brahman alone is being enjoined as qualified by three distinct meditations.
This must be considered: how is it that there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*)?

It is appropriate that in cases such as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), there is an injunction of a sacrifice qualified by the accessory (guṇa) of Soma and so forth, because that which is qualified by those accessories is the object of the injunction (*vidhi*) as something not previously established (*apūrva*).
But here, Brahman, being established in its own nature, cannot be the object of an injunction,
because it is not something to be brought into being;
for there is a rule that only that which has the nature of an action (bhāvārtha) can be the object of an injunction.

Furthermore, since the realization of Brahman is already established through other statements, it is merely restated (anūdyate); thus, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*)—namely, meditation (*upāsanā*), which has not been previously established—is what must be enjoined. And because of that, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the repetition of the injunction (*vidhi*) would be extremely clear;
however, the Commentator did not point this out, as he has already expressed [this] through his own explanation. Thus, all is clarified. //31//
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the Bhāmatī, which is the commentary on the [Brahma-]Sūtra-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra. //1//
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter, titled "The Concordance of Śruti Passages Containing Clear Indications of Brahman."
The second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter: 1.2.1.1.
Now, desiring to commence the second quarter, [the author] recalls the matter previously stated for its utility in what is about to be said:
"In the first quarter."
For later on, the pervasiveness, eternity, and other attributes of Brahman will be taught as established reasons;
yet, since these have not been directly demonstrated previously, one might ask how they can be taught as reasons.
To this it is said: "of the cause of the entire world."

The meaning is this: although these [reasons] were not previously stated explicitly by name, they were nonetheless introduced by way of establishing Brahman as the cause of the world's birth and so forth, according to the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context of a discussion). Therefore, their presentation later on as logical reasons is justified.
This applies even to those [terms] whose meanings are well-known in other contexts.

Where even terms such as "ether," "vital breath" (prāṇa), and "light"— which are well-known to have other meanings— are explained as referring to Brahman because of the hearing of characteristics that are never-deviating from it,

what need is there to mention the determination of terms like "consisting of mind" (manomaya) as having Brahman as their referent, given that they are already well-known to have other meanings? This is the intended sense.
However, we shall demonstrate the intention of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) later on.
"Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere.
This is recorded in the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
"All this, indeed, is Brahman.
Why?
Because it originates from that, dissolves into that, and breathes in that.
Because it is born from that Brahman, it is "tajjam"; because it dissolves into it, it is "tallam";
and because it breathes—that is, acts—within it during the period of its maintenance, it is "tadanam. Therefore, this entire world is indeed Brahman.

Therefore, being free from passion and hatred and remaining tranquil, one should meditate [on the Self], considering: "Who is attached to what, and who hates whom? Now, indeed, a person consists of volition (*kratu*); as is his volition in this world, so does he become after departing from here. He should form a volition: "He consists of mind (*manomaya*), has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for his body," and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) taught here as the object of meditation by means of these attributes such as "consisting of mind," or is it Brahman?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the individual soul is corporeal.
Why?

Having referred back to the meditative cultivation of sacrifice (*kratubhāvanā*) enjoined by the sentence beginning with "sacrifice" (*kratum*), the sentence beginning with "all" (*sarvam*) is an injunction regarding the quality of tranquility (*śama*).
Thus, although the sentence "All this, indeed, is Brahman" is recited first, by consideration of the meaning it comes later; for it depends upon the meaning of that [subsequent injunction].

And thus, this first injunction regarding the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), being without an object, not reaching completion, and dependent on an object, cannot by itself be subsisted upon by another injunction because it lacks a complement.

Therefore, it is connected with the passages such as "consisting of mind, having breath for its body," which provide the object, even prior to the injunction of the quality of tranquility (*śāntatā*).

Furthermore, since qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) are firmly established as belonging to the individual self (*jīvātman*)—which is of the nature of a composite of cause and effect—an adoration colored by the individual self as the object of meditation cannot subsequently be connected with Brahman, because it is barred by the qualities [already] enjoined at the time of its origin.

Nor does the sentence "All this, indeed... refer to Brahman; rather, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to induce tranquility, serving as a statement of praise for the injunction to become tranquil.

It is not as in the case of [the injunction] "One offers with a winnowing basket" followed by "For with that food is prepared," where even though the statement has another purpose, it is accepted because of its requirement for Brahman; for here,

since the attributes such as "consisting of mind" (manomayatva) and so forth are well-known in relation to the individual soul (jīva), there is no requirement [for Brahman] once they have been assigned to the subject of the individual soul.
However, the possession of all functions and so forth by the individual soul (jīva) will occur successively;
in this way, its minuteness is also logically established.
But for the Supreme Self, which is immeasurable, such [minuteness] is impossible.

The quality of being "greater" (jyāyastva) must be explained as being subordinate to the previously understood quality of being "smaller" (aṇīyastva). And this is how the author of the Bhāṣya explains it.

Likewise, the designation of [the Self] as both object and agent, and the use of the locative case ending and the word "bowing down," should be understood—even though there is no actual difference between the individual self (jīvātman) and [Brahman]—as a figurative attribution of difference, similar to the expression "the head of Rāhu."
And the phrase "this is Brahman" refers to the individual soul (jīva), because the soul is also called "Brahman" in the sense that it nourishes (bṛṃhaṇa) the body and other constituents.
This being so, qualities such as having true resolve (satya-saṃkalpatva), which reside in the Supreme Self, are also possible in the individual soul.
Because it is non-different from that [the individual soul],
it follows that the individual soul alone is intended here as the object of meditation,
and not the Supreme Self.
This being the case, it is stated in reply: "A compound whose referent is a pronoun requires something proximate;
even the general sense of a secondary derivative (taddhita) does not remove that requirement."
Therefore, Brahman, being required [for the context], must be understood even from a passage whose primary purport is something else;
and thus, the literal reality of attributes such as "whose resolve is true" (satyasaṃkalpa) is established.

This might be so if, having reached the referent of all names as "breath" (prāṇa) and "body" (śarīra), the designation were to terminate there. In that case, the term "consisting of mind" (manomaya)—its own meaning having been fully exhausted—would be sufficient for the completion of that designation.
However, it is still not understood for what purpose [the text] uses either "a modification of mind" (manovikāra) or "abounding in mind" (manaḥpracura).
Therefore, where this word has a combined meaning, that is the meaning of the compound;
and it is not correct to say that this [word] has its combined meaning in the individual soul (jīva) alone and not in Brahman,
because its separation from those [attributes] is established by such passages as "for He is without breath, without mind," and so forth.
Because that [Brahman] is the cause of all modifications,
and because modifications are non-different from their own cause, and because those [modifications] consist of mind, it is logical that Brahman, as their cause, consists of mind (*manomaya*).
This might be so.
The qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (manomaya) belong directly to the individual soul (jīva),
whereas they belong to Brahman only by way of that [soul]. In this regard, since the door [the soul] is first present to the intellect, let that alone be the object of meditation.
But Brahman is not inferior;
moreover, since the individual soul (jīva) is non-different from Brahman, the characteristics of Brahman will also apply to the individual soul.
Therefore, this must be considered here: is it that the individual souls, being non-different from Him, possess those [Brahmanic] attributes by virtue of the characteristics of Brahman?

And thus, since the individual soul (jīva) is first understood through its qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (manomaya), does it alone possess the status of the object of meditation? Or rather, even though the soul is non-different from Brahman, does Brahman not likewise possess the marks of the soul; for by the marks of the soul, Brahman is characterized as possessing those very attributes?
Thus, because the marks of Brahman are observed [in this passage], and because those marks are untenable in the case of the individual soul (jīva), Brahman alone is the object of meditation.
However, we observe: "The object may take on the form of that which is superimposed upon it, but the thing superimposed does not take on the form of the object."
For when a snake is superimposed, it is the rope that possesses the form [of the snake] by way of its terrifying nature and so forth;
however, the snake does not possess the form [of the rope] by way of its accessibility and so forth.
At that time, since the snake itself is non-existent, what could possibly possess a form?
In the case of a snake, however, it is not that the rope does not exist in reality;
likewise here, it is appropriate for Brahman— which exists as a reality— to appear in the form of the superimposed individual soul (jīva),
yet the jīva cannot possess the nature of Brahman through attributes such as eternity and so forth.
Because that [state] is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) at that time;
therefore, since the marks of Brahman are observed and because those marks are impossible in the case of the jīva, it is established that Brahman alone is to be meditated upon, not the jīva.
And this statement, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," has been cited as an illustration of this point. //1// 1.2.1.2.
Regarding the phrase "even though it is not of human origin" (apauruṣeya):

although the Lord is the source of the scripture, He is designated as "not of human origin" because His composition depends upon the textual arrangements fashioned by each preceding creation, and thus lacks independence;
accordingly, it has been stated that there is no intention to speak [of the scripture] due to this lack of independence.

The terms "acceptance" (*parigraha*) and "relinquishment" (*parityāga*) refer to "appropriation" (*upādāna*) and "non-appropriation" (*anupādāna*), and not merely to the state of being capable of being appropriated.

Otherwise, since the act of grasping and so forth would not be intended as the object of the injunction, it would follow that the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) would apply even to the *camasa* cups and other such items.
Therefore, even though it is not something to be adopted (*anupādeya*), the cup (*graha*) is intended (*vivakṣita*) as that which is grasped by virtue of being the objective (*uddeśyatayā*).
However, the singularity residing in it is not intended, as it is excluded from being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*).
This intention or non-intention is based on figurative usage (*bhakti*).
This is what has been stated:
[the meaning] is understood through the primary purport and the non-primary purport of the Vedic sentences.
Whatever the Vedic sentence aims at, that alone is adopted as intended by it.
And that which is not intended by one who is not devoted to it is "not meant to be expressed"— this is the meaning.
Just as [qualities] such as having true resolve are appropriate for Brahman, so too will they be appropriate for the embodied soul (śārīra).

Because of the non-difference of the embodied one from Brahman, qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth might be attributed to Brahman just as they are to the embodied one; therefore, the author of the Sūtras says: "But on account of impossibility, it is not the embodied one. (1.2.1.4) "But on account of the impossibility [of the qualities], it is not the embodied one. (1.2.1.5) "But on account of the impossibility [of the qualities], it is not the embodied one. (1.2.1.6)
This is the origin of what we previously stated: that superimposed properties may exist within the object of superimposition, but the properties of the [actual] object are not superimposed.
This is its source.
Here the opponent objects:
"Who, then, is this so-called embodied self?

It has already been stated that both difference and non-difference cannot be real in one and the same thing, because difference is denied while difference is also taught, and because such a state is contradictory.

Therefore, among these, one is real and the other is unreal; for the Vedāntas are intent upon establishing non-duality through their sequential progression, and there exists no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends duality, since such a cognition would be sublated by the Vedāntas. Thus, non-duality alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Consequently, the [Sūtra] beginning with "But because of the impossibility" (*anupapattestu*) would be inconsistent in meaning—this is the sense.
He refutes this: "This is indeed true;
the Supreme Self alone, when not distinguished by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is figuratively designated as the 'embodied' (śārīra) by the ignorant."
The Supreme Self alone, having attained the state of an individual soul (*jīva*) through the limitation of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), appears as if distinct by its own nature;
and such ignorance belongs to these individual souls,
but not to Brahman, which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).

Nor is it correct to argue that there is a mutual dependence— namely, that the differentiation of individual selves (jīvātman) occurs only when ignorance exists, and ignorance subsisting in those selves exists only when the differentiation of individual selves exists—
because, being beginningless, the relationship between the individual self and ignorance is as unavoidable and inseparable as that between a seed and its sprout.
Nor should it be argued: "How could one who is omniscient and omnipotent become a transmigrating being (saṃsārin) spontaneously or without cause?
For it is one who is dependent that might be cast into a prison by another, but not one who is independent."
For that portion of the self which is the individual soul (jīva) has not undergone a recent imprisonment in a prison-house such that it would be subject to questioning;
rather, its condition is beginningless, bound by the impressions (saṃskāra) of prior actions and ignorance (avidyā), and thus does not deserve such inquiry.

Nor does this much [requirement of instruments] imply a lack of sovereignty on the part of the Lord; for the dependence of a creator upon instruments and the like does not destroy his independence. Therefore, whatever has been said [by the opponent] is also [refuted]. (6) 1.2.1.7. (7) 1.2.1.8. While it should have been stated as "because of distinction" (*viśeṣāt*), the use of the term "particularity" (*vaiśeṣya*) is intended to demonstrate an absolute distinction.

For thus, attachment to pleasure and so forth, which is imagined by ignorance, is appropriate only for that which is characterized by ignorance; it is not, however, appropriate for the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure, awakened, and liberated, and from whom all ignorance along with its latent impressions has been wiped away—this is the meaning. The remainder of the text has a self-evident sense. //8// 1.2.2.9.

The Self [is the cause], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving. In the Kaṭhavallīs it is recited: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are but food, for whom death is the sauce—who indeed knows where He is? (KaṭhU 1.2.25).
And here, some eater is understood who is sprinkled with the sprinkling of the water-offering (audāna) that is to be consumed;
and this state of being an eater would consist either in the capacity for enjoyment or in the capacity for swallowing.
However, the supreme self under discussion does not possess the capacity for enjoyment.
Because the scripture "The other looks on without eating" prohibits the state of being an enjoyer,

and because the state of being an enjoyer is prescribed for the individual self (jīvātman) in the passage "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit," if "eating" here signifies the state of being an enjoyer,
then it must undoubtedly be understood as the individual self alone.
Furthermore, its aggregate of causes and effects— beginning with the *brahman* and the *kṣatriya*— exists either as the locus of experience or directly as the object of experience.
Moreover, it possesses the nature of both the agent of withdrawal and the experiencer.

Consequently, since questions and statements regarding three—the fire, the individual soul (jīva), and the supreme self (paramātman)—are found, and since their status as the "consumer" (saṃhartṛ) is indistinguishable, a doubt arises: is the "eater" (attā) the fire, or the individual soul, or the supreme self?
