In this regard, because food is well-known in the world as an object of enjoyment, the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) first presents itself to the mind, whereas the state of being a consumer (saṃhartṛtva) comes last; thus, the "eater" must be the enjoyer.
And thus it is the individual soul (*jīva*) itself;
the statement "it is neither born nor dies" is a praise of that very [soul],
because even at the time of dissolution, it persists in the form of mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, its difficulty of being known is due to its subtlety.
Therefore, it follows that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the eater who is to be meditated upon here.
Even if "eater-ness" (*attṛtva*) is understood as the quality of being a destroyer, in that case too, Agni would be the eater.
On account of the well-known scriptural texts, "Agni is the eater of food," it might thus appear that [the eater] is Agni;
to this, it is replied: the Supreme Self is the eater here.
Why? Because...
Because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving;
for it is heard in scripture: "Both of which are his boiled rice" and "Death is his condiment.
In that context, if the aggregate of causes and effects exists as the locus of experience and the means of experience for the individual soul (jīva), [then the following applies].
In that case, it is not boiled rice;
for boiled rice is neither the locus of enjoyment nor the means of enjoyment.
Rather, it is that which is to be enjoyed (*bhogya*).
Furthermore, the status of being "to be enjoyed" does not primarily belong to the locus of enjoyment or the means of enjoyment;
nor, in this context, is death conceived as a condiment (*upasecana*).
Furthermore, the aggregate of causes and effects consisting of the *brahmanas*, *kṣatriyas*, and so forth, is not to be eaten by the individual soul (*jīva*).
While this might apply to some cruel being such as a tiger, it does not apply to every single living being in every way.
Therefore, even with respect to *brahmanas* and *kṣatriyas*, the status of being an eater does not extend to all living beings.
How much more so, then, the case of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, which is permeated by the sprinkling of death?

Nor is it correct to argue that the quality of being an eater (the subject) should be applied according to the possibility of the situation, in conformity with the state of being food (the object) understood first from the word "rice" (*odana*). For the word "rice" does not denote the state of being food through direct primary denotation (*śruti*).
However, it is by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
And the two scriptural passages— “Death is its condiment” and “Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood”— do not deserve to be restricted merely on account of the figurative nature of their enjoyability.
Nor are only the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya intended here, because by means of "death as a condiment" there is the presentation of all living beings;
and it is appropriate to mention the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya among living beings because they are the most prominent.
And because it would be purposeless;
for likewise, the power of destroying all things moving and unmoving belongs to the Supreme Self alone,
not to fire.
Nor does it belong to the individual soul (jīva).

Thus, there will be no abandonment of what is under discussion in the passage, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and the difficulty of knowing [the soul's location] expressed in "Who indeed knows where he is? will be appropriately established.
But since the individual soul (*jīva*) is well-known throughout all the worlds, it is not difficult to understand [that it is not the subject here].
Therefore, it is established that the Eater is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
[The two who have entered the cave are] the two selves, for that is seen [in scripture]. (1.2.3.11)
He states the doubt with the words "therein" (tatra).
He states the purpose of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) as follows:
If [it be argued] that "the intellect and the individual soul" are meant;
[the author] states the purpose of his own established conclusion (siddhānta):
"Now, [if it be argued] that 'the individual soul and the supreme self' are meant."

Thinking that, due to the predominance of the general rule (*autsargika*) and the impossibility of the previously established prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*), another position will be postulated, the objector raises a doubt:
"Here the objector says... *Ṛtam* means truth.
This means that it is necessarily so. He provides the resolution:
"To this, it is said."
Since the context concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), it is impossible to conceive of two other drinkers [besides the Self].

Therefore, in this case, because the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient and the Supreme Self is the one who drinks, the word "drinker" (*pibat*) indicates [the Self] by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) without abandoning its own primary meaning; thus, the sense is that [the verse] refers to the drinking and non-drinking associated with the moving and the unmoving.
Or, let it be taken in its primary sense alone.
Nevertheless, he says "or else" (yadvā) to show that there is no fault:
for agency is characterized by independence, and since that [independence] exists in the one who causes another to drink just as it does in the one who drinks, he too is an agent.
For this very reason, they say: "He who causes another to act, he indeed acts himself.
Likewise, by intending to express the independence of an instrument as well, it may in some sense possess the status of an agent, as in the expression, "the pieces of wood cook."
Therefore, even if [the term] is used in its primary sense, there is no contradiction.
Having thus resolved the doubt, he takes up the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
"The intellect and the knower of the field (buddhi-kṣetrajñau)."
"A fixed substratum is not possible by the power of the intellect;
it is not reasonable to imagine [such a substratum] due to affliction within the all-pervading Supreme Self."

Nor is it appropriate for the word "entered" (praviṣṭa) to be figurative, as in the case of the phrase "the two drinking," because when a primary meaning is possible, a figurative meaning is unjustifiable;
furthermore, the entry into the cave is logically possible for both the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva).

Furthermore, by the phrase "in the world of well-done deeds" (*sukṛtasya loke*), it is stated that there is no transcending the sphere of karma through the established order of the world of well-done deeds.
And both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) have not transcended the sphere of karma;
for the soul stands within the sphere of dharma as the enjoyer, and the intellect as the instrument of enjoyment.
But it is not Brahman,
because [the world] is dependent upon that;
furthermore, "shadow and light" refers to darkness and illumination.
In that regard as well, since there is doubt concerning the deceased, it is stated that the soul which goes to the next world must be shown as distinct from the intellect;

thus, the following view is set forth: "By the drinking of the *ṛta*, the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is determined; its second [companion] is Brahman alone, who is of the same nature, and not the intellect, which is of a different nature. (1.2.3.12)
"Once it is first understood that Brahman has a companion,
its abiding in the cave should be explained last, in order to avoid contradiction.
When it is said, 'The cow has a companion,' it is understood to be another cow of the same species."

But it is not with something of a different genus, such as a horse or the like. Thus, here the conscious individual soul (jīva) is perceived as having a companion that is of the same nature— namely, Brahman, which is itself conscious— and not with the insentient intellect (buddhi), which is of a different nature.

Thus, in this case, since Brahman is first understood from the phrase "the two drinking the *ṛta*," the subsequent mention of its abiding in the cave must be explained in accordance with that [primary understanding], just as Hari is said to abide in the Śālagrāma stone.
For the Śrutis frequently declare that Brahman abides in the cave.
This very point has been stated:
"Because it is seen [in scripture]" means because the fact that this Brahman resides in the cave (guhā) is observed in the Vedas.

And thus, in accordance with the Brahman understood first, its existence in the world of the well-performed (sukṛta) must also be understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), according to the maxim of the umbrella-bearers (chatrinyāya).

Even the relationship between shade and sunlight must be understood as being due to the individual soul (*jīva*) having ignorance (*avidyā*) as its substrate, while Brahman, whose nature is pure light, does not have that [ignorance] as its substrate.

(1.2.3.14) Applying this very same principle to the illustrative example of "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*), he states: "This is the same principle. (1.2.3.15) This is done by way of a hypothetical application (*kṛtvācintā*).

Regarding this point as well, a doubt arises as to whether the two are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), or the individual soul and the supreme self (*paramātman*). Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the intellect and the individual soul are intended here—on the grounds that even though the intellect is an instrument, it may be metaphorically designated as the agent (just as in the expression "the fuel cooks")—the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) must be established. And this final conclusion has been elucidated by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*).
Regarding the phrase "from seeing that," it refers to the mantra: "A person is immersed in the same tree.
Since it is not appropriate to resort to a metaphorical attribution of agency to the instrument when primary agency is possible, another [author] introduces a deliberation on this point by saying:
"Another says..."
"Sattva" means intelligence (buddhi). He raises an objection: "The word 'sattva'... [etc.]
The meaning is that he explains the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the established doctrine (siddhānta). He refutes this, saying: "That is not so."
"By which one sees a dream":
by the word "by which," he teaches the instrument;
and from that, [it follows] a distinct agent, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
"Who is this embodied one who is the witness?

[If it is argued: "Let the meaning of the Brāhmaṇa passage then be that of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of this section, because when there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement, reasoning is merely fallacious"—to this he says:
Nor does it follow the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of this section;
for it would follow the prima facie view of this section only if it were to conclude with the transmigrating individual as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
The meaning is that, since it culminates in the nature of Brahman, it does not even accept the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Furthermore:
"These two... [tāvetau].

"The two—the individual soul (sattva) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)—do not indeed suffer from passion for one who knows thus. Passion means ignorance; "does not cause to fall" means that it does not bring about attachment in one who knows thus. Since the instruction on knowledge concludes with just this much, he says that the purport of this [passage] is perceived to be the identity of the individual soul with Brahman: *na ha vā evaṃvidi raja ādhvaṃsate*. "Passion does not indeed afflict one who knows thus. Passion (*rajas*) is ignorance; "affliction" (*ādhvaṃsana*) means it does not cause [ignorance] to adhere (*saṃśleṣa*) in one who knows thus. By the conclusion of the teaching on knowledge at this very point, it is indicated that the intent of this [text] is the state of the individual soul being the Self of Brahman. Thus he says:
"And by that much" means:
he asks, "But how? to indicate this.
He refutes this, saying: "It is replied—this is not a scriptural statement.
When it is stated that "the individual soul (jīva), not eating, gazes upon Brahman," an objection is raised.
If the individual soul (jīva) does not eat by means of its nature as Brahman, how then is there the cognition of it as an enjoyer?
For the state of being an enjoyer appears as having the same locus as consciousness (caitanya).
To refute that [objection], the Śruti says: "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit.
What is meant by this is as follows: this state of being an enjoyer does not belong to the individual soul (jīva) in reality;

rather, it is the intellect-substance (buddhisattva), which has undergone transformation into the form of pleasure and so forth, and which—as if endowed with consciousness through the falling of the reflection of consciousness—enjoys [the fruit], but the individual soul, who is the Supreme Self, does not enjoy it in reality.
This has already been explained in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*. By this, the discussion of a hypothetical inquiry (*kṛtvācintā*) has been introduced. //12//
"Because of the intermediate position.
[Objection: Is this not already covered by the sūtra "On account of the teaching of its attributes, [it is Brahman] within"?
For indeed, here too there exist attributes of Brahman, such as immortality and fearlessness, which are impossible for a reflection, a living being (jīva), or a deity.
Therefore, because of the instruction on the nature of Brahman, it is Brahman alone that is intended here;
this is also because the word "Brahman" is explicitly employed.
It is said: "The phrase 'this is seen' is used with reference to an object of direct perception."
Brahman is not perceived directly; however, it is appropriate [to perceive it] in its reflection. //1//
"For indeed, because of the force of the initial [introduction], the description of the others was made first according to that very logic; therefore, that [logic] is certainly applied here as well.

For in the passage "the two who drink the Truth," the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) are understood first; consequently, in accordance with that, the entry into the cave and other attributes were explained later.

Therefore, here too, since the person seen in the eye is first understood through direct designation in the words, "This person who is seen in the eye," the attributes such as immortality and fearlessness must be explained in some way as mere praise in accordance with that shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*).
In that context, immortality consists in its remaining for a few moments,
and fearlessness consists in its being insentient.
It is "manhood" because it has the form of a man;
it is "selfhood" because it is the locus of the pupils of the eyes;
and it is "the nature of Brahman" because of its connection with the aforementioned immortality and other qualities.
In this same way, qualities such as being "vāmanī" (the dwarf) and so forth must also be understood as somehow pertaining to praise alone.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "kaṃ ca khaṃ ca" cannot be restricted to the words of the teacher [Uddālaka], as it concerns the fires.
Moreover, the statement "The teacher, however, will tell you the path" refers to a different kind of path.
But it does not intend to refer to what was stated as the remainder.
Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the shadow-person alone is to be meditated upon here;
the individual soul (jīva) and the deity (devatā), however, were merely mentioned for the sake of possibility.
And since this [objection] is not seen here for the purpose of demonstrating another sublation—
because it has already been refuted by the sūtra "On account of the teaching of His attributes within"—
this being the position reached, it is said in reply:
Regarding the phrase "ya eṣa" (who this):
"When two pronoun-words whose referents are not yet established exist,
they become denoters of the object that is proximate [to them]."

Furthermore, the words "person" (puruṣa) and "self" (ātman) are present; and as long as they do not denote their own specific meanings, no portion of meaning can be expressed by the two pronouns. Therefore, how could there be direct perceptibility of that object?

Moreover, the words "person" and "self" naturally refer either to the individual soul (jīva) or to the Supreme Self (paramātman), independently of the pronouns. Nor is there any perception of these two in the eye. Consequently, in accordance with the meaning conveyed by the independent word "person," the phrases "this one who" and "is seen" must be explained as best as possible.

And it has been explained that the use of the term as if [the fact] were already established (*siddhavat*) depends upon the scriptures and so forth, and refers to the subject matter of the injunction for the sake of generating enthusiasm.

The meaning is that for the knower, the very attainment [of the result] through the scripture is presented as if it were a direct perception (*pratyakṣavat*) for the sake of praise, because of its firmness.
Furthermore, only that which is capable of being led, and which is minor, is led [into a different position] by making it conform to what precedes it.

In this case, however, many [qualities] such as immortality (*amṛtatva*) and others cannot be [logically] extended [to the individual soul]. For immortality does not consist merely in abiding for the duration of one's own existence; if that were so, what indeed would not be immortal? Thus, the term "immortal" would be redundant.
Furthermore, fear and fearlessness are attributes of a conscious being and cannot possibly exist in that which is unconscious.
Likewise, qualities such as "leading downward" (vāmanītva) and so forth cannot be attributed to anything other than Brahman.
Moreover, the designation of [Brahman] as being directly perceived has already been established.
This has been stated by the word "because of logical possibility" (*upapatteḥ*). When it is said, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman," a doubt might arise:
"Why is the eye specifically designated as the location for the omnipresent Lord?"
The scripture refutes that [objection]: "Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water upon this [fire], it flows only along the two tracks.
"Tracks" (vartmanī) refers to the locations of the wings.
This is what is meant: for the stainless Lord, a stainless eye alone is the appropriate locus.
This has been stated [in the sūtra]:
"In that same way, it is in accordance with the Supreme Lord," and there is also the teaching of qualities such as being the "receptacle of all blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*) in that Brahman.
It is appropriate and logical, because its meaning is inherently connected [to the object];
however, in the case of reflections and the like, the meaning is not so connected.
The term *vāma* refers to things that are desirable (*vāmanīya*), worthy of being resorted to (*saṃbhajanīya*), beautiful (*śobhanīya*), and the fruits of merit (*puṇyaphala*).
Because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the means by which these desirable things come together and unite (*saṃyanti saṃgacchamānāni*), He is called *saṃyadvāma*.
Since the production of the fruits of merit occurs through Him as the instrument, the fruits of merit unite with Him.
He alone leads the world toward the desirable fruits of merit; thus he is Vāmanī.
He alone is Bhāmanī.
Because he leads the world toward lights (bhānāni), he is Bhāmanī.
This has been stated by the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. //13//
"And because of the designation of place and so forth.
This sūtra is a response to an objection.
He states the objection:
But how so?
For it is observed that the abode of those who dwell therein is vast, just as the ocean is the abode of aquatic creatures.
The meaning of the objection is: "How can the locus of the eye of the Supreme Self be so extremely small, when the Supreme Self is infinitely great?
He provides the answer: "To this it is said."

Those things which have "places" (sthāna) as their first [characteristic] are the "place-and-the-rest" (sthānādi) categories of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Because of the designation of these, the restriction of the omnipresent [Brahman] to a single place is not tenable.
However, its having various places is not like the case of space (nabhas), which has various locations such as needles, loops, and so forth.
Specifically, since those are the respective places for the meditation upon Brahman, its designation by means of them is appropriate. //14//
Moreover, following the context of the subject matter, Brahman alone must be understood here, and not the reflected image, the individual soul (jīva), or a deity; thus says the author of the Sūtras:
"And because of the mention of that which is distinguished by bliss."
Thus, indeed, it is related: Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla. He tended the sacrificial fires for that teacher for twelve years.
And that teacher, having caused the other students to master their sacred study, had them perform the ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*).
The teacher did not initiate that very Upakośala alone; and although he was requested by Upakośala’s wife for his initiation, the teacher disregarded her words and departed on a journey.
Then, the three Fires—whose minds were overcome with compassion—approached Upakośala, who was deeply dejected in spirit but skilled in the service of the sacred fires.
Having approached him, they spoke of the knowledge of Brahman to this faithful and steadfast devotee, saying: "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman.
Then Upakosala said:
"I understand that breath is Brahman."
For that very *sūtrātman* is called "Brahman" because it manifests in the form of Brahman through its possession of manifold powers (*vibhūti*).
However, [the sage says], "I do not understand what is meant by 'Ka' and 'Kha' as Brahman.

Indeed, the pleasure born from the contact of the senses with their objects—which is impermanent and well-known in the world—cannot be Brahman; nor can the ether (*kha*) of the physical elements, which is insentient, be Brahman.
Then the fires replied to him: "That which is indeed *kaṃ* is the same as *kha*; that which is indeed *kha* is the same as *kaṃ*.
Having spoken thus collectively, they each spoke of the knowledge pertaining to their own domain, beginning with: "The earth, fire, food, and the sun," and so forth.
Then they spoke to him again collectively.
"O dear one, this knowledge regarding each of us has been told to you individually, as well as the knowledge concerning our own respective domains;
and previously, we told you collectively the knowledge of the Self, namely, 'Breath is Brahman' and 'Kaṃ-khaṃ is Brahman.
But the Teacher will tell you the way."
"This knowledge of Brahman has been declared by us; however, the destination alone remains unspoken.
Our teacher Jābāla will explain that for the sake of attaining the fruit of this knowledge. Having said this, the fires ceased speaking.
This being the established context, the Commentator explains the passage: "That which is indeed *kaṃ* is the same as *khaṃ*; that which is *khaṃ* is the same as *kaṃ*."
In that context, the phrase "the word *kham*" is used with the intention of referring to a *pratīka*.
A *pratīka* is the superimposition of a cognition belonging to one substratum onto another substratum;
for example, the word "Brahman," which refers to the Supreme Self, is superimposed upon names and so forth.
One might have the notion that "this very thing which is the name is Brahman to be known," or likewise, "this very thing which is the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) is Brahman. However,
this status of being a mere symbol (pratīka) is not intended here.

The means for attaining worldly pleasure are dependent on external factors and are subject to decay; because suffering (*āmaya*) coexists with them, such pleasure is "associated with suffering" (*sāmaya*).
Having thus stated the defect in the case of their separation, he states the merit in the case of their conjunction: "But when distinguished by the former and the latter."
Because their referents have been specified, the two words themselves are also said to be specified.

For the word *kham*, being in grammatical apposition with the word *sukha*, abandons its meaning as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and functions by way of attributing a quality to Brahman. And when *sukha* is qualified by such a *kha*, it becomes free from affliction (*nirāmaya*), excluded from that which is subject to affliction (*sāmaya*).
Therefore, the inclusion of both [terms] is justified.
He states the purpose of the repetition of the word "Brahman" with the words: "Therein, the second..."

The word *brahma* used above the word *kaṃ* constitutes the head; likewise, the word *brahma* is the head of the word *khaṃ*. Those two words, *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*, are thus "Brahma-heads" (*brahmaśirasī*), and their state is "the condition of being Brahma-heads" (*brahmaśirastvam*).
To the question, "Let that be so; what follows for the present context?", he says: "Thus, at the commencement of the discourse...
[Now, one might object: "But let Brahman be pointed out first by the fires."
Regarding the teacher's statement, "That which is this in the eye," why must that very same thing be followed? To this he says:
"But the teacher will tell you the way" (*ācāryas tu te gatiṃ vaktā*) indicates the teaching of the way alone.
Although these two statements have different speakers, they are nevertheless brought into syntactic unity with the preceding speaker.
Because only the goal has been stated.
What is meant is this:
"The knowledge of Brahman has been taught to you by us."
However, the destination for one who knows that [truth] has not been stated; and the Teacher will explain it after completing that which remains slightly deficient in what is to be studied.
Thus, by this, any intention to speak of a different subject matter unconnected with the preceding is precluded.
Then, after the fires had thus instructed him, the teacher returned after some time; having arrived and observed Upakosala, he said:
"My dear, your face shines serene like that of one who knows Brahman."
"Who instructed you?

Upakosala, however, being ashamed and afraid, initially thought, "Who indeed would instruct me while you, O Blessed One, were away? But when pressed, he spoke of the instruction regarding the fires exactly as it was. Having heard that, the teacher, who had been greatly distressed for a long time, his heart becoming tender with compassion toward Upakosala, replied:
"My dear, it is said that the fires did not explain the Brahman to you in its entirety;
therefore, I shall explain it to you in its entirety.
By the greatness of the resulting experience, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this."
When Upakosala had spoken thus, the teacher said to him,
"Let the Blessed One tell me," and the teacher spoke to him, intending to explain the path beginning with light.
In order to fulfill what was stated by the Fires—"Prāṇa is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman"—it is said: "This person is seen in the eye," and so forth.

This is what is meant: those who, under the instruction of their teacher, meditate upon the Bliss that is Brahman, which has its locus in the eye and possesses such qualities as being the "Saṃyadvāma" (the center of blessings), the "Vāmanī" (the leader of blessings), and the "Bhāmanī" (the leader of light), together with Prāṇa—they all become freed from evil, whether they perform other rituals or not.
They reach—that is, they attain—the deity presiding over the light (arciḥ);
from the light, they reach the deity of the day;
from the day, they reach the waxing fortnight, which is the deity of the bright half of the month.
Then, for six months— those months during which the sun moves toward the northern direction— those six months constitute the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); they reach that deity,
and from those months, they reach the deity who is the year (*saṃvatsara*).
From there, one goes to the sun; from the sun, to the moon;
from the moon, to lightning.
There, a certain person— a non-human being born of the non-human creation,
that is to say, one who exists in the world of Brahmā— descending from the world of Brahmā, leads these [beings] to the effected Brahman residing in Satyaloka.

This very path is called the "path of the gods" (*devapatha*) because it is characterized by the gods—the guides consisting of light (*arcis*) and so forth—and it is also called the "path of Brahman" (*brahmapatha*) because it is characterized by Brahman as the goal to be reached.

Those who proceed by this path reach Brahman residing in Satyaloka; they do not return to this human creation of Manu, which is of what nature? It is a whirlpool (*āvarta*), meaning a recurrence of birth, old age, and death; that which performs this recurring cycle is a whirlpool.
The world of Manu does not return;
and so says the Smṛti: "When the time of universal dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā]. (15)
By this explanation of the narrative, the sūtra "And because the path is described for one who has heard the Upaniṣads" (sūtra 3.4.16) is also explained.
"And because of instability and impossibility, it is not the other.
The expression "this which is in the eye," heard as a permanent statement, is not applicable to the shadow-person, which is impermanent.
Furthermore, he says that in this view, the fault of conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) would follow.
Nor is it the case that [meditation] occurs only at the time of worship;
likewise, this applies to the cognitional self (*vijñānātman*) as well.
For meditation upon the cognitional self has never been observed to take place in a specific location other than [the heart].
The meaning is that it was heard there previously from Brahmā; "miṣā" means through fear;
"asmāt" refers to this Brahmā.
The remainder has its meaning not hidden. //17//
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is [Brahman] because His attributes are designated in relation to the divine realm and so forth:
"By means of that [Self], one controls the body acquired through one's own karma as well as other things;
however, a carpenter or the like, being bodiless, cannot possess the status of the Inner Ruler of another Self. (Verse 1)

For an effect characterized by the regulation of activity is observed in an embodied conscious being with respect to its own body, sense organs, and so forth, or with its body with respect to tools such as an axe; it cannot belong to the bodiless Brahman.
Indeed, a sprout of a *vaṭa* tree never arises from a *kuṭaja* seed. By this, it should be understood that the [sūtra] "from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" is also refuted.
Therefore, since the Supreme Self, being devoid of a body, senses, and so forth, cannot be the inner ruler (antaryāmin), the inner rulership must belong either to the Pradhāna,
or to a deity possessing conceit regarding the earth and other elements, or to a yogin endowed with powers such as atomization (aṇimā), or to the individual self (jīvātman). In this regard,
although the Pradhāna possesses the qualities of not being seen, not being heard, not being thought, and not being known, [the following applies].

Nevertheless, because that insentient [pradhāna] lacks the qualities of seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing which are mentioned in scripture, and because it is not the Self, the scriptural statement "This is your Self" would be untenable; thus, the pradhāna cannot be the Inner Ruler (antaryāmin).
Even though the deity who presides over the earth and other elements possesses the nature of a Self, [the pradhāna does not].
Furthermore, qualities such as being unseen are compatible with qualities such as being a seer, because of the connection with a body, sense organs, and so forth,
as evidenced by scriptural passages such as: "For whom the earth itself is the abode, fire the world, and the mind the light."

Nevertheless, because that [soul] is restricted by its own specific determination, it is untenable [to claim it is the universal ruler], as it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "He who rules all worlds from within," and "He who rules all beings from within.

As for the yogin, although he is indeed capable of ruling all worlds and all beings—since he can assume various kinds of bodies, senses, and so forth in different places, as evidenced by scriptural texts such as, "He becomes onefold; he becomes threefold"—[the universal ruler must be distinct].

Nevertheless, according to the principle to be stated later—"excluding the activity regarding the world, because of the context"—since there is an absence of activity for those who have attained knowledge with respect to the realm of modifications, he too cannot be the Inner Controller (antaryāmī).

Therefore, by the method of exhaustion (pāriśeṣya), it must be the individual soul (jīva) alone who is the conscious one, possessing a body, senses, and so forth, endowed with the capacity for seeing and other such functions, yet himself invisible and so on, because of the contradiction of an action directed toward oneself;
and he is immortal, because he does not perish even upon the destruction of the body, senses, and so forth.

Otherwise, due to the absence of enjoyment of fruits in the next world, there would follow the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).

Furthermore, in the passage "He who dwells in the self," although there is non-difference, a distinction is figuratively attributed in some way, as in the statement, "In what, O Blessed One, is he established? In his own glory.
And the phrase "whom the self does not know" intends to express the contradiction of [an action] operating upon itself.
And all such passages as "whose body is the self" (yasyātmā śarīram) should be interpreted in the same manner as [the passage] "in his own majesty" (sve mahimni).

Furthermore, if there were a controller or knower other than the Self who is itself the controller, then there would be an infinite regress, as there would have to be yet another controller for that one as well.
Moreover, the status of the individual soul (jīva) as the controller of all beings in the world occurs only through the medium of its unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa).
For it is through this means—namely, that dharma and adharma acquired by him restrain [the body]—that the individual soul (jīva) restrains [the body].
And the singular number is used with reference to the genus.
Therefore, the inner ruler (antaryāmī) is indeed the individual self (jīvātman).
"It is not the Supreme Self.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "In the case of the regulation of the body, senses, and so forth, he has no other body or senses;
if that [body] is acquired through his own karma, then the world is acquired through ignorance (avidyā)."
In the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas, it is understood that the venerable Supreme Lord—who is omniscient and omnipotent—is the source (yoni) of the universe.
This cannot be denied by a fallacious inference based on the common experience of ordinary people that contradicts scripture.

Thus, the entire collection of modifications is a transformation of His power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti), which exists in the place of His body and senses; and through the respective effects and instruments of the deities of earth and so forth, He is able to bring about those very deities of earth and so forth.
It is not to be restrained,
nor is there an infinite regress;
for no other restrainer is restrained by it.

However, it has been stated repeatedly that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the controller established by worldly consensus, is in fact the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself, described as such through the distinction imagined by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
therefore, how could there be another controller, and how could there be an infinite regress?
Thus, even scriptural passages such as "There is no other seer but He" become consistent in their meaning.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no knower other than the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), because no other individual self (*jīvātman*) exists as a seer. However, the scriptural texts concerning the distinction between the knower and the known, as well as the means of valid cognition such as perception, have their basis in the distinction between the individual self and the supreme self (*paramātman*) as constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
There is the experience of saṃsāra and the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions;
and in this way, the recognition of the one Inner Ruler (antaryāmin) alone within the divine and other realms becomes consistent.

In the passages "He who [rules] all worlds" and "He who [rules] all beings," the use of the singular pronoun "he" (yaḥ) is appropriate; furthermore, immortality is fitting only in the Supreme Self and not elsewhere.
Moreover, in such passages as "He who dwells in the self," there will be no need for the cumbersome resort to figurative attribution of difference where there is actually non-difference.
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) and not the individual soul (jīva) or other such entities.
That which begins with "He who [dwells] in the earth" and ends with "in the thundercloud" refers to the divine realm (adhidaiva).
That which begins with "He who [dwells] in all worlds" refers to the world-realm (adhiloka).

"He who [is present] in all the Vedas" refers to that which pertains to the Vedas (adhideva). "He who [is present] in all sacrifices" refers to that which pertains to sacrifice (adhiyajña). "He who [is present] in all beings" refers to that which pertains to beings (adhibhūta).
The internal self (adhyātma) extends from the vital breath (prāṇa) to the self (ātman).
Since the term "perception" (saṃjñā) is not well-established [in this context], the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is merely an introductory statement. //19//
Because activity toward the agent of actions such as seeing is contradictory;
that is to say, because activity toward the self, which is the agent, is contradictory. //20//
[The Self] possesses qualities such as invisibility because of the declaration of its attributes. Now, that higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is attained— that which is invisible,
being beyond the range of the sense organs of cognition.
It is ungraspable, being beyond the range of the organs of action;
it is without lineage, being devoid of a cause;
it is without color, being free from such qualities as being a Brahmin and so forth.
It is not only that the objects of the senses do not exist for him;
he states further that even the senses themselves do not exist for him by saying,
"without eyes or ears."
It indicates the sense organs by the phrase "without hands or feet";
it refers to the organs of action.
It is eternal, all-pervading, and extremely subtle because it is difficult to discern.
This may be so;
[one might ask] whether that which is eternally existent is a changing eternal. He says "no"—it is immutable (*avyaya*).
The meaning is that it is immutably eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*).
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) or illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is observed only for that which possesses a similar nature (*sarūpa*);
however, a similarity between the conscious self (*cidātman*) and insentient things (*jaḍa*) is not possible. //1//
Therefore, let it be understood that the insentient *pradhāna* alone is the source (*yoni*) of the world.
If the word "source" (*yoni*) means a "causal agent" (*nimitta*), then why should the individual soul (*jīva*) be rejected?
For all observed transformations are seen to be of the same nature as their transforming substrates.
Just as the threads produced from the transformation of a spider's saliva are of the same nature as that [spider],
so too transformations (vivarta) are indeed of the same nature as that which exists [the substrate] and not of a different nature;
just as the transformations of a rope, such as a snake or a stream, are of the same nature as the rope.
People never mistake a rope for an elephant,
nor does a spider's thread undergo a transformation into gold.
For what reason is that?

Because of their absolute dissimilarity. Therefore, it is logical that the Pradhāna alone, being insentient, is the source of the insentient world. That which is "unheard" regarding its own transformations is the Imperishable (akṣara).
Furthermore, the statement "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" is a description of that which is higher than the high Imperishable.
This is because of the scriptural text: "Higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme.
Indeed, other than the Pradhāna, no other "Imperishable" (akṣara) is possible that exists beyond the Supreme Self and beyond the entire collection of its evolutes.
Therefore, that Supreme Self who is higher than the Pradhāna is the All-Knowing One.
The source of beings is indeed the Imperishable (akṣara), which is none other than Pradhāna;
let that be exactly as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.
Now, if you are not satisfied with that because it lacks authoritative proof, [then consider this:]

Let it be, then, that the unmanifest subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which is the potentiality of the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), is the *pradhāna*, for by it the modifications are produced. Indeed,
that which is insentient and indefinable is fit to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the indefinable, insentient world-process (*prapañca*), because of their similarity.

Is it not the case that the conscious self (cidātman) is inexpressible, for it is indeed formless? The commentary stating "of non-conscious things" is intended to establish a similarity [between the self and those things].
It might be argued:
"Since this too is almost certainly refuted by the very refutation of the Smārta [view] as the primary one, why then is there any doubt regarding it? To this, he says:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it was not seen previously":
the meaning is that while this [principle] is not resorted to when there is a subverting argument (bādhaka), here, however, no such subverting argument exists.

Therefore, in passages such as "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), let the status of Brahman as the source of the world be understood figuratively, by virtue of its being the substratum for the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*).

But here, since the power of ignorance itself can be the source of the world, it is not appropriate to posit the relationship of the medium and the mediated; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) alone that is called the source of the world in this sentence.

Alternatively, even if the word "source" (*yoni*) refers to an efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), there is still no decisive reason to conclude that Brahman alone is the efficient cause and not the individual soul (*jīvātman*); thus, due to this doubt, the prima facie view is maintained.

To this it is replied: "Having first stated that the Imperishable is the source of the universe, that [source] is subsequently declared to be omniscient by the Śruti text beginning with 'He who is all-knowing'. (1)

Therefore, due to the commonality of the description and because of recognition, it is clear that the syllable (akṣara), which is the source of the universe and the omniscient one, cannot be insentient. //2//
The scriptural passage "beyond the Imperishable" (akṣarāt parataḥ) is considered to refer to the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta).
Because it has not manifested its own effects, it is therefore called the "Imperishable" (akṣara).
There is nothing here that is even slightly obscure.

As for the claim that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the conscious self (*cidātman*) due to the absence of similarity (*sārūpya*), that is certainly true; however, this phenomenal world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) from Brahman, which is non-transforming.
"Arising from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it does not depend upon similarity [with an external object].
(1) Indeed, there is no restrictive reason to maintain that every error is necessarily based on similarity with an external object;
for various errors are observed to arise even from internal mental faults—such as desire, anger, fear, insanity, and dreams—which do not depend upon similarity.
Furthermore, while such an inquiry is appropriate regarding an error concerning a cause because of its absence,
one who has fallen into the stream of beginningless ignorance and its latent impressions does not deserve such inquiry.
Therefore, since the phenomenal world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the Supreme Self, that Self is its source.
Like a snake [appearing] through the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of a rope, [the world] has that [Brahman] as its source, but not through its transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Therefore, from the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the statement regarding omniscience—which is an attribute of that [Brahman]—it is Brahman alone that is taught as the object of knowledge in the passage, "That which is invisible... and so forth.
Thus it is established that neither Pradhāna nor the individual soul (jīvātman) is the object of meditation.
This is not only known from the internal indicative marks (liṅga), but also from the designation (samākhyā) "higher knowledge" (parā vidyā); thus he says:
"Moreover, there are two kinds of knowledge."
He states another inferential mark:
"In whom, O venerable one?
[This refers to] enjoyments, which are objects of enjoyment, and the enjoyer who is distinct from them.
For the individual soul (jīvātman) is indeed limited and distinct from the objects of experience; therefore, by the knowledge of it, everything is not known.
He states another designation:
"Moreover, he [instructed him] in that knowledge of Brahman which is the foundation of all knowledge."
"For these eighteen forms of sacrifice are indeed rafts, unstable.
They are called "rafts" because they float away—that is, they are non-enduring;
for this very reason, they are unstable.
What are those whose form is sacrifice? "Form" (rūpa) means that by which something is formed;
those for whom sacrifice is the form—that is, the limiting adjunct (upādhi)—are "those whose form is sacrifice."
These sixteen, however, are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
since the term *ṛtvij* is applied by way of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of performing the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu-yajana*), the priests have the sacrifice as their limiting condition.
In the same way, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) also has the sacrifice alone as his limiting condition.
Likewise, the wife [is included], according to the Smṛti rule: "The word *pati* [is used] for the husband when joined with sacrifice.
These eighteen are the forms of sacrifice, in which—the officiating priests and others—the performed action is called sacrifice.
The meaning is that it is the substratum of sacrifice;
and that action is inferior because its fruits, such as heaven, are inferior.
They go to, that is, they attain [it].
This is because the intended meaning of what was stated—that [the property] is not [present] in both the example and the thing exemplified—is as follows. //21//
"And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is not the other two.
He explains the reason through the term "distinction" (viśeṣaṇa) with the words:
"For [the scripture] distinguishes..."
The mention of "from the embodied one" (śārīrāt) is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood as "from the primal matter" (pradhānāt).
He explains the designation of difference:
"Likewise, [the same applies] even from the Pradhāna.
This might be so;
what is this Pradhāna favored by the Sāṃkhyas that is based on scripture?
And so that many things may be consistent, he says: "In this context, there is no such thing as a 'pradhāna' (primordial matter). //22//

And because of the presentation of form (*rūpopanyāsāt*). Having explained this through the objections and resolutions according to the view of another, he explains it according to his own view: "Others, however, think... (*anye punar manyante*).
The word "again" (*punar*), by indicating a distinction from what precedes it, suggests that this [view] is the intended one.

Since there is the possibility of [Agni] being born as something falling within the category of those currently being born—possessing forms such as "Fire is the head"—it is not reasonable to assume a status as a creator without cause.
Indeed, this context concerns the birth of Viśvakarman.
If it is argued that proximity (*saṃnidhi*) applies to those things being produced,

and since context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than proximity, one should therefore abandon what is being produced and accept that the description of forms refers only to the source of the universe (*viśvayoni*), who is the subject of the context— we say no,
because it is a contradiction for the subject of the context, who is devoid of body, sense organs, and so forth, to possess a physical form (*vigraha*).

Nor is it correct to say that, because of a conflict with the context (*prakaraṇa*), the scriptural passages concerning the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and so forth must abandon their own literal meaning and be understood as referring merely to the state of being the Self of all; for scripture (*śruti*) is more powerful than context when its meaning is not extremely remote.

Furthermore, the Commentator has stated that being situated within a section dealing with something currently arising is the reason for including [the passage] in the mention of "what is arising," provided that no connection with the subject of the context has been established.
Therefore, it is correct that the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha himself, existing within all beings as the self of the vital breath (prāṇa), is indicated as the effect.
One might ask: "In that case, is the Sūtra then not to be taken into account? He says, "No," [adding]: "In this view..."
Because of the context. //23//
Vaiśvānara [is the Self] because of the specific common term.
Prācīnaśāla, Satyayajña, Indradyumna, Jana, and Buḍila, having come together, conducted an inquiry:
"Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"
When it was said, "The Self," let there be no misconception that it refers to the individual soul (jīvātman); therefore, he asked, "What is Brahman?
Deliberating upon this and failing to reach a certainty, they approached the King of Kekaya, who was a knower of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā. Having approached him, they said:
Having begun with, "You are now studying this very Self as Vaiśvānara; remember it, tell it to us," [the text continues] with "of heaven, sun, wind, ether, water, and earth.
The meaning is this: of the Blessed Lord Vaiśvānara, heaven is the head, which is of excellent luster (*sutejas*).
The eye is the Sun of universal form;
the vital breath is Vāyu, whose path is manifold—Vāyu is "pṛthagvartman" because his course is diverse—and he whose very nature (ātmā) is that [manifold path] is "pṛthagvartmātmā.
The trunk (*saṃdeha*) is the middle portion of the body; it is Space (*ākāśa*), for it is vast due to its omnipresence.
The bladder itself is wealth and water;

since food comes from water and wealth (rayi) comes from food, therefore water is called wealth. And since the bladder is the receptacle for those waters when they have become urine, it is said that "the bladder itself is wealth. The feet are the earth, because it is there that one finds support.

Thus, for those such as Prācīnaśāla and others who, by means of a perverted meditation, worship each individual limb of Vaiśvānara—namely heaven, sun, air, ether, water, and earth—as being respectively the head, eyes, breath, trunk, bladder, and feet of Vaiśvānara, the scripture records their punishments—the falling of the head, blindness, the departure of the breath, the decay of the body, the bursting of the bladder, and the withering of the feet—in order to censure such meditations; and having thereby taught that he is the totality of the head and all other parts, it is declared: "But he who meditates on him thus as the measure of a span, the all-pervading one... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1).
In all the worlds, including heaven and earth;
in all beings, both stationary and moving;
and in all selves—consisting of body, senses, mind, intellect, and the individual soul—food exists.
The meaning is that one obtains the fruit associated with all [the fires].
Now, the Śruti speaks in order to establish the nature of the Agnihotra for this Vaiśvānara, who is the enjoyer of the food:
"The chest itself is the altar," because of its similarity to an altar (vedi).
The body hairs are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), because of their similarity to the strewn sacrificial grass;
the heart is the Gārhapatya fire,
because it follows immediately after the heart.
The mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire,
for it is there that that food is offered as an oblation.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the words "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman" are conventionally established as referring to the Supreme Self in the opening statement, "What is the Self? What is Brahman?", the cognitions colored by those terms would lead one to conclude that words such as "Vaiśvānara" and "Agni" must somehow be interpreted as referring to the Supreme Self alone;
for it is not proper to alter the meanings of the words "Brahman" and "Self," which are first encountered, in accordance with the words "Vaiśvānara" and so forth, which are encountered later.

And although the two words "Self" (ātman) do not occur at the beginning of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā among the Vājasaneyins—in the passage, "Venerable sir, you indeed know Vaiśvānara; tell that to us"—nevertheless, the Chāndogya passage, which has the same meaning, serves as its introduction.
Therefore, the meaning of the Vājasaneyi passage is determined in accordance with that Chāndogya passage whose meaning is already established.
For a passage of uncertain meaning is settled by one of certain meaning, but not by one of uncertain meaning.
And just like ritual action (*karman*), Brahman too is one and the same, being the object of knowledge across all Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, attributes such as having heaven as its head and so forth are not possible for any of the following: the sacrificial fire (*agni*), the deity (*devatā*), or the individual self (*jīvātman*) who has become the sun.
Nor is it possible for any of these to possess the status of being the recipient of the fruit that is the support of all worlds.
And since it has been determined—by the method of elimination—that Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Self alone because he is the burner of all evils, how can there again be this doubt:
"If it be said that [it is not so] on account of [the mention of] sound and so forth, and on account of abiding within"?
It is replied: That very [conclusion] is led otherwise in accordance with the introductory statement (upakrama).
The proponent's intention is that it is impossible to interpret [the terms] otherwise, for the words "Vaiśvānara" and "fire" cannot possibly be interpreted differently. Furthermore,
the qualities of being established within and having the size of a span are not possible for the Supreme Brahman, which is all-pervading and immeasurable.
Furthermore, it is not possible for anything other than the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) to serve as the locus for the oblation of the vital breaths;
nor is it possible for Brahman to possess the nature of the Gārhapatya fire and so forth, or the heart and so forth.
Therefore, Vaiśvānara must be one of these: either the digestive fire, the elemental fire, the deity, or the individual soul (jīva), according to what is appropriate.
But it is not Brahman;
and thus, although the words "Brahman" and "Self" appear at the beginning [of the passage], they must be interpreted otherwise,
and the attributes such as being the "head" and so forth are merely for the sake of praise.

Alternatively, the intention of the objector is that the attributes such as having heaven as the head are possible for a deity whose body is fire, due to its possession of sovereign power (*aiśvarya*).
To this, the reply is: "No."
Why?
Because the teaching is seen to be thus:
indeed, that which is understood last, being otherwise unestablished, sublates what was previously apprehended.
But in this case, there is no finality or necessity [of the literal sense],

because it is possible to explain it either as a figurative instruction— like "the mind is Brahman"— or as an instruction regarding its limiting adjuncts— like "consisting of mind, having prāṇa for a body, having the form of light."

Alternatively, since the words *vaiśvānara* and *agni* denote Brahman through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), there is no possibility of establishing them otherwise. Thus, it is logically consistent that the attributes of *vaiśvānara* and the attributes of Brahman may coexist in Brahman— which is the object of meditation— either by superimposing upon it the gastric fire called *vaiśvānara* as its substrate, or by means of the gastric *vaiśvānara* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
He explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "asaṃbhavāt" (on account of impossibility):
"And if the Supreme Lord were not intended here... He then explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "puruṣamapi cainamadhīyate" (and they also read him as the Puruṣa).
And if it is "only" [the Self],
the meaning is that it is neither by way of being an adjunct (*upādhi*) to Brahman nor by way of being a symbol (*pratīka*).
The sense of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only the Self established within, but the person (*puruṣa*) as well.
Therefore, in the passage "That person who... (*yatpuruṣa*), Vaiśvānara is not being enjoined by referring to the person;
for if that were the case, one would be instructed to view the person as Vaiśvānara.
And thus, it would contradict the Bhāṣya which states: "Indeed, the meditation on the Supreme Lord is here taught with respect to Vaiśvānara in the form of the digestive fire."
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with scripture.

For in the passage, "He who knows this Vaiśvānara Agni as a person, having the form of a person, established within the person," it is the knowledge of Vaiśvānara’s being a person that is restated here, not the knowledge of a person’s being Vaiśvānara.

Therefore, since the word "yat" (which) has its connection with the preceding [phrase], it is logical that in the statement "This Agni Vaiśvānara is that," the instruction regarding the Puruṣa is an instruction of the perception of the Puruṣa therein. //24 // // 25 // // 26 //

For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being (bhūta). For this very reason—meaning, on account of these reasons: its connection with attributes such as having heaven as its head as understood from Śruti and Smṛti; its possession of the fruit of being the support of all worlds; and the sequence of words such as "Brahman" and "the Self that burns away all evils"—the Vedic verse, "He who by his splendor [overspread] the earth and this heaven," does not speak of such greatness for the elemental fire (bhūtāgni), which possesses only the power of heat and light.
Rather, the sense is that it is so by virtue of being a modification of Brahman, and thus possessing its nature. //27//
Jaimini [holds that] there is no contradiction even with the literal sense.

With reference to this construction—wherein the parts of Vaiśvānara, whose self is the three worlds from heaven down to earth, have been superimposed upon the parts of the person from the head down to the chin, thereby conceiving him as "having the form of a person"—it is said: "He who meditates on him as having the form of a person... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1). Thus, it is not meant that he is literally a person.
"One knows it as established within the person.

Here, its "human-likeness" (puruṣavidhatva) is due to the perfection of its parts; and its being "established within the person" is due to its being established within the head and ending at the chin—the parts of the person who is a composite of causes and effects—because those constituent parts reside within the whole.
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration: "Just as a branch on a tree.
The meaning is that a branch, which is established upon the aggregate of branches, trunk, roots, and stem, is included within that [aggregate].
He states another interpretation with the words "or else" (athavā).
"Abiding within" (antaḥpratiṣṭhatva) means being situated in the middle; by this, he indicates its nature as a witness (sākṣitva).
This is what is meant: Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self, the witness of the moving and the unmoving.
He uproots the lingering doubt of the opponent with the words, "And when [this] is ascertained."
Because he is the self of all, the Pratyagātman (the inner self) is Vaiśvānara; or, he is the "Man" (nara) of all (viśva),
because the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) is a modification of him.
All men are his living selves; thus, by that very identity. //28//
"Because of manifestation," says Āśmarathya.

Since it is impossible for [the Lord] to be perceived in His entirety, the Supreme Lord, though infinite, manifests Himself as being only the size of a span (prādeśamātra) for the sake of favoring His worshippers; thus he says:
"Even of that which exceeds all measure."
"Excessive" (*atimātra*) means having transgressed the limit or measure.
It is "for the sake of the lay followers" (*upāsakānām kṛte*),
which is to say, for the purpose of the lay followers.
He states another explanation: "Or in the locations," [sūtras 29 and 30].
"Jaimini [holds that it is] on account of the correspondence.
For the region of the body beginning from the crown of the head and ending at the chin is indeed a span in measure.
It is precisely there that the text, by correlating the limbs of Vaiśvānara—who is the self of the three worlds—with those parts, shows Vaiśvānara to be a span in measure. (3.1.31)
On this very point, the author of the Sūtras states the corroboration from the Jābāla Śruti: "And they record him in this.
In the *Avimukta*—that is, in the individual self (*jīvātman*) whose limitation is imagined through the adjunct of ignorance—he is indeed *Avimukta*.
The Supreme Self is established in that [space], due to their identity (*tādātmya*).
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "By means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*).
However, the relationship of container and contained (*ādhāra-adheya-bhāva*) is based on the distinction imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).
The Varaṇā is the eyebrow. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //32//
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, titled "The Concordance of Non-Explicit Śruti Passages Denoting Brahman as the Object of Meditation.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter: 1.3.1.1.
"The Abode of Heaven, Earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word."
Here, Brahman is introduced as that which is to be known.
In this regard, because it possesses limits and is thus a "bridge," and because of the use of the genitive case [to denote a relation] between them,
the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth can logically be something other than the immortal Brahman at any time.
For in the world, a bridge is seen to be that which spans both banks and, being delimited by those two, holds back the water;

it is not merely a cause of bondage. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying the term "bridge" even to things such as shackles and fetters. Furthermore, Brahman does not experience the state of being a bridge unless it is delimited.
It is not logical to say that Brahman, which is existent, is a "bridge" for the immortal;
nor is there any other immortal apart from Brahman for which it could serve as a bridge.
Furthermore, the use of the genitive case is never observed when there is non-difference;
this is what was stated [in the commentary]:
"because of the scriptural statement, 'This is the bridge to immortality.'"
The construction is: "because of the mention of 'of immortality'.
In that context, it was not explained as being free from duality (viśabdatayā) [in the previous statement], "because of the mention of 'of immortality'";
rather, he explains it as: "because of the mention of 'a bridge' (setu)."

Regarding the term "having a further shore" (*pāravān*): thus, when a bridge possessing a further shore is being referred to as something distinct from immortality (*amṛta*), it would either be the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṃkhyas.
For that indeed, having its limits defined by its own effects, reaches as far as the *puruṣa* (spirit), and is therefore "having a further shore."
And that which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, exists [as Brahman],
because it is their material cause,
and because modifications have the material cause as their abode.
And there exists a self, because the word "self" denotes intrinsic nature (svabhāva), just as in the expression "a lamp whose nature is light.
And its knowledge is conducive to liberation.
For in its absence, there would be no liberation from suffering, because the Puruṣa could not be discerned as distinct from Pradhāna.
If, however, you are not satisfied by this due to a lack of evidence,
then let it be that the unmanifest subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which is the potentiality of the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Because everything stated is logically consistent within that authoritative [scriptural] context;
this too has been indicated by the presentation of the Pradhāna.
However, if one were to instead honor the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth as explicitly stated in the Śruti, [then...]
Therefore, let it be air alone, according to the Śruti: "By air, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together.
Furthermore, if you are still not satisfied even here because of the scriptural teaching of its omniscience regarding that which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
Let it be, then, that the Blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha himself—the omniscient one who is the self of the Sūtras—is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
for in his case, all such things as being limited due to being an effect, and his distinction from the immortal Supreme Brahman, are logically consistent.
This [position] was also indicated by the one who cited the scriptural text: "By the thread of Vāyu, O Gautama."
Therefore, when it has been argued that this [ether] is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, it is stated in reply:
the supreme Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, and not the Pradhāna, the Unmanifest, Vāyu, the embodied soul, or Hiraṇyagarbha.
Why? Because of its own word [in the scripture].
"Because it supports immortality, or because it is the means to attain it, it has the nature of a bridge.
Even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the primary meaning of the word "bridge" is not accepted [as applicable here].

For we do not accept that the term "bridge" (setu) refers to a physical structure made of earth or wood, situated between this shore and the far shore, which is well-known in the world as a supporter of waters—whether it be *pradhāna*, the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), wind, the individual soul (*jīva*), or the *sūtrātman*.
Rather, the word "bridge" must be accepted here as figurative, referring merely to the state of having a far shore.

For us, it will function by abandoning its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) and proceeding solely through its etymological connection (*yoga*) with the mere quality of supporting, excluding the aspect of having a far shore.
The fact that the knowledge of the Self is the means for living beings to attain the state of immortality will be indicated only later [in the text].
Furthermore, the word *amṛta* (immortal) has its primary significance in the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).
Just as in the rule "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one" (*dvyekayordvivacanaikavacane*), the meanings of the words *dvi* and *eka* are duality and unity.
Otherwise, it would have been stated as "in two and one";
this very point has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
"because it is the means to attain immortality."
Thus, both the terms "of immortality" and "the bridge" will be appropriate for Brahman as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.

And here, [the Sūtra] indicates this by the word "from its own term," which refers to the word "Self" (ātman) mentioned repeatedly in the text; by the word "being" (sat) in the phrase "having being as their support"; and by the word "Brahman.
For all these are its own terms.
It might be argued that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— such as "the state of being the abode and the non-abode is all Brahman"— is possible even in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha;
and thus, suspecting that he alone might be the one here who is the bridge to immortality, the author provides the answer by means of a restrictive scriptural statement:
Regarding the phrase "because of hearing about the state of being like a sense-field and its object":
one who has the intention directed toward a modification that is "inexpressible" (anirvācya) is so described;
that is to say, one who conceives of the manifold of difference (bhedaprapañca) as real.
A refutation of that [view] is heard as a fault:
"from death," and "but everything is Brahman."
Whatever is superimposed by ignorance, all that is the absolute Brahman; however, it does not mean that whatever is Brahman is all [of that]. Thus says another.
In this context, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is not described by means of a "bridge" (setu), which would imply having a further shore;
rather, it refers to that knowledge which is proclaimed by the words "know ye," and to that relinquishing of speech expressed by "relinquish speech."
In that context, it is called a "bridge" because it is the means to attain immortality;
and both of these [immortality and the bridge] belong to the one who has gone beyond (pāraga).
Nor is the Self alone—the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—referred to by the pronoun "this" (eṣa) on account of its primacy.
But it is not correct to say that this applies to the release of knowledge and speech;
for it is precisely the cultivation of self-knowledge and the release of speech that are primary as things to be enjoined,
whereas the selves, being substances, cannot be enjoined because they lack causal activity (*avyāpāra*).

Because it is the very activity of that which is to be enjoined which possesses the capacity [to be understood], even a quality (guṇa) is referred to. 1.3.1.2 "On account of the designation of being approached by those who are liberated" (muktopasṛpyavyapadeśāt): The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is designated as that which is to be approached by those freed from defects such as ignorance, in passages such as, "The knot of the heart is untied," and so on.
Therefore, that [passage] has as its object only the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Furthermore, that Brahman is to be approached by the liberated is well-known from another scriptural text, such as "When all are utterly released," and so on.
Therefore, because it is to be approached by the liberated.
It is determined that Brahman is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
and the "knot of the heart" consists of ignorance, passion, hatred, fear, and delusion—
wherein delusion is despondency and sorrow.
That Brahman which is superior to Hiraṇyagarbha and inferior to none is described as such;
"in that Brahman" means in that vision which is seen therein, or for the sake of that [vision],
just as in the expression "one kills the leopard for its skin," it is understood to be for the sake of the skin.
The phrase "the desires that reside in his heart" intends the sun of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-āditya*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*);
by the word "desires," it indicates ignorance. (1.3.1.3)
"Because there is no such word, it is not inference.
The phrase "it is not inference" is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood as "it is not unmanifested (avyākṛta)."
Because the reason is the same in both cases. 1.3.1.4. *praṇabhṛt* (the breath-bearer) also [is not a name].
By the word "also" (*ca*), the reason—that it does not consist of those words—is drawn forward.
And the author of the commentary himself states the reason for this here:
"Nor [is it possible] for that which is delimited by limiting adjuncts.
This does not properly hold.
The meaning is that it is not direct.
For it is problematic [to claim] that being a basis consists in being an object of enjoyment.
This might be so:
If the reason "because of the absence of that word" is also to be drawn over here [into the previous rule], then alas, why was a separate rule formulated?
Why was not a single rule—"not in the case of inference based on the vital breath"—made instead? To this, he says:

Regarding the word "separately" (*pṛthak*): by the statement beginning with "because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśāt*), it is indeed the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*) that is negated,
not the *pradhāna*.
And that [knowledge] would be difficult to comprehend if it were presented as a single unified practice. (Sūtra 4) 1.3.1.5. Because of the context:
Indeed, when Hiraṇyagarbha and others are known, everything is not thereby known; rather, it is only when Brahman is known. (Sūtra 6) 1.3.1.7. Because of the topic. (Sūtra 7)
And because of abiding and eating:

if the individual soul (jīva) or Hiraṇyagarbha were the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, then the mention of the Supreme Self in the passage, "While not eating, another looks on," would result in being rendered accidental.
Nor is Hiraṇyagarbha indifferent,
for he too is an enjoyer;
nor is the individual soul (jīvātman) alone the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
That being the case, it must be said that it is precisely that [Brahman] which is being discussed here; and for the sake of discussing that, Brahman is also mentioned,
otherwise even in the final conclusion (siddhānta), the discussion of the individual self (jīvātman) would be arbitrary.

For it is well said that the Veda, by its very nature of making known objects not previously understood, teaches the transcendent Brahman—which is absolutely unknown—to bring about the realization of the individual self (jīvātman) as established among all living beings;
this is so even according to the interpretation provided by the Paiṅgi Upaniṣad.

For there, in the passage "One eats while the other looks on," the individual self is shown to be non-enjoying and indifferent, possessing the essential nature of Brahman in its form devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
For that very reason, it was stated that the insentient *buddhi-sattva* possesses a non-ultimate status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).

Thus, by this scriptural passage describing the *jīva* in such a manner, it is shown that Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, and the *jīva* as delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is thereby refuted.
The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the *Pauṅgi-brāhmaṇa*.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of elaboration" (*prapañcārtham*): the meaning is that this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been undertaken as a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*), on the grounds that [the subject] was not recited among those [texts]. //7// 1.3.2.8.
The Infinite [is Brahman] because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith (saṃprasāda).

Indeed, the divine seer Nārada, considering himself pitiable because he was knowledgeable in ritual action but ignorant of the Self, approached the blessed Sanatkumāra—a knower of the Self, perfected from birth, and a great yogi.
Having approached him, he spoke:
"O Blessed One, may the Blessed One ferry me across to the further shore of the ocean of sorrow born from the lack of knowledge of the Self.
Having heard that, Sanatkumāra said, "Worship Name as Brahman. Thereupon Nārada asked: "Is there anything greater than Name?"
In that regard, Sanatkumāra’s reply is: "Speech, indeed, is greater than name.

Thus, in this manner, through the dialogue between Nārada and Sanatkumāra concerning what is greater, having begun with the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*), the inquiry culminates in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), proceeding through the mind (*manas*), volition (*saṃkalpa*), thought (*citta*), meditation (*dhyāna*), discernment (*vijñāna*), strength (*bala*), food (*anna*), water (*āpa*), fire (*tejas*), air (*vāyu*), space (*ākāśa*), memory (*smṛti*), hope (*āśā*), and heaven (*svarga*).

Discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done is *saṃkalpa*; its cause is the mind (*citta*), which consists of the investigation of antecedent and subsequent objects, causes, and purposes;
*smara* is recollection.

Having described the preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— by way of its distinction as the agent and fruit of all actions, its identity with the father and others, its being the hub of the spokes of the chariot, and its being the support of all—

and having stated that it is greater than the entire expansion beginning with Name because one who perceives the greatness of the *prāṇa* is an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādin*), Sanatkumāra, even though not asked by Nārada, spoke in a single continuous passage: "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker who exceeds by means of Truth (*satya*)."
Having taught [the categories] beginning with truth and ending with action, [Sanatkumāra] instructed: "But happiness alone is what one should desire to understand.

Upon hearing that, Nārada said, "O Venerable One, I desire to understand happiness alone. Thereupon, Sanatkumāra began by stating, "That which is the Infinite (bhūman) is happiness," and proceeded to explain the Infinite with the words, "Where one sees nothing else," and so forth.
An inquiry is now commenced regarding such a subject.
In this regard, there is a doubt: could the *prāṇa* be the *bhūman*, or rather, the Supreme Self?

The Commentator has stated that the seed of this doubt is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) intended to express the identity between the state (*bhāva*) and that which possesses the state (*bhavitṛ*).

In this context, that which is stated more extensively than what has already been said in this sequence of texts is here called "the further explanation" (bhūyaḥ), and it is presented preceded by a question.
Nor was it asked, "What is greater than prāṇa? nor was it replied, "The bhūman is indeed greater than this.
