Therefore, since the bhūman is being mentioned immediately after the statement regarding the superiority of prāṇa, without having been asked about, it must belong to prāṇa itself.

Furthermore, since a state (*bhāva*) cannot be defined without an agent (*bhavitṛ*), it requires such an agent; and because the intellect (*buddhi*) is in immediate proximity to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the term "state" finds its fulfillment by reaching that very intellect as the agent. This is analogous to the case in the passage, "If both sacrificial oblations (*havis*) should meet with ruin (*ārti*)," where the word "ruin" refers to the ruined oblation.
As they say: "We tolerate the qualification by means of the oblation.
Nor is it logical that, because the Self is the subject under discussion, the Self itself should reside in the intellect and thus the "plurality" (bhūman) would belong to that [intellect] alone;
for Sanatkumāra said, "Worship Name as Brahman."

For, since the answer in the form of a figurative instruction (pratīkopadeśa) has Nārada’s question as its object, there is no occasion for a separate section on the instruction regarding the Supreme Self (paramātman). Furthermore, if the answer did not have that as its object, there would be a lack of correspondence between the question and the answer, resulting in the consequence of invalidity due to inconsistency.
Therefore, in the absence of such a context, it is logical that the "Bhūman" refers to the vital breath (prāṇa) because of its immediate proximity.
Thus, since the author of the Bhāṣya has indicated the argument for the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by pointing out this very seed of doubt, it is not redundant.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that Nārada sought to know only the Supreme Self (paramātman) through repeated questions,
because his inquiry ceased immediately after the instruction regarding the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus, since it is established that *prāṇa* alone is the *bhūman*, whatever statement appears to be in contradiction with that must be interpreted in accordance with it;
and this has already been done by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*).
This might be so.

But as for the phrase, "However, he indeed speaks beyond [the ordinary]," since it distinguishes the speaker of the beyond from the one who sees the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of the word "however" (tu) while declaring that one speaks beyond through Truth, how could it then assert the abundance (bhūman) of the vital breath?
To this, he says: "But [he speaks beyond] only through the vital breath," and thus the status of being a speaker of the beyond belongs to the one who sees the vital breath.
The meaning is that it transcends everything from name up to hope, and thus possesses the quality of being "speech.
This is what is intended: this word *tu* (but) does not exclude the state of being a "speaker of the vital breath" (*prāṇātivāditva*);

rather, without abandoning that state of being a speaker of the vital breath, it actually draws it along, for the sake of realizing that very same vital breath which is Truth, through hearing, reflection, faith, steadfastness, and practice.

"One speaks beyond the truth for the sake of certainty" refers specifically to the *prāṇa-vrata* (the vow regarding the vital breath) as "speaking beyond"; the word "but" (*tu*) excludes the status of being a "speaker beyond" with respect to name and so forth.
One who speaks beyond is not merely one who speaks beyond name and the rest up to hope (*āśā*).
Moreover, it means one who speaks with truth as their life-breath and is beyond all extremes.

In this context, the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the truth occurs through scripture (*āgama*) and the instruction of the teacher (*ācāryopadeśa*). Then, reflection (*manana*) is the application of reasoning that is not in contradiction with scripture.
Having understood [the truth] and having deliberated with his teacher, disciples, and fellow students who are free from envy, he places his faith in it.
Immediately following that faith, the one who perceives other objects becomes detached from them and turns away from them to practice the cultivation of the knowledge of reality;
this is his action, his effort (*prayatna*).
Now, when there is steadfastness in the practice of the knowledge of reality, immediately after which the realization of reality as direct experience manifests—
this is the external [means].

Some have said: "The knowledge of the yogin arises from the culmination of the intensification of the meditation on the real object (*bhūtārtha*). Here, the culmination (*paryanta*) of the intensification of meditation means its final limit; from that, the experience of reality (*tattvānubhava*) is born.

Therefore, when it is argued that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the *bhūman*, the following is stated: after saying, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly through Truth (*satya*)," the *bhūman* is described.
In this context, the word "Truth" has a conventional usage established in the sense of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); thus, by means of the Scripture (*śruti*), it denotes the ultimate reality.

And the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is none other than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For everything else, being a collection of modifications (*vikāra*), is unreal; it is called "true" only in some sense and in relation to something else. Thus, the Śruti declares that Brahman alone is the "supreme speaker" (*ativādin*), independent of anything else: "But he indeed speaks supremely who speaks supremely by means of Truth."

How can that which has been understood as stronger than the indicative mark (liṅga) and so forth be explained in any way as referring to the vital breath (prāṇa) merely on the basis of proximity (saṃnidhāna)— a factor that is exceedingly weak when compared to direct statement (śruti) and the rest?
And thus, since it is understood to reside in Brahman after the vital breath, it cannot possibly have the vital breath as its object.
However, [the teaching] is of the True Supreme Self alone.

Thus, Sanatkumāra— possessing the intention, "In response to the question of Nārada, who does not know the Self and desires to know the Self, I shall explain to him the Supreme Self alone"— proceeds by the logic of ascending a staircase, beginning from the gross and explaining each successive stage, because the Infinite (bhūman) is exceedingly difficult to comprehend.

He elucidated this most subtle point through an easily understood commentary, demonstrating that there is no rule requiring every answer— though it may follow in the flow of a preceding question— to necessarily be preceded by a question; furthermore,
he explained the succession of means for attaining knowledge, such as reflection, faith, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the section concludes with that much alone following the instruction regarding the end of life, the dependence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) on anything else would not be stated;
for if that were mentioned, the section would not be concluded due to the resulting state of expectancy.
Therefore, this is not a section concerning the vital breath itself, but rather concerning that upon which the vital breath depends.
And since that [self] is the "Self," the context concerns the Self alone; he raises an objection:
"At the end of the context."
The meaning is: "at the conclusion of the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).
He refutes [this objection] with the words: "No, O Venerable Sir."
For, by the logic of the tongs (*saṃdaṃśanyāya*), this section belongs to the eyebrows;
and since that [pair] is the vital breath (*prāṇa*),
this section would belong to the vital breath.
And that [position] has been declared to be incorrect. 1.3.2.9.
Not only is the identity of the Supreme Self with the *bhūman* established by scripture (*śruti*), but also by an indicative mark (*liṅga*); thus says the author of the Sūtras:
And because of the logical consistency of the doctrine (*dharmopapatti*).
Having restated that which was somehow interpreted by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), the author of the Commentary refutes it: "As for that [state] in the condition of deep sleep... and so forth.
In the state of deep sleep, it is the self alone that is dissociated from the senses and so forth,
not the vital breath (prāṇa),
because this occurs within the context of the Supreme Self.
"Afflicted" means perishable; the rest is self-evident. //9// 1.3.3.10.
"The Imperishable (akṣara), because it supports that which has the sky as its limit.
The word "akṣara" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "phonemes" (*varṇa*) by virtue of its well-known collective usage;
however, with respect to the Supreme Self, it is etymological (*yaugika*), based on the meaning of its constituent parts.
Furthermore, since the established meaning of a whole is stronger than the established meaning of its parts, the phonemes themselves are the syllable (*akṣara*).
Nor is it untenable for space to be woven warp and woof within the phonemes,
because every manifested form consists essentially of name.
For every form is experienced as permeated by a name, such as "this is a cow" or "this is a tree"; yet,
because it serves as a means [to realization], that permeation cannot ultimately exist.
For the cognition of fire based on smoke does not apprehend fire as conjoined with smoke— such that one thinks, "This smoke is fire"—
but rather apprehends fire as distinct from smoke, in the form "Fire [is] from smoke. However, there does occur a cognition of a visible form conjoined with a name, such as "This is Ditttha."
Furthermore, even in the case of a cognition of a form that does not depend on words—such as that produced by the sense organs and their marks—the non-separation from names is observed.
Therefore, the elements beginning with earth and ending with the sky are permeated by names and pierced by them;
and names themselves have the syllable *oṃ* as their essence, because they are pervaded by it.
As the scripture states: "Just as all things are pierced by a pin, so all speech is [pervaded] by the syllable Om.
Therefore, it follows that the earth and the rest, up to the ether, consist of the syllable Om; thus, the phonemes alone are the Imperishable (akṣara), not the Supreme Self.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the Imperishable is indeed the Supreme Self alone.
But it is not the letters;
why?
Because they sustain everything up to the end of space.
Indeed, the elements beginning with earth, ending with space, are not capable of sustaining colors;
rather, it is the Supreme Self alone,
because they are transformations of that Supreme Self.
Nor is it logical that the thing to be designated (rūpadheya) is identical in nature to the name (nāmadheya),
because of the difference in their intrinsic natures and the difference in their means [of apprehension].
There is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

To explain: names, which consist of the universal *śabdatva* (wordness), are perceived as being graspable by the auditory organ, having as their causal efficiencies the denotation and the cognition [of the object].

However, physical objects such as jars and cloths, which consist of universals such as *ghaṭatva* (jar-ness) and *paṭatva* (cloth-ness), are perceived distinctly as being ungraspable by the visual and other sense organs, yet possessing causal efficiencies such as holding honey or providing clothing.
Thus, how could there be a confusion of names?
Nor is there a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "this is Ḍittha.
Indeed, there is no experience [of the form] that "this physical mass is of the nature of the word."
However, that aggregate which is merged with various places and times is what is meant by "proximate place and time.

As for the name (saṃjñā), because of extreme familiarity, it is remembered as being directed toward the appearance of the aggregate itself, having arisen through the simultaneous awakening of latent impressions (saṃskāra) once the relationship [between the name and the object] has been grasped.
As they say: "In that case, the remembrance of the name is not caused by anything else."
For it is the physical form itself, when perceived, that is capable of causing the recollection of the name. //1//
"For even when a name is being remembered, it does not subvert the perceptual nature [of the object];
for that name stands apart from the named thing and is incapable of obscuring its form. (Verse 2)

Furthermore, there is no worldly consensus regarding the term "syllable" (akṣara) or "word" (pada) referring to a non-worldly entity called *sphoṭa* that is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*). Nor will it be demonstrated later on that this [theory] is authoritative; we have already explained this in our *Tattvabindu*.

Therefore, since it is impossible for letters— which are perceivable by the ear— to support everything up to the sky, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is the Imperishable (akṣara), by means of the etymological derivation of its parts (avayava-prasiddhi) which overrides the conventional meaning of the whole (samudāya-prasiddhi).

As for those who, having proposed the Pradhāna as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), establish with this Sūtra that the Imperishable is indeed the Supreme Self, they must explain how the Pradhāna is refuted by the phrase "because of supporting everything up to the sky" (ambarānta-dhṛti).
Now, even if "support" (*dhṛti*) does not consist merely in being a locus, the phrase "because of the support of everything up to the ether" would still be redundant;
one should have simply said, "the Imperishable [is Brahman] because of its presiding" (*praśāsanāt*).
For by this much alone, the refutation of the Pradhāna is established.
Therefore, its meaning is precisely the negation of being composed of letters and phonemes.

Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of doubt regarding the letters because the negations such as "not gross" would be untenable if grossness and so forth were never attributed to them;
for negations do not necessarily require a prior attribution [of the thing being negated].
Because we observe permanent restatements (*nityānuvāda*) even with respect to things that have not been previously established;
for example, "neither in the intermediate space nor in heaven" is a restatement of the prohibition regarding the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*).
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial. //10// 1.3.3.11.
And that [Brahman] is [the cause] because of its presiding over [the world].
Presiding means commanding; this is an attribute of a conscious being and cannot belong to the unconscious *pradhāna* or to the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*).
The sense is that when the primary meaning is possible, it is not appropriate to resort to a figurative sense, as in the expression "the bank wishes to fall. //11// 1.3.3.12.

And because of the exclusion of other entities: the Śruti, beginning with "That indeed, O Gārgī, is this imperishable," completely excludes the existence of any other entity— whether it be the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth, or the phonemes (varṇa), or primordial matter (pradhāna), or the unevolved (avyākṛta)— from that Imperishable which supports everything up to the ether.
By this very scripture, the imperishability of the individual soul (jīva) is also negated; therefore, he says "likewise" (tathā).
For by the scriptural passage beginning with "not other" (nānyat), the difference between the Self [and the Supreme] is prohibited.

And thus, the meaning is that the individual souls (jīvas), though differentiated by the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), are shown to be non-different because their non-difference is declared.
For this reason also, he states "without eyes" (acakṣuṣkam) to show that the term "Imperishable" (akṣara) does not refer to the embodied soul (śārīra).

The meaning is that the Śruti, by negating the adjuncts such as the eye for the Imperishable (akṣara), denies the state of being the Imperishable to the individual soul (jīva) which is conditioned by those adjuncts.
Therefore, since it is impossible for the phonemes, the unevolved (avyākṛta), or the individual soul to be [the subject],
and possible for the Supreme Self, [it must be the latter].
It is established that the Imperishable (akṣara) is indeed the Supreme Self. 1.3.4.13.
"Because of the designation of it as the object of the act of seeing, it is He.
[This is so] because the fruit is the attainment of the world of the effected Brahman, and because there is a difference in meaning.
Through both vision and meditation, the lower Brahman is attained as the object of meditation.

Based on the Vedic scripture, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," when one attains the state of that [Brahman] through the knowledge of the omnipresent Supreme Brahman, it would not be logical for there to be an attainment of a specific location, as in the text, "He is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman.
Therefore, it is the lower Brahman alone that is enjoined here as the object of meditation.
Nor can it be argued that because the act of seeing is well-known in the world as having reality as its object, it must therefore refer to the Supreme Brahman.
And because it has the same object as the root *dhyai*,
it is correct to say that meditation (*dhyāna*) has the Supreme Brahman as its object;
however, this is not so, because the fact that they have the same object is unproven.
For the higher person is the object of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while that which is even higher than the high is the object of direct vision (*darśana*).
Furthermore, not every instance of vision has reality (*tattva*) as its sole object.
For that [seeing] is observed even with respect to an unreal object;
nor is it correct to say that "seeing" is "reflection," and that [reflection] has only reality as its object.
This is because reflection (*manana*) is taught as being distinct from that [hearing] in various places;
furthermore, even reflection—which is synonymous with reasoning (*tarka*)—does not necessarily have reality (*tattva*) as its object, as they say: "Reasoning is unstable" (*tarko 'pratiṣṭhaḥ*).
Therefore, it follows that here in this context, the non-supreme Brahman alone is the object of meditation, and its supremacy is relative to the body.
To this, it is replied: "Between the acts of seeing and meditating, which stand in the relation of cause and effect, there is one [and the same object]."
The meaning is that, as in the case of perception, there is a general rule regarding the fact that [cognition] has reality as its object.
For the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). And direct realization, as a general rule, has reality (*tattva*) as its object;
however, in some cases, when an obstructing factor intervenes, it may have a superimposed (*samāropita*) object as its domain.
Furthermore, when there is no sublation by a false statement, it is not possible to abandon the general rule.
Likewise, because this [knowledge] has reality as its object, its cause—meditation—must also have that reality as its object.
Moreover, when it is possible to achieve syntactic unity through the remainder of the sentence, a split in the sentence is not appropriate.

Moreover, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is possible because there is a recognition of the same object through the reference to the Supreme Person (*parapuruṣa*), as well as through the immediate verbal connection (*samabhivyāhāra*).
In accordance with that, in the phrase "higher than the high" (*parātpara*), the word "from the high" (*parāt*) should be understood as referring to the mass of individual souls (*jīvaghana*).
Therefore, the Supreme Person is both to be meditated upon and to be seen.
This has been stated:

here, the term "mass of living beings" (jīvaghana) does not refer back to the Supreme Person who is the object of meditation in the preceding context; rather, it is used to speak of that which is beyond the mass of living beings—the one who is to be meditated upon and seen—and thus "jīvaghana" refers to the individual soul (jīva).

That [Self], having attained the state of being a fragment (*khilya*) due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is called the "mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*). Alternatively, the "mass of living beings" refers to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) mentioned in the immediately following passage: "He is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman.

For that world is the "mass of living beings" because it is the abode of the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha—the *sūtrātman*, who is the self of all the organs—and thus it constitutes a collection (*saṃghāta*) of individual souls (*jīva*) enveloped by their instruments.
Thus, the supreme Brahman itself, as the abode of the three-measured *oṃkāra*, is to be meditated upon.
For this very reason, its attainment of a specific location is a fruit resulting from the presence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
and through the gradual arising of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), there is liberation.

"But 'He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself'—this scripture refers to the knowledge of Brahman without attributes (nirupādhi). However, it should be understood that the other [Brahman] is to be meditated upon as having the single measure (ekamātra) as its abode. //13// 1.3.5.14.
"The small [space] [is Brahman], on account of the subsequent [arguments]. //14//
"Now, as for this small, subtle, cave-like dwelling in the form of a lotus within this city of Brahman— 'that small space within it, what is inside that,
is what one must seek,' [this refers to] hearing through scripture and the instruction of the teacher,
and reflection by means of reasoning not inconsistent with them."
The search for that [knowledge] is the preliminary step.

And through the ripening of the practice of meditation—cultivated with diligence, continuity, and over a long period of time preceded by that search—there arises direct realization, which is "knowledge.
For that knowledge is indeed superior to the previous [forms of knowledge].
The desire for that [Brahman] is the inquiry.
Regarding this, he states a doubt: "In that regard... (tatra).
In this regard, first of all, there arises this doubt: is something other than the small ether (daharākāśa) that which is to be sought after and understood, or is it the small ether itself?
Even when the small ether is that which is to be sought after, is it the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), or the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), or the supreme self (paramātman)?
He asks for the cause of this doubt:
Why is this so?
He states the reason for it:
"by means of the two words 'ether' (ākāśa) and 'city of Brahman' (brahmapura)."

In this regard, first of all, the opponent establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) itself is the "small" one, on the grounds that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the elemental ether. However, because this prima facie view contradicts the extensive subsequent context, it is trivial; thus, dissatisfied with it, the opponent resorts to another position: "Or rather, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the small one. This is the conclusion reached.

The meaning is that this is logical. In this regard: "Because it is that which is contained within and because of its particularity, the body is declared to be the city of the individual soul (jīva); it is not logically the city of Brahman, due to the absence of those two reasons."
For designations are made by way of what is unique [to a thing].

For example, although a sprout is produced from the convergence of a collection of conditions such as earth, water, wind, and seed, it is designated by means of the rice seed as a "rice sprout," but not by means of the earth and so forth.
Because those [causes] are common to other effects as well; therefore,

although this body is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman, it should not be designated by the term "Brahman," since Brahman, as the cause of all modifications, is too common [a designation for this specific effect].
It is logical that this [body] is designated by the term "living being" (jīva) because it is acquired through the merit and demerit of the living being, owing to its being the specific cause;
furthermore, since the locative case in "the city of Brahman" (brahmapura) denotes a locus, it must be connected with this [body] which is contained therein.

Furthermore, for Brahman, which is established in its own majesty and is incapable of having anything added to it, a connection with a substratum cannot be postulated. The individual soul (jīva), however, being the size of the tip of an awl, is something that can be supported.

Therefore, the word "Brahman" must be explained as either etymological (*yaugika*) or figurative (*bhākta*) when applied to the individual soul—either by abandoning its conventional meaning or by taking it to mean "that which nourishes" (*bṛṃhaṇa*) the body and so forth.
And consciousness is devotion;
the distinction lies, however, in the presence or absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Expressibility is [the state of being] what is directly denoted, while suggestibility is [the state of being] what is implied.
This might be the case:
let the body be the city of the individual soul (jīva),
but the state of being within the lotus-heart would belong to another.
Since it is as if in the city of Ujjayinī belonging to Vatsarāja, [the author] says "of the lord of the city" (tatra purasvāminaḥ) to indicate the residence of Bhairava.

This is the meaning: a house is indeed a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for which no substratum (*ādheya*) has been specified; when there is a requirement for a specific substratum, because the "lord of the city" is the subject under discussion, the house is connected with that very substratum and thus requires nothing else, nor any other substratum.
[The opponent] postulates a connection [between the Self and the heart].
But even so, since the body alone is its locus of experience, what is the special distinction of the lotus of the heart such that it alone is its abode? To this, he says:
"And the individual soul (jīva) has the mind as its limiting adjunct (upādhi)."
But is it not the case that the mind also, due to its mobility, functions throughout the entire body in succession? To this he says:
"And the mind, for the most part.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (ākāśa) is applied figuratively to the individual soul (jīva) on the basis of common attributes such as formlessness.
Or, let this word "ether" (ākāśa) refer to the elemental ether itself, as in the passage, "In this small ether within," even so there is no fault; thus he says:
"And here, it is not the small ether that is to be sought."

This being the case, the following is stated: First of all, the elemental ether cannot be "small," because that would contradict the comparison [in the scripture]: "As large as this external ether is, so large is the ether within the heart.
For indeed, its being the object of comparison with that [ether] is like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.
When a way [of understanding] exists, it is not appropriate to superimpose a distinction out of necessity.
However, there is a way to understand the comparison of the small ether (*daharākāśa*) with the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) on the basis of its being Brahman;
for that which possesses unlimited magnitude cannot become limited,
since if it were so, limitation would be logically impossible.
In this context, it is not being enjoined that Brahman has the same measure as the elemental ether, which would contradict the scriptural statement "greater than the ether";
rather, by means of the comparison with the elemental ether, the smallness [of the heart] resulting from its limiting adjunct, the lotus, is set aside.
Moreover, all the subsequent reasons serve to exclude the possibility that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the elemental ether; thus he says:
"And not a difference based on imagination.
Nor is the small ether the individual soul (jīva); thus he says:
Regarding the phrase "even though the word 'self'":
"The body is accepted as the substratum of perception for Brahman;
because of its uniqueness, the body becomes the city of Brahman."

For since Brahman is perceived within the body, the body is designated as the "city of Brahman" (brahmapura) by virtue of this unique relationship, and not because it is a modification (vikāra) of Brahman;
in this way, the meaning of the word "Brahman" remains primary.

Or let it be that the city of Brahman is the city of the individual soul; nevertheless, just as the palace of Maitra is located within the city of Ujjayinī, the king of Vatsa, so too will the lotus of the heart be the abode of Brahman within the city of the soul.
Because Brahman is determined by the subsequent marks of Brahman;

for it is only when there exists a stronger subverting authority regarding Brahman and a supporting authority for the individual soul (jīva) that the marks of Brahman are somehow interpreted as applying to the jīva with the intention of expressing non-difference.
But here, there is no subverting authority regarding Brahman.
There is no evidence for the existence of the individual soul (jīva).
Furthermore, the designation "city of Brahman" has been established as referring to it being the locus for the realization of Brahman;
and its having a small abode has also been stated.

Therefore, since it is possible [to interpret it] as Brahman, it is not appropriate to explain its characteristic marks as referring to that which is not Brahman; thus, the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is Brahman alone, and not the individual soul (jīva) or the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
Having understood through hearing and reflection, and having realized Brahman, their "wandering" (caraṇa) consists in wandering among their desires—this is the meaning.
It might be argued:
once it is established that the small ether is to be sought after, an inquiry into it would be appropriate; however, it is not actually something to be sought after.
Furthermore, he restates what was said— that there is something else entirely which serves as its substrate— by saying, "As for this [which you said]...
He then refutes that restatement by saying, "To this we reply..."

The meaning is this: if something other than space were to be accepted as its support, then that alone should be explained above; what, then, would be the use of explaining space? He raises an objection:
"But even this," [he says].
Even the mention of space is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the existence of the objects contained within it.
To the question, "Why should it not refer to space itself? he replies:
If they should say this:

for when the teacher has taught, "In this small inner space (ākāśa), that which is within it is what must be sought, that indeed is what one must desire to understand," the student objects: "What is there in this that must be sought?"
The lotus is indeed subtle;
the space enclosed within it is subtler still.
Within that which is most subtle, what else can there be?
The meaning is that it does not exist at all.
Thus, what is there to be sought?
When this objection has been concluded, the teacher’s speech, beginning with the analogy of space as the resolution, is as follows: "Both heaven and earth are contained within this."
Therefore, the meaning is that heaven and earth alone, which rest upon the space enclosed within the lotus, are taught as what must be sought, not the space itself. He provides the rebuttal:
"This is not so; for it would be thus.
This might be the case.
It is exactly so; for indeed, mere admissions are not themselves faults. Therefore, he says:
"In that regard, there is a remainder of the sentence."
For the supplementary passage declares that the knowledge of the Self as the small ether possesses a fruit;
and that which possesses a fruit is enjoined as something to be performed,
and that which is to be performed is desired— thus, the statement "that is to be sought after, that indeed is to be desired to be known" remains fixed upon the small ether as its subject.
It might be argued: "Heaven and earth themselves will be the two selves;
by means of these two alone, the self will be characterized."
It is like the word "space" (ākāśa). Therefore, those two alone, which have space as their support, are being referred to; hence he says:
"In this, desires are contained"—that is, established.
"This Self is free from evil"—
by this [statement], the ether (ākāśa), which is the subject under discussion and the substratum for the support of heaven, earth, and so forth, is drawn forward.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "even though it is separated by the mention of heaven and earth.
[Objection: But surely this is the fruit of the knowledge of one whose desires are true, because it is mentioned immediately after that.
But this is not the case for one who knows the small ether; therefore, he says:
"by the word *ca* (and) in the sense of conjunction.

Since both "in this [ether] are desires" and "this" are in the singular number, they cannot refer to the two, heaven and earth; thus, the collective meaning is that the small ether alone is what must be referred to.

Thus, by this sequence, it is stated that in the passage "that which is within it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1), the word "that" (tat) refers to the lotus of the heart, bypassing even the immediately preceding ether.
The meaning is: that ether which is within that lotus of the heart is what must be sought. 1.3.5.14.
On account of the movement and the word; for thus [it is] seen, and there is an indicative mark.

The following is an elaboration on the phrase "from those that follow": Having introduced this very same small ether (*daharākāśa*), [the text says]—"Alas! How painful is this situation for living beings who are devoid of the realization of reality, in that they do not attain Brahman even though it is within their own grasp.
This is just as when pieces of gold, long buried under thick, firmly settled impurities, have fallen upon a path, yet remain [unrecognized] right above them.

Even by travelers passing by, who are seeking wealth, these [stones] are not picked up because they are mistaken for a heap of gravel; with this intention, the Śruti proceeds as if in wonder and as if with sorrow: "All these creatures go to this world of Brahman day after day, yet they do not find it."

For at the time of sleep, this entire world of living beings— both the wise and the ignorant— having reached the world of Brahman known as the small ether (daharākāśa) which resides within the lotus of the heart, does not know, "I have become Brahman," because its vision is veiled by the cataracts of the darkness of beginningless ignorance.
Thus, both the term "world of Brahman" and the mention of going to it refer daily to the fact that the small ether itself is the world whose nature is Brahman for the world of living beings.
The author of the Bhāṣya states this very point:
"For this reason also, the Supreme Lord alone is the 'small' one, because [the word 'small'] occurs in the remainder of the passage concerning the small [space].
By this, the two terms "going" (gati) and "word" (śabda) have been explained.
He explains the portion of the sūtra beginning with "for it is seen thus" (*tathāhi dṛṣṭam*) as follows: "For it is seen thus, day after day, among living beings"—
that is, it is seen both in the Veda and in the world.
Although there is no other worldly means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the state of being Brahman in deep sleep,
nevertheless, it is stated in order to establish the Vedic consensus itself—
that such is indeed the Vedic consensus that it is sung about even in the world.
The construction is as follows: "Just as in another Vedic passage and as in common worldly usage, so too here the word 'Brahma-world' [is used].
He introduces the explanation of the portion of the sūtra beginning with "And the indicative mark" by means of an objection:
"But [does it not also refer to] the world of the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā)?"
He refutes this: "If it were to mean 'he should cause [him] to go to the world of Brahman'—
" here, first of all, it is already established by the principle of the *niṣādasthapati* that a *karmadhāraya* compound is stronger than a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound.

Nevertheless, in this context, there is also an additional indicative mark (*liṅga*) for establishing a *karmadhāraya* compound by rejecting a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound; that too has been stated by the author of the Sūtras.

To explain: the very mention of attaining the world of Brahman day after day—which is well-known in both common usage and the Veda—is the indicative mark. Since this attainment is impossible in the case of the opposite view (the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*), it excludes that suspicion and remains fixed upon the attainment of the space within the small lotus-seated world (*daharākāśa*).
Nor is the small ether the world of Brahman; rather, it is established as a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is Brahman and that which is the world" (*tad-brahma tat-lokaś-ca*).
It is called "world" (*loka*) because it is perceived (*lok-yate*). Indeed, this [Brahman] residing within the lotus of the heart is what is perceived.

Indeed, when that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which resides in the lotus [of the heart] is purified—having been withdrawn from other organs—the yogis perceive the Brahman, whose nature is the light of consciousness, as being exceedingly clear, like the reflection of the moon in pure water. //15// 1.3.5.16.
And because its greatness, consisting of support, is perceived in this [internal organ].
The word *dhṛti* in the Sūtra denotes an abstract state (*bhāva*).
And the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is none other than the Supreme Lord.
Why? Because this greatness, characterized by sustaining (*dhāraṇa*), is found in this very Lord in other scriptural passages (*śruti*).
The commentary on this is explained by the word itself (nigada-vyākhyāna). 1.3.5.17.
"And because of its well-known meaning" (prasiddheśca):
Nor is this application of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) to Brahman—based on the connection with qualities such as omnipresence that are indicated here—a merely figurative one.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that while the term *rathāṅga* (chariot-part) refers to the *cakravāka* bird through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this [usage] is one that has become completely conventionalized (*atyanta-nirūḍhā*).
As for those who claim that the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is indeed primary even when referring to Brahman, just as it is with the physical sky (*nabhas*), [that is not the case].
By these [arguments], the seal of the Mīmāṃsakas— namely, "it is unjust for a word to have multiple meanings" and "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained by other means"—
has been broken.
For Brahman can indeed be obtained even through the connection with qualities such as omnipresence from the word *ākāśa*.
Nor should it be argued that [the term ‘ether’] is used in its primary sense for Brahman alone, while it applies to the physical ether only through a connection with those same qualities;
for the relationship between word and meaning is determined by worldly usage, and the comprehension of Vedic word-meanings is preceded by that [worldly usage].

An objection may be raised: since there is a distinct indication [of difference] in the passage, "As far as this external ether extends, so far extends this ether within the heart," figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate.
For when one intends to say "the bank of the Gaṅgā," the expression "Gaṅgā’s Gaṅgā" does not occur;
so, is the Vedic usage in "one should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the Paurṇamāsī" and "with the Amāvāsyā on the Amāvāsyā" now incorrect?
Moreover, the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are not primary (*mukhya*) in reference to the Āgneya and other sacrifices.

As for what was stated— that where there is the cognition of a word’s meaning, there is indication (lakṣaṇā), whereas where a word is not employed when its meaning is already ascertained elsewhere, there it possesses only denotative power (vācakatva)—
that is incorrect, because both cases are subject to deviation.
From the word "one should sacrifice with Soma" (somena yajeta), the meaning is understood;
and here, there is no figurative usage (lākṣaṇikatva) for anything except for the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha).

Furthermore, in the passage "He who, knowing thus, should sacrifice on the full moon day (paurṇamāsī); he who, knowing thus, [should sacrifice] on the new moon day (amāvāsyā)," the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* are not figurative.
Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence. 1.3.5.18.
"If it be argued that he [is the soul], because of the reference to the other, we say no, on account of impossibility.

In this state, the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes perfectly serene; it abandons the turbidity produced by the contact between the sense organs and their objects. Thus, *samprasāda* (perfect serenity) is a specific state of the individual soul, not of Brahman. Likewise, the rising out from the body [is also a state of the soul].
This refers to the individual soul (jīva) which has the body as its support,
and not to Brahman which is without any support.

Therefore, just as Brahman is understood to be the ether within the small lotus (dahara-ākāśa) by means of the previously mentioned indicative marks found in the supplementary passages, [so too is it understood here].

Thus, why is it that the small ether (daharākāśa) is not understood to be the individual soul (jīva) precisely from the "serenity" (saṃprasāda) and the "arising" (samutthāna) mentioned in the remainder of the passage?
Therefore, the meaning of the doubt is that there is no decisive reason [to choose one over the other].
[The answer is: "No, because of impossibility. (nāsaṃbhavāt).

For the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) arising from the states of serene confidence (*saṃprasāda*) and emergence does not concern the individual soul as such, but rather concerns its true nature as Brahman;
thus, this reference pertains to Brahman alone, and therefore the signs of the individual soul do not apply to the states of serene confidence and emergence.
However, it will be stated later that [the attributes] belong to Brahman alone because they exist for its sake.

As for the comparisons with space and so forth, since they never deviate from Brahman and are intended to refer to Brahman, there is a definitive criterion; this is the meaning. (1.3.5.9) "If it be said [that the soul attains omniscience] on account of what follows, [we reply: its true nature has indeed become manifest."
The small ether itself is introduced by way of a narrative: "Having sought that Self, one obtains all worlds and all desires.
Desiring to know that Self, Indra and Virocana, the kings of the gods and the asuras, approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands to serve him.
Having arrived, they dwelt there in celibacy for thirty-two years, intent on his service.
Then Prajāpati said to them, "What is your desire, you two who are staying here?
They replied, "We wish to know that Self which is free from evil."
Then Prajāpati said:
"This person who is seen in the eye is the Self, characterized by qualities such as being free from sin;
through the knowledge of whom there is the attainment of all worlds and all desires."
This is the immortal and fearless. Now, having heard this, because their veil of impurity was not yet destroyed, they took hold of the shadow-person and questioned Prajāpati.
Now, O Blessed One, regarding that which is seen in water, that which is in a mirror,
and that which is in one's own limbs and so forth— which among these is it? Is it that very same single [Self] present in all of them?
Having heard this question from the two of them, Prajāpati thought: "Alas! These two have wandered very far astray;
we pointed out the Self as residing in the eye, yet these two have identified it with the person in the reflection."

Thinking, "If we were to say that you are in error, then these two, who have arrogantly attributed great wisdom to themselves, would feel insulted; being thus dejected, they might not receive the instruction as it truly is," he replied with the intention of making them grasp the truth by conforming to their disposition: "Look at yourselves in this water-pot and tell me what you see."
Seeing them, their hearts were filled with satisfaction, yet they said nothing.
Then, the Creator, desiring that these two should not hold a perverted view, asked:
"What did you see there?"

The two of them said, "Just as we possess nails, hair, and so forth, produced by our recent practice of religious studentship (*brahmacarya*), we saw in the water-jar a reflection of ourselves that likewise possessed nails, hair, and so forth.

Then, wishing to remove their delusion regarding the self in the reflected image, [the teacher said]: "For just as the person in the reflection—being perceived through its nature of arising and passing away and lacking the characteristics of a self—is not the self itself, even so is this body."

However, intending that they should understand these two [the Self and the reflection] as distinct from each other through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), Prajāpati said:
"Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look again at yourselves in the water-pan;
whatever you see there, report that."
Having adorned themselves well, dressed in fine garments, and trimmed their nails and hair, the two acted exactly as before.
When questioned again by Prajāpati, they identified that very shadow as themselves.
Hearing this, Prajāpati thought, "Alas! Even now, their delusion has not subsided."
I shall now explain the true nature of the Self exactly as it is intended.
Thinking that when their impurities have been exhausted over time, they will realize the true nature of the Self by themselves through a careful examination of the sequence of my discourse, he said:
"This is the Self; this is the immortal; this is the fearless; this is Brahman."

Of these two, Virocana—because he identified the shadow as following the body—concluded that the body itself was the true essence of the Self; having returned to his own abode, he taught the Asuras exactly so.

Indra, however, before reaching his own abode, while still on the way, perceived certain defects due to the excellence of his [former] merit, reflecting upon each of those defects inherent in the shadow-self which conforms to the qualities and faults of the body; thinking, "I see nothing enjoyable in this perception of the shadow-self," he went back to the presence of Prajāpati.
With sacrificial fuel in hand, he returned once more; and when Prajāpati asked him the reason for his coming, he told how the world had been distressed on the way.
Prajāpati said, "Although the reality of the Self was well-explained, you did not grasp it because the veil of your impurities was not yet exhausted.
Therefore, practice the life of a student (*brahmacarya*) for another thirty-two years in order to destroy those impurities."
Then he said, "I shall explain this very Self to you again, once your impurities have been destroyed.
And Surendra, having thus practiced the life of a religious student, approached Prajāpati. To him who had arrived, Prajāpati spoke.

That Self which was shown in the previous section as characterized by freedom from evil and other such qualities—that very same Self is this one who "wanders about" in the dream state, being honored in various ways by women and others, and experiencing the enjoyments of dreams.
Even with respect to this [state], Devendra perceived fear;
for although this [Self] does not follow the attributes of the body like a shadow-person, [it is still subject to change].

When Maghavan had spoken thus—that even there, because of the experience of various afflictions such as grief and fear, there is no attainment of well-being—the Lord of Creatures replied: "Wander for another thirty-two years in pure celibacy; even now, you have not exhausted your defilements."
Then, when Maghavan had approached him in this manner, Prajāpati said:

"That very Self which was shown as possessing qualities such as being free from evil, and which is present in the eye and in the dream state—that same Self is the one who is serene in the state of deep sleep due to the absence of contact with objects and senses.
Even regarding this, Indra did not find peace.

For just as one who is awake or one who has entered a dream recognizes "I am this" and "these beings exist," so it is not at all that one who is in deep sleep perceives anything; then, indeed, being without consciousness, he becomes as if he has reached non-existence.
What, then, in this case, is the bliss?
When Maghavan had spoken thus, Prajāpati said, "Alas! Even until now, the destruction of your defilements has not occurred; therefore, practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for another five years.
In this manner, ninety-six years passed for that Maghavan through three such cycles.

And in the fourth section, for Maghavan, who had practiced the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) for five years— thus completing one hundred and one years in all— the [five fires] approached him. Then, for that Maghavan, whose impurities had been wiped away by the perfection of his studentship, Prajāpati clearly explained that very Self— which is threaded through the eye, in dream, and in deep sleep, and which possesses qualities such as being free from evil—
by means of the passage beginning, "O Maghavan, the body is indeed mortal."

This is the intended meaning [of the passage]: whatever pleasure or pain there is that comes and goes, all of that pertains to the body, the senses, and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), but not to the Self (ātman). However, due to the power of the impressions of beginningless ignorance (avidyā-vāsanā), this Self is mistakenly perceived as being these very things—the body and so forth. Consequently, imagining itself to possess the pleasure and pain residing in them, it grieves.

But when it becomes established in its own nature—which is dense with consciousness and bliss, characterized by freedom from sin and other such qualities—and remains indifferent, it attains all the desires of the world.
For all desires are merely portions of this very supreme bliss;
since suffering is a fabrication of ignorance, the man of knowledge does not experience it.
However, delusion arises here for those who have not practiced the Upanishads.
For their benefit, I have related this narrative.

Thus, from the subsequent textual context established in this manner, it is the individual self (jīvātman) alone—characterized by qualities such as being "freed from evil"—that is spoken of by the Śruti in the fourth section concerning the eye, the dream state, the state of deep sleep, and the state of liberation, in the passage: "This serene being (saṃprasāda), having risen up from this body...
Indeed, the abode of the eye is not possible for the Supreme Self.
Nor is there any connection with states such as dreaming,
nor is there any emergence from the body;
therefore, he to whom all this belongs is the one described by the Śruti as possessing qualities such as being free from evil.

Since all this belongs to the individual soul (jīva), it is that very soul which is described by the Śruti as possessing qualities such as being "free from evil" (apahatapāpman); therefore, the supreme Brahman is not understood through the attributes of being free from evil and so forth.
But has it not been stated that freedom from evil and the like are impossible for the individual soul?
They will exist [for the soul] on the basis of scriptural statement.
What kind of statement would it not carry out? There is no obstacle to its word, nor is there any contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

The meaning of the doubt is this: the individual soul (*jīva*) does not have sin and so forth as its inherent nature; rather, its sin and so forth arise from the activity of speech, intellect, and body. Therefore, in the absence of the body and other such instruments, sin and so forth do not exist, just as smoke does not exist in the absence of fire. [The author] refutes this:
To that one, he should say: "But [the Self] whose true nature has become manifest.

This is the intended meaning: upon a thorough consideration of the preceding and following passages, it is understood that the purport of the Upaniṣads is this—that Brahman is one, pure, awakened, liberated, and devoid of phenomenal expansion (aprapañca), while everything other than that is its illusory manifestation (vivarta), like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope.
And thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) is also a form of Brahman conditioned by the body, senses, and so forth, which are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), but it is not its natural state.
Consequently, qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and the like are not possible for the soul while it possesses that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance;
however, when the nature of Brahman has become manifest and is devoid of adjuncts, these qualities are possible only for Brahman itself, not for the individual soul.

Thus, since Brahman alone is described in the Śruti as possessing qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmā*), it is that very Brahman which is the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) and not the individual soul (*jīva*).
This might be so;
if, upon the manifestation of its true nature, it is indeed Brahman and not the individual soul, [then what follows...]
In that case, it would be a contradiction to state that "the individual soul (jīva) has manifested its true nature"; therefore, he says:
"by way of having been so in the past," as illustrated by the example of the water in the cup and Brahman.

For just as the reflections of Indra appearing in water are not the Self—because they are subject to appearance and disappearance and lack the characteristics of the Self—so too the body, senses, and so forth, being subject to appearance and disappearance, are not the Self.
Thus, by means of the illustration of the water-jar, the notion that the body is the Self is set aside and sublated.
He raises an objection: "But how [is it] its own form?"
For gold, stars, and so forth, which are mixed with other substances and overwhelmed by them, become manifest when separated from those [substances].
But how could there be manifestation through separation for that which is unchangingly eternal (*kūṭasthanitya*) and not mixed with anything else?
Furthermore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not unmanifest during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

For vision and the other [faculties] constitute its very nature, and since they manifest during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), how could the form of the individual soul (jīva) not manifest? This is the meaning. He provides the rebuttal:
"—prior to the arising of discriminative knowledge.

This is the meaning: although this immutable and eternal [Self] has no real association with anything else, and although it appears in the form of seeing and so forth during the state of transmigratory existence;

Nevertheless, due to the power of beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*anirvācyānādyavidyā*), his nature—which is actually unconnected with the body, senses, and so forth that are merely imagined by ignorance—manifests as if it were connected and as if it were non-distinct, even though it is distinct;
thus, through the suffering and other states residing in the body, senses, and so forth, he appears as if he himself possesses suffering and the like.
This has been established in detail in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*, and therefore it is not further elaborated upon here.

Although crystals and the like are in proximity to hibiscus flowers and the like, and this proximity consists of a conjunction with that which is conjoined (saṃyuktasaṃyoga), and thus they are indeed conjoined;
Nevertheless, the mere fact that [the mind] is not directly conjoined with the *japā* flower does not constitute an inconceivable [cause].
Sensations (*vedanā*) refer to joy, fear, sorrow, and so forth. He applies this to the subject of the analogy:
Likewise, regarding "the body and so forth":
he analyzes the scriptural passage, "The serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form," as follows:
"the discriminative knowledge produced by the scripture."

Thus, having described the discriminative knowledge (*viveka-vijñāna*) resulting from the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditation, he states that the fruit of that discriminative knowledge is the direct realization of the nature of the absolute Self, which is its manifestation in its own true form.

And that realization, being of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), dissolves itself—just like the clearing-nut (*kataka-phala*)—while dissolving the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), since it too is of the nature of the phenomenal world.

Consequently, the light of the Self (*ātma-jyotis*) becomes established, with the entire web of the phenomenal world wiped away, free from afflictions, and possessing an illumination that is not dependent on anything else.

This has been stated: "having attained the highest light. And here, the use of the gerund suffix *ktvā* even for an action occurring at a subsequent time should be understood as being like the expression, "he sleeps with his mouth open.
Furthermore, the direct realization of the isolated [Self] is the "rising out from the body."

But movement does not have the body as its point of departure; rather, it is possible even for one who possesses a body prior to the exhaustion of the karma that has begun to bear fruit. Thus he says:
"In this way, by the mere presence or absence of discrimination."

Not only is the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from the Supreme Self (paramātman) established by such scriptural texts as, "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," but this very same conclusion must also be understood through a careful consideration of the context of Prajāpati’s discourse; thus he asks:
"And for what reason should this be understood in this way?"
It might be argued:

"Just as with the self that is a reflection, Prajāpati, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is in reality distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), first causes it to grasp [the Self] as being immortal and fearless, and subsequently teaches that the Supreme Self possesses immortality, fearlessness, and so forth;
he does not, however, declare this [identity] of the individual soul with the Supreme Self, as is the case with the reflected self. To this, he says:
Nor is this self perceived as a reflection in the eye;
for even though it is pointed out as being "in the eye," it is the Self itself that is taught, not a reflected image.
Therefore, the illustrative example is unestablished.

Furthermore, because each subsequent section begins with the words, "I shall explain this very same thing to you further," it shows that the person in the reflection mentioned in the first section is not the one intended, but rather something other than that—a perceived Self;
otherwise, Prajāpati would be guilty of deception. Therefore, he says:
The same applies to the second [case] as well.
Now, why should the reflection-man (chāyāpuruṣa) not be the individual soul (jīva)? And thus, why should this reflection-man alone be referred to by the word "this" (etam)? To this, he says:
Furthermore, the phrase "I [saw] an elephant today in a dream" expresses a conjunction of certain cognitions along with the aforementioned logical justification;
and this is done by way of dispelling doubt.
The meaning is that while the shadow-person is non-abiding, this self shines forth as abiding, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
"Indeed, it is not thus"—
this refers to the one who is in deep sleep;
"now" means during the state of deep sleep.
"I" refers to the self, the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). He does not know that self.
To the question "In what manner does he not know it?", he says:
"I am this one, and these are the beings"—

just as in the waking state and in the dream state. By the statement, "For there is no loss of the knower's consciousness, because of its imperishability," the author establishes imperishability as a proven reason and thereby explains the recognition of the Self by one who has awakened from sleep.
"He who was I that slept after waking is indeed the same one who now wakes"— this is the view of those who follow the teacher's instruction; he states this with the words "But some," etc.

For if, by the words "if indeed this," one were to refer to the person who is the substratum of the eye mentioned immediately prior and declare that person to be the Self, then it would not be the shadow-person;
however, this is not the case,
because [the text] refers to the Supreme Self indicated at the beginning of the passage.
The meaning is that, indeed, the qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva) cannot possibly belong to the individual soul (jīvātman). He refutes this [objection] with the words:
"teṣāmetam" (of these, this...).
This is easily understood.
He states another opinion: "But other proponents," etc.
If the soul were not,
in reality, both the agent and the enjoyer,
then the injunctions regarding ritual action, which depend upon it, would be rendered null and void.
Furthermore, the statement of the author of the Sūtras, "Not so, on account of impossibility" (BS 2.3.29), would be contradicted;
for that [sūtra] indeed declares the impossibility of the qualities of Brahman in the individual soul (jīva).
Their intention is that there can be no impossibility of the qualities of Brahman in the souls if the souls are non-different from Brahman.
An answer has been given to those disputants by the *Śārīraka* itself;

for, upon a thorough examination of the preceding and succeeding passages, it is understood that the purport of the Vedāntas is this: the reality of the Self is one and non-dual, whereas individual souls (*jīvas*) are merely imagined through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, the qualities of Brahman, which exists as a reality, cannot possibly exist in the individual souls (jīvas) who are superimposed [upon it]. Indeed, the properties of a real rope, such as its fitness for being used, cannot belong to a snake that is merely superimposed upon it;
nor is the superimposed snake distinct from the rope.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtras. Furthermore, it has been stated that the injunctions for ritual action proceed by relying upon the agency and enjoyership imagined through ignorance as established in common worldly experience—just as the injunctions for the Śyena sacrifice and others proceed by relying on a person who, despite the prohibition "one must not harm any living beings," transgresses that prohibition in the pursuit of the intended result, namely malevolent magic (abhicāra); for the scripture has as its locus the person characterized by ignorance.
This is what he says:
"of all these" (teṣāṃ sarveṣām). Now, it might be objected that since Brahman is what must be discussed here, the reference to the individual soul (jīva) was unnecessary; to this, he replies:
Furthermore, this reference has another purpose:

the identity of the individual soul (jīva), which is conceived through limiting adjuncts (upādhi), with Brahman is what must be taught; and since that cannot be taught without first referring to the individual soul, the soul is referred to throughout the three states.
The meaning is that the dissolution of its state [of being limited] is intended to demonstrate its ultimate nature as Brahman. //20// 1.3.5.21.
"If it be argued that [the individual soul is not Brahman] because of the scriptural mention of smallness, that has already been answered.
This has been explained by the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which requires no further verbal explanation. //21// 1.3.6.22.
"And because of its imitation of that [fire]:
'Since the non-appearance of fire is observed when another fire is present,
another element of the nature of fire is therefore understood from this imitation.'"
For it is observed that a weak light, such as that of the moon or the stars, is overwhelmed by the more powerful solar radiance,
but never by anything other than light.
Furthermore, those things which obstruct a lamp, such as houses or jars, are not capable of illuminating the lamp by means of their own luster.
And it is heard [in scripture]: "By its light all this shines. The word "all" refers here to the sun and other luminaries under discussion.
Furthermore, imitation in the form of "shining after" (anubhāna) is not possible between things that are not of a similar nature.
For it is not the case that cows run after black birds; rather, it is fitting for cows to run after such boars.

Therefore, although Brahman was the subject under discussion in the passage, "In which heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven," [the subsequent reference to the sun as the eye does not contradict this].
Nevertheless, by the mark characterized as the capacity to imitate the overpowering [of other lights], the element of fire (tejo-dhātu) is understood through the sublation of the context,
and not Brahman, because the mark is inapplicable to it.
In those cases, the pronominal words *tam* and *tasya* will simply obscure what is to be demonstrated.
Furthermore, there is no rule that the word *tat* must refer back to something previously mentioned;
for instance, in expressions such as "dyed by that" (*tena raktaṃ rāgāt*) or "the offspring of that" (*tasyāpatyam*), there is nothing whatsoever previously mentioned.

Therefore, since it is argued that another form of light, though not perceived through other means of knowledge, is understood from the word as an object of meditation because it is extraordinary, we reply: "For that mark belongs to Brahman alone, and not to an extraordinary light;
therefore, it is not Brahman that is to be known as the object of meditation, but rather [Brahman] is understood [as the subject]."

Regarding the doubt as to whether, in the passage "upon Him alone [they shine]," one should assume some extraordinary light (*alaukika-tejas*) to account for the shining of the sun and other luminaries,

or whether the shining of the sun and others should be accounted for by the shining of Brahman— as well-known from another scriptural text which states, "He is of the nature of light, whose resolve is true"—
the conclusion is that when what is heard in scripture is possible, the assumption of what is not heard is not appropriate; thus, an unestablished entity is not to be assumed.
It is not logical that some extraordinary light should be meditated upon;
rather, it is Brahman, well-known from the Śruti, that must be known. This is what he says:
The Self must indeed be of the nature of consciousness;
he states the contradiction [with the opponent's view] by saying, "and because of equality."
But surely, in one's own perception, the sun and other luminaries depend upon visual light;
for these are not seen by a blind person.
Likewise, that very same visual light, when nourished by external light such as that of the sun, illuminates form and so forth, but not when it is not so nourished.
Since it would follow that one could see forms even in darkness, he says: "following the radiance of which [it shines].
For we do not deny that one light requires another light.
But its manifestation is a subsequent manifestation (anubhāna).
And the sun and other luminaries do not manifest following the manifestation of the eye.
This is what was stated:
"Not indeed [like] a lamp":
having restated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "as for what was also said."
This is what is meant: if imitation is rejected on the grounds of an absence of similarity in essential nature (*svarūpa*), then that is a non-sequitur.
But if it is on the grounds of an absence of similarity in action (*kriyā*), that [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For there exists a similarity of action—namely, the act of blowing in a fixed direction and location—even between wind and dust, though their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) are dissimilar.

As for fire and an iron ball, although the action of burning is not different, the similarity of action is to be explained by postulating a difference in action based on the difference in substance (*dravyabheda*).
Having thus analyzed the portion of the sūtra beginning with "anukṛteḥ," he now analyzes the part of the sūtra beginning with "tasya ca."
"And of that" refers to the fourth [state].
The meaning is that Brahman is the light that illuminates the lights, such as the sun and others.
It is not established that the light of the sun and so forth shines by means of another light that has attained the state of a sense organ.
For the natural function (*vṛtti*) of the word "all" (*sarva*) is to denote everything without exception.
This function would be restricted in the case of the non-worldly element *tejas* (fire), which illuminates only form;
however, with respect to Brahman, which illumines the entire universe, the function of the word "all" is not restricted.
Regarding the phrase "introducing the word *tatra*":
in all cases, this word *tatra* refers back to what has been previously mentioned.

Even in rules such as "that which is dyed by that [is called *rakta*] because of the color" (*tena raktaṃ rāgāt*), when a suffix is prescribed after a base (*prakṛti*) in the sense of a different meaning, the referent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) exists as having occurred previously; therefore, because of the reference to it by the word "by that" (*tena*), [the rule applies].
It is not inconsistent;
for in this way, the very mention of a pronoun brings Brahman to mind.
Thus, let it be that the indicative mark (liṅga) is indeed stronger than the context (prakaraṇa).
Since direct scriptural statement (śruti) is stronger than indicative mark (liṅga), it follows that here Brahman alone is understood through the scripture.
Furthermore, between the denotation of what is required and what is not required, the denotation of what is required is more appropriate because it serves a visible purpose; thus he says:
And immediately thereafter, in the passage "in the supreme golden sheath," it is stated that [Brahman] is "the light of lights.
To the inquiry as to how it is the light of lights, this [subsequent text] presents itself:

"There is no sun there" [is said] because, if it were stated independently, it would be unnecessary and would serve only an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). Furthermore, the negation of their manifestation would not be possible even with respect to Brahman.

The intended meaning is this: in the statement "the sun does not shine there," this is not a locative absolute (satisaptamī), for if it were, one would perceive the eclipsing of the sun and other luminaries while that [Brahman] exists; rather, it is a locative of object (viṣayasaptamī).
Therefore, when that Brahman is to be illumined, the sun and other luminaries do not shine as its illuminators;
rather, it is Brahman alone that shines as the illuminator within the sun and others which are themselves to be illumined.
And that [Brahman] is self-luminous.
"Because it is ungraspable, for it is not grasped," and so forth, according to such scriptural passages (Śruti).
Furthermore, it is also recorded in Smṛti:
"It does not illuminate that [Brahman]"; thus, the ungraspability of Brahman has been stated.
By the statement "That which is situated in the sun," its very nature as the perceiver is declared. 1.3.7.24.
"He is known from the word alone": "There is no direct difference in the means of knowledge regarding the Supreme, which is devoid of all measures."
Since the lordship over the past and the future does not directly apply to the individual soul (jīva), there is doubt [regarding its identity].

Should this passage be taken as being concerned with the meditation on the individual soul (jīva) in order to conform to the scriptural mention of "the size of a thumb," and the term "Lord" (īśāna) be explained in some way to accord with that; or rather, should it be taken as referring to Brahman in order to conform to the scriptural mention of "Lord"?

In accordance with that [latter], the scriptural mention of "the size of a thumb" should be interpreted in some way. Regarding the question of which of the two should conform to the other, it is logical that the first should be followed; thus, the scriptural mention of the "Lord" (Īśāna) must be interpreted in conformity with the mention of the "thumb.
Furthermore, it is appropriate for the Supreme Self to have its abode within the small lotus of the heart.
This is because there is merely a mention of a measurement;
furthermore, in the phrase "in the middle of the self," no distinction of location is understood.
For this word "self" (ātman) may denote either intrinsic nature, the individual soul (jīva), or Brahman.

In that regard, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) depends upon its possessor (*svabhavitṛ*) for its determination, and because its possessor is not specified, it is not known of what the "middle" is.
Furthermore, there is no middle between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) in a direct sense; thus, this indication of location is not clear.
However, the indication of magnitude (*parimāṇa*) is clear.
Furthermore, since a difference in dimension is impossible in the Supreme [Self], it is the individual self (jīvātman) alone that is "the size of a thumb.
Indeed, this is a portion of the Supreme Self, conceptually constructed by limiting adjuncts such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
And the internal organ generally has its locus within the sheath of the heart-lotus.

Furthermore, since the lotus-bud of the heart of human beings is the size of a thumb, the individual self (jīvātman), being delimited by it, is also the size of a thumb—just as space, when delimited by the joint of a bamboo, is the size of a cubit.
Moreover, the thumb-sized nature of the individual self is clearly recorded in traditional scripture (*smṛti*): "Yama forcibly dragged out the person the size of a thumb."
For it is not possible for the extraction of the Lord of All, Brahman, from [the body] by force by Yama;
indeed, Yama declared: "I am subject to Hari and my Guru; Viṣṇu is not powerless even in restraining me.

Therefore, since the state of being the size of a thumb is certain to belong to the individual soul (jīva), the soul's lordship over some past and future beings must be explained as being merely relative.
And by the words "This indeed is that," [the text] refers back to the form of the living self (jīva) as perceived through direct perception.
Therefore, it follows that the living self alone is the object of meditation here.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "Because it is the answer to a question, and because the mention of the Lord (Īśāna) occurs without distinction."
The statement is intended to convey that the individual soul has the nature of Brahman.
For here, absolute sovereignty over all that has been and all that is to be is perceived;
moreover, Brahman was previously asked about in the passage beginning with "Other than dharma, other than adharma.
Since the subsequent textual context is intended as a reply to that question, it is appropriate that Brahman be denoted by the words "This, indeed, is That."

And likewise, although the individual soul (jīva) is understood to be the size of a thumb, nevertheless this statement does not have that as its primary meaning; rather, it is intended to establish that the thumb-sized soul is of the nature of Brahman.
In this way, the unrestricted lordship (īśānatva) must not be restricted.
Nor should the status of this as an answer to the question regarding Brahman be abandoned.

Therefore, just as in the statement "That [Truth] exists," the identity of the individual self—the referent of the term *tvam*—with the Supreme Self denoted by *tat* is established, so too here it is logical that the state of being Brahman is established for the individual self measured by the thumb through the scriptural declaration of its being the *Īśāna*. //24// 1.3.7.25.
"But with reference to the heart, [it is said so] because the qualification belongs to human beings.

This means that even though the Supreme Brahman is omnipresent, its "abiding in the heart" is stated with reference to the individual soul (jīva). Furthermore, since no one other than the Supreme Self can be grasped here, the meaning is that this statement does not concern the individual soul.
"Only humans" means only those belonging to the three higher castes (traivarṇika). "Because of their desire [for liberation]" means...
It negates the eligibility for rites performed with a desire for rewards for those who possess internal consciousness and who seek liberation—

on the grounds that they lack the capacity— and it excludes animals, gods, and sages who likewise lack such capacity. Furthermore, by means of scriptural injunctions regarding initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites, it demonstrates the lack of eligibility for Śūdras.
As for what was also stated, namely, "because of the teaching of a limited size and because of the Smṛti," if this refers to the Supreme Self, why then is the individual soul (jīva) mentioned here?
Should it not rather be the Supreme Self alone that is mentioned?
And it is called the "living self" (jīva); therefore, the sense is that it refers specifically to the living self. He refutes [this objection]:
To this it is replied:
for the reality of the individual soul (jīva) is its state as the Supreme Self (paramātman),
and that must be explained.
The meaning is that since it is not possible to speak of that [liberation] without first designating the individual soul (*jīva*), the soul is therefore mentioned. 26.
"And Bādarāyaṇa [holds that there is eligibility] even for those above [the gods], because it is possible.

To show the incidental connection of this discussion—namely, the consideration of whether celestial sages (*devarṣis*) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman—which might seem irrelevant to the section on "Harmony" (*samanvaya*), he states the context:
Regarding the scriptural statement that [the self] is "the size of a thumb":
this might be the case;
since gods and others enjoy various and manifold experiences of bliss, they lack dispassion and thus have no desire for the knowledge of Brahman. To this, he says:
In this context, "desire" (arthitva) refers, for the time being, to the object of liberation.
The meaning is that there is detachment (vairāgya), because even in the enjoyment of heaven and the like, there exists the possibility of decay and excess.
