Now, an objection is raised: since gods and others lack a physical body (vigraha) and so forth, the functioning of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and so on—which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects—is impossible; thus, due to their ignorance and lack of capacity, they have no qualification (adhikāra). To this, he says:
"—then their capacity [is established] by those [means].
And how that understanding is derived from mantras and so forth will be demonstrated later on.
Now, one might object: "Since, like Śūdras, they cannot undergo initiation (upanayana), there is an absence of formal study; therefore, they lack qualification. To this, he says:
Nor [is it so] by means of the injunction for initiation (*upanayana*).
Indeed, the Veda being received from the mouth of a teacher according to the prescribed rule is not, in itself, the cause for the realization of fruitful ritual acts or Brahman;

rather, it becomes so when it is recollected by a person who, subsequent to his study, has understood the connection between words and their meanings through grammar, etymology, lexicography, and the like, and who possesses knowledge of the principles of verbal testimony and logic.
And for him, just as in this present life among humans, the Vedic scripture (*āmnāya*) studied according to rule in a previous birth is remembered in this life;
therefore, the meaning is that the Veda can manifest spontaneously (*svayaṃ pratibhāta*).
Furthermore, he states that there is no lack of qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) simply because of a lack of qualification for ritual action (*karma*):
As for the statement that there is a reason for their lack of qualification for ritual acts:
for indeed, among the Vasus and others, there is no other Vasu or the like;
nor, among Bhṛgu and others, is there another Bhṛgu or the like.
The meaning is that because the ancient ones such as Vasu, Bhṛgu, and others have now exhausted their *adhikāra* (spiritual office), they no longer exist as celestial sages (*devarṣi*). 27.
"If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple attainments.

The meaning perceived through the coherent connection of words in the mantras and other scriptures is to be accepted provided there is no contradiction with other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but not when there is such a contradiction.
Furthermore, this corporeality and so forth of the deity contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, like the statement "The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the sacrificer," the mantras and other such texts must be explained as having figurative meanings.

And thus, since there is an absence of a body and so forth, whether the deity is the object qualified by the word or the word qualified by the object, it is insentient; for this reason, the meaning of the doubt is that it has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to anything whatsoever.
He refutes this:
No.
Why?
Because there is the realization of manifold forms.
Why is that? To this he says: "Because it is seen" in the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
To explain: the creation of many bodies by a single being is not tenable either because it is not observed, or because its contradiction is observed.
In this regard, the claim that it is not observed is unproven (*asiddha*).

Because it is seen through both Śruti and Smṛti. For that which is not seen by worldly means of knowledge does not become "unseen" (inadmissible) simply because it is seen through scripture; otherwise, the fact that sacrifices and the like are the means to attaining heaven would also be "unseen. Furthermore, since it is a rule that a human body is produced from the union of mother and father, how could there be such a birth when the parents themselves have not come into existence?

If it is argued that there is an observation of sublation— namely, that smoke might exist even without fire, since [smoke] can arise from other sources— then alas, why do you wish to prove by the reason "being a body" that even the bodies of gods and others are born from the union of a mother and father?
In that case, the reason is fallacious due to being inconclusive (anaikāntika).
If it is argued that the bodies of those born from moisture or sprouts do not have this [divine power] as their cause,
and that the creation of bodies and so forth by mere will has never been observed, we say no;
for since they are derived from the primary elements (*bhūta*), it is not established that they are created by mere will.

For when those who have mastery over the elements— such as gods and others— desire to produce various bodies, the activity of the elements arises through their mutual conjunction, thereby generating various bodies.
And the activity of one who possesses mastery is indeed seen to follow the power of his will,
just as a master of the science of poisons causes a fragment of poison to move by mere wish.

Nor should it be argued that because those who know the science of poisons do not see the substratum when they see the poison, and because beings that are obstructed or distant are not seen, how can there be a substratum for gods and others?
This is because such an argument is invalidated by the observation of planets such as Mars and Saturn, which are distant and obscured by glass or clouds yet are still perceived.
Furthermore, the unimpeded vision of gods and others is not obstructed by the earth, mountains, and so forth, in the same way that it is not obstructed by glass, clouds, and the like.
Nor should it be argued that, like those such as ourselves, their inability to perceive things that are distant or obstructed due to possessing a body can be inferred;
for an inference that contradicts scripture cannot arise.
Furthermore, the power of invisibility (antardhāna) is possible for those lords, just as it is for humans through the use of collyrium and other means.
Therefore, there will be no perception of those [deities] even when they are present within the sacrificial site;
thus, it is well said that "there is a manifold way of understanding," for it begins with the question, "How many gods are there?"
For in the *nivid* of the *vaiśvadeva-śāstra*, having begun with "How many gods are there?", Yājñavalkya gave the answer to Śākalya by means of the *nivid* itself:
"Three and three hundred, and three and three thousand.
A *nivid* consists of mantra-words expressing the number of deities to whom the recitation is addressed.

This is what is meant: when Śākalya asked how many deities were enumerated as being praised in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva [hymn], Yājñavalkya’s reply was, "Three hundred and three," and so forth, up to the point of stating that there are as many deities as are enumerated in the Vaiśvadeva *nivid*.
Furthermore, when Śākalya asked, "Who are they? regarding those to be numbered, Yājñavalkya’s reply was:
"These are indeed its powers; there are only these thirty-three gods.
The thirty-three gods are the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, and Indra and Prajāpati.
Among them, Agni and the Earth, Vāyu and the Atmosphere, Āditya and the Sky, and the Moon and the Stars constitute the Vasus.
For these, transforming into the form of the aggregate of causes and effects based on the fruits of the actions of living beings, cause this entire world to dwell;
therefore, they are the Vasus.
As for "Who are the Rudras?", these are the ten vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person, namely the ten organs of perception and action.
And the eleventh is the mind; thus,
these are the vital breaths (prāṇas),
because they function as its modifications.
For they are called *rudras* because, at the time of departure, as they ascend, they cause the person to weep (*rodayanti*).

"Which are the Ādityas?"—the twelve months, which are the constituent parts of the year; because they revolve again and again, causing living beings to take up their lifespans and the enjoyment of the fruits of their actions, they are the Ādityas.
Lightning is Indra.
For she is strength;
she is the supreme sovereignty of Indra;
for by her he causes all living beings to perish.
Therefore, the thundercloud, the lightning bolt, Indra, the sacrifice, and Prajāpati—
both the means of sacrifice and the sacrificial form itself, the cattle, are Prajāpati.
These very thirty-three gods are the manifestations (*mahimānaḥ*) of six—namely, Agni, Earth, Vāyu, Antarikṣa, Āditya, and Div; they do not differ from those.
There are, however, only six gods.
But by making Agni and Earth one, Vāyu and Antarikṣa one, and Div and Āditya one, there are three worlds and thus only three gods.
And these three, being included within food and vital breath, become the two deities, food and vital breath;
even those two constitute one deity, Adhyardha.
Which one is Adhyardha?
This wind which blows—how is it that this one alone is "one and a half" (*adhyardha*)?
Because when it exists, all this attains increase (*vṛddhi*) by one and a half; therefore, it is called "one and a half."
What is the "one"?
That very same vital breath (*prāṇa*), being one and a half, is the "one Brahman.
It is called "Brahman" because of its greatness (*bṛhat*) by virtue of being the self of all the gods; that very thing is designated by the word *tyat*, which is an indirect expression.
Therefore, the Śruti declares that by virtue of the majesty of the one God alone, he simultaneously assumes the forms of many deities; and the Smṛti has already been explained accordingly.

Furthermore, even among ordinary people who have attained powers such as *aṇimā* through the practice of means, there is the simultaneous attainment of being subordinate members [of a ritual], which is understood as their becoming auxiliary parts.
From the observation of that [fact].
To demonstrate that very point clearly, he first states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "In some cases, one... and so forth.

Indeed, a single Brāhmaṇa cannot simultaneously occupy the status of a subordinate member (*aṅga*) in respect to many acts of faith (*śrāddha*). Regarding the fact that one person may occupy the status of a subordinate member in multiple places at once, he says:
"And sometimes one."

Just as a single salutation is performed simultaneously by many people directed toward one Brāhmaṇa, so too, while directed toward a single deity situated in her own abode, oblations are offered simultaneously by many sacrificers residing in various locations; and although she is not physically present there, she becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the rite.
For it has been established that she possesses the capacity to perceive multiple objects situated at a distance simultaneously. (1.3.8.28)

If it is argued that [the relationship between word and meaning] is eternal because of the word itself, we say no; for they originate from this [Eternal Word], as is known through perception and inference.

Like "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, words such as "Vasu" and others are denotative of individuals, because there is no prior recollection [of a universal] and because no single common attribute (upādhi) is perceived—as is the case with words like "cook" or "ether. Since that individual is eternal, the relationship with it must also be eternal.

But in the case of a connection with a body and so forth, because the Vasus and others are non-eternal due to their having parts, the word "Vasu" and so on was not previously connected with its own referent, since that referent itself did not exist.

Consequently, when the Vasu and others are produced, the connection of the word "Vasu" and so on with them arises—just like the connection of words such as "Devadatta"—as originating from human intellect; and thus, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is preceded by that [connection].

The meaning of the objection is this: [the validity] would also be dependent upon human intellect; and since human intellect arises in dependence upon other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), the validity of the Veda would be undermined by its dependence on other means of knowledge. The reply is: "No."
"Because it originates from that":

from words denoting a genus, such as "wealthiness" (*vasutva*) and so forth, there arises—residing in the intellect—the manifestation of an individual belonging to that genus which one intends to produce;
this is what is meant by "originating from that."

This is what is meant: although the word is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of Vasu and the other deities—since Brahman is their material cause—it is nevertheless their efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) in the manner described.
And yet, this does not entail the non-eternality of the relationship between word and meaning.
"Because of the eternity of the genus *vasu* and so forth, or of that which is delimited by some form (*ākṛti*) serving as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
He analyzes this very point through objection and resolution: "But [it is said], 'from which the birth and so forth of this [world proceed']" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.2).
These have been explained by way of paraphrase (*nigada-vyākhyāta*).
Now, one might ask: has this [Veda] been produced by the Self-existent One (*svayambhū*) like the *Kumārasambhava* and other works by Kālidāsa and others?
And if so, does it not follow that it lacks authority because its sentences depend upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*)? To this, he says:
This "utterance" (utsarga) of speech consists in the initiation of the tradition (saṃpradāya). Tradition is the study [of the Veda] through the lineage of teacher and pupil.

What is meant is this: although the Self-existent One (svayaṃbhū) is the author of the Vedas, he does not possess independence like Kālidāsa and others; rather, [he acts] in accordance with a previous creation.
This has been established by us, and the author of the Commentary will establish it further below;
moreover, this is observed even today.
He says— “Moreover, [it is] what is intended to be done”— because from seeing that, the same state of even former agents is inferred. He objects:
"But what is their nature?

This is the intended meaning: for it must be admitted that the gods originate from expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*), because they cannot be inscribed upon the intellect by means of non-expressive words.
In this regard, the individual phonemes such as *va* and so forth are not the denoters of [the word] *vasu* and the rest,
because they are distinct with each utterance and thus it is impossible to grasp their relationship [to the meaning];
and if that which has not had its relationship grasped were a denoter, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Moreover, do these [phonemes] express the meaning of a sentence either individually or collectively?
First, they cannot do so individually, because no cognition of the meaning is observed immediately after the utterance of a single phoneme.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the utterance of subsequent phonemes would be purposeless.

Nor are they combined, because for those [phonemes] uttered by a single speaker— which perish moment by moment both in terms of their form and their manifestation— it is impossible for them to possess mutual concomitance.

Nor is any mode other than the individual or the aggregate possible. Nor is it tenable to claim that, even in the absence of coexistence in their own form (*svarūpa*), there exists a coexistence of the phonemes by way of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), as in the case of the Āgneya and other sacrifices; for this cannot withstand logical analysis.
What indeed is this "disposition" (saṃskāra) intended to be? Is it something unprecedented, produced by [rituals] such as the Āgneya sacrifice,
or is it that which has another name, "cultivation" (bhāvanā), and serves as the seed for the production of memory?
The first alternative is not tenable;

for a word that is unknown either in its own form or in its constituent parts, and whose relationship [to its meaning] is unknown, cannot be a cause for the cognition of an object, just like a sense organ.
This is because a word that has been uttered but is not perceived by a deaf person, or is perceived but its relationship is not grasped, does not produce cognition.
Therefore, it must be accepted that a word—whose connection is known and whose constituent parts for conveying meaning are known—is a communicator, just like smoke and other such signs.
And thus, its *saṃskāra* (latent impression), which denotes the *apūrva*, must be understood as a constituent part of the communication prior to the cognition of the object;
yet at that time, there exists no means for its comprehension.

But one who attempts to justify the comprehension of that [word-meaning] through the cognition of the object falls into an inescapable circularity: the cognition of the object arises from the determination of the linguistic impression (*saṃskāra*), and the determination of the linguistic impression arises from that [cognition of the object].
The latent impression (saṃskāra), which is designated as "cultivation" (bhāvanā), is the capacity of the self to produce memory.
It cannot, however, be the very same capacity that produces the cognition of an object;
nor can there be another capacity belonging to that very capacity itself.

For the very power of fire that burns is not the same as its power to illuminate, nor is the power to illuminate the same as the power to burn. Furthermore, if the letters were uttered in a reversed order, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the very same seed of memory—the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—would produce the cognition of the meaning;
yet this does not occur.
Therefore, the phonemes (varṇas) are not in any way the causes of the comprehension of meaning,
nor is there a self-nature called *sphoṭa* distinct from them,
because such a thing does not ascend to [the level of] experience.

As for the cognition of an object, if that [eternal entity] were understood through its effect, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence; this has already been largely stated. Furthermore, if that eternal entity were the cause of the cognition of an object by its mere existence, there would follow the consequence that the cognition of objects would arise at all times, because a cause that is independent [of other factors] must be ever-present.
Therefore, the claim that the production of the signified arises from the word as the signifier is untenable.
Regarding this, a teacher-like [proponent] says: "He said 'the sphoṭa'... and so forth.
We do not tolerate the view that phonemes are the conveyors [of meaning],
yet we do not tolerate the view that it is the *sphoṭa*.
This is because, immediately following the experience of those [phonemes], the cognition of the object arises for one who has known the linguistic convention (*saṃgati*).
Nor is it the case that there is no experience of that [word] which is distinct from the phonemes;

for the cognition of a single word and a single sentence— such as "gaur" (cow) as one word, or "gām ānaya śuklām" (bring the white cow) as one sentence— as being distinct from the various phonemes and words, is common to all people.
Nor can this experience of a single word or sentence as "this is not a horse" be said to be false;
nor is it adventitious (aupādhika).
For an adventitious condition (upādhi) would indeed have to be either the state of being grasped by a single cognition, or...
Or [it might be] the state of being the cause for a single cognition of an object.
First of all, there is no cognition appearing as a single entity for the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees, which are the objects of a single cognition;
if that were the case, the expression "the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa*" would never occur.
Nor can they be the cause of a single cognition of an object, because the status of being such a cause has been refuted in the case of the phonemes; furthermore,
if their simultaneity were postulated on the grounds of being that cause, it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence.
Because there is coexistence (*sāhitya*) there is the state of being its cause, and because there is the state of being its cause there is coexistence;

therefore, this uncontradicted and unconditioned experience of a single manifestation within the domain of words and sentences, which rests upon a single expressive entity distinct from the phonemes, is *sphoṭa*. And although the sounds (*dhvanis*) manifest it individually, they do not make it clear all at once.
For by means of this, the cognition of the meaning would arise immediately; rather,

as in the case of the knowledge of the true nature of the Jewels, when the final consciousness— born from a mind accompanied by the ripening of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by two, three, four, five, or six successive insights— shines forth clearly with the reality of the words and sentences, then the cognition of the meaning arises immediately thereafter, having not arisen previously.
Thus, there is no pointlessness regarding the later sounds (dhvanis),
nor regarding the preceding ones;
for in their absence, there would be no assistance due to the lack of the mental impressions (saṃskāras) produced by them and the lack of their maturation.
Because the final consciousness alone is not productive [of the cognition of meaning],
nor do the preceding phonemes produce an indistinct cognition of the object individually, as is the case with the cognition of words.
But it is logical that its assistant, the *sphoṭa*, [is perceived] even more clearly;
for there is a restriction regarding perceptual cognition such that it must manifest as either manifest (*vyakta*) or unmanifest (*avyakta*),
and the cognition of the *sphoṭa* is indeed perceptual.

However, since the cognition of meaning arises from another means of knowledge and is not itself perceptual, its manifestation would either be clearly evident or it would not occur at all; it could not be indistinct. Thus, the resolution [of the difficulty] is not equal. Therefore, the eternal *sphoṭa* alone is the signifier, not the phonemes (*varṇas*).
He refutes this view of the teacher’s school while establishing his own position:

"But it is the phonemes themselves that are the word, not something else. For the sphoṭa would have to be accepted as something distinct from the phonemes only if the capacity of the phonemes to signify were impossible.
And that [word] must abide within the path of experience.
Furthermore, there are two ways in which letters could possess denotative power:
either because it is impossible to grasp their relationship due to their momentariness, or because of the absence of both the individual and collective modes [of occurrence].
The first alternative is not tenable, because there is no evidence for the momentariness of phonemes (*varṇa*).
[Objection: Is it not well-known to all people that phonemes are different with each utterance? [Response: No.
Because it is recognized as being the same;
nor is it correct to say that this recognition is based on similarity— like that of a flame— even in the absence of actual identity.

Whether this [cognition] is based on similarity would have to be accepted either because of the occurrence of a powerful sublation (*bādhaka*), or because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in certain cases, such as with a flame.

Regarding that, when one conjectures it due to the observation of deviation in some instances, those who maintain that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) say: "For he who, out of delusion, might conjecture a sublation even though it is unknown—"
In all worldly affairs, such a person, being of a doubting nature, shall go to ruin.
Thus [it has been said].
And this has been explained by us at length in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*.
Nor is this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) concerned with universals (*jāti*) such as "g-ness" (*gatva*), nor is it concerned with individual instances (*vyakti*) such as the letter "ga."

Because a distinction is perceived among those [utterances] for each individual person, and precisely because a distinction in sound is perceived, it is logical that a difference between speakers is inferred from such expressions as, "Somaśarman is studying, not Viṣṇuśarman.
Therefore, let experience be carefully examined when many people are pronouncing the letter *ga*:

just as for one observing both a Kālākṣī and a Svastimatī cow, while the manifestation of the difference between the individuals is indeed present, a single universal (*sāmānya*) that conforms to them manifests itself.
Likewise, when the individual sounds such as *ga* and so forth manifest with distinction, does a single universal *gatva* shine forth as that which persists through them?

Or rather, is it like the case of "cowness" (*gotva*), which is inherently one, yet—due to the differences in the limiting adjuncts of individual cows (such as their location, size, shape, and manifestation)—appears as if it were in different locations, as if small, as if large, as if long, or as if short; similarly, although the individual manifestation of the sound *ga* is inherently one, does it follow those properties due to the difference in its manifestors?
Let your honors yourselves understand that it is "extended" (*prathata*).

In this regard, even if one accepts a difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), the effort required to postulate a distinction based on the proximity of other factors for a single phoneme *ga* would be better applied to the individual instance of *ga* itself. What is the use of accepting a superfluous *ga*-ness (*gatva*) as an internal burden?
As they have said: "Therefore, whatever is sought from a universal (*jāti*), that will be obtained from the phoneme itself."
But since the individual [phoneme] is obtained from the sounds, the cognition of [abstract properties] such as *gata* is futile.
Furthermore, unlike [the case of] "Svastimati" and so forth, there is no clear cognition of a difference between individual utterances (gavyakti) at each pronunciation.
If that were the case, the cognition would be "Caitra uttered ten *ga*-sounds," rather than "He uttered the sound *ga* ten times."
Nor is this repetition intended to imply identity of class, as in the expression, "Devadatta ate partridges a hundred times.
For in this case, even though people cry out beating their breasts, the cognition of the practice of pronunciation regarding the manifestation of the phonemes *ga* and so forth still arises.
The opponent raises an objection that contradicts recognition:
For how could many people utter [the same sound] at one and the same time?
Whatever possesses a simultaneous conjunction with contradictory properties is manifold,
just as cows, horses, and so forth possess two hooves, one hoof, manes, dewlaps, and so on.
Furthermore, this phoneme possesses simultaneously contradictory properties such as being acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta);
therefore, it must be manifold.
Nor are the acute and other tones properties of the manifesting agents (vyañjaka).
It is not correct to say that they are the properties of color (varṇadharma). For its manifestors are the winds; if those [winds] are not audible, how could their properties be audible?
This much must first be said here:
a sense faculty whose object is a quality does not also take the possessor of that quality as its object;

otherwise, earth, water, and space—which possess smell, taste, and sound—would become the objects of the olfactory, gustatory, and auditory faculties, even though those faculties have only smell, taste, and sound as their respective objects.
And let it not be that the ear has wind as its object; rather,
it will take as its objects the qualities of that [wind], such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth,
and because these are apprehended in conjunction with sound, they are determined to be properties of sound.

Furthermore, it is not possible for mutually contradictory properties such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others to coexist simultaneously in the very nature of a sound whose unity is determined by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Therefore, just as a single face appears to have various distinctions of location, size, and shape due to the influence of different adjuncts such as a gem, a sword, or a mirror,
so too this illusion of the association with various contradictory properties belongs to a single phoneme (*varṇa*), being dependent upon its manifesting sounds (*vyañjaka-dhvani*).
But since it is established that there is no real conjunction of various properties, the author of the Bhāṣya states a rebuttal by way of concession:
"Or rather, it is produced by sound.
The word "or rather" (athavā) sets aside the prima facie position.
Granted that the quality and the possessor of the quality might both be apprehended by a single sense-faculty, even so there is no fault;
for sounds, like words, are also audible.
He distinguishes the true nature of *dhvani* from the phonemes (*varṇa*) by means of a question: "But what, then, is this?

Nor is it correct to say that this is merely a cognition of the commonality of phonemes whose specific differences have not been determined, and not a cognition of a manifesting *dhvani* distinct from the phonemes.
Because there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of this [sound]— which is divided by distinctions such as nasality— as there is for individual instances of the letter *ga* and so forth,
and because that which is not recognized lacks unity, the existence of a universal (*sāmānya*) is untenable. Therefore, this sound is not of the nature of a phoneme (*varṇa*).

Whether sound (*dhvani*) is admitted as distinct from the word (*śabda*) or as the audible manifester of the word, in either case, qualities such as nasality (*ānunāsikatva*)— which are perceived through the mediation of various specific sounds (*dhvani*) in both vowels and consonants— are understood as properties belonging to those sounds themselves; they are not properties of the word *per se*.
And so, let those sounds (dhvanis) in which mutually contradictory properties such as nasality appear be impermanent;

for there is no recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of them. However, as for those phonemes (varṇas) in which there is recognition, they do not possess properties such as nasality; therefore, they are not impermanent.
And this being the case,

[the phrase] "having an object" (sālambanā) is used; for if the opponent's position is that when the substratum (dharmin) is not apprehended, its attributes (dharmas) cannot be apprehended either, [then our argument follows].
"Let it be so named; let the other person be satisfied in that way.
The meaning is that even so, there is no fault.
Thus, by this continuous argument, the lack of expressive power attributed to phonemes on the grounds that their connection cannot be grasped due to their momentariness has been refuted.
Desiring to refute that which has been proposed on the grounds that neither of the two modes—individually nor collectively—is possible, [the author] says:
"And because the cognition of meaning arises from the phonemes.
An opponent, unable to tolerate this conceptualization, says:
"I do not conceptualize"—he refutes this, saying: "No;
for even this cognition..."
Let the venerable one first examine the cognition that "gauḥ" is a single word:

does this [cognition] apprehend only the previously experienced phonemes, such as the letter *ga*, in their totality; or does it apprehend something distinct from the letters *ga* and so forth, just as a *gavaya* is distinct from animals such as the boar?
If it were to manifest as something distinct from the letter *ga* and so forth, then the cognition would not be colored by the form of the letter *ga* and so forth;
for a cognition of a boar does not apprehend a boar that is colored by the form of a buffalo.

The sounds (*dhvani*), differentiated by variations in effort, each manifesting the single reality of a word (*padatattva*), produce—by virtue of being produced at identical places of articulation (*sthāna*) and instrumental organs (*karaṇa*)—a resemblance to the various sounds that manifest other words. Through this resemblance to the respective sounds manifesting other distinct words, they cause the single reality of the word to appear as if it were many distinct words, possessing mutual dissimilarities. Due to these differences in the superimposition of resemblance, even though the word is a single, partless entity, they make it appear as if it were manifold and possessed of parts.

Just as a single primary [form] possesses distinctions of color, dimension, configuration, and arrangement, yet gems, swords, mirrors, and so forth possess many such distinctions of color, dimension, configuration, and arrangement— if you argue that its constituent parts, the phonemes (*varṇa*), are thus merely imagined, then why do you now resolve to declare these distinctions of phonemes to be false even in the absence of any subverting evidence?

If it is argued that a single cognition itself appears as manifold, then alas! Since various colors are manifested within that [single cognition], why does the appearance of manifoldness not sublate its oneness?
Alternatively, oneness and manifoldness are not contradictory, just as in the case of cognitions such as "forest" or "army."
Indeed, the cognitions "army" and "forest" do not arise by negating the distinction between elephants, foot-soldiers, horses, and so forth, or between *campaka*, *aśoka*, *kiṃśuka*, and other trees;
rather, they bring about a state of unity for those very things that are distinct, by delimiting them through a single common adjunct (*upādhi*).
Nor does the unity derived from such an adjunct contradict their inherent plurality.
For the metaphorical firehood of a boy does not contradict his inherent humanity;

therefore, it should be understood that the letters appearing in a single recollective cognition— which arises from the accumulation of mental impressions produced by the experience of each individual letter and which encompasses all those letters— possess a metaphorical unity, either by virtue of being objects of that single cognition or by virtue of being the cause of a single cognition of meaning.

Nor is there a circularity such that their being the cause of the cognition of a single object depends on their unity, and their unity depends on their being the cause of the cognition of a single object;

for it is not the case that, prior to the cognition of the object, these many phonemes do not appear as ascending into a single recollection. Nor is it the case that the elder’s cognition of the object cannot be inferred immediately after their appearance.

And because their status as a single causal factor (*kāraka*) toward the cognition of a single object is understood through that inference, the superimposition of "single-word-ness" follows; thus, there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*).

Nor should it be argued that since phonemes (*varṇa*) ascending into a single memory cannot be non-distinct when employed in succession, non-succession, or reversed succession, it would follow that meaning-cognition would arise from these phonemes regardless of how they are employed.
For it has been said: "As many as there are, of whatever kind, and which [phonemes] are involved in the communication of a word-meaning..."
The phonemes, whose capacities are well-known, are likewise the means of comprehension.
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: even though there is no sequence in the single cognition of a row, it is appropriate that the row of houses and so forth appears as such because a real row exists for them;
however, in this case, there is no real sequence for the phonemes, since they are eternal and all-pervading.
If it is argued that there may be an adventitious condition (*pratyayopādhi*),
and since that too is one, from where could this sequence of these [cognitions] arise?
This is because, even in a single act of memory, there is a recollection of the sequence of prior experiences, just as there is [a perception] of the form of the phonemes.

For instance, when the two words *jāra* and *rāja* are being presented, although the phonemes are identical, a difference between the words is clearly manifested due to the difference in their sequence.
Thus, there is no lack of distinction in a single cognitive act of memory regarding phonemes employed in a specific sequence, as opposed to those employed out of sequence or in reverse order.
As they have said: "The wise desire many means for determining the words [of the Veda]:
order, deficiency, excess, accent, syntactical connection, direct revelation (śruti), and traditional law (smṛti)."
Thus [ends the citation].
The remainder has its meaning not obscure. Only a mere indication of the direction has been shown here.
The detailed account, however, should be understood from the *Tattvabindu*.
Or rather, enough with this dispute with the Naiyāyikas;

even if phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed non-eternal, nevertheless, the apprehension of linguistic convention and worldly usage such as "cow" will be established precisely through the delimitation of universals such as *g-ness* (*gatva*). Thus he says:
"Or even if [it were not so]," etc.
(28). And for this very reason, there is eternality.
Now, one might object: "Since the eternality of the Veda was already established in the previous Mīmāṃsā, why is it being proved again? To this, he says:
For it is established that the Veda is eternal precisely because no independent author is remembered;
indeed, the world cannot arise from that which is non-eternal, since even such a thing, being itself subject to origination, would be dependent on other causes.

Therefore, the Veda is eternal because it is the cause of the origin of the world, just like Īśvara; thus its eternity is established and merely reinforced by this [argument]. The remainder has a self-evident meaning. //29// 1.3.8.30.

"And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, on account of [scriptural] vision and Smṛti. Since this sūtra follows upon a point of doubt, he reads: "Now, it might be argued..."
For the eternity of the relationship [between word and meaning] would exist only if there were no interruption in the continuity between the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*).
Likewise, the eternity of the Veda would depend on the uninterrupted succession of teachers and students.

However, if the world were to dissolve without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*), and if something entirely non-existent and unprecedented were to arise, then both the signifier and the signified would be utterly destroyed; what, then, would be the basis for their relationship?
Furthermore, if the lineage of teachers and students were to be interrupted, what would the Veda have as its substratum?
Nor should it be said that there are individual souls (*jīva*) permeated by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
for since they are constructed by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they cannot persist once those adjuncts have ceased to exist.
Nor can that impression belong to Brahman,

because it is impossible for Him— whose nature is pure and whose essence is knowledge— to possess such impressions. Furthermore, at the beginning of creation, when the internal organs and the individual souls (jīvas) delimited by them come into being, they cannot possibly be endowed with the impressions of past karma or ignorance.
Because it would be unprecedented (*apūrva*).
Therefore, this eternality of the relationship between word and meaning is contradicted by the acceptance of creation and dissolution.
By the mention of the "designator" (*abhidhātṛ*), both the teacher and the student are implied.
To dispel this doubt, he introduces the Sūtra:
"In this regard, it is said: 'Because of the identity of names and forms.

Although at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) the internal organs and other faculties do not exist with their functions actively manifest, nevertheless, [they persist] in their own cause.
"Absorbed in ineffable ignorance (*avidyā*), they remain indeed in a subtle state as power (*śakti*), along with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma, distraction, and ignorance.
And thus says the *Smṛti*: 'This was once enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without defining marks, beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.'"

Thus it is said. And those [souls], having reached the place of dissolution (avadhi), impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord, emerge from it— just as limbs that were retracted within the body of a tortoise come forth from it,

or just as the bodies of frogs, which had attained the state of earth at the end of the rains, experience the state of being frog-bodies once again when nourished by the drenching showers of thick rain-clouds due to being permeated by their latent impressions (vāsanā).
Likewise, by the force of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [beings] are born with names and forms similar to those of the past.

This is what is meant: although the sphere of cyclic existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*) originates from Īśvara, nevertheless, Īśvara creates only in accordance with that [prior state], having the karma and ignorance of living beings as his auxiliary causes.

And since this [creation and dissolution] is not possible without the beginninglessness of the stream of creation and dissolution, even when one accepts creation and dissolution, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is not contradicted. This has been stated:
"It is both logically established and observed."
Regarding the phrase "from scripture":
it might be argued that while the beginninglessness of saṃsāra may indeed be granted, [the objection remains].
Nevertheless, one might ask: "How can there be a recollection of the Vedas when separated by a great dissolution (mahāpralaya)? To this, he says:

"And in the beginningless cycle of transmigration, as in the cases of sleep and waking. Although there is a difference between the states of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution in that, in the former, only the vital breaths remain while in the latter, they are entirely absent; [nevertheless, the recollection occurs].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that there is no difference between the states of deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, because they are identical in their commonality of being a residue of ignorance characterized by dissolution accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the distraction of karma.
Now, an objection may be raised: "But surely not everyone is in the state of deep sleep simultaneously, since some are awakened at that time."

Since it is possible for them to grasp [the relationship] upon waking from sleep, and since there is no destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) due to the absence of the two causes of such destruction— namely, death and the great distance of time— the continuity of linguistic usage regarding the relationship between words and their meanings is logical, provided that the *vāsanā* exists. However, the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) affects all living beings simultaneously.

Since the long duration of time and the distance from the time of departure are there the causes for the total destruction of the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), how can it be that the activity of a subsequent awakening occurs just like the activity of a previous awakening—as in the case of deep sleep?
To this objection, he says: "It might be so:
[as in] sleep."
He refutes this: "This is not a fault,
even though there would be the cessation of conventional usage."
This is the intended meaning: neither the time of death nor the distance of time can destroy all saṃskāras;
for otherwise, it would be impossible for a newborn to experience joy, fear, or grief through the continuity of memories from previous practice.
Furthermore, it would follow that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of human birth—separated by thousands of other births—could never be manifested again by the karma that brings about a human birth.
Therefore, if even for those of inferior intellect there is a persistence of prior latent impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*) despite the remoteness of the time of death and other such factors,

what need is there to mention the case of those of great intellect, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, who— by the grace of the Supreme Lord— are endowed with excellence in dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty?
Just as a decline in knowledge and other qualities is experienced among all beings from humans down to worms, [so too is their excellence].
Thus, even among humans, up to the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, there is the possibility of an excellence of knowledge and other qualities.
And so, the statements of the Vedas and Smṛtis that proclaim this attain unimpeded authority.

In this way, it is possible for these venerable ones, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others who are graced by the Supreme Lord, to maintain a continuous connection with all worldly transactions belonging to other kalpas.
The rest is easy to understand.
This might be the case:
let there be for them a continuity of conventional usage based on other conceptual constructions.
But in this creation, the land is indeed different, their objects are indeed different, and the castes and stages of life are indeed different.
From dharma comes misfortune and from adharma comes prosperity;
likewise, what is desired becomes misfortune and what is undesired becomes prosperity, because this creation is unprecedented.
Therefore, there is no need here for the consideration of conventions from other kalpas.
Because it would be ineffective;
and furthermore, due to the destruction of prior linguistic convention, both the relationship between word and meaning and the Veda itself would result in being non-eternal. To this, he says:
"And for the sake of living beings attaining happiness."
For creation proceeds according to the power of the intrinsic nature of things as they actually exist; indeed, it is not possible to alter that intrinsic power.
For happiness can never be abandoned in its true essence.
And suffering will be sought after;
moreover, the causal capacity of dharma and adharma never undergoes reversal,
for a cloth does not arise from a lump of clay.
Furthermore, a jar is produced from threads;

if that were so, then because there would be no restriction on the causal capacity of things (*vastu-sāmarthya-niyama*), everything could arise from everything. Thus, even one who is thirsty might quench his thirst by bringing fire, or one afflicted by cold might alleviate the chill by bringing water.

Therefore, even in another creation, it is established that the sequence remains the same: acts such as the killing of a Brahmin are causes of misfortune, while acts such as sacrifice are causes of merit.
Likewise, the very same Vedas that exist in this kalpa exist in other kalpas as well; their meanings are the same, and the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramas) are likewise the same.

When the possibility of observed similarity exists, to postulate its dissimilarity contradicts both inference and scripture. Furthermore, many scriptures— known as Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇa— which have been shown here by the author of the Bhāṣya, would otherwise be subverted.
Therefore, it has been well said:
"And because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence," as in the passage, "Agni, indeed, desired."
Based on the future function [of the fire], the sacrificer himself is called "Agni";
for there is no other Agni-fire that is a separate deity from the one already present.

(JS 1.3.8) Jaimini [maintains] that there is no entitlement [to Vedic rites] for those who are not human, because such [rites] are impossible in the case of honey [offerings] and the like. (JS 1.3.31)
One who asserts that the gods and sages possess eligibility for all Brahma-vidyās becomes subject to the following inquiry:
Is it by way of no distinction that all [beings] have eligibility for all Brahma-vidyās, or is it only for certain [vidyās] that certain [beings] have eligibility?
If it is without distinction for all [vidyās],...
Consequently, [the meditations] on honey and so forth would be impossible.
How so?
For in the passage, "The sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," human beings would have to worship the sun by superimposing the nature of honey upon it.
For the relationship of the object of worship and the worshiper is based on difference; it cannot exist within the very self of the deity Āditya.
Nor is there another Āditya, because the previous Ādityas of this kalpa have exhausted their office.
Furthermore, having commenced with the five [forms] beginning with the red, which have the sun as their support—this is the meaning:
"That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.1.1); it is called "honey" because, like honey, it is a cause of joy for the gods.
The Śruti describes its similarity to the honey of bees: "Of that honey, the sky itself is the cross-beam."
The atmosphere is the honeycomb;
for the atmosphere, or the ether, is the "comb"— the layer— of the honey that is the sun, because it is situated therein.

Furthermore, those substances such as Soma, clarified butter, and milk which are offered into the fire, having undergone digestion by means of the solar rays conjoined with the fire and having attained the state of nectar (*amṛta*), are carried to the solar orb by the *ṛc* mantras, which act like bees. For just as bees, having gathered honey-nectar from flowers, bring it to their own abode, so too the bees that are the *ṛc* mantras—

by means of the recollection of the meanings inherent in the ritual performance and other factors— having gathered [the essence] from the ritual-flowers prescribed in the *Ṛgveda*, bring forth what is produced therefrom.
They bring the nectar from the solar orb by means of its eastern ray-tubes, which are red;
the Vasus subsist upon that nectar.
Now, from this honey of the sun, they draw [the nectar] by means of its southern ray-tubes, which are white, from the flowers of the rites prescribed in the Yajurveda.

Having been offered into the fire as before, Soma and other substances attain the state of nectar; the bees that are the mantras of the Yajurveda bring this nectar to the solar orb, and the Rudras subsist upon this very nectar.
Then, from the flowers of the rites prescribed by the Sāmaveda, [the bees draw] through the western rays of this honey of the sun, which are like dark-colored tubes.

Having been offered into the fire, the soma and other substances, as before, attain the state of nectar; the bees that are the Sāman mantras and hymns bring this nectar to the solar orb, and the Ādityas subsist upon that nectar.

Then, from the Atharva-veda and Veda-enjoined ritual flowers, the bees that are the Atharva-Aṅgiras mantras bring [the offering] into the fire; having been offered, the soma and other substances, as before, attain the state of nectar through those northerly, exceedingly dark-colored rays which are like tubes.
Likewise, from the flowers of the rituals of the Aśvamedha and Vācastoma, bees in the form of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas bring [nectar] to the solar orb.
Because of the scriptural statement, "In the Aśvamedha and the Vācastoma, they recite the Pāriplava," there is indeed the employment of the mantras of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as well.
The Maruts subsist upon that nectar.

Now, those upward-tending tubular vessels of his which belong to the honey of the sun and are to be protected—by means of them, the bees that are the practitioners of meditation bring [the nectar] from the flower of the syllable Om and carry it to the solar orb;
the Sādhyas subsist upon that nectar.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: these five tubular vessels, beginning with the "red" (rohitā), which depend on the sun and are connected to the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas, are taught in their proper sequence.

Having seen and obtained this very nectar (amṛta) according to their respective capacities through all their instruments—the ear and so forth—and having obtained that nectar consisting of fame, splendor, the integrity of the senses, vigor, food, and nourishment within the sun, they are satisfied.
Indeed, because it provides delight to the gods, such as the Vasus, by means of that nectar, the sun is "honey" (madhu).
What is meant is this: it is not only the relationship of the object of meditation and the meditator that is contradictory in a single entity; [rather, the same applies to other relations].
Moreover, there is the relationship between the knower and the known, as well as the relationship between that which is attained and that by which it is attained.
Likewise, the statement "fire is a foot" was indeed spoken for the purpose of enjoining the contemplation of Brahman upon the ether with respect to the divine sphere (adhidaivata).
For the all-pervasiveness of space and its lack of form and other qualities constitute its similarity to Brahman;
and of this very space that is Brahman, the four feet—Agni and the others—are shown by the passage beginning with "Fire is a foot.
Just as the feet of a cow are not separated from the cow, [so too are these feet not separate from Brahman].
In this way, fire and the others also do not [encompass] space, even though it is all-pervading; thus, they are the "feet" of space.

Having thus enjoined the meditation on space as Brahman by means of its four feet, the text now magnifies air—whose quality is "absorption"—in order to enjoin it as the object of meditation in its own form: "Air, indeed, is the absorber.
Likewise, in order to enjoin the sun as the object of meditation through the vision of it as Brahman in its own form, the text magnifies it:

"The instruction that 'the sun is Brahman' is the teaching (*upadeśa*). The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. If it should be argued that there is no qualification [to the contrary] such that all gods and sages have the right (*adhikāra*) to all knowledges of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*):"
But as far as possible, this [objection] presents itself:
"And because of existence in light."
For in the world, the application of words such as "sun" and the resulting cognitions are observed with respect to the orbs of light and so forth;
yet these possess no consciousness,
for in them no activities corresponding to those [of conscious beings] are seen, as is the case with Devadatta and others.
It might be argued:
[the proof is] "from mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, purāṇas, and common usage.
In that regard, there is the mantra: "O Indra, we have grasped your right hand, which laughs with joy. And:
And [the verse] "Kāśir indra it": *kāśiḥ* means a fist.
Likewise: "With powerful neck, pot-bellied, and strong-armed, in the intoxication of the soma-juice..."
The mantra-explanatory passages (*mantrārthavāda*) declare that the deity possesses a physical body, stating: "Indra slays the Vṛtras.

Likewise, they show that the deity partakes of the sacrificial oblation, as in: "Eat, O Indra; drink of what has been set forth," and so on. Similarly, regarding lordship: "Indra rules over heaven, Indra rules over the earth, Indra rules over the waters, and Indra rules over the mountains."
"Indra is the increaser; Indra is the wise among the wise; Indra is to be invoked in peace and in exertion"—thus [it is said].
Likewise, "The Lord of this world, the beholder of heaven, the Lord of the mortal"—thus [it is said].

Furthermore, it shows the grace of the deity toward one who honors her, and the granting of fruits by her when she is pleased: "By oblations alone he pleases the gods who eat the offerings; pleased with him, they grant food and strength."
And they grant [their favor], as it is said:
"Indra, being satisfied himself, satisfies him with offspring and cattle.
The authors of the Dharmaśāstras also say: "Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires."
Thus, numerous Purāṇic statements establish the fivefold expansion beginning with the embodied form of the deities;
even worldly people remember and represent this fivefold expansion of the deities' forms and so forth.
For instance, they depict Yama as holding a staff in his hand.
They speak of Varuṇa as having a noose in his hand and Indra as having a thunderbolt in his hand;
and they call the deities "consumers of the oblation."
Likewise, they say of this [goddess] that she is the village of the gods and the field of the gods.

And they speak of her favor and the granting of fruits by her when she is pleased: "Paśupati is pleased with him; a son has been born to him," or "Dhanada is pleased with him; wealth has been obtained by him."
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) refutes this as follows:
"No," it is said;
for there is no such thing as what is called "the world" (loka).
Indeed, there is no such thing as "worldly consensus" (*loka*) that is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinct from perception and the others;
rather, worldly consensus derives its status as truth when it is rooted in perception and the like.
In their absence, however, it collapses due to the lack of a foundation, like a line of blind men following one another.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition, such as direct perception and the like, regarding the creation of the world and so forth;
nor can it be that history (itihāsa) and similar sources serve as its foundation,
since they too, being of human origin, depend upon direct perception and other such means of knowledge.
And because perception and the other means of knowledge are absent here, he says:
"Even the Itihāsas and Purāṇas [do not establish this]. Now, it was argued that the fivefold set beginning with the embodied form is established through mantras and arthavādas; therefore, he says:

"Even the explanatory passages (arthavādas)" means that since the explanatory passages form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive statement, they are intent upon characterizing the excellence of the object of the injunction; they cannot be authoritative with respect to their own literal meaning.
For those who know the logic of verbal testimony hold that "whatever a word is primarily intended to signify, that is its meaning."
However, where [a property] is established even regarding its own referent by means of another instrument of knowledge—
as, for example, the swiftness of the wind—
it is accepted there on account of that other instrument of knowledge, and not through the power of the word itself.
But where there is no other means of valid cognition, as in the case of the fivefold group beginning with the embodied form (vigraha), that meaning must be understood from the word alone.
And a word that is not primarily intent upon something cannot be capable of making that thing understood;
therefore, even in that case, one must admit that there is a primary intent toward understanding that very thing.
Furthermore, since a single sentence cannot be intent upon two things simultaneously, the sentence would otherwise be split.
Furthermore, when a single unified sentence is possible, it is not proper to assume a split of sentences (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, the idea that the possession of a physical body and so forth—which is not apprehended by other means of knowledge—is to be understood from words intended for another purpose, is merely a vain wish; this is the meaning.

Moreover, mantras, being employed here and there through direct statement (*śruti*) and other criteria like the rice-grains (*vrīhi*), enter into the process of ritual production (*bhāvanā*) as authoritative means.
When the question arises as to how those [words] are employed in their respective ritual acts, since a visible mode of operation is possible, it is not appropriate to assume an invisible one.
And the visible mode is the recollection of the meaning inherent in the performance;
for indeed, performers carry out the constituent elements of the rite only after having recollected them.

Furthermore, since words generally possess a primary intention toward their own referents (*arthaparatā*), it is not appropriate for mantras—which are intended to cause the recollection of meanings connected with the required ritual performance—to have an intention directed toward things such as the physical form (*vigraha*) of a deity that are not already known. Therefore, since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the existence of a deity’s corporeal form and so forth, it follows that this [matter] falls within the domain of the sixth means of knowledge (*ṣaṣṭhapramāṇa*). This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). //32// 1.3.8.33.
This being the case, it is replied: "But there is existence, according to Bādarāyaṇa; for [it is so].
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view.
The passage beginning with this and ending with "the insentience of the element of the elements in the sun and so forth is admitted" has its meaning not obscure.
"Because of the usage of mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and so forth.
By the inclusion of "and so forth," the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras are understood.
This means because one observes the usage—that is, the application—of mantras and the other aforementioned texts.
He restates the prima facie position with the words, "As for what was also said...
He first offers a rebuttal according to the view of a certain school of thought.
—To this we reply:
having raised the opponent's prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes it. Here the opponent says:
This is indeed the nature of verbal cognition, namely that its function is dependent upon the intended meaning (tātparya);
for a word whose primary purport lies elsewhere cannot serve as a means of valid knowledge regarding anything else.
For the sentence "The white [dog] runs" (śveto dhāvati), which is intended to describe the washing away of a leper's mark, cannot imply from this context the movement of a dog;
nor can a positive injunction in the form of a subordinate sentence-meaning be understood within a great sentence containing a negative particle (nañ);
nor does that meaning belong to it merely by virtue of the suffix alone.
This is because that cognition is erroneous;
however, this is not the case for perception and the other means of valid cognition.
For one who seeks to fetch water, the eye opened upon seeing a jar does not fail to perceive the jar and cloth, or the cloth alone.
When the proponent of the partial view (ekadeśin) has been thus refuted by the opponent, the proponent of the final established doctrine (paramasiddhāntavādin) says:
"To this it is replied: the presentation is unequal.

The underlying intention is this: in the world, words are employed to convey a qualified meaning; they do not terminate merely in the recollection of their own individual referents in the absence of that [qualified meaning].
Indeed, the use of words in the world has never before been observed for the mere purpose of reminding one of their own individual meanings;
rather, it is seen to function toward the meaning of the sentence.

And since these words are not capable of directly conveying the sentence-meaning without first reminding one of their own meanings, the intermediate operation of words—namely, the reminding of their own meanings—is postulated as the means for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, that for whose sake something exists does not reach its completion without it; thus, words do not terminate in the expression of their own primary meaning alone.
Nor does a sentence containing the negative particle *nañ* terminate in a positive injunction;
for if that were the case, the word *nañ* would be meaningless.
As they have said: "Although the phonemes directly effect the communication of word-meanings, they nevertheless do not terminate in that [process], which would otherwise be fruitless."
In their activity toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the presentation of word-meanings is an indispensable factor,
just as fire is for wood in the process of cooking.
Thus,
this is the method for a single sentence.
However, where one sentence is connected with another sentence, there, in accordance with worldly usage, the understanding of the actual meaning [is derived].
Furthermore, this connection is established because each individual sentence has its function exhausted by conveying its own specific qualified meaning;

subsequently, when there arises an expectation for another purpose due to some cause, the syntactical connection is postulated. This is as in the passage: "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity; one should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu. In this case, the connection is understood later.

For in this context, if the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) did not lead the collection of Vedas—denoted by the term *svādhyāya*—toward the status of being a human goal, then the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), which terminate merely in [the description of] existing facts, would never attain syntactic unity with the injunctive statement.

Therefore, by virtue of the injunction for the study of one's own Veda, when there arises an expectancy as to the purpose (*kaimarthyākāṅkṣā*), these passages—having as their domain historical events and so forth—indicate the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the enjoined act by means of making those events known; they do not, however, have the power to indicate it while their own literal meaning remains unintended.
If that were the case, there would be no indication (lakṣaṇā) at all,

because the seed of indication— the inseparable connection with the primary meaning— would be absent. For this very reason, in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the word "Ganges" indicates the bank as something connected to its own primary meaning, but not the ocean shore.
For what reason?
Because there is an absence of proximity to one's own purpose.
And none of this is possible if there is no intention to express one's own purpose.
For this very reason, in cases where explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are seen to contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
such as "The sacrificial post is indeed the sun" or "The grass-bundle is the sacrificer," and so forth,
[the interpretation] must be such that there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

And as to how they serve the purpose of praise, Jaimini, for the sake of establishing both [the literal meaning and the figurative], composed two sūtras: "But it is a figurative statement" (*guṇavādastu*) and "The establishment of that" (*tatsiddhiḥ*).

Therefore, where the literal meaning of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) is contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there the definition of excellence is indicated through figurative speech (*guṇavāda*); this is a case of "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

However, where there is corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that object is established through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) just as it is through that other means of valid cognition; for both function with mutual independence regarding a single object, like perception and inference.
Nevertheless, from the perspective of the cognizer, [the arthavāda] is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*).
For an unlearned knower does not understand an object from the Veda in the same way he understands it through perception and other means,
because in that case [the Veda] depends upon learning and so forth;
but this is not due to a dependence on the means of knowledge themselves.
It has been stated that "because two [means of knowledge] are independent with respect to their own objects.
Now, one might ask: even when there is a contradiction with another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), why does it become a figurative statement (*guṇavāda*)?
For, when there is a contradiction with verbal testimony (*śabda*), why is it not the other means of knowledge itself that is sublated?

Just as the categories of perception and so forth, which have the phenomenal world as their object, are set aside by the Vedāntas whose subject matter is non-duality, why then are the Vedāntas not also interpreted through figurative description (*guṇavāda*), like explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)?
To this it is replied: according to worldly convention, the objects of words are indeed twofold.
Both by way of the door and by way of the purport.

Just as in a single sentence the meanings of the words are the object by way of the door and the meaning of the sentence is the object by way of the purport, so it is also in the case of two sentences forming a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
For example, "This cow belonging to Devadatta is to be purchased" is one sentence.
"This cow has much milk"—this is another [instance], where the demonstration of its having much milk serves as the door (dvāra).
However, the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in the sense of another sentence, namely, "it should be purchased.
In that case, what is presented by way of the door is interpreted otherwise when it contradicts other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Just as the sentence "Eat poison" is intended to convey the meaning of another sentence, such as "Do not eat in his house," so too, where there is a primary intention (*tātparya*), human testimony remains a valid means of knowledge even when contradicted by other means of knowledge. However, the Vedantas, upon thorough examination of their preceding and succeeding parts, are devoted solely to establishing Brahman, in which the manifold world of difference has been entirely sublated.

Because it is not of human origin, a statement that is inherently established as having ultimate validity—even if it purports to establish that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the sun—is in fact intended as a praise of the post.
Therefore, when there is a contradiction with another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the subject matter, acting as a means, is interpreted through figurative description (*guṇavāda*).
However, where no contradicting means of knowledge exists, [the literal meaning stands].
Just as in the case of a drought caused by a deity and so forth, there the object, even when perceived through the gateway [of the senses], cannot be dismissed;
nor can it be interpreted as being figurative speech (*guṇavāda*).
For when the primary sense is possible, one should not resort to a merely figurative sense, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that "in that case, the sentence would be split (*bhidyeta*) while explaining the unestablished etymological analysis (*vigraha*) and so forth," this is certainly true;
this sentence is indeed split.

If it is argued that this being so, there would also be a difference in intention (*tātparya*), we say no; for when that [meaning] is understood even by way of a secondary door (*dvāra*), it is impossible to postulate a further intention.
Nor is there a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding a matter where a certain [text] has no intention.

That being the case, the principle that "a sentence intended for the qualified [object] is not an authority regarding the qualifiers" would imply that even a sentence intended for the qualified could not be authoritative,
because it would not have the qualifiers as its object.
However, if one attempts to imply those qualifiers by means of the qualified object itself, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

For if the qualifiers are understood through implication, then the status of having a qualified object follows; and conversely, if there is a qualified object, then the implication of those qualifiers occurs.

Therefore, even in cases where the intention is directed toward a qualified cognition, the qualifiers being perceived must be admitted—even by one who does not wish to do so—as the very objects of that sentence, just as in the following example:

Therefore, when forms and other attributes of deities are understood even from other explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), they ought not to be discarded provided there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For figurative interpretation (*guṇavāda*) is not tenable when the primary meaning is possible;
nor does even a non-human (authorless) statement, when it conveys a factual matter, depend upon another means of valid cognition regarding its own object.
By this it was stated that [the scripture] would be non-authoritative because another means of knowledge is impossible.
This might be the case:
even if there is unity of purport, if there were a division of sentences, [it would follow].

How, then, is it that "a sentence is one because its meaning is one"? It is not so; for in each case, it is possible for the cognition to culminate in a single object qualified by its respective various word-meanings.
However, the distinction is merely this: in some cases that single object qualified by other word-meanings serves as the means (*dvāra*), while in others it is the end (*dvārī*).

[Objection: If that were the case, then even in the sentence "Having eaten rice, he goes to the village," there would be the undesirable consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), for the connection [of meaning] in "having eaten rice" is one thing, while that in "he goes to the village" is another. [Reply: No.
Because the cognition [of the gerund] does not terminate in a single instance;
for by the word "having eaten" (*bhuktvā*), both the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) and anteriority in time (*pūrvakālatā*) are cognized.
And this cognition does not reach its conclusion without the perception of another action occurring at a subsequent time.

Therefore, since the comprehension of a qualified object reaches its conclusion within as many as five or six words, there is no contingency of multiplicity in a single sentence consisting of that many words. Even if the qualifiers are multiple, the qualified object remains one;
and because that principal element, having been heard only once, cannot be repeated merely to conform to its subordinate qualifiers.
But if there were a difference in the primary objects (pradhāna), there would indeed be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda).

Therefore, it is established that the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is distinct from the injunctive sentence (vidhivākya); thus, since the operations of both sentences are completed by the cognition of their respective sentence-meanings, their mutual connection occurs only later when some requirement arises.
Furthermore, it is precisely by means of the injunctions themselves that [the rites] have Indra and others as their deities.
The essence of a sacrifice (*yāga*) consists in the relinquishment of ownership over an oblation with reference to a deity after having touched it.
Now, a deity cannot be designated unless it is inscribed in the mind;

nor can that which lacks form be inscribed in the mind. Therefore, by the very injunction of the sacrifice, which requires such a form, whatever form is understood from other sources—namely, from mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) whose primary intent lies elsewhere—that form must be accepted.
Because there is no evidence for postulating a different form [of the person],
and because it would entail that the *mantras* and *arthavādas* function regarding something entirely beyond perception;

for just as in the case of the injunction, "The *vrātya* sacrifices with the *vrātyastoma*," when the specific nature of the *vrātya* is required, the definition provided by the injunction— "he whose father or grandfather does not drink *soma* is a *vrātya*"— is what is expected, rather than [the meaning] from the *arthavāda*.
That which is being understood is established by the authority of an injunction;
likewise is the form of the deity.
Now, it may be argued that the mention [of the deity] requires knowledge of its form, but not even the existence of that form.

Since the cognition of form is possible even through the superimposition of the deity, it is precisely the superimposed form that is spoken of as the deity by means of mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas).
True, it depends upon the cognition of form;
and since that is not possible from any other source, it arises only from mantras and explanatory passages.
Furthermore, since there is no sublation of that form, it is improper to abandon its existence as it is established in experience and instead imagine it to be otherwise when such is not experienced.

Therefore, it is logical that the form of the deity—being presented to the mind by mantras and arthavādas which, though having other purposes, are required by the injunction—is indeed based on the authority of the injunction itself.
This may be so.
An object understood even from a sentence with a different purpose is accepted only when there is an expectation for an injunction; however, in this case, such an expectation does not exist,
because the deity consists of the form of the word itself.
And because that [form] is cognizable by other means of knowledge, he says:
"Nor is it mere word.
The establishment of the embodied form and so forth does not arise from mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) alone.

Rather, he says— “itihāsa,” etc.— whether [the knowledge] is derived from the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and traditional recollections (smṛti) which have their root in the explanatory passages (arthavāda) of the Mantras, or from direct perception which has no such root;
it “coheres” (śliṣyate), that is, it is logically consistent.
The rest has been explained merely by way of summary.

Thus, since the embodied form and other attributes of the deity are established through mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and so forth, the sacrifice consisting of the worship of the deity—just like the worship of teachers and others—is logically possible as being fruitful by means of the deity’s grace and the like.
However, for that which is insentient, such worship is impossible because it cannot receive it.

Nor, because the sacrificial act (*yajñakarman*) is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the deity, must one abandon the scripturally stated fruitfulness of the sacrificial productive activity (*yāgabhāvanā*) in the production of the fruit from the deity, nor the scripturally stated instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the sacrifice with respect to that deity or its portion of the fruit.

For it is precisely the sacrificial productive activity, being fruitful, that possesses as its intermediate operation— characterized by the sacrifice— the feeding of the deity, [its] satisfaction, and so forth.
Just as in the case of agricultural work, each intermediate operation is a means for obtaining the harvest;
or just as, according to your own view, the rites such as the Āgneya sacrifice possess the capacity to produce heaven through the intermediate operations of the originary and ultimate *apūrva*s;
