therefore, because the action—whether by way of the intermediate operation of the *apūrva* or the intermediate operation of the deity’s grace—is possessed of the fruit, its status as the primary factor is equal in both positions.

However, it is not the case that the deity—possessing a physical form and so forth—is the primary factor; thus, there is no contradiction with the *Sūtra* of the *Dharmamīmāṃsā*: "Or rather, because it is preceded by the [Vedic] word, the sacrificial act is primary, while the mention of the deity is subordinate.
Therefore, it is established that deities generally possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). //33// 1.3.9.34.
For it is indicated by the hearing of Śuka’s disregard [for the world] and his rushing toward that [state].
Establishing the intermediate connection, he states the purport of the section: "Just as [the scriptures] have human beings as their qualified recipients."
He states the seed of doubt with the words "therein" (tatra):
for what conscious being, indeed, would there not be a desire for that eternal bliss from which all connection with suffering has been wiped away?
On account of which [lack of qualification], a Śūdra would not be entitled [to Vedic study] due to the absence of need;
nor is there an absence of capacity for him regarding the knowledge of Brahman.
For capacity is indeed twofold: innate and adventitious.
If it is argued that, while the innate capacity for hearing and so forth is unimpeded for Śūdras just as it is for the twice-born,
they lack qualification because of the absence of such capacity due to the lack of Vedic study,
then alas!

It may be argued that in the absence of the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), there is an absence of fire, and thus there can be no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to those rites accomplished by means of fire;
however, since fire is not a requisite means for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), why should those who have not established the sacred fires be excluded from it?
Nor is it correct to say that they lack entitlement to the knowledge of Brahman because they lack the entitlement to its means—namely, Vedic study—due to their failure to establish the fires.

For it is logical that since the *āhavanīya* fire is prescribed as the locus for the oblation in the injunction "one offers in the *āhavanīya*," its specific nature is non-worldly (*alaukika*), being unattainable from any source other than the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) enjoined by a text not connected to a specific ritual context; and since that *ādhāna* is prescribed as pertaining only to the twice-born (*dvija*), the fire produced thereby is non-worldly and does not belong to a *śūdra*.
Thus, a *śūdra* has no entitlement to rituals accomplished through the *āhavanīya* and other such fires.
Furthermore, there is no extraordinary means for the knowledge of Brahman that would not be available to a Śūdra.
If it is argued that this is due to the restrictive rule regarding Vedic study, we say no; for such an argument cannot withstand scrutiny.
That study would either be restricted to the human goal,
as in the case of receiving gifts and so forth for the acquisition of wealth;
or it would be restricted to the purpose of the sacrifice.
For example, threshing in the injunction "one threshes the rice" is not for the sake of the sacrifice; likewise,
the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" is not recited with reference to any particular sacrifice.
Just as, with reference to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is said, "One threshes the rice-grains";
nor does that which is taught independently (anārabhyādhīta) bring to mind a sacrifice by virtue of an inseparable connection with one,
such that the study [of the text] would be connected with that sacrifice solely through the sentence itself.
For the Veda (svādhyāya) is not invariably connected with a sacrifice in the same way that the sacrificial ladle (juhū) and other implements are;
therefore, the restriction is neither for the sake of the sacrifice nor for the sake of the person.

The sequence of actions (*itikartavyatā*) is indeed based solely on human desire; however, engagement in those sequences, both generally and specifically, is entirely dependent upon injunction (*vidhi*).
For one who has not yet understood the distinction between the instruments (*karaṇa*) cannot properly engage in the sequences of action.
Therefore, because their activity is dependent upon an injunction (*vidhi*), the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) have the sacrifice as their purpose (*kratvarthatā*).
By the word "sacrifice" (*kratu*), one refers to the injunction (*vidhi*) which is the object of the injunction by means of its subject.
That which is sought after—that is, that which is made the object—is "for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvartha*).
Furthermore, neither study, nor private recitation (*svādhyāya*), nor the knowledge of its meaning, prior to the injunction, functions through a motivation dependent on human desire,
such that it would constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Moreover,
if the comprehension of meaning were restricted by the act of study itself, there would be a contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

Since that [knowledge] can be attained even without formal study—that is, even by reading from books and the like—it follows that, as in the case of the expression "a load of gold," the fruit must be understood as resulting from the study itself. Consequently, because the injunction for study would lack restrictive force, a Śūdra would possess the capacity either through formal study or through reading from books and the like; thus, he too would be entitled to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).
Let it not be that there is no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman everywhere due to the absence of Vedic study;
however, it will exist in the case of the Saṃvarga-vidyā,
because that [instruction] was imparted after addressing a Śūdra with the words, "O Śūdra, you have indeed brought [the fuel]."

Furthermore, this word "śūdra" cannot be applied to a non-Śūdra through any etymological derivation of its parts, because the conventional meaning of a whole word is stronger than the meaning derived from its individual components due to its independence.

Therefore, just as a Niṣāda carpenter has the right to perform the Iṣṭi sacrifice by virtue of the power of the scriptural injunction despite not being a student, it follows that a Śūdra will likewise have the right to the Saṃvarga-vidyā. This is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
This being the case, we reply:
there is no entitlement for a Śūdra because of the absence of Vedic study.

This is the intended meaning: although the injunction for study, "One's own Veda is to be studied," is not recorded as being introduced in connection with any specific fruitful ritual action, [it nevertheless implies its own fruit].
Nor does it pertain to a word-meaning whose connection to a sacrifice (*kratu*) is invariable;
for the Veda (*svādhyāya*), unlike the *juhū* ladle and so forth, does not have an invariable connection to a sacrifice.

Nevertheless, the injunction for the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of studying the Veda, by making known that study is a required means [to an end], [does not lead to a result] like the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, nor to heaven, or—

In this matter— whether one should assume a fruit based on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as in the injunction "gold is to be worn," and thus interpret the application (*viniyoga*) by breaking its syntactical connection to mean "one should study for the sake of Vedic recitation" (*svādhyāya*); or whether, having attained from elsewhere what is required for the supreme goal, one should find fulfillment—

it is not appropriate to assume an unmentioned unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭa*) arising solely from the act of study by breaking the application prescribed by the scripture, when it is possible to justify the application exactly as heard through a visible means, even if indirectly, and when the attainment of what is required from elsewhere is already established.
Moreover, the refinement resulting from the study and recitation of the Veda is observed;
for by that means, the person attains it,
and once attained, it produces the fruit of the knowledge of karma and Brahman, which has the purpose of both worldly prosperity and the supreme good.
However, in the case of wearing gold ornaments and the like, there is nothing required by a person even indirectly through a visible means;
therefore, setting aside the indirect application, a result is postulated directly from the act of wearing itself by breaking the rule of syntactical connection (*viniyoga*).

And when, through the *svādhyāya* (Veda) refined by study, the realization of ritual action and Brahman—which brings about prosperity and the supreme good—is being cultivated as the result, [the Veda serves its purpose].

Thus it has been established that the comprehension of ritual action (*karma*) and Brahman, which has prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as its purpose, belongs only to him for whom there is study (*adhyayana*), and not to anyone else;
and study belongs only to him for whom there is the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*);

and since that [initiation] belongs only to the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the comprehension of the meaning produced by the recitation of the *svādhyāya* read from books and so forth—due to the absence of the study-sacrament resulting from the absence of initiation—is [not valid].

It is established that because Śūdras do not possess the capacity prescribed by the scriptures— as indicated by the statement "it does not lead to fruit for Śūdras"— a Śūdra is not entitled to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). The mention of "the sacrifice" (*yajña*) is intended as an illustration.
It should also be understood that [the person] is not qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*).
This is because the statement is made as an established fact (*siddhavat*) based on reasoning (*nyāya*), and that reasoning is the same in both cases.
He restates the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):
As for the argument that this is stated in the *Saṃvarga-vidyā*, he refutes it:
"That is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*)."
Why?
Because there is no logical justification.
For a Śūdra is not directly mentioned in the Saṃvarga-vidyā.
For example, there is the case of "one should cause the Niṣādasthapati to sacrifice with this [offering]," where the term *niṣādasthapati* occurs;

however, the Mīmāṃsakas of the Adhvara school maintain that this word *śūdra* occurs within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and as such, it merely illuminates a meaning already established by other means rather than enjoining it as a new rule.

For us, however, even from another person's statement, when the meaning is understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), and is required by an injunction (*vidhi*), it is certainly accepted. And the reasoning regarding this point has been stated as a sublater [of the opponent's view].
Furthermore, there is no requirement for an injunction [in this case].

Because the injunction reaches its conclusion through the attainment of the qualification for the twice-born, this logical principle is set aside by the force of the direct statement (vacana), as in the case of the Niṣāda-sthapati; however, it has been stated that this [passage] does not fall under the heading of an injunction.
Therefore, the sense is that the eligibility of Śūdras is not established by a mere arthavāda.

Furthermore, on what basis is the eligibility of a Śūdra for knowledge in general, or specifically for the Saṃvarga-vidyā, established by the force of an explanatory passage (arthavāda)? It is not for knowledge in general;
as he says: "And let this [be so] at will.
For the explanatory passage heard in the context of the Saṃvarga-vidyā does not establish eligibility for knowledge in general, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
"Let it be then that the Śūdra has the entitlement only in the Saṃvarga-vidyā"; to this he says:
"Because it occurs in an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Does this mean that the word "Śūdra" here was uttered by mistake?
Nor is it appropriate [to apply this] to a shrine (caitya) and so forth, for that which is traditional is equal [in both cases]; therefore, he says:
"And this word 'śūdra' can [be explained]."
Thus, indeed, this story is told here: Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man who gave much, who was worthy of gifts through his faith, who prepared many kinds of food, and who was fond of guests.

In various villages, towns, and crossroads, he had guest-houses constructed, filled with diverse kinds of food and drink, thinking, "People coming from all directions will enjoy my food and drink in these guest-houses when they are in need."

Then, the virtuous celestial sages (*devarṣi*), delighted by the excellence of the virtues of that king who was so devoted to giving, assumed the form of swans and, for the sake of bestowing their favor, came at night during the summer season; they arrived above him as he stood upon the roof of his palace, having fastened a garland [around him]. Addressing the leading swan among them, one swan flying behind him spoke with wonder: [The text continues: "O King, you have indeed attained the fruit of your merit! For this reason, the gods, having become swans, have come to you. Having thus spoken, he descended from the sky and alighted upon the palace roof. Then, having honored those swans, the king, out of curiosity, asked them: "Who are you, O birds, that have come here? They replied: "We are celestial sages (*devarṣi*). We have come to you because we were pleased by your virtue. The king said: "I am indeed fortunate, since I have been graced by the presence of such holy ones. What can I do for you? Tell me. They replied: "O King, we have no need for anything else; we have come simply to behold you. The king said: "If you have no other purpose, then please accept this palace. They replied: "O King, we do not dwell in palaces; rather, we dwell in the forest. The king said: "If you have no need for this, then please accept this city. They replied: "O King, we do not dwell in cities; rather, we dwell in the forest. The king said: "If you have no need for this either, then please accept this kingdom. "O Bhallākṣa! Do not touch that light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa which extends through day and night into the heavenly world; let it not burn you!
To him who had spoken thus, the leading swan replied:

The meaning is this: he says "vara" (excellent) ironically, implying "not excellent" (*avara*). Alternatively, *vara* means "miserable," referring to this Jānaśruti;

Then, having heard from the words of the swan both his own extreme degradation and the pinnacle of excellence belonging to Raikva, Jānaśruti became dejected in mind;

Then, while still upon his couch, the king heard the sound of auspicious musical instruments mingled with thousands of hymns commenced by throngs of unrestrained bards proclaiming the end of the night; hearing this, he immediately summoned his charioteer and commanded him:
"Friend,..."

"Search diligently for that knower of Brahman named Raikva, who delights in solitude and possesses a yoked cart, in those various extremely secluded places such as forest thickets, mountain bowers, and riverbanks; having found him, report it to us.
And so, searching here and there, he saw in a certain very secluded spot a member of the Brāhmaṇa caste scratching an itch beneath a cart.
Having seen him and being convinced that "this must be Raikva," he sat down and questioned him with humility.
"O Blessed One, you are Raikva with the cart.
And having inferred from various gestures Raikva's consent to his state and his desire for the householder's life and wealth, the charioteer informed the king.

Having arrived, he addressed him:
"O Raikva, here are these six hundred cows, this gold coin, this necklace, and this chariot drawn by mules."
"Accept this;
instruct me, O Blessed One.

The sense is: "Let the chariot, which is drawn by horses (hāretvā), together with the horses (gobhiḥ), remain yours alone; what is the use of this wealth of mine, which is insufficient for the maintenance of a household life that lacks all necessary resources? However, the reading *āharetvā* has been criticized by the teachers because it is semantically redundant and because no correlate is provided for the word *gobhiḥ* ("with cows").

And because of his connection with the officiating priest Kāpeya, Abhipratārin is identified as one who is worthy of sacrifice (*yājya*).
And his status as a Kṣatriya follows from his being a Caitrarathi, according to the statement: "From him was born a certain lord of the Kṣatras named Caitrarathi.

She too did not know [the answer].

Therefore, Gautama proceeded to initiate Jābāla and instruct him, thinking, "Since there is no possibility of his being a Śūdra in this matter, I shall initiate you who are born of the twice-born.

And although the entire world is perceived as being accompanied by air, nevertheless the word "all," even though its application is relative, does not abandon its own primary meaning; rather, its scope becomes contracted.
The two words "prāṇa" and "vajra," however, when referring to Brahman, completely relinquish their own literal meanings.
Therefore, the contraction of one's livelihood is better than the abandonment of one's own purpose, because at least a trace of that purpose remains.
Furthermore, even the word "immortal" (amṛta), while denoting the absence of death, does not express its absolute absence for all time.
Since that [immortality] is possible even through the light of life—
as in the expression "the gods are immortal"— it follows,
on account of the scriptural passages concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the thunderbolt (*vajra*), that it is air alone that is intended here, not Brahman. This is the prima facie position.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply:
"Because of trembling.
Because the entire world, together with its wind, trembles.
The phrase "the Supreme Self alone" from the preceding passage is supplied here by *maṇḍūkapluti* (frog-leap), as it is understood through the word "from scripture" (*śabdāt*).
For this entire world does not differ from Brahman; it proceeds regularly in its own functions and does not overstep its boundaries.
What is meant is this: the mere contraction of a scriptural statement is not the reason for abandoning the literal meaning of that scripture.
Rather, there is a restriction of the literal sense (śruti) conditioned by the syntactic unity of the preceding and following passages as well as by the context.
This has been stated:
"In both the preceding and following portions of the text, we perceive that Brahman alone is being indicated."
"How could we understand that the wind is being pointed out here itself, or in the intermediate space?
By this, the unity of the sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*) has been shown.
Furthermore, by the commentary stating "also from the context" (*prakaraṇād api*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) has been explained.
Indeed, that which is asked must be answered primarily; this constitutes the relevant context (*prakaraṇa*).
If something other than what was asked were stated, the scripture would become invalid due to the fault of irrelevant prattle.
As for the statement that immortality is attained through the knowledge of *vāyu*, that is merely relative (*āpekṣika*).
For by the scriptural text, "He conquers repeated death," the conquest of *apamṛtyu* (accidental or premature death) is stated, but not the conquest of *paramamṛtyu* (the ultimate death);
this is because [the text] introduces a different context right there for that reason.

Furthermore, it is not only on the basis of that [specific] scriptural passage that [the conquest] is relative; rather, after designating the Supreme Self, the text declares, "Everything else is afflicted (*ārtam*)," thereby stating that the body and so forth are subject to affliction.
The meaning is that one who is afflicted by suffering does not become free from suffering through mere practice.
1.3.11.40. Because of the perception of light;
for in this context, the word "light" (jyotis) has its primary meaning in the sense of radiance (tejas).
Because [the word "self"] would be used in a secondary sense with respect to Brahman,
because direct scriptural statement (śruti) is more powerful than context (prakaraṇa), and because, as in the previous case, there is no restriction of the scriptural statement here.

On the contrary, in the case of the "Brahman-light" (brahmajyotis) view, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the *ktvā* suffix, which signifies a prior action; furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of "arising," light (*tejas*) alone is the light.
For it is said that "arising" means "going upward."
But it is not the knowledge of discrimination [that is meant].
Furthermore, "ascending" is possible in the case of light by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*).
And since the sun is the supreme light in relation to the light and so forth, having reached that—that is, having come into its proximity—one becomes manifest in one's own true form.
Upon reaching the world of the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahmaloka*), one is liberated gradually.
But in the view that [the goal] is the light of Brahman (*brahmajyotis*), what further "attainment of one's own nature" (*svarūpaniṣpatti*) could there be after having already become Brahman?

Furthermore, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the nature of Brahman as distinct from the body and so forth—which takes the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*)—is not itself the "attainment."
For that [light] precedes the state of becoming Brahman and does not follow it;
thus, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural use of the gerund suffix *ktvā* in the phrase "having reached this" (*etām upasaṃpadya*).
Therefore, since the three scriptural passages override the context, it follows that light alone is the "light" mentioned here.
This being the case, it is replied: the word "light" (jyotis) refers to the Supreme Brahman itself.
Why?
Because it is seen;
for its continuation is observed here in this context.
Indeed, that which is proposed as a thesis—
That which is examined in the middle and that which is concluded is precisely the primary meaning of the context.

However, all those elements falling within that context must be interpreted in accordance with it; they are not to be extracted from the context merely by following the literal force of the scriptural statement—such is the established rule of worldly practice.

Otherwise, in the case of the sentence concerning the *upāṃśuyāja*, which begins with the mention of the defect of monotony (*jāmitā*) and concludes with its remedy, the injunctions such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently" (*aviṣṇur upāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*), which fall within that context, would have to be followed according to the direct scriptural statement alone.
Various [absurd] consequences would follow.

Therefore, why now— disregarding the force of the well-established collective designation obtained through the context that "there should be exactly three *upasads* for the *sāhna* and twelve for the *ahīna*," and setting aside the name *ahargaṇa*— should the word *ahīna* somehow, by means of a forced etymological derivation, denote the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice (the *sāhna*) and apply [its characteristics] to that very same [rite]?
Let it enjoin twelve *upasads*;
for since its entire procedure is prescribed, it is not deficient in any respect from the sacrifice, and thus it may be called an *ahīna* (non-deficient).
Do not say so.

Since the establishment of a whole is stronger than the establishment of its parts, the direct statement (śruti) overrides the context (prakaraṇa); thus, it cannot enjoin [the twelve upasads] in relation to the Jyotiṣṭoma which possesses the quality of being a *sattra* (*ahīna*). Nor can it, being displaced from that context, enjoin them for a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), because enjoining a property belonging to one thing within the context of another is improper.
Because it would involve the hardship of reconnecting a context that has been interrupted by the intervention of unrelated words,

the twelve-fold number of *upasads* prescribed for the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice— which is established as the archetype (*prakṛti*) and thus extended to all *ahīna* sacrifices— is restated here like the *nivīta* rule and other such cases, in order to praise the injunction that "for the *sāhna*, three *upasads* are to be performed," while that [twelve-fold number] remains unremoved by the sentence "of the *dvādaśāha*."

Therefore, although the context (*prakaraṇa*) is set aside by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) "ahīna," there is no displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the sentence "of the twelve [stotras] for the ahīna" from that context.

As for the displacement of the mantras for the invocation of Pūṣan and others—which are recited within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma—due to the force of their indicative power (*liṅga*), that occurs because there is no other way; for those mantras possess purposefulness (*arthavattva*) in that specific ritual action, such as the sacrifice to Pūṣan.

In this context, however, since the instruction on the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) pertains to the means for attaining a result that has already been introduced, the sentence "This is the serene state" (*eṣa saṃprasādaḥ*), which conveys only a single indistinct part of that very clear exposition of the path of means, would be purposeless.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that the statement "This is the serene state" merely restates the path beginning with light in order to praise the practice of the aforementioned meditation on the Self—just as in the case of the phrase "of the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhīnasya*)—because such an interpretation as figurative praise (*stuti-lakṣaṇā*) would entail abandoning the primary intention of the word's own literal meaning. As for the phrase "of the twelve-day sacrifice," however...

Since a sentence whose purport is the connection of its own constituent meanings has no purpose in merely restating what is already established by context or interrupted by the context, it is indicated that [the statement] serves the purpose of praise (*stuti*). Furthermore, out of fear of this defect, one cannot abandon the well-known meaning of the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) and rely instead on the meaning of the parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*) in order to enjoin that the *sāhna* sacrifice itself must have twelve *upasads*.
Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of an option between the numbers three and twelve;
and because an option is not logical when a way out exists;
and because it would result in the meaninglessness of the terms *sāhna* and *ahīna*, which denote the Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion.

Because that [meaning] is understood from the context alone; however, in this case, since the intention concerns the connection with its own primary meaning, the aforementioned defect does not arise. Thus, by considering the preceding and following passages and in accordance with the context, even setting aside the conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) and the state of being prior in time, the Supreme Brahman is understood as "light" (*jyotis*) in conformity with the context.
As for what was stated— that the attainment of the Sun is taught for one desiring liberation—
that is not ultimate liberation,
but rather the attainment of the world of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahmaloka).
Nor does the statement "he manifests in his own form" refer to liberation by stages;
for there is neither going nor departure from the body for one who knows the reality of Brahman as described in this context.
Thus says the Śruti: "The vital breaths do not depart from him; they are merged right here."
Nor is there gradual liberation by means of that [attainment of the effected Brahman-world],

for the path beginning with light (arcirādi) leads to the world of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahmaloka), but it does not serve as a cause for becoming Brahman. As for the individual soul (jīva), since its liberation is caused by the direct realization of its own nature as the unconditioned, eternally pure, and enlightened Brahman, what purpose is served by reaching the world of the effected Brahman via the path of light?
In this case as well, there is no difficulty for the knower of Brahman, because that [attainment] is logically possible.
Therefore, the direct realization of the self—the serene living being (*jīva*)—in its own true nature as the ultimate Brahman upon reaching the light of the sun is not strained by the scripture.

Furthermore, since the term "light" is established as referring to the Person (*puruṣa*) rather than to physical radiance, by means of the subsequent qualification, "That is the highest light; He is the Supreme Person," which distinguishes it from mere luster.
It is established that the light is indeed the supreme Brahman, and not mere physical fire. 1.3.12.41.
"Because of the designation of space as being a different entity and so forth.

Although it was demonstrated in the section "Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks" that space is the Supreme Self due to the observation of the characteristics of Brahman, [the present discussion continues].

Nevertheless, because there is no observation of characteristics of the Supreme Self (paramātman) here as there was in that [previous] case, and because the "issuing forth" (nirvahaṇa) of names and forms is possible even in the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) by providing space for them, it is improper to abandon the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) without cause; furthermore,
the phrase "Brahman between name and form" does not state that the ether is situated between name and form, but rather that Brahman is.
Therefore, the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) is the "conductor" (*nirvahitrī*) of name and form;
and Brahman is the "interval" (*antara*), that is, the middle or the essence between these two.
But Brahman is not merely the conductor.
Or rather, the "intermediate space" (antarāla) is the one that leads out [to liberation];
therefore, because of this well-known usage, it follows that it is the elemental ether and not Brahman.
To this objection, it is replied: the supreme ether itself is Brahman.
Why? Because of the designation as being something other than the object [of the elements], and so forth.
Here, "space" is said to be that which sustains mere name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
however, how could the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), being a modification and thus included within name-and-form, sustain itself?
For even a highly trained and wise person does not venture to carry himself on his own shoulder;

nor is it proper—when possible—to restrict the term *nāmarūpa*, which is applied without distinction, to exclude the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and apply it instead to another kind of *nāmarūpa*; furthermore, it is not appropriate to interpret with some forced difficulty as dependent upon something else a mark of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*) that is understood to signify an unimpeded capacity for sustaining all things.
Furthermore, in the passage, "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva), let me evolve names and forms," the creatorship of Brahman is perceived as an extremely clear characteristic (liṅga).
And since the living self acts as the evolving agent only by virtue of being of the nature of Brahman, it is Brahman alone that is said to be the evolving agent.

Thus, because the one who brings about the manifestation is none other than the one within, the assumption of a difference in meaning—that the bringer-about is one thing and the one within is another—is also not tenable.
And thus, the designation of space as something distinct—namely, that "name-and-form are within it"—is logically established for space.
Therefore, because of this designation as a distinct entity, and likewise because of the designation "that Brahman is immortal," it is established that space is indeed Brahman. //41// 1.3.13.42.
"On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure.
Since the transmigrating soul is presented at the beginning, middle, and end [of this section],
the entire context of the textual composition is to be applied to that very subject.
First of all, the transmigrating self (saṃsāry-ātman), which is the locus of the ego (ahaṅkāra) and is surrounded by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, is established for all people.

And since the collection of scriptural passages beginning with "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths" refers to that very self at the beginning, middle, and end, this [text] must be intended as a restatement (anuvāda) of that.
Thus, the transmigrating self itself is "great" in relation to something else.
Because saṃsāra is beginningless, it is called "unborn" (aja) due to its lack of a beginning;
however, no entity distinct from that, characterized by being eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated, is here intended to be established.
As for your notion of a distinction based on the statement that [the self] is "embraced by the conscious Self" during deep sleep and departure, [that too is not a true distinction].
This is not a case of actual difference; rather, this word "self" (ātman) denotes intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

Therefore, because there is an absence of specific objects during the states of deep sleep and departure, one whose cognition is as if contracted is embraced by the wise self—that is, by one's own intrinsic nature—and thus "knows nothing. Even though there is no actual difference, this should be understood as a figurative expression of difference where there is non-difference.
As they say: "The wise one is one whose wisdom is fully integrated.

Furthermore, terms such as "Lord" (pati) and so forth must be applied only to the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin), since the world—consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects—is acquired through the karma of that soul and is its object of experience.
Therefore, it follows that it is only the transmigrating soul that is being referred to (anūdyate), and not the Supreme Self (paramātman) that is being established (pratipadyate).
This being the case, it is replied: "Because of the designation by distinction in deep sleep and departure" (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.42) is understood to carry over.
The intention is this: Is there no Supreme Self other than the transmigrating soul?
Therefore, does the statement, "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths," refer to the transmigrating self?

Or rather, since the Supreme Self is not mentioned here apart from the transmigrating soul, and because the transmigrating soul is referred to at the beginning, middle, and end [of the text], this [Upaniṣad] concerns the self of the transmigrator;
yet, it is not that such a Self distinct from the transmigrator does not exist.

For hundreds of scriptural traditions establishing that [Self] have been set forth in the collection of sūtras beginning with "Because of seeing, it is not that which is based on scripture" (BS 1.1.5) and "On account of the uniformity of the way of going" (BS 1.1.10).
Moreover, even here there is no absence of mention of the Supreme Self as distinct from the transmigrating soul, because that Supreme Self is mentioned in connection with deep sleep and departure.

Furthermore, when it is possible, it is not appropriate to treat the mention of the wise one— the Supreme Self— as figurative— like the expression "the head of Rāhu"— by way of a distinction from the individual soul.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to explain the word *prājña*—which has a conventional meaning established for one possessed of excellence of wisdom—as referring in any way to an ignorant person.
Nor is such excellence of wisdom, whose function is unrestricted, possible in anyone other than the omniscient one who has known everything that is to be known;
and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is not of this nature.

Therefore, because the wise one, the supreme Self (prājña), is designated as distinct from the individual soul (jīva) in the states of deep sleep and departure, the text— beginning with "this which consists of consciousness" (vijñānamaya)— restates the individual soul as established in common experience and teaches its status as the supreme Self, a state not previously understood. Moreover, these statements do not have the mere restatement of the individual soul as their sole purpose.
For verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition must be intent upon the comprehension of an object not previously attained;
it cannot be restricted to mere restatement.

For this very reason, the consideration [of the Self] as something not subject to origination at the beginning, middle, or end is appropriate for the purpose of establishing the transmigrating soul's identity with the Supreme Self.

And thus, since greatness and immutability are possible for the all-pervading, eternal Self, they will not be conceived as merely relative. As for the statement, "because of the presentation of states such as being a Buddha in the middle," it is not intended by this that the Self possesses states.

Rather, because the various states possess the nature of arising and passing away, [the text] intends to refer to the Supreme Self, which is distinct from them and devoid of such states, as seen by considering the context of the subsequent passages. 1.3.13.43.
[This is known] from words such as "Lord" (pati).
"Master of all": *vaśa* means power; he has mastery over the entire world, meaning he is capable of manifesting various emanations (*vyūha*) and maintaining them.
For this very reason, he is the Lord (īśāna) of all; for by virtue of what has been stated, he rules over all through his power, since the world conforms to his will.

Therefore, he is the sovereign of all, the controller of all— that is to say, the inner ruler (antaryāmī). Furthermore, such being the case, scriptural passages such as "this person, who is the internal light consisting of consciousness, does not become greater or more exalted by good action," refer to the Supreme Self alone, which is beyond transmigratory existence.

Therefore, it is established that the textual sequence beginning with "This which consists of consciousness" (yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ) is intent upon demonstrating the state of Brahmanhood by restating the individual soul (jīvātman), which is already established through other means of knowledge. //43//
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Bhāmatī, which is a commentary on the Śārīrakabhāṣya of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, composed by the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra. //3//
Thus ends the third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, titled "The Concordance of Non-Evident Śruti Passages Teaching the Brahman to be Known.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the first chapter. 1.4.1.1.

"If it be argued that for some [the Pradhāna] is also inferential, we say no; because [the text] shows that what is grasped is that which was set forth as the metaphorical body of the embodied soul, and [scripture] further demonstrates this."
This might be so:
having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the definition of Brahman was stated as "from which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this [world].
And this definition does not apply to the Pradhāna or other such entities.
If [the definition] were otherwise, it would be non-definitive due to deviation;
however, it has been established in the sūtra "Because of seeing, that which is not based on scripture [is not Brahman]" that this applies to Brahman alone.
Furthermore, there exists a uniformity of purport among the Vedānta passages regarding the doctrine that Brahman is the cause.
The doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause has already been refuted by the preceding section of the Sūtras.
What, then, remains for which this subsequent section is commenced?
Furthermore, there is no lack of consistency even if [terms] such as "the Unmanifest beyond the Great" (mahataḥ param avyaktam) were to be construed with Pradhāna.
For these [Sāṅkhyas] do not assert that the Pradhāna is the cause of the world; rather, they merely assert its existence.
And by the mere existence of that [Pradhāna], nothing is subtracted from the definition of Brahman as "that from which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed]."
Therefore, the subsequent section is not purposeless; hence he says: "having proposed the inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsāṃ pratijñāya*).
Passages such as "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great" (*mahataḥ param avyaktam*) and "the one unborn female" (*ajāmekām*) do not merely establish the existence of the Pradhāna.
However, [some hold] that the *pradhāna* is the cause of the world;
for in the phrase "beyond the Great One" (*mahataḥ param*), the word "beyond" (*para*) denotes a state of being temporally remote from what precedes it,
and thus signifies causality.
In passages such as "the one unborn," however, the designation of [Prakṛti] as the cause is extremely clear.
Thus, since there is a deviation from the definition [of Brahman], the commencement of the subsequent section is appropriate in order to ensure non-deviation.
He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
Regarding the phrase "therein, that which indeed":
this expresses the established tradition of the Sāṃkhya school—
namely, "therein, the unmanifest."
It is not merely through conventional usage that this meaning is understood based on its establishment in the Sāṃkhya Smṛti;
rather, he says "not manifest" (na vyaktam) to show that this very same meaning is also understood through the well-known meaning of its constituent parts.
And because it is devoid of such qualities as being peaceful, terrible, or deluded;
thus the Śruti has been cited,
as well as the Sāṃkhya Smṛti.

And the reasoning is as follows: "Because of the finite measure of distinct objects, because of their homogeneity, because of their activity proceeding from a potentiality, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the manifold universe."
"The Unmanifest is the cause" [is stated].

Nor can the term "Unmanifest" refer to the body, based on the context and the method of elimination (pariśeṣa) from the statement "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great," because it is impossible for the body to be "unmanifest" given that its nature consists of the words "peaceful," "terrible," "deluded," and so forth.
Therefore, when it is argued that the unmanifest (avyakta) must be the Pradhāna itself, we reply:
this is not so;
for this is not a passage from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad [referring to the Pradhāna].
For worldly renown (*laukikī prasiddhi*) is the basis for determining the meaning of the Veda, because it is the means to that end.
As they say: "Those very words which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic, and their meanings are the same."
But for investigators, it is not technical; for that [convention] is human-made and does not serve as a basis for establishing the determination of the meaning of the Veda,
unlike the well-known usage of terms such as "oṣadhi" (herb).
Therefore, the Pradhāna is not understood from the term *avyakta* by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
As for its etymological application (*yoga*), that is common to other things as well.

Thus, since the scriptural mention of the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta-śruti*) is established otherwise, this word "unmanifest" refers to the body by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the remainder of the passage (*pariśeṣa*).
He will demonstrate later how it is established that this [consciousness] has those as its object. Among those things, such as the body and so forth, know the objects to be its domain.
Just as a horse moves by taking a path as its support, so too do the horses of the sense faculties move by taking their respective domains as their support.
The wise say that the self is the enjoyer.
How so? Through its connection with the senses and the mind, according to the manner of yoga.
For it is by means of the contact between the sense organs, their objects, and the mind that the self is the enjoyer of odors and other sensations.

It should be understood that "context" (*prakaraṇa*) is the statement of one who has a desire for the principal subject; thus, it introduces the desire for that principal subject—namely, "Viṣṇu’s supreme abode"—by means of the phrase, "with those senses and so forth being unrestrained.
The mention of "non-restraint" is intended to bring about a state of restraint by way of contrast (*vyatirekamukhena*).
The word *para* signifies "superior.
Now, if superiority were based on being internal, then the sense organs themselves would be superior to external objects such as odors and the like; therefore, he says:
"the objects which are sound and so forth."
Superiority does not consist in being internal, but rather in being primary;
and that [primacy] depends on what is intended to be expressed.

Since the Śruti intends to express the primacy of the objects over the sense organs—the "seizers" (atigrahas) relative to the "seized" (grahas)—the objects' status as "beyond" (para) arises from their primacy over the sense organs.
Indeed, the eight sense organs—namely the nose, tongue, speech, eye, ear, mind, hands, and skin—are declared in the Śruti to be the "seizers" (grahas).
For these seize and bring under control the human beast;
yet they are not able to bring one under their control by means of their own inherent nature.
As long as they do not offer to this human corpse the fragrance, taste, name, form, sound, desire, action, and touch,
for that very reason these eight— fragrance and the rest— are called "seizers" (*atigraha*), since it is through their offering that the [senses] acquire the status of being "seizers" (*graha*).
This has been stated:
"The sense organs are called *grahas* (seizers) and the objects are called *atigrahas* (over-seizers)," because this is well-known from the Śruti.
Although the mind shares the status of being a *graha* with the sense organs, [the author] declares its superiority over the objects by means of a distinction inherent to itself.
And [the text states] that the mind is superior to the objects. Why is the person (puruṣa), who was introduced as the charioteer, understood [to be the Self]? To this he says:
"Because of the word 'Self' (ātman)."
The meaning is "because of the recognition of that.
He states the reason for its preeminence with the words "and of the enjoyer."
Thus, by this, the individual soul (jīvātman) is described as "great" by virtue of its lordship;
or else, he says "or else" to indicate that, according to both Śruti and Smṛti, the intellect belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha is denoted by the word "Self" (ātman).
"Pūḥ" means city. Since the intellect (*buddhi*) is the substratum for the entire range of objects of experience, the intellect is the "city.

Thus, because all individual intellects have their single common abode in the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha—the first-born—there is both the greatness (*mahattva*) and the nature of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) belonging to the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha.
For this very reason, its separation from mere intellect is logically established.

Now, an objection is raised: "In this view, since the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha is the Self, the Self—the enjoyer—is not presented here as the charioteer; thus, it is not merely the chariot that remains, but the driver of the chariot as well.
To this, he says: "But in this view... [etc.]

For just as a reflected image superimposed [upon a mirror] does not differ from the original object in reality, so too the conscious self (vijñānātman) does not differ from the supreme self (paramātman) in reality; thus, it is the supreme self alone that is taken here as the rider of the chariot, and by that, only the chariot remains. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of this metaphorical construction of a chariot and so forth with respect to the body and other things? To this, he says:
"Of one who is indeed disconnected from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and objects.

*Vedanā* is the experience of pleasure and so forth. That which moves toward each object (*pratyartham añcati*) is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), intended here as the individual soul (*jīva*); its realization is the comprehension of Brahman.
Furthermore, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman is not established by any other means of knowledge, such that one might think scripture is unnecessary here;
thus he says: "And so... (tathā ca).

The word "vāk" (speech) is used with the elision of the accusative case ending according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The remainder of the text has a meaning that is not obscure. The following sūtra is intended to refute the seed of doubt held by the opponent: "But it is subtle, because it is capable of that. (1.4.1.2)
Because the modifications are non-different from their material cause, the unmanifest nature of the cause is figuratively attributed to the modification.

Just as in the expression "mixed with cows," the word "cow" refers to its product, milk; so too, since the modifications are non-different from the unmanifest cause, they are fit to be designated by the term "unmanifest. He states the authority for this:
"And so says the Śruti.
*Avyākṛta* (the undifferentiated) and *avyakta* (the unmanifest) are synonymous.
But if this is so, does it not follow that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) itself is being accepted?
For the world, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, must arise from a cause of such a nature,
since the effect possesses the nature of its cause;
and that which constitutes its nature of pleasure is *sattva*.
That which constitutes its nature as suffering is *rajas*;
that which constitutes its nature as delusion is *tamas*. Thus, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is accepted as being nothing other than the primal source (*pradhāna*). //2// 1.4.1.3.
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states:
"Because it is dependent on that [the Supreme Lord], it is purposeful.

For the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) of the Sāṃkhyas—whether they maintain the existence of a Lord (*seśvara*) or not—is possible to define as being substantially distinct from the Lord or from the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*).
This power of Brahman, denoted by such terms as *māyā* and the like, is this very ignorance (*avidyā*); it cannot be defined as being either identical to or different from [Brahman].
Its unmanifest nature (*avyaktatva*) consists precisely in this state of being indefinable (*anirvācyatva*).
This, then, is the distinction between the doctrine of the unevolved (*avyākṛtavāda*) and the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhānavāda*).
Furthermore, the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti) is dependent upon Īśvara because He is its substratum;
nor is a mere substance capable of producing an effect without power, which establishes the functional utility of power.
This is what was stated: "it is meaningful.
This might be so.

If the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) were perceived through the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*) belonging to Brahman, then alas, there would be the undesirable consequence of the rebirth even of those who are liberated, since that power remains as constant as *pradhāna*.

Alternatively, if that power were destroyed, there would be the total cessation of the entire cycle of transmigration, because its root—the power of ignorance—would have been utterly eradicated. To this, he says:
Furthermore, for those who are liberated,
there is the non-arising of bondage.
Why?
"By knowledge" means through the burning away of its seed-potency (*bījaśakti*).

This is the intended meaning: we do not declare ignorance (*avidyā*) to be one and the same for all individual souls (*jīva*), as we do with the *pradhāna*, such that we might be censured in this manner.
However, this [avidyā] differs for each individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, only the avidyā of that specific soul for whom knowledge (vidyā) has arisen is removed, not that of another soul,
because there is no contradiction between knowledge and ignorance when they reside in different substrates.
Therefore, how could there be the consequence of the total eradication of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)?
This fault, however, belongs to those who maintain the doctrine of *pradhāna*.

Since *pradhāna* is a single entity, if it were eradicated, everything would be eradicated; if it were not eradicated, nothing would be eradicated, leading to the consequence of no liberation at all. Even if *pradhāna* were diverse, [the bondage and liberation] would still be dependent on the presence or absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by the non-discrimination (*aviveka-khyāti*) [of puruṣa and prakṛti].
In that case, the assumption of *pradhāna* is superfluous, since that [distinction] is established solely through the existence or non-existence of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Nor is it correct to argue that the distinction between individual souls (*jīva*) depends on the distinction between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of ignorance, while the distinction between those adjuncts depends on the distinction between the individual souls— resulting in the non-establishment of both due to mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
Because they are beginningless, both are established like the seed and the sprout;
and by virtue of being merely ignorance (*avidyā*), there is a metaphorical designation of unity, such as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*) and "the undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*).
Now, if it is argued that ignorance alone is the seed of the world, making the Lord (*īśvara*) redundant, he says:

"Having the Supreme Lord as its substratum" (parameśvarāśrayā): for that which is insentient is not capable of producing an effect unless it is presided over by consciousness; thus, in order to perform its own work, it relies upon the Supreme Lord either as its efficient cause (nimitta) or as its material cause (upādāna).
Indeed, the world-appearance has the Lord as its substratum, just as the illusion of a snake has the rope as its substratum.
Therefore, just as the delusion of a snake has the rope as its material cause (*upādāna*), so too the delusion of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) has the Lord (*Īśvara*) as its material cause.

Consequently, although nescience (*avidyā*) has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus, it is said to "reside in the Lord" because the Lord is its efficient cause (*nimitta*) and its object (*viṣaya*),
but not because He is its substratum (*ādhāra*).
Because that [bondage] is impossible in Brahman, whose nature is knowledge;
for this very reason he says:
"In which the transmigrating individual souls (jīvas), devoid of the awakening to their own true nature, lie dormant."
While that ignorance exists, living beings lie;
since the true nature of living beings is Brahman, they are said to be "lying" (in dissolution) when devoid of the knowledge of it.
The term "those who transmigrate" expresses distraction,
because the state of being an individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Although the priority between the individual soul and the Unmanifest is indefinite due to their beginninglessness, this statement was made with a view toward the priority of the Unmanifest.
"Even though [the senses and so forth exist] like the body"—
this is to be understood as being like the expression "the cow and the bull.
He states the opinion of one who is like a teacher (ācāryadeśīya):
"—'Others, however'": he refutes this with the words "But by them...
[taistviti].
Since both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the remainder of the section (*pāriśeṣya*) are equal in both cases, there is no reason for a restrictive rule regarding the mention of only one.
He raises an objection: "It is for the sake of the traditional scripture (*āmnāya*)."
The meaning of the objection is that the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) itself is the cause for the exclusion of the gross body, because that [gross body] is manifest (vyakta). He refutes this, saying:
"No; because it depends on syntactical unity" (ekavākyatādhīnatvāt).

Since it is possible for there to be a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) by avoiding the abandonment of the subject matter under discussion (*prakṛtahāni*) and the introduction of a new subject not under discussion (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*), a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not appropriate. Furthermore, there can be no single syntactical unity without mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); and since both [the self and the body] are subjects under discussion, both are required here as objects to be grasped. Thus, even a word that expresses a single thing has a dual reference (*dvipara*).
Nor does it become merely figurative on the grounds that it is not intended in its primary sense;
for instance, when the word "crow" (*kāka*) is employed with no further requirement than to denote a destroyer, it is understood as a term for everything that destroys, such as dogs and so forth.
As they say: "Even a child, when instructed by the words 'The food must be protected from crows,' [understands it to mean all destroyers]."
Because its primary function is to cause injury, it does not protect against dogs and similar creatures.
Thus [it is said].
Now, one might object: there is no need here for two bodies;
rather, it is only the subtle body that requires attention because it is so difficult to purify.

But it is not [the case that this refers] to the gross body composed of the six sheaths; for since this [gross body] is easily purified as an object of detachment due to its visibly loathsome nature, he says:
"And one should not think thus."

The meaning is that the Supreme alone is introduced here as the subject to be established for the purpose of leading one to Viṣṇu’s highest abode, and not the purification [of the self] for the sake of dispassion.
Or, enough with this dispute; let it be that the subtle body itself is what must be purified.
Nevertheless, he says "But in every way" (sarvathāpi tu) [Sūtra 3.1.4.1.4], while provisionally accepting that the *pradhāna* favored by the Sāṃkhyas is not the supreme [reality] here,
because of the non-mention of its being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).
For this reason as well, this term "unmanifest" (avyakta) does not refer to the Pradhāna as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas.

Indeed, for the Sāṃkhyas, the Pradhāna is proposed as an object of knowledge so that the Puruṣa may be known through its distinction from it, either for the sake of the highest good (niḥśreyasa) or for the sake of worldly power (vibhūti).
But here, there is no mention of an injunctive suffix such as "one should know" (jānīyāt) or "one should meditate" (upāsīta).

However, it is merely the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). The point is that one cannot recognize the Sāṃkhya tradition based on this alone. [Sūtra 1.4.1.5]—anticipating the objection that the non-mention of "being an object of knowledge" (*jñeyatva*) is unproven—the following sūtra is presented to demonstrate its proof:
If it be argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one [is meant], according to the context.
The commentary on this is explained by the word itself (nigada). And thus there is the presentation and the question regarding these three alone. //5// 1.4.1.6. Trayāṇāmeva caivamupanyāsaḥ praśnaśca.
Indeed, the discourse between Mṛtyu and Naciketas in the Kaṭha Upaniṣads is observed to commence with the granting of boons and continue until its conclusion.
It is said that Mṛtyu, being pleased with Naciketas—who had been sent by his father in anger—granted him three boons. With the first boon, Naciketas chose the restoration of his father’s good humor.
By the second [question] he [taught] the knowledge of fire, and by the third, the knowledge of the Self,
according to the statement: "This is the third boon, O Varaṇā."
But surely, in that granting of boons, the question and the reply refer to the primary subject;

therefore, in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, the course of the discourse must concern only the fire, the individual soul, and the supreme Self, and cannot possibly concern the Pradhāna which was not introduced at the outset.
To this he says: "For this reason also, the Pradhāna is not denoted by the word 'unmanifest' (avyakta)."

The construction is as follows: by the words "Come, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman," [the text] connects this with the response concerning the individual soul (jīva) that was previously interrupted, beginning with "But as the self becomes, O Gautama, upon reaching death," and so forth.
Here, the challenger asks: Is the question regarding the individual soul and the supreme self (paramātman) one and the same?

Or rather, is the individual soul (jīva) different from that which is addressed in the question, "This which one hears regarding the deceased man," and is the Supreme Self (paramātman) different from that which is addressed in "Other than dharma," and so forth?
If they were identical, there would be a contradiction with the three [categories] mentioned in the Sūtra.

If, however, there were a distinction [between the questions], then the granting of the three boons—consisting of joy, the attainment [of immortality], and the knowledge of the Self as Fire—would not be included within the granting of the boons, because of the question beginning with "other than dharma" and so forth.
Alternatively, if one were to postulate yet another boon for the fourth [question], it would result in the contradiction of the scriptural statement that it was the "third.

If the question is not included within the granting of the boons, then by the same logic, the primary narrative [of the creation] should also not be included in the granting of the boons; thus arises the objection: "That which is beyond the Great is the Unmanifest."
He refutes this, saying: "To this it is replied: we do not say so here.
Since, in reality, there is no difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman), there is only one question, because the object of inquiry is non-different."
For this very reason, the reply is also one;
however, the Sūtra intends the non-difference [of the two] in a figurative sense,

whereas the actual non-difference between the individual self (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) has been demonstrated by the venerable commentator through the citation of various scriptural passages.

Likewise, regarding the question of the existence or non-existence of the soul (jīva), and so forth; for, having heard Naciketas's question, "This which [is] after death," and perceiving his lack of desire for those various objects of longing, Death praised Naciketas with the words, "I consider Naciketas to be one who desires knowledge," and so on.
Praising even that question of his, he stated "Brahman alone" as the answer to this question: "Him, difficult to see...
For if the wise one were different from the individual soul (jīva), [the answer would not have been so].
The question concerns the domain of the living, while the answer concerns the domain of the wise; how, then, could these two be consistent?

Furthermore, if Naciketas, having heard the question concerning that very subject, were to ask about it again after being praised by Death, and if Death were to explain the answer to him, then the praise would have served a visible purpose.
But he says that this state, when expanded within another question, would have its object seen as truth:
"yatpraśna... (that which is the question). "Yatpraśnaḥ" means that in which there is a question.
The remainder has its meaning not hidden.
Regarding the phrase "and like the Great One" (mahadvat):
by this, it is stated that because there is a contradiction between the Sāṃkhya tradition and Vedic tradition, the Sāṃkhya tradition should not be accepted in the Veda.

For the Sāṃkhyas, the principle of Mahat is "mere existence" (sattāmātra). Existence (sattā) is the state of being capable of performing the purposeful activity of the Puruṣa; that which consists of this alone is the principle of Mahat. Whatever purposeful activity there may be—characterized by the experience of sound and other objects, as well as characterized by the discernment of the difference between the Sattva and the Puruṣa—all of that culminates in the Great Intellect (mahatī buddhiḥ); thus, the principle of Mahat is called "mere existence."
Thus [ends section 7]. 1.4.2.8.
*Camasavad aviśeṣāt*:

Although the word "ajā" is conventionally established in the sense of a goat, nevertheless, because this context pertains to the science of the supreme self (*adhyātmavidyā*), it cannot be taken in that [conventional] sense here.
Therefore, since a conventional meaning (rūḍhi) is impossible, it must be understood through etymological derivation (yoga).

In this regard, is the independent Pradhāna being referred to by this Vedic mantra-text, or is the supreme Lord’s power of illusion (māyā-śakti), which is the cause of the differentiation of fire, water, and earth, being spoken of? What, then, is the initial position?
That it is indeed the Pradhāna.
For instance, exactly as the *pradhāna* is described by the Sāṃkhyas, so too is it perceived here, neither deficient nor excessive.
That *prakṛti*, characterized as *pradhāna*, is "unborn" (*ajā*) because she is not born; she is "one" (*ekā*); and she is "red, white, and black.
Although the colors red and so forth do not actually exist within the qualities of *rajas* and the rest, [they are used metaphorically].
Nevertheless, just as safflower and the like dye [the cloth] red,
and dust also dyes it, it is called "red" (*lohita*); likewise, clear water is "white" (*śukla*).
Sattva is also white because it is serene;
likewise, that which obscures, such as clouds and the like, is black, and tamas is also black because it is obscuring.
Nor can it be maintained that even by another [means] there is a connection with redness and so forth in the neutral (avyākṛta) in its own nature;
rather, the causality of redness and so forth must be figuratively attributed to fire, water, and earth, which are its effects.
Or else, it should be conceived in the cause by way of the similarity of the effect.

That is equally true for us as well. Since the scripture declares a plurality of selves—“For one unborn, enjoying [her], lies alongside her; another unborn leaves her after she has been enjoyed”—it is precisely the Sāṃkhya tradition that is recognized here in this Vedic verse, and not the doctrine of the unmanifest (avyākṛta), because in that doctrine, due to the acceptance of a single self, there is no plurality of selves.
Therefore, it follows that the independent *pradhāna* is not supported by scripture.
Regarding the phrase "by the qualities of the constituents of their state of equilibrium":
the constituents (*avayava*) of the single *pradhāna* are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; their qualities (*dharma*) are redness and so forth; [the state of equilibrium is characterized] by those.
"Beings are endowed with the three qualities" means they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
For instance, there is pleasure for Maitra when he is with Narmadā, the wife of Maitra.
For what reason?
Because of the arising of affection toward him;
and likewise, there is suffering for his co-wives.
For what reason? Because passion arises with respect to them; likewise, for Caitra, who does not find her, there is delusion and despondency.
For what reason?
Because darkness arises in relation to that;
and all entities have been explained by means of the river Narmadā.
This is the state of being endowed with the three qualities (traiguṇya) of living beings; he explains [the phrase] "it lies latent" as follows:
"by that very ignorance."

For objects such as sound and the rest—which are modifications of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion through the three qualities (*triguṇya*)—enter the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*) by way of the channels of the senses, mind, and ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

Consequently, that *sattva* of the intellect, being a modification of primordial nature and consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, transforms itself into the forms of sound and the other objects.

However, the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), though unchanging and non-transmigrating, perceives its own distinction from the *sattva* of the intellect; yet, through the error of ignorance (*avidyā*), it identifies with the pleasure and other states residing in the intellect by means of the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) itself.
It becomes as if possessed of pleasure and so forth;
thus it has been said:
"Through lack of discrimination, thinking 'I am happy,' 'I am miserable,' or 'I am deluded,' one wanders in saṃsāra."
One [remains bound],

while another— whose attachment to ignorance and all latent impressions has been utterly uprooted by the discriminative discernment of the difference between the spirit (puruṣa) and primordial matter (prakṛti)— abandons this prakṛti.
This is what was stated:
Regarding the phrase "another,
however," he explains "one whose enjoyment has been experienced" as "one for whom enjoyment and liberation have been accomplished."
Experience is the perception of sound and other objects;
liberation is the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the qualities (guṇas) and the self (puruṣa),
for by means of that, the self is liberated.

This being the case, it is replied: First of all, the verse "The one unborn [Self], indeed, while enjoying [her], lies down; another unborn [Self] leaves her after having experienced enjoyment" does not aim at establishing a plurality of selves; rather, it takes for granted the established plurality of selves and teaches bondage and liberation.

And that assumed plurality is merely conceptual, because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings," which aim at establishing the unity of the Self.

Thus, since there is no recognition of the Sāṃkhya method [in this passage], the statement regarding the goat (*aja*)—like the statement regarding the *camasa* cup—is merely ambiguous and not sufficient to establish an independent *pradhāna*.
This very point was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "As in the case of the *camasa*, because there is no distinction" (Sūtra 1.4.8). 1.4.2.9.
He raises an objection in order to introduce the subsequent sūtra: "In that case, however, this is its head.
He then introduces the sūtra.
To this we reply: "But she begins with light, for so it is studied by some.

Since Brahman is one and the same as recognized across all Vedic branches, this "Unborn" (aja)—who possesses the qualities of being red and so forth mentioned in another branch, and who is characterized by fire, water, and food—is the primordial material cause of the fourfold collection of beings: those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from a sprout.
Regarding the phrase "red, white, and black," this is because that very [Prakṛti] is recognized through its red and other forms;
it is not the *prakṛti* postulated by the Sāṃkhya school.
For that [Sāṃkhya *prakṛti*] lacks scriptural authority, which would entail the fallacy of abandoning what is stated in scripture and imagining what is not stated.
Furthermore, since it is improper to apply figurative designations such as "red" (rohit) and so forth by means of coloring and the like when the primary meaning is possible,
this has been stated:
"of the words *rohit* and so forth."

Furthermore, in the case of the word *ajāpada*, there is the fault of abandoning the conventional meaning of the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) and resorting to the etymological meaning of its parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*)—namely, "that which is not born" (*na jāyate*).
However, in this instance, for the purpose of constructing the metaphor (*rūpaka*), one accepts the conventional meaning of the whole without any regard [for etymology].
Moreover, he says that even this collection of scriptural passages is in accordance with our own philosophical system (*darśana*), and not in accordance with the Sāṃkhya tradition (*smṛti*).
"So it is here as well.
Why? Because the inquiry begins with "What is Brahman?
First of all, the essential nature of Brahman cannot be the cause of the world.
Because of its purity;
as they say, "For a pure person, there can be no impure transformation"—with this intention, as it were, the Śruti asks:
"What is the reason?"
The meaning is: "Of which Brahman there is the origination of the world—that Brahman is the cause.

The construction is: those knowers of Brahman, having reached and attained the Self through the yoga of meditation, beheld it. [This refers to the verse] beginning with "yo yoniṃ yonim" (who [presides over] each womb).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the power that is the source (*yoni*); and it has been stated that this [power] is manifold for each individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is justified. The remainder of the passage has a self-evident meaning. //9// 1.4.2.10.
He raises an objection in order to introduce another Sūtra: "But how?
The generic form (*jāti*) of a goat does not exist within fire, water, or earth.
Nor can the word *ajā* (the unborn) be applied to fire, water, and earth on the grounds that they are heard to have an origin; thus he says:
"Nor [can it be so] for fire, water, and earth.
He introduces the Sūtra:
To this, he recites the following:

"And because of the teaching of a figurative conception, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. Now, one might object: "Is the goat necessarily red, white, and black? For goats of other appearances are also observed. To this, he says:
"By chance" (*yadṛcchayā*):
she has many kids and many lambs.
The rest is explained by the literal reading (*nigadavyākhyāta*). //1//
"Not even by the inclusion of a number [is the objection removed], because of their diversity and because of the excess.
He states the intermediate connection:
"Even though it has been refuted in this way..."
For the meaning of the compound *pañcajanāḥ* is connected with the number five;

nor should it be argued that this word *pañcajana* is conventionally established as referring to human beings due to the rule for compound formation, "When direction and number [are compounded] in a technical name" (*diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*),
because if that were the case, it would have to be *pañcamanujāḥ*.
Thus, the claim that the self, the five elements, humans, and space have their foundation [in Brahman] is devoid of purpose,
since everything indeed has its foundation [in it].
Therefore, since a conventional meaning (rūḍhi) is impossible here, one must not resort to etymological derivation (yoga) by abandoning that [conventional sense].
And the word *jana* must be explained in some way as referring to the [five] principles (*tattva*).
Even there, one must consider whether the five beginning with breath (*prāṇa*) mentioned in the supplementary passage are intended, or whether some others entirely distinct from those are meant.
This is because, upon examining the preceding and following context, there is a contradiction between the Kaṇva and Mādhyandina recensions of the text.
For in one case there is a fivefold state by means of light, while in the other it is by means of food; moreover, an option is not possible here as it is in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup,
because it is the performance that is optional, not the reality itself.
This is a discourse on the reality of things, not a discourse on ritual practice, because there is an absence of injunctions.
Therefore, only certain principles here— each consisting of a group of five— constitute the twenty-five principles.

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the twenty-five principles, beginning with *prakṛti*, are recorded in traditional scripture (*smṛti*); therefore, it is these very principles that are expressed by this mantra, and thus the *pradhāna* and so forth are not "unscriptural" (*aśabda*).

Furthermore, [the *pradhāna* is not unscriptural] because the Self is established as its substratum, whereas it is a contradiction for the relationship of container and contained to exist within the Self itself, and because space (*ākāśa*) is excluded [from being such a substratum].
If it be argued: "It should be said that there are twenty-three persons (*jana*), rather than five groups of five persons (*pañca-pañcajana*);

for even though space (*ākāśa*) and the Self (*ātman*) are distinct, the number twenty-five is established by the constituents of primordial nature (*mūla-prakṛti*), namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

And if that were so, with the addition of the Self and space, the number would become twenty-seven, which would contradict your own established doctrine of 'twenty-five principles' (*pañcaviṃśati-tattvāni*)."
It is not by identifying the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* merely as the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) that the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) are established;
rather, when they are treated as distinct entities, there is no contradiction in their number being twenty-seven.
Therefore, it follows that the Sāṃkhya tradition is not based on the Veda.
The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is the primary matter (pradhāna). It is not a modification of anything else, but rather is itself the primal source; thus it has been stated: "the root."
The Great Principle (mahat), the I-principle (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements (pañcatanmātra) are both evolvents (prakṛti) and evolutes (vikṛti).
To explain: the principle of the Great (mahattattva) is the evolvent of the distinct principle of the I-principle, but it is the evolute of the Root Evolvent (mūlaprakṛti).
Likewise, the principle of the I-principle is the evolute of the Great.
That same [ego] when characterized by tamas is the nature (prakṛti) of the five subtle elements (tanmātras);
that same [ego] when characterized by sattva is the nature of the eleven organs.
Furthermore, the five subtle elements are the transformation (vikṛti) of the ego and the nature (prakṛti) of the five [gross elements], beginning with space.
This has been stated:
"The seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both evolvents and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is only evolute."
The group delimited by the number sixteen is indeed a modification (*vikāra*).
The group of sixteen consists of the five gross elements (*bhūta*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the eleven organs (*indriya*).

Although earth and the other elements are the material causes (*prakṛti*) of cows, jars, and so forth, they are not a distinct principle (*tattva-antara*) from [the subtle elements] such as earth; therefore, they are not the *prakṛti* [in this context].

In this context, "being the material cause" (prakṛtitva) is intended to mean being the material cause of another principle (tattvāntara), not merely being a material cause; thus there is no contradiction.
The Puruṣa, however, being immutable and eternal, is non-transforming; he is neither the material cause of anything nor a modification.
This being the case, it is replied:
