Space is not a part of space,
because it is its very essence.
If it is argued that it is a part delimited by the circular rim of the ear, [we reply:]...
Well then, by distinguishing between what is reached and what is not reached, it is effectively stated that [the cause] is either the circle of the ear's rim or its conjunction [with the sound].
And if you say it is a portion delimited by the circle of the ear's rim,
well then, by distinguishing between what is reached and what is not reached, it is effectively stated that [the cause] is either the circle of the ear's rim or its conjunction.
Nor is the circular rim of the chariot wheel a part of space,
because it is distinct from it.
If it is argued that its conjunction with space is a part of space because it is a property of space, we say no.
Because it is untenable.
For if it were of the nature of space, it would be partless and undifferentiated everywhere; thus, its conjunction would be perceived everywhere.
Indeed, it is impossible for that which is partless to exist without pervading [its locus].
Therefore, if it exists there, it must exist as a pervader; if it does not pervade it, then it simply does not exist there.
If you argue that it exists as a pervader alone, but is not perceived everywhere because its determination depends upon its correlate, [we reply:]...
Let it not be defined as "name" [itself].
However, since the ether (*nabhas*) conjoined with that [name] exists everywhere and is fit for hearing, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing occurring everywhere.
Furthermore, a part cannot be defined by either difference or non-difference, nor by both.
It has been stated that two contradictory things cannot coexist in one place.
Therefore, it is logical that the portion of space [perceived as such] is merely imagined through beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*anirvacanīyāvidyā*) and is not real.
Nor can it be argued: "How can that which is purely imaginary, whose very existence depends solely upon cognition, exist when it is not being cognized?"
It must be said: how can a non-existent part serve as the cause for an effect characterized by the hearing of sound?
For a snake that is not being perceived in a rope is never capable of producing effects such as fear or trembling.
This objection is invalid because it is unproven that [the part] is unknown, since it is manifested by its very effect.
If it is asked, "How can that which is unknown prior to the production of the effect be a factor for the production of the effect? we say: no.

Because it is manifested by the successive production of preceding effects, its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) persists even in the absence of knowledge; and since the stream of those impressions is beginningless, such a conceptualization is possible.
Alternatively, let there simply be no logical consistency [between cause and effect], because they are of the nature of illusion (*māyā*).
For indeed, the very impossibility [of its existence] strengthens the case for it being an illusion, since the nature of an illusion consists in having an impossible object.

Furthermore, according to the view of those who maintain that there is a real part [of the self], liberation—which is accomplished through knowledge and meditation—could not occur, because that real part cannot be destroyed by knowledge.
Thus, like the aspect of space, the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*).
Thus it is established that the view of Kāśakṛtsna—that the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman—is correct. 1.4.7.23.
"And [Brahman] is the material cause (prakṛti), because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.
This might be so.

When it has been shown that the Vedāntas are in harmony with Brahman, one might raise the objection: "The section on harmony (samanvaya-lakṣaṇa) is thus completed; what else remains for which this [next] section is commenced? To dispel this doubt, the author states the connection (*saṃgati*) with the words:
"Just as prosperity...
Here, having stated the connection of this section with the [preceding] definition, the connection of this specific topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) with that definition is explained.
This is what is meant: it is true that the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas has been stated with respect to Brahman as the cause of the world.
However, since causality is observed in two ways, is the status of Brahman as the cause of the world solely as the efficient cause (*nimitta*), or also as the material cause (*upādāna*)?
In that regard, if the first position is held, then upon investigating the material cause, one must accept the *pradhāna* established by the Sāṃkhya tradition.
Consequently, the definition of Brahman— "from which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed"— would be invalid,
because it would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), as it would also apply to the *pradhāna*.
Or [it is excluded] because of impossibility.
If, however, the latter alternative is accepted, then there is neither over-extension nor under-extension; thus the definition is sound.
This is the "remainder" (avaśeṣa).

In that regard: "The state of being an agent preceded by deliberation, sovereignty, and dissimilarity [from the effect] belong only to efficient causes (nimittakāraṇa), never to material causes (upādāna)."
This is what he says:
"In that regard, first of all, it is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*)," etc.

Since scripture (*āgama*) culminates in [establishing] the mere cause, he says that scripture does not reject the restriction of inference (*anumāna*) to its specific [object], but rather indeed approves of it.
"By the method of elimination, [it is] other than Brahman":

when the possibility that Brahman is the material cause has been negated, since it cannot apply to anything else, the *pradhāna*—known from the Sāṃkhya tradition and established through inference—is what remains.
Furthermore, the promise of knowing everything through the knowledge of one, expressed in the passage beginning with "But that instruction... (*uta tam ādeśam*), [is fulfilled only by this].
And the illustration, "As, my dear, by one clod of clay," indicates the primacy of the Supreme Self;
just as, when Somaśarman is known, all the Kaṭhas become known.
This being the position reached, it is said:
"And [Brahman is] the material cause.
It is not only Brahman that is the efficient cause; [it is also the material cause].
Why?
Because there would be no contradiction between the proposition and the example;
however, if it were merely a causal factor as a motive (nimitta-kāraṇa), those two would indeed be contradicted.
For it is said: "When a primary meaning is possible, a secondary sense is not desired;
nor is that which is inferential proper when sublated by direct scripture."
Indeed, when all the Vedāntas are examined in their proper sequence,
they are seen to be exclusively devoted to non-duality by means of the negation of mere duality.

Therefore, in this case as well, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are properly understood in their primary sense alone; they are not to be interpreted through the attribution of figurative qualities (*guṇakalpanā*), as in the statement "The sacrificial grass-bundle is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), because that [latter] explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not intended to convey its literal meaning.

However, since the sentences concerning the proposition and the example are devoted to non-duality (*advaita*), and because the entire range of effects (*kāryajāta*) which is derived from a material cause is of the same nature as that cause, the knowledge of those effects is logically established through the knowledge of the material cause.
However, since an efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) is absolutely distinct from its effect, knowledge of the effect does not arise from knowledge of it.
Therefore, Brahman is the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) of the world;
nor is it logical to hold that there is any efficient cause of the world other than Brahman.
Precisely because it contradicts both the proposition and the illustrative example;
for at that time, when Brahman is known, everything is not yet known,
since there remains something other than Brahman— the efficient cause of the world— which falls within "everything" and is not known by the knowledge of that [Brahman].

Furthermore, the ablative case in the word *yataḥ* is not prescribed for a cause in general, but rather for the material cause (*prakṛti*), according to the rule: "The material cause [is designated by the fifth case] of that which performs the act of being born. From this also, we understand its status as a material cause.
The mention of the "drum" (*dundubhi*) and the "beating of the drum" is for the purpose of indicating the commonality (*sāmānya*) of sound residing therein. (23) 1.4.7.24.
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) of desire for what has not yet come.
By this, indeed, its status as a causal factor (*nimittatva*) is shown through agency (*kartṛtva*) characterized by autonomy (*svātantrya*).
And by the phrase "May I be many," its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) with respect to itself has been stated. 1.4.7.25.
"From space alone" (*ākāśādeva*): the meaning is "from Brahman alone."
Having cited the portion of the Sūtra, "sākṣāt ca," he explains its meaning:
"From space alone" (ākāśādeva).
The Śruti, by ascertaining that Brahman is the material cause of the world, shows directly that there is no other material cause.
The construction is that this is shown by the phrase "directly" (*sākṣāt*) within the sūtra. 1.4.7.26.
*Ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt* (Because of self-making and transformation).
The mention of "prakṛti" (primordial matter) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be regarded as the "efficient cause" (nimitta), because it is the object and the material cause [of the world], while it is the efficient cause with respect to that [world] by virtue of being its agent.
But how so? [The sūtra asks: "How again? (kathaṃ punaḥ).
"The non-coexistence of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished in one place is due to contradiction;
therefore, we say it is because of transformation (pariṇāma).

This means that even that which is already established undergoes transformation into the form of an indefinable modification; and because this [modification] is itself indefinable, it appears as if non-different from the [original] despite being different—thus, even that which is established possesses the status of being "to-be-accomplished."
Having explained [the previous point] as a single syntactical unit, he explains the term "from transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*) by means of the phrase "or from transformation" (*pariṇāmād iti vā*).
The two forms of Brahman are the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*tyat*).
That which is real is directly perceptible and definable by way of its general and particular characteristics,
characterized as earth, water, and fire;
whereas that which is beyond perception is for that very reason indefinable in terms of "this-ness," characterized as air and space.
And how could that be the form of Brahman if Brahman were its material cause?
Therefore, because of that transformation, Brahman is the *prakṛti* (material cause) of beings.
Having restated the inference of the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), [the author] refutes it by means of contradiction with scripture.
Regarding the phrase "but as for that which..."—

this is what is meant: God is merely the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) of the world, because he is the creator of the world preceded by volition (īkṣā), just like a potter who is the maker of a jar.
In this case, since Īśvara is unestablished, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), and the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualification.
As they have said: "The method of reasoning (*nyāya*) does not operate with respect to that which is not perceived.
If it is argued that his existence is established through scripture (*āgama*), [the response follows].
Well then, one must accept the Lord exactly as scripture reveals Him; and that scripture makes known the Lord as both the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

Since inference cannot arise due to its contradiction with the scripture—which is to be accepted as the basis for the subject—how can there be a determination of His being the efficient cause through it?

Furthermore, this terminology regarding the "transformation of the material cause" (*upādānapariṇāma*) is not intended to imply actual modification; rather, just as a rope is the material cause of a snake [in an illusion], so too should Brahman be understood as the material cause of the world.
Indeed, it has been stated that transformation— either as a whole or in part— is not possible for Brahman, who is eternal and devoid of parts, because of its eternity and lack of spatial extension;
nor do pots, shards, and the like differ from the clay.
Nor are they non-different, nor both different and non-different, but rather they are simply indeterminable (anirvacanīya).
As the Śruti says: "Only 'clay' is real."
Therefore, since they begin with non-duality and conclude with it, all Vedāntas are exclusively devoted to non-duality; some state non-duality directly,
some do so by negating duality,
and some do so by [showing] that the world has Brahman as its material cause.
By this much alone, the difference [between the cause and the effect] is refuted;
however, one should not assume the apprehension of a modification merely by the mention of "material causality" (upādānatva).
For there is no such thing as the meaning of a mere fragment of a sentence. //27// 1.4.8.28.
It might be argued as follows: even if the *pradhāna* were not the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, nevertheless, it is not established that Brahman is its material cause,
because other candidates for that role, such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), are also appearing [as possible causes].
To dispel the doubt that even for those [other systems] there exists some Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*) as a supporting factor, the author of the Sūtras says:
"By this, all are explained; they are explained.
The Sūtra is explained by the commentary (*bhāṣya*), which is self-evident (*nigada-vyākhyāta*).

It has been established in this very context—and not elsewhere—that the definition of a proposition consists in the syntactic coherence of words within the object being defined, and that such coherence belongs specifically to the Vedic [text]. //28//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śrīmacchārīrakabhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra.
Thus ends the fourth quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, titled "The Harmonization of All Doubtful Terms Beginning with the Unmanifest" (Avyaktādi-saṃdigdha-pada-mātra-samanvaya).
This concludes the first chapter, titled "Harmonization" (Samanvaya), in the venerable Śaṅkara Bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras.
Chapter 2.
Now begins the second chapter.

**"If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis."** To demonstrate the connection between what has been discussed and what is about to be discussed—namely, the characteristics of resolving contradictions regarding the harmony (*samanvaya*) [of the Vedas]—and for the sake of easy comprehension, he states the essential meaning of the two sections in brief: [The Sūtra: "If it be argued that there would be the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis, we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. (2.1.1) [Commentary: The first chapter established the harmony of the Vedas with respect to Brahman. Now, the second chapter is commenced to resolve contradictions concerning that same harmony. An objection is raised: "If the Vedas teach that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), then there would be the fault of leaving no room for those Smṛtis which describe Brahman as possessing attributes (*saviśeṣa*). To this, the author replies: "No, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis"—that is, for those Smṛtis that support the doctrine of the attributeless Brahman. Thus, by showing the consistency of all Smṛtis with the Vedas, the contradiction is resolved. Furthermore, the purpose of this section is to show that the Smṛtis do not contradict the Vedas, thereby establishing the authority of the Smṛtis as a means of knowledge. This is the concise purport of the two sections.
"In the first chapter" means:

because an objection and its resolution are provided through the refutation and reconciliation of contradictions regarding the characteristic of "harmonization" (samanvaya)—which is established by the natural sense of the Vedānta texts independently [of other means of knowledge]—there exists a relationship of subject and object between this [chapter] and that characteristic.
For the meaning of the preceding characteristic is the subject, since the objection and its resolution have that as their scope, and this [first chapter] is the subject-matter (viṣayin).
Having thus introduced the chapter, he introduces its constituent part, the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), with the words: "First of all, therein...
A *tantra* is that by which the means to liberation is systematized (*tantryate*) and explained (*vyutpādyate*).
That which has this very name is the Smṛti known as Tantra, composed by the supreme ṛṣi Kapila, the primordial knower;
other Smṛtis composed by Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and others follow that same tradition.
Indeed, it cannot be said that these Smṛtis have any other scope than the illumination of the means for liberation, in the manner of the Smṛtis of Manu and others.
If they were not to assert even that, then the truths, having no scope, would result in being invalid.
Therefore, the Vedāntas must be interpreted in some way so as not to contradict that [Smṛti]. He objects to the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):
But how [is it established] from the words "seeing" (īkṣati) and so forth?

Indeed, this was already established in the *Dharmamīmāṃsā* at the point where it says: "In case of contradiction, however, there should be no reliance [on Smṛti], for when [contradiction] is absent, there is inference.

Just as Smṛtis that contradict Śruti are not to be relied upon due to their weakness, it is therefore not proper to provide an exposition of the more powerful Śrutis in accordance with weaker [Smṛtis].
"Rather, it is logical that the Śrutis, whose status as valid means of knowledge is established by their own nature, do indeed sublate the weaker Smṛtis.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) replies: "This might be so... [end of fragment].

The meaning is that even though the point has already been established, it is being established once more for those who are dull-witted due to a lack of faith. Having stated a superficial resolution, the proponent states the ultimate resolution:
"And the scripture of Kapila and others is [authoritative]."
This is its intended meaning: Brahman has indeed been stated to be the cause of the scripture in the sūtra "Because it has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt).
Therefore, this collection of the Vedas, being born from Brahman, is preceded by a cognition whose object is solely the unobstructed reality established by innate knowledge (*ājānasiddha*).

In the same manner, the Smṛtis of Kapila and others—who are renowned in Śruti and Smṛti as possessing an innate nature—also originate from a cognition of theirs that has all things as its object and is free from obstruction.

Thus, there is no distinction between these [Smṛtis] and the Śrutis; nor can it be maintained that these [Smṛtis] are not intended to propound the Pradhāna and other such principles more clearly than the Śrutis. Therefore, in accordance with them, the Śrutis themselves must be interpreted in some way.
Moreover, even reasoning (tarka) accords with the Smṛtis of Kapila and others; therefore, this very [conclusion] is established.
When this has been established, he says:
Regarding the phrase "his concentration":
for while there is no contradiction among the Śrutis with respect to Brahman because of the uniformity of their purport (*gatisāmānya*),
such non-contradiction does not exist among the Smṛtis with respect to the Pradhāna.
For we observe in various places that the majority of those [Smṛtis] are intent upon establishing Brahman as the material cause.
Therefore, because there is no contradiction, the meaning established by Śruti alone must be accepted, and not that which is Smārta, due to its contradictions.
To the objection, "In that case, would all Smṛtis be rejected simply because of mutual contradictions?", he says:
And regarding the phrase "in the case of conflicting traditions" (*vipratipattau ca smṛtīnām*),
the expression "and not [concerning] objects beyond the senses" (*na cātīndriyārthān*) refers to the perspective of one who perceives only what is within range of the senses (*arvāgdṛk*).
He raises an objection: "It is possible [to establish the authority] of Kapila and others. He refutes it: "No."
Regarding the phrase "even from [the attainment of] perfection":
Kapila and others were not, like the Lord (Īśvara), established by birth;
rather, for them—who had ascertained the authority of the Vedas and practiced them in a previous life—perfection was attained in this present birth.

For this very reason, they are said to be "established without being born" (*ajānasiddha*). This is because in this life, no means for attaining those perfections has been practiced by them; rather, those perfections have arisen from having practiced the meaning of the Vedas in previous births.
Thus, for those who have ascertained the authority of the Vedas, any statement of a matter contrary to them is sublated and is indeed non-authoritative.

Furthermore, it is not proper to cast doubt upon the meaning of the Veda by means of what is non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), because that [meaning] is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, having stated that a statement concerning an established fact (*siddha*) is non-authoritative when it contradicts the Veda, he recalls what was said previously—that there is no confidence in the words of even those who are established (*siddha*) when they contradict one another—by saying:
"Even in the case of a conceptual construction based on the authority of the *siddhas*... (*siddhavyapāśrayakalpanāyām api*).
He awakens those who are dull-witted due to faith, stating:
"even for one whose wisdom is dependent on others.
Now, if the Śruti indeed makes known the excellence of the knowledge of Kapila and others, which has as its object the reality that is free from obscuration, [then...]
How can their word be non-authoritative?
For if that were non-authoritative, it would follow that the Veda (*śruti*) would also be non-authoritative; therefore, he says:
"But as for the Veda... [yā tu śrutir iti].
First of all, the mutually contradictory statements of the perfected ones (siddhas) cannot constitute valid authority;
nor can there be an option regarding a real entity, because such an option is impossible once the entity is established.
The performance [of ritual action] is conceptualized as something yet to be produced, not as something already established, because it is that which is to be determined.
Therefore, the delusion arises from the mere similarity of the word; thus, Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya, is considered "one who follows the Śruti."
It might be argued:
"Kapila alone is authoritative according to the Śruti, not others such as Manu and the rest;
therefore, their Smṛti, being in contradiction with Kapila’s Smṛti, should be rejected. To this, he says:
And there is another [verse] by Manu;
and he states its corroboration by another scripture, saying: "In the Mahābhārata also..."
Not only is Manu’s Smṛti in agreement with other Smṛtis, but it is also in agreement with Śruti; thus he says:
"And Śruti."
He summarizes [the argument] with the words "therefore" (ataḥ).
This might be so.

"Let it be that the Kapila doctrine is contrary to the Veda; nevertheless, since both originate from human intellect, what is the reason for the decisive conclusion that the Kapila doctrine, being opposed to the Veda, is not to be respected? [The answer is:
'For the Veda is independent.
This is the intended meaning: it is true that the Lord has the scripture as His source, yet He does not possess independence in the act of composing the scripture, as Kapila and others do.
For that Blessed One composed the scripture in this present creation according to the same manner as he had composed it in the previous creation.

Thus, following the precedent of what was even further prior, he composed it in the previous [creation], and following the precedent of that which was further prior, he composed it in the one before that; in this way, this causal relationship between the scripture and the Lord is beginningless.
In that regard, the Lord’s composition of the scripture is not preceded by his own knowledge of the scripture's meaning, such that his independence would be comparable to that of Kapila or others.
Furthermore, although the knowledge of the meaning of the scripture may manifest to him spontaneously, it does not become the cause of the scripture itself,

because both [the scripture and the knowledge] manifest simultaneously and not sequentially. And the scripture, by virtue of its self-evident capacity to convey understanding and its lack of dependence on a person— thereby being free from the suspicion of defects— is an independent authority (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own subject matter directly.
The words of Kapila and others, however, were composed by independent authors such as Kapila and are preceded by their recollection of those meanings;
and those recollections of meaning are themselves preceded by the experience of those meanings.

Therefore, for the sake of determining the validity of those [words]—which is a factor in the cognition of their meaning—as long as the recollection and the experience are required, they are [valid] intrinsically (*svataḥ*).

Since the meaning of the Veda is determined by the Veda itself, which functions independently of any established means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical that the meaning of the Smṛti is sublated by the Veda, which operates with far greater speed. 2.1.1.2.
To begin with, the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the Ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) are not well-known [in common experience].
Since the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are also unestablished by virtue of having ego (*ahaṅkāra*) as their material cause, they cannot be remembered [as objects of recollection]; thus he says:
"And of the others...
Now, one might object that the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest are well-known from the scripture stating, "Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest" (*mahataḥ param avyaktam*); to this he replies:
Regarding the phrase "yadapi" (even that which),
he states the purport of the Sūtra:
"kārya" (the effect), etc.
The meaning is that it is determined that the Sāṃkhya Smṛti possesses no authority regarding Pradhāna, just as it lacks authority regarding the Mahat and other principles.

Even if the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is sublated, how could its stated arguments be sublated? It is reasonable [to ask] how the knowledge of a seer (*ārṣajñāna*) can be established as the basis here. Therefore, it is proven that the world does not have Pradhāna as its material cause according to the Smṛti of Kapila. //2// 2.1.2.3.
By this, Yoga is refuted.

This does not mean that the authority of the Yoga treatises of Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, and others is rejected in every respect; rather, it is stated that they possess no authority regarding the independent Pradhāna—which is the material cause of the world—and its evolutes, namely Mahat, Ahaṅkāra, and the five Tanmātras.
Nor can they be rendered invalid by this much alone;
for those [scriptures] would incur invalidity only if they were intended to establish that [primary object],
whereas these texts do not have the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth as their primary purpose.

However, [these texts] are devoted to the exposition of the nature of yoga, its means, its intermediate results consisting of supernatural powers (*vibhūti*), and its ultimate result which is liberation (*kaivalya*).
And since that [liberation] must be expounded by taking something as its occasion, the primary cause along with its modifications has been taken as the occasion—

just as in the Purāṇas, which are devoted to expounding those [topics], the account of creation, secondary creation, genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of dynasties are presented.
But that is not what is intended there;
for even from a statement whose primary purpose is something else, another meaning might be accepted as implied, provided it is not contradicted by another means of valid cognition.
However, it has been stated that there is a contradiction between this [Yoga system] and the Vedāntic scriptures.
Therefore, the existence of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and other such principles is not established even by the Yoga-śāstra, which is itself a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For this very reason, the venerable Vārṣagaṇya, the expounder of the Yoga-śāstra, said: "The supreme form of the *guṇas* does not come within the range of vision."
But that which has come within the range of vision is merely an illusion, utterly void.
Thus,
by one desiring to explain yoga, the qualities (guṇas) have been mentioned here merely as a cause, but not in their actual state.
The meaning is that this is because they lack ultimate reality (*atāttvikatva*).

It is logical that even things like *pradhāna* and so forth—which are not established in the world and are merely imagined through fallacious reasoning in beginningless prior disputations—are fit to be restated (*anuvādyatva*).
With this intention, he says:

By this refutation of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, it should be understood that the Yoga Smṛti as well is refuted insofar as it concerns the Pradhāna and other such principles. [The author] raises an objection regarding the commencement of a new section (adhikaraṇa):
"If this is so, then by the principle of equal logic... [he asks]. He provides the resolution:
"There is here a further objection."
Granted that the existence of *pradhāna* might be understood from the Sāṃkhya treatises;
however, the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth will be made known through the Yoga treatises as well, for a great deal of agreement between the Yoga treatises and the Veda is observed.
Furthermore, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is the means to the Upanishads, requires yoga.

Indeed, the direct realization of the Upaniṣadic reality of the Self cannot arise at all without abandoning the external means prescribed in the Yoga-śāstra—such as the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama)—and without the internal means such as concentration (dhāraṇā) and the rest.

Therefore, because it is not contradicted by the Upaniṣadic knowledge of reality and because of its great degree of agreement with them, the Smṛti on Yoga is authoritative, just like the Smṛtis concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites.
Consequently, since the primordial matter (pradhāna) and other principles are understood from this authoritative source, they are not "unscriptural" (aśabda).

Nor is it reasonable to claim that [the scripture] is not authoritative regarding the primal matter (pradhāna) and so forth, while being authoritative regarding the restraints (yama) and so forth; for if it were unauthoritative in that case, there would be a lack of confidence in its authority elsewhere as well.
As they have said: "For as long as monkeys do not find scope anywhere, so long do they not attack piśācas within their own domain."

Thus, this demoness of the invalidity of Yoga—which has gained its footing in [the existence of] Pradhāna and so forth—would be irresistible everywhere; therefore, by one who seeks to block its progress, Pradhāna and the like must be admitted. This is the meaning of the doubt: "Pradhāna is not without scriptural authority. That [demoness].
This further objection is also refuted by extension [to the previous case].
He states the reason for its refutation:
"even when there is agreement regarding a portion of the meaning."
If the Yoga-śāstra were intended to establish the existence of Pradhāna and other such principles,
it would be invalid due to its contradiction with the Vedāntic scriptures perceived through direct perception;
and consequently, there would be a lack of confidence even in the restraints (yamas) and other practices prescribed therein.

Therefore, it has been stated that the [scripture] does not have the Pradhāna and so forth as its primary subject; rather, having made those [entities] its occasion, it has as its primary purpose the exposition of Yoga.
Furthermore, a lack of authority regarding what is not its subject matter does not undermine its authority regarding its own subject matter.
For the eye, which is not an instrument of valid cognition regarding taste and so forth, cannot likewise be an instrument of valid cognition regarding form.

Therefore, because it contradicts the Vedāntic scriptures, the primary principle (Pradhāna) and so on are simply not its objects; the ultimate point is that this does not imply a lack of authority [in the scriptures].
This might be so.
There exist thousands of internal systems of tradition (smṛtis), such as those of the Buddhists, the Ārhatas, the Kāpālikas, and others;
why then are these not also refuted? To this he says: "Even though they exist... (satīṣvapi).

The meaning is this: since those [Smṛtis] are for the most part inconsistent with the meaning of the Vedas, disregarded by the learned, and accepted only by certain base men—beasts among men such as Mlecchas and others—the very suspicion that they might be rooted in the Veda does not even arise, and thus they have not been refuted;
however, the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya and Yoga are the opposite of that, and therefore they are set aside as being concerned with the Pradhāna and other such [non-Vedic principles].
"Not by means of Sāṃkhya knowledge independent of the Veda" means:
by means of that which has the Pradhāna and so forth as its object.
For those Sāṃkhyas and Yogas are indeed dualists.
The meaning is that those who explain that scripture by treating its primary subject as *pradhāna* (the primordial matter) and so forth [are the Sāṃkhyas].

They are called Sāṃkhyas because they proceed with *samyag-buddhi*, which is Vedic wisdom (*vaidikī*). Likewise, "yoga" refers to meditation (*dhyāna*), where the means and the end are intended to be non-different.
Yoga is indeed the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; its means is meditation (*dhyāna*), which is one-pointedness of consciousness.

This is an illustration; other means of yoga, both external such as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), and internal such as concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth, are also to be understood.

By this, the formulation is that for those such as Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and Akṣacaraṇa (Gautama), who accept the authority of the Veda, all [their] treatises on logic (*tarka*) are merely recollections (*smaraṇa*).
The rest is easy to understand. 2.1.3.4.
"Not so, because of its dissimilarity; and its being such [as you claim] is due to verbal testimony."
He states the intermediate connection:
"of this position that Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of this world. He raises an objection:
How much less so, then?
For contradiction would exist only if there were identity of object;
yet here there is no identity of object.

The meaning is that, like Dharma, Brahman is also not the object of other means of knowledge; being beyond ratiocination (atarkya), it is the exclusive province of the independent Vedic revelation (āmnāya).
He provides the resolution:
"This may be so."

"Let it be that dharma, which consists of something to be accomplished (kārya), is not the object of another means of knowledge because it apprehends an already established entity; however, Brahman, being an established reality, is the province [of another means of knowledge]."
Therefore, because they have the same object, there is scope here for reasoning (*tarka*).
[Objection: Let there be contradiction; nevertheless, what is the reason for heeding reasoning? To this, he says:

"And as in the case of the Śrutis" means that just as many Śrutis, even if they possess scope (*sāvakāśa*), are interpreted in conformity with a single Śruti that lacks scope (*anavakāśa*) when there is a conflict between them, so too, when there is a conflict with a single argument lacking scope, even many Śrutis must be explained through the postulation of secondary qualities (*guṇakalpanā*) and other means in accordance with that [argument]. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, the direct realization of Brahman (brahmasākṣātkāra), by removing beginningless ignorance through its very nature as its opposite, is accepted as the means to liberation in its visible form.

In this regard, since the direct realization of Brahman is the primary means to liberation, inference—having an unseen object based on similarity with the seen—is proximate (*antaraṅga*) in terms of its object;
whereas verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*), which has an entirely imperceptible domain, is remote (*bahiraṅga*).
Therefore, he says— “And by similarity with what is seen”— that inference alone is more powerful even due to its proximity to the primary means [of knowledge].
Furthermore, he says that reasoning (tarka) is also respected regarding Brahman by scripture itself:
Regarding the term "Śruti":

this objection concerning Brahman’s being the material cause of the world is now further introduced by means of reasoning: "Even according to the *Prakṛti* [Sāṅkhya] doctrine and according to Śruti, the world exists as a modification (*vikāra*) that is similar in nature to Brahman; yet, for that [Brahman], there is no actual transformation (*vikriyā*)."
The Brahman is pure consciousness, while the world is insentient and subject to impurity;
therefore, due to its similarity with the Pradhāna, it is the Pradhāna itself that undergoes transformation.

For instance—a single female body, by virtue of its nature consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, simultaneously produces pleasure, pain, and despondency for the husband, for her rivals, for Caitra, and for the one who desires women but does not possess her; and by this, all states [of existence] are explained through the example of the woman.

Therefore, because it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and because it manifests as the diverse multiplicity of high and low states such as heaven and hell, the world is both impure and insentient.
Brahman, however, is conscious and pure because it is unsurpassed;
therefore, it is logical that the world is a modification of the primary matter (pradhāna), which is impure and unconscious, and not of Brahman.
To those, however, who assert that the world is conscious because it is a modification of the conscious Brahman, he says: "And this world is insentient.
He raises an objection regarding a deviation [from their premise]: "But is it not also conscious?"
He refutes this, saying: "Not even between master and servant.
Now, it may be that a conscious being does not directly assist another conscious being; however—
But [the opponent might argue] that [the Self] will assist [the body] by means of the employment of the intellect and other faculties which perform those functions; to this he says:
"For consciousnesses are unsurpassed and non-agents.
"Surpassing" (atiśaya) is the connection with attributes subject to arising and passing away.
Their absence is their state of being unsurpassed.
For this very reason, because they are devoid of activity, they are non-agents;
therefore, the meaning is that they also lack the status of being instigators of the intellect and so forth.
The challenger exposes the seed of the latent tendency (anuśaya-bīja) with the words "yopi" [even he]. He states a provisional resolution by way of concession:

he introduces that very point with a portion of the Sūtra in order to state the ultimate proof:

He states the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) of a portion of the Sūtra:
"For this [consciousness] is indeed not perceived [in them].

Indeed, since the earth and other elements possess consciousness as their inherent nature (*prakṛti*), the consciousness [of these elements] which is understood from the meaning of the words is strengthened by another means of knowledge (*māna*); thus, even if non-consciousness were heard directly [from the text], it would be set aside.
The meaning is that in the absence of another means of knowledge, the object [established by] the object [of perception] must be set aside by the meaning of the Vedic revelation;
however, the meaning of the revelation should not be altered on the strength of that [perception]. //4// To introduce the next sūtra, he raises an objection:
[Objection: But is not consciousness also [found] somewhere?
[Response: It is not that consciousness belongs to earth and the other elements merely by way of inference;
rather, the meaning is that it is the direct meaning of numerous Śruti texts.
He introduces the Sūtra:
therefore he recites the following—“But there is a designation of the presiding deities, because of distinction and because of following.
He analyzes it:
Regarding the word "tu" (but):

these scriptural passages do not directly state that clay and the like, or speech and the like, possess consciousness; rather, they refer to the presiding deities who are of the nature of consciousness.
Therefore, on the strength of this scriptural authority, one should not suspect that clay and the like, or speech and the like, possess consciousness.
Why, then, is this so? To this he says:
"Because of [the mention of] specific distinctions and because of the inclusion [of all things]."
In this regard, he explains the distinction: "For the distinction...

Since the enjoyers are those who are benefited and the elements and senses are those that provide benefit, such a relationship would be impossible if there were equality; furthermore, this is well-known to all people.
Furthermore, the distinction characterized by sentience and insentience mentioned previously would not be tenable on account of the scriptural text, "And consciousness came into being. Or rather,
he says that the distinction here is expressed by the word "distinction" (viśeṣa) as being caused by the word "deity" (devatā)—
namely, "Moreover, in the Kauṣītaki [Brāhmaṇa], in the dialogue of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda)."
He explains the "concomitance" (anugati) with the words:
"and they are concomitant.
Mantras and other authorities teach that deities, in the form of presiding agents (abhimānin), are concomitant everywhere—in all things such as the elements and the sense organs.

Moreover, many scriptural passages—such as "Fire, having become speech, entered the mouth; Air, having become breath, entered the nostrils; the Sun, having become sight, entered the eyes"—show that the deities reside within the specific sense organs.
And these deities are conscious, being distinct individual knowers of the field (kṣetrajña).
Therefore, consciousness does not belong to the sense organs and so forth by their very nature.

Furthermore, in the supplementary portion of the *Prāṇasaṃvāda* (the Dialogue of the Vital Breaths), it is shown that the vital breaths—just like the bodies of ourselves and others—are engaged in worldly activity only when presided over by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*); thus, in the supplementary portion of the *Prāṇasaṃvāda*, the consciousness of the vital breaths is established through their being presided over by the Knower of the Field.
"Even [the statement] 'That fire thought'...

"Therefore" (tasmāt) //5// 2.1.3.5. This is the sūtra of the established conclusion (siddhānta-sūtra): "But it is seen" (dṛśyate tu).
He refutes the alternative [view] regarding similarity as the cause for the relationship between material cause and modification by stating,
"and because of the cause being of a different character.
Not conforming to the nature of all things is not incompatible with the relationship between material cause and modification.
In following that [position], because there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra*) through identity (*tādātmya*),
the middle term (*liṅga*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
As for the third [alternative], the meaning is that it is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) due to the absence of an illustrative example (*nidarśana*).
Now, one might ask: why is it not argued that the inference has its object sublated by scripture (*āgama*), since Brahman is understood through scripture as being the source of the world?
To this he says: "But there is a contradiction with scripture.
Furthermore, there is no room for any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this Brahman, which is to be known solely through scripture.
Intending to show how that [scripture] might imply the attainment of those means, he says: "As for what was stated, that Brahman is [known] because of its being fully established"—

for just as, despite the lack of distinction in their being effects, statements such as "one desiring health should eat wholesome food" and "one desiring a beautiful voice should eat sand" depend upon other means of knowledge (mānāntara), [so too does this scripture].
But this does not apply to such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
For what reason?
Because this distinction of the task (kāryabheda) is beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition.

The meaning is this: although there is no difference in their being "thus-existent" (evambhūtatva), earth and the other elements are within the scope of other means of knowledge, whereas Brahman, though it is also "thus-existent," is not;
therefore, because its object is exclusively the Veda, it transcends the boundaries of all other means of knowledge, and is established by Smṛti and Āgama.

If Brahman’s being beyond the scope of reasoning is established by tradition and scripture, how then is there an injunction for reflection (*manana*) distinct from hearing (*śravaṇa*)? To this, he says:
"As for that which [is said] to be apart from hearing..."

For reasoning (*tarka*), being the means of discerning the objects of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), constitutes their procedural application (*itikartavyatā*) and is dependent upon them; thus, in the absence of the instruments of knowledge, it is disregarded because, lacking its support, it would be "dry" (i.e., baseless).

However, that which is supported by the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*), which discerns its object, and which is not in contradiction with it—that is enjoined as "that which is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*).
[This is expressed in the phrase: "supported by revelation" (*śrutyanugṛhīta*).
"Subsequent to the scripture, i.e., hearing (śravaṇa), it is grasped as the 'how-to' (itikartavyatā).

for reflection (manana), when being cultivated, becomes experienced as the object of the creative contemplation (bhāvanā); thus, reflection is a limb of experience."
"The Self's state of non-attachment" means its lack of contact with states such as dreaming;
that is to say, its state of indifference.

Moreover, for those who maintain that consciousness is the cause [of the world], it is possible to apply the statement "it became both conscious and unconscious" to the cause of the universe by means of the manifestation or non-manifestation of consciousness in the effect, even though the effect shares the same characteristics as its cause. However, for those who maintain that the insentient *pradhāna* is the cause, this is difficult to reconcile.
For it is not possible for an insentient cause of the world to possess the nature of consciousness.

However, in the case of a sentient cause of the world, even though it exists during states such as deep sleep where consciousness is unmanifest, it is possible to somehow attribute to it a lack of conscious selfhood; thus he says:
"He who [attributes this] by the force of the scriptural teaching that the cause is sentient..."
However, this would not be tenable for the Sāṃkhya alone, who maintains that the non-intelligent *pradhāna* is the cause;
for the difference [between cause and effect] has already been refuted.
This was stated by accepting the premise that there is no relationship of cause and effect when there is a difference in nature.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), we do not accept this. 2.1.3.7.
If it is argued that [the effect] is non-existent, no; because it is a mere negation.
The effect is not non-different from the cause.
Because if there were non-difference, the status of being an effect would be untenable;
because, as with the cause itself, there is a contradiction in [the effect] acting upon its own self; and because of the association with contradictory attributes such as purity and impurity.

Now, if there were a difference between the conscious Self as the cause and the world as the effect, then this world as an effect would not exist even though the conscious Self as the cause exists prior to its production; and if it does not exist, then that which is non-existent is produced, which would contradict the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). To this, he says:
If it is argued that consciousness is pure, he refutes this by stating:
"This is not a fault."
Why?
Because it is a mere negation.
He analyzes [the point]:
For this is a mere negation;
he will indeed establish this in the section beginning with "The non-difference of that [effect from the cause], on account of such terms as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa)," etc.,
where it will be shown how the effect cannot be defined as either existent or non-existent by its own nature.
Rather, it can be defined as existence by way of its causal form.

And thus, the very existence of the cause is the existence of the effect; it is not other than that. Therefore, how could that which is non-existent prior to its arising exist while the cause is existent? However, in terms of its own nature (*svarūpa*), that which is prior to arising, or which has perished after arising, is indefinable in terms of being either existent or non-existent. Consequently, there is no production of either an existent or a non-existent thing. Thus, the meaning is that the refutation of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is without a valid object.

But it is not because of the mere existence of examples. Dissolution is not merely non-distinction; rather, it is the non-distinction of the effect within the cause.
And regarding the coloring of that [cause] by the attributes of the [effect], there are thousands of examples.
The meaning is that, in your view, there is not even a trace of an illustrative example for the dissolution of the effect into the cause while it remains stained by the properties of the effect.
This might be asked: if the non-distinction of the effect from the cause occurs [only] when the effect has dissolved, how can the cause be stained by the properties of the effect? To this, he says:

"Even in the case of non-difference" means that just as the ultimate nature of superimposed silver is nacre— and nacre is not itself the silver— so it is here as well. Furthermore, the Śruti, which declares the non-difference of the effect from the cause throughout all three stages of persistence, origination, and dissolution, is beyond doubt for all proponents of the Veda.
In that regard, the refutation concerning [the world's] persistence and origination applies equally to its dissolution as well; namely, that the effect is merely superimposed by ignorance (avidyā).
Therefore, he says—"this which is said is far too little"—to show that one should not object merely on the grounds of [the world's] destruction.
And there is this other illustration:
"Just as a single dreamer" refers to an ordinary person.
Thus, [the Lord] is the sole witness of the three states.
The "three states" are origination, maintenance, and dissolution.

As for what was further stated:

"Because the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) is restricted, there is a restriction regarding [the order of] origination"—this is the meaning.
