The objection that there would be the undesirable consequence of the rebirth of liberated souls due to the specific determination of the power of false knowledge has been refuted;

for the absence of an effect is strictly determined by the absence of its cause, and false knowledge, along with its latent power, has been destroyed root and branch by the knowledge of reality. //9// 2.1.3.10.
And because of the defect in our own position:
first, the dissimilarity between cause and effect is indeed equal in both positions;

furthermore, the objection that the effect does not exist prior to its production applies equally to both, as does the consequence that [the world] would re-enter the cause at dissolution—this applies specifically to the position that the Pradhāna is the material cause.

Although we shall demonstrate later that this is not our position, it should be understood that for the time being, this [objection] is set aside as being equivalent to "sweetening the tongue with molasses" (*guḍajihvikā*).

It is easy to understand the rest: "This acquisition of pleasure and pain belongs to this person; this [acquisition] belongs to that person," [arising] from afflictions, karma, latent dispositions (*āśaya*), and so forth. //10// 2.1.4.11.
Also because of the instability of reasoning (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*).

Regarding a matter that is accessible only through scripture (*āgama*) and lies outside the domain of independent reasoning, one should not employ reasoning based merely on similarity or dissimilarity—as the Sāṃkhyas and others do—by which the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth might be established.
For such reasoning is "dry" (*śuṣka*), being inherently unstable.
As it has been said: "Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skilled inferents may be established in an entirely different way by others who are more proficient."
Nor can any reasoning be established on the grounds of being accepted by great persons,
because even among those very great persons who are logicians, there is mutual disagreement.
In the Sūtra, an objection is raised: "If it be argued that the object of inference is otherwise.
This is analyzed as follows: "We shall infer it in another way."
One should not suspect that inference is subject to deviation because of the deviation of fallacious inferences,
for that consequence would then apply to perception and other means of knowledge as well due to their respective fallacies.
Therefore, the inferer must be skillful in following a logical mark (liṅga) that possesses an intrinsic necessary connection (svābhāvikapratibandha).
The implication is that, consequently, the primary [goal] will be established without obstruction.

Furthermore, he states that the very reasoning by which one asserts the non-establishment of reasonings must itself be accepted as established; for if that were not established, there could be no non-establishment of the others. Thus he says:
For reasoning (*tarka*) is not itself established.
Moreover, if reasoning were unestablished, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the entire worldly course of action.

Furthermore, the determination of the true meaning of the Śruti does not occur merely by refuting fallacious appearances of its meaning; thus he says: "And if all reasoning were unestablished... and so forth.
Moreover, reasoning (*tarka*), which consists of investigation, permits the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) after abandoning the previously reasoned prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
And this [reasoning] proceeds against the prima facie position when that position is devoid of a firm foundation,
for it is only in the absence of such [a foundation] that the process of investigation commences.
This is what he says:
"And this very thing is the ornament of reasoning.
He dispels this doubt with the Sūtra: "Even so, there would be the consequence of non-liberation."
We do not rely on anything other than inference as a means of valid cognition;
however, regarding the existence of the cause of the world, there is no inferential mark (liṅga) possessing an essential connection (svābhāvikapratibandha).
As for that which is merely similarity and dissimilarity, [it is insufficient].
"One is not liberated because of the fault of non-abiding in that [state]. By means of another argument, he states the meaning of the term "non-liberation":
"Moreover, liberation comes from right knowledge."
For in the world, it is observed that correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), which has real objects as its domain, is established by having well-defined entities as its object,

just as in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*). And this Vedic cognition— which concerns the conscious material cause of the world, employs the ritual procedures of reasoning arising from the Vedas, and is produced by the Veda— is likewise established.

However, for the logicians (*tārkika*) who establish the diversity of the cause of the world by means of reasoning independent of the Vedas, there is no determination of reality because of their mutual contradictions and the absence of any means for ascertaining the truth; thus, from that [reasoning], there is no establishment of reality, nor is there right knowledge from it. And from the lack of right knowledge, there is no liberation from *saṃsāra*; this is the meaning. //11// 2.1.4.12.
By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained.

The effect is not non-different from the cause; for if there were non-difference, the status of being an "effect" would be untenable—just as it is with the nature of the cause—and the meaning of the verbal root *kṛ* (to produce) would also be untenable.
For its purpose is the manifestation of what was previously non-existent;
yet, if it were of the nature of a cause, there would be nothing non-existent therein for which this person would strive.
If it is argued that [the effect exists] for the sake of manifestation, no; for even that manifestation exists by virtue of being of the nature of the cause.
Alternatively, if it were non-existent, then by the same logic, the manifested object would also be non-existent, which would result in a contradiction of its being of the nature of the cause.
For it is not logical that the very same thing should both exist and not exist at that very same time.

Furthermore, what kind of jewel, mantra, medicine, or sorcery has been learned by this effect, such that for a person whose sense organ remains in that same state— [perceiving] that very object which possesses no excellence of being unarisen or unceased, and which is neither obstructed nor distant—
it is sometimes perceptible and sometimes imperceptible?
If it is argued that its perception is sometimes direct, sometimes inferential, and sometimes based on scripture—
its indirectness being caused by the intervention of other effects— this is not so,
because the class of effects is eternal.

Now, it might be argued that other effects, such as the lump, the potsherd, the gravel, the powder, and the dust, intervene between [the clay] and the jar; therefore, the jar might occasionally be beyond perception.
That is not so.

Because that collection of effects, being of the nature of its cause, would always exist as an eternal entity, it would follow that the jar would never be perceived at all due to constant concealment;
or, if the collection of effects were only occasional, it could not be of the nature of its cause,
because the association of contradictory properties characterized by eternality and non-eternality constitutes a distinction.
And it has been stated that difference and non-difference, being mutually contradictory, cannot coexist in one and the same thing.
Therefore, for that reason, the effect is absolutely different [from the cause].
Nor is it correct to argue that if there were difference, the relationship of cause and effect would be untenable, as in the case of a cow and a horse.
Because it has already been stated that [the relation] is untenable even if there were non-difference due to the presence of the nature of the cause;
and because, in the case of absolute difference, the relationship of efficient cause and effect is observed between a pot and its maker.

Therefore, although there is no distinction in their being other than one another, it is precisely the distinction of inherence (*samavāya*) that is the cause for the restriction of the relationship between material cause and effect.
That which, having not previously existed, comes into being, and whose constituent parts (samavāyikāraṇas) are smaller in dimension than the cloth and other effects, [is an atom].

However, for the conscious self (cidātman), which is of the nature of the supreme magnitude (paramamahat), it is impossible for an effect to be of an extremely minute dimension relative to its material cause.
Therefore, that wherein this gradation of minuteness reaches its limit—that from which nothing smaller can possibly exist—is the atom (paramāṇu), the fundamental cause of the world.

Anticipating further objection— that the Śruti, which declares the world to be an effect and thus something to be accepted as minute, might somehow be explained through a secondary sense (jaghanya-vṛtti) due to conflict with well-established authoritative reasoning, just like the scriptural mention of a "year" in the context of a sacrificial session lasting a thousand years— the author extends the refutation of Sāṃkhya by means of the sūtra beginning with "etena."

The meaning of this is as follows: we shall refute the difference between cause and effect in the section beginning with "Non-difference from that [cause], on account of such words as 'originating material' (BrSū 2.1.14).
Furthermore, we shall disregard the deficiency or excess of the effect resulting from its superimposition through ignorance, because such factors are irrelevant to the ultimate purpose.
Therefore, since the reasoning (tarka) favored by the Vaiśeṣikas and others is "dry" (śuṣka) and lacks a firm foundation, this Sūtra extends the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position to them as well.

If this is the fate of the Sāṃkhya doctrine, which follows the Veda in some respects and has been accepted by the learned authorities such as Manu and others, then what need is there to mention the theory of atoms (paramāṇuvāda), which is entirely outside the Veda and was disregarded by Manu and the rest?
[The phrase] "in some respect" [is used].

For the creation and other topics are indeed what are to be explained; they are not explained by merely citing some example imagined through the logic of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), whether it be existent or non-existent. Thus it was said, "in some respect. The rest is easy to understand. 2.1.5.13.
"Because of the attainment of the enjoyer, there would be no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman], as in the case of the world. (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14)
It might be argued:
it has been stated that reasoning (tarka) does not have as its object the cause of the world, which is exceedingly profound, and that this [cause] is accessible through scripture alone.
How, then, can there be a challenge based on reasoning? To this he says:
"Even though scripture is a means of valid knowledge.
For scripture, having proceeded as a self-evident authority by virtue of its independence, does not depend upon any other means of valid knowledge.

Furthermore, when [a statement] proceeds, it is displaced from its primary sense and reduced to a secondary figurative function due to contradiction with reasoning whose validity is firmly established;
this is the meaning [of the phrase], as in the case of mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas).
The commentary is of self-evident meaning.
Regarding the phrase "just as at present":
if this distinction between the past and future creations did not exist,
then that very [non-distinction] would subvert the distinction of the present.
The perception of the waking state is like the perception of a dream;
however, this is not the case.
The meaning is that because the present perception is uncontradicted, one can infer that those two [the dream and waking states] are likewise [unreal].
The author of the Sūtras dispels this doubt by merely presenting an example established in common worldly experience without further investigation:
"It may be as in the world" (syāl lokavat). He states the secret of the refutation: [Sūtra 2.1.6].
"The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning 'origination' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.

He states the distinction between this section, which begins with the declaration of a specific point, and the preceding one—which was based on the absence of contradiction—by saying: "And having admitted this... and so on.
It might be argued:

"If the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is an effect, is non-different from its cause, which is the ultimate reality, then why does the defect mentioned by the Vaiśeṣikas and others not apply here? To this, he says:
"The non-existence of the effect is understood through its distinction [from the cause]."
Indeed, we do not assert non-difference by claiming they are identical; rather, we deny their difference.
Consequently, the fault that follows from relying on non-difference does not apply.

However, by those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who deny non-difference, assistance is actually rendered to us. He explains the reason for denying difference: "First, the word 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*)," and so forth.

For the entire world would be known in its true nature through the knowledge of Brahman only if Brahman alone were the reality of the world—just as when a rope is known, the reality of the snake [superimposed upon it] becomes known.
For that alone is its reality;
and knowledge of reality is true knowledge, whereas anything other than this is false knowledge and is indeed no knowledge at all.
On this very point, there is a Vedic illustration:
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay," [it is said].
This might be asked: when clay is known, how does a jar or other object made of clay become known?
For it has been demonstrated above that the [effect] does not have clay as its essence;
therefore, it is different in reality. Furthermore, when one thing is known, another thing is not thereby known; hence the Śruti says: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name."
The entire collection of transformations is undertaken by speech alone,
but it does not exist in reality, since it is merely a name.

Just as "consciousness of a person" or "the head of Rāhu" are mere conceptual constructions (vikalpa), as those who know conceptual construction have said: "Conceptual construction is that which follows upon word and cognition but is devoid of an objective reality";
likewise, the entire collection of transformations is unreal because it lacks substantial reality.
"Only 'earth' is real. Therefore, the true nature of jars, bowls, water-pots, and so forth, is earth alone; thus, when earth is known, the true nature of all these things becomes known.
This has been stated:
"And otherwise, the knowledge of all things through a single cognition would not be accomplished.
Demonstrating two other illustrations, he concludes:
Therefore, as in the case of the spaces within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth:
for those things whose nature is seen and then lost are not real entities, just like the water of a mirage and the like; and since the entire collection of modifications is thus, it is unreal.
For instance, that which exists truly exists,
just like the conscious self (*cidātman*);
for that [self] never, nowhere, or in no way does not exist.
However, it exists always, everywhere, and in every way, and is never non-existent;
whereas the collection of transformations is not like this,
because it exists only at certain times, in certain ways, and in certain places.
For form never, nowhere, or in any way becomes odor; rather, those two properties— existence and non-existence— which belong to a thing,
occur only at certain times because their arising is dependent upon their own causes.
In that case, if that collection of transformations were persisting as a continuous entity, then no transformation would belong to anything.
Alternatively, if it does not exist at the time of non-existence,
then to what does the property of non-existence belong?

For if the substratum (dharmin) is not present, its property (dharma)— non-existence— cannot logically be present. If, on the other hand, non-existence is not a property of this [substratum] but rather the existence of some other thing,
what does that have to do with the entity in question?
When a jar is produced, nothing at all happens to a cloth.
If it is argued that non-existence (*asattva*) is the opposite of existence (*bhāva*), we say no; for that which effects nothing cannot logically be considered a real entity.
Or, even if it were to have some effect, that same objection would apply there as well because of its non-existence.

Now, if you say that what is called "non-existence" does not arise as something at all, but rather that very thing simply does not exist—as they have said: "Nothing happens to it; it simply does not exist."
Now, let this non-affirming negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) be defined: does it have the nature of an entity, or is it the nature of an entity?
In the first case, because entities would possess that nature and thus be void, it would follow that the entire world is empty.
And thus, there would be an absence of both existence and non-existence.
However, in the latter case, because of the permanence of its own nature, the conventional designation of "non-existence" could not occur.

Even if negation were based solely on conceptual construction, the consequence of the permanence of existence would remain exactly as it was. Therefore, the collection of transformations exists as something distinct from the cause, but it is not a real entity.
Therefore, the collection of modifications is indefinable and unreal.

By this means of valid cognition, the unreality of the collection of modifications is established; the Śruti then reiterates, by way of illustration through the continuous passage beginning with "Only clay is real," the reality of the cause by virtue of its being definable.

The Nyāya sūtra, "An example is that wherein there is a consensus of understanding among worldly investigators," is intended to mean that an example is one established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
it does not, however, intend to imply that it must be something already established in common worldly experience.
Otherwise, things such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) would not serve as examples for them.
For the atom and so forth are not established for worldly people who lack both innate and acquired excellence of intellect; thus, he now raises the proponent of non-absolutism (anekāntavādin):
"But surely [the object] consists of multiple natures."
Since there are various activities consisting of the production of manifold effects by means of numerous powers, Brahman is both one and manifold.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says:
"In that regard, by way of its aspect of oneness... (tatraikatvāṃśena).

If, on the other hand, unity alone were the actual reality, then, due to the absence of multiplicity, the entire worldly and Vedic practical activity based upon the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) would be utterly destroyed; furthermore, all activities within the domain of Brahman, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and so forth, would result in being abandoned. Thus, if Brahman possesses a manifold nature, the analogies of clay and the like will be appropriate.
He refutes this doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) by stating:
"It could not be so.
First, it must be said here:
For one who asserts that there is identity in the form of clay and plurality in the form of jars, bowls, and so forth, is it intended that there is mutual non-difference between cause and effect,
or rather difference, or perhaps both difference and non-difference?

In that case, if non-difference were absolute, both the two expressions—“in the form of clay” and “in the form of a jar, a bowl, and so forth”—as well as the restriction [of the effect to those specific forms] would be untenable. If, however, there is difference, the two expressions and the restriction are both tenable;
yet, the expression “in the form of [the cause] itself” (ātmanā) would be inconsistent.

For one thing cannot be the self of another, nor is there a doctrine of non-exclusivity (anekāntavāda). Even if one were to assume both difference and non-difference, there would still be two distinct descriptions.
But such a restriction is illogical;
for it is not possible that when two substrata—the cause and the effect—are intermingled, their properties—unity and plurality—should not likewise become intermingled.
Consequently, as long as there is unity in the nature of the clay, there would have to be unity even in the forms of the jar, the bowl, and so forth.
In this way, as long as there is multiplicity in the form of jars, bowls, and so forth, there must likewise be multiplicity in the form of clay.
This rule necessitates either an absolute difference between cause and effect,
or else the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of the effect.
This has already been thoroughly investigated by us in the first chapter;
let it rest for now.
He cites a scriptural passage that reiterates what has been refuted by reasoning:
"Only 'earth' is the truth.
This might be the case:
the state of the individual soul (jīva) belonging to Brahman is not merely conceptual.
However, he is real, for he is a constituent part [of Brahman]; since the state of being Brahman is bestowed upon him through knowledge conjoined with action, the author says:
"For [he] is well-known by himself."
Regarding the phrase "of that which is innate and beginningless":

as for what was stated— that worldly and ritual activity based on the *karmakāṇḍa* will be established through the aspect of manifoldness— he replies to that with the words "and when [it is] sublated."
For as long as there is no sublation, all this worldly transaction is like the transaction with the collection of objects presented in the state of a dream.

And just as that [transaction] ceases upon the occurrence of a sublation in the waking state, so too does it cease through the sublation consisting of the direct realization of the identity of the embodied self with Brahman, which arises from the ripening of the practice of meditating on such sentences as "That thou art."
It might be argued as follows:

by such passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?", it is not that worldly activity—characterized by action, agent, and so forth, which is dependent on false knowledge—is removed by right knowledge; rather, worldly activity, which rests upon a particular state [of consciousness], ceases through the attainment of another state.

Just as for a child, [the capacity for] acting, speaking, and eating according to desire ceases upon reaching the initiation ceremony (*upaneyana*), yet he does not thereby become one whose [previous state] was based on false knowledge; so it is here as well. Therefore, he says: "And this is not an absence of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)."
Why?
Because [the sentence] "That thou art" teaches the identity of the self with Brahman;
for this sentence does not indeed teach the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman as being restricted to a particular state.
Moreover, it does not refer to him as eternal in the same way one says "this is a rope, not a snake.
Furthermore, he states that even by speaking of both the real and the unreal, this very point is appropriate, saying:
"and by the example of the thief."
And it is not the case that in this perception [one thing sublates another];
for indeed, the cognition of being coiled in a piece of wood that possesses a staff, a water-pot, and earrings does not sublate its possession of a staff or its possession of a water-pot.
Why is that?
Because those earrings and so forth exist as real (*bhāvika*) within that [gold],
so too here, by means of the knowledge of oneness which has the real as its object, the reality of multiplicity is not to be negated;
for a thing is not removed by knowledge.
Rather, the meaning is that it is superimposed by false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). He objects: "But surely, this implies the absolute acceptance of oneness (*ekatvaikānta*)."

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is defined as that which produces a cognition that is uncontradicted, not previously apprehended, and free from doubt; it is by virtue of this general definition of *pramāṇa* that perception and the other [means of knowledge] attain the status of being valid cognitions.

However, if the absolute oneness (*ekatvaikānta*) of all things were accepted, then all these [means of knowledge], which have difference as their object, would result in being invalid because they would be contradicted.

Likewise, even the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions would be undermined, since it depends upon the distinctions between the cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), the agent (*bhāvaka*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And likewise, there would be nihilism;

furthermore, since the entire Veda is sublated by the sublation of even a single part, the Upanishads (Vedāntas) would also lack authority, resulting in the loss of the doctrine of absolute non-duality. He states that this treatise on liberation is not only sublated by the sublation of injunctions and prohibitions, but is itself dependent upon difference in its very nature: [He says: ... [the sublation of this treatise on liberation occurs] not only through the sublation of injunctions and prohibitions, but because it too depends upon difference in its essential form. Thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the treatise on liberation" (*mokṣaśāstrasyāpi*): furthermore, in this view, since letters, words, sentences, contexts, and so forth are unreal, the non-dual knowledge arising from them would be incorrect; for indeed, knowledge of fire does not arise correctly from what is unreal. Thus he says: "And how [could there be liberation] by means of an unreal treatise on liberation? (*kathaṃ cānṛtena mokṣaśāstreṇa*).
He addresses this objection: "To this it is said.
Although perception and the other means of knowledge do not possess ultimate non-sublation, [they are nonetheless valid].
Because it is sublated by both reasoning and scripture, nevertheless, since there is no sublation within the sphere of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), this non-sublation is merely conventional.
Indeed, no one engaged in worldly existence, having determined an object through perception and the other means of knowledge, is ever found to be contradicted in their practical activity.
Therefore, since they are not sublated, perception and the other means of knowledge do not deviate from the definition of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Because of the establishment of truth" means:
because of the establishment of the conviction of truth.
This is the summary statement; he analyzes it as follows:
"For as long as there is no realization of the oneness of the Self with Reality..."

The construction is as follows: one regards the very modifications, such as the body and so forth, as "I" through the sense of selfhood (ātma-bhāva), and sons, cattle, and so forth, as "mine" through the sense of possession (ātmiya-bhāva).
The phrase "and Vedic" refers to the justification for the practical application of both the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) and the treatises on liberation (mokṣaśāstra).
He analyzes [the phrase] "just like the conventional usage of dreams" as follows:
"as in the case of an ordinary person who has fallen asleep.
Having restated what was said [by the opponent], namely, "how can liberation be attained through a scripture that is false," he refutes it:
But how [can it be said] "by that which is unreal"? It can be said here:
even this collection of knowledge arising from the Vedānta, beginning with the means such as hearing and culminating in the direct realization of the Self, is unreal.

For even that [attainment] is of the nature of a function and, as an effect, is subject to cessation; however, the direct realization of the state of Brahmanhood is not an effect, because its very essence is that [Brahman].
Therefore, this objection—namely, "how can the real arise from the unreal?"—is not to be raised.
Indeed, that which is real does not arise; how, then, could there be the arising of that which is unreal?
And whatever arises is entirely unreal.
However, the conventional reality (*sāṃvyavahārika-satya*) is common to both the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, as well as the realization of Brahman in its active form.

Therefore, it should be understood that by accepting the ultimate reality of the direct realization of Brahman—which is the very nature of the state [of liberation]—one is merely pointing out a logical deviation [in the opponent's argument].

Even though real death arises from a conventionally real fear, nevertheless, the cause of that fear—the snake or the cognition of it—is unreal; thus, it is said that real fear is produced from the unreal, which constitutes the production of the real from the unreal.

Furthermore, although the cognition of the snake exists in its own right, it is not the cause of fear in its capacity as a mere cognition, but rather by virtue of being qualified by the form of an indeterminable (anirvacanīya) snake.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of fear arising even from the cognition of a rope, since there is no distinction between them insofar as both are cognitions.
Therefore, it is established that knowledge itself, when colored by an indefinable snake, is also indefinable; thus, the production of the real from the unreal is proven.
However, we do not say that the production of everything real arises from everything unreal.
For if it were so, the cognition of fire arising from a "smoke-cow" (dhūmamahiṣī)—which is merely a superimposed state of being smoke—would have to be true.

It is not the case that because a visual cognition of form arises as true, a cognition of taste and so forth must also arise from it as true. For such is the restriction regarding true cognitions: that something specific arises only from something specific.
Thus, there is a restriction even among unreal things: from some unreal thing truth arises, and from others untruth;

just as, although the superimposition of length and so forth upon syllables is indistinguishable in both cases, from the word *ajīnam* people correctly understand the absence of a bowstring (*jyāni*), whereas from the word *ajinam*, those who understand the absence of a bowstring due to the superimposed state of length become deluded.
And there is no difference whatsoever regarding the superimposition of length in both cases;
therefore, it is logically established that the arising of the real can occur even from the unreal.
He states another illustration:
Regarding the phrase "of one in the state of seeing a dream":

just as a worldly person, having seen a snake while awake, flees and consequently does not suffer the pain of its bite; or just as one who is thirsty, perceiving water, proceeds to drink and, having reached it, experiences happiness by drinking again and again.

Thus, since everything remains in that same state even within a dream, the accomplishment of an effect cannot proceed from what is unreal. An objection is raised: "That effect, too, is indeed unreal."
The meaning is that even so, it has been stated that the establishment of the real does not proceed from the unreal. He offers a rebuttal: "To this we reply."
Regarding the phrase "of one in the state of seeing a dream":
for an ordinary person who has awakened from sleep, they consider the object perceived to be sublated, but not the cognition itself.
Therefore, although investigators determine that cognition—being colored by the indefinable—is itself indefinable, this was stated according to the perspective of ordinary people.
In this context, he refutes the view of the Lokāyatikas with the phrase:
"by this non-sublation of the cognition of the dreamer.

For instance, when Caitra [sees] a female jackal with a mouth made terrifying by wide, formidable fangs, with a tail raised up and touching her whirling head, and with large, round eyes fixed and blood-red with extreme rage—
When one who has assumed a human body— whose form is terrifying due to its bristling horripilation and is reflected in the walls of a crystal mountain—
awakens from a dream and perceives his own human body, he then realizes that the self transcends the body, identifying the self as persisting through both bodies.
It determines [the self], but not as being merely the body;
for if it were merely that, there would follow the consequence of an absence of recollection, just as there is none regarding the body itself.

And how could this be possible if the cognition of the dreamer were uncontradicted? For if that were contradicted, there would be no subsequent recognition. Furthermore, he states that the perception of the real from the unreal is established by scripture and established through positive and negative concomitance: [The verse: "Even from the unreal, the real is perceived; thus it is seen in the world. Just as the form of a woman is seen in a painting, so too is the Self seen within the body. [The commentary: In this world, even from what is unreal, the perception of the real is observed. For example, just as the form of a woman is seen in a painting, so too is the Self seen within the body. Therefore, the perception of the real from the unreal is established. Thus, the objection that "the cognition of the dreamer is contradicted" is refuted. This is because the dreamer’s cognition is not contradicted by another waking cognition; rather, it is contradicted by the dreamer's own subsequent waking cognition. Since the dreamer’s cognition is not contradicted by another waking cognition, it is established that the perception of the real from the unreal occurs even in the absence of a real object. Therefore, the objection that "there is no subsequent recognition" is also refuted. This is because the subsequent recognition is established by the dreamer’s own waking cognition, which is not contradicted by another waking cognition. Consequently, the perception of the real from the unreal is established both by scripture and by positive and negative concomitance. Thus, the objection that "the cognition of the dreamer is contradicted" is refuted. This is because the dreamer’s cognition is not contradicted by another waking cognition; rather, it is contradicted by the dreamer’s own subsequent waking cognition. Since the dreamer’s cognition is not contradicted by another waking cognition, it is established that the perception of the real from the unreal occurs even in the absence of a real object. Therefore, the objection that "there is no subsequent recognition" is also refuted. This is because the subsequent recognition is established by the dreamer’s own waking cognition, which is not contradicted by another waking cognition. Consequently, the perception of the real from the unreal is established both by scripture and by positive and negative concomitance. Thus, the objection that "the cognition of the dreamer is contradicted" is refuted. This is because the dreamer’s cognition is not contradicted by another waking cognition; rather, it is contradicted by the dreamer’s own subsequent waking cognition. Since the dreamer’s cognition is not contradicted by another waking cognition, it is established that the perception of the real from the unreal occurs even in the absence of a real object. Therefore, the objection that "there is no subsequent recognition" is also refuted. This is because the subsequent recognition is established by the dreamer’s own waking cognition, which is not contradicted by another waking cognition. Consequently, the perception of the real from the unreal is established both by scripture and by positive and negative concomitance. "And so says the Śruti. Regarding "the letter 'A' and so forth": although the nature of the lines is real, nevertheless, according to convention, they are unreal.

For those who establish conventions do not establish them by saying, "This letter is to be understood through such a distinction of lines," but rather, "Such a distinction of lines is the letter *a*, and such is the letter *ka*. Thus, it is established that the comprehension of the correct letters arises from an incorrect convention. As for what was said—that through the aspect of unity, the practical activities of cognition and liberation will be accomplished—[that too is untenable].
"But worldly activity based on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) will be established through the aspect of diversity"; to this he replies:
"Moreover, this is the final means of valid cognition.
Indeed, if there were any worldly activity whatsoever that were based on the comprehension of unity, [then this would not be the case].
Because the realization of that [truth] sublates everything else;
for instance, the realization of identity in the form "That thou art" arises without subverting the entire range of means of knowledge, their results, and worldly transactions,
and beyond this realization there exists nothing either favorable or unfavorable.

Since there is nothing further to be desired beyond this— because it prevents what is favorable and unfavorable regarding that which is depended upon and that by which this [negation] would be rejected.
And this comprehension is not like rice-water; thus he says:
"And this [is] not...
It might be argued as follows:
If this final comprehension were purposeless, then it would not be undertaken by discerning persons;
or, if it were possessed of a purpose, it could not be "final. To this, he says: "And this comprehension is not without purpose. Why?"
Because it is observed that its fruit is the cessation of ignorance.
For this [knowledge], having arisen, does not subsequently remove ignorance such that it would not be final;
rather, by virtue of having a nature opposed to ignorance, it arises as the very essence of that cessation.
Furthermore, the cessation of ignorance is not a fruit by virtue of being its effect, but rather by virtue of being desired;
for a fruit is defined by the characteristic of being something desired.
To refute that which is contrary [to liberation] and directed outwardly, he says:
"Or is it an error?
Why?
"Because there is a sublater."
It might be argued:
let there be no conventional usage based on unity; however, there is one based on plurality, for that alone sustains the entire course of worldly affairs.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing that [multiplicity], its reality must be postulated; to this he says:
"And previously" (prāk ca). For practical activity (vyavahāra) is established through the intellect of those who act with deliberation.
However, it is not [real] in an ultimate sense,
for it has been explained that such [a cognition] is possible even through error;
and it is true because it is non-contradictory.
And falsehood (*anṛta*) consists in being indefinable due to its inability to withstand critical inquiry.

He concludes the present topic by stating that the final knowledge of the oneness of the Self is subverting because it is independent, whereas the knowledge of multiplicity is subverted because it is weak, depending as it does upon the apprehension of a counter-correlate.
Therefore, [it is said] "by the final means of valid cognition.
This might be so:
we do not postulate the ultimate reality of multiplicity for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of multiplicity.
But he raises an objection, claiming that its reality is based solely on scripture: "Now, from clay... He answers:
It is said: "No.
For although some kind of transformation might be inferred by means of examples such as clay and the like, it is not possible to infer [such a transformation here].
Because the statement, "Only 'earth' is true," establishes that the effect is unreal by determining that only the cause is real;
and because there are thousands of scriptural passages directly teaching that Brahman is immutable and eternal, Brahman does not possess the quality of undergoing transformation.
Now, as to why even the immutable should not undergo transformation, he says:
"For not of one" [is the phrase].
He raises an objection: "Like staying and moving."
"Just as there is both motion and its cessation based on a single arrow, so too, in a single Brahman, there will be both transformation and its absence, resulting in immutability (*kauṭasthya*).
He refutes this with the words: "No, because of the qualification 'of that which is immutable'."
For immutability (*kūṭasthanityatā*) is indeed perpetual, consisting in the non-deviation from one's own nature. How could that not be contradicted by [the occurrence of] deviation?
Nor is a property (*dharma*) separate from its substratum (*dharmī*), such that the substratum would remain immutable even when that property arises or perishes.
Because where there is absolute difference, as between a cow and a horse, there can be no relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*).
However, arrows and such things are subject to transformation; they transform through both staying and moving.

Furthermore, not even a single syllable of the mass of the Vedas—which has its purpose established by the injunction for Vedic study—can be meaningless, let alone this entire [passage] which establishes that the world has Brahman as its source.
By means of the context of the passage:

therein, the fruitless nature of being the source of the world, which is mentioned in proximity to the scriptural teaching of the fruitful vision of Brahman, exists for the sake of that [vision] as a means to it, and not for the sake of some other purpose; thus he says:
"And not as in the case of Brahman."
Therefore, the meaning is that this [scripture] does not have transformation as its primary purport.

He raises the objection regarding the contradiction with the initial proposition and the contradiction with the Śruti of the aphorism "tadananyatvam" (non-difference from That), specifically for one who maintains the doctrine of the self as the immutable Brahman.
He refutes this, saying: "No; it is of the nature of ignorance.
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are themselves the seed; their differentiation is the manifold of effects (kāryaprapañca), because sovereignty depends upon that.

This is what is meant: the lordship and omniscience of Brahman are not real (tāttvika), but rather are conditioned by the limiting adjunct of ignorance (avidyopādhika). Therefore, there is no contradiction between the *pratijñāsūtra*, which has that [conditioned state] as its basis, and the *tadananyatvasūtra*, which has the reality (tattva) as its basis.
The rest is easy to understand. 2.1.6.15.
*And because of the perception of existence*:

the existence (*bhāva*) of the cause—that is, its being (*sattā*)—and its perception (*upalambha*); [the inference follows] from the perception and the existence of the effect when that [cause] exists.
This is what is meant: the term "object" (viṣaya) refers to both the object and the subject, and the term "subject" (viṣin) also refers to both the subject and the object;

by that reason, the meaning of the sūtra results in [the statement]: "because of the presence or absence of the perception of the effect, there is the presence or absence of the perception of the cause."

And thus, there is no deviation [of the reason] with respect to visual perception that conforms to the presence or absence of light-form, nor with respect to the distinction of smoke that conforms to the presence or absence of fire; this is established.
In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya begins by stating one part of the aforementioned reason:
For this reason as well, there is non-difference— that is, the absence of distinction— between the effect and the cause; because, for this reason, the effect is indeed the very being of the cause.
He states its capacity to convey [the meaning] by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"And not necessarily...
[The point is that] by the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (kākatālīya), one thing is perceived when another exists.
The meaning is that it is not, however, by way of necessity.
He raises an objection regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in order to qualify the reason (*hetu*): "But even when another exists... and so forth.
He offers a rebuttal according to the view of a certain school:
"It is said, 'No'.
Having refuted the rebuttal of that school by addressing the objection, he states the rebuttal according to the ultimate truth:
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates that by this [word], a qualification of the reason has been stated.
By means of an alternative reading, he explains this very same sūtra as follows:
"It is not from the word alone" means:
by the perceptual cognition "cloth," it is the very threads in the state of being stretched lengthwise and crosswise that are apprehended as the object,
but no cloth distinct from them is perceived through direct perception.

Unity, however, belongs to the threads because they are delimited by a single purposeful action characterized as a single garment, even though they are many— just as many trees such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa*, when delimited by a single place and time, are called a "forest. Furthermore, it is observed that even things incapable of performing a purposeful action individually are seen to perform it when combined, without having produced any other distinct entity.
Just as stones constitute a single support for a cooking pot, so too, without being directed toward any other purpose, the threads, when combined, will produce a single garment.
Nor is it correct to say that because of inherence there is no perception of difference even between distinct things; for such non-perception would be untenable.
Because they are mutually dependent:
for inherence is established only if difference is established, and difference [is established] through inherence;
yet there is no other means of proof for difference.

It has been established that [the distinction between] causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and verbal designation (*vyapadeśa*) is possible even when there is no difference [between the two]. Therefore, this [objection] is trivial. And by this same line of reasoning, Brahman alone, as the fundamental cause, is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
And he states that all intermediate causes, such as the threads and so forth, are likewise indeed indeterminable:
"And thus, in the case of the threads... (2.1.6.16). And because of the existence of what follows.
He analyzes [the point] with the words "for this reason also":
not only is there scriptural authority, but...

And here the following argument arises: "Whatever exists in whatever form does not exist there in that form. For oil does not exist in sand by way of being of the nature of sand, just as a jar exists in clay by way of being of the nature of clay.
For a present jar is perceived as having the nature of clay;
however, present oil is not perceived as having the nature of sand.
Therefore, just as oil is not produced from sand, so too the world would not be produced from the Self.
And since it is born, it is understood that "the self existed by means of the self. He states another argument:
Just as the cause is Brahman:

for just as a jar is always and everywhere a jar and never at any time or place becomes a cloth, so too Being (sat), being everywhere and at all times Being alone, can never at any time or place become non-being; this has been established above.
Therefore, the effect is indeed existent throughout the three periods of time.
If it is asked, "What follows if the *sattva* is thus?", he says:
"And furthermore, it is one.
That is, the *sattva* of both cause and effect is one and the same.
For existence (*sattva*) does not differ with each individual instance;
therefore, because they are non-different from that undivided existence, these two also do not differ from one another.
Nor is it logical to claim that existence itself is differentiated because it is non-different from those two.
For if that were the case, it would follow that the existent (sattva) is merely superimposed.

In that regard, when conceiving one of the two— difference or non-difference— as superimposed, should the conception of non-difference be based upon real non-difference, or should the conception of non-difference be based upon real difference?

We, however, observe that since the apprehension of difference depends upon the apprehension of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and since the apprehension of a counter-correlative is possible even without the apprehension of difference—otherwise there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—and since the apprehension of non-difference is independent and thus not subject to such [dependence], and because difference resides in each of the two terms individually such that it is impossible when either one is absent, the conceptualization of difference is based solely upon the apprehension of non-difference; this is entirely established.

If it is argued that [the Self] is not so [non-different from Brahman] "because of the designation of unreality" (*asadvyapadeśāt*), we say: no, for [this designation refers] to another attribute, as is clear from the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣāt*).
The two properties of being determinate and being indeterminate are themselves indeterminable.
This Sūtra has been explained by a commentary that requires no further verbal explanation. (17) [Sūtra 2.1.6.18:
"Because of reasoning and because of another scriptural statement."
"Because of the possession of excellence (*atiśaya*) in the prior state. For excellence is a property (*dharma*), and it cannot exist in an effect that lacks excellence.
[Objection: But surely it is not the excellence of the effect that is the cause of restriction, but rather a specific capacity (*śaktibheda*) of the cause.
And since that [effect] exists even when the effect is non-existent because the cause exists, he says:
"and power" (śaktiśca).
It is not something other than the effect and the cause.
Nor can it be joined with the phrase "not as something non-existent in the form of an effect.
Furthermore, regarding the words "of cause and effect":
although this point was already stated under the sūtra "And because of perception due to existence" (2.2.16), it is introduced again here for the purpose of refuting inherence (samavāya).

And if the relation of inherence with its two substrata (the inherent things) is not admitted, there follows the consequence of disjunction between parts and wholes, substances and qualities, and so forth.
For inherence, being unconnected with its substrata, cannot connect those substrata together. [The opponent] objects:
Now, as for the claim that "inherence itself [is real]":

just as substances, qualities, and actions exist through their connection with existence (*sattva*), whereas existence itself is real by its very nature and thus does not depend on a further connection with another existence; so too must inherence be.
Likewise, inherence does not require the application of another relation in order to be connected with its two inherent relata,
because it is itself of the nature of a relation.
He refutes this by showing that it leads to a contradiction with other established doctrines:
"Then conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as well [would require inherence]," it might be argued.

However, one should not say that conjunction is [inherently related] because conjunction is an effect, and because an effect must arise dependent upon an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), which would be impossible if there were no inherence;
for if that were so, it would follow that eternal conjunction (*ajasaṃyoga*) lacks [inherence].

Moreover, since inherence (samavāya) is defined in dependence upon its relata, just as it does not differ when there is a difference between the two relata, nor is it destroyed when they are destroyed, but rather is eternal and one— so too might conjunction (saṃyoga) be.
What fault would there be in that?

Now, if—out of fear of this same consequence—it is accepted that inherence (*samavāya*), like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), is divided according to its pairs of correlates and is non-eternal, then it follows that just as [an effect] arises from a single efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) alone, so too would conjunction arise from an efficient cause alone; thus the two cases are identical.
And because there is the cognition of identity (*tādātmyapratīti*).
For when a relation is understood, it is the understanding of that relation—not identity—that serves as the seed for the conceptualization of a relation;
this is because identity is incompatible with a relation between multiple things sharing a single substratum.
He refutes the existence of a whole distinct from its parts by means of the dilemma regarding its subsistence (vṛtti):
And how is it to be performed?
It is "entire" (samasta),
because the middle and rear parts are not separated by the front part.
Now, [it might be argued that] although [the whole] is connected to all its parts, it will be perceived as residing in only a few parts; to this, he says:
"For multiplicity...
and then, "If [it is argued that it is perceived] part by part..."

For the number "many" exists by its very nature as a distributed whole across the things to be numbered; thus, even if one thing is not apprehended among those to be numbered, the number is not apprehended, because that form [of "many"] is distributed over the totality.
A composite object, however, does not pervade its parts by its own nature.
Rather, it is by way of its parts.

The point is this: just as a thread, while pervading flowers through its parts, does not require the grasping of all the flowers because it is perceived even in the place of just a few flowers, so too is the case with the whole (avayavin).
He refutes this with the words "even then" (tadāpi).
He raises an objection with the words "like cowness and so forth" (gotvādivat).
He refutes this, saying "no.
Even though the particulars of the universal "cowness" are indefinable and not ultimately real, and thus how could it be fully present in each individual? [The opponent's objection stands.]
Nevertheless, this should be understood as having been stated even while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]:
since it would have no agent, it would therefore be without a self (nirātmaka).
For in the absence of a cause, what indeed could an unproduced effect possibly be?
Therefore, the meaning is that [the pot] is devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*).

If it were argued that the word "pot" is applied metaphorically—on the basis of its being intended for that purpose—to the parts of the pot which have entered into a temporal sequence by being engaged in activity and are oriented toward the production of the pot, and that since these parts possess agency by virtue of their established existence, the usage "the pot comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*) is justified; to this he says:
And as for the statement "the production of the jar is being described":
for production is indeed the activity of already established factors such as the potsherds and the potter; it is not [itself] production.
Nor is production identical to the act of producing.
This is because there is a distinction between the activity of the one who causes to act and the one who is caused to act;
otherwise, if they were non-distinct, it would follow that one could say "the jar arises" just as one says "he produces the jar.

Therefore, just as in the case of "he does" and "he causes to do," one must admit a difference in locus for the arising and the causing to arise, which pertain respectively to the servant and the master with respect to the object, the jar.

In this regard, since established agents such as weavers and potters possess the capacity for production and maintenance (*utpādana-adhiṣṭhāna*), they do not possess the status of being the locus of origination (*utpatti-adhiṣṭhānatva*). Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be accepted that the jar alone is the locus of origination as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore, since that which is non-existent cannot be a locus, its existence (*sattva*) must be admitted. And thus, in the expression "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), because the activity of the jar is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), its status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) therein is logically established.
Just as in the case of rice grains, they undergo softening when there is softening;
thus one might object: "Now, origination is simply the connection with the existence of its own cause."
This is what is meant: "origination" (utpatti) is not some kind of activity by virtue of which one might be questioned how an unestablished entity can possess agency here;
rather, it is inherence in its own causes.
Or [it might be argued that] it is its own existence or its own nature, and that is not contradictory even for a non-existent thing;
to this he says: "That too is impossible for a non-existent thing."
"How is it that [the effect] has not attained its own nature?

Furthermore, since the effect is non-existent prior to its production, it is illogical to establish a boundary between the absence of the effect and the existence [of the cause]; thus he says: "And of the non-existence... etc.

This might be the case: let there be no boundary for the absolute non-existence of the son of a barren woman, for he is indeed indefinable; however, the prior non-existence of a jar does have a boundary, since it is definable by the future jar. To this, he says:

If it is argued that "the son of a barren woman [arises] from the operation of an agent," this has already been addressed below: just as a jar never becomes a cloth, so too that which is non-existent (asat) cannot become existent (sat).
Therefore, if the jar were non-existent in the lump of clay, its non-existence would be absolute.
Here, the proponent of the theory that the effect does not pre-exist (asatkāryavādin) objects:

"But if this were so... [The author replies: "Even if the effect were already established beforehand, the operation [of the cause] might still be purposeful in joining it with the cause at some point. To this he says: "And because of its non-difference from that."
He refutes [the objection], saying: "This is not a fault.
It has already been stated how the reality of the serpent does not differ from that of the rope.
For it is indeed just a rope,
while the difference is merely conceptual;
likewise, in reality, the nature of the effect does not differ from the cause, for it is simply the very essence of the cause.
However, the effect, being inexpressible, appears as if distinct and yet as if non-distinct;
this is what was stated by the phrase "the non-difference of the reality."
In reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), distinctness does not arise merely from the perception of difference;
rather, the meaning is that conventional distinctness and identity do indeed occur in some way. For it is precisely along these lines that this textual composition is to be applied.

He states another refutation against the proponent of the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavādin): "But for whom [it is so]," etc. The meaning is that only if the effect is non-different from the cause would the operation of the causal factors have an object; otherwise, it would not.
He explains the portion of the sūtra beginning with "Brahman is the root cause" by taking up the phrase "and from another scriptural passage," stating:
"Thus, on account of reasoning, [it is the cause] of the effect."
The meaning is not obscure.
2.1.6.19. And like a cloth;
and as in the case of the vital breaths and so forth.
Thus, [the point] has been explained in the Sūtra by means of a commentary (bhāṣya) that requires no further verbal explanation. 2.1.6.20. // 20 // 2.1.7.21.
*Itaravyapadeśāddhitākaraṇādidoṣaprasaktiḥ* (The objection that defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others] would follow because of the designation of [Brahman] as the other).
Although the Śrutis speak of the difference between the embodied soul and the Supreme Self, nevertheless many Śrutis also demonstrate their non-difference.
Furthermore, difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same thing due to their mutual contradiction,
nor has it been stated that difference is ultimately real;
therefore, the embodied self does not differ from the omniscient Supreme Self in reality.

However, that very [Self] appears as differentiated due to the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of ignorance, like space within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth. Its conditioned form is the embodied self (śārīra);
therefore, let it be that the individual souls (jīvas) do not experience their own identity with the Supreme Self.
The Supreme Self, however, experiences them as non-different from itself;
for if it did not so experience them, its omniscience would be contradicted.
And if it were so, it, while binding these individual souls (jīvas), would bind itself alone.
Regarding this, it has been said:
"Indeed, no one who is not dependent on another would build a prison for himself and then enter it," and so forth.
Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the world does not have a conscious being as its cause. //21// 2.1.7.22.
"But there is a distinction because of the specific designation.

This is true: although he perceives these individual souls as non-different from the Supreme Self in reality due to the latter's omniscience, he does not perceive them as such in their actual state; for these souls have no connection with the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, yet by the power of ignorance they possess a conceit [of such experience] corresponding to that.

And thus, since I am indifferent even toward their experiences of pleasure, pain, and so forth, there is no injury whatsoever to me even if they are cast into a prison; therefore, the fault of failing to act for their benefit and the like does not arise.
This is what was stated:
"Moreover, when [it is said] 'That thou art'..."
Furthermore, the word "ca" (and) indicates the conjunction with the preceding argument, not the introduction of a separate argument. 2.1.7.23.
This might be so.
If the world were an emanation from Brahman, then alas, it would follow that everything must possess consciousness like a living being; therefore, he says:
"And as in the case of stones and the like, that is untenable."
This has been explained by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) whose meaning is not obscure. 2.1.8.24.
"If it be argued that [Brahman cannot be the material cause] because we observe a withdrawal [of the effect], we say no; for it is like milk.
Indeed, Brahman alone, being non-dual and independent of anything else, is accepted as the material cause of the universe—which arises in succession and possesses diverse forms—yet this is untenable.
Indeed, a diversity of effects cannot arise from a single form, for that would entail the consequence of its being causeless;
for it is the diversity of causes that is the cause of the diversity of effects.
Because we observe a difference in effects— such as sprouts and snakes— corresponding to differences in their causes, such as seeds from milk or other sources,
it is not logical for an effect to arise sequentially from a cause that is non-sequential.
For that which is capable cannot endure delay, and because it is non-dual, it is impossible for it to encounter auxiliary conditions (sahakāri) in a sequential manner.
This is what was stated: "For here in the world...
Each individual factor, such as clay and so forth, is a causal agent (*kāraka*), but their collection (*sāmagrya*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
For it is from that [Brahman] alone that the effect is indeed accomplished;
therefore, since Brahman is not non-dual, it cannot be the material cause of the world—this being the position reached, it is said: "Like milk, indeed."

First, please explain this which you have been asked: is this spoken with reference to its ultimate (tāttvika) nature, or is it its conceptual (kālpānika) omniscience and omnipotence accompanied by the beginningless seeds of name-and-form (nāmarūpa)?
Regarding the former alternative, what indeed could arise from that which is non-dual and without companion?
For there exists no real effect (vastusat-kārya) for that whose intrinsic nature is pure, awakened, and liberated.
And thus says the Śruti: "For him, there exists neither effect nor instrument.

However, in the subsequent alternative, if it is sought to prove that [Brahman] is not a material cause (anupādānatva) due to the absence of auxiliary causes entirely distinct from itself—like a potter and so forth—then there is a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to milk and the like.
For even those [entities] reach another state of transformation by themselves alone through the influence of time, without depending on external causes such as consciousness;
here, the reason is stated as their independence from internal causes,
but that is unproven (*asiddha*).
This is because it is assisted by the seed of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which is itself inexpressible.

Thus, scripture says: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. Furthermore, the sequential ripening [of effects] from that [cause] must also be understood as occurring in a sequence. Moreover, it is observed that even from a single cause possessing diverse powers, the production of multiple effects occurs.
Just as from a single fire there arise both burning and cooking, or from a single action there arise conjunction, disjunction, and latent impression (saṃskāra). 24.
If, however, one qualifies [the reason] by adding "provided it possesses consciousness," then there is no deviation [of the reason] by the case of milk and so forth;
for potters and others are indeed seen to depend upon external materials such as clay.
And regarding the statement "Brahman is volition," this [sūtra] is presented as a counter-argument: "Even as in the world, like gods and so forth."

That by which something is perceived is "loka"; [here] it refers specifically to sound. 2.1.9.26. [The objection: "There would be the consequence of the whole [Brahman] undergoing transformation, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its partlessness.
[Reply: But surely, Brahman does not undergo transformation in reality (tattvataḥ), such that it would be subject to the dilemma of whether it is transformed as a whole or in part.

However, through a differentiation of form characterized by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) imagined by ignorance—which consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and which is indefinable as being either identical to or different from reality—Brahman becomes the locus for conventional transactions such as transformation;
yet, this imagined form does not touch the actual reality.
For the imagination of a double moon by one suffering from ophthalmia does not bring about a duality in the moon itself.
Or rather, it is through the impossibility of that [transformation] that the moon itself becomes impossible.
Therefore, although this conceptualization of transformation is unreal and untenable, it does not bring about the impossibility of Brahman, which exists in the ultimate sense.
Consequently, since there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), this section (adhikaraṇa) need not have been commenced; to this, he says:
"Consciousness is one.

Although transformation is in fact precluded by hundreds of scriptural passages dedicated to establishing absolute non-duality, nevertheless, by means of the analogies of milk and other substances and deities, there arises once again the possibility that it is real; thus, through the reasoning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), this [objection] is addressed in every respect.
The meaning is that, having set aside the position that [the world] cannot be logically established,

the meaning of the Śruti— characterized as absolute non-duality— is purified by strengthening the doctrine of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) through the two sūtras, "And thus in the Self" and "For [the powers] are manifold.
Therefore, Brahman exists unmodified in reality.
The objection, "Is it not so even by means of verbal testimony? is intended to expose the fact that [the world] is constructed by ignorance (avidyā).
For there is no third alternative between being partless (niravayavatva) and having parts (sāvayavatva), because the negation of one necessarily entails the affirmation of the other.

Therefore, since no other mode is possible and both modes—being partless and having parts—are untenable, the meaning of the objection is that verbal testimony would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), like the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning stones floating on water.

For the self that perceives dreams creates chariots and other such things by means of the mind alone, without destroying its own essential nature. [28] 2.1.9.29.
And because of the defect in his own position, he objects:
"Is it not so? [The opponent] replies:
"Not by such a kind."
Although the aggregate possesses parts, nevertheless each constituent— sattva and the others— is partless.
For it is not possible that sattva alone undergoes transformation while rajas and tamas do not,
since it is accepted that all three transform collectively.
Furthermore, for each of those things that are partless, if there were a transformation of the whole, it would follow that their very root is destroyed;
or, if there were a transformation of only one part, the undesirable consequence of having parts (sāvayavatva) would ensue.
This applies equally to those who maintain the doctrine of qualities (guṇavādinaḥ).

For according to the Vaiśeṣikas, the process is as follows: from two atoms (paramāṇu) joined together, one dyad (dvyaṇuka) is produced; and from three of those dyads, one triad (tryaṇuka) is produced.
In that case, the conjunction of two partless atoms would have to pervade both of those atoms.
Or, if it did not pervade [the space], it would not exist there;
for it is impossible that the very same thing should both exist and not exist in that place at that time.

Furthermore, since the six atoms situated above, below, and on the sides would occupy the same location, extension could not be established, and it would follow that even a composite mass would be no larger than a single atom.
Alternatively, if there were no pervasion [of space], the atom would have six parts, which would contradict its partlessness.
Furthermore, it is impossible to admit that it has parts;
for if that were the case, since it would possess infinite parts, it would follow as a logical consequence that Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed would be equal in magnitude.

Therefore, the fault is equal. This equality was stated merely from the perspective of the initial appearance; however, in ultimate reality, this fault is unavoidable for those who maintain that there is a real transformation (*pariṇāma*) or a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), but not for us, the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādins*). Thus he says:
"But it has been refuted" (parihṛtas tu).
2.1.10.30. It has been stated that Brahman possesses manifold powers; regarding this, the following sūtra is intended to present scriptural authority:

"And [the soul] is endowed with all [powers] upon seeing Him. (Sūtra 30) This sūtra is intended to resolve the objection [raised against the preceding statement]: "If it be argued that [the soul does not possess powers] because it is devoid of instruments, that has already been answered. (Sūtra 31)

To begin with, just as the distinction observed through valid means of knowledge between the creation of gods and others—which does not depend on external instruments—and that of potters and others—which does depend on external instruments—cannot be denied;

and just as the creation of chariots and so forth seen in dreams—which is accomplished by the internal instrument alone without depending on external instruments—is observed during the waking state’s creation that does depend on external instruments and cannot be denied;

even so, the creation of the universe heard in scripture as belonging to the Supreme Deity, who possesses all powers and does not depend on an internal instrument, does not deserve to be denied on the mere basis of what is observed in general. //31// 2.1.11.32.
It is not so, because [the world] possesses the nature of a *paryāya*.
To begin with, the process of the world does not arise from a delusion of intellect on his part, like that of a madman, because it is impossible for one who is deluded to be omniscient.
Therefore, this world must have been created by a wise being.

Furthermore, the activity of a wise being—having as its purpose the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful for oneself and others—does not occur without a purpose, even if that activity involves little effort;
how much less so the creation of the world’s manifold, diverse, and vast array of phenomena, which is a great exertion?
For this very reason, even *līlā* (divine play) is refuted;
for that is accomplished with little effort.
Nor is this [play] purposeless, [since it serves a specific function].
Because that [activity] also possesses happiness as its purpose;
or because, since it exists for the sake of that [happiness], it would be impossible for it to have fulfilled its purpose in the absence of that [happiness];
and because, in the absence of others who are to be benefited, activity directed toward benefiting them would also be untenable.

Therefore, it follows that the activity of a discerning person is pervaded by having a purpose; since such activity is impossible in its absence, [the lack of purpose] must reject the view that Brahman is the material cause of the world. To this prima facie position, it is replied: "But as in the world, there is mere sport. (2.1.11.33)
This would indeed be so if the activity of a discerning person were pervaded by having a purpose; consequently,
upon the cessation of that [purpose], the activity would cease,
just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* ceases when the state of being a tree ceases.
But this is not the case, because we observe that even among discerning people, there is engagement in certain activities even when no purpose is consciously intended;
otherwise, the prohibition by the authors of the *Dharmasūtras* stating "one should not perform useless exertion" would be rendered meaningless.
Furthermore, this sūtra is not meaningful for those who are insane, because it is impossible for them to understand its meaning or to carry out its practice.
Moreover, among discerning people, an activity characterized by inhalation and exhalation— which arises from an unseen cause— is observed to occur even without a consideration of a specific purpose.
Nor is it correct to argue that consciousness is useless for the conscious being even in this state, because it exists even in the state of profound serenity (*saṃprasāda*);
for even in the state of the supreme knower (*prājña*), consciousness does not fall away.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of respiration occurring even in a dead body.

And just as those who have attained all their desires through the perfection of their own and others' welfare— being free from all longing because they have accomplished what was to be done— do not act with a view toward that [result] even though the result arises as a byproduct of their mere play (*līlāmātra*), so it is with Brahman.
Thus, the activity of [the Lord] in creating the world is not logically untenable.

It is observed that what is impossible or extremely difficult for those of little strength, vigor, and intellect becomes easy or even effortless for others who possess no small strength, vigor, and intellect. Indeed, the unfathomable ocean was not bound by trees by monkeys such as Māruti; for great beings, nothing is impossible.
Nor was this not bound by Pārtha with his stone-tipped arrows;
nor was it not drunk up in a single gulp, as if in sport, by the great sage Agastya, whose birthplace is the water-jar.

And even today, the magnificent palaces and pleasure groves of the illustrious Nṛga kings—which would be difficult for other lords of men to conceive even in their minds—are still seen, constructed as mere playthings.
Therefore, it is logical that the creation of the world by the Lord Maheśvara occurs either by chance, or from inherent nature, or as a mere sport.
Furthermore, this is not an ultimate creation for which a purpose could be questioned;
rather, it is based upon beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).
Moreover, ignorance by its very nature tends toward its effects and does not depend upon a purpose;
for delusions such as the double moon, the circle of fire from a whirling torch, or a city of Gandharvas, do not arise with a specified purpose.
Nor do their effects—such as astonishment, fear, trembling, and so forth—require a purpose for their own production.
And since that [Prakṛti], being permeated by consciousness, is the cause of the production of the world, it is called the "conscious source of the world"; thus he says:
"Nor does this [scriptural statement] have the ultimate reality as its object.
Moreover, even the scriptures do not intend to teach that Brahman is the cause of the world in that sense, but rather that Brahman is the Self (ātman) within the world.
And thus, with the intention that if the creation is not intended [to be taken literally], the defect based upon it becomes entirely without a subject, he says:
"The state of being Brahman and the Self... (Sūtra 2.1.12).
2.1.12.34. "There is no partiality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He has regard for [the karma of beings]; for so [the scripture] shows."
The prima facie position has already been refuted;

now the reply is stated: [This world] belongs to that venerable one who, aided by the latent impressions of merit and demerit acquired through the distinctions among living beings, fashions the manifold diversity of living creatures—distinguished by high, low, and middling varieties of pleasure and pain—as well as the various causes of pleasure and pain, such as nectar, poison, and so forth.
Neither partiality nor cruelty is attributed to the Supreme Lord.

For a member of an assembly appointed to a court does not become hateful or biased merely by declaring that one who speaks rightly is "speaking rightly" and one who speaks wrongly is "speaking wrongly"; nor does the presiding judge become hateful or biased by favoring the one who speaks rightly and restraining the one who speaks wrongly.
