Rather, he is described as being impartial, free from passion and hatred.
In the same way, Īśvara, while favoring those of meritorious karma and punishing those of non-meritorious karma, remains truly impartial; he is not partial.
For he would be partial only if he were to favor one who performs what is unwholesome and punish one who performs what is wholesome, but that is not the case.
Therefore, there is no fault of partiality;
for this very reason, there is also no cruelty on the part of the Destroyer when he annihilates all living beings,
for that [destruction] is simply the time for the cessation of the activity of the latent dispositions (*karmāśaya*) of those living beings.
If he were to leap over that [karma], he would be acting improperly;
nor does the sovereignty of Īśvara suffer any impairment when there is dependence upon karma,
for a Lord who bestows different fruits in dependence on the differences in actions such as service does not thereby become powerless.

Nor can it be argued that, according to the scriptural text, "For He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; He alone makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead down," it is the Lord who, through partiality and aversion,
causes one to perform good and evil actions and then leads them to the world of heaven or hell.
Therefore, it must be stated that the Lord is not the cause, because that would entail the fault of partiality;
for this is contradicted by the fact that it is understood from scripture that the Lord creates living beings as happy or miserable after having caused them to perform their respective actions.
Therefore, it is contradictory to assert that [the Lord] does not create.
Furthermore, one should not say: "We are not here asserting mere partiality (vaiṣamya), but rather we are refuting the status of the Lord as the cause.
What follows from this being so?

Therefore, this [objection]—that [the Lord] desires to lead some upward and others downward, thereby contradicting the numerous Śruti texts which declare that the Lord does not take account of the afflictions (kleśa) along with their latent impressions (vāsanā)—is to be understood as follows: living beings [act thus] due to the force of the practice of previous karma of a similar nature.
As they say: "Whatever has been practiced birth after birth—be it charity, self-restraint, study, or austerity..."
By that very same yoga of practice, the person practices that very [object] again.
Thus [it is said].
And this was stated having accepted the reality of creation;
however, one must not forget that even here, creation is inexpressible (anirvācya).

And so, just as for a magician who displays various living beings through the distinction between the completeness or deficiency of their limbs, there is no fault of partiality, nor is there any cruelty when he suddenly withdraws them; likewise, for this Blessed One, who displays and withdraws the universe—which is a manifold, diverse, and ineffable proliferation—there is no fault whatsoever, whether it be by his very nature or out of sport (*līlā*). //34// 2.1.12.35.
This being the case, there is the following sūtra intended to resolve the doubt:

"If it be argued that [the world] did not exist because of the non-differentiation of karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness. The doubt and its resolution have been explained by the commentary (bhāṣya) whose meaning is not obscure. 2.1.12.36.
The statement "because it is beginningless" was made as an established fact; to prove that, the Sūtra says:
"And it is logically possible, and it is also perceived."
If the fruit of an action— whether meritorious or sinful— were to reach the enjoyer even when that action has not been performed,
then the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would become useless due to the absence of engagement and desistance;
furthermore, the uselessness of the scriptures on liberation has already been stated.
And ignorance is not alone [in producing this].
This refers to the state of dissolution (*laya*).
However, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance characterized by distraction (*vikṣepa*), being an effect, requires a prior distraction for its own production.
And distraction (*vikṣepa*), which is synonymous with delusion (*moha*) and is the cause for the engagement in merit and demerit, has as its basis passion and hatred;

and that [delusion], accompanied by passion and the rest, cannot exist through its own effects without a body that serves as the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain. Nor can there be action (*karman*) without passion and hatred.

Furthermore, passion and aversion do not exist without delusion accompanied by enjoyment, nor does delusion and the rest exist without a previous body; thus, delusion and the rest depend upon each preceding body, and each preceding body depends upon each preceding instance of delusion and the rest. Therefore, this process is indeed beginningless.
To this effect, he says:
However, ignorance (*avidyā*), depending upon karma projected by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*), would produce inequality.

Passion, hatred, and delusion are "passion and the rest" (*rāgādayaḥ*); for it is these very things that afflict the person by causing him to experience the suffering of saṃsāra, and thus they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*).

Their "latent impressions" (*vāsanāḥ*) are those conforming to the operation of karma; "karmas projected" (*ākṣiptāni*) by them means set in motion by them. Ignorance, characterized by dissolution (*laya*), depends upon those [karmas].
It might be argued that designation by means of what is yet to come is observed, as in the case of "he winnows the husks with the sacrificial cake's pan.
To this, he says:
"And it will not maintain [itself] from this" (na ca dhārayiṣyati ityataḥ).

Thus, since beginninglessness has been established, the scriptural determination of non-differentiation prior to creation—expressed as "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent, one only, without a second"—is intended to negate the manifestation of qualities such as passion (rāga) and so forth, but it does not exclude these [qualities] even when they are in a state of dormancy. Therefore, everything is clear. //36// 2.1.13.37.
And because all phenomena arise [from it];
herein,
[it is said] "the omniscient one."
It is observed that in the world, the activity of everything occurs only when presided over by a conscious agent; thus, conformity with worldly experience has been demonstrated.
Regarding the term "possessing all powers" (*sarvaśakti*):
it has been established that [Brahman] is both the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of the entire universe.
Regarding the term "mahāmāyā" (the great illusion):
all doubts concerning its logical impossibility have been dispelled.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the cause of the world. //37//
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* of the venerable Pāda, composed by the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra. //1//

Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Removal of Contradictions to the Concordance of the Vedānta through the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the Doctrine of Primordial Matter, and by the Reasoning Employed by the Sāṃkhyas and Others.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter:
"And because the arrangement [of the world] is untenable, [the world] is not [produced by] inference. This might be so.
For here, in this chapter, the arguments of the Sāṃkhyas and others—which are independent, indifferent to the Veda, and concerned with the establishment of Pradhāna and so forth—will be refuted.
That is incorrect, because this is not a limb of the Veda.

This treatise does not proceed like a treatise on unbridled logic; rather, it is intended to determine, through the presentation of prima facie and final positions, that the Vedānta passages have Brahman as their ultimate purport.
In this regard, what relevance is there for the refutation of independent reasoning that resembles dry logic? To this he says:
"Even though this [is the case] regarding the Vedānta passages...
For it is not the case that the Vedānta passages, which ought to be determined, are themselves being determined [here].
However, for those seeking liberation, it is for the purpose of generating the knowledge of reality.
Just as Brahman is understood to be the material cause of the world from the Vedānta statements,
so too is a non-conscious principle such as *pradhāna* understood to be the material cause of the world through the inferences of the Sāṃkhya and other systems.
Nor can it be maintained that this [self] is both the substratum of consciousness and the substratum of unconsciousness, because of their contradiction.
Furthermore, an alternative (vikalpa) is not tenable regarding an established entity.

Nor is it correct to argue that inference does not even arise because its object is sublated by scripture; for since the scriptures of the Sāṃkhyas and others were composed by an omniscient being, they are equal in status to the Vedic scriptures, and thus the inference spoken of therein [remains valid].

Because it is unassailable due to its similarity to a lion in its counter-argument, the systematic coherence (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman cannot be established on account of that contradiction; therefore, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) cannot be proven by means of it.
And since liberation does not exist apart from the knowledge of reality, the refutation here in this treatise of even those independent inferences is entirely appropriate.
If this is so, then why was the refutation of the opponent's inference not performed first? To this he says:
"And because of the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta... [and so on].
Now, one might object: in a discussion among those free from passion (*vītarāga*), only the determination of the truth is useful, and not the disparagement of the opponent's position.
He raises an objection, saying, "For that [attachment] brings about a state of passion," with the words, "Now, for those seeking liberation... He then provides the rebuttal.
— "Certainly so; nevertheless... [The meaning is as follows: Discussion among those free from passion culminates in the ascertainment of truth.

And since the ascertainment of truth cannot be achieved without the refutation of the opposing position, even one who is free from passion refutes the opposing position for the sake of ascertaining the truth, and not because it is an opposing position; thus, there is no contradiction in its being a discussion among those free from passion.
Having raised the objection regarding redundancy, he provides the resolution:
"But [it is so] because of seeing" (nanv īkṣateḥ).
In that context, the word "number" (saṃkhyā) [is used].
For those things which, from grossness down to subtlety, are endowed with a certain nature are seen to have that as their cause;
just as jars and the like, and necklaces and the like, being endowed with clay and gold respectively from grossness down to subtlety, have those as their causes;
and so too this entire collection of external and internal objects is perceived as being endowed with the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Therefore, that [world] too must have as its common cause pleasure, pain, and delusion.
In this regard, that which is the nature of pleasure in the cause of the world is *sattva*;
that which is the nature of pain is *rajas*.
And that which is the nature of moisture is darkness (*tamas*); thus, the proof for the cause consisting of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) is established.

For instance—each entity is experienced as possessing the three qualities. For example, among Maitra’s wives, there is pleasure for Maitra toward Padmāvatī; [there is pain toward another wife]; and [indifference toward the third]. Thus, all entities are observed to possess the three qualities.
For what reason?
Because of the emergence of virtuous qualities in him,
there was suffering for his co-wives.
For what reason?
Because those [women] arise from the quality of passion (rajas);
however, for Caitra, who is lustful and does not obtain her, there is delusion and despondency.
For what reason?
Because that [state] arises from the quality of darkness (tamas) in relation to her;
and by means of Padmāvatī, all states of being have been explained.

Therefore, it is understood that the entire world, being permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion, has a cause; and that cause is the Pradhāna, which possesses the three qualities (guṇas). It is called Pradhāna because the world is produced (pradhīyate) by it, or because the world is deposited (pradhīyate) within it at the time of dissolution.

And that [Prakṛti], being insentient like clay or gold, proceeds by its very nature to accomplish the purpose of the sentient Puruṣa—characterized as experience and liberation—but it is not impelled by anyone. For thus they say: "The purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause; the instrument is not set in motion by anyone.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "by size etc.," [the following are included]: "and because of activity from power," and so forth.
By the statement, "From the distinction between cause and effect, and from the non-distinction of the manifold universe," the reasons for establishing the Unmanifest (avyakta) are grasped.
Having explained these later on, they will be refuted.
He now refutes this inference for the existence of Pradhāna:
To this we reply:

If it is first of all the insentient *pradhāna* [that you posit as the cause], then because it lacks a presiding intelligence, this contradicts the observed pervasion in the subjects of the examples, such as clay and gold;
for clay, gold, wood, and so forth, do not produce jars, bracelets, chariots, and the like without being presided over by a potter, a goldsmith, a chariot-maker, and so on.

Therefore, just as "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is contradictory when employed to prove eternality because it is pervaded by its opposite, so too "homogeneity" (samanvaya) and the like are shown to be contradictory when "not being presided over by a conscious agent" is the probandum; this is what is indicated by the phrase "because the formation [of the world] is otherwise inexplicable.
If it were argued that, at least in the case of the subject of the example, a non-conscious material cause is observed...

In this regard, although it is observed that [the material cause] is indeed impelled by consciousness, nevertheless, being impelled by consciousness is not a necessary factor for the cause, because it is an external condition; rather, the internal condition— mere insentience as it inheres in the material cause— is what renders the cause effective.
As they have said: "And since pervasion is observed, some property must be the determinant.
To this, he replies:
"Nor [is it determined] by clay and so forth."
For that which is pervaded, being tied to its own nature, causes one to understand the pervader;
and that tie to its own nature is ascertained when there is the removal of suspected or superimposed conditions (*upādhi*).
And that ascertainment depends upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, those two—positive and negative concomitances—are not as clear-cut regarding the insentience of the material cause as they are regarding its being impelled by a conscious agent. The sense is that there is no need for further internal deliberation on this point. Even so, the state of being impelled by a conscious agent would not be accepted if it were contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
On the contrary, he states that the Śruti is even more consistent [with this view] by saying,
"And this being so... By the word "and" (ca), he indicates the inclusion of the fact that the reason characterized by the "concordance with pleasure, pain, and so forth" is unestablished (asiddha).
—And because of the impossibility of [the required] positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.

Indeed, these internal states of pleasure, pain, delusion, and despondency are perceived by direct observation to be distinct from external objects such as sandalwood, which are cognized through entirely separate modes of awareness.

If, however, these [internal states] were of the very same nature as the [external objects] such as pleasure and pain, then, because it would be their inherent nature, sandalwood would be pleasant even in the depths of winter.
For sandalwood is never non-sandalwood;
likewise, even during the summer heats, saffron paste remains pleasant,
for it is never non-saffron paste.
In this way, just as a thorn is pleasant to a camel, it would likewise be pleasant to humans and other living beings;
for that thorn is not pleasant only to some specific individuals.

Therefore, it is more reasonable to hold that sandalwood, saffron, and the like, though not having the nature of pleasure or pain in themselves, become causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth depending on the species, time, and condition [of the experiencer], rather than being inherently of the nature of pleasure and so on.
Therefore, the endowment of entities with the nature of pleasure and so forth is unestablished; thus, the unmanifest cause is not inferred from this as having that nature.
This is what was stated:
"And even though there is no difference in sound and so forth, [the diversity of effects arises] from the particularity of mental impressions (bhāvanā)."
Cultivation (*bhāvanā*), latent impression (*vāsanā*), and formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*)— it is from their specific distinction [that this occurs].
For indeed, karma that brings about birth as a camel manifests only that cultivation appropriate to a camel,
such that thorns alone are pleasing to it.
The same should be understood in other cases as well.
He introduces the Sāṃkhya argument based on "limited magnitude" (parimāṇa) with the words:
"likewise, of limited distinct entities."

For if conjunction (*saṃsarga*) were preceded by [prior] conjunction, it would be impossible for it to exist in that which is one and non-dual; therefore, one must postulate various instruments of differentiation residing in a single object as being conjoined, and these are none other than *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. This is the intended meaning. He refutes this by showing that such "limitedness" (*parimitatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when examined in light of the Sāṃkhya tenets: The intended meaning is as follows: if conjunction were preceded by [prior] conjunction, it could not possibly exist in that which is unitary and non-dual. Consequently, one must postulate various causes of differentiation—which are themselves conjoined—as inherent in a single object, and these are nothing other than *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. He refutes this very point by demonstrating that such "limitedness" is inconclusive when considered from the perspective of the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas.
Regarding the phrase "of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*":

if "limitedness" means a specific quantity (*iyattā*), then that [quality] does not exist even in the case of space (*nabhas*); therefore, the reason "because of being limited" (*parimāṇāt*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).
Now, we do not say that the dimension of space consists in its being measured by a distance such as a *yojana*, but rather that it is non-pervasive;
and space is non-pervasive with respect to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and so forth.
For an effect does not pervade its cause.
However, the reason—that the cause pervades the effect—is limited, because the ether and its subtle elements (tanmātras) do not pervade one another.
Alas! Even the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas do not pervade one another, nor are these preceded by any other ontological principle (tattva); thus, there is a logical deviation (vyabhicāra).
For those [elements] do not enter one another in the same way that they enter into the collection of effects;
this is because there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect between them.
Furthermore, there is no mutual contact or penetration into the power of consciousness (citi-śakti).
For the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), being immutable and eternal, is not conjoined with those [guṇas];
consequently, since the guṇas do not pervade it, they are limited.
Likewise, the power of consciousness is also not conjoined with the guṇas, and thus it too would be limited; therefore, the reason "being limited" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Likewise, he states that even the distinction between cause and effect is contradictory, just like the [doctrine of] homogeneity (samanvaya): "But as for the relation of cause and effect... (verse 1).
And because of the process of manifestation:
not only do various arrangements not occur without the superintendence of an intelligent being, but there is also a departure from the state of equilibrium and the emergence of diversity;
thus, that which arises as more powerful becomes the primary factor (aṅgin), while that which is overcome remains subordinate (aṅga) by conforming to it.
For if there is such a relationship of subordinate and principal [between the constituents], what activity could there be for this [Prakṛti] in its effects, such as the Mahat and so forth?
That activity also leads to the inference of a presiding conscious being;
for without the direction of a conscious being, the wheel, staff, water, string, and so on, do not remain in a state of subordination within the lump of clay which is the primary material cause.

Therefore, since activity also establishes the existence of a conscious supervisor, it has been stated by way of an indirect argument that this Sāṃkhya reason, "because of activity from power," is indeed contradictory.
Here, the Sāṃkhya objects: "But surely there is activity even for a conscious being."

The intention is as follows: you, it seems, having refuted our reasons on the basis of the Upaniṣads, seek to establish that the conscious principle alone, independent of anything else, is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the world;
that is incorrect, because the activity of a solitary conscious principle is not observed in any instance serving as an example.
But the follower of the Upaniṣads, intending to say, "Let this Sāṃkhya first accept that activity has consciousness as its cause; afterwards, I shall refute his own position from within it," says:
"This is true;
activity is not observed to belong to a solitary conscious being alone."
The Sāṃkhya says:
"But not [the agency] of that which is conjoined with the non-conscious.
The word "but" (tu) excludes the position of the followers of the Upaniṣads.
Every activity is observed to have a non-conscious basis, and not even a single one is seen to have a conscious basis;
therefore, the meaning is that there is no activity on the part of a conscious being toward the creation of the world.
Here, the Upaniṣadic author, possessing a hidden intention, reflects by means of a question:
"What then here?"—at this point, the Sāṃkhya says: "But [in the case of] that in which... etc.
A conscious being is not perceived through direct perception either as the substratum of activity or as its instigator;
rather, it is only the insentient body, chariot, and so forth—the substratum of that activity—that is cognized by direct perception.
In that case, the activity of the insentient entity is caused solely by that [insentient thing] itself, and not by a conscious being.
However, in that case, only the mere existence of consciousness is perceived in the living body because of its distinction from things such as chariots;
yet, the status of being a cause is not established by mere existence alone.
Let it not be that space is the efficient cause of produced things like jars, for [if mere existence were sufficient], space would indeed exist everywhere.
Thus, it has been stated that even though there exists a conscious principle distinct from the body, that principle does not possess the status of being the cause for activity.

And because this [conscious principle] lacks the status of being the cause of activity, for this very reason the Lokāyatikas have concluded that since activity is observed when the body is present and not observed when it is absent, consciousness belongs to the body alone;
and thus it is established that activity is not caused by a conscious self.

Therefore, the follower of the Upaniṣads (the Aupaniṣada) refutes the claim that the world’s status as having consciousness as its cause is established by either its composition or its activity, stating:
"To this it is replied: We do not say so.
That is to say, neither the embodied soul nor the Supreme Self—which are already established through perception, inference, and scripture—is something we must now prove anew.
One must simply state that it is the cause for its activity.

In this regard, since activity is not observed in a dead body or in a chariot and the like when they are not presided over by a conscious being, whereas activity is observed when the opposite is the case, it follows through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that consciousness is the cause;
it is not [the cause] merely by the presence of consciousness.

He says, "Even for the Lokāyatikas," because there would otherwise be an over-extension [of the argument]; for even among those who maintain that consciousness is derived from the elements (bhūtacaitanika), there is no dispute regarding the point that the activity of insentient things occurs through the presiding presence of sensation (vedanā).
It might be argued as follows:
It is reasonable that the body itself, being conscious and possessing hands, feet, and so forth, acts by means of its own activity;

however, it is not reasonable that there should be a conscious being distinct from it—one who is immutable, eternal, devoid of activity, and whose sole nature is knowledge—acting as an instigator, because such a being lacks any impulse toward action. Thus he raises the objection:
"Is it not yours? He replies:
"No."
"Like a magnet and like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Regarding "and as in the case of color-form and so forth":
according to the Sāṃkhyas, color-form and the other [sensory objects], while remaining in their own location, produce a transformation in the sense organ.
Therefore, it is established that when the sense-faculty has reached the object, it transforms into the form of that object.
Now, the opponent reveals his own intention:
"Because of oneness."
For those who maintain that both the insentient and the sentient exist, it is appropriate to say that the insentient proceeds when presided over by the sentient,
as is the case for the Yogins who propound the existence of Īśvara. However, for the Advaitins, there exists nothing apart from consciousness.
The meaning is: in the absence of those [factors] to be set in motion, toward what would the conscious being possess the quality of being a mover?
He provides the answer: "No, because of ignorance."

That name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) which is presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by dissolution and acting as the cause, and by the impressions of distraction (*vikṣepasaṃskāra*) accumulated prior to creation—that alone is *māyā*. This is because this objection is repeatedly applied through its pervasion. What is meant is this: this creation is not substantially real, such that the non-dualist (*advaitin*) would be questioned regarding the absence of a second [entity] that is substantially real.
In the case of an imagined creation, however, there exists an imagined second assistant consisting of *māyā*.
As they say: "The assistants are exactly like that which is destined to be."
Nor does this contradict Brahman’s status as the material cause;

for it is Brahman alone who, through the influence of Māyā, serves as the material cause, since the world-delusion has Brahman as its substratum—just as the mother-of-pearl, which is the substratum of the delusion of silver, is its material cause. Thus, the position is faultless. //2//

"If it be argued that it is like milk and water"—the meaning of this objection is that just as milk and water, being devoid of a conscious controller, proceed spontaneously by themselves, so too does the *pradhāna*.
To this, we reply: even in that case, the fact of being controlled by a conscious agent remains to be proven.
Nor is there a deviation from the probandum itself;
for if that were the case, it would follow that inference as a whole would be abolished, since such a deviation would be easily found everywhere.
Nor is it unprovable;

for here too, the fact that the directing of consciousness is established by scripture is the meaning of dispelling the doubt that there might be a deviation from the rule regarding similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
The phrase "in the case of the probandum" (*sādhyapakṣe*) is an elliptical indication; it should also be understood as "because it is included within the similar instances" (*sapakṣanikṣiptatvāt*).
Now, [one might object]: "In the [sūtra] 'Because of the observation of application' (*upasaṃhāradarśanāt*), the operation of that which is independent was shown."
But since it is established here that the activity of everything depends upon consciousness, how is there no contradiction? To this he says:
"Because we observe the withdrawal [of the world].
The meaning is that this was stated in accordance with the perspective of people who perceive only gross objects, but not from the standpoint of ultimate reality. //3//
"And because of the non-establishment of the distinction [between cause and effect] due to independence.

Even though, according to the Sāṃkhyas, the *pradhāna*—perfumed by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of diverse actions—is likewise present even in its state of equilibrium, nevertheless the impressions of action do not have mastery over creation;

rather, it is the *pradhāna* itself that, when proceeding toward its own effects, is unable to produce a creation consisting of happiness as long as it is obstructed by demerit (*adharma*). Thus, the obstruction of demerit is removed by merit (*dharma*).
Thus, in this creation consisting of suffering, the obstruction to dharma caused by adharma is removed;
and Pradhāna itself proceeds toward creation without depending on anything else.
As they say: "The efficient cause is not the motivator of the primal natures (prakṛtis); rather, it serves to break through their covering, like a farmer."

Furthermore, since the impressions of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are also present as the means for removing obstacles, there would be no external factor to depend upon; consequently, the transformation would always occur either in a state of equilibrium or in a state of disequilibrium, and this occasional variation in transformation could not be accounted for.

However, in the case of the Lord—who possesses great *māyā*, is conscious, and acts either through sport (*līlā*), by chance (*yadṛcchā*), or due to the diversity of His own nature—the engagement in activity or cessation from it is indeed possible when He depends upon the ripening of karma. //4//
And because [the effect] does not exist elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth.

For grass, shoots, and the like, when consumed by a cow, transform into the state of milk by their very nature without depending on consciousness; the consciousness of the cow is not required for that transformation, as she is required only for the act of consumption.
The meaning of the objection is this: "In the same way, primordial matter (pradhāna) will transform by its very nature; what is the use of an intelligent agent here?
Is it merely being denied that there is some other efficient cause for grass and so forth being turned into milk when consumed by a cow, or is an intelligent agent being denied?
It is not yet a different cause,
because a different cause— such as the internal fire residing within the body of the cow— is possible. However,
the purpose [of this discussion] is to refute the doubt that even in that case, the omniscient Lord alone could be the conscious agent.
This is what was stated:
"Some things are to be accomplished by destiny. //5//
Even if [the existence of the Self] were admitted, it would be because of the absence of an object [for action];
for it would follow that there is no dependence upon human purpose.
This is what was stated:
Thus, even some purpose will not be required;
or rather, it should be construed as "due to the absence of a human goal" (puruṣārtha).
This is what has been stated:
Nevertheless, the purpose for which the primary cause (pradhāna) operates must be discerned.

Not only is actual experience impossible for the Puruṣa— who is eternally immutable and incapable of having any excellence added to him— but there would also follow the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation.

For whatever purpose the Pradhāna was set in motion, that must be accomplished by it; and since it was set in motion for the sake of experience (bhoga), it would perform only that and not liberation (mokṣa), because liberation was not the purpose for which it was set in motion— this is the meaning.
If it is argued that liberation exists even prior [to the realization of truth], [we reply:
because consciousness (cit) is eternally pure, the impressions of karma and experience never exist within it;
rather, it is primordial matter (pradhāna) that serves as the substrate for those beginningless impressions.
And thus, since consciousness is already liberated prior to the activity of the Pradhāna, that activity cannot even be for the sake of liberation.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of not perceiving sound and other objects,
because the Pradhāna would not have been active for their sake.
Regarding the objection "nasya" (it is not so): even if one accepts that [the *pradhāna*] acts for both purposes,
liberation (*apavarga*) cannot be the goal to be accomplished, because it is established merely by the cessation of the activity of the *pradhāna*.

If, however, it were to proceed for the sake of enjoyment, then since enjoyment is accomplished merely by the once-and-for-all perception of sound and the other objects, the Pradhāna would not proceed again for that purpose; thus, liberation would be achieved without effort.
Furthermore, because the complete enjoyment of all sounds and other objects is impossible due to their infinity, there would follow the consequence of no liberation at all.

If it is argued that primordial matter (*pradhāna*), even though its enjoyment has been completed, continues to cause [the self] to experience through the repetition of activity until the discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between *sattva* and the Puruṣa occurs—
then for what purpose does it, having already set out for the sake of the Puruṣa’s goal, produce this discriminative discernment of *sattva* and the Puruṣa?
If it is said to be for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*), [we reply:]...

Once the purpose of *pradhāna* has been accomplished through the single enjoyment of sound and the other objects of experience, its cessation follows from that alone; therefore, there is no need to wait for the discernment of the difference between *sattva* and the *puruṣa*.
Nor does this [discernment] constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) in its own right.
Consequently, since the activity of *pradhāna* cannot be justified even for the sake of both [the *puruṣa* and itself], it is established that there is an absence of a purpose (*arthābhāva*).
The rest is easy to understand.
He raises an objection: "The power of vision... and so forth.
For the Puruṣa is the power of seeing;
and that [power] would be purposeless without an object to be seen,
nor is it purposeful with respect to itself.

Because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself, and because the primary cause (*pradhāna*) is the power of creation, that power would be purposeless without an object to be created; therefore, the objection is this: "That very thing, such as sound and so forth, which is created by the *pradhāna*, becomes the object of the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*); thus, creation exists for the sake of both [powers] being purposeful."
He refutes [this objection] with the words: "just as the power of creation is not cut off.
For just as the power of creation belonging to the Pradhāna, although it has fulfilled its purpose with respect to one Puruṣa, continues to operate toward other Puruṣas because it is not cut off.

In this way, the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) would also continue to function at all times toward that Puruṣa because it possesses an object and is indestructible; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation.

Alternatively, if its purpose were fulfilled by seeing the object only once, it would not function again; consequently, the liberation of all [beings] would occur simultaneously, and saṃsāra would be suddenly cut off. //6//
"If it is argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so,
there is no escape from the fault"— this is the remainder of the sentence.
Let it be that neither the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) nor the possession of capacity (*śaktyarthavattva*) functions as the motivator.

The doubt is that the Puruṣa alone, endowed with the power of vision, will set in motion the Pradhāna—which is like a blind man—endowed with the power of activity, just as a lame man [directs a blind one].
To show that there is no liberation from this defect, he says: "First, there is the abandonment of what has been accepted."
Not only is there an abandonment of what has been accepted, but this is also logically untenable when examined through your own philosophical system; thus he says:
"And how can it be indifferent?"
The proof for its being devoid of activity is "because it is devoid of qualities" (nirguṇatvāt). The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. //7//
And because the state of being a constituent member is untenable:
if the state of the Pradhāna were immutable and eternal, then there could be no falling away from it, as that would entail the consequence of impermanence.
As they have said: "The wise call that eternal which is its own nature and does not perish.
This very point has been stated [in the commentary] as "out of fear for the destruction of the life-force of one's own nature."
Now, there is the "transforming eternal" (*pariṇāminitya*). As they say: "That which, even while undergoing transformation, does not lose its essential nature—that too is eternal."
Thus it is said;
regarding that, he says:
"And of the external."

The meaning is: how could that very [primordial matter], which for a very long time remained inclined toward a state of equilibrium, ever fall into a state of disequilibrium in the absence of the encounter with a distinct cause? For if it were to become unbalanced either spontaneously or independently [of a cause], there would never again be a state of equilibrium. //8//
And in the case of inference by another [means], there would be a lack of the capacity for cognition; thus,
even so, we shall explain that you are unable to avoid the defect characterized by the impossibility of the Pradhāna being the principal factor (aṅgin).
The meaning is that even if one were to concede that this is not a fault, it is stated [as follows].
Now he demonstrates the impossibility of its being a constituent part:
"even those capable of undergoing transformation into inequality" (verse 9).
And because of contradiction, [the theory] is inconsistent.
In some places it says "seven sense organs.
For the organ of cognition (buddhīndriya) is actually only the skin, which is a single entity capable of perceiving multiple forms and other objects.
There are five organs of action,
and with the mind as the seventh, there are seven organs;
in some contexts, there are three internal organs.
Intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas)— in some places, it is taught that there is only one, namely intellect;
the rest has a meaning that is not obscure.
Here the Sāṃkhya objects:
"But surely [this is true] for the followers of the Upaniṣads as well.
For the state of being the sufferer and the causer of suffering is not possible in a single entity.

For *tapi* (to heat) is not like *as* (to exist), which has its state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*), but rather like *pac* (to cook), which has its state residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*).
And an object (*karman*) is that which possesses the fruit of an action inherent in another [the agent].
And thus, the object of suffering (*tapyam*)—which possesses the fruit of an action inherent in the sufferer (*tāpaka*)—must necessarily be distinct from the sufferer.

For if it were non-distinct, there would follow the absurd consequence that [the self], despite possessing the attainment of the city which is the fruit of the act of going inherent in itself, would not be the object of the action, just as Caitra, the agent of going, is not his own object.

On the other hand, if there is distinction between the object of suffering and the sufferer, the status of being the object of suffering is logically established for the former, just as the city, which is the goal of the act of going whose fruit is enjoyed by Caitra, is the object of that going.
Therefore, since non-difference [of the two] is the case, the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is not tenable.
He states another refutation with the words "And if... (yadi ca).
The meaning is that an entity cannot be separated from its own nature (*svabhāva*).
For instance, waves, ripples, and foam are the very nature of the ocean; though they possess the properties of appearing and disappearing, the ocean is never at any time released from them.

He states that not only is the one who suffers distinct from the cause of suffering due to their functional difference, but this distinction is also established by direct experience: He says: [the verse follows].
And this is well known.
For instance: even an object (*artha*), being an evil (*anartha*) due to the perception of the defects of acquisition, preservation, decay, attachment, increase, and violence, afflicts the seeker;
thus, that object is both the afflicted (*tāpya*) and the afflictor (*tāpaka*).

Moreover, these two are well-known as distinct in the world, and faults have been stated regarding their non-distinction; therefore, the meaning is: how could they possibly exist within a single, non-dual entity?
Having thus stated that the Upaniṣadic doctrine is inconsistent, the Sāṃkhya establishes liberation within his own system by asserting the difference between the sufferer and the cause of suffering—
namely, "But when there is a state of being different classes" (jātyantarabhāve).
For it is indeed the conjunction of the powers of the seer and the seen that is the cause of suffering.
Its cause is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of non-discriminative perception, which is ignorance (*avidyā*);
and because it is opposed by knowledge (*vidyā*), which is the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), it is brought to cessation.
Upon its cessation, the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) caused by it ceases.
And upon the cessation of that [ignorance], the suffering which is its effect ceases.
This was stated by the teacher Pañcaśikha: "From the avoidance of the cause of that conjunction, there shall be this absolute remedy for suffering.
And in this regard, bondage and liberation do not belong directly to the Puruṣa, who is unchanging.
Rather, it belongs to the intellect-substance (*buddhisattva*) itself, which has acquired consciousness through the reflection of consciousness (*citicchāyāpatti*).
For instance, its experience (*bhoga*) consists in the determination of the nature of desirable and undesirable qualities, which has attained non-distinction [from consciousness].
Liberation is the ascertainment of the true nature of the enjoyer;
for by that [ascertainment], it is the intellect (*buddhisattva*) alone that is liberated.
Nevertheless, just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the soldiers, is attributed to the king because of his preeminence, [so too is liberation attributed to the Self].

In this way, bondage and liberation, though residing in the *buddhi-sattva*, are somehow attributed to the *puruṣa*, for he is the experiencer of their fruit due to the state of non-discrimination (*avibhāga*). With this in mind, it is said:
"It might even be that liberation could possibly occur"—
to this it is replied: "No."
Because the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is untenable precisely due to oneness;

since the relationship of sufferer and causer of suffering is not possible when there is oneness, for that very reason of oneness, we must accept that the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is based upon conventional distinction.
For it has been stated more than once that suffering (*tāpa*) is merely conventional and not ultimate.

This objection would apply if, within the state of oneness, the sufferer and the cause of suffering were to enter into a relationship of object and subject with one another; this is our position, as the sense of the passage implies.
For even the Sāṃkhya, while asserting that the relationship of sufferer and cause of suffering is based on difference, cannot claim that the *puruṣa* is the object of the act of suffering.
Because it cannot be established that the activity of heating possesses a fruit produced by itself unless it is transformed,
one must simply accept that sattva is the object heated and rajas is the heater.

However, because the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses objects presented to it, it suffers; and through its non-differentiation [from the Self], the Puruṣa also appears as if suffering, though it does not actually suffer due to its changelessness (*apariṇāmitva*).
This non-differentiation is ignorance (*avidyā*);
thus, you must admit that the relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering is produced by ignorance.
Why does this which we are stating appear harsh to you?
Furthermore, because of the admission of the permanence of the sufferer, there follows the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of liberation. [The opponent] objects:
"Even though the powers of the heated object and the heater are eternal...
[This refers to the argument that] the conjunction is "with a cause" (*sanimitta*) because it exists with the cause of non-perception;
[the author] refutes this, saying: "No."
Regarding the phrase "of non-perception, which is darkness":
it has already been stated that there is no affliction for the *puruṣa*;
rather, this [affliction] is produced by the *rajas* of the *buddhi-sattva*, which acts as the afflictor.
And for that sattva of the intellect, which—due to tamasic error—fails to perceive the distinction between itself and the Puruṣa, there arises the conceit that "the Puruṣa suffers";
yet the Puruṣa is not joined even by a speck of error.
However, this tamasic non-discriminative cognition of that sattva of the intellect must be dispelled by sattvic discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti).
Furthermore, it is not possible to eradicate that root of darkness completely;

for even if it is severed like a split jujube tree, it would arise again through the emergence of darkness, overpowering purity (*sattva*) and obstructing discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), thereby manifesting ignorance with its hundred peaks. Alas!
This discourse on liberation would result in a miserable situation where the final libation of water has already been offered to the ascetic.
But he says that in our own position there is no such fault:
"But for the follower of the Upanishads...
Just as a face, though naturally pure, assumes a state of impurity when its distinct reflection is produced by the limiting condition (upādhi) of a soiled mirror-surface; so too [is the case here].
And yet, that reflection is not actually soiled,
nor does the reflection differ from the original object in reality; nevertheless, in that reflection, the quality of dirtiness finds a foothold due to its proximity to the dirty mirror.
Likewise, Devadatta suffers when he perceives his own face as soiled;

however, when—through the removal of the adjunct (upādhi)—he understands by means of conceptualization that the reflection is in fact the original image itself and that it is pure, then his suffering subsides, and he no longer thinks, "My face is soiled. In the same way, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a semblance of the reflection of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) with its limitations imagined through the adjunct of ignorance (*avidyā*), suffers due to contact with imagined objects such as sound and the like, but not in reality, for the Supreme Self does not [suffer].

But when there arises in him a direct realization produced by the culmination of the excellence resulting from the ripening of the practice of hearing, reflecting upon, and meditating on the sentence "That thou art," then the individual soul (jīva), experiencing his own self as having the nature of pure, awakened reality, becomes solitary and established in its own state, with the entire web of afflictions along with their latent impressions completely wiped away.
Furthermore, he has no fear of saṃsāra, because its cause has been eradicated along with its very root by virtue of its unreality;
for the Sāṃkhya, however, since *sattva* and *tamas* are real, they cannot be utterly destroyed.
This is what was stated:
And because it is heard in scripture that the differentiation of modifications is merely a matter of verbal designation. //10//
Regarding the phrase "the doctrine of Primordial Matter as the cause":
just as the doctrine of Primordial Matter as the cause is opposed to the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, so too is the doctrine of atoms as the cause; therefore, that too must be refuted.
An elaboration of the sūtra, "By this, those not accepted by the learned are also explained," is now commenced—therein, the Vaiśeṣikas sought to refute the view that Brahman is the cause.
If consciousness were the material cause of space and so forth, then space and the rest, being produced from it, would themselves be conscious;
for it is observed that qualities are produced in an effect according to the sequence of qualities in the cause,
just as cloth produced from white threads is white.
That which is produced from consciousness never becomes non-conscious; likewise, space and so forth, when initiated by consciousness, would be conscious and not unconscious.
Therefore, the world has only that which is unconscious as its material cause.
And that [effect] is insentient; the atoms [are its cause].

Indeed, the production of the gross is seen from the subtle, just as cloth is produced from threads, and threads from fibers; in this way, by successive reduction, the causal substance remains as something extremely subtle and partless.
And that [atom] is the *paramāṇu*.

However, if its possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*) were admitted, it has been stated that there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and a mustard seed would be equal in magnitude because both would possess an infinite number of parts.
In that regard, first of all, motion arises in the atom from the conjunction of the *kṣetrajña* (the conscious soul) with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Then that [atom], having conjoined with another atom, begins a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). However, many atoms in conjunction do not suddenly begin a gross object,
because they possess plurality while still being atoms,
like the atoms contained within a jar.
For if atoms were to originate a jar while being grasped by the jar, then when the jar is being broken down, shards, gravel, and so forth would not be perceived,
because those [atoms] would not have originated them;
rather, it is the jar alone that is originated by them.
If that were the case, nothing would be perceived when a jar is destroyed by a blow from a hammer, because those [atoms] have not begun [to form a composite],
and because the atoms which are its parts are beyond the reach of the senses.
Therefore, many atoms do not possess the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to a substance; rather, only two atoms initiate a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).

And its dimension of minuteness (*aṇutva*)—which is distinct from the spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) of the atom—is initiated by the number "two" (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*), which has arisen in dependence upon the intellect of the Lord (*īśvarabuddhi*).
Nor can a substance be originated from two dyads,
because that would result in the fallacy of redundancy;
for that too would be merely a dyad and not something large.
For the production of magnitude arises from a plurality of causes, from magnitude itself, or from a specific accumulation;
however, there is no magnitude in two dyads (dvyaṇuka), such that a large object could be produced by them.
Nor is there a plurality of those two, precisely because they are only two; nor is there a difference in accumulation, as in the case of balls of cotton.
Because its parts lack further parts, it is devoid of the distinction of loose conjunctions between parts.
Therefore, by that [reasoning], it too must be atomic (*aṇu*), just like the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) which is its cause.

And thus, since there is no excellence in human experience and since the creation of the universe has *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) as its motive, it is for the sake of experience; and since that is accomplished by the dyad which is its cause, what is the use of postulating a substratum consisting of a dyad?

Because [if it were produced] by another dyad, the act of origination would be purposeless; rather, for the sake of making the act of origination meaningful, a substance such as a triad or a tetrad—whether large or long—must be originated by many dyads alone.
For there exists a distinction in experience in each respective case.

Furthermore, there exists a source for the dimension of largeness (*mahattva-parimāṇa*) which arises in dependence upon the cognition of a Lord (*īśvara*) regarding the number of plurality (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*).

As for the effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*) initiated by triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, it becomes large either due to the plurality of its causes, or due to the largeness of its causes, or due to a specific aggregation (*pracaya*) of its causes; such is the process.
By this very process, the refutation—that qualities inhering in the cause initiate a quality of the same genus in the effect-substance—is rendered non-refutable.
He states that [the argument] is inconclusive: "Or like the large and the long from the short and the spherical" (VS 4.2.10).
Just as a large substance such as a triad (tryaṇuka) is produced from a short dyad (dvyaṇuka),...
But in the production of the quality of magnitude, it does not depend on the magnitude residing in a dyad, because that [dyad] is minute; or rather,
just as that very triad and so forth, being long, is produced from a minute dyad.
But it does not depend on the length residing in that [object], because such length is absent there.
The word "vā" (or) has the sense of "ca" (and), serving to include what has not been explicitly stated.

Just as a dyad (dvyaṇuka), which is minute and short in dimension, is produced from a spherical atom (paramāṇu) that is not itself spherical, so too the insentient world is produced from the sentient Brahman— this is the application of the Sūtra according to the Commentary,
[as stated in the phrase] "But the specific quality of the atom... (paramāṇuguṇaviśeṣastu).
The mention of "spherical dimension" (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is illustrative.
It should also be understood that even "atomic dimension" (*aṇutva*), though residing in an atom, does not initiate [the production of] spherical dimension in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*),
because the latter has its origin in the number two (*dvitvasaṃkhyā*).
The sūtra "from two minute and spherical [atoms]" refers to the possessor of qualities (guṇin) and not to the quality itself.
For when it should have been read as "two by two [form] dyads," one instance of the word "two" was omitted through error;
thus, the formation of the tetrad (caturaṇuka) and so forth is logically established.
For otherwise, as it has been stated, that too would be merely a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and not something large;
or else, "two" refers to duality, just as in the rule: "The dual and singular endings are used for one and two."
For here the meaning is "in the two [dualities] and the one [unity]";
otherwise, it would have been "in some" (*ekeṣu*), because the things to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) are many.

It should therefore be construed as follows: when those dualities which reside in the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) initiate a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*), then—because they are the initiators of the four dyads that are the things to be numbered—the two numbers of duality residing in each of them [are the cause].
The meaning is that they are merely initiatory.

When the Vaiśeṣika system is established in this way, the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in its refutation has been stated. But even if it is not so established, the fallacy of deviation remains in that same state; thus he says:
"Even when there are many atoms"—the construction is: "it is not born as minute, nor is it born as short. He raises an objection:
Now, if you think that [the destruction of the prior dimension] occurs because it has been superseded by a contradictory subsequent dimension through its own cause,
he refutes this: "Do not think so."

The meaning is this: since the qualities residing in the cause do not initiate another quality of the same genus in the effect, our desired conclusion is established by this much alone; therefore, one need not weary the mind by following after that [further] reasoning.
Moreover, a real [entity] pervades another dimension, but prior to its production, the other dimension is not real; how then could it pervade it?
Nor does that [dimension] pervade the cause.

Intending to show that there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that neither effect would be produced because the two causes—spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya) and its homogeneous cause—are of equal strength due to the presence of a reason for their mutual obstruction, he says:
"Nor is there a transcending of another dimension.
Nor is there an engagement in the commencement of another dimension on the part of spherical dimensions and the like.

And he states that the proximity or non-proximity of the multiplicity of causes and so forth does not apply to spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*)— namely, "nor in the production of another dimension. He then states another instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*):
"And because of conjunction. He raises an objection: "Since substance is the subject under discussion..."
He refutes this: "No;
by means of an example.
Nor is this lack of restriction [of ours] arbitrary.
He says, "It is for you as well," meaning that even the author of the Sūtras [says so].
He explains the Sūtra:
"Just as in the case of the perceptible and the imperceptible.
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //11//
In either case, there is no action; therefore, there is an absence of that [creation].

Whether one accepts or does not accept a cause for the initial action of the atoms, there is no action, and consequently, there is an absence of creation through the sequence beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
Alternatively, whether the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) is inherent in the atoms or inherent in the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), [the same result follows].

In either case, since that insentient [atom] does not act when it is not presided over by a sentient being, there is no state of action; consequently, there is an absence of that [action], which is the absence of creation.
Furthermore, the Lord's status as a presiding agent merely as an instrumental cause will be refuted later on.

Alternatively, whether for the purpose of producing conjunction or for the purpose of producing disjunction, in both cases there is no action; thus, due to the absence of conjunction—which is the cause of creation—and the absence of disjunction—which is the cause of dissolution—there is an absence of that [creation].
The meaning is that there is an absence of those two, namely creation and dissolution.
He explains that sūtra according to its intended purport:
"Now, [regarding] the doctrine of atoms as the cause."
He states the nature of that which is to be refuted,
accompanied by its logical justification: "And that is the doctrine (vāda)," [meaning] by means of those things that follow from it and are connected to it.
And the relation here, which is the cause of the notion of "inherence" (ihapratyaya) and consists of the supported and the support, is inherence (samavāya).
Because the fifth element is partless,
these are said to be the four elements.
In that regard, concerning the theory of atoms as the cause, this aphorism is stated.
Therein, he states the first explanation:
"of those possessing action" (karmavatām).

By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "from impact and so forth," impulsion (*nodana*), momentum (*saṃskāra*), gravity (*gurutva*), and fluidity (*dravatva*) are included. Since impulsion and momentum share the same status as impact, and since gravity and fluidity residing in atoms are eternal, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the continuity of action. He states the second explanation preceded by an objection:
Now, the "unseen" refers to merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).
Regarding the phrase "of the first action," it refers to the self, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
"Of one whose consciousness has not arisen" means "by a person possessing unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)"; the meaning is that the relationship is one of inherence in the conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya).
"Because of the continuity of the connection.

Although the conjunction between the atom and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is produced by the motion of the atom, the point is that there is a continuity in its stream. If [the atoms] were joined in their entirety, there would be no increase in size;

for when there is conjunction by way of a single part, those two parts of the two atoms that are contiguous are such that the other parts remain unoccupied by the conjunction—thus the first [possibility] is established.
The meaning is that if [atoms] were to occupy one another entirely, then even other atoms would fit within a single atom; consequently, there would be no first atom.

He raises an objection: "Even though atoms are partless, their conjunction is nonetheless non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti) because such is its very nature. To this he replies: "What kind of logic is this—that a conjunction can fail to pervade what is partless?"
Such is the logic of speech: that whatever is perceived in such a manner is accepted as being so. To resolve this doubt, he says:
"The atoms are conceptualized."

For it is impossible that a single partless entity could at one and the same time be both conjoined with and not conjoined with that very same thing, because existence and non-existence are contradictory within a single, non-dual reality;
or, if there were no contradiction, then contradiction would find no scope anywhere at all.
But that which is perceived is also conceptualized through the construction of spatial divisions;
this is what was meant by the statement: "the spatial divisions are conceptualized."
And thus, [the author] extracts it,
saying "this is pure," because imagined things lack reality;
he then states the third explanation:
Regarding the phrase "and as at the beginning of creation":
one might ask why striking, pushing, and so forth—which are causes for action that initiates division—do not occur at the time of the commencement of dissolution; therefore, he says:
"for even there, nothing is fixed."
Striking and so forth may occur sometimes and in some places,
but not simultaneously in everything;
the meaning is that there is no cause for such a restriction.

"Not for the sake of establishing dissolution" means that although there is the experience of suffering at the commencement of the dissolution of the body and so forth, this statement was made with the intention that such [suffering] does not exist during the dissolution of the earth and other elements; thus it should be understood. //12//
"And because of the acceptance of inherence, there is an infinite regress due to parity.
He explains:
"And because of the acceptance of inherence," and so forth.

In the first place, an independent inherence that is absolutely distinct from the two relata of inherence cannot connect those two relata, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it must be connected to the two relata by means of being itself related to them through inherence;
and thus, if another relation were admitted for inherence to connect it with the relata, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Now, this relation does not require another relation for its connection with the two related entities, because the connection between the related entities is its ultimate reality.
For instance, it is not perceived as independent of the related entities even when they are distinct;
nor do the two related entities become unrelated while that [relation] exists.

Therefore, he raises the objection that inherence (samavāya) exists between the two inherent entities (samavāyin) by its very nature and not through another relation, so there is no infinite regress: "But [it is argued] here that these are grasped by the cognition of 'here' (ihapratyaya). He replies:
"No," it is said; "conjunction also is thus.
For indeed, conjunction too has as its ultimate reality the connection between related entities.
Furthermore, even though it is distinct [from its relata], it cannot be defined without the two conjoined things;
nor do the two conjoined things become non-conjoined when that [conjunction] exists—thus the argument is equal.
If it were said that conjunction is a quality (guṇa),...
Furthermore, a quality does not exist without inhering in a substance, nor can it possess the state of inherence (samavetatva) without inherence itself;
therefore, he dispels the doubt that conjunction must possess inherence—by stating: [the following].
And as for the argument "because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*): if its non-quality-ness (*aguṇatva*) follows from its not being an inherence [cause], let it be so; we have no objection whatsoever.
This is what was stated:
And regarding the "refutation of qualities":
although it was stated that [a substance] "resides in a substance" from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
that [residence] is indeed possible for conjunction by its very nature even without *inherence* (*samavāya*).

Nor is it correct to argue that because [inherence] is an effect, it must depend upon inherent and non-inherent causes such that conjunction is its inherent cause; for this would entail the undesirable consequence that eternal conjunction is not so.

Furthermore, since inherence also has its existence dependent upon the related entities, and since those related entities—whether one or two—are perishable, inherence itself is perishable and thus an effect.
Indeed, it is impossible for a quality and its possessor, or parts and the whole, to exist while their relation does not exist.
Therefore, inherence must be accepted. And just as its production depends solely on efficient causes, so too would conjunction.
Alternatively, if inherence also requires inherent and non-inherent causes, then that same infinite regress remains.
Therefore, like inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also does not depend upon another relation.

If it is argued that it connects the two related entities but does not connect itself with those two related entities, then is it not the case that it is entirely unrelated to those two related entities?
If it were thus absolutely distinct and unrelated, how could it connect two related things?
Or, if it did so connect them, it would likewise connect the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.
Therefore, it must be stated that conjunction is connected to the two conjoined things by means of inherence (*samavāya*).
This same [problem] applies equally to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) in its connection with the inherent substratum (*samavāyin*), except for one's dogmatic attachment to it;
thus, the sense is that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). //13//
"And because [the cause] exists eternally"—the remainder of the sentence is "of activity or non-activity. The commentary on this is of self-evident meaning. //14//
And because it possesses form and other qualities, the opposite [of permanence] follows from observation:
for you indeed accept that the ultimate cause of the elements and elemental derivatives is an atom (paramāṇu) possessing form and other qualities and that it is eternal;
yet, if its possession of form and other qualities were accepted, then grossness and non-eternality—which are incompatible with atomicity and eternality—would necessarily follow.
This is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) regarding the necessity of another property when one property is accepted;
for the definition of a *prasaṅga* is indeed the certain consequence [of an undesired conclusion].

Thus, by means of this *prasaṅga*, the proof (*sādhana*) undertaken to establish a cause of the world is diverted from the establishment of eternal atoms possessing form and other qualities, and is led toward the domain of Brahman.
He states this, preceded by the presentation of the Vaiśeṣika tenets:
"Of substances that possess parts.
And having set forth their proofs for the eternity of atoms, he refutes them.
And as for that which is the reason for permanence:
the term "existent" (sat) excludes [the possibility of] prior non-existence (prāgabhāva),
while the term "without cause" (akāraṇavat) excludes [the possibility of] things such as jars.
As for the second point regarding permanence:
indeed, something that has already acquired its form in one place is what is negated elsewhere.
Therefore, by means of that worldly negation "it is impermanent," one must postulate the existence of permanence elsewhere,
namely in those other atoms;
but that is not so.
Furthermore, permanence is established even with respect to the self;
for we observe that designations, which are preceded by cognition, occur even without such [cognition] being present,
as in the expression, "There is a yakṣa here in this banyan tree."
As for the third reason for permanence,

namely ignorance (*avidyā*): if the non-perception of a cause by direct perception regarding existing atoms that produce the gross effects we observe constitutes "ignorance" and thereby establishes their permanence,
then, in that case, the binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*) would also be permanent.
Now, if it were qualified by the condition "being non-substantial" (*adravyatve sati*), then there would be no deviation in the case of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*),

because since that [dyad] consists of multiple substances, it is impossible for it to be non-substantial. Even so, the very state of being causeless (*akāraṇavattva*) would result as the cause of eternality.
Since "non-substantiality" (adravyatva) is said to mean the absence of a substance that serves as its cause, he states— "And of that"— to show that [otherwise] it would be a mere repetition.

Moreover, since the desired conclusion is already established by the reason "because it exists while being non-substantial," the term "ignorance" (avidyā) is redundant. Alternatively, if by the word "ignorance" one means the absence of the two causes for the destruction of a substance—

since there are indeed two types of causes for the destruction of a substance, namely the destruction of its parts and the destruction of the conjunction of its parts— [then the term is still unnecessary].
Neither of those two exists in an atom;
therefore, the atom is eternal.
Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] by means of pleasure and so forth.
He says that they are not substances because "even so" (athāpi); he then refutes [this objection].
"Not necessarily.

For if the process were established such that many substances, assisted by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), would originate another substance, then it would follow that those two very substances are the cause of its destruction.
This is not so, because the nature of substance has not been fully understood.

It has already been stated above that there exists no such thing as a "cloth" distinct from the threads that could be produced by the threads acting in conjunction with their contact. Furthermore, he will later refute the six categories of existence.
Rather, the effect is simply the cause itself undergoing a particularized state of transformation,
and that [effect] is of the nature of a universal.
For instance: clay or gold is experienced as the commonality (sāmānya) that persists through all [products] such as jars and earrings;
and it has already been stated—and will be further explained below—that these jars, earrings, and so forth, are not distinct from the clay and the gold.

Therefore, it is only clay and gold that undergo transformation into various forms and are designated as "jar" and "necklace," or as "potsherd, gravel, and grain," and as "fragment, particle, and powder," because in each case there is recognition of the two respective materials, clay and gold.

However, jars and the like are not recognized within the potsherds and the like, nor are potsherds and the like recognized within the jars and the like; nor are necklaces and the like recognized within the fragments and the like, nor are fragments and the like recognized within the necklaces and the like—wherein the relationship of cause and effect [is otherwise established].

It might be argued: "The moment of the potsherd arises in dependence upon the very moment of the pot that is perishing, and thus it does not arise without a material cause (*anupādāna*); so what is the use of recognizing a material cause?
This must be addressed, for this very nihilistic (*vaināśika*) procedure will be refuted later on.
Therefore, the particular states, which are subject to appearance and disappearance, are the derived effects (*upādeya*) of the universal,
while the essence of the universal is the material cause (*upādāna*).
This being established, just as the substance gold, having abandoned its state of solidity, is reckoned by its state of fluidity;
Moreover, even if the division of parts exists there, it is not the cause of fluidity;
for according to your own view, since that [division] is absent in atoms, fluidity would be untenable.
Therefore, just as qualities and so forth are not defined independently of substances and the like, [so too is the case here].
Rather, whenever they are examined, they manifest only in that very form; however, they possess no independence within their manifestation.
Therefore, they are not distinct from substance (*dravya*); instead, the meaning is that substance itself, in its universal form, manifests in various ways.
Considering that the dependence of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth upon substance consists merely in their being effects of substance, [the opponent] objects:
"Surely [this applies] to fire and other things as well?
He answers: "Because there is the cognition of difference."

We do not assert that [the cognition] has dependence on that [object] in the sense of having its production dependent on that; rather, we assert that it has dependence on that in the sense of having the form of that.
And thus, there is no deviation [in the definition]. This is the meaning. He raises an objection:
If it is argued that qualities are dependent on substance because substance and quality are inseparable (ayutasiddha), [we reply]:
for when two things possessing distinct forms are perceived through those different forms, they appear as having different loci (vaiyadhikaraṇya), whether they are actually connected or unconnected—
just as "curd in this bowl" or "a cow and a horse."

It is not so with qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*); for since these lack any other form apart from being the form of the substance (*dravya*), they do not exist as distinct from the substance which serves as their substratum, and thus there is no separate establishment of them as formal constituents. This is what is meant by "inseparability" (*ayutasiddhi*). And thus, the meaning is that they are perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Having proposed this non-separateness (*ayutasiddhi*), he refutes it with the words: "Now, as for that non-separateness...
He states that, in that case, the state of not occupying different locations contradicts what has been accepted [by the opponent].
Regarding the phrase "not being in different locations":

if, in the case of two conjoined effects, *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) consists in their occupying different locations from their respective relata, then *ayutasiddhi* (non-separate existence) is its opposite;
however, in the case of two eternal conjoined things, whether both or one of them possess separate motion constitutes *yutasiddhi*, and *ayutasiddhi* is its opposite.

Thus, the separateness-in-existence (*yutasiddhi*) of ether and an atom, as well as of two conjoined atoms, is established; and the inseparability-in-existence (*ayutasiddhi*) of quality and qualified, such as whiteness and cloth, is established.
For in that case, the whiteness and the cloth do not exist in different locations from their respective correlates.
Even though the cloth occupies a location distinct from those other threads, whiteness does occupy the location of its substrate, the cloth;
therefore, that [argument] is not valid.
For in the case of the eternal conjunction between the self and space—which are both partless—there is an absence of "separate existence" (yutasiddhi) for either of the two.
For those two do not have a relationship of support and supported as separate entities, because they lack a physical substrate;
nor do either of the two, or both together, possess separate motion, because both are immaterial and thus devoid of action.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no conjunction of the unborn, for such conjunction is established through inference.
For instance: "Space is conjoined with the self,
because it is conjoined with corporeal substances,
like a jar and so forth"— this is the inference.

Although "non-separate existence" (*ayutasiddhi*)—defined as being distinct from "separate existence" characterized by having different substrata, being supported by different bases, and possessing different movements—does not bring about a contradiction with what has been accepted [by you], it nevertheless cannot account for the manifestation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
