For even if inherence (*samavāya*) were accepted as having such a characteristic, when it is postulated between a quality and its possessor, there would arise the cognition that they are "connected," but not the cognition of their identity (*tādātmya*); yet it is precisely for the sake of establishing this [identity] that you maintain the existence of inherence.

If, even when [the relation] is present, one does not produce this cognition [of inherence], then enough with that conceptualization. Furthermore, the perceptual cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not have inherence as its object,
because it has a meaning contrary to that [inherence].
For if that [quality] were the object [of the cognition], the form would be "the cloth is white" (paṭe śuklaḥ) and not "the cloth is white" (paṭaḥ śuklaḥ).
Nor is it correct to argue that such a presentation occurs precisely because the word "white" refers to the substratum qualified by the quality;
for perception does not conform to the operation of words.
For a boy to whom the state of being fire is metaphorically attributed—as in "the boy is fire"—does not manifest through perception as having the nature of burning.

Nor should it be said that this delusion of non-difference between two distinct things is caused by inherence (*samavāya*), because there is no means of valid cognition other than direct perceptual experience for the existence of qualities and so forth and their distinction; and if that perception were erroneous, it would follow that everything is non-existent.
However, since it is impossible for a proof of difference that has that very thing as its substratum to arise from something contradictory to it,
this has been stated:
"because it is perceived precisely as being identical with that."

Furthermore, the term *ayutasiddha* (inseparable) is primary in the sense of non-distinct origination; and that [non-distinct origination] does not exist between substance and quality according to your view,
because the substance is established prior and the quality arises subsequently.
Therefore, he says that this is a false statement:
"of two things established separately" (*yutasiddhayoḥ*).
Now, let it be granted that the cause is established separately; [what follows?]
Anticipating the objection that the effect is non-different from the cause because it does not exist apart from it, he refutes this in another way:
"Even so," etc.
For a relation, whose very existence depends upon two related entities, cannot exist if even one of those related entities is non-existent.
Furthermore, it has been stated previously that inherence (*samavāya*) is neither eternal nor independent.
Nor can it be asserted that the production of an effect is non-different from its inherence in the cause;
for if that were the case, since inherence is admitted to be eternal, it would follow that the cause is redundant.
Furthermore, if inherence (*samavāya*) were to arise [simultaneously] with the effect, let that [inherence] itself be the cause of the effect; what is the use of a separate inherence?
If, however, it is held that inherence exists as a relation between two already established entities, there follows the consequence of their being separately established (*yutasiddhi*).
And it has already been stated that no other form of non-separate establishment (*ayutasiddhi*) is possible.
Consequently, what was stated by the Vaiśeṣikas— that because there is no separate existence (yutasiddhi),
conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect— would be a poorly stated argument, precisely because the absence of separate existence itself does not exist.
By this, the definition that "separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*) consists in non-attainment (*aprāpti*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also untenable.
Let it be granted that there is no non-attainment between cause and effect;
however, why should their attainment not simply be conjunction?
In that case, since it is non-conjunction, its inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*) must be stated;
and so let that very [inseparability] be asserted—what is the use of this [conjunction], which is seized by the fault of mutual dependence?
Furthermore, it has already been stated that no other [relation] is possible.
If it were argued that conjunction is a reaching that was previously unattained, arising from the action of one or from the action of both—
such as in the case of a post and a hawk, or two wrestlers— and that the relationship between a thread and a cloth is not like that;
Because the cloth exists precisely at the moment of its production due to its connection with the threads, [the opponent claims] that this is simply inherence (samavāya). To this, he says:
"And just as for that which has just been produced... and so forth.
For you also admit that conjunction is produced by conjunction, and not solely by action;
nor is conjunction merely the attainment [of what was previously] non-attained,
because that is absent in the case of the eternal conjunction between the self and space.
And because, in the case of an effect that has just arisen in a single moment, there is an absence of contact with its cause;

furthermore, if a relation were established as something distinct from the nature of the related entities, then one might resort to different definitions for its various sub-types. But that very relation, existing apart from the related entities, is unproven;
for it will be stated later that a relation distinct from the two related entities, being itself unrelated, cannot be intended to connect those two related entities.
Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress regarding the relationship of related entities.
Therefore, based on both logical reasoning and experience, the effect is not something other than the cause;
rather, it is simply an indescribable modification (*pariṇāmabheda*) of the cause itself.
Therefore, since the effect is not distinct from its cause, what is related to what?
And since conjunction is not distinct from the two conjoined things, what is the conjunction between them? To this he says:
"Nor [is there a relation] of conjunction... and so forth.
Not yet contemplating its indefinability due to its inability to withstand critical inquiry, he raises an objection:
"Apart from being denoted by words related to [its parts]...
He refutes this: "No."
"Even in the case of oneness, it is with respect to its own nature and its external form.
This means that even in a single entity, the application of various cognitions and designations is possible with respect to its various distinct states of indescribable particularities;
just as a single Devadatta is called a "human," a "Brāhmaṇa," and "pure" depending on his own internal particularities.
In relation to the distinctions of his own states of being, he is a child, a youth, or an elder;
in relation to the distinctions of his own activities, he is a Kṣatriya; but in relation to others, he is a father, a son, a grandson, a brother, or a son-in-law.
He states another illustration:
"And just as even though it is one, it is called a 'line'"; he then applies this to the point at hand.
Likewise, regarding "of two related things":
conjunction is the lack of interval between two fingers,
while conjunction is the state of one being above and the other below, as in the case of curd and a bowl.

Even though there is identity between cause and effect, the phrase "of the two related things" (*saṃbandhinor*) was stated with the intention of expressing the distinction of the effect, which is indeterminable (*anirvācya*).
Furthermore, the statement that "the word and the cognition of relation do not have the related things as their object" also intends the distinction of the indeterminable.

Furthermore, you maintain that the initial action of atoms and the mind arises from conjunction with the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) as if it were an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), because of the statement: "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial actions of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen.
Yet, a conjunction of the atom and the mind with the soul is not possible through a spatially extended part of the soul.
Furthermore, if [the soul] were to exist [only in part], since the soul would pervade the atom and the mind, it would follow that it lacks atomicity due to its being of supreme magnitude.
Nor can there be a conjunction of these two with the soul occurring in a specific location (pradeśavṛtti), because the soul has no parts (apradeśatva);
moreover, conceptual construction (kalpanā) is incapable of establishing the true nature of reality, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Thus he says:
Likewise, regarding atoms, the self, and the mind:
furthermore, it is impossible for a composite effect consisting of two atoms (dvyaṇuka) to come into contact with space, given that it is composed of two causal atoms.
"Adhesion" (*saṃśleṣa*) is cohesion (*saṃgraha*), such that when one related entity is pulled, another related entity is also pulled; the impossibility of this [is the reason for its distinctness].
For this very reason, the relationship of support and supported between the causal substance and the effect-substance is other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*); otherwise, it would not be so.
If it is argued that "inherence must necessarily be postulated because [otherwise] it would not be possible," he refutes this:
No.
Why?
Because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). He analyzes this as follows:
"For [the relation] between cause and effect," and furthermore,
"of atoms."
For whatever is limited is composed of parts,
such as jars and the like;
and so too are atoms.
Therefore, they would be composite and impermanent.
Furthermore, if they were unlimited, their status as atoms would be contradicted, just like space and so forth. [The opponent] raises this objection with the words:
"Those which you... [etc.]
He refutes this: "No;
[it is not so] because they are gross. Does it mean that atoms do not perish because of their subtlety, or because of their partlessness? Regarding the former alternative, this has been stated:
Regarding the phrase "even though they have become real entities": anticipating and refuting a subsequent argument from your perspective,
he says, "even while perishing through the disjunction of parts."
For just as in the case of clarified butter, gold, and so forth, even when their constituent parts are not being divided;
for just as a lump of flour, while its internal conjunction of parts remains undestroyed,
expands, and while expanding, being shaped into the form of a horse's hoof, attains the state of a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
In that case, while the lump perishes, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) arises; for it is not the conjunctions of the parts of the lump that perish,
but rather, being already conjoined, they are merely pushed apart by the expansion and come to occupy a larger space.

In this way, through contact with fire, the constituent parts of the substance gold attain a state of liquefaction while remaining in conjunction; they do not, however, become separated from one another.
Therefore, just as a lump of gold may perish even without the destruction of the conjunction of its parts, [so too may other things perish].

Furthermore, just as liquidity arises in gold without the production of another conjunction, so too atoms will perish and others will arise even without the destruction of the conjunction of parts; thus everything is clarified. //17//
Even if both causes were present for the aggregate, that [result] would not be attained.
He states the intermediate connection: "In the Vaiśeṣika tenet," and so forth.
The Vaiśeṣikas are indeed partial nihilists (ardhavaināśika).

For they accept the eternal nature of atoms, space, direction, time, self, mind, as well as generality, particularity, inherence, and certain qualities; yet they maintain the total, traceless destruction (niranvayavināśa) of all remaining things.
Therefore, they are called partial nihilists.
Therefore, by introducing that [example], he reminds one of all nihilists through their commonality of being nihilists; hence, the refutation of the nihilistic doctrine follows immediately after.

While the commencement of a composite whole might be possible for the semi-nihilists who maintain the existence of stable entities, we shall demonstrate that this is utterly remote from the case of those who maintain the doctrine of momentary existence.
Therefore, it was said: "all the more so. Now, in order to refute this, he states the various types of that [doctrine] by setting forth the system of the Nihilists (Vaināśika):
"And that [system] is of many kinds" means:
indeed, due to the diversity of proponents,
some adopt the existence of all things as their established doctrine (*siddhānta*), while others adopt the existence of consciousness alone.
Some [assert] the emptiness of all things.
Now, since a difference in the realization of reality is not possible for those who possess omniscience—
because reality is of a single nature— he says the following out of dissatisfaction with that [view]:
Or [it is taught] due to the differences among those to be trained (*vineya*).
For disciples possess inferior, middling, or superior intellects.
Among them, those of inferior intellect are introduced to emptiness by means of the doctrine that everything exists, in accordance with their disposition.
Those who are of middling capacity are introduced to emptiness through the existence of mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
However, for those of superior intellect, the reality of emptiness is explained directly.
As it is said in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*: "The teachings of the Lords of the World follow the inclinations of the dispositions of sentient beings."
In this world, they are divided again in many ways by numerous means. //1//

Although the teaching is differentiated by way of the distinction between the profound and the superficial—and in some cases possesses both characteristics—it is undifferentiated in its characteristic of non-dual emptiness. //2//
Thus,

although there is a difference in their internal views between the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas, nevertheless, since they are in agreement regarding the existence of all [dharmas], they are presented here as a single group.
And thus, the state of being three is established:
earth has the nature of solidity,
and water has the nature of moisture.
Fire has heat as its intrinsic nature;
wind has motion as its intrinsic nature;
"motion" means impelling.
Having spoken of the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika), he speaks of the mind and mental factors (citta-caittika): "Likewise, form" (tathā rūpa).

According to the etymologies "that by which things are formed" (rūpyante ebhiḥ) and "those which are formed" (rūpyante), the sense-faculties together with their objects constitute the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Although earth and the other elements are external when being transformed, they nonetheless become internal because they reside within the body or because they are connected with the sense faculties.

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is that which has the aspect of "I," which takes form and so forth as its object, or which is produced by the sense faculties and so on, and which extends like a staff.

The aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is that particular state of the mind which arises upon contact with an object—whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neither—which consists of pleasure, pain, or that which is devoid of both.

The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is a conceptual cognition characterized by a mental appearance capable of being associated with a name, such as "Devadatta," "one who wears earrings," "fair-complexioned," "a Brahmin," or "he goes"— that is, of such a kind.
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as attachment and the rest.
The secondary afflictions include pride, intoxication, and so forth,
as well as merit and demerit;
thus, the collection of these constitutes the five aggregates.
Regarding the phrase "even in that which has both as its cause":

when one intends the external collection of the earth element, which has dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) as its cause, and the internal collection, which has the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form and consciousness as its cause, there is the non-attainment [of a whole], meaning that such a collection is untenable.
Why?
Because the constituents of the aggregate are insentient.
For it is observed that a sentient being, such as a potter, having gathered all the materials—clay, staff, and so forth—fashions a jar consisting of an aggregate.

For indeed, in the absence of an intelligent potter who exerts activity over the clay, the staff, and so forth, the insentient clay, staff, and other implements never produce a jar by acting on their own;
nor do the threads, the loom, and other tools weave a cloth in the absence of a weaver.
Therefore, the production of an effect depends upon the conjunction of causes conducive to it, and in the absence of those [causes], it does not occur.

Furthermore, the convergence of causes conducive to the production of an effect depends upon the observation of an intelligent agent; in the absence of such observation by an intelligent agent, it is not capable of occurring. Thus, the production of an effect is pervaded by dependence upon the observation of an intelligent agent. By the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), this production, being excluded from causes that are not presided over by an intelligent agent, establishes itself as being presided over by an intelligent agent.
The establishment of the necessary connection:
if it were argued that the production of an effect is certainly dependent upon volition (*cetanā*),
yet there exists a mind (*citta*) which is volitional;

For when there is contact with the objects of the senses and so forth, that [consciousness] blazes up; and as that circle of causes becomes increasingly sufficient for its effect, it illuminates accordingly, presiding over the insentient causes and bringing the effect into being.
This is because the blazing up of consciousness is dependent upon the accomplishment of the aggregate.
Indeed, without the accomplishment of the external and internal aggregate, there is no blazing up of consciousness.

Therefore, one who desires that [result] would fall into a circular argument that is difficult to resolve. Furthermore, the radiance of the mind belonging to a previous existence does not bring about the formation of the subsequent aggregate,
because at the time of that formation, it has long since passed away and thus lacks efficacy.

This is because, unlike our own established conclusion, you do not admit the existence of another intelligent being— whether as an enjoyer or a ruler— who is permanent and the agent of the formation of the aggregate;
for it is only one who knows the specific arrangement of the causes that can be a creator.
And one cannot understand that distinction in the application [of the reason] without positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Nor is it possible for a single person, existing only at the time of [observing] positive and negative concomitance, to comprehend those two concomitances.
Therefore, it has been said:
Regarding the phrase "of the stable" (*sthirasya*):

if it were argued that causes, being independent of one another, will produce the effect even when not brought together, and thus there is no need for a conscious agent to assemble them, [the author] says:
And regarding the acceptance of [the world] proceeding without dependence [on a cause]:

if it is argued that "there exists the ālayavijñāna, which is the locus of the ego and the synthesizer of the preceding and succeeding moments; that itself will be the synthesizer of the causes," to this he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the intention as well":
for if that which is one were maintained to be stable, then it would be the self itself under a different name;
but if it is momentary, [then...]
Consequently, the aforementioned fault would ensue.

For if that continuum is distinct [from the moments], it is the self accepted under another name; if it is not distinct, it is simply consciousness itself, and since that is momentary, the aforementioned fault ensues.

The *āśaya* (basis) is that in which the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the experience of karma reside; this refers to the *ālayavijñāna*. Furthermore, "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is the operation of a collection [of factors], and the operation of momentary things is not tenable.
For in the world, it is well known that an activity (vyāpāra) has a substratum for its activity and that [substratum] as its cause.
Therefore, that which possesses the activity must exist prior to the activity and at the time of the activity;
otherwise, the status of being a cause and having a substratum would be untenable.
Furthermore, there is no relationship of cause and effect between two things that exist at the same time,
nor is there a relationship of container and contained between two things existing at different times;
thus, [the opponent] states that momentariness would be lost:
And because of the acceptance of momentariness. //18//
If it is argued that [the world] exists because of mutual conditionality (*itaretarapratyayatva*), we say no, because that is merely the cause for the arising [of phenomena].
As for the phrase "even though":
this is the meaning—the Buddha briefly stated the definition of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as "this is the result of conditions" (*idaṃ pratyayaphalam*).
"Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains established;
it is the stability of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, and the conformity with dependent origination.
Furthermore, this dependent origination occurs by way of two causes: connection through cause and connection through condition.
That, moreover, is twofold: external and internal.

Therein, the causal connection of external dependent origination is as follows: from the seed comes the sprout, from the sprout the leaf, from the leaf the stalk, from the stalk the stem, from the stem the bud, from the bud the awn, from the awn the flower, and from the flower the fruit.
When the seed is absent, the sprout does not arise; likewise, up until when the flower is absent, the fruit does not arise.
But when the seed is present, the sprout arises.

As long as there is a flower, there is a fruit. In that process, it does not occur to the seed to have the cognition, "I am producing the sprout," nor does it occur to the sprout to have the cognition, "I am produced by the seed."

In this way, it does not occur to the flower, "I am producing the fruit," nor does it occur to the fruit, "I have been produced by the flower. Therefore, even though seeds and the like lack consciousness, and even though there is no other presiding agent, a fixed law of cause and effect is observed.
The causal nexus has been explained; now the conditional nexus of dependent origination is being stated. A condition is the conjunction of causes.
They depend upon one cause after another as further causes; the state of these [causes] being thus dependent is "pratyaya" (condition),
which is to say, "samavāya" (inherence).
Just as a sprout arises from the conjunction of the six elements with the seed as its cause—
therein, the earth element performs the function of supporting the seed, whereby the sprout becomes firm,
and the water element moistens the seed—
The fire element ripens the seed;
the wind element brings forth the seed from which the sprout emerges;
and the space element performs the function of non-obstruction for the seed.
The season also brings about the transformation of the seed; thus, when these elements are present in their entirety and come together, the sprout arises from the seed, and not otherwise.
In this regard, it does not occur to the earth element, "I am performing the function of supporting the seed."
As long as the season does not think, "I am bringing about the transformation of the seed," nor does the sprout think, "I have been produced by these conditions.
In the same way, internal dependent origination occurs through two causes: connection by way of cause and connection by way of condition.

In this regard, its causal connection (*hetūpanibandha*) is as follows: namely, that conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise, up to and including how, conditioned by birth, aging, death, and so forth, come into being.
In this process, it does not occur to ignorance, "I am producing the formative forces," nor does it occur to the formative forces, "We have been produced by ignorance."
In this way, even up to birth (*jāti*), it does not occur that "I bring about old age, death, and so forth.

Nor does it occur to old age, death, and the rest that "we have been brought about by birth and the others. Nevertheless, when ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors exist—though they themselves are insentient and not presided over by another conscious agent—the conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*) and the subsequent links arise.
Just as in the case of seeds and the like—which are insentient, not presided over by another sentient being, yet produce sprouts and so forth—only this much is observed:
"having depended upon this, having reached this, that arises," and no presiding by a sentient being is perceived.
This is the causal nexus (*hetūpanibandha*) of internal dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Now, as for the conditional dependence: the body arises from the coming together of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.
Therein, the earth element produces solidity in the body;
the water element moistens the body.
The fire element digests what has been eaten and drunk by the body;
the wind element performs functions such as respiration for the body;
the space element creates the state of internal cavities within the body.

That which brings about the sprout of name-and-form— the tainted mental consciousness associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness— is called the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
For when the internal elements, such as earth and the rest, are complete, then from the assembly of them all, the production of the body occurs.
In this regard, it does not occur to the elements such as earth and so forth, "We produce the hardness and other qualities of the body.
Nor does it occur to the body, "I am produced by these conditions.
And yet, from the insentient elements such as earth and so forth—which are not presided over by another sentient being—there arises the production of the body, just like that of a sprout.
Thus, this dependent origination, having been seen as it is, is not to be altered.
In that regard, among these very six elements, there is the notion of unity and the notion of a whole.
the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure,
and the notion of a sentient being;
the notion of a person, the notion of a human being,
and the notion of mother and daughter;
The notions of "I-making" (ahaṅkāra) and "mine-making" (mamakāra)—
this is ignorance (avidyā), the root cause of the entire mass of miseries in saṃsāra; for as long as that ignorance exists...
The formative forces (*saṃskāra*)— namely passion, hatred, and delusion— operate upon objects.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the representation whose object is the thing-in-itself (*vastu*).
From consciousness arise the four formless aggregates of clinging; that is "name.
Depending upon these, form is produced. These, taken together as a single unit, are [called name-and-form].
"Name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is defined as the various stages of the body itself, such as the embryo (kalala), the bubble (budbuda), and so forth;
the "six sense-bases" (ṣaḍāyatana) are the sense-faculties conjoined with name-and-form; and [the third link] is the coming together of these three: name, form, and the sense-faculties.
From contact arises feeling, such as pleasure and so forth;
when feeling exists, there occurs craving, which is the determination: "I must experience this pleasure again."
From that, grasping arises; from that, the activity of speech and body occurs.
From that...
"Becoming" (bhava) refers to merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), because from them birth arises;
"birth" (jāti) is the manifestation of the aggregates (skandha) caused by that [becoming].
Subsequent to birth, there are aging, affliction, and so forth;
these are the maturation of the aggregates that have been born.
Old age is the decay of the aggregates; death is their destruction.
Grief (śoka) is the internal burning of a dying fool who is attached to his children, wife, and so forth;
from that arises lamentation, such as "O mother! and so on.
"Alas, father! Alas, my son, wife, and so forth!"— this is lamentation.
Suffering associated with the activity of the five sensory consciousnesses consists in experiencing what is undesirable;
and there is also mental suffering.
Mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and other such means are included among these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
these are mutually causal.

Ignorance and the rest have birth and the rest as their cause, while birth and the rest have ignorance and the rest as their cause; thus, they revolve incessantly like a waterwheel. Therefore, it is said that "the aggregate is projected by these factors, beginning with ignorance. He refutes this as follows:
— Why is that? Because it is the cause of mere origination.
This is the intended meaning: indeed, an effect that is bound by its cause may well arise as something independent of anything else, since its production depends solely upon the cause.
The collection of the five aggregates, however, is dependent upon conditions; its arising is not governed by causes alone. Rather, it is born from the convergence of various causes.
And it has been stated that there is no other agent besides consciousness to bring these causes together.

Because even the arising of a sprout from a seed—which is dependent upon conditions—is itself subject to dispute and thus falls within the scope of the thesis (*pakṣa*); and because if one were to point out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the thesis itself, it would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of negating all inference.
This might be argued:
It is precisely those factors such as earth and so forth, having reached their final moment, that initiate the sprout;
however, their mutual conjunction occurs by virtue of the conditions for their approach.
Nor should it be argued: "Since the effect is established from a single cause alone, what is the use of other causes?"
Since the effect arises immediately after the causal complex, it is not established that [the effect] exists [prior to them].
Nor is it logical to say that even if one [cause] is capable of producing that effect, others remain indifferent;
for they are not conscious beings who would deliberate, "Since even one among us is capable of the effect, our presence is unnecessary."
However, those [causes], whose mutual proximity arises dependent upon the conditions of their approach, are not able either not to arise or not to be in proximity.

And depending upon all of them as independent factors, the effect also cannot fail to arise. Nor do they, while producing the effect by their own power, desire various different effects, because their capacity is restricted to that very [single] effect.
Nor does a difference in the effect follow from a difference in the cause, because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is a single unity;
for it is observed that it is precisely the differentiation of that complex which is the cause of the diversity of effects.
That is not so;
for if those [causes] that have reached their final moment are independent in producing their own effects,
then alas, by this same sequence, all those preceding them, and those preceding them as well, would be independent in producing their respective effects.

Thus, although there is no difference in their remaining within the granary, that seed-moment situated in the granary which is to produce—through a series of its own effect-moments—a seed-moment capable of generating a sprout, must be independent in the production of its own effect; and in this way, all the intervening seed-moments that follow in succession would likewise be independent. Consequently, the farmer would achieve his purpose simply by placing the seed in the granary.
Enough with this laborious work of agriculture!

For if that single moment of the seed were to produce the sprout through a succession of its own moments, then that entire succession of moments would produce the sprout within the granary itself, since it would be independent [of other conditions].
Therefore, one must say that the final, intermediate, or initial moments are mutually dependent for the production of the effect.
As they have said: "Nothing arises from a single cause alone; everything arises from a causal complex (sāmagrī).

Furthermore, this conjunction of causes is observed to be preceded by an intelligent being who knows the specific arrangement of those causes and their purpose; therefore, it cannot originate from something insentient.
This is what has been stated:
The aggregate would be established if some cause for the aggregate were perceived;
this refers even to the case of mutual conditionality—
that is, even if they were mutual causes.
Not understanding the intended meaning (abhisandhi) that was stated, he raises an objection:
"But surely [the cause] is implied by implication through ignorance and the rest. He replies:
To this it is replied: "If, first of all...
What is meant by "inducing"? Is it production, or rather making known?
In that regard, a cause does not produce an effect simply because it cannot otherwise be accounted for; rather, it does so by its own inherent capacity.
Therefore, the process of making [the effect] known must be explained.
And thus, another producer must be stated for that which has been made known;
and that is not possible even in the case of a permanent entity, despite the existence of an enjoyer, without a conscious presiding agent— how much less so, then, in the case of momentary phenomena?
The aggregate might perhaps be impelled by the experience of an experiencer;
however, since even such an experiencer does not exist, [the author] demonstrates that [the aggregate] is utterly cast aside with the words:
"in those devoid of an experiencer."
Moreover, many things produce an effect by existing in a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor;
however, in the case of momentariness, such a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor does not exist,
because a thing lacks a locus for receiving benefit.
Because a moment is indivisible, it is impossible for it to be either assisted or unassisted;
or, if such [assistance] were possible through a difference in time, the nature of momentariness would be contradicted.
This is what he said:
And regarding the phrase "in those things empty of basis and based":
this is the intended meaning.
For if dependent origination were merely a connection of conditions, then one might require a conscious presiding agent.
But it is not dependent on conditions (pratyaya), rather it is dependent on causes (hetu).
And thus, there is no need for a presiding controller (adhiṣṭhātṛ);
the meaning is that the cause alone, by its very nature, will produce the collection of effects.
Granted that for the time being the effect does not arise from a cause alone;
however, with the intention of showing that this position entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), he asks:
"How [could it be] that very same..."?
Now, setting aside the dependent origination based on conditions, he raises an objection:
"But perhaps you think that they are merely aggregates.
For even unstable entities always arise and perish only as aggregates.
Furthermore, they do not remain there [in that state] and then get gathered into a mass by some conscious agent;
rather, the sense is that such a thing has been done here by a conscious unifier.
By the term "beginningless" (anādau), he removes the charge of mutual dependence (parasparāśraya).
Having thus formulated this [position], he refutes it with the words:
"Even so, because of the aggregate" (*tathāpi saṃghātāt*).

That series of impressions (*saṃskāra-santāna*) called merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), which exists within the continuum of the aggregate, would either produce pleasure and pain according to their respective natures by itself, without depending on anything adventitious, or else it would do so by depending [on something].
Alternatively,
if it were produced without depending [on other causes], it would always produce pleasure and pain; for that which is capable and independent cannot be delayed.
Having encountered its cause of production, a discerning person must accept that [cause];
thus, dependent origination is not merely a connection between conditions.

Therefore, one must maintain that the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the continuity of the aggregate-series—which is independent of external threads—consists in the production of either a similar or a dissimilar [result].
And thus the refutation stated in the Bhāṣya applies.
Furthermore, as for the argument that "the aggregate would exist for the sake of experience":
it is established by individual self-evidence that one who has not yet attained experience, desiring to attain it, engages in the means for its attainment.

This process of activity is postulated in relation to an enjoyer who is distinct from the enjoyment itself, who is stable, and who persists through the time of the enjoyment and its means; it is not postulated in relation to one who is unstable, nor in relation to one who is non-distinct from the enjoyment. For enjoyment does not serve for the sake of enjoyment, nor does one thing serve for the sake of another.
The same should be understood regarding liberation as well.

In that case, if those desiring enjoyment and those desiring liberation were to remain fixed [in their respective positions], there would be the abandonment of what was previously accepted; or else, if they were not fixed, it would follow that activity would arise—this is the meaning.
But the aggregate cannot be established because of the absence of an enjoyer;
since activity is untenable in the absence of an enjoyer, there is an absence of an agent.
Consequently, due to the absence of action, the aggregate is not established—this is the meaning. //19//
"And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises.
He states the connection of this [sūtra] with the previous sūtra:
"This has been stated."
Having accepted dependent origination as a causal connection (*hetūpanibandhana*), dependent origination as a conditional connection (*pratyayopanibandhana*) has been refuted.
Now, the meaning is that he refutes even that [aspect of] causal connection.
He states the refutation:
Regarding the phrase "this now": as for the term "of that which is ceasing," one should not define its state of ceasing as the proximity of a cause of cessation, as the Vaiśeṣikas do.
Furthermore, "ceased-ness" and "long-ceased-ness" are intended [as the reasons];
and thus, since both are seized by non-existence, their status as logical reasons is untenable. He raises an objection:
Now, regarding the phrase "become existent" (*bhāvabhūta*):
the meaning of existence prior to the production of the effect is purposeful for the cause, but not its existence at the time of the effect;
for at that time, since the effect is already established, existence serves no purpose toward its establishment—this is the sense.
He refutes this from the perspective of worldly experience with the words:
"of that which has become an entity" (bhāvabhūtasya).
For in the world, entities are generally seen to perform an action after having come into being and having become active.
And thus there is stability; otherwise, however, there would be contradiction with worldly experience. Again, he raises an objection:
Now, [the opponent argues] that it is indeed existence (*bhāva*) itself.
As they say: "That which is the coming-into-being (*bhūti*) of things is itself the action (*kriyā*), and that very same thing is called the causal factor (*kāraka*).
While it is true that there is thus an activity (*vyāpāra*), even so, a momentary entity cannot possess causality; to this he replies:
Nevertheless, the causal status of that which is momentary is simply not tenable.
For jars and the like, as well as necklaces and the like, produced from clay and gold, are experienced as being of the very nature of clay and gold.
And if the cause does not exist at the time of the effect, how could those effects be experienced as having that [cause's] nature?

Nor should it be said that the effect possesses similarity to the cause rather than identity with it; for if no single form persists [from cause to effect], even similarity is untenable. If, however, such persistence does exist, then that very [persisting form] is the cause.
And thus, its identity with the effect is established; the meaning is that non-momentariness is proven.

However, if there were total dissimilarity, the relation of cause and effect would result even in the case of threads and a jar, which would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); thus he says: "or even without [identity]," etc.
Nor is the presence of that [cause] the determining factor,
because it cannot be apprehended in a single moment,
and because a universal is not a cause.
The sense is that if [the entity] were a cause, there would be the loss of its momentariness and the consequence of falling into our own position.
Furthermore, even among the three alternatives regarding arising and cessation, there is the consequence of the entity being eternal; thus he says:
"Moreover, as for what are called arising and cessation..."
Even if one were to establish [the self] as a synonym [for the entity], it should be understood that this entails its being eternal;
for if it were unassociated with the arising and ceasing of the entity, it would follow that the entity is permanent.
Furthermore, even if there were association, association with what is non-existent is logically impossible.
If one accepts the existence of a sentient being, it should be understood that there is eternalism, or the state of being eternal.
The remainder has been explained by the words themselves. //20//
If [the two were] non-existent [simultaneously], there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity.
For the mind that has the appearance of blue derives its form as blue from the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya), which is the blue object;
it derives its nature as consciousness (bodha-rūpatā) from the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), which is the prior cognition.
The specific determination of the apprehension of form arises from the eye as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
its clarity arises from light as the cooperative condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*).
Likewise, for mental factors (*caitta*) such as pleasure and so forth, which arise from causes not distinct from those of the mind, these same four causes apply.
This proposition— that mental states and their concomitants arise depending upon four kinds of causes— would be contradicted if [the cause] were a non-existent cause.
Alternatively, if it were to persist until the arising of the subsequent moment,
then arising would be non-different from the entity that is arising.
And thus, because momentariness would be lost, there is a relinquishing of the original proposition. //21//
The non-attainment of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is due to their lack of interruption.
*Pratisaṃkhyā* is a cognition that is contrary to existence;
cessation by means of that [cognition] is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the nature of cognition that takes the form "I am making this which exists non-existent" is the subversion of existence (*bhāvapratīpatva*).
By this, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is also explained;
or rather, cessation has as its object the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
Or [it has] the continuum and the moment as its object.
First of all, the cessation of a continuum is not possible;
for continua are simply those possessors of the continuum which, established through the relation of cause and effect, are subject to the nature of arising and passing away.
In that regard, as for that final member of the continuum— the cessation of which must result in the severance of the continuum— does it initiate any fruit or not?
If it begins, it is not the final one;
and thus there would be no cessation of the continuum. But if it does not begin, then it would be the final one.
But it might be non-existent, because it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*), which is the defining characteristic of existence.

Since that [continuum] is non-existent, its producer is also non-existent by virtue of being the producer of a non-existent thing; by this sequence, all members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*) are non-existent, and thus their continuum is utterly non-existent. Therefore, of what could there be cessation through analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
Furthermore, the continuum (*saṃtāna*) is not merely the causal relationship between similar members of a series; rather,
the cessation of that continuum is the arising of a dissimilar [moment], and the very moment that produces this dissimilar arising is the final moment of the continuum.
If that were the case, when a cognition of taste or the like arises within a stream of cognitions of form, it would follow that the continuum is severed.

Alternatively, if there is some degree of similarity—even if the objects are of a different class—then because they ultimately share the commonality of existence (*sattā*), the continuum is not severed.
With this intention in mind, he says:
Because in all continua (*saṃtāna*), due to the uninterrupted relationship of cause and effect among the members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*), the interruption of the continuum is impossible.

Furthermore, the two cessations—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—cannot have existent things as their objective domain.
In this regard, first of all, cessation through deliberation is not possible for an existent thing that has just arisen and has not yet begun to function.
Since that [view] lacks dependence on human effort, the aforementioned objection certainly remains; nevertheless, he points out another defect in both cases regarding cessation:
"For it is not [the case] of entities," and so forth.

Since destruction without a trace (niranvaya-vināśa) is impossible, therefore even that which is indefinable (nirūpākhya) is not possible; for even a thing that has perished remains definable by that very nature which persists through continuity (anvaya).
He states the reason for the impossibility of destruction without a trace:
"In all states" means:
whatever possesses a persisting nature (*anvayirūpa*) is that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasadbhāva*);
whereas the states (*avasthā*), known as specific modifications, are subject to arising and passing away.
Since all of these [states] are inexpressible as such, they do not possess ultimate reality in themselves.
Rather, their true nature is that which persists through them;

and because that [nature] is recognized everywhere, it does not perish. Thus, since the possessor of the states does not perish, there is no destruction of the states without a persisting substrate (niranvaya-vināśa).
Because their reality (tattva) persists as a continuous thread everywhere.
This might be argued:
"In the case of a lump of clay, clay, a jar, shards of clay, and so forth, let it be so, since the reality of 'clay' is recognized as persisting throughout all of them."

What persisting form remains recognizable in a drop of water that has fallen upon a heated stone and vanished, by virtue of which its destruction could not be considered a total annihilation? To this, he says:
"Even when recognition is indistinct."
In this case as well, it should be inferred that those waters are led by fire to the orb of the sun to become clouds, because we observe the uninterrupted continuity of earth and other elements;
for it can be said there: "The state of being water does not differ in a drop on a lotus leaf and in the ocean."
Even when that drop has perished, its continuity persists within the ocean.
Therefore, it is established that there is no destruction whatsoever that is without continuity. //22//
And because there are faults in both cases:
the "accessories" (parikara) are the causal complex for right knowledge, such as the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), hearing (śravaṇa), reflection (manana), and so forth;
the "paths" (mārgas) are the meditations on momentariness, selflessness, and so forth.
The rest is self-evident. //23//
"And space, because it is without distinction.
He explains this with the words:
"And that which belongs to them..."
Even for those who disagree with the authority of the Vedas, it must be stated that space (ākāśa) is inferable from the quality of sound.

For instance: since sound is distinct from generality, particularity, and inherence by virtue of possessing a genus (jāti), and since it is intangible yet perceptible by a single external sense organ, its status as a quality is inferred—just like odor and other such qualities.
Furthermore, this [sound] is not a quality of the self (ātman), because it is an object of the external senses.
For this very reason, it is not a quality of the mind,
because its qualities are imperceptible;
nor is it a quality of earth and the other elements.
Because its qualities, such as odor and so forth, are not perceived in association with it;

therefore, having become a quality, like odor and the rest, that substance which is inferred from what is perceptible by a specific sense-organ is the fifth element, the entity called space (*ākāśa*).
Furthermore, they maintain that space is the absence of obstruction (*āvaraṇābhāva*).
Negation is defined in dependence upon the definition of the locus of that which is to be negated; it cannot be defined without the definition of its locus.
And that locus of the absence of obstruction is space (*ākāśa*), which is a real entity (*vastu*). The rest is self-evident. //24//
And because of recollection (*anusmṛti*).
He analyzes this: "Even for the nihilist (*vaināśika*), of every entity... and so forth.

But for one who, even while accepting this difference between the perceiver and the rememberer, is not satisfied with the argument that memory is possible due to the causal relationship within a common continuum (*saṃtati*), [the author] states the contradiction with the perception known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): "Moreover, [it would have to be] the agent of both seeing and remembering... and so forth.
The meaning is that one should understand "tato 'ham adrākṣam" as "I remember, but another saw";
the subsequent detailed exposition concerns the contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"From birth until the final exhalation"— that is to say, until death.
Furthermore, recognition is not based on similarity.
Since that [recognition] is impossible in the absence of a single entity that perceives both the preceding and succeeding moments,
he raises an objection:
"This is similar to that."
The meaning is this: this is a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*), and a conceptual cognition determines its own internal form as being external;
it does not, however, in reality grasp either the preceding and succeeding moments or the similarity between them.
"How then can there be the consequence of a single, stable [entity] being seen as many?
He refutes this: "No;
because [the cognition] 'this is by that' takes up distinct entities."

This conceptual construction (vikalpa) manifests as an appearance of a sentence-meaning composed of various word-meanings; one who asserts that these various word-meanings do not manifest therein would contradict his own self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).
Furthermore, it is impossible for a single cognition to possess multiple forms, because that would contradict its unity.
Nor is it logical that there are only as many cognitions as there are objects;

for if that were the case, since cognitions would terminate with each individual form, and because they would lack any knowledge of one another's affairs, the very notion of "manifoldness" (nānātva) would not exist.
Therefore, it must be stated that cognition has as its object both preceding and succeeding moments along with their similarity.

And this [cognition] cannot exist without a single cognizer who persists through preceding and succeeding moments; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence of the refutation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

If it should be argued: "In that conceptual construction, the employment of the two words 'this' and 'similar to that' does not intend to refer to two distinct entities as the loci of 'that-ness' (*tattā*) and 'this-ness' (*idantā*), nor to a similarity between them; rather, it is intended that such a form is merely imagined by the cognition," to that he replies:
For when a thing is well-known in the world, [it is as follows]:

debate (*vivāda*) is the acceptance of two contradictory properties residing in a single locus. In that case, one party establishes his own position, while the other refutes the proof for that [position].

And all of this would not be possible if conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) did not have external objects as their objective supports, nor if they did not possess meanings established by worldly consensus.

For if [the properties] such as permanence and impermanence—which appear in conceptual constructions—were merely forms of cognition (*jñānākāra*), there would be no commonality of object (*ekārthaviṣayatva*) between them; and since the cognitions themselves, which serve as the subjects (*dharmin*), are distinct, there would be no contradiction.
Indeed, two people who assert respectively the permanence of the self and the impermanence of the intellect do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, one who employs the word "impermanent" (anitya) with the intention of expressing omnipresence (*vibhutva*) in the self by means of that word's non-worldly meaning does not contradict one who employs the word "permanent" (nitya) in the self with its worldly meaning.

Therefore, by this person who wishes to establish his own position and intends to refute the proof of the opposing position, it must be stated that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have objects established in the world as their referents and that they possess external objective supports.
If it should be argued: "For the object of conceptual constructions is twofold: the grasped (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*)."
In that context, the internal form (svākāra) is the apprehended object, whereas the external object is the one determined (adhyavaseya).
Thus, the contradiction characterized by the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, as well as the status of having well-known referents, becomes logically consistent. Therefore, he says:
"Only that which is ascertained as 'this is exactly the meaning' should be stated."
To state anything else than this would merely demonstrate one's own prolixity.
This is the intended meaning: what is this "state of being determinable" (adhyavaseyatā) for the external object?
If it is "being graspable" (grāhyatā), then there is no twofold division [between perception and determination].
Now, let another point be considered:

has it not already been stated by those very [opponents] that activity occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within what is actually one's own non-objective mental appearance? Furthermore, what is this "determination" of the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Is it an instrument (*karaṇa*), or a conjunction (*yojana*), or an imposition (*āropa*)?
It cannot first be an instrument,
for one thing cannot be made into another.
Indeed, even a thousand artisans could never turn a jar into a cloth,
nor could they join an internal part with an external one;
moreover, if that were the case, there would be the cognition that it is "joined."
And yet, such [external object] does not exist.
Furthermore, as for this superimposition, is it performed while the external object is being perceived, or while it is not being perceived?
If it occurs while it is being perceived, then is it by means of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) or by a non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpaka*) arising at that same time?

First of all, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whose object is capable of being associated with verbal expression, cannot take as its object the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is impossible to express by convention and does not persist across space and time.
As they have said: "The nature of pleasure and the like is incapable of being associated with conventions, as it is not shared by others;
therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal discourse."
Thus,

when an external object is being grasped by a non-conceptual cognition occurring at that same time, but is not itself grasped by the conceptual cognition, that conceptual cognition cannot superimpose its own form upon it.
For it is not possible for a cognition of silver to superimpose "silver" upon an object standing before one that does not appear in that cognition of silver.

If an external object were not being apprehended, there would only be "one's own form" (svākāra) and not "the external"; and in that case, there would be no superimposition (āropaṇa). Furthermore, does this conceptual construction (vikalpa), while being self-cognized, first grasp its own form as a real entity and subsequently superimpose the external?
Now, when it grasps its own form, at that very moment it superimposes [the object].
Since cognition is momentary and devoid of succession, successive acts of grasping and superimposing are not possible for it.
Therefore, one must say that at the very time it grasps the non-object which is its own form, it simultaneously superimposes the object.
And this is not tenable;
for one's own form is extremely vivid by virtue of being a self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*),
whereas the external object being superimposed is indistinct and must therefore be something other than that [vivid form], rather than being the superimposed form of one's own nature.
Nor can superimposition be designated merely by the non-apprehension of difference,
because it has been stated that the apprehension of difference consists in the forms of clarity and lack of clarity.

Furthermore, if activity directed toward an external object occurs through the non-apprehension of its difference from a non-external particular (svalakṣaṇa) while that external object is not being apprehended, [then the following would ensue].
In that case, since no distinction would have been apprehended by this [cognition] from the three worlds themselves, it would apply to anything whatsoever without distinction.
By this, the superimposition of externality upon the light of the very form of cognition is also refuted.
Therefore, it was well said: "To speak of anything other than that would merely reveal one's own prolixity."

Furthermore, conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*) is based on similarity; it is grounded in a cognition of the form "this is similar to that," and not grounded in a cognition of the form "this is that very same thing. Thus he says: "And this conventional usage does not arise from similarity. Now, one might object: in cases such as a flame, even when the cognition of similarity is absent, conventional usage is observed to be based on the recognition of its continued existence, as in "it is like that" or "it will be so. Anticipating dissatisfaction with this [previous] argument, he says:
It might even be possible in the case of an external object;
for instance, common people mock a Pāśupata who, while entering a city through a gateway crowded with various folk, makes a unique mark to distinguish himself from other men. //25//
"Because that which is non-existent has not been observed.
For this reason as well, the doctrine of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) is untenable.
Desiring the production of an effect from an unstable cause, the Nihilists effectively assert the production of an entity from non-existence itself.
This has been stated below:
if the effect were produced independently [of causes], human effort would be rendered useless;
and if there were dependence [on causes], it would be impossible for a momentary entity to be assisted, given its indivisibility.
Furthermore, since there can be no dependence upon that which provides no assistance, it follows that [the entity] would be non-momentary.

Because the negation of either dependence or independence is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other, there is no other alternative; thus, the production of an entity from a non-stable entity is impossible.
Consequently, within the position of momentariness, it follows by implication that the production of an entity must arise from a non-entity (abhāva). This is the meaning.
It is not only implied by the sense,
but they also explicitly show it:
"because [the effect] does not manifest without having destroyed [the cause]."
This is analyzed as follows:
"From that which has perished, indeed...
The particle *kila* indicates a lack of conviction.
If an effect were to arise from an immutable cause, then everything would arise from everything.
This is the intended meaning: for an immutable entity must either have the nature of producing an effect or not have that nature.
If it has the nature of producing an effect, then it would produce all its effects simultaneously, as soon as it was required to do so.
Because it is impossible for that which is capable to delay [its action];
however, if it were not of that nature (atatsvabhāva), it would never produce [the effect] at all.
If it is argued that even though it is capable, it produces effects sequentially by means of successive auxiliary conditions (sahakāri-saciva), [we reply:]...
That is incorrect, because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
Do these auxiliary causes (sahakārin) provide some benefit to it or not?
If it were not the substratum, they would not depend on auxiliary causes because of their lack of utility.
Even if it were the substratum, they would have to produce either a distinct or a non-distinct benefit.
If it were non-distinct, then that very [entity] would be what is produced, and thus its immutability (*kauṭasthya*) would be contradicted.

However, if there is a distinction [between the entity and its capacity], then because the effect exists when that assistance (upakāra) is present and does not exist when it is absent—and because the effect is not produced even though the immutable entity persists—it follows from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that it is the assistance alone that produces the effect, not the entity itself.
Thus, the entity would not be a producer of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
As it has been said: "What do rain and sun do for space? Their fruit is seen upon leather."
If it is like a hide, it is impermanent; if it is like a balance scale, it yields no fruit.
Thus it is said;
and likewise, if an effect were to arise even from an unchanging [immutable] cause that is incapable of action,
then everything would arise from everything— this has been well stated.
He summarizes: "Therefore, from those seized by non-existence.
To this, the following is said:
"Because it is not seen [to arise] from the non-existent. An effect does not arise from a non-entity. Why? Because it is not observed.
Because it is not observed.
For the production of effects such as sprouts from things like a rabbit’s horn is never seen.
If, however, the arising of an entity were to occur from non-existence, then, since there is no distinction in their being non-existent, a sprout would arise even from a rabbit’s horn and the like.
For non-existence is not differentiated;
or rather, if it were to possess a qualifier, it too would be an existence and not something indefinable—this is the meaning.
Having accepted the connection of a qualifier with non-existence, he says:
Nor is non-existence the cause of the production of anything.
Furthermore, that which is not connected with something else cannot be a modification of it;
for example, jars, bowls, and cups, being unconnected with gold, are not modifications of gold.
Moreover, these modifications are not connected with non-existence;
therefore, there is no modification of non-existence,
but rather they are modifications of existence.
He says that because an entity is endowed with that [non-existence]:
"And because an entity arises from non-existence.
Having restated the statement of the proponent of non-existence as the cause, he refutes it:
As for what was said:
"Even a stable entity produces effects sequentially through the conjunction of successive auxiliary causes;
and these auxiliary causes are not non-beneficial."
Furthermore, the assistance being conferred upon it by its auxiliary causes is neither different nor non-different;
rather, it is simply inexpressible (*anirvācya*). And from that which is inexpressible, an effect that is likewise inexpressible arises.

And it has been stated that the permanent entity does not become a non-cause merely by this much, because the effect has that as its material cause (*upādāna*), just as the snake has the rope as its material cause.
And thus says the Śruti: "Only 'clay' is real.

Furthermore, even for those who maintain that particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are distinct in every respect, are real entities, why is it that from seeds of a certain kind only effects of the same kind, such as sprouts, are produced?
But they do not belong to the species of a camel;
for there is no distinction whatsoever when another seed or a camel is absolutely dissimilar to the [original] seed. Nor are the universals "seed-ness" and "sprout-ness" ultimately real.
By means of this, there would be a real causal relationship between these two;

therefore, one must accept that the restriction on the production of a specific type of sprout from a seed of a specific type arises solely from an imagined substrate of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference based on the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*).
Only a mere indication has been given here;
however, since the detailed exposition was composed in the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā* and the *Nyāyakaṇikā*, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of prolixity. //26//
And thus, there is accomplishment even for those who are indifferent;
this is easily understood from the commentary. //27//
"Not non-existence, because it is perceived.
He states the connection with the preceding section:
"In this way," etc.

He states the distinction of the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*) from the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), on the grounds that it is the intended view of the Sugata, with the words:
"It is said that for some...

Now, the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the resulting knowledge (*pramiti*)—in these four categories, the totality of reality (*tattva*) is fully exhausted; for even in the absence of any one of these, reality cannot be established.
Therefore, by one who establishes the mere aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as reality, four modes must be accepted;
and thus, the mere aggregate of consciousness is not reality. For it is impossible that there should be both the mere consciousness and the four modes; hence he says:
And regarding that Vijñānavāda (doctrine of consciousness), it says "in the form mounted upon the intellect" (*buddhyārūḍhena rūpeṇa*).
Although there is no object of experience, experiencer, or act of experiencing other than the experience itself, nevertheless,

it should be understood that this entire conventional usage of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and results, as well as the conventional usage of the knower, exists precisely as something distinct [from the experience], by way of being mounted upon the intellect— that is, through conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) by the intellect.
The meaning is that it is not ultimate.
And thus, there is the proving of what is already established;
for the proponents of Brahman do not admit a cognition possessing forms such as blue and so forth.
However, it is indescribable as being [identical to] blue and so forth.

For instance: the intrinsic nature of consciousness, when endowed with an unreal aspect, is the object of cognition (*prameya*); the manifestation of that object is the fruit of the means of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*); and the power to manifest that [object] is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He states that even for the two externalist schools, the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas, the conventional usage of "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) and "result" (phala) is intended to be merely conceptual, by saying:
"even though the external object exists."
For if the instrument and its result had different loci, that relationship between them would not exist;
indeed, when an axe is applied to a *khadira* tree, the splitting occurs in the *palāśa* tree. Therefore, it must be stated that these two share a common locus.
And how does that come to be?
If both the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) reside in the cognition itself,
then it is not logical for cognition— which is a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and partless— to be connected with two distinct parts of a real entity.

That very cognition is the result (*phala*), consisting of the aspect of "cognition" as conceptually constructed through the exclusion of non-cognition (*ajñāna-vyāvṛtti*). It is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting of the aspect of the power to manifest self and non-self as conceptually constructed through the exclusion of incapacity (*aśakti-vyāvṛtti*).
Its object of cognition (*prameya*), however, is strictly external.
The same applies at the time of the Sautrāntika system:

the conformity of cognition to the object (*arthasārūpya*), which consists in the exclusion of non-blue forms and the possession of an imagined blue form, is established as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause for establishing [the object].
And the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*), which is imagined through the exclusion of non-cognition, is established as the result (*phala*) because it is that which is to be established.
And so they have said: "It is not logical that the mere existence of a cognition constitutes the awareness of its object, because that existence is indistinguishable in all cases.
Rather, it is by entering into similarity with the object that the cognition, by making itself similar, can bring about the apprehension of that object."
He states the arguments for the non-existence of external objects by way of a question: "But how, again, is this known?"
For that external object, which is considered to be the objective support (*ālambana*) of consciousness, cannot possibly be an atom (*paramāṇu*).
Indeed, cognition appears as a single, gross, blue form; it does not appear as an extremely subtle atom.
And it is impossible for that which appears as one thing to have another thing as its object.
Because it would lead to the over-extension [of the argument] that everything is the object of all, resulting in the absurdity that everyone is omniscient;
nor is it logical to claim that grossness is a property of appearance,
because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
Is this a property of the cognition that appears, or is it a property of the object at the time of its appearing?
If the former alternative is held, then [it follows that] there is no [external object].
For if that were the case, consciousness would be admitted to have its own part as its object;
and in that case, who could be opposed to one who acts in accordance with what is favorable?
If you say it is the second [part], then:
For instance: it is precisely atoms of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) that, having arisen in immediate proximity and being presented to a single cognition, constitute grossness (*sthaulya*).
And there is no delusion regarding this;
for those are indeed atoms of form.
Nor is it the case that they do not arise in immediate succession,
nor that they do not follow upon a single cognition;
therefore, let it be that the atom is not a property [of the object] like blueness and so forth.

Because [the nature of] each individual atom is non-existent, however, for those atoms that have entered into the state of appearing [to cognition], there will be a conventional (sāṃvṛta) grossness, just like [their] plurality and so forth. As they say: "When many [atoms] are grasped by a single [cognition], some form indeed is grasped."
The conventional exists as a manifestation, because that [multiplicity] is impossible within a single essence. //1//
Nor is that perception erroneous, because it apprehends various entities;
conventional apprehension is not elsewhere, and the apprehension of an entity is not a delusion. //2//
Thus [it is argued]; but that is not so,
because the appearance of continuity is an illusion.
For those atoms of form are separated by atoms of odor, taste, and touch; they are not contiguous.

Therefore, we observe that this cognition of grossness regarding atoms that are actually separated is merely an error—just like the cognition of a single dense forest regarding trees that are at a distance and separated.

Consequently, even though it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), the cognition of a jar and so forth lacks the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) because it is erroneous, just like the knowledge of a yellow conch shell and the like, if one accepts that its object is atoms.
This has been stated:
first of all, atoms cannot be the objects determined by the cognition of pillars and the like;
nor can their aggregates, such as pillars and so forth, be wholes (*avayavin*).

If they were non-different from the atoms, they would be nothing but atoms, and the refutation of that has already been stated. But if there is difference, then there is an absolute disparity like that between a cow and a horse, and thus no identity exists.
And since inherence (*samavāya*) has also been refuted,
one should likewise reject universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth by means of the analysis of their difference or non-difference.
Therefore, because everything that appears is incapable of withstanding critical investigation, [it is all empty].
Furthermore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of that which does not appear, cognitions do not have external objects as their support.
Moreover, consciousness cannot perceive an object in a hidden manner like a sense faculty;
for just as a sense faculty produces a cognition whose object is the external thing, one consciousness is not capable of producing another consciousness in that same way.
In that case as well, because the inquiry would be identical, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress;
nor is it capable of producing a result characterized by manifestation (*prākaṭya*) supported by an object,
because such a result is impossible in the case of past and future objects.
For it is impossible that the substratum (dharmin) be non-present while its attributes (dharmas) are present;

therefore, the direct perception of the object must be admitted as being nothing other than the direct perception of the nature of cognition itself. And since that [cognition], being devoid of forms (anākāra), lacks any distinction for one who does not perceive [forms], how could it establish a distinction between objects? Thus, in order to establish that distinction, a distinction of forms must be sought for this [cognition].
As it has been said: "For it is not logical that the mere existence of a cognition constitutes the awareness of its object, since that [existence] is indistinguishable in all cases;
rather, it is by entering into similarity with the object that the cognition, being itself similar, can bring about the apprehension of that object."
Furthermore, this single form is experienced; yet there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an object apart from that consciousness. Thus he says:
"Moreover, by mere experience, [there is no proof] of a cognition whose nature is common [to all]."
Moreover, [the argument] "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*):
whatever is invariably apprehended simultaneously with something else does not differ from that thing, just as a second moon does not differ from a single moon.
And since the object is necessarily perceived together with the cognition, this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

For the difference [between object and cognition] that is to be negated is pervaded by the lack of necessity in their simultaneous perception; just as the two Aśvins, being distinct, are not necessarily perceived together, since sometimes one or the other is perceived when they are covered by clouds.
Here, this necessity—which is the opposite of the non-necessity that pervades difference—is observed, and thus it excludes the difference which is pervaded by that non-necessity.
As it has been said: "Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof;
yet their difference is perceived by erroneous cognitions, just as [the duality] in the case of the non-dual moon."
Thus it should be viewed as being like a dream and so forth:
whatever cognition there may be, all of it is without an external objective support.
Just as the cognition of dreams, illusions, and so forth, so too is this cognition under dispute; thus, it is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

For the state of being a cognition is invariably concomitant with the lack of an external object, just as the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is invariably concomitant with the state of being a tree. Therefore, when the lack of an external object is to be proven as that which is invariably concomitant with the mere state of being a cognition, the state of being a cognition [serves as the reason].
This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
At this point, the Sautrāntika raises an objection:
"But how, then, [is there the cognition] 'this is blue,' 'this is yellow,' and so forth, regarding an external object?"
