The diversity of conditions is thus established.
For he [Dignāga] held that those things which occur only occasionally, even when a certain factor is present, must depend upon causes other than that factor;
just as, for example, while I am neither desiring to speak nor desiring to walk, the appearances of speech and movement depend upon another mental continuum.

And thus, the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is as follows: those [six] active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which are the subject of dispute, are indeed sixfold active cognitions even while the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists.
And that which is distinct from the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness and serves as the cause for the occasional variety of active cognitions is the external object.
If it is argued that their production occurs only occasionally because the conditions for the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are themselves occasional; [we reply: no.
Now, [the opponent might argue: "The *vāsanā* is the capacity of the *ālayavijñānas* falling within a single continuum to produce those evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Its 'ripening' (*paripāka*) is its orientation toward the production of its own effect, and its 'condition' (*pratyaya*) is the preceding moment existing within its own continuum, since the dependence on another continuum is not admitted.
And thus, all [moments] falling within the *ālaya*-continuum would be causes for ripening."
Or rather, not even any [of them],
because there is no distinction in their being included within the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna*.
If it is argued that there is a difference in capacity due to the difference between moments, and that the occasional nature of the effect arises from the occasional nature of that [capacity]:

But surely, in this way, the capacity to produce the cognition of blue and the capacity to awaken that [impression] would belong to one and the same [moment], and this would not belong to a subsequent moment. Or, if it were to exist [in the subsequent moment], how could there be a difference in capacity due to the difference in moments? For all [moments] existing in the continuum of the ālayavijñāna would be equally capable; thus, since the efficient cause is present, the non-production of the effect is untenable. If the negandum—occasional occurrence—is dependent solely upon its own continuum, then its opposite, permanence, is perceived; by the perception of that [permanence], occasional occurrence being excluded, it is established that [the cognition] depends upon another cause.

Thus is established the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Furthermore, even by the proponents of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*), it is not maintained that all active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are based on another stream of consciousness; rather, it is only certain active cognitions—those appearing as interrupted movement or speech—that are so regarded.
Moreover, if it were caused by the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) of another sentient being, then because that [continuum] would also be constantly present, it could not be occasional.

For there can be no spatial or temporal remoteness with respect to the mental continuum of another sentient being; this is because in the Vijñānavāda system, no space distinct from consciousness is admitted, and since consciousnesses are immaterial, they do not possess spatial extension. Furthermore, this would entail the consequence that *saṃsāra* has a beginning, as it would imply the manifestation of a previously non-existent sentient being, which is not accepted.
Nor is there the possibility of remoteness even in terms of time.
Therefore, since the diversity of cognitions would be untenable if external objects did not exist, the Sautrāntikas maintained that external objects exist as inferential entities;
[the author] now refutes them:

The Vijñānavādin says: "Due to the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The underlying intention here is as follows: even if it is established that the occasional nature of cognitions is possible through their arising solely from one's own mental continuum (*svasaṃtāna*), the logical reason (*hetu*) remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the opposite case (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. For instance, even if external causes were involved, how could there be the cognition of blue at one time and the cognition of yellow at another?
If it is argued that this is due to the presence or absence of external blue and yellow [objects],
then why, even when yellow is present, does there not arise a cognition of blue, but rather a cognition of yellow?
If it is argued that [the distinction] exists there because of its capacity and in the other case because of its lack of capacity,
then from what does this difference between capacity and incapacity arise?
If it is argued that it arises from a difference in causes, [then...]
If that is the case, then even for moments (kṣaṇas), there will be a difference in capacity based on the difference in their own causes.
For moments are the members of a continuum (saṃtānin) that serve as the causes for the diversity of effects, and they differ with respect to each effect.
Furthermore, there is no single entity called a "continuum" that produces the moments such that, due to its non-difference, the moments themselves would not differ.
But has it not been said that the difference or non-difference of capacities does not follow from the difference or non-difference of moments,
because even distinct moments are observed to possess a single capacity?

Otherwise, if the capacity to produce the cognition of blue resided in only a single moment, then further cognitions of blue would not arise, since that which possesses such capacity would have already passed away.
And because subsequent moments lack that capacity,
there is no difference in capacity despite the difference between moments;
however, when there is a difference in the continuum, the capacity does differ.
That is not so;
for if there is no single capacity belonging to distinct continua,

then alas, since even the various continua of blue objects— which are mutually distinct— would lack a single capacity to impart the form of blue, a cognition of blue would not arise even when another continuum of blue is in proximity.

Therefore, just as in the case of different mental continua, it must be stated that among the various moments produced by their own specific causes, some possess a particular capacity while others do not.

Likewise, among the moments of cognition falling within a single continuum of the same person, only a certain moment of cognition possesses such a superior capacity—known by the name *vāsanā* (latent impression)—which is acquired from its own preceding conditions;
it is from this that an active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arises in the form of blue, and not in the form of yellow.

However, for some, that [external object] is of such a nature that the cognition has the form of yellow and not the form of blue; thus, since the variety of cognitions is established solely from the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) acquired through one's own internal conditions, we see that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the existence of an object distinct from that [cognition]. Latent impression is simply a cognition belonging to the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) that remains unperceived; from its variety arises the variety of experiences of blue and so forth.

Furthermore, because the variety of the experience of prior blue and other objects results in a variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), these two—consciousness and its latent impressions—are beginningless. Therefore, there is no possibility of the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*), as is the case with the continuum of seed and sprout. He states that, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is precisely the variety of latent impressions that is the cause of the variety of cognition, and not the variety of external objects: [The verse: "Because of the variety of the experience of prior blue and so forth, there is a variety of latent impressions; thus, these two—consciousness and its latent impressions—are beginningless. Therefore, like the continuum of seed and sprout, there is no occurrence of the fault of mutual dependence. Furthermore, by means of positive and negative concomitance, it is the variety of latent impressions alone that is the cause of the variety of cognition, and not the variety of objects. [The commentary: The meaning is this: since the variety of the experience of blue and other objects in the past gives rise to a variety of latent impressions, the sequence of consciousness and its latent impressions is beginningless. Consequently, just as in the case of the seed and the sprout, there is no fault of mutual dependence. Moreover, based on the observation of positive and negative concomitance—that when there is a variety of latent impressions there is a variety of cognition, and when there is no such variety there is no such variety—it is established that the variety of latent impressions alone is the cause of the variety of cognition, and not the variety of external objects. Thus, the claim that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of objects" is refuted. This is because even in dreams and the like, where there is no variety of external objects, a variety of cognition occurs due to the variety of latent impressions. Therefore, the statement that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of objects" is untenable. Furthermore, the statement that "the variety of latent impressions arises from the variety of objects" is also untenable. For if that were so, then since the variety of objects is constant, the variety of latent impressions would also be constant, and consequently, the variety of cognition would never cease. However, we observe that the variety of cognition does indeed cease. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of objects" is incorrect. It is only the variety of latent impressions that is the cause of the variety of cognition. Thus, the statement that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of objects" is refuted. This concludes the section on the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of objects. Now follows the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of atoms (*paramāṇu*). [The verse: "The variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of atoms, because atoms are imperceptible. Nor does it arise from their aggregation, because that [aggregation] is not distinct from them. Furthermore, since the atoms are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. [The commentary: The meaning is this: the variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of atoms. Why? Because atoms are imperceptible. That is to say, since atoms are beyond the range of the senses, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the aggregation of atoms. Why? Because that aggregation is not distinct from the atoms themselves. Since the atoms are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of atoms" is untenable. This concludes the section on the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of atoms. Now follows the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of parts (*avayava*). [The verse: "Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the variety of parts, because those parts are not perceived. Nor does it arise from the whole (*avayavin*), because that [whole] is not distinct from its parts. Furthermore, since the parts are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. [The commentary: The meaning is this: the variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of parts. Why? Because those parts are not perceived. That is to say, since the parts are not perceived, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the whole. Why? Because that whole is not distinct from its parts. Since the parts are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of parts" is untenable. This concludes the section on the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of parts. Now follows the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*). [The verse: "Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the variety of universals and particulars, because those are not perceived. Nor does it arise from the relation (*saṃbandha*), because that is not distinct from the relata. Furthermore, since the universals and particulars are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. [The commentary: The meaning is this: the variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of universals and particulars. Why? Because those are not perceived. That is to say, since universals and particulars are not perceived, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the relation. Why? Because that relation is not distinct from the relata. Since the universals and particulars are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of universals and particulars" is untenable. This concludes the section on the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of universals and particulars. Now follows the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of mental constructs (*vikalpa*). [The verse: "Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the variety of mental constructs, because those are not perceived. Nor does it arise from the object, because that is not distinct from the cognition. Furthermore, since the mental constructs are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. [The commentary: The meaning is this: the variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of mental constructs. Why? Because those are not perceived. That is to say, since mental constructs are not perceived, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the object. Why? Because that object is not distinct from the cognition itself. Since the mental constructs are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of mental constructs" is untenable. This concludes the section on the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of mental constructs. Now follows the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of the sense-faculties (*indriya*). [The verse: "Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the variety of the sense-faculties, because those are not perceived. Nor does it arise from the object, because that is not distinct from the cognition. Furthermore, since the sense-faculties are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. [The commentary: The meaning is this: the variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of the sense-faculties. Why? Because those are not perceived. That is to say, since the sense-faculties are not perceived, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the object. Why? Because that object is not distinct from the cognition itself. Since the sense-faculties are not perceived individually, they cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of the sense-faculties" is untenable. This concludes the section on the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of the sense-faculties. Now follows the refutation of the variety of cognition arising from the variety of the mind (*manas*). [The verse: "Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the variety of the mind, because that is not perceived. Nor does it arise from the object, because that is not distinct from the cognition. Furthermore, since the mind is not perceived individually, it cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. [The commentary: The meaning is this: the variety of cognition does not arise from the variety of the mind. Why? Because that is not perceived. That is to say, since the mind is not perceived, it cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Nor does the variety of cognition arise from the object. Why? Because that object is not distinct from the cognition itself. Since the mind is not perceived individually, it cannot be the cause of the perception of a gross object. Therefore, the view that "the variety of cognition arises from the variety of the mind" is untenable. This
Moreover, [it is argued] "by means of positive and negative concomitance.
This being the case, we reply:
"There is no non-existence, because [the world] is perceived."
Indeed, the non-existence of an external object cannot be determined;
for that [non-existence] could only be determined either through the absence of apprehension,
or even when apprehension exists, because that [apprehension] does not have an external object as its domain.

Even though there is an external object, [the cognition is not valid] because of the existence of a means of knowledge that sublates the external object; or rather, it is not the case that there is no apprehension at all. He states this, preceded by a question:
"Why?"
"Because of perception" (upalabdheḥ): the meaning is that when there is a perception so clear as to be common to all people, it is impossible to assert its non-existence.
He now takes up the second position:
"Now, do you not say, 'I do not speak thus'?
He refutes this: "Certainly, you do speak thus."
The meaning is that when perception is apprehended by a witness who apprehends that very perception, it is apprehended precisely as having an external object, and not as mere perception alone.
The phrase "ataśca" (and therefore) refers back to the reasoning that will be stated hereafter.
He now adopts the third position:
"Now, [it might be argued] that this is because an external object is impossible. He refutes this:
"This determination is not correct. The underlying intention here is as follows: jars, cloths, and so forth appear as gross (*sthūla*), and not as supremely subtle (*paramasūkṣma*).

In this regard, although this grossness—characterized by the pervasion of various directions and locations—is [present] in the form of the cognition (*jñānākāra*) by way of its characteristic of being either obstructed or unobstructed...

It is joined with the association of contradictory properties precisely because the limiting adjunct of cognition (*jñānopādhi*) is unobstructed; nevertheless, the multiplicity resulting from the association of contradictory properties—characterized by being in that location and not in that location, trembling and not trembling, being colored and not colored—is impossible to prevent, even by Śakra himself, even if [the object] exists as a form of cognition.
Furthermore, the dilemmas regarding whether [atoms] exist as distinct or non-distinct, as well as the fact that atoms possess parts, have been established in the *Vaiśeṣika-parīkṣā*.
Therefore, as in the case of external objects, grossness is not possible even in cognition;
nor can a single cognition have the appearance of atoms,
because it is impossible for a single entity to possess a manifold nature.
Alternatively, because the forms would be identical in nature to the cognition, it would follow that they are one;
nor is it the case that there are as many cognitions as there are forms,
for if there were that many cognitions, they would be mutually unaware of one another, which would entail the impossibility of experiencing a gross object.
Nor is it correct to say that a single, coarse conceptual construction (*sthūla-vikalpa*), consisting of a synthesis of all the forms of cognition, manifests subsequently to that [perception];
for even that [conceptual construction], by virtue of having a form, cannot be considered coarse.
As Dharmakīrti said: "Therefore, there is no appearance of coarseness either in the object or in the cognition, because its nature [is otherwise]."
Because it is prohibited in one case, its occurrence is impossible even in many cases.
Thus,

therefore, even by you who seek to establish the grossness of the form of cognition, the possibility and impossibility [of external objects] must be accepted as being preceded by the operation or non-operation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, that which is the locus of this [cognition]— the external object distinct from cognition— is impossible to deny. Furthermore,

as for the conformity to the object (*viṣayasārūpya*) which has been posited to account for the determination of cognition with respect to each respective object, the object cannot be denied by means of this [conformity].
He says, "And not because of the similarity of cognition to the object," because if the object does not exist, both its similarity [to cognition] and the determination of that [object] are untenable.
Furthermore, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) which was stated is also incapable of withstanding analysis.

If the apprehension of cognition and the object occurs as a concomitance (*sāhitya*), then that reason is contradictory and cannot establish non-difference (*abheda*), because concomitance is pervaded by difference— which is its opposite— and such concomitance would be untenable if there were non-difference.
Alternatively, [the reason might be] the rule of their being apprehended as one.
The word "together" (saha) does not denote oneness.
Furthermore, is there apprehension as one, or is there a single apprehension of both the cognition and the object?
It is not the case that there is apprehension as one; thus he says:
And because the object is perceived externally.
Now, if it is argued that there is a rule of simultaneous perception, he says in response:

"Therefore, it must be understood that even the rule of simultaneous perception regarding the cognition and its object is caused by the relationship between the means and the end (upāya and upeya), not caused by non-difference."
For just as all visual objects, being permeated by the form of light, are invariably perceived by humans as being cognizable by the intellect,
yet for this reason the form of a jar or other object does not become identical with light;
rather, the rule exists because light serves as the means [of perception].
Thus, here too, because the object is apprehended through the means of experience witnessed by oneself (*ātmasākṣika-anubhava*), there is a necessity for the simultaneous perception of the object.

Furthermore, in cases where a jar and a cloth are both within the scope of a single cognition, cognizers determine that there is a difference between the objects and a difference between the cognitions.
This would not be possible if they possessed a single nature; thus he says:
Likewise, there is the perception of a jar and the cognition of a cloth. Thus,

since a difference in cognition is observed even when the object is not different, he says— “likewise, the perception of a jar and the recollection of a jar”— to show that the object does not have cognition as its essence.

Furthermore, since a cognition that terminates solely in its own nature is ignorant of the report of any other cognition, those two [cognitions] are not apprehended; thus, the difference residing in them is also not apprehended.

In this way, even such properties as momentariness, emptiness, and selflessness—which are to be established through the difference between multiple cognitions of propositions, reasons, and examples—are likewise [unapprehendable].
Similarly, a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) which is unique to a thing and excluded from others—that which is excluded and that from which it is excluded—is also established by multiple cognitions.

In this way, even a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), whether it be of the nature of a positive affirmation (vidhi) or of the nature of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), is cognizable through multiple cognitions.
Likewise, the relationship between the perfumer and the perfumed (vāsyavāsakabhāva) is established by multiple cognitions.
Similarly, by the power of the affliction of ignorance (avidyopaplava), there is the state of being a real or unreal property; for example, "it is blue" is a real property (saddharma).
"A human horn" is a non-existent property;
"formless" is a property that is both existent and non-existent,
for it is possible to say that a rabbit's horn is formless.
And it is possible to say that consciousness is formless,

as it has been stated: "The referent of a word, established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless habitual tendencies, is a threefold property based on existence, non-existence, or both."

"Thus, the proposition regarding liberation—that he who is liberated, that from which one is liberated, and that by which one is liberated—is to be accomplished through manifold cognitions. Likewise, in order to instruct one who is mistaken, the proposition is that which is being instructed, that by which it is instructed, and he who instructs; this too is to be accomplished through manifold cognitions, provided there exists no single synthesizer of the cognitions of multiple objects."
That is not tenable.
He says that all of this is untenable if consciousness takes its own part as its object:
"Furthermore, regarding two cognitions at earlier and later times..."
Moreover, the relationship between action and its fruit must depend on a distinction; it cannot exist in a non-distinct cognition.
Indeed, it is not the act of cutting that is cut, but rather the wood;
nor is it the act of cooking that is cooked, but rather the rice grains.

Therefore, here too, cognition is not known by its own part as its object, because that would involve a contradiction in self-operation; rather, it is an object distinct from it, just as rice grains to be cooked are distinct from the act of cooking.
Having first established the arrangement of the elements, he says:
—Furthermore:
"One would have to admit that consciousness is consciousness. Thus he objects.
— "But surely, [the objection is] that consciousness has as its object something distinct from its own nature.
This is the meaning: if consciousness were to grasp an object distinct from its own nature, then, being itself imperceptible, it would be unable to render the object perceptible;
for, unlike the eye, it does not impart any excellence to the object by being in contact with it.
By means of which one might perceive an object that is not itself perceived;
rather, the very perception of that [cognition] is the perception of the object.
As they say: "For one whose apprehension is not itself perceived, the seeing of the object is not established."
If that [cognition] were to be cognized by another cognition, then being itself unperceived, it would not be able to make the cognition whose object is the thing manifest as immediate.
In this way, there would be an infinite regress of "that and that"; therefore, fearing such an infinite regress, it is better to maintain that [cognition] has its operation upon itself.
Moreover, just as a lamp does not require another lamp, [so too does cognition not require another cognition].
"In this way, knowledge also ought not to require another knowledge, because they are equal. He refutes this as follows:
"Both of those [arguments] are incorrect."
Since the desire to apprehend the witness of consciousness does not arise at the very moment of the apprehension of consciousness itself, the fear of an infinite regress (anavasthā) is untenable.
This is the meaning: it is true that for an apprehension that is not itself perceived, the perception of an object is not established;
however, another apprehension need not be sought in order to make that [first] apprehension perceptible to the knower.

Moreover, as soon as a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) arises from the contact between the sense-organ and its object, both the object and the apprehension become perceptible to the knower.
For the object, whose nature is inherently hidden, requires the experience—which is a specific modification of the internal organ—to become perceptible to the knower;
whereas experience, though insentient (*jaḍa*), does not require another experience because, through its transparency, it is capable of receiving the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*).
By which there would be an infinite regress;
for it is not possible that experience has arisen and yet does not become perceptible to the cognizer.
Just as in the case of blue and so forth;
therefore, just as the cutter pervades the object to be cut, such as a tree, by means of the act of cutting, but the act of cutting does not [pervade] another act of cutting.
Nor is the cutter itself the agent of cutting; rather, it is Devadatta or another who acts by his own nature.
Or, for example, as a cook pervades the object to be cooked through the act of cooking—not indeed by means of one cooking through another cooking.
Nor is the act of cooking itself the cooker; rather, it is Devadatta and others who cook by their own nature.

Likewise, the knower pervades the object of knowledge, such as blue and so forth, through the act of knowing, but he does not pervade the act of knowing through another act of knowing, nor is the act of knowing itself the knower.
However, the knower (*pramātṛ*) is by its very nature the pervader of valid cognition (*pramā*).

Furthermore, there can be no requirement for valid cognition with respect to the knower, who is the immutable and eternal consciousness (*kūṭasthanityacaitanya*); for if the knower required another knower for his own valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, it has been well said: "At the very moment of the apprehension of the cognition, there arises no desire for the apprehension of the knower—the witness of cognition—who is the immutable and eternal consciousness."
Regarding what was stated— "because of their equality, the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator is untenable"— it is replied:
"And because of the difference in nature between the witness and the cognition, the relationship of perceiver and perceived is tenable."
Let it not be that the relationship of grasped and grasper exists between two cognitions due to their equality;
rather, it is indeed possible between the knower and the cognition because of their inequality.
Furthermore, the status of being the grasped for a cognition is not due to its possessing a fruit produced by the activity of a grasper, as is the case with an external object.
Because one fruit cannot logically arise from another fruit, as they say: "Consciousness is not perceived as an object, because it is itself the fruit.
Rather, it exists through a manifestation that is self-established for the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Even an object of perception becomes manifest to the subject when consciousness is present; and consciousness itself is likewise manifest.
As others have said: "There exists no state of being an object for this [witness].

It might be argued that whatever is manifest is manifested by another, as in the case of knowledge and its object; and since the witness is likewise [manifest], there is no disparity between the cognition and the witness. To this, he says:
"And because the self-established witness cannot be denied."

For instance: since this witness is always free from doubt and error, its nature as eternal direct perception is consistent with its being non-accidental luminosity. To explain: even when the knower is doubting, [the witness] is not doubtful; even when he is erring, it is not erroneous; even when he is conceiving an object indirectly, it is immediate; and even when he is remembering, it is experiential. This is true for every living being, and this would not be possible if its consciousness were dependent on something else.
Furthermore, the consequence of infinite regress has already been stated.
Therefore, its self-establishment cannot be denied even by one who does not wish it, because it is the very essence of the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Moreover, according to the sequence already explained, since cognition lacks the capacity for self-comprehension, if the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is not admitted—

Furthermore, by asserting that consciousness, like a lamp, manifests by itself without depending on another illuminator, one would be saying that consciousness is not accessible through any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇagamya*) and lacks a cognizer;
it would be like the manifestation of a thousand lamps situated in the interior of a solid rock.
If it does not shine forth for anyone at all who could be its cognizer, then what is the use of its being "self-luminous" (*svayaṃprakāśa*)?
Thinking that consciousness alone is the cognizer, he raises an objection:
"Certainly so;
because it is of the nature of experience."
He offers a rebuttal, stating that since the fruit (the result) possesses neither agency nor objecthood, another agent must be sought for it, as in the case of a lamp;
thus, his position is not one of proving what is already established: "No, because there is another cognizer."

One might object: "Let it be that our own desired consciousness resides in the position of the witness; thus, there is disagreement only regarding the name, not regarding the actual thing. To this, [the author] replies by pointing out the self-established nature of the witnessing knower: "By intending that [witness], it is precisely this [consciousness] which manifests of itself."
He refutes this with "no.
For the properties such as arising and so forth are indeed accepted as belonging to consciousness; and thus, because it is a result, it does not possess the status of being a cognizer.
Because the relationship between agent and fruit is contradictory in a single entity;
rather, the meaning is that it is similar to a lamp and so forth. //28//
"And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams and so forth.
The difference in nature consists in sublation and non-sublation:
the cognition of a dream is sublated, whereas the cognition of the waking state is not sublated.
You too must necessarily maintain that the cognition of the waking state is unsublated;
for it is by that [waking cognition] that the dream-cognition is understood to be sublated and false.
If, however, the waking cognition were itself subject to sublation, it could not serve as the sublater of the dream-cognition.
For that which is itself sublated cannot possibly be the sublator.
Consequently, the example "like a dream" would be deficient in its probandum, as it would follow that the cognition of a dream is not false.

Therefore, because of this dissimilarity regarding sublation and non-sublation, it is not possible to determine that waking cognitions lack an objective basis by using the cognition of a dream as an example.
"Afflicted by sleep" refers to a defect of the instrument (the sense organ). He states another point of dissimilarity regarding falsity:
Moreover, it is memory alone [that is defined as such].
For a cognition produced solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is memory;

whereas a cognition arising from a causal complex characterized by the presence of currently functioning sense-faculties, logical marks, words, similarity, or the non-arising of other possible means of knowledge, is apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
Thus, in this case, because one who is asleep lacks other causal conditions, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) remains as the sole residue;
therefore, it is a memory (*smṛti*) by virtue of being born from that impression.
Furthermore, due to the defect of sleep, even though [the father and so forth] are not actually present, they appear as if present through a distorted manifestation.
Therefore, there is first of all a distinction between memory and perception, and furthermore, there is a reversal of that memory;
thus, the meaning is that there is a vast difference.
Moreover, once self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is established, the fact that waking cognitions correspond to reality—which is established by direct experience—cannot be overturned by inference.
Because that [inference] does not arise due to contradiction with experience;
furthermore, even the state of having an unperceived object is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being grasped by the causal complex for the production of inference.
And since an effect cannot possibly arise in the absence of its cause, the author, holding this intention, says:
Moreover, because it would entail a contradiction with direct experience. // 29 //
There is no [existence of objects] because they are not perceived.

Furthermore, when positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are relied upon according to worldly observation, it is the object itself that comes to be perceived, not the mental impression (vāsanā) independent of the object.
The meaning is that even mental impressions are seen to be dependent upon the perception of objects.
Furthermore, worldly *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) is not tenable even due to the absence of a substratum (*āśraya*).
Nor can the momentary *ālayavijñāna* serve as the support for *vāsanā*,
because between two things arising simultaneously, there can be no relationship of support and supported, just like the left and right horns of a cow.

Furthermore, [the author], intending to show that there would be a contradiction of momentariness for that which has already arisen but is non-existent at the time of the arising of the effect to be produced, says:
"Moreover, as for what is called 'impression' (vāsanā)... The remainder of the text has its meaning not obscure. //30//
And because of momentariness. It might be argued as follows:

if consciousness with an aspect (*sākāra*) is possible, yet an external object—whether gross or subtle—is impossible through analysis, then alas, in this way, both the object and the cognition cannot withstand investigation by means of their existence.
Nor by way of non-existence, because that which is non-existent cannot manifest;
nor by way of both.
Because of contradiction, existence and non-existence cannot coexist in one place;
nor can it be by way of being neither, because the negation of one is inseparable from the affirmation of the other.
Therefore, let the very inability of things to withstand analysis be their true nature.
As they have said: "This is what the wise declare to be the force of reality:
the more objects are reflected upon, the more they are found to fall apart."
Thus.
The meaning is that they do not establish themselves in any position whatsoever.
Desiring to refute this, [the author] says:
"But the position of the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); therefore, no effort is made to refute it."

For worldly means of valid cognition have existence and non-existence as their objects. By these, that which is apprehended as "existent" is established as reality, being just as it is and non-erroneous; and that which is apprehended as "non-existent" is established as reality, being just as it is and non-erroneous.

Furthermore, by one who establishes that both the existent and the non-existent are incapable of withstanding analysis, everything becomes established as contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, due to this contradiction with all *pramāṇas*, this [your] establishment is not tenable.
If it should be argued: "By this analysis, the ultimate validity (*tāttvika-prāmāṇya*) of the means of valid cognition is excluded, but not their conventional validity (*sāṃvyavahārika*)."

And thus, since they have different objects, there is no contradiction with all means of valid cognition; therefore, he says: "For this worldly transaction, established by all means of valid cognition, cannot be denied without apprehending another reality.
For the means of valid cognition, when operating within their own respective domains, operate precisely with the thought, 'This is the reality.'"
However, their lack of ultimate reality (atāttvikatva) must be understood from another source, namely a sublater (bādhaka);
they do not, however, proceed with the thought, "Our validity is merely conventional (sāṃvyavahārika) and not ultimate.
And the sublater would demonstrate their lack of ultimate reality by pointing out a reality that is the opposite of the object of those [cognitions].

Just as one determines that "this is mother-of-pearl, not silver," "these are rays of light, not water," or "this is a single moon, not two moons," and so forth— in the same way here too, the unreality of these means of valid cognition must be demonstrated by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) that establishes another reality which contradicts the entire range of objects of those means of valid cognition;
for it is not possible to subvert means of valid cognition by means of something else whose reality has not been established.

If it is argued that establishing the reality of things as being incapable of withstanding analysis demonstrates the non-ultimate nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what is this "incapability of withstanding analysis" which is intended as the reality of things?
Is that thing, in ultimate reality, one of the categories such as existence (*sat*) and so forth, which simply does not withstand analysis?
Now, if it is devoid of reality precisely because it cannot withstand analysis,
then it is contradictory to say that, from the perspective of ultimate truth, it does not withstand analysis as being any one of "existent" and so forth.
If it does not withstand analysis, then it is not any one of "existent" and so forth.
If it were one [of the two], how could it not tolerate investigation?
Now, if it is devoid of reality (*nistattva*), how can it be possible to speak thus without first establishing one of the two as reality?
Furthermore, the very state of being devoid of reality is not itself the reality of things.
For if one were to seek it, there would be an absence of reality; and you yourselves have stated that even such [reality] cannot withstand analysis.
Furthermore, that which is superimposed must be negated.
Furthermore, superimposition is observed to have a real substrate, as in the case of silver and the like being superimposed upon mother-of-pearl and so forth.
If there were no reality whatsoever, of what would there be superimposition, and upon what?

Therefore, the non-dual Brahman, which is the ultimate reality beyond all conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), is superimposed as the nature of an inexpressible phenomenal world (*anirvācyaprapañca*).
And we consider it logical that, having established that reality as being non-ultimate, the conventional validity of the means of cognition is sublated by a sublating cognition. //31//
And because it is untenable in every respect—why say more?
It shines forth.
What need is there for further words?
In whatever way one examines it, both in terms of its textual composition and its meaning, this is a doctrine of the Nihilists (vaināśika).
First, regarding the textual composition, one observes the improper use of words such as *paśyanātiṣṭhan*, *asiddha*, and *poṣadha*.

Furthermore, by accepting selflessness in meaning yet asserting the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the substratum for all latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), one accepts an imperishable self.

Likewise, by accepting momentariness while asserting that "whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*) remain constant," one accepts permanence. Many such [contradictions] are to be inferred;
thus, [the Buddha's teaching is not contradictory], because multiple [attributes] cannot coexist in a single [entity].
The system of the Sugatas who wear their lower garments loose has been refuted;
now the system of the naked ones is being refuted.
He states that system both concisely and in detail.
"And seven categories (padārthas) are accepted among them.
Regarding this, he states the summary:
"In brief, however, there are only two categories."
The soul (jīva) consists of consciousness, while the category of the non-soul (ajīva) is insentient;
they describe this further elaboration (prapañca) of those two, soul and non-soul, as appropriate.
He states it as follows:
Regarding the term "five astikāyas":
it refers to all their respective internal subdivisions as well.
The *jīvāstikāya* (the category of living beings) is threefold: the bound (*baddha*), the liberated (*mukta*), and the eternally perfected (*nityasiddha*).

The categories of substantial entities (*astikāya*) are sixfold: the four elements beginning with earth, the stationary, and the mobile; the category of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), which is inferred from movement; the category of rest (*adharmāstikāya*), which is inferred from stability;

and the category of space (*ākāśāstikāya*), which is twofold: world-space (*lokākāśa*) and non-world-space (*alokākāśa*). Among these, world-space is that which exists within the worlds situated one above the other; above those, the place of liberation is non-world-space.
For in that [realm], worlds do not exist.
Thus, the two categories of soul (jīva) and non-soul (ajīva) have been explained in five ways.
Now, the three categories characterized by activity—influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), and dissociation (nirjarā)—are being explained.
Activity is of two kinds: correct and false.
Among these, false activity is *āsrava* (influx). Correct activity, however, consists of restraint (*saṃvara*) and shedding (*nirjarā*).
Activity of the senses is called *āsrava* because it causes the person to flow toward sense objects.
For it is through the doors of the sense-faculties that the light of the person (pauruṣaṃ jyotiḥ), touching upon objects, transforms into the form of cognitions such as those of color and so forth.
Others, however, call karma "influx" (āsrava);
for these [actions] flow toward and pervade the agent, following after the agent; thus they are called influx.
This is false activity because it is the cause of harm;
restraint (*saṃvara*) and the wearing away of karma (*nirjarā*) are right activities.
Among these, activity consisting of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, is restraint.

For it is called *saṃvara* (restraint) because it closes the door to the stream of the *āsravas* (influxes). *Nirjarā* (dissociation), however, is the cause for the abandonment of merit and demerit—which have been defiled by passions (*kaṣāya*) and have operated since beginningless time—such as [the practice of] climbing upon heated stones and so forth.
For it is called *nirjarā* because it completely wears away (*jarayati*) merit and demerit through the experience of pleasure and pain.
Bondage consists of eight kinds of karma. Among these, the destructive karma (ghātikarma) is fourfold;
namely: knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇīya), deluding (mohanīya), and obstructive (antarāya).

Likewise, there are four non-obstructive karmas (aghāti-karmāṇi), namely: that which is to be experienced (vedanīya), the name-determining (nāmika), the lineage-determining (gotrika), and the life-span-determining (āyuṣka).
In this regard, right knowledge is not the means to liberation.
The notion that "the establishment of reality does not follow from knowledge because that would lead to over-extension" is called the *jñānāvaraṇīya* (knowledge-obscuring) karma.
The belief that "there is no liberation through the practice of right vision" is the *darśanāvaraṇīya* (perception-obscuring) karma.
The failure to ascertain the distinction among the many mutually contradictory paths to liberation shown by various teachers is the *mohanīya* (deluding) karma.
For those who have set out upon the path to liberation, that knowledge which acts as an obstacle is the *antarāya* (obstructive) karma.
Because these [other] karmas destroy what is beneficial (*śreya*), they are called the *ghāti* (destructive) karmas;
the non-destructive karmas are the *aghāti*.
For example, karma to be experienced [in this life] is the cause for the maturation of a pure person;
for although it is a bond, it does not obstruct the supreme good because it does not impede the knowledge of reality.
Furthermore, there is the "nominal" (nāmika) karma which is concordant with the karma to be experienced that initiates a pure person.
For that [gotra] initiates the first stage of a virtuous person (śuklapudgala), beginning with the embryonic stages such as the *kalala* and *budbuda*.
It is the neutral (*avyākṛta*) gotra; even more so than that, it is the primary [element] existing in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*).
As for the life-force (*āyuṣka*), it is called "life-force" because it makes known (*kāyati*) or declares (*kathayati*) the lifespan by way of its production.
These aforementioned actions are non-destructive (*aghāti*) because they have as their basis individuals who are pure (*śukla-pudgala*).
This group of eight actions is called "bondage" (*bandha*) because it binds the person.

According to some, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the abiding above [the world] of the self (*ātman*), whose afflictions and their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have completely fallen away, whose knowledge is unobstructed, and who is absorbed in bliss.

Others, however, maintain that liberation is simply this: since the soul (jīva) has the nature of moving upward, it is bound by the categories of merit and demerit (dharma-adharmāstikāya); when it is released from those, it moves upward—this indeed is liberation.
Thus, these seven categories, beginning with the soul, have been presented along with their internal subdivisions.
Among them:
And they apply this logic known as the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgīnaya) everywhere: "in some sense it exists," "in some sense it does not exist," and so forth.
It may both exist and not exist; it may be inexpressible; it may both exist and be inexpressible.
"It may be that it does not exist and is inexpressible," and "it may be that it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible.
Indeed, this word *syāt* is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).
It indicates non-absolutism (*anekānta*).

As they have said: "In sentences, the particle *syāt* indicates non-absolutism; it is understood as a qualifier for each [predicate]. Because it is connected with meaning, it is a nipāta (indeclinable) that resembles a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)."
Thus.

If, however, this word *syāt* were not an indicator of non-absolutism (anaikānta), then in the sentence "it may be" (*syād asti*), the word *syāt* would be meaningless. This is what was stated: "because of its connection with meaning. But if it indicates non-absolutism, then [the phrase] "it may be" means "it exists in some way" (*kathañcid asti*); thus, through the word *syāt*, the sense of "in some way" (*kathañcit*)—which is not explicitly stated by the word "exists" (*asti*)—is understood, and so there is no lack of meaning. And thus: "The doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*) results from the abandonment of absolute one-sidedness (*sarvathaikānta*) due to the application of the particle *kim* (in the form of *syāt*)."
It is based on the method of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅganaya) and effects the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

Indeed, when an interrogative suffix (*kiṃvṛtta*) is present, by means of this rule for the particle *cit*, through the total abandonment of absolute exclusivity (*ekānta*), the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*)— being dependent upon that perspective (*naya*) which exists within the sevenfold alternatives (*saptabhaṅga*)— is capable of distinguishing between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
For instance, if a thing were absolutely existent alone, then it would necessarily exist in every way, at all times, in all places, and in its entirety.

Neither through the desire to obtain nor through the desire to avoid would anyone ever, anywhere, or in any way, engage in activity or desist from it; for that which has already been obtained cannot be further obtained, and the abandonment of what is to be discarded is likewise impossible.

However, in the case of the position of non-absolutism (anaikāntapakṣa), since existence occurs somewhere, at some time, for someone, and in some manner, the rejection and acquisition [of things] are possible for those who act with discernment.
He refutes this very method of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgīnaya) with the following:
"Because [contradictory properties] cannot exist in one [thing]. He explains:

For it is not possible for properties such as existence and so forth— which, being ultimately real, are mutually exclusive by nature— to coexist simultaneously within a single entity that is ultimately real.

This is what is meant: it is true that whatever exists as a reality exists in every way, at all times, everywhere, and in its entire essence, as an indefinable form, and does not not exist—just like the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
However, that which is said to exist in some place, in some manner, at some time, or by some aspect [is different].
Just as conceptual proliferation exists through conventional usage and not from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it cannot withstand analytical investigation.
Moreover, mere conditionality (*pratyayamātra*) does not establish reality, for it would follow that silver, water, and so forth in mother-of-pearl, mirages, and the like would also be real.

If, however, reality were established merely by non-sublation for worldly people, then since the identification of the body with the self is also uncontradicted for them, it would be ultimately real; this would result in the consequence of nihilism through the adoption of the Lokāyata doctrine.
For those who appear to be wise, however, the sublation of the conceit of the body being the self through inquiry is equal to that of the manifold world (prapañca), which is itself indeterminate.

Furthermore, since existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, there can be no conjunction between them; thus, there would be an alternative (vikalpa). Yet, an alternative is not possible regarding a real entity (vastu).

Therefore, just as in the case of the cognition "Is it a post or a person?", when there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the result—the determination of sevenfoldness or fivefoldness—as well as the determiner, the cognizer; the instrument, the means of knowledge; and the object of that knowledge, the sevenfoldness or fivefoldness itself, the author has successfully established his own status as a teacher of the heterodox schools (tīrthakara).
And since a definitive determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) exists only where there is absolute existence, there can be no doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) everywhere; thus he says:
"These which are the seven categories. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. //33//
And thus, there would be non-omnipresence of the self.
The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and thus" (evaṃ ca) indicates a conjunction.
For if the self were subject to transformation through the body, it would follow that it is non-omnipresent, that is, limited in extent.
And likewise, there is impermanence:
for whatever is limited is all impermanent, just like jars and so forth; and such is the self.
This is what he says:
"Just as in the case of a single substratum" (yathaikasmindharmiṇi).
And he states that this is also indicated by the sūtra through its incompleteness:
"And because the dimensions of bodies are not fixed" (śarīrāṇāṃ cānavasthitaparimāṇatvāt).

For if the *jīva* were of the same size as the human body, it would not be capable of pervading the entire body of an elephant due to its smallness; thus, because the self does not pervade the whole body, it would lack completeness (*akārtsyam*).

Consequently, it would not be of the same size as the body. Furthermore, when [the soul], having abandoned the body of an elephant, becomes embodied in the form of a tiny insect, it could not then be fully contained within that tiny insect's body; thus, there would be incompleteness of the self.
The rest is easy to understand.
He raises an objection: "This might be so."
"Having infinite parts":

the meaning is that just as a lamp situated inside a small jar or a great palace possesses contraction and expansion, so too does the individual soul (jīva) within the bodies of an ant and an elephant.
He refutes this by means of a dilemma:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of those which are infinite":
first of all, a lamp cannot serve as an illustration here,
because that would entail the consequence of [the self] being impermanent.
For the constituent parts of a lamp are perishable,
and the lamp as a composite whole possesses the nature of arising and ceasing at every moment;
therefore, because of its impermanence, neither the soul nor its constituent parts can be admitted to be stable.
And thus, the refutation stated regarding the two alternatives applies.
Furthermore, he says that the assertion of the infinity of the soul's parts is even more untenable: "Moreover, [if it were] only the size of the body... (3.2.34).
Introducing another sūtra preceded by a doubt, he says: "Now, in turn" (atha paryāyeṇa).
To that also, it is said:
Nor can there be non-contradiction even through figurative interpretation, because of [the necessity of] transformation and so forth.
The eight types of karma, beginning with knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), have been mentioned.

Furthermore, if the eternity of the self is accepted, liberation (apavarga) cannot occur because there would be no knowledge of the self due to the inability to determine the exact measure of the parts that come and go; this is the intended meaning.
"Therefore, because of the consequence of such defects as these.
We shall state the defect indicated by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi).
Furthermore, would these parts of the individual soul (jīva) be conscious individually, or would their aggregate be conscious?

If each of those [atoms] were individually conscious, then because there would be no rule ensuring that many conscious entities share a single intention, the body might at times be torn asunder by their actions in opposing directions.

However, if the consciousness belongs to the aggregate, then when the body of an elephant becomes the body of a gnat, the living being—consisting of only two or three remaining parts—would not be conscious;
for the aggregate would cease to exist due to the dissolution of the many components that constituted it within the gnat's body.

The word "or" (*athavā*) introduces this sūtra in response to the suspicion that, following the previous sūtra, the soul might be non-eternal like a Buddhist *saṃtāna* (continuum). The sūtra states: "Nor can there be no contradiction even through succession, because of transformation and so forth. Nor can there be no contradiction between bondage and liberation on the grounds that the soul is eternal due to the admission of a *saṃtāna*, even though its dimensions do not remain constant through successive states (*paryāya*). This is because [the soul] undergoes transformation and other such changes.
Why?
Because of faults such as transformation (pariṇāma).
If the continuum were a real entity, it would undergo transformation; consequently, faults such as impermanence would follow, just as in the case of leather.

And if [the self] were a non-entity, there would follow the fault of falling into the view of selflessness (*nairātmya*), as indicated by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). The *visica* are those who are naked (*vivāsana*). //35//
"And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both would be eternal, there would be no distinction.
For in this way, the size of the individual soul existing in the state of liberation would be eternal, provided that it did not come into being after having previously not existed.
Because things such as jars, which come into being after not having existed, possess a finality [of change];

and how could they not have come into being after not having existed if they had already existed previously? Furthermore, when another dimension [or size] has been occupied, it is impossible for something new to arise.
Therefore, since the final dimension must have existed even previously, there would be no difference [between states];

and thus, there would only be the dimension of a single body, with no attainment of bodies that are increased or decreased, because this would contradict the admission that the dimension is coextensive with the body.
Furthermore, in this case, the logical connection is that it would follow that both dimensions are eternal.
And in the first [explanation], it is illuminated that there is indeed the same size as a single body;
whereas in the second explanation, the construction is "in both states," and thus the state of having the same size as a single body is not illuminated.
However, the distinction is merely that one has a single measure, whether it be minute or large. //36//
"Because of the inconsistency with the Lord [as the cause].
To dispel the misconception that the doctrine of God as the cause is being refuted here without distinction, he says: "only."
Those who rely on Sāṃkhya and Yoga, such as Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, and others,
have declared that the Pradhāna is the power of seeing (dṛkśakti).
The Puruṣa is the witness of the intellect (pratyaya).
And that Supreme Person, the Lord (Īśvara), who is untouched by the various afflictions (kleśa), karmas, fruitions (vipāka), and latent impressions (āśaya), is distinct from both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
There are four types of followers of Maheśvara: the Śaivas, [the Pāśupatas, the Kāpālikas, and the Kālāmukhas].
The Pāśupatas, the Kāruṇikasiddhāntins, and the Kāpālikas.
These four are also called Māheśvaras because they follow the established tenets propounded by Maheśvara.
The cause is Īśvara;
the effects are those derived from Pradhāna, such as Mahat and the rest.
Yoga consists of meditation on the syllable *oṃ* and so forth, as well as concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and other such practices.
Ritual (*vidhi*) includes bathing at the three junctions of the day and so forth, ending with living in concealment.
The end of suffering is liberation (*mokṣa*).
The "beings" (paśu) are the selves; their "fetter" (pāśa) is bondage, and liberation from that is the end of suffering.

This is their intended meaning: [it is argued] that it is impossible for a conscious presiding agent, such as a potter, to be the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of an effect such as a jar; thus, this position is reached.
To this position, the following is stated:
"Because of the inconsistency with the Lord" (patyurasāmañjasyāt).
The underlying intention here is as follows: it has been stated more than once that [this sūtra] is intended solely to establish that the Lord is merely the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa).
Therefore, another means of valid knowledge (pramāṇāntara) must be accepted for this matter by means of this [sūtra].
In that regard, inference is first of all not possible; for it functions in accordance with what has been perceived, and in accordance with that, there is inconsistency. Thus he says:
"Inferior and middling" means this:
when the Lord is established through scripture (*āgama*), one need not follow what is perceived by the senses.
For when heaven, the unseen merit (*apūrva*), deities, and so forth are understood from scripture, there is nothing among them that is perceptible.
For scripture does not function by means of observed similarity;

therefore, even if one postulates a great many unseen things whose nature is the opposite of what is seen for the sake of establishing what has been heard, they do not incur the "odor of iron" (i.e., the taint of being base or unproven), because they possess valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
Any conformity to what is seen that is made therein is done merely out of a friendly disposition.
But inference, which operates by means of similarity with what is observed and does not depend on scripture, fears even a mere husk when confronted with the opposite of what has been observed.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the process] depends upon the karma of living beings, we say:
no.
Why?
Because if there were a mutual relationship of the impelled and the impeller between karma and God, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) would follow.
This is the meaning: if God, being dependent on compassion and free from passion, were [the sole cause], then He would not impel living beings toward evil action (*kapūya-karma*).
Even if that [evil] has arisen, he should not preside over it,
because suffering does not arise for living beings by that alone;
for people are not dependent on God [in such a way that they could act] independently to perform wicked deeds.
Or else, how could an action that is not presided over by Him produce a fruit?
Therefore, even though the Lord is independent, you must conceive of Him as being impelled by actions; this would be a conception contrary to what is observed.
Furthermore, this would result in another "boil upon a boil": the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
"Karma must be set in motion by Īśvara, and Īśvara by karma. He raises an objection:
"If it is argued that this is not so because of beginninglessness..."
[The opponent argues: "One is impelled toward present action by past karma; by that [past] karma, the present action is then impelled toward its own effect.
He refutes this: "Not as in the case of the present time."

Now, how can prior karma—which was not set in motion by Īśvara—perform an effect characterized by being set in motion by Īśvara? In that case as well, [one would have to say] it was set in motion by Īśvara, who was himself set in motion by prior karma; thus there is the fault of an infinite regress (*andhaparamparā*).
For indeed, a blind person is led by one who has sight, not by another blind person.
Likewise here as well, since both [the mover and the moved] must be set in motion, the meaning is: who could set whom in motion?
Furthermore, he states "Moreover" (apica) because the Naiyāyikas' claim that God is faultless contradicts their own established tenets.
The meaning is that this is not our [accepted] position.
Now, one might object: "Is it not observed that people also act out of compassion?
And yet, compassion is not a fault. To this, he says:

"And [one] who is motivated solely by self-interest. For when there is compassion, suffering arises for that person; therefore, one engages in activity to eliminate it. Thus, even those who possess compassion engage in activity only because they are motivated by their own interest.
Now, one might object: "Let them indeed engage in activity while being motivated solely by self-interest—what is the fault in this? To this, he says:
"Because of having its own purpose, etc.
means because of being desirous [of liberation].
And since it is admitted that the person (puruṣa) is indifferent (audāsīnya), there is no real activity [on his part]. //37//
Furthermore, he states another refutation based on observation:
"And because a relation is impossible.
For conjunction is observed to exist between things that have parts and are not all-pervading.
For conjunction is an attainment that was previously non-attainment; it is not possible for those things that are all-pervading, because there is no prior non-attainment and because they lack parts.
Indeed, the nature of conjunction is to exist without pervading [its locus].
And it has already been stated that the existence of conjunction without pervading its locus is impossible in the case of partless entities.
Therefore, the point is that since the non-pervasive occurrence of conjunction is excluded, there is the exclusion of conjunction itself, which is pervaded by it.
Nor is it characterized as inherence (*samavāya*);

for that is accepted as the relation that is the cause of the cognition "here" (*ihapratyaya*) between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of substrate and superstrate.
The meaning is that there is no mutual relationship of container and contained between Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara;
nor is there a relationship inferable from effects characterized by mere fitness (yogyatā). Thus he says:
"Nor any other."
For the status of Pradhāna as the cause of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and so forth is not yet established; thus, he raises an objection:
"by the proponents of Brahman" (brahmavādibhiḥ).
He refutes this: No. Why?
In his view, the relationship characterized by identity with that which is indeterminable (anirvacanīya) is established;
furthermore— apiceti.

For scripture (āgama), in its operation, does not depend upon an illustrative example; thus, it is capable of operating even with respect to that which has never been seen before or that which is contrary to it.
Inference (anumāna), however, follows what has been observed and is therefore unable to operate in such cases. Thus, he raises an objection:
"Of another as well"— he refutes this, saying:
"No."
The intended meaning is that, for us, since both God and the scripture are beginningless, there is no contradiction even though the scripture has God as its source. //38//
And because a substratum is untenable.
It should not be forgotten here either that inference proceeds according to what is observed and does not have as its object a thing beyond the world of experience.
The rest is easy to understand. //39//
If it is argued that [the Lord] is like an instrument, we say no, because of [His] experience and so forth.

"Devoid of form and the rest" means that its form is unmanifest. For the presiding over an instrument devoid of form and the rest is observed only in the case of a person's own experience and so forth, and not elsewhere.
For no one is ever observed employing an external instrument, such as an axe, without perceiving it;

therefore, for the Lord who employs an instrument devoid of form and other qualities, there would follow the consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain, and thus his lack of lordship (anīśvaratva). This is the intended meaning. He states another alternative:
"Otherwise" means as follows:
previously, "presiding" (*adhiṣṭhiti*) was the act of presiding; now, however, "the locus of presiding" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is explained as the body, which is the seat of experience.
Likewise, by the consequence of [accepting] experience and so forth, the lack of lordship (*anīśvaratva*) was previously established.

But now, the distinction is that because [the Lord] would possess a body, there would follow the consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain, and thus He would not be the Supreme Lord (anīśvara). //40//
Either there would be finitude or a lack of omniscience.

Furthermore, for one who accepts inference as the sole means of valid cognition, it must be inferred that even Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara possess numerical diversity and finitude, because they are substances—or because they are objects of knowledge while being distinct from number;
consequently, there would be either finitude or a lack of omniscience.
The sense is that, regarding a matter accessible through our own scriptures (*āgama*), inference has no power because its object is sublated by that scripture.
Furthermore, "the nature and dimension" refers to whatever [dimension] a thing may have—whether minute, large, infinitely large, long, or short.
Now, the subsequent alternative is proposed so that this fault may not occur.
The non-apprehension of that which has an end would result in non-omniscience because of its finite nature;
however, for that which has no end at all, the non-apprehension of it does not entail non-omniscience.
The point is that one does not become ignorant simply by not knowing things such as a rabbit's horn.
He refutes this with the words "tataḥ" (therefore).
It has been stated that inference, independent of scripture, makes known their finitude. //41//
Because of the impossibility of its arising.
Elsewhere, due to non-contradiction with the Vedas, that portion in which there is contradiction is rejected;
he states that portion as follows:
Furthermore, as for this which is said— that from Vāsudeva arises Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is the individual soul (jīva)—
if the individual soul were to possess a cause, it would follow that it is non-eternal.
The meaning is that because there would be no one who goes to the next world if the soul were impermanent, there would be an absence of the next world;
and consequently, since this would lead to the non-existence of heaven, hell, and liberation, it results in nihilism. Furthermore, he states that the production of a soul is untenable:
And he will also refute [this]. //42//
And there is no instrument for the agent;
for even though one who is proficient in many arts might fashion an axe and cut down a *palāśa* tree with it,

and even though one perceives an object by employing the instrument of knowledge— characterized by the contact of the sense organ, the object, the self, and the mind— with effort, [the self does not become the instrument of that very action].

Nevertheless, how could Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is without instruments (akaraṇa), produce the instrument called Pradyumna, which is the mind? Or, if one who lacks instruments possesses the power to create instruments, then what is the purpose of creating instruments at all? The point is that the accomplishment of all effects follows from the very absence of instruments. //43//
Or, if they exist as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that;
these [beings], Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, are indeed Vāsudevas— faultless, meaning free from defects such as ignorance.
They are without a basis and without a substrate;
for this very reason,
they are irreproachable, being free from defects such as impermanence and the like.
Therefore, the meaning is that the impossibility of origination is not a fault, because it is consistent [with our position].
To this it is replied: "Even so" (evamapi).
Let there be no fault by way of [our] admission; [nevertheless...]
However, this same fault applies by way of another method.
He states this other method preceded by a question:
"How so?"
Regarding the phrase "If, first of all":
these various Lords, being distinct from one another, cannot possibly possess mutually contradictory wills;
for if their desires were contradictory, the production of any effect would be impossible.

Alternatively, if their desires were unimpeded and each were individually a Lord, then since the act of ruling would have been accomplished by one alone, the others would be purposeless. If, on the other hand, they ruled collectively, no single one would be a pure Lord,
and there would be a loss of the established tenet.

Since it is accepted that the Blessed One alone is Vāsudeva, the supreme reality (*paramārthatattva*), another alternative must be maintained. And since the impossibility of origination (*utpattyasaṃbhava*) is a fault in that case, [the author], intending this, presents another alternative and refutes it by means of the impossibility of origination:
Now, as for the phrase "this is the intended meaning":
the rest is easy to understand. //44//
And because of contradiction:
having indeed spoken of qualities such as knowledge as distinct from the selves who possess those qualities, he then declares their non-difference, saying,
"These venerable ones are Vāsudevas themselves."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), another [contradiction] is subsumed: having asserted the difference of Pradyumna and Aniruddha from the Self by characterizing them as mind (*manas*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*), there is the subsequent assertion of their non-difference from that very Self in the statement "these are of the Self.
Thus, the contradiction with the Veda has been explained. //45//
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhagavatpādabhāṣya* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "Demonstration of the Faultiness of the Doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and Others.
The third quarter of the second chapter begins: 2.3.1.
Space [is not produced], because it is not mentioned in scripture.
Previously, the contradiction of the Śruti with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was refuted;
now, however, the mutual contradiction among the Śrutis themselves is being refuted.
In that regard, he states the mutual contradiction among the Śrutis concerning creation:
"In various places in the Vedāntas" means that,

just as the irrelevance of the opposing views has been established due to contradictions with the Śruti, so too is the irrelevance of one's own position [established] due to contradictions with the Śruti.
"The clarity of its meaning" consists in the demonstration of the true nature of reality through the removal of fallacious appearances.
The fruit of this [discussion] is the removal of the doubt regarding the independence of the world’s cause being Brahman within one's own school.
For here, in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), a mutual contradiction among the Śruti texts is set forth, whereas in the established conclusion (siddhānta), there is no contradiction.
In this regard, the statement of a certain proponent of a partial conclusion (siddhāntyekadeśin) is: "The ether is not produced, because there is no scriptural text [to that effect].

His intention is as follows: although there is a scriptural text in the Taittirīyaka regarding the production of the ether, nevertheless, due to its contradiction with other means of valid cognition and its conflict with many other scriptural texts, it must be understood figuratively.
Thus, since the ether is eternal, creation begins only with fire and the subsequent elements.
And thus, there is no contradiction among the Śrutis.
This very point has been stated: first of all, having recourse to the ether, it is considered whether this ether has an origin or not.
