If it does not exist, there is no apprehension of contradiction with scripture; but if it does exist, then there is a contradiction with scripture, and thus another effort must be undertaken to resolve that—this is the meaning. 2.3.1.2.
In this regard, the sūtra of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows:
However, there is [a difference].
For in the Taittirīya, within the section on creation, the first creation heard of is that of space alone;
whereas in the Chāndogya, the first creation is that of fire alone.

Furthermore, it is not proper to assume that what has been understood as being without a companion possesses a companion merely to conform to another scriptural passage, because that would contradict the comprehension of its being without a companion. Indeed, what is not explicitly stated is postulated for the sake of establishing what is stated; it is not for the purpose of subverting it. And the state of being without a companion, which is stated, is contradicted by the assumed state of having a companion.
Furthermore, there can be no option between things that are mutually independent, like rice and barley;
for it is the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) that is optional, not the thing itself. Indeed, an option such as "it is a post" or "it is a person" does not find a basis in the actual reality of the object.
Nor can this regulation be established on the basis of a difference between cycles of creation, because as in the present cycle, so too was it in previous cycles;
for it is certainly not the case that in this cycle curd is produced from milk, while in another cycle milk is produced from curd.
Therefore, the scriptural passages concerning creation, being mutually contradictory, cannot serve as authoritative evidence for this matter; such is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa). 2.3.1.3.
A partisan of the final conclusion (siddhāntin) reveals his own position through the Sūtra: "Because [creation] in a secondary sense is impossible. (gauṇyasaṃbhavāt)

The meaning is that there is no contradiction because this scriptural statement regarding the origin of space is figurative, due to the impossibility of the origin of space both on account of its conflict with other means of valid knowledge and its conflict with many other Vedic texts.
He states the conflict with other means of valid knowledge: "For [there is] no [origin] of space... and so forth.
For the production of an effect from its inherent, non-inherent, and efficient causes is a necessary rule; in their absence, it cannot come to be, just as smoke does not arise in the absence of fire.
Therefore, space (*ākāśa*), being existent and lacking a cause, is eternal.
Furthermore, regarding those things that are produced, neither experience nor causal efficiency is perceived prior to their production, yet both are observed once they have been produced.
Just as in the case of fire and so forth,
space does not possess such a distinction between arising and non-arising;
therefore, he says that it does not arise.
"And of those things that possess origination" means that manifestation (*prakāśa*) is the illumination of objects such as jars and cloths;
"and because of the dissimilarity with earth and the other [elements]" means...

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is understood that space (*ākāśa*) is eternal because, while possessing substantiality (*dravyatva*), it lacks tangibility (*asparśavattva*), like the self (*ātman*).
Regarding the phrase "in the spaces of the forest":
even in the Veda, the plurality of the single space is merely figurative (*aupādhika*), based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). //3// 2.3.1.4.

Thus, having stated that [the term] is figurative because it contradicts other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states that it is also figurative because it contradicts another scriptural passage (*śruti*): "And on account of the word" (Sūtra 5).
This is easy to understand. 4 // 2.3.1.5.
And it may be that the word alone is to be supplied, as in the case of the word "Brahman," rather than the meaning of the word;
for that [meaning] is primary in some instances and figurative in others, depending on what is possible or impossible, and thus there is no contradiction.
He raises two objections—
namely, "How so?"—
and first resolves the initial objection:
"Ekameva" (only one) means "tāvat" (just that much). "Kulaṃ" means the household.
"Amatrāṇi" means vessels.
"Vessels" refers to jars, bowls, and so forth.
The meaning is that this restriction is relative and does not apply to all objects.
He states another argument:
"And not even by space" (naca nabhasāpi): the word "even" (api) implies admission.
The meaning is that even if [the cause] were dependent on everything, including space, there would still be no fault.
"And not prior to its origination"—
the word "of the world" is to be supplied.
He thus dispels the second objection:
And for this very reason, it is said: "by means of the knowledge of Brahman.
This is because, due to the absence of any difference in defining characteristics, space is non-different from Brahman.
Furthermore, space does not exist apart from its location or time; it is [non-different] from Brahman and from the effects of Brahman, since its essential nature is not distinct from them.

He says that just as when a few drops of water are thrown into a jar of milk, the sky [the space] becomes known once Brahman and its effects are known: "Moreover, every effect being produced... (Sūtra 5). When a partial conclusion of this kind has been reached, he says the following:
There would be a loss of the initial proposition because there is no difference from words [denoting the world].

Since the world has the nature of being an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, it is in reality non-different from Brahman; thus, when Brahman is known, knowledge of the world is logically established.
For the reality of the world is not other than Brahman.

Therefore, since space is also a modification (*vikāra*) of that [Brahman] by virtue of being its illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), it becomes known through the knowledge of that [Brahman], and not otherwise.
If, however, it were not a modification, it would be a distinct reality from it, and thus it would not become known when Brahman is known.

Furthermore, even if two distinct things lack a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and there is no difference in space or time, the knowledge of one does not entail the knowledge of the other.
For when milk is being drawn from a jar full of milk, even though drops of water are present, there is no cognition of the reality of water;

therefore, for the sake of not contradicting the accumulation of propositions and examples—that those [elements] are known when milk is known—one must, even against one's will, accept the origination of space (*ākāśa*).
Thus, when the proponent of a partial conclusion has been refuted, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) states a distinction regarding his own position:
The truth has been shown;
for this very reason,
however, that [position] is contradictory.
He states the essence of the established conclusion (siddhāntasāra):
"This is not a fault;
[it is] light—"
Regarding the statement "of creation, [the authority of] the Taittirīyaka":
between two scriptural passages, one that can be explained otherwise and one that cannot be explained otherwise, the Taittirīyaka passage, which cannot be explained otherwise, is stronger;
whereas the Chāndogya passage, which can be explained otherwise, is weaker.
Now, it was argued that fire, when understood initially as being without a companion, is contradicted by its having a companion; to this he says:

"For this scriptural statement does not have the production of fire as its primary purport. The connection with creation is what is directly stated in scripture (śrauta), whereas the distinction [of having a companion] is merely implied (ārtha).
And that [position] is sublated by another scriptural passage that contradicts it, because it is of inferior authority;
nor is its state of being without assistance [independent of Brahman] scripturally established in the same way as the connection with the creation beginning with fire.
However, [the order of creation] is obtainable through negative inference (*vyatireka*).
Nor does the contradiction of that [order] by the scriptural statement [of simultaneous creation] entail the impossibility of the scriptural account of the creation of fire;
this is what has been stated: "having the production of fire as its primary [subject]."
This might be the case:

if a single sentence cannot have multiple meanings because it is impossible for one [sentence] to possess two functions, then, alas, how is it not contradictory for a single creator to possess multiple functions? To this, he says:
"But even the Creator is one alone.
The determination [of meaning] is dependent upon the usage of the elders;
it is not observed that a word, when used without repetition, can function toward multiple meanings simultaneously through both sequential and non-sequential orders.
The meaning is that it has been observed that even a single agent possesses multiple functions through both sequential and simultaneous action.
Furthermore, he states— "Nor by us..."— to show that in this matter, the function does not belong to a single sentence, but rather to distinct sentences.
This is easy to understand. He objects: "Is it not for the purpose of prescribing tranquility?"
Whatever a word aims at is its meaning;
and this [word] does not aim at creation, but rather aims at tranquility—this is the sense. He refutes [this objection]:

The phrase "not indeed by following the priority of light" means that because order is a subordinate quality (guṇa) and a matter of secondary import (ārtha), its abandonment is improper when it contradicts the primary elements (padārtha) as heard in the scripture; such is the meaning.
By way of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita) maxim, he addresses the one who maintains that ether (viyat) is not produced:
Furthermore, regarding the *Chāndogya*:
he refutes that which was previously set forth as an alternative justification for the proposition.
As for what was stated:

because the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika) conforms to the illustration (dṛṣṭānta), and since the latter consists of the relationship between material cause and its modification (prakṛti-vikāra), the former must likewise possess that same nature.
Furthermore, this statement, "one only, without a second," is based on error— like the perception of milk in water—
or it is figurative— like saying "the boy is a lion.
To show that it is not, in fact, erroneous, he says:

"According to the principle of milk and water" means that since error and the intention to deceive are attributes of a person, they are impossible in that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya). Nor is it figurative; thus he says:
And this [statement] is restrictive;
while unity may indeed exist through figurative usage,
the two terms of restriction are not tenable.
For worldly people do not say, "Having metaphorically attributed the nature of a lion to a boy, there is not even the slightest bit of a boy other than the lion.
Therefore, the Śruti intends the absolute identity of the world with Brahman, and not a merely figurative one.
For in repetition, the meaning increases; it does not diminish, much less become figurative—this is the sense.
"And not with respect to its own effect.

The meaning is that the word *sarva* (all), by its very nature denoting "without remainder," cannot be restricted to a partial scope when there is no contradiction with another scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Having restated the objection regarding the contradiction with other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) concerning the origination of space (*ākāśa*), [the author] states that since that other means of knowledge is itself non-authoritative due to its contradiction with yet another means of knowledge, it lacks the power to establish that [the scriptural statement] is merely figurative (*gauṇa*).
"But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world.
This is the formal argument: ether, space, time, mind, and atoms are modifications, because, while being distinct from the Self, they are divided.
"As in the case of a jar, a bowl, a water-pot, and so forth"—
this means that if every effect were devoid of a self (nirātmaka),
it would follow that it would be without a material cause (nirupādāna).
Furthermore, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) has been refuted by the Scripture itself through the presentation of the passage, "How could being arise from non-being?
And the refutation of that view has already been established below.
Precisely because it is the Self, the inner Self (*pratyagātman*)—[is not subject to origination].
The doubt regarding the impossibility of [the Self] being the material cause is thus resolved.
This is what is meant: if the effect has a material cause, then since the Self alone is taught by scripture as that material cause, it is impossible to postulate any other material cause.
This might be so.
Let it be that the Self is the material cause of this world; however, one might argue that there may exist another material cause for that [Self], even if it is not heard of. To this, he says:
"For the Self is not adventitious, nor is it something to be produced by any other material cause."
Why?
Because it is self-established (*svayaṃsiddha*).
Its existence or its manifestation is established by itself.
In this regard, he states the non-accidental nature of the perfection (siddhi) which consists of luminosity: "For the Self does not [belong] to the Self.
This has been established as follows: because it is never the locus of doubt, error, or mediacy, the Self is never dependent on another for its manifestation.
But the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth have their manifestation dependent upon Him.
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
And for such a Being, no other cause is possible.

The meaning is that even negation, which derives its very existence from that [subject], cannot arise as something contradictory to it. He states the non-accidental nature of existence [of the self] as follows: "In this way, I myself know now.

Even though the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the acts of knowing (*pramā*) exist in the present, past, or future, the knower (*pramātṛ*)—because he is experienced as always being present and his essential nature never departs—is not of accidental existence.

For adventitiousness is pervaded by limitation to the three periods of time; since that [adventitiousness] is excluded from the knower who exists eternally in the present, adventitiousness—taking its own pervader with it—is thereby excluded.
Otherwise, it would follow that even that which undergoes change must be known.
By means of the base and the suffix, the transformation of both knowledge and the object of knowledge has been shown.
Now, one might object: "Let there be no such transformation for the cognizer while he is alive, but it will certainly occur when he is dead"; to this, he says:
"Likewise even in the case of becoming ashes."
Indeed, that which possesses an existent nature established by experience must have its indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva) understood from some other subverting evidence (bādhaka).

And for things such as jars, the subverting evidence consists in their deviation from their own nature as presented by valid cognition (pramāṇa). However, for that whose nature is not [thus] [subverted], it is not logical to imagine such indeterminability.

Because there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the hypothesis that the existent nature (*satsvabhāva*), which is established by uncontradicted experience, is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*);
this is what was stated [in the verse]:
"it cannot be conceived."

Having thus refuted the inference for the non-origination of space by means of this series of counter-inferences, he further refutes it on the grounds of its being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with regard to what was stated as "of the same genus": nor does a single material cause (*upādāna*) initiate a single effect (*upādeya*).

For where milk transforms into the state of curd, one should not admit that multiple constituent parts (*avayava*) act as the material cause (*upādāna*); rather, it is the single, already-appropriated milk itself that transforms into the state of the effect, the curd—just as, for those who maintain that atoms are partless, a milk-atom transforms into the state of a curd-atom. The remainder [of the commentary] has its meaning self-evident. //7// 2.3.2.8.
By this, Mātariśvan (the wind) is explained.
If, upon repetition, there is an increase in the meaning and not a decrease—let alone any figurative application—then, alas! it would follow that the wind is eternal.
Having stated the immortality of both by saying, "The wind and the intermediate space—this is the immortal," he speaks again specifically regarding the wind:
"This deity, namely the wind, is never-setting.
Therefore, due to this repetition, it follows that the immortality of the wind is not merely relative, but rather innate.
This has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
"Because of the denial of setting and because of the hearing of [attributes] such as immortality. By the word "and" (ca), which has the sense of conjunction, repetition is indicated.
This being the case, it is said in response: because of the proposition that through one cognition all cognitions [are known],
because the meaning of the proposition is primary,
and because other statements serve to support that [proposition].
Furthermore, since many of those [scriptural passages] that establish non-duality also establish the sequence of the origin of Mātariśvan,
these Śrutis are stronger due to their preeminence and abundance; therefore,
in accordance with them, the prohibitions against immortality and dissolution must be interpreted as being merely relative.
Having regard for many scriptural passages, both of these two scriptural statements are declared to be mere words. [Sūtra 2.3.3.9:
"But the origination of Being is impossible, because it is not logically tenable.

[Objection: But surely, since there is a scriptural statement regarding the Self as Being that it has no cause—namely, "And there is no progenitor of this"—how can there even be a suspicion of its origination?

Nor is it logical to claim that the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is established without seeing the [opposing] statement, for it would be untenable for one who has studied the Vedas to have no opportunity to engage in the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*); therefore, he says:
"Of space and air... (*viyatpavanayoḥ*).

Just as the scriptural declarations regarding the immortality and non-setting of the ether (*viyat*) and the wind (*pavana*) are interpreted as being relative due to their contradiction with other scriptural passages, so too the scriptural declaration that the Self has no cause must be explained as being relative, because it contradicts the scriptural statement of the analogy of sparks from a fire and because it contradicts other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor does the fact that the Self possesses a cause lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—which would bring a "stink of iron" [i.e., logical fallacy]—because the succession of cause and effect is beginningless; this is the intended meaning.
Likewise, regarding the phrase "from modifications," a contradiction with other means of valid cognition has been shown.
This being the position reached, it is said: the origination of the state of the One Being is impossible.
Why?
Because it is untenable.
For Brahman is heard in scripture to have the single nature of existence; therefore, in the absence of a subverting factor, that [nature] must not be altered.

This has already been stated: although modifications (vikāras) are experienced through the quality of goodness (sattva), they are seen to perish after the lapse of a certain period of time; thus, because they are delimited by the three periods of time, they are indeterminable (anirvacanīya).
But the Self (ātman) is not like that, for it is well-known—both from scripture and from experience—to have the nature of existing solely in the present. Therefore, he says this:
"Brahman is indeed pure Being" (sanmātraṃ hi brahma).
This is what is meant: that which deviates from its own nature is inexpressible, and it is logical that it should have something expressible as its material cause (*upādāna*), but not the reverse.
Just as a snake has a rope as its material cause, but a rope does not have a snake as its material cause.

Furthermore, between those two which do not deviate from their own nature and are thus indefinable, there can be no relationship of the effect and the material cause, as in the case of a rope and mother-of-pearl.
Nor is there an error without a substratum; thus he says:
Nor [is it] from what is non-existent;
nor is there an infinite regress of baseless errors, as he states: "because, if a fundamental material cause (mūlaprakṛti) were not accepted, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress."

For the ultimately real relationship of cause and effect is beginningless; thus, it is not vitiated by an infinite regress. Furthermore, it has been established in the section refuting the Madhyamaka position that the superimposition of transformation does not have a superimposed material cause;
this should not be forgotten here.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is not appropriate to justify an error (*vibhrama*) that lacks a real substratum (*asad-adhiṣṭhāna*) on the grounds of its beginninglessness.
The scriptural mention of sparks from fire must be understood as referring to the forms of the *aupādika* (derived) [elements].
The remainder of the text has its meaning not obscured.

However, those who have described this section as concerning the origin of qualities (*guṇa*), space (*diś*), and time (*kāla*) would have to explain the phrase "because it is impossible for that which exists" with great difficulty.
Furthermore, its connection [to the chapter] must be stated in the context of establishing non-contradiction;
for there is no comprehension of any scriptural passage teaching the production of space, time, and so forth, as there is for water and the other elements.
Let that matter rest for now. //9// 2.3.4.10.
Fire [arises] from that; for thus he has said.

Although, according to the rule "the case-ending expressing the *kāraka* is stronger than the case-ending expressing the *upapada*," the ablative in "from air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*) ought not to be taken as referring to immediate succession, nevertheless, because it would otherwise contradict many scriptural passages, it is more appropriate here to follow the weaker *upapada* case-ending itself.

Consequently, this scriptural statement, "From air [comes] fire," is intent upon showing immediate succession. And when direct birth from Brahman is possible, it is not proper to resort to an indirect birth through being a descendant of that lineage, as in the case of the sacrificial animal and the post for the Vājapeya sacrifice; such is the prima facie position.

This being the case, it is replied: It is appropriate that in the case of the animal sacrifice and the Vājapeya—which possess distinct auxiliary and principal elements—there should be recourse to an indirect succession when there is no direct connection with the Vājapeya, as this involves some difficulty.

Here, however, since even air, which is a modification of Brahman, is in reality non-different from Brahman, it is possible for Brahman to be the material cause directly even when air is the material cause; therefore, the scriptural texts, which can be interpreted in both ways, follow the superior strength of the case-terminations (kāraka-vibhakti).
The final conclusion (rāddhānta) is that it is logical that they are restricted by the "analogy of those who eat from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojinyāya*).
Regarding the phrase "even though produced through a succession," this refers to the conceptualization of difference; for he speaks of ultimate non-difference:
"having attained the state of air."
"Brahman" is [the subject].
As for the phrase "as its boiled [milk]," this is an illustration based on a similarity of mere succession and not on a similarity in every respect; thus everything is clarified. 10 // 2.3.5.
Water.
This has been explained by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which requires no further verbal explanation. 2.3.6.12.
*Pṛthivyadhikārarūpaśabdāntarebhyaḥ* (On account of the context of earth, the form, and other words).

This word "food" (*anna*)—both by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and by common usage (*prasiddhi*)—applies to rice, barley, and the like, as well as to their derivatives such as boiled rice (*odana*).

Moreover, direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), and that [statement] is further reinforced by the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) "wherever it rains. Therefore, what is intended here is that rice, barley, and so forth—which are fit for consumption—arise from water;
for even blackness is possible in some edible things.
For even the earth is not exclusively black,
since it is observed to have red and other colors as well;
consequently, there would be a contradiction with another scriptural passage, such as "from water comes earth, from earth come plants," and so forth— this is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position.

When there is a conflict between two scriptural passages (śruti), since an option (vikalpa) regarding the actual entity is untenable, one must be interpreted in conformity with the other. In this regard, when the doubt arises as to whether the word "earth" in the passage "from water, earth [was produced]" should be led to refer to food, or whether the word "food" in "it created food" should be led to refer to earth— the answer is that, in accordance with the context of the great elements (mahābhūta) and because of the common black color [of both], as well as the statement "that which was the froth of the waters," [the latter is to be understood].

Furthermore, because of the conformity with scripture (*śruti*) and because the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) can be explained otherwise, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that the word "food" (*anna*) refers to the earth, which is the cause of food.
"But from the meditation on that alone [arises the world], on account of its characteristic mark.
The absence of contradiction regarding the order of the elements in the process of creation has already been stated.

Now, a doubt arises: do the deities presiding over the elements, such as space (*ākāśa*) and the rest, proceed independently toward the successive production of the elements, since there is no evidence for their dependence on the Supreme Lord? Furthermore, since both the introductory context (*prastāva*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) can be consistently explained through the lineage of causes ultimately reaching Brahman, the root cause, it follows that space and the others are the independent causes of air (*vāyu*) and so forth; thus, the doctrine that the world has Brahman as its source (*brahmayonitva*) would be contradicted. This is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
This being the case, it is replied:
statements such as "from ether, air" describe ether and the others merely as material causes (upādāna), but not as independent presiding agents (adhiṣṭhātṛ).

Nor is it an absolute rule that sentient beings possess independence regarding their own effects, for they are frequently observed to be dependent on others, like servants, apprentices, and so forth. Therefore, to ensure the consistency of the discussion concerning the inferential mark (liṅga), it is logical that it is that very Lord who, abiding as the material cause in various forms such as space and so on, presides over himself as the instrumental cause and creates each respective modification,
such as the egg and the rest.
Otherwise, the mention of the *liṅga* and the introduction would be rendered difficult;
[the reason is] "by virtue of the penetration (*āveśa*) of the Supreme Lord.
That is to say, the Supreme Lord himself, having entered [the body] in the form of the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), is the beholder (*īkṣitṛ*).

Therefore, it is established that for the entire range of effects, the Supreme Lord alone is the presiding cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and not [the Lord] having attained the state of ether and so forth; whereas [the Lord] having attained the state of ether and so forth is the material cause (*upādāna*). 2.3.8.14. "But the sequence is justified by the reverse order from this."
The sequence for the arising of the great elements is indeed heard in scripture, but not for their dissolution, since only dissolution in general is mentioned.
Since a specific order is possible there, an absence of order is not tenable;
for that [absence of order] would be devoid of any established regulation.

Furthermore, when there is an established order, a lack of order is not tenable. In this regard, regarding the question of which sequence to rely upon— the observed sequence of the dissolution of jars and other objects,
or the scriptural sequence of origination— within this dilemma, the scriptural [sequence] is more worthy of preference than another scriptural one, due to their being of the same kind.
This is because it is due to the proximity of that very [intellect].
It is not perceived, because of its belonging to a contradictory class.

Therefore, the conclusion reached is that the order of dissolution is regulated by the very order of origination mentioned in scripture; however, it is said in response: indeed, the order of origination would serve as the regulator only if there were a requirement for an order of dissolution.
However, there is no dependence on a sequence for dissolution,
because the sequence of dissolution according to scripture is sublated by the distinctions of sequence brought forward by perception and inference;
for if that [sequence] were to exist, it would follow that even when the material cause has ceased, the effect still exists.
But this is not the case;
therefore,
because it is constrained by the observed sequence that is contrary to it, there is no expectancy at all for another sequence, as that would be unfit to be a condition.
This very point was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "And it is possible.
The author of the Bhāṣya also says:
"Nor is this [liberation] desired through dissolution into that which is unfit."
Therefore, the sequence is the reverse of the order of origination; thus has the Smṛti been stated as being rooted in this principle. 2.3.9.15.
"If it be argued that the intermediate consciousness and mind [arise] in sequence because of their indicative marks, we say no, because there is no distinction.

Having thus investigated the origination and dissolution of the elements as they pertain to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he now investigates the sequence of the intellect, the sense organs, and the mind.
And here, according to the etymology "that by which one discerns" (*vijānāti*), the word *vijñāna* denotes both the sense organs and the intellect (*buddhi*).
In that context, when considering their sequential order, because they are mentioned between the self and the elements, the sequence is determined by that very textual reading.
Therefore, there would be the undesirable consequence of violating the previously established order of origination.
Since it is understood that the organs arise from the Self and the elements arise from the organs, it follows that "from the Self [comes] space.

Furthermore, since the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term *annamaya* does not signify a modification—just as in the case of *ānandamaya*—this being the position reached, it is stated in reply: first of all, because the mind and so forth are distinct [from the Self].

Since there is scriptural evidence such as "the mind consists of food" (*annamayaṃ manaḥ*) which depends on a specific cause, it is appropriate that the suffix *mayaṭ* here has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), in order to state the required meaning;
otherwise, something unintended would have been stated.
And even that [unintended meaning] is not tenable.

For just as it is impossible for the mind to consist of food in the sense that "sacrifice consists of food," so too it is logical that the mind and other organs, having manifested their modifications, arise from beyond the primary elements (bhūtas). Having provisionally accepted this position for the sake of argument, he says:
Now, as for the claim that they are non-material (*abhautika*):
let it be that the instruments (*karaṇa*) arise from the self alone;
however, it does not follow from this that the self must not arise from the material elements (*bhūta*).
And thus, there is no consequence of violating the stated sequence; it is distinguished (*viśiṣyate*), that is, it is divided (*bhidyate*), meaning it is partitioned (*bhajyate*). //15// 2.3.10.16.
But that designation [of the Self] based on the moving and the non-moving must be figurative, because it exists only when that [body] exists.
To begin with, names such as "Devadatta" belong to the individual soul (jīvātman) and not to the body,
because it would be illogical to perform funeral rites (śrāddha) and so forth for the body under that name.
The prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position belongs to one who considers the designation "Devadatta has been born" to be primary when Devadatta has died.

However, since a primary sense would result in an inconsistency with the scriptures—given that the connection with fruits such as heaven in the hereafter, as taught in the scriptures, would be impossible—the worldly designation must be explained as figurative (bhākta).
And this figurative usage [is based on] the production and destruction of the body, and consequently, its conjunction [with the self].

Furthermore, rites such as the *jātakarman* are for the purpose of purifying the sins of the living being arising from the seed and the womb, but not for the purpose of destroying the sin produced by the birth of the soul itself.
For this very reason, they record in tradition: "In this way, the impurity arising from the seed and the womb is pacified."

Therefore, it is established that the birth and death of the individual soul (jīva) do not occur through the birth and destruction of the body. This discussion was conducted by assuming that worldly designations are rooted in non-delusion; however, it was stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* that these [designations] are actually rooted in delusion. //16// 2.3.11.17.

Lest it be thought that while the gross origination and destruction [of the body] do not belong to this [self], there will nevertheless be origination and destruction of the *jīva* at the beginning of a great creation and at its end— just as in the case of ether and other elements— this [sūtra] is commenced to remove that further doubt:
"The self is not [produced], because of the scriptural statement of its eternity, and because of those [scriptures]."
He states the seed of doubt rooted in deliberation:
"Because of the conflict of scriptural texts.
He demonstrates that very conflict:
"In some scriptural passages" refers to the presentation of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "In that regard, it follows [that the soul is not eternal]."

First of all, the individual souls (*jīva*) are distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) due to their association with contradictory attributes, such as being "afflicted by sin" versus being "free from sin.
If they are not modifications (*vikāra*) [of Brahman], then their status as a different reality would contradict a great many scriptures on non-duality (*advaita*),
as well as the declaration that "by the knowledge of Brahman, everything is known."
Therefore, the status of being a modification (vikāratva) is authorized by the Śruti.
Furthermore, another means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) is stated here: "Because they are distinct, like space," and so forth.
Moreover, the Śruti passage, "As from a fire tiny sparks fly out," directly shows that individual souls (jīvas) are modifications of Brahman.

And by the words, "As from a well-kindled fire," it directly shows both the origin of the individual souls (jīvas) from Brahman and their dissolution therein. Now, one might object: "It is understood that the origin and dissolution of entities (bhāvas) proceed from the Imperishable (akṣara), but not of the individual souls. To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "of the individual selves" (jīvātmanām):
this might be asked—
just as the origin of ether and the other elements is mentioned in the scriptural accounts of creation, why is the origin of the individual selves not likewise recorded?
Therefore, since that which is fit for being recorded in scripture is not so recorded, we understand its non-existence; to this he says:
"And there is no non-hearing [of it] anywhere.

For if this were the case, one would not be able to incorporate the subsidiary parts belonging to other recensions into a ritual action that is recorded in a particular recension along with only a few of its own subsidiary parts.

Therefore, because it contradicts many scriptural passages, the scripture concerning "entering" must be explained as referring to the production of the individual self through a state of modification.

Thus, the position being reached is that individual selves are produced like space; to this it is replied: this would indeed be so if the individual selves were different from Brahman, but that is not the case.

Having created that, He entered into it—by this living self—and so forth; for since the scripture teaches non-distinction, and since difference is merely adventitious due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as in the case of the ether within a jar or a pot, the association of contradictory attributes is thus intelligible. Furthermore, there are numerous scriptural passages regarding the mind-made self and other such adjuncts, as well as many scriptures concerning its eternity, birthlessness, and so on. Moreover, non-distinction is established in various ways through questions and answers, such as "of the conditioned [self] by the dissolution of the adjuncts."

And since it has been stated by the Śruti itself that "The one God is hidden in all beings," it is established that the individual selves (jīvātman) are eternal, not modifications [of Brahman], and there is no contradiction with the proposition of non-duality (advaita).
Furthermore, the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa has already been explained above, so it is not explained here. //17// 2.3.12.18.
For this very reason, [the self] is the knower.
For the meaning of "knowing" is pervaded by an object; in the absence of that [object], it does not exist, just as smoke does not exist in the absence of fire.
Furthermore, in states such as deep sleep, because the object of knowledge is absent, there is an absence of knowledge, which is pervaded by that [object].
And thus, consciousness is not the inherent nature of the self, since consciousness is absent even when the self persists.

Therefore, because the presence and absence of knowledge follow the presence and absence of the sense organs and other factors, this consciousness—which is produced by the contact of the sense organs and so forth—is an adventitious property of the self and not innate.
For this very reason, the sense organs and other factors possess purposefulness.
Otherwise, the sense organs would be rendered purposeless;
furthermore, the scriptural passages concerning eternal consciousness must be explained as referring to potentiality.
For the individual selves possess an innate power to produce cognition.
But it is not the case that this [Self] fails to produce knowledge even when there is contact with the sense organs and so forth, as is the case with the ether (*vyoman*).

Therefore, when the position has been reached that the individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed insentient (*jaḍa*), it is replied: that which is adventitious knowledge and is insentient by nature is sometimes indirect (*parokṣa*), sometimes doubtful (*saṃdigdha*), and sometimes erroneous (*viparyasta*), just like a jar or similar objects.
And it is not so by means of the self;
for thus, even one who infers is not non-perceptual,
and even one who remembers is experiential.
Even while doubting, it is free from doubt; even while erring, it is unerring—the Self of all.
And such is its very nature.
Nor is there an absence of consciousness, which is of that very nature,
because it is eternal. Therefore, the mental modifications (vṛttis), which are of the nature of activity, cease in states such as deep sleep when there is an absence of karma.

Thus, it is established that consciousness is the very nature of the Self. Consequently, the scriptural texts proclaiming eternal consciousness need not be explained through any forced or strained interpretation. Furthermore, the purposefulness of the sense organs is realized in the production of modifications directed toward objects such as fragrance; thus, everything is clear. //18// 2.3.13.19.
Regarding "the departing, the going, and the returning":

although the individual soul (jīva) is in essence the unmodified Supreme Self and thus possesses no atomic dimension, this section is established through objection and resolution for the sake of reconciling the scriptural texts concerning departing, going, and returning with the direct scriptural hearing of its atomic dimension. Thus he says:
"Now, if it be so" (nanu ceti): he takes up the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)—"In that regard, first of all, it is established... (tatra prāptaṃ tāvad iti).
For the production of disjunction and conjunction is indeed the result of departing [from the body] and so forth;

however, these two do not exist for that which is omnipresent, for it is impossible for them to occur in something that is either eternally present everywhere or identical with the self of all. //19// 2.3.13.20.
And by its own self, [the soul is the agent] of the two subsequent actions.
For "departure" (utkramaṇa) is firmly established as occurring at death;
and that is possible even for one who does not move, provided he remains there, through the cessation of his ownership of the body—but this is not the case for going and returning.

Since it is impossible for [the soul] to pervade [the body] when the two [states of] being established in movement—wherein the action resides in the agent—are present, the intermediate dimension of the body is its largeness (*mahattva*).
And that has been refuted in the *Arhatparīkṣā*.
Furthermore, going and coming are not possible for one who is not of supreme largeness; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), atomicity (*aṇutva*) is established.

Since the soul's localized nature is established by its going and coming, it is proven that death is simply the soul’s departure from the body, rather than merely the cessation of its ownership over it while remaining therein; thus he says:
"And since going and coming are real... For this reason as well, he states that the soul’s death is indeed its departure from the body:
Regarding the phrase "of the regions of the body":
therefore, the departure (utkrānti), which depends upon going and coming, also has a point of departure (apādāna) and thus serves as a proof for its atomicity; this is the meaning.
It is not only because of the scriptural mention of a point of departure.
He states that the scriptural passage concerning the soul's departure from other parts of the body is also to be understood in this very same way:
"He [takes] these particles of light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6).
"If it be argued that the soul is not atomic because of scriptural statements to that effect, we say no, because of the context of the other. (Sūtra 2.3.13)

Since the atomicity of individual souls (jīvas) has been established by scriptural texts concerning departure from the body and so forth, their distinction from the all-pervading Supreme Self (paramātman) follows from their being its modifications.
Thus, the meaning is that there is no contradiction, as the scriptural texts regarding "greatness," "non-duality," and so on, refer to the Supreme Self and not to the individual soul.

One might object: "If the individual souls are atomic, then how is it that the embodied self is referred to in the passage, 'This one consisting of consciousness among the highest,' as being connected with greatness? To this, he raises the objection:

Regarding the word "nanu": he provides the answer— by the perspective of the scripture (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*), that is, from the ultimate standpoint (*pāramārthikadṛṣṭyā*), the designation is like that of Vāmadeva.

For just as the individual soul Vāmadeva, while still in the womb, realized his identity with Brahman through the vision of ultimate reality, so too, because modifications are in reality non-different from their material cause (prakṛti), they are designated by the measure of that [cause]. This is the meaning. 2.3.13.22.
"And on account of its own word and of measurement."
He analyzes the term "its own word" (svaśabda):
"directly indeed.
He analyzes "measurement" (unmāna):

"Likewise, there is also 'measurement by subtraction' (unmāna). Having subtracted a measurement, it is "measurement by subtraction"; that is, a hundredth part subtracted from the tip of a hair, and from that hundredth part, another hundredth part is subtracted—this is what is meant by "measurement by subtraction.
Measurement subtracted from the tip of an awl is "merely the size of the tip of an awl. //22// 2.3.13.23.
He raises an objection in order to introduce another sūtra: "But [if it were] devoid of qualities...
The meaning is that since the self is atomic and not pervasive of the body, there would be no perception of coolness extending over all limbs.
"There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood.

For the individual soul (jīva) is conjoined with the skin, and the skin pervades the entire body; thus, the connection of the self, through its pervasion of the skin, is capable of perceiving coolness throughout the whole body—this is the meaning.

"If it be argued that there is a distinction due to the specific location [of the soul], we say no, because it is admitted [that the soul resides] in the heart. For [the scripture] states that [the soul] is indeed in the heart.
The meaning of the objection is this: having directly perceived the smallness of a drop of sandalwood paste, a logical inference [of smallness] is appropriate;

however, for one whose minuteness is doubtful yet whose effects are observed throughout the entire body, this inference finds no room, as it would require setting aside the soul's natural pervasiveness.
Nor can the soul's minuteness be inferred by the example of the drop of yellow sandalwood paste.
He states that [the argument] is inconclusive because a counter-example is possible, saying:
"And there is no inference here.
He then dispels this doubt:
To this it is replied: "It is said here.

Although the atomicity of the Self has been established by the previously cited scriptural texts, nevertheless, another scriptural passage is introduced to demonstrate its all-pervasiveness. 2.3.13.25.
"Or [the soul is all-pervading] because of its quality, as in the world."

To those, however, who think that there is a disparity because the pervasion of the body by a drop of sandalwood paste is possible through the movement of its constituent atoms due to its having parts, whereas the movement of atoms is not possible for the partless self, this is said in reply: "Or [it is] on account of its quality, as in the world. This is now analyzed: The text continues with the analysis of this point. The intended meaning is that just as the fragrance of sandalwood, though located in one place, pervades the entire body through its quality (the scent), so too the self, though partless, can pervade the body through its quality (consciousness). Thus, there is no actual disparity between the two cases. The phrase "as in the world" (lokavat) refers to common worldly experience where such phenomena are observed. This establishes that the analogy holds despite the difference in the nature of the substances involved.

Regarding the term *caitanya* (consciousness): although the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic, its quality, consciousness, pervades the entire body. Just as the light of a lamp, though the lamp itself is small, pervades the interior of the entire house. //25// 2.3.13.26.
Having refuted this as well by way of an objection, he states another illustration:
"The distinction is like that of fragrance;
for even though it is not being consumed, it [remains]."
He raises the objection that destruction might be imperceptible due to its extreme subtlety with the words "this might be so.
The phrase "because of the smallness of the separated parts" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
It should also be understood that this is due to the entry of other substantial atoms.
Furthermore, although separation exists through both disjunction and entry, it is not perceived because of its subtlety. He refutes [this objection]:
No. Why?
Because it is beyond the reach of the senses.

Because atoms are extremely subtle, odor, like the color and other qualities residing within them, would not be perceived; or, if it were perceived, it would be perceived as subtle and not as gross—this is the meaning. The rest has a self-evident sense. //26// 2.3.13.13.27. // 27 // 2.3.13.28.
Because of the separate instruction [of the two]. The commentary on this has been explained by the word itself (*nigada-vyākhyāta*). 2.3.13.29.
But that designation [of the self] is due to its having those qualities as its essence, as in the case of the "intelligent one" (*prājña*).
"Even in the case of piercing with a thorn":
the conjunction of the large and the small obstructs the small, not the large;
for the conjunctions of jars, water-pots, and the like never pervade the ether, but rather [obstruct] only the small jars, water-pots, and so forth.
Otherwise, since space exists everywhere, jars, water-pots, and so forth would be perceived everywhere; it would follow that those objects too would have the same dimensions as space.
Furthermore, for the atomic soul (*jīva*), experience extending throughout the entire body would not be possible.

Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is atomic, nevertheless, because it is connected with the skin and the skin pervades the entire body, the skin situated even in one part is as good as situated over the whole; thus, the soul (*jīva*), which pervades the body, is able to experience the coldness extending over all limbs through the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*) when in the Ganges.

The soul (*jīva*), being atomic (*aṇu*), would experience [sensation] only in that specific part of the body where it resides, and not throughout the entire body, because it does not pervade the whole body.
Thus, there is a discrepancy: whereas the sensation of a thorn's prick is localized, its perception is not experienced throughout the entire body.
"For this indeed is their quality-ness" means that this very thing is the quality-ness of qualities, namely, their having a location in a substance.

For this very reason, although the extremely dense cold touch residing in a substance composed of closely packed water-particles is experienced during winter, its unmanifest color is not perceived, just as [in the case of fire].

Likewise, when the extremely dense fragrance of musk and other substances—whose subtle particles are dispersed by the wind—is being experienced, their color and touch are not perceived. For what reason?
Because those two [color and touch] are unmanifest (*anudbhūta*), whereas the fragrance is manifest (*udbhūta*).
Nor does this entail the dissolution of the substance.
Because it is filled with parts consisting of a different substance;
for this very reason, its foul odor is perceived due to the influence of the passage of time.
Furthermore, that which is called consciousness is not a quality of the soul, as qualities belong to substances.
However, there is the state of being a form;
and since the nature [of a thing] is all-pervasive, the entity itself cannot be non-pervasive, for that would entail a loss of its true essence. Thus he says:
And if it is argued that "consciousness" [is the nature of the soul]—
thus, when the soul's identity with the Supreme Self is established by Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa as being non-modifiable,
and likewise its supreme greatness is established by Śruti and other authorities;

He states that those scriptural passages which speak of the soul's atomicity (*aṇutva*) are to be explained in accordance with them as referring to the fact that the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*) constitute its essence;
thus he says: "Because its essence consists of those qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*).
He explains this [sūtra]:
Regarding the phrase "of that cognition":
because it is presented by the cognition associated with the self (ātman), there is a subsequent reflective reference (parāmarśa) to it.
For the true nature (tattva) of the self—which is pure, awakened, and liberated—is not experienced by those in the cycle of transmigration (saṃsārin).
Moreover, that which is associated with false knowledge, aversion, and so forth, is precisely what falls within the range of one's own individual experience.

And since it is impossible for the individual self (*jīvātman*), whose nature is Brahman and who is immutable and eternal, to be spontaneously attached to desire and aversion, these qualities—which actually belong to the intellect (*buddhi*)—are superimposed upon it through the superimposition of non-difference; thus, their status as its attributes is a mere superimposition.
This has been established in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* by the analogy of the reflection of the moon, where the shaking of the water leads to the superimposition of shaking upon the lunar disc itself.

And thus, since its status as a *jīva* (individual soul) is produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, it also receives the designation of being "atomic" (*aṇu*) due to the atomicity of the intellect—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—just as the ether (*nabhas*), when confined within a water-pot (*karaka*), is said to have the dimensions of that pot. Consequently, the departure (*utkrānti*) and other such states of the soul are logically established. The rest has been explained by the very words [of the text].

[If it were argued that] at the time of departure [from the body], there is non-existence or a lack of transmigratory state, then there would follow the consequence of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛta-vipraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). [Reply: But there is no fault because [the self] persists as long as the existence of the soul; for that is seen [in scripture]. (2.3.13) 30. *yāvadātmabhāvitvāt tu na doṣas taddarśanāt*.
The meaning is: "as long as it has the nature of being transmigratory.
"Being common" means being common with the intellect (*buddhi*), because its essence consists of the qualities of that [intellect].
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "through false knowledge":
the meaning is that not only is the transmigrating nature of the self established through scripture, but also through logical reasoning.
"Of the color of the sun" means having the nature of light;
[it is said] "of darkness."
The meaning is "of ignorance.

The construction is: "Having known—that is, having directly realized—that very [Self], one transcends death, which is ignorance. (2.3.13) 31. The proponent reveals the seed of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*):
"Now, [as for the objection] regarding deep sleep and cosmic dissolution:
[the soul is] with the existent Supreme Self.
Here, the removal of the seed of residual karma (*anuśaya*) is addressed as follows:
"But because the existent [Self] is manifested like intelligence and so forth.
The commentary on this is explained by its very recitation. 2.3.13.32.
"Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either eternal perception or non-perception, or else the necessity of one or the other."
It might be argued as follows:

Even though the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) exists, since it is eternally present, why do constant perception and non-perception not result? Or, [it may be argued that] because the ripening of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa-vipāka*) is occasional, this consequence does not apply due to the presence or absence of the internal organ's capacity being obstructed or unobstructed.

Whether those two [the merit and demerit] reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or in the self (*ātman*), or in the senses (*indriya*), what is the use of this superfluous internal organ? Thus he raises an objection:
"Or else, in one or the other of these, namely the self... and so forth.
The phrase "or rather" sets aside the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The proponent of the conclusion says:
"Nor [is it the case] of the Self..."
Attention is indeed either the desire to understand or the desire to hear;
and these two are not attributes of the Self, because the Self is changeless.
Nor are they the sense-faculties, because we observe blind people and others even when individual sense-faculties are absent;
furthermore, those [faculties] being experienced as internal cannot possibly exist externally.
Therefore, there exists some internal principle distinct from that,
and these [faculties] have that as their internal organ (*antahkarana*).
This is what has been stated:
"Of whom [it is] the attention...
Here, he shows the scriptural authority for this very point: "And thus... //32// 2.3.14.33.

"The soul is an agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. Now, one might object: "Since the soul's status as both agent and enjoyer has already been established by the sūtra *tadguṇasāratvāt* (II.3.29), its further exposition here is redundant. To this he replies: "By way of the section on *tadguṇasāratva*"—this is an elaboration of that very point for the purpose of refuting the view that the soul is merely an enjoyer and not an agent.
"The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its defining characteristic," so said the venerable Jaimini.
"To the performer" means to the one who carries out [the action],
that is to say, to the agent.
The fruit of the scripture consists of heaven and so forth. Why?
Because the scripture, that is, the injunction, is characterized by being the means for achieving the fruit of the agent.
For an injunction (*vidhi*) is indeed the status of being a means sought by an agent.

If the intellect (*buddhi*) is the agent and the self (*ātman*) is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), then that which is the means sought by the enjoyer does not possess agency, and that which possesses agency does not have [the status of] a means sought [by the enjoyer]. Thus, what connection is there between one and the other? Consequently, the scripture would be purposeless, meaning it would lack a subject matter (*anarthakatva* = *avidyamānābhidheyatva*).
And thus, it would follow that [the Self] is devoid of purpose.

Just as its status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), though not substantially real, is merely conventional due to its having the qualities of the *guṇas* as its essence, so too its status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) is merely conventional and not ultimate.
Furthermore, it has been established in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* that the scripture has as its object one who is possessed of ignorance (*avidyāvat*). Thus, everything is clear. //33// 2.3.14.34.
Because of the teaching on "dwelling" (*vihāra*).
"Dwelling" means movement or action;
in that regard, independence is not possible for one who is not an agent.
For this reason also, the living being (jīva) is the agent. [Sūtra 35:
"Because of taking up.

For these vital breaths and sense organs, having taken up—that is, having appropriated—their cognition, namely the power of apprehension by means of the intellect (buddhi), there is independence in this act of taking up; such independence is not possible for one who is not an agent. [Sūtra 36: "..."

And because of the designation; if it be argued that this refers to an action, there would be a reversal of the grammatical indication. This is merely an additional argument; the logical proof is not complete. Consciousness is the agent that performs the sacrifice.
For everywhere else, the intellect (buddhi), being of the nature of an instrument, is designated precisely as an instrument and not as an agent;
here, however, it is [designated] as an agent,
which would constitute a reversal in its designation.
Therefore, the self itself is designated as consciousness;
by that [consciousness], it is the agent.
To introduce another sūtra, he raises an objection: "Here he says, 'If...'"
One who possesses wisdom and is independent would accomplish what is desired for oneself and not what is undesired;
yet the attainment of the undesired is observed for him as well.
Therefore, he is not independent, and thus he is not the agent.
The meaning is that this is because it possesses those characteristics.
The answer to this is:
"There is no restriction regarding perception."

The agent employs other factors of action, such as the instrument and so forth, but he himself is not employed by those other factors; this much alone constitutes his independence. It does not mean, however, that he does not depend on other factors in the performance of the action to be accomplished. For if such were independence, even the venerable Lord (Īśvara) would not possess it, and thus the very concept of an "agent" would be destroyed.

And thus, because this [agent] might—due to the ripening of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)—desiring a desired object and, through a confusion regarding its means, employ a means to what is undesired and thereby obtain the undesired, there is no contradiction between agency and the lack of necessity;
for [agency] has as its sole purpose the mere conceptualization of objects.
Indeed, for the Self, whose nature is eternal consciousness, the instruments such as the sense organs present their respective objects [to it].
Therefore, consciousness (caitanya) as delimited by an object is designated as "modification" (vṛtti) and as "cognition" (vijñāna);
the meaning is that in this state, it possesses independence (svātantrya). 2.3.14.38.
Because of the reversal of power (śakti-viparyayāt).
Previously, the reversal of the case-terminations denoting causes (*kāraṇa*) was stated;

now, however, it is the reversal of the causal capacities (*kāraka-śakti*) that is addressed, and thus there is no tautology. But if one were to postulate other instruments (*karaṇa*) in order to avoid this reversal, there would be a contradiction regarding the name [of the factor]. //38// 2.3.14.39.
And because of the absence of *samādhi*.
By the term "concentration" (*samādhi*), one indicates "restraint" (*saṃyama*);
for *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* are indeed to be designated by the term "restraint."
As they have said: "The triad [of hearing, reflection, and meditation] united in one is *saṃyama*.
Here, "it is to be heard" and "it is to be reflected upon" is the instruction for *dhāraṇā*;
"it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) is the instruction for *dhyāna*.
"It is to be seen" is the instruction regarding *samādhi*.
As they say: "That very meditation (*dhyāna*), when it manifests as the object alone and is, as it were, empty of its own form, is *samādhi*.
The meaning of the aphorism is this: when this agent-self (*kartṛ-ātman*) is instructed here in *samādhi*, it realizes its own state of being an agent. //39// 2.3.15.40.
And as with the carpenter in both ways;
he states the intermediate connection [between the sections] with the words:
"In this way, for now..."
He reflects: "That, moreover... He takes up the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa):...
Regarding the word "therein":
for the reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures (śāstrārthavattva) and so forth establish the agency of the Self.
And since inherent agency is possible and there is no sublation [of it], it is not logical to claim that it is merely adventitious (aupādhika), for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor does the consequence of the non-existence of liberation serve as a refutation of this [position];

for just as one whose nature is knowledge does not cease to be a knower even in the absence of an object of knowledge, so too one whose nature is agency does not cease to be an agent even in the absence of engagement in action.
Therefore, when it is argued that his agency is indeed inherent, the following is stated in reply:
For Brahman is repeatedly heard in scripture to have the nature of being eternally pure, enlightened, and free;

therefore, its state of being "enlightened" (buddhatva) is logical even in the absence of anything to be known, just as fire possesses the quality of being a burner even in the absence of anything to be burned.
This is because it is understood from its nature;
however, its agency is to be understood as resulting from its engagement in action.
And such agency is not possible for that which is eternally indifferent, immutable, eternal, and repeatedly heard [in scripture] to be so.
And since that [liberated soul] is never in contact with anything else, how could it possess that capacity? For a capacity cannot exist without an object.

Thus, if one were to admit the entry of activity into that object in order to establish that capacity, then—since there can be no destruction of its own nature for that which has such a nature—it would follow that the entity itself is destroyed.
Furthermore, there is no connection with activity for one who is liberated.
With the intention that liberation cannot be a state of supreme bliss from which all suffering has vanished because action is itself suffering, he says:
"Agency does not belong to the Self by its own nature. Not understanding this underlying intention, an objector challenges him:
[Objection: "But even when [the cause] persists... [The author] answers: "No;
because even the causal conditions..."

The power that rests upon the capable and the incapable necessarily implies its object by its very existence; thus, the sense is that the object implied by such power would always exist. He raises an objection:
[Objection: "But surely [liberation exists] because of the injunctions for the means to liberation. [The author] refutes this: "No;
because it would be dependent upon a means."
But for us, liberation is not something to be accomplished; rather, it is the very nature of Brahman, and that is eternal.
He reveals this intended meaning:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "eternally pure": an objection is raised— “In that case, the transmigrating being must be the Supreme Self itself.”
The meaning is this: if that which transmigrates were the Supreme [Self], then upon the dissolution of its ignorance and liberation, all would be liberated without distinction;
consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all saṃsāra.
If, on the other hand, it were something other than the Supreme, then it would be nothing but the aggregate of the intellect and so forth.
"In that case, liberation and saṃsāra would belong to that [intellect] alone, and not to the Self. He refutes this: "No, because they are presented by ignorance (avidyā)."
Liberation and saṃsāra do not belong to the supreme self,
because it is eternally liberated;
nor do they belong to the aggregate consisting of the intellect and so forth.
Because it is insentient;

rather, due to the differentiation of the aggregates of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self—though unitary—is as if divided, and though pure, is as if impure, through the conditioning of each respective differentiation of the aggregates of intellect and so forth. Consequently, upon the disappearance of a particular aggregate of intellect and so forth...

In that case, it is as if liberated in one place and bound in another, just as a single face appears as if manifold—long, round, dark, or fair—due to the differences in adjuncts such as a jewel or a sword; yet when any particular adjunct is removed, it is as if liberated there and as if still constrained elsewhere. Thus, the liberation of one [instance] does not entail the liberation of all.

Therefore, neither birth nor transmigratory existence belong to the Supreme Self, nor do they belong to the aggregate of the intellect and so forth; rather, the ultimate truth is that they belong to the essential nature of the Self when it is conditioned by the intellect and so forth and has attained the state of a living individual (jīva).
In this very context, the scriptures demonstrate the method of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka):
"And so it is" (tathā ca):

for this reason as well, the limiting adjuncts [are not real], since scripture shows that the appearance and disappearance of this [Self] result from the appearance and disappearance of the limiting adjuncts; thus he says:
"And so it is."
Regarding the phrase "of dream and waking":
he explains the sūtra on this very point with the words "he says this."
"Samprasāda" refers to deep sleep.
This might be argued:
"A carpenter has hands and other limbs; by employing tools such as adzes with them, he may indeed become subject to suffering."
But how can the Supreme Self, being partless, set the mind and other organs into operation? This disparity compared to the example of the carpenter is addressed by the statement:
"And the example of the carpenter. Just as the carpenter is happy while remaining indifferent with respect to his own body, [so too is the Self].
One who employs the instruments such as speech and so forth is miserable;
likewise, one who remains indifferent to the self by means of the self is happy.
However, one who employs the instruments such as the mind and so forth is miserable; it is only in this sense that there is equality for him, but not in every respect.

Just as the self (ātman) and the living being (jīva), without depending on other parts, set their own body into motion, so too do they set other instruments such as the mind (manas) into motion; since this is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), neither a mandatory injunction (niyoga) nor an objection (paryanuyoga) is applicable.
Having restated the reasons for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), he refutes them with the words: "As for what was said... and so forth.
For that which is the ultimate purpose of a scripture is indeed the true meaning of that scripture.
A scripture whose primary aim is the cultivation of the means sought by an agent does not have the essential nature of the agent as its primary subject.

Therefore, a scripture that operates within its own domain with reference to an agent established according to worldly convention is not capable of making known an inherent agency belonging to the person.

Therefore, because it would contradict such teachings as "That thou art," that [distinction] remains as something created by ignorance. He raises an objection: "But [the scripture speaks of] the intermediate state (saṃdhya-sthāna)..."

The meaning is that agency, being dependent on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), is not possible when those adjuncts are removed; therefore, it is logical that it is inherent (*svābhāvika*) [to the Self].
Furthermore, even where there is an instrument (*karaṇa*), since the agency of the isolated Self is heard of in scripture, it is logical that it is indeed inherent; thus he says:
"Likewise, even with respect to the material cause (*upādāna*)."
He refutes this as follows:
"First of all, it is not the state of transition (saṃdhyā).
The meaning is that the removal of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is unestablished, because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serves as the adjunct, persists even during the state of transition.
Furthermore, he states that "the dwelling is also like that" (*vihāro 'pi ca tatra*) because the dwelling is of the same nature as the cognition in a dream;
likewise, it is so even with respect to appropriation (*upādāna*).

Although the agentive case-ending is heard [in grammar] with reference to the agent alone, nevertheless, this agency belongs to it only when it is assisted by the object and the instrument, not to it in its pure state;
for one who cuts with the aid of an axe is not a "cutter" in isolation.
Now, if agency does not belong to the isolated entity, but only to that which is accompanied by instruments and so forth, [then...]
If that were the case, the agentive case-ending would apply even to instruments and the like;
since this is not so, he says:
"In common usage, it does not occur."

The meaning is that even in the case of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, the agentive case-ending (*kartṛvibhakti*) sometimes indeed occurs by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Furthermore, this scriptural mention of "appropriating" (*upādāna*) is intended merely to denote the cessation of the instrument's activity, not its independence; the agentive case-ending, however, is figurative (*bhākta*), because—as in the expression "the bank wishes to fall"—the cessation of an instrument's activity is observed to occur even without prior conscious intent. Thus he says:
Furthermore, regarding the statement "appropriation in this [case]":
as for that designation which was mentioned by us as being merely an incidental elaboration, it has arisen from this very point.
[The phrase] "of all causal factors indeed" refers to this.
"Rice grains soften, logs burn, and the pot [cooks]"—thus, all things possess agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to their own respective functions.
Therefore, one might ask: is it that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other factors possess only agency and not the status of instruments (*karaṇatva*)? To this, he says:
Rather, their status as instruments is dependent upon cognition (*upalabdhi*).
Now, if this is so, one might argue that the self’s agency should be natural (*svābhāvika*) with respect to that very cognition; to this he says:
"And not even with respect to that cognition is this [agency] natural."
Why does agency exist?
Because the self has the nature of eternal cognition;
for there can be no activity on the part of an entity whose nature is eternal. This is the meaning.

Thus, it has been stated that the perceiver does not possess an innate agency with respect to perception. Nor is the agency of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth superimposed upon the Self in the same way that the agency of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and other functions belonging to them might be; for he says:
"Even agency preceded by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) cannot belong to the perceiver."
Why?
Because the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is also perceived [as an object].
For that which is the object of motion in a particular action cannot itself be the agent of that same motion.
This is what is meant: if cognition were itself the act of apprehension, then its status as the apprehender would be attributed to the self;
but this is not the case.
Because it is perceived as being insentient, it is impossible for it to be the agent of perception.

And since the intellect is not the agent in the act of perception, that which was previously stated—that if the intellect were the perceiver, another instrument would have to be postulated, and thus there would be a mere disagreement over names—is no longer tenable; so he says:
And this being so, there is no need to postulate another instrument,
because the intellect lacks the capacity for perception.
Since consciousness is now without an instrument, and the intellect is the perceiver while the self is not the perceiver, he says:
Because consciousness is admitted to be the instrument [of the self].

This is the intended meaning: since consciousness, which is apprehension, is the very nature of the self and is eternal, the self has no agency therein, nor does the intellect possess the status of an instrument.
However, it is consciousness itself, when delimited by an object, that is designated as both "modification" (vṛtti) and "apprehension" (upalabdhi).

When that [consciousness] is delimited by various objects through such a modification, it is logical that the intellect and other factors function as instruments (karaṇa), while the Self, conditioned by them, possesses agency preceded by the sense of "I" (ahaṅkāra). 2.3.16.41.
But [the activity of the agent arises] from the Supreme [Lord], because of the scriptural statement to that effect.

This agency of living beings, which is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), does not require the postulation of another impeller in the form of God, as long as passion and the like—characterized by incitement—exist; for otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can God, who is devoid of hatred and partiality, be capable of impelling living beings toward good and evil actions.
By means of which [cause] the world would attain its diversity in dependence upon dharma and adharma—
that very Dharma, being independent and compassionate, would impel living beings toward dharma and not toward adharma.
Consequently, all beings impelled by it would be solely righteous and thus happy, not miserable.
It is logical that autonomous beings, impelled by passion and other afflictions, engage in action and thereby experience diversity while possessing merit and demerit.
In this way, injunctions and prohibitions become meaningful; otherwise, if souls were entirely dependent and set in motion solely by God, what would be the use of injunctions and prohibitions?
Indeed, instruction is not meaningful for one who is being driven by the forceful current of wind and water.

Therefore, since the scriptural passages such as "For He alone makes one perform good action" would otherwise conflict with all the scriptures concerning injunctions and prohibitions and contradict worldly experience, they must be interpreted as being intended merely to praise His sovereignty— this being the position reached, we reply:
those scriptural passages such as "For He alone makes one perform good action" indeed declare that in all their activities, living beings are dependent upon the Lord.
Therefore, in the absence of any obstacle, it is not appropriate to explain this as being intended for the purpose of praise.
Nor is there any need to postulate what is already established by scripture,
such that the postulation of such [an injunction] would be contradicted while passion and other motivators are present.
It is not logical to claim that if [the world] were dependent on Īśvara, there would be only merit for living beings and thus only happiness, rather than diversity;
