for even though this Īśvara is free from passion (*vītarāga*), he is neither partial through hatred or favoritism nor devoid of compassion, as he impels living beings toward merit and demerit in dependence upon the successive actions of those very beings.
Furthermore, it is not correct to say that there is no beginning to the accumulation of karma because saṃsāra is beginningless,
nor that injunctions and prohibitions are rendered useless because [the individual] is dependent on the Lord;
for the Lord does not impel living beings like a powerful wind, but rather acts by conforming to their consciousness through the medium of the presentation of passion and so forth.
Thus, for one who desires to attain the desirable and avoid the undesirable, injunctions and prohibitions become meaningful.
With this intention, it was said: "Even though agency depends on another, the individual soul (jīva) indeed acts.

Therefore, because of the contradiction with the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions, because people are of superficial vision, and because of such scriptural texts as, "For He alone causes one to perform good deeds," [the soul is not entirely independent].
"This creature is ignorant and not master of its own pleasure or pain;
impelled by God, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell."
Thus, it is established by the Smṛti that the agency of living beings is dependent upon the Lord alone, and not independent.

If the Lord himself were the one appointed to the place of injunctions and prohibitions— such that the fruit of injunctions and prohibitions were produced by the Lord independently of the merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) established by them— then injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered useless.
He says that not only would there be pointlessness, but the opposite would also result: "one who acts according to what is prescribed.
Furthermore, the previously mentioned defect—the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done—would follow.
The rest has its meaning obvious. //41// 2.3.16.42.
// 42 // 2.3.17.43. "A part [of Brahman], because of the designation of diversity, and also because otherwise the status of being a 'giver' (dāśa) and 'servant' (kitava), etc., is taught by some.
He states the intermediate connection:
Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)":
the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary is the relationship of the instigator and the instigated.
Here, because there is initially no decisive reason for preference, it is stated that there is no fixed certainty.
Having observed fallacious reasons for [the opponent's] certainty, he states "Alternatively" (*athavā*) by resorting to the position of difference:

the relationship of ruler and ruled, the relationship of seeker and sought, the relationship of knower and known, the relationship of controller and controlled, and the relationship of substratum and superstratum are not possible if there is no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Furthermore, Vedic texts such as "Brahman is the fisherman, Brahman is the gambler," which aim to establish that the fishermen are Brahman and the gamblers are Brahman, would not be tenable if there were a difference between the individual souls and Brahman.

Nor can the individual souls (jīvas) be established as parts of the Lord on the basis of these scriptural passages intended to demonstrate difference and non-difference, nor from the Vedic mantra-text which directly establishes the state of being a part, such as "All beings are one foot of Him," nor from the Smṛti passage "A part of My very self.

It is, however, logical that the Lord— through His possession of unsurpassed adjuncts (upādhis) and His connection with divine manifestations (vibhūti)— rules over even those parts of Himself whose adjuncts are inferior.
To begin with, individual souls cannot be parts of a partless Lord.
Moreover, if the souls were parts of Brahman, then the sensations experienced by them would belong to Brahman,
just as sensations occurring in the feet and other limbs belong to Devadatta.

Furthermore, for one who has attained the state of Brahman, there would follow the consequence of experiencing the sensations belonging to all living beings; thus, worldly existence (saṃsāra) itself would be preferable to liberation, for in that state one experiences only one's own sensations and does not undergo manifold suffering. But the liberated one [would] share in the sensations of all living beings; therefore, liberation, being fraught with such great misfortune, ought to be avoided through diligent effort.
Likewise, because difference and non-difference, which are mutually contradictory, cannot coexist in one place, the individual souls (jīvas) cannot possess parts.

Nor is it tenable to say that Brahman alone is real while the souls are unreal, for this would entail the absence of the established order of pleasure, pain, liberation, and saṃsāra, as well as the impossibility of injunctions and prohibitions.

Therefore, it follows that only the individual souls (*jīva*) are ultimately real, and not the one non-dual Brahman; as for the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*), they are merely figurative (*upacāra*) due to the conditions of genus, place, time, and so forth. To this, it is replied: means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and especially verbal testimony (*śabda*), function to make known objects not previously apprehended.
In that regard, since difference (*bheda*) is already established by worldly experience, it is not what needs to be propounded by the word.

Non-duality, however, because it has not been previously apprehended, deserves to be established by way of restating distinctions that have already been apprehended. Furthermore, the purport of a statement lies precisely where it begins, is referred to in the middle, and is concluded at the end. And since the Upaniṣads begin with non-duality, refer back to it in their middle sections, and conclude with it, they are rightly understood as being solely devoted to non-duality.
Nor is it reasonable that what has been refuted should be merely figurative;
for it has been stated that through repetition there is an increase in the reality of the meaning, not even a diminution, let alone a figurative status.

Therefore, since duality is established as being sublated, the state of being a living soul (jīva) belongs to that very Brahman due to the distinction created by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (avidyā); just as there are distinctions among reflections of a single original object due to the distinctions among limiting adjuncts such as mirrors.
In this way, the worldly and Vedic injunctions and prohibitions, as well as the established order of pleasure and pain, liberation and saṃsāra, become logically consistent.
Furthermore, there is no abundance of suffering in liberation;

for, just as the qualities of darkness or whiteness belong only to reflections and not to the original object, so too the connection with various experiences belongs only to the individual souls (jīvas) and not to Brahman, which is like the original object.

Just as when a mirror is removed, that reflection remains in the state of the original object (*bimba*) and no longer exists as a reflection in a sword, so too, upon the removal of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) exists in the state of Brahman. Thus it is established that the *jīva* is like a part of Brahman by virtue of its dependence on Him, but it is not actually a part; such is the intended meaning. 2.3.17.44. 44.
A collection or group consisting of seventeen members is called "the seventeenfold" (*saptadaśaka*).

For example: the ten external organs of cognition and action; the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is considered one by unifying the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*) despite their difference being merely a distinction in function (*vṛtti*); and the body as well as the objects [of the senses]. Thus, there is a seventeenfold collection. //47// 2.3.17.48.
The intended rule is one of authorization (*anujñā*), and not an instigation of one already engaged in action;
for in that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), it is impossible for there to be compliance with the intention of an instigator,
and because an instigation of one already engaged in action is untenable in the case of the injury to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-hiṃsā*) which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
Even when one is engaged in the portion consisting of restrictive rules (*niyamāṃśa*) for the sake of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), [one must ask]: "What, then, is the connection with the body?

For there can be no conjunction, inherence, or any other kind of connection between the Self—which is immutable, eternal, and non-extensive—and the body; this is because the intended meaning is that the Self transcends all attributes (*dharma*).
The answer is: this is the arising of a contrary cognition within the self, namely, "I am indeed this aggregate consisting of the body and so forth.
The meaning is this: it is true that there is no ultimate, real connection of the self with the body and other such things.

However, there is a contrary mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the self, produced by the intellect and other faculties, which takes the form: "I am indeed this aggregate of the body and so forth.
In this [modification], the aggregate of the body and so forth appears through identity with the self.
The meaning is that this relationship, characterized by identity, is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtta*) and not ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
With a hidden intention, he objects:
"In that case, for one who possesses right vision... The reply is: "No."
Regarding the word "tasya" (of him):
if it is intended that the aggregate of the subtle and gross bodies and so forth, which is presented by ignorance, is the right vision— namely, "I am Brahman, the one without a second"— then indeed,
for one who possesses such a vision, injunctions and prohibitions are utterly useless.
He clarifies this very point with the words: "of that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted.
The challenger reveals his hidden intention: "only for one who perceives the distinction from the body."
And he refutes [the objection] that there is a state of being enjoined (*niyojyatva*) with respect to rituals such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which have results pertaining to the next world:
"No, because of the conceit of their being combined with that.
He analyzes this point:
"It is true":
for he who knows the self to be non-different from the body composed of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*),
but not as being non-different from the entire aggregate of the intellect and so forth, [is one who speaks the truth].
He has authority over the fruits pertaining to the next world;

however, for one who perceives [the self] as distinct from the entire collection of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, and who is devoid of the conceit of being the enjoyer of karma, there is no authority over action. Thus, there is no acting according to whim, because even that [acting at will] is absent in one who is free from such conceit. //48// 2.3.17.49. // 49 // 2.3.17.50.

However, for those Sāṃkhyas or Vaiśeṣikas who maintain that there are many all-pervading selves and who assert that the distribution of pleasure and pain is ultimately real, this very confusion (vyatikara) necessarily follows.
Regarding this, he first states the contradiction concerning the Sāṃkhyas by way of a question: "How so? (katham).

Since the connection with qualities (guṇasaṃbandha), regardless of its specific nature, is indistinguishable with respect to all persons, the resulting pleasure and pain would likewise be indistinguishable for all.
Nor can the established order [of experience] be based on karma;
for since karma is composed of the material constituents (prakṛti) and Prakṛti is common to all, the lack of a fixed order remains an unavoidable consequence.
He objects: "It might be so.
The meaning is this: the Pradhāna does not act for the purpose of proclaiming its own manifestations.
However, [the *guṇas* act] for the sake of the *puruṣa*.

And toward that *puruṣa* for whom enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)—the two purposes of the *puruṣa*—have been accomplished by this [manifestation of the *guṇas*], [the *guṇas*] cease because their mandate is fulfilled; but toward another *puruṣa*, they continue to function, their mandate being unfulfilled.

Thus, he refutes [the objection] by showing that the distinction between the liberated and the transmigrating is established, and consequently, the distinction between pleasure and pain will also be established.
"No," [it is replied].

Because all *puruṣas* are omnipresent (*vibhu*) and because *pradhāna* is common to all, it is simply not the case that "this purpose has been accomplished for this particular *puruṣa* by this [evolution of *pradhāna*].
Therefore, a fixed order must be maintained without a motive based on a specific purpose.
And that [position] is incorrect because there is no reason for it; this is the meaning.
Let the Sāṃkhyas’ lack of systematic consistency stand, since for them the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) arises from inherence in the Pradhāna.
Furthermore, because *pradhāna* is common to all, [the system of the Kaṇādas and others faces difficulties].

For the followers of Kaṇāda and others, however, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) inhering in the self is unique to each individual self; and the relationship between the self and the mind, characterized by the state of owner and owned, is beginningless, since the various types of unseen merit are themselves beginningless.

Thus, even though the conjunction of the self [with the mind] is common to all, the systematic arrangement of intentions and so forth is indeed possible due to the uniqueness of the owner-and-owned relationship.
Nor is conjunction itself common [to all]; for the conjunction of that mind with one self is not the same as its conjunction with another master,
because a conjunction between selves differs according to the difference in each respective conjunct.

Therefore, since the oneness of the Self is established by scripture, and since the systematic arrangement of experience is possible even if there is only one Self, there is no need to postulate a plurality of Selves.
Because it would entail unnecessary complexity and contradict the scriptures;
and because, if one were to postulate a distinction based on the possession of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*):
for the distinction would depend upon that postulation, and that postulation would depend upon the distinction.
This itself constitutes the refutation of the Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣika) doctrine.

However, the author of the Bhāṣya, speaking with the confidence of one who asserts a bold position (*prauḍhavāditayā*), has applied such sūtras as "because of the lack of restriction regarding the unseen force" (*adṛṣṭāniyamāt*) even against the followers of Kaṇāda.
Some, however, prefer to hold that these [sūtras] are intended solely for the refutation of the Sāṃkhya doctrine; let that matter rest for now. (50, 51, 52, 53)
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Bhāmatī, a commentary on the Śārīrakabhāṣya of the venerable Pāda, composed by the illustrious Nācaspatimiśra. //3//
Thus ends the third section (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "The Resolution of the Apparent Contradiction between the Śrutis concerning the Five Great Elements and the Living Self.
Now begins the fourth section of the second chapter. 2.4.1.
And so is the vital breath (prāṇa).

Although the scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) at the beginning of creation ought to be interpreted in some other way—just as the scriptural passages concerning the non-remembrance of the ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth must be interpreted otherwise—because it contradicts the promise that "by knowing Brahman, everything is known," contradicts the explanatory scriptures, and contradicts the numerous Śruti texts on non-duality;

nevertheless, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) argues from this position, thinking: "If one does not know how to interpret it otherwise, even a single scripture that cannot be explained otherwise might cause many [other scriptures] to be entangled. Thus, he sets forth the prima facie argument.
And here, by virtue of its extreme height, he recalls the reasons for the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument regarding the ether as the substratum—beginning with "In that regard, first of all":

for the production of the gross elements is to be understood solely through the authority of scripture; therefore, wherever the scriptural word ceases, the absence of those elements is recognized due to the non-existence of that means of knowledge.
The meaning is: "just as in the case of the nature of the dharma consisting of the worship of a caitya and its ritual action.

Here, having provisionally raised an objection through a superficial misconception and lack of firm conviction, he introduces the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) stated with the words "or rather" (athavā).
His underlying intention has thus been shown.

In the [sūtra] "And the [penance for] drinking [Soma] is likewise," what is referred to is the similarity to the meaning of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) sūtras concerning the "Aśvamedha-sacrifice for receiving a horse" and others. However, the final conclusion (rāddhānta) is as follows: this would be so if the scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths (prāṇa) at the beginning of creation were established as being incapable of another explanation;
but rather, this is established in quite another way.

For it must be stated that at the intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*), there is a creation of the means for fire; thus, the opening of the passage regarding "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is for that purpose.

In that context, the sovereign person Prajāpati remains undestroyed while only the three worlds have dissolved; therefore, with respect to his vital breaths (*prāṇa*), that scriptural statement is consistent in meaning. Consequently, [this interpretation] favors the majority of the scriptures and serves to establish the subsequent portion, which aims to justify the promise of universal knowledge.

But if the context were secondary, it would follow that the subject matter is unnecessary due to the absence of conformity with the intended meaning; thus, even the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) would be mere modifications of Brahman, like space.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no scriptural mention of the origin of the vital breaths at all, as there is in the case of the worship of a shrine (*caityavandana*) and similar acts.
Indeed, in some places there is no mention of their origination, yet in various other places their origination is shown;
therefore, there is a disparity [between them] and such acts as the veneration of shrines (*caityavandana*) and the ritual fast (*poṣadha*).
Some explain the Sūtra—“because figurative usage is impossible”—by means of the discussion concerning space (*viyat*).
"The scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is secondary because their origin is impossible"—
this is incorrect,
as it cannot withstand critical analysis.

To explain: it would be impossible for the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) to have the nature of the unmodified Brahman, either in the same manner as the individual soul (*jīva*), or by being a different principle from Brahman.
First of all, they cannot have the nature of the unmodified Brahman in the same manner as the soul, because they are insentient (*jaḍa*).
Therefore, one must accept that these [effects] do not arise as distinct realities from Brahman.
And in that case, there would be a contradiction of the proposition that "by the knowledge of Brahman, all is known," as well as a subversion of the entirety of the Vedānta; this is what he states:
"In the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa), for [it is said] 'hi' (for/indeed)... //2// 2.4.1.3.
"And because it is heard before that... The commentary on this is self-explanatory (nigada-vyākhyāta). //3// 2.4.1.4.
"Because speech is preceded by that [mind].
The term "speech" (vāc) is an elliptical expression for speech, breath, and mind.

The meaning is this: even in those cases where you claim that the creation of the vital breaths is not mentioned in the account of the creation of fire and the other elements, [the breaths are nonetheless implied].
To this we reply that it has already been stated there.

For instance, in the section where the fact that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by fire, water, and food is recorded in the passage beginning with "For [speech] consists of food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.1),
if that were taken in its primary sense, then by analogy with that, the creation of these very vital breaths would have been stated.

Now, as for the passage concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*): even so, since the differentiation of names and forms is performed by Brahman, and considering the beginning and conclusion [of that section], as well as its renown in other scriptural texts (*śruti*), it has been stated that the description of the vital breath and the rest as being "made of water" and so forth is solely for the purpose of illustrating the manifold nature of Brahman’s effects.
Thus, it is established that the creation of the vital breath is indeed mentioned there as well. //4// 2.4.2.5.
And because the seven [types of] destinies have been specified.
He states the intermediate connection:
"with regard to the subject of birth."
He states the cause of the doubt:
"because of a contradiction in the scriptures.
*Viśaya* here means doubt.
In some cases there are seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*), namely: eye, nose, tongue, speech, ear, mind, and skin. In other cases there are eight vital breaths.
They are proclaimed as "graspers" (graha) by virtue of their quality of being bonds;
namely, the nose, tongue, speech, eye, ear, mind, hand, and skin—
these are the graspers.

The objects of these [senses], however, are the eight *atigrahas* (over-graspers), which have been stated in the textual passage beginning with: "Breath indeed is the *graha*; it is seized by the *atigraha* that is the out-breath (*apāna*), for by means of the out-breath one smells odors. In some places, there are nine;
for example:
There are indeed seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in the head and two directed downwards.
There are two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, and one speech— thus they are seven.

The anus and the generative organ, or the intellect and the mind—these two are downward-directed; nor is it anywhere stated that there are ten. Indeed, it is said that there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, with the navel as the tenth.
In some places there are eleven, as in: "These ten are the vital breaths (prāṇas) in a person;
namely, the five sense organs beginning with the nose, the five organs of action beginning with the hands, and the self as the eleventh."

It is called the "self" (*ātman*) because it attains [objects] through its presiding presence; this self is the mind (*manas*), which is the eleventh [organ], though in some places it is the twelfth, as in the passage:
"The skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations."
Namely: skin, nose, tongue, eye, ear, mind, heart, hands, feet, genitals, anus, and speech.
In some places, these same vital breaths (*prāṇas*) plus the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) make thirteen. Thus, the scriptural traditions (*śruti*) are at variance regarding the number of vital breaths.
Here, he presents the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) by means of a question: "What, then, is the conclusion?
That there are exactly seven."
There are exactly seven vital breaths (prāṇas). Why? Because of their departure and because they are understood from such scriptural passages as, "The seven prāṇas come forth.
This understanding is not derived from scripture alone; [it is also supported by other evidence].
He says that it is exactly so even because of the qualification: "And because of being specified," namely,
"There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head."

When it is stated that "those seven which are located in the head, beginning with the ears, are the prāṇas," it is understood that the others—the non-head-residing [organs] such as the hands and so forth—are not prāṇas.
Just as when it is said, "he sees with the right eye," it is understood that he does not see with the left;
this is what is meant: even if there is a contradiction with the Vedic text, and even if the subsequent numbers do not [subsume] the preceding numbers.

Even so, since it is impossible for many numbers to function as delimiters (*avacchedaka*), when only one must be postulated, it is logical that it be seven, due to its primacy and its simplicity (*lāghava*).
However, by intending merely to distinguish the different modes of functioning (*vṛttibheda*), the number eight and others are to be understood. This is the conclusion reached. //5// 2.4.2.6.
This being the position reached, it is said: "But hands and so forth [exist] while [the body] persists; therefore, it is not thus.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not only seven; rather, the hands and so forth are also vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Since the number of vital breaths is established as eleven by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the word "ekādaśatve" is used] with the suffix *tasi* functioning as a substitute for all case endings.
It is not so;
the literal meaning is that there are seven [categories] because of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of being primary (*prāthamya*).

What is meant is this: although the scriptures (*śruti*) are independent as they are intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥpramāṇa*), nevertheless, due to mutual contradictions, they are not sufficient for the determination of the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, an option (vikalpa) is not possible regarding an established entity in the same way it is regarding a ritual performance;
therefore, [the alternatives] are determined by the force of the objects presented by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
As it is said: "Just as 'inferior'... and so forth.
Just as it is established that one "cuts with the *sruva* [ladle]" because it is impossible to cut portions of meat or sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) with it,
whereas it is possible to cut liquid substances, and thus the rule "liquids are cut with the *sruva*" is established;
so too here, from the determination of the five effects— the cognitions of form and so forth— the five instruments, the sense organs of cognition such as the eye, are established.

For the blind and others do not perceive visible forms and so forth, even when the other [faculties]—the sense of smell and the rest—are present and their existence is inferred by the perception of odors and so forth.

Likewise, from the established fivefold set of effects characterized by speaking and so forth, there is the establishment of the fivefold set of organs of action characterized by speech, hands, and so forth.

For the mute and others never possess the capacity for speaking and so forth, even when the feet and other [organs], as well as the sensory organs, are present and their existence is known through activities such as walking.

Thus, the internal organ is inferred through the established functions of volition and so forth, which cannot belong to the organs of action or the organs of perception. Furthermore, even though it is a single internal organ, it will perform multiple functions,
just as a single lamp is the cause for illuminating forms, transforming the wick, and drying up the oil.
Therefore, there is no difference among the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Rather, it is a single internal organ that is designated as "mind" (*manas*) because of its function of thinking, as "ego" (*ahaṅkāra*) because of its function of self-conceit, and as "intellect" (*buddhi*) because of its function of determination.
Although it is non-different, it is figuratively treated as if it were three distinct things due to the difference in its functions.
In reality, however, there is only one, because there is no evidence for any division.
Thus, since the eleven effects are established in this way, the scriptural statement that "there are eleven prāṇas" is direct and primary;
other scriptural passages should be interpreted in accordance with it.

In this context, the scriptural mentions of the numbers seven, eight, nine, and ten are restatements of what has already been established, in accordance with such passages as "he chooses one," "two," or "three.

However, the scriptural mentions of the numbers twelve and thirteen must somehow be interpreted as referring to meditations (*upāsana*) and the like, by intending a distinction based on a difference in function.
Therefore, it is established that there are exactly eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and not others.
Furthermore, as for the designation of the vital breaths located in the head as being seven, that too must be established as residing in only four,
because it contradicts other means of valid cognition; for there are certainly not two eyes.
Because there is no difference in the effect characterized by the apprehension of form;
however, for one with one eye covered, the apprehension of form is not such as it is for one with both eyes intact.
Therefore, there is only one eye, though it is figuratively treated as if distinct due to the difference in its locations.
Even for one who is one-eyed, there is perception by means of a portion of the eye located in a single eyeball;
by this, the nose and the ear are also explained.
This is another way of applying the two sūtras:

One might raise an objection to explain that there are only seven vital breaths— namely sight, smell, taste, speech, hearing, mind, and skin— that possess the power of departure, because the scripture specifically mentions the departure of only these seven: "But [the opponent] objects here that even the word 'all' is used."
The answer to this is:
"Because they are specified.
For it is the organs beginning with the eye and ending with the skin that are specified in relation to the departure [of the soul].

Therefore, since the word "all" (sarva) depends on what has been previously mentioned, it follows that only the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) depart, and not the hands and so forth. An objection is raised: "But surely here consciousness (vijñāna) is the eighth," as it was enumerated in the passage, "They say he does not perceive."
He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault.
He states the established conclusion:

"But other vital breaths, such as the hands and so forth, are understood to be distinct from the seven and to undergo departure, because of the scriptural statement that the hands and others are 'seizers' (grahas)."
In this way, indeed, their designation as "grahas" (seizers) would be logically consistent;
for if they were to bind the self until liberation, otherwise—just like the body composed of the six sheaths—their status as grahas would not have been recorded in the tradition.
And for this very reason, the Smṛti declares that their limit is liberation.
—by means of the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka).
Likewise, this Atharvaṇa Śruti also declares the departure of these eleven [elements].

Therefore, since the departure of all [the elements] is established by other scriptural passages, by Smṛti, and because there is no restriction on the meaning of the word "all," that which was stated—that there are only seven—is not so.
However, it is established that the number seven is for the sake of illustration. 2.4.3.7.

*And [the senses] are atomic.* Regarding this, the Sāṃkhyas say: because the sense organs are derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), and because the ego-principle pervades the entire cosmic egg, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are all-pervading.
They hold that their function is localized because they occupy a specific region of the body, and that the scriptural accounts of their coming and going are based on that [localization].

In response to them, he says: "And the vital breaths are atomic. Their atomicity consists in having unmanifest color and touch; it is not the state of being a *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom), because that would entail the impossibility of producing effects that pervade the entire body.
It has already been stated that for one afflicted by heat who has immersed himself in a cool lake, there is a perception of a cold touch extending over all limbs.
This is what is meant: if the sense-faculties were all-pervading (*sarvagata*), then it would follow that there would be perception of objects that are obstructed or distant.

If it is argued that even though they are all-pervading, only those [faculties] delimited by the body function as instruments (*karaṇa*), and therefore there is no consequence of perceiving obstructed or distant things—well then, since their status as instruments and as sense-faculties (*indriyatva*) consists in being delimited by the body through the distinction between what is reached and what is not reached, they cannot possess the nature of sense-faculties if they are omnipresent.

Thus, there is a discrepancy only regarding the name and not the object; for we call them "organs" (*indriya*), whereas you call them "functions" (*vṛtti*). It is established, therefore, that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are atoms (*aṇu*).
And [the text says]: "The best [breath] also.
Not only are the other vital breaths modifications of Brahman, but this one is as well.
And [the opponent] maintains that the vital breath (prāṇa) is a modification of Brahman;

for, in the *Brahmasūkta* known as the *Nāsadāsīya*, which begins with "Non-being was not," there is heard a reference to the activity of the vital breath prior to creation in the words "breath existed" (*ānīt*), and since activity is impossible in the absence of [an underlying substance], and because of the scriptural declaration of its primacy (*jyeṣṭhatva*), the vital breath is not a modification of Brahman. This is the view of one who so thinks.
Furthermore, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arises for one who, despite the contradiction with numerous scriptural passages, perceives no way to reconcile these two Vedic texts.

The established conclusion (rāddhānta), however, is that precisely because of the contradiction with numerous scriptural passages, the word "anīt" does not intend to describe the functioning of the vital breath;
rather, it means "it breathed," "it lived," or "it existed," referring to the cause of creation.

Therefore, it should be understood that this [passage] is intent on establishing the actual existence of that [breath], and that its status as "the eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) is relative to the ear and other senses. Consequently, in accordance with many scriptural passages, it is established that even the primary vital breath (*prāṇa*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman. //8// 2.4.5.9.
"Nor [is the chief vital breath] the function of air, because it is taught separately.
Now, the nature of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is being determined.
For here, based on the scriptural statement, "That which is the vital breath is air," it appears that the vital breath is indeed just air.

Alternatively, since the Prāṇa is heard of as distinct from Vāyu in the passage, "Prāṇa alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it [shines] with Vāyu as its light," and because of the contradiction [otherwise], it is better to accept the view of another system (tantrāntarīya). Furthermore, the two scriptural passages regarding Prāṇa may somehow be interpreted as having contradictory meanings. Thus, let Prāṇa be simply the common function (sāmānyavṛtti) of the organs. Nor is there a contradiction here with the scriptural enumeration of Prāṇa as separate from the organs, because of the distinction between the function (vṛtti) and that which possesses the function (vṛttimat). This is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not the collective function of the sense organs. For it would have to be either the function of the senses combined or the function of each individually;
first, it cannot be the function of them combined.
Because if one, two, three, or four sense-faculties were absent, there would necessarily follow the non-existence of that [consciousness].
Indeed, the red quality produced by the conjunction of turmeric powder and lime cannot exist if either of those two is absent.
Nor can the carrying of a palanquin, which requires many porters, be accomplished by two or three porters.
Furthermore, it is not accomplished by the skin alone;
for if that were the case, its existence as a common property (sāmānya) would be untenable.

Moreover, when causal factors (kārakas) act in combination to produce an effect, they do so only through intermediate operations (avāntara-vyāpāra) that are conducive to the primary operation, just as the individual actions of birds are conducive to the movement of a cage.
Furthermore, when the primary function of the vital breath (prāṇa) is to be produced, there is no such intermediate activity of the sense organs that is conducive to it.
And those cognitions of form and so forth are not conducive to it;

therefore, the vital breath is not the common function (sāmānyavṛtti) of the sense organs. Thus, although there is a distinction between the function and the possessor of the function, one should not understand their separate instruction as being intended to express some kind of difference between them.
Therefore, *prāṇa* is neither action nor merely air; rather, it is a specific modification of air that has entered into the body (*adhyātma*), consisting of fivefold manifestations. //9// 2.4.5.10.
It might be argued as follows:

Just as the eye and other organs are subordinate to the living self (jīva), and because the living self is preeminent, the living self alone is independent; so too, because the vital breath (prāṇa) is primary and preeminent, it would follow that it is independent.

However, it is not possible for two independent entities to function as a single unit within one body; otherwise, the body would be torn asunder by their simultaneous and contradictory movements in different directions.
This being the position, it is replied:
"But [the vital breath] is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons.

Although the vital breath possesses superiority and preeminence in comparison to the eye and the rest, nevertheless, because it is composite, insentient, and material, it is similar to the eye and the other organs.
Furthermore, because it is taught together with them and because it serves the purpose of the person, the breath (prāṇa) must be dependent upon the person, just like the bed, the seat, and so forth.

And thus, just as a minister, even though he is the principal among other officials appointed by royal decree, is nonetheless not independent insofar as he depends on the king; so too the breath, even though it is the principal among the eyes and other organs, is not independent insofar as it depends on the living self (jīva).
This might be the case if the breath were merely an instrument taught along with the eyes and other organs.
This being the case, just as the eye and so forth have objects such as visible form, one would have to state another object for this [mind] as well;
yet that cannot be stated.
Furthermore, it would contradict the enumeration of eleven instruments. To avoid these faults, he says:
And there is no fault because it is not an instrument; for the scripture shows this:

we do not accept that the vital breath (prāṇa) is an instrument for functions such as discerning or supporting, whereby one would have to search for another object for it, and the number of instruments would be disturbed by reaching eleven. Rather, the vital breath is the cause for the maintenance of the body and the senses, which cannot be accomplished by any other vital breath.
And this has been demonstrated by a series of scriptural passages; its function is not merely the maintenance of the body and the senses.
Furthermore:
"It is designated as having five functions, like the mind. (VS 3.2.1)
"Error is false knowledge not established in its own form," such as the cognitions of water and so forth in the case of mirages in the desert and the like.
And the state of being "not established in its own form" exists even in doubt, because that [doubt] is not established in a single [aspect].
Therefore, that too is included.
"Conceptual construction (vikalpa) is that which follows upon the cognition of words and is devoid of a real object.
Although the state of being devoid of a real object also exists in the case of false cognition (mithyājñāna), nevertheless, it lacks the status of being a cause for linguistic usage (vyavahāra).

However, this [conceptual construction], even though it cannot withstand the scrutiny of the learned, certainly possesses the status of being a cause for linguistic usage due to the power of the cognition of words.
For example, in the expression "the consciousness of a person" (*puruṣasya caitanyam*),
there is no relation denoted by the genitive case here, because such a relation is based upon difference.
Because consciousness (*caitanya*) is absolutely non-different from the *puruṣa*.

Although, in this context, a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the cognition of non-existence as its object is not admitted, nevertheless, a mental modification characterized by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of distraction certainly exists here; thus, it is clearly established that [the mind] is endowed with consciousness. 12.
2.4.6.13. And [the mind] is atomic (*aṇu*).

Since the breath (prāṇa) is heard to be all-pervasive in the statement, "Equal to the three worlds," it is omnipresent; as for the scriptural texts such as "equal to a gnat," these will apply to the omnipresent [breath] through its limitation [by specific bodies].
Just as the all-pervading ether (ākāśa) attains equality with a pot and so forth due to its limitation by a pot, a water-jar, and the like—this being the position reached, he says:
And [the prāṇa] is atomic.
On account of the scriptural texts concerning its departure, movement, and return, the internal prāṇa is limited and not all-pervading.

Furthermore, it has been stated previously that its "atomicity" is merely a figurative designation for its extreme difficulty of perception, even though it pervades the body; it does not mean that it is actually atomic in size.

However, that measure which belongs to it by virtue of its omnipresence is in relation to the *sūtrātman*—the divine self existing as both the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*)—and not in its internal (*ādhyātmika*) form.

And the scriptural passages beginning with "He is equal to a gnat," which have that [divine aspect] as their basis, declare only the equality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with the body; they do not mean that it is somehow smaller than the body due to the influence of another limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), as in the case of the space within a jar.
But its presiding over light and so forth is because of the traditional teaching regarding that.

For it is a general rule that whatever is observed performing an action does so by its own power alone; any dependence upon another, however, occurs only through the force of some other stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It might be argued:

"Since we observe that insentient tools such as axes perform their functions only when presided over by a carpenter or the like, one should likewise postulate a presiding deity for the sense organs because they are insentient.
This is not so, because there already exists a sentient presider residing within the living being (*jīva*).
Nor is it appropriate to accept that even the deities act as presiding controllers on the basis of such scriptural passages as, "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth," and so forth.
For if one were to accept multiple presiding controllers, no action whatsoever could be accomplished due to contradiction, as there would be no cause for regulating them toward a single intention.

Furthermore, since he who is the controller of the sense organs is himself the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*), the deities—by virtue of being the experiencers—would possess ownership over the body; consequently, the individual soul (*jīva*) would neither be the owner nor the experiencer.

Therefore, it follows that the metaphorical application of terms such as "fire" to speech and the other organs must be understood through some cause, such as their quality of being illuminators, and not that the deities of fire and so forth actually enter into the mouth and other parts in their own essential form.
This being the position reached, it is replied: In various Śrutis and Smṛtis here and there, the presiding of deities such as fire over speech and the other organs is clearly perceived;
and since there is no contradiction or impossibility, it is not appropriate to explain this away with forced interpretations.

Furthermore, for the individual soul (jīva), which lacks knowledge of the specific nature, functions, and distinctions [of the senses], the status of being the presiding controller of the sense organs is not possible;

however, it is possible for the deities (devatās), who have directly perceived them through their divine knowledge, to possess the cognition of their specific natures, distinctions, and the distinctions of their functions.
Therefore, it is logical that those very deities are the presiding controllers of those respective instruments, and not the individual soul.

Or, let it be that the individual soul (*jīva*) is also a controller; even so, there is no fault. There exists a single Supreme Lord as the controller and inner ruler (*antaryāmī*) of many controllers; by His power, even those who wish to act in opposition are not able to oppose Him. Thus, through this unity of purpose, there is no obstruction to the production of its effects.
Nor does this much imply that the deities are the enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*) in this body;
for although a charioteer stands upon a chariot, he is not the enjoyer of the victory or other results achieved by it, but rather the owner alone.
In the same way, although the deities are presiding agents (*adhiṣṭhātrī*), they are not the enjoyers, because scripture teaches only their status as such.
The enjoyer, however, is indeed the individual soul (jīva).
Furthermore, even the gods are not entitled to experience the pleasure that consists of enjoyment abounding in suffering, which is appropriate for human bodies and the like.
Therefore, it is established that the presiding deities are those of the vital breaths (prāṇas).
The remainder has its meaning not obscured. //14// 2.4.7.15. // 15 // 2.4.7.16. // 16 // 2.4.8.17. // 16 //
Those [organs] are the senses (indriyas), because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one. Let it not be that prāṇa is merely a function of the senses;
rather, the senses themselves will be the functions of this eldest prāṇa.
The fact that the existence and non-existence of the sense organs follows the existence and non-existence of that [prāṇa] is established by both scripture and experience;
thus, there will be no inconsistency in the single word "prāṇa" having multiple referents,
because the functions (vṛttis) are not essentially different from the possessor of those functions (vṛttimat).
If, however, the sense organs were distinct principles from the vital breath, it would follow that the word "prāṇa" has multiple meanings,
or that its application to the sense organs is merely figurative.
Furthermore, when the primary sense of a word is possible, metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate because it is more remote.

Nor does designation by distinction constitute proof of actual difference; for instance, since there is a designation of the mind as distinct from the senses in such passages as "From this [Self] the vital breath (prāṇa) is born," it would follow that the mind is not an organ. If, however, its status as an organ is established on the basis of Smṛti, then even though the organs are designated as distinct from the vital breath, they too possess the nature of the vital breath, as the Śruti states: "Come, let us assume his very form."
Therefore, on account of both reasoning and scripture, it follows that the eleven organs are merely functions of the vital breath (prāṇa) and not distinct principles.
This being the position reached, it is replied: the organs are indeed distinct principles from the principal vital breath, because they are designated as separate in various places.
This is because of the scriptural teaching regarding the conjunction of contradictory properties characterized by having attained or not yet attained death,
and also because of the difference in their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For the maintenance of the body is the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while the observation of objects and reflection are the functions of the sense organs.
Furthermore, the fact that something follows the presence and absence of another does not entail that it resides within that other;
for there is a deviation in the case of the body.
Indeed, breath and the like follow the positive and negative concomitance of the body, yet they do not reside in the body as its self.
Furthermore, regarding the scriptural statement that the sense organs have the nature of *prāṇa*,

the Commentator has stated that upon examining the preceding and following contexts, it is precisely their difference [from *prāṇa*] that is understood. Therefore, because it contradicts many scriptural passages and because it is internally inconsistent, the assertion that the sense organs have the nature of *prāṇa* must be understood as figurative, based on their dependence upon *prāṇa*.

As for the mind (*manas*), since its status as a sense organ (*indriya*) is understood from the Smṛti, its mention in some places as distinct from the [other] senses is according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).
Alternatively, it is mentioned separately because the senses have only the present as their object, whereas the mind has all three periods of time as its sphere.
However, it is not appropriate to interpret the abundance of distinct designations for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the same way.
Furthermore, the movement [of the soul] has been shown on account of the scriptural statement regarding its nature as *prāṇa*.

Likewise, since the word *prāṇa* is used in its primary sense for the vital breath (*jyeṣṭha-prāṇa*), it is logical that the word *prāṇa* is used figuratively for the sense organs and, subsequently, for other principles.
Moreover, it is not reasonable to establish identity between two things whose difference is already understood merely by following the primary sense of a term.
"Let there not be an identity between the Gaṅgā and so forth with their banks and such.

Others, however, fearing the need to supply the word "difference" (*bheda*) and fearing redundancy in the phrase "and because of the scriptural mention of difference," have explained it otherwise—since the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the immediately preceding "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*).

[They ask: "Are the sense organs only the eleven beginning with speech, or is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) also one? In this doubt, an "organ" (*indriya*) is that which is a mark (*liṅga*) of Indra, the Self.

And thus, since the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses the characteristic mark of Indra (indraliṅga) just like speech and the other organs, it follows that the vital breath is also an organ, just like speech and the rest.
This being the position reached, the following is stated: "The organs—speech and the others—are distinct from the supreme vital breath.
Why? Because they alone, namely speech and the others, are designated by that term "organ" (indriya).
For the word "indriya" is never observed to be used in its primary sense for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Its status as being "characterized by Indra" (*indraliṅgatā*) is merely a basis for etymological derivation, just as [the word] "cow" (*go*) is derived from the fact that it "moves" (*gacchati*).
However, the actual ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the state of being an instrument for the perception of color and so forth, while having the body as its locus.
Furthermore, this body serves as its locus insofar as the body’s benefit and injury result in its own benefit and injury.
Thus, there is no consequence of light being classified as a sense organ.
Therefore, it is established that by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), only speech and the others are the sense organs, and not the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The section of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), however, is to be understood in the context of the sūtras beginning with "Because of the scriptural statement of difference" (B.S. 3.3.1) and so forth. [Sūtra 18] 2.4.8.19.
[Sūtra 19] 2.4.9.20. "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching [in the text].

In the section concerning the Existent (Sat-prakriyā), after prescribing the creation of fire, water, and food through the textual sequence beginning with "That fire thought," it is taught: "This [earth],"...
The Deity thought: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms; let me make each one of them threefold.
The meaning of this is: the purpose of the aforementioned desire to become many has not yet been fully accomplished in every respect; therefore, there is a further reflection.

Having accomplished the purpose of becoming manifold, [the Self thought]: "Ah! Now, how may I enter these three deities—Fire and the others—as previously described, by means of this individual soul (jīva), the sustainer of life, which was brought into proximity through memory;
having entered them as a mere reflection, like the image of a face in a mirror or the image of the moon in water, within the subtle elements such as intellect and the rest?"
"I shall differentiate name and form; I shall make this clear, [determining] 'this is its name' and 'this is its form.
Of those three deities, I shall make each one threefold—threefold in essence through fire, water, and food.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is this differentiation of name and form performed by the individual soul (jīva), or is it performed by the Supreme Lord?

If [the world] were created by the individual soul (jīva), then there would be uncertainty due to contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form. However,
if it were created by the Supreme Lord (parameśvara),
then there is no contradiction.

In that regard, since the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is observed in the creation of names such as "Ḍittha" and "Ḍavittha," and in the creation of forms such as jars and cloths, there is likewise a possibility here for the soul to be the agent in the tripartite differentiation (trivṛtkaraṇa) and the creation of names and forms.
Thus, by virtue of its fitness, the phrase "by this living soul" is connected with the principal action, "I shall manifest," and not with the immediately preceding phrase "having entered."
For a direct connection with the principal word-meaning is the general rule for all subordinate word-meanings, since they exist for the sake of that [principal meaning].
However, when such a direct connection is impossible in certain cases, recourse is taken to an indirect (mediated) one;
and the possibility of a direct connection has been demonstrated by way of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).
But is it not heard that the Supreme Lord is the agent in the passage "This, indeed, was the deity"?
True;
however, that will be so by way of being the instigator.

Just as in the world one might say, "Having entered the enemy's army by means of a spy, I shall gather it together," if, on the other hand, the state of being the direct agent belonged to this [individual soul], the phrase "by means of this living self" would be redundant; for otherwise,
it is not possible for the living self to function as an instrument.

The instrument (karaṇa) of the instigating agent (prayojaka-kartṛ) is that which directly effects [the action] on behalf of the instigator, because the instigator causes the prompted agent (prayojya-kartṛ) to act toward the primary action.

Therefore, since there is a contradiction—namely, that the soul (jīva) possesses agency in the differentiation of names and forms (nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa), while elsewhere the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) does so—it follows that there is no definitive conclusion to be reached.
To this position, it is replied: even here, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught to be the differentiator of names and forms, and not the soul.
Because he is unfit for connection with the primary action [of creation].

If it is argued that fitness is possible here as well—since agency is observed elsewhere in the case of objects named Ḍittha, Javittha, and so forth, as well as in the case of objects such as jars and bowls—[we reply: no.
For any such possibility is sublated by the absence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), which is determined by the incapacity [of a human] to create things such as mountains, rivers, and oceans.
Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught here as the direct agent, not the individual soul (jīva).
However, the word "having entered" (anupraviśya) is connected with this [agent] because of its proximity and suitability.
Nor is it purposeless; for the mention of that entry is meaningful, as the threefold compounding (trivṛtkaraṇa) is for the sake of the individual soul who is the enjoyer.
This might be so:

because the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed when there is a common agent (in the sense that "having entered, I shall explain"), it is taught that the very soul (*jīva*) who is the agent of entering is also the one who explains; otherwise, if the Supreme Lord were the explainer and the soul were merely the enterer, [the rule would not apply].

He says—"And the so-called individual soul (jīva) is not [the agent]"—lest the use of the suffix *ktvā* be contradicted by the fact that there would be different agents; the rest has a self-evident meaning. //20// 2.4.9.21.
"Meat and so forth belong to the earth, as does [the air] according to its name; and the same applies to the other two.
Here, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt) has explained this Sūtra as being intended to present the subject matter, serving as a supplement to the subsequent Sūtra.
However, it is also possible to state that its purpose is to dispel a doubt.

For instance, regarding the statement that "the subtlest part of food is the mind (manas), while the subtlest part of fire is speech (vāk)," there is indeed a disagreement between the followers of Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣikas) and the Sāṃkhyas. In this regard, the Vaiśeṣikas declare the mind to be eternal,
whereas the Sāṃkhyas maintain that both speech and the mind are derived from the ego (ahaṃkāra).
The statement regarding "partaking of food," however, is intended to indicate its connection with food;
for when one enjoys food, the mind becomes healthy.
In the same way, one should infer that the eloquence of speech is equal to [the vigor of] fire.
In this regard, the following verse is presented:
"From meat... (Māṃsāt).

Although it should have been stated as "from speech and mind" (*vāṅmanasaḥ*), the mention of "meat" and so forth is for the purpose of providing an illustrative example by presenting the thing to be established (*sādhya*) along with the established (*siddha*).
Just as flesh and so forth consist of the elements such as earth, so too speech and mind consist of fire and earth; this is the meaning.

What is intended is this: there is nothing whatsoever that exists eternally apart from Brahman, because [if there were], it would contradict the proposition that through the knowledge of Brahman, all things are known.
Furthermore, because it contradicts the *Bahuśruti*, it cannot be derived from the *ahaṅkāra* either;

for the category of *ahaṅkāra* as accepted by the Sāṃkhyas lacks scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*). Therefore, since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), it is not appropriate to interpret the direct Vedic statement otherwise in any way. Having stated that some fault exists, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) demonstrates that fault:

"If all [is fire]," [it is replied: "But on account of its predominance, there is that designation; indeed, there is that designation. (2.4.9.22) The meaning is that although the process of triplication (*tribṛtkaraṇa*) is common to all, a thing is designated by that which is most abundant in it. (22)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, an exposition on the *Śrīmad-Bhagavatpāda-Śārīrakabhāṣya* composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra.
Thus ends the second chapter, named "Non-contradiction," in the Śrīmad-Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-bhāṣya. Now begins the third chapter. 3.1.1.
At the time of entering another body, the soul departs enveloped [by the subtle elements], as is established by both questions and answers.

Showing the relationship between the second and third chapters as characterized by the state of being the cause and the effect, he states a summary of the subject matter for the sake of easy comprehension:
"In the second chapter...

By means of removing contradictions with Smṛti, Nyāya, and Śruti, the lack of authority characterized by indecisiveness is indeed set aside; and thus, when [the first chapter] has been made firm, the investigation of the third chapter occurs, whereas otherwise it would be without foundation.
"It would not be established"—

in order to show the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṃgati*), it was stated therein that "the principles distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) are the instruments (*upakaraṇa*) of the individual soul."
Having stated the summary of the meaning of the chapter, he states the summary of the meaning of the quarters (pādas):
"In that regard, first, in the [first] quarter...
He states its purpose: "...[namely], detachment (vairāgya)."
He prepares the foundation for the subsequent and preceding purifications by stating: "The individual soul has the chief vital breath as its minister.
This is because, unlike the case of the instruments [of action], there is no scriptural statement regarding the soul's taking up the primary elements.

And here, since the instruments (karaṇas) are material according to the very scriptural statement regarding their material cause, the fact that the elements (bhūtas) are their material cause is established; thus, this section is commenced with the intention of discussing elements distinct from the material cause of the sense organs.
If the self were to depart taking the elements along, then those too would have been heard [in the scripture] as being included in the material cause of the instruments.
But they are not so heard; therefore, even when departing swiftly, the self is enveloped by the instruments alone, and not by the elements.
For when a matter is accessible solely through scripture (*āgama*), the absence of that [scripture] is not capable of determining the absence of the object of knowledge.
Nor is it reasonable to assume that the soul departs enveloped by the elements merely because the commencement of another body would otherwise be inexplicable; thus he says:
"And the subtle elements (*bhūtamātrā*) are easily obtained everywhere."

"Day and Parjanya," etc. For here, having divided the commencement of the body— which is characterized by the transformation of the *apūrva* of the Agnihotra— into five parts according to its nature as faith and so forth,
the author speaks with the intention of describing the meditation upon these as things to be offered into the fires beginning with the Sky (*dyu*), which is the means for attaining the Northern Path.
The Śruti says: "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," and so forth.

Here, when the morning and evening Agnihotra oblations have been offered—using milk and other materials as the means—with faith, [the sacrificer] becomes transformed into the fuel, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks of the Āhavanīya fire.
And when impelled by the causal factors such as the agent, these two— having gradually ascended from the intermediate space and entered the heavenly world— become subtle elements;
they are designated by the word "water" (āpas) due to their connection with liquid substances such as water,
and they are designated by the word "faith" (śraddhā) because they are caused by faith.
The substratum for those two oblations is fire, and other elements—kindled wood, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks—are indicated by way of metaphor.

"That world of heaven, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. Just as the Āhavanīya fire is the substratum for the Agnihotra sacrifice, so too the world of heaven is the substratum for those subtle waters—which are the transformed state of the Agnihotra oblation denoted by the word *śraddhā* (faith) and permeated by *śraddhā*.
The sun itself is its fuel;

for by it that world of heaven is kindled and shines, and thus, because of this kindling, it is the fuel. The rays of that sun are its smoke, because the rays arise from the sun just as smoke arises from fuel. The day is its flame.
Because it shares the common quality of luminosity and because it is a product of the sun,
the moon is a coal.
In this fire, the gods— the vital breaths of the sacrificer— exist in the form of Agni and the other deities with respect to the divine realm (adhideva).
They offer faith, and faith is said [to be the oblation]. Parjanya indeed, O Gautama, is the fire; Parjanya is a specific deity presiding over the instruments of rain.
Of him, the wind alone is the fuel.
For by means of the wind the rain-cloud is kindled as fire,
since rain is observed when the east wind and others are strong;
the smoke is the cloud.
Because it is an effect of smoke and because it resembles smoke;
lightning is like a flame because of the commonality of their luminosity.
The thunderbolt consists of embers due to its hardness and its connection with lightning;
the roar is the sparks because of their common quality of being scattered.
In that [cloud], the gods—whose nature is fire and who are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the sacrificer—offer King Soma as an oblation; from that offering of Soma, rain comes into being.

This is what is meant: the waters called "faith," having entered the heavenly world as an oblation, are transformed into the form of the moon; then, in the second stage, being offered into the fire of Parjanya, they transform into rain.
"The earth, O Gautama, is indeed the fire"—for that fire called the earth, the year itself is the fuel.
For after a period of one year, the earth, fully kindled, becomes fit for the production of rice and other crops.

Smoke is the sky; just as smoke rises from fire upon the earth, the sky appears like smoke. Night is the flame; corresponding to the darkness of the dark earth, night is like a flame corresponding to fire.
The quarters are the coals, because they are seen as tranquil and serene when the flames of night have subsided at dawn.
The intermediate directions are the sparks, due to their similarity in minuteness.

Into that fire, the gods offer the waters—which have arrived through the process of the transformation of faith and Soma and have ripened into the form of rain; from that oblation, food such as rice and barley comes into being.
"Man, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. His speech is the fuel;

for by means of speech—abiding in the eight locations such as the palate and so forth, and manifesting the collection of meanings through the sequence of the revelation of syllables, words, and sentences—he is kindled.
His breath is the smoke."
The mouth is like smoke because it issues forth from the face; the tongue is like a flame due to the similarity of its redness;
and the eyes are like embers because they are the locus of radiance.
The ear is the sparks, because of its scattered nature.

Those very waters, having arrived through the sequence of transformations beginning with faith, and having been transformed into the form of rice and other grains, are offered as oblations into the fire that is the person; their transformation results in the production of semen.
Woman indeed, O Gautama, is the fire; her lap is the fuel.
Therefore, she is kindled for the production of sons and so forth; that which he addresses her with is the smoke.
Because the addressing arises from the woman, the hair is the smoke, and the womb is the flame because of its redness.
That which he performs within—sexual intercourse—is the embers.
Delights are mere fragments of pleasure, like sparks, because of their insignificance.
Into this very fire, the gods offer semen; from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
Thus, having reached the fire of the woman through the sequence of faith, soma, rain, food, and semen as oblations, the waters become what is called the embryo.
Because they consist primarily of water, those waters come to be designated by the word "person" at the fifth oblation.
Since the waters come to be designated by the word "person" at the fifth oblation, it is understood that the living self (jīva) departs enveloped by the waters.

This is what is meant: he will later state that water is what is denoted by the word "faith" (śraddhā); because these [elements] have been made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), and because fire and food are inseparable from water, it will also be stated that by the mention of water, fire and food are likewise included.

Even so, the departure of the individual soul (jīva) enveloped by the elements is not understood by this much alone, because the scriptures merely state that fire, water, and food attain the state of being called "man" (puruṣavacastva) at the fifth oblation.

Nevertheless, because the scriptural statement, "They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation King Soma arises," possesses authority alongside the scriptural passage, "From space [he goes] to the moon; this is King Soma," which describes the attainment of the lunar world by those who perform sacrifices for desired objects via the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) through smoke and so forth, it is understood that the soul departs enveloped by the elements.

For it is thus: those very waters which, having been offered in the second oblation, have attained the state of Soma—it is with these that this living being (jīva), the performer of sacrifices and other rites, being enveloped, attains the state of the moon and reaches the lunar world.

Now, one might object: let the waters themselves, independently, attain the state of Soma through the sequence beginning with faith; but let the living being go there without being enveloped by them, as a mere possessor of the senses, and experience the state of Soma.
What is the harm in that?
This is the objection: namely, that there would be a transgression of the commonality of the scriptural statement.

For the commonality of the scriptural statement would be maintained only if the soul's transformation into Soma occurred in the same form and by the same sequence as that of the waters' transformation into Soma.
Otherwise, however, there would be no commonality of scriptural statement (*śrutisāmānya*).

Therefore, regarding the question of whether the soul departs while embraced or unembraced, it is determined—on the basis of the commonality of scriptural statement—that the soul departs while embraced.
Consequently, because of their preponderance of fluidity, the substances such as curd and milk, once offered as oblations, become subtle and adhere to the performer of sacrifices and other rites.

When the body is being offered according to the method that is not [merely] material wealth, the Truths, having been offered as oblations, surround those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* and lead them to the heavenly world. Thus he objects:
"But surely there is another scriptural text"—this is the meaning:
for the subtle body would have to travel enveloped [by the gross body] only if it did not possess a gross body while traveling;
however, by the illustration of the caterpillar, this [subtle body] maintains a connection with its current gross body until the attainment of another body.
Therefore, because it contradicts the scriptural illustrations, [the soul] does not depart enveloped by the subtle body. He refutes this with the words:
"Even there... (tatrāpi).
First of all, transmigration is not possible for the Supreme Self, because its nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated; rather,
it belongs to the individual souls (jīvas).
The Supreme Self alone, when its limitation is imagined through adjuncts (*upādhi*), is designated as the individual soul (*jīva*).
Since those adjuncts—such as the body and the senses—are localized, the soul, while residing therein, cannot go to another body.

Therefore, it must be understood that [the soul] moves away enveloped by the subtle body, brought forward by its karma; the comparison with a leech serves merely to illustrate the prolongation of the process of generating and reaching the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the body that is to be attained.
He states the Sāṃkhya hypothesis:
"of the all-pervading organs.
Since the organs are derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra), and since the ego pervades the entire sphere of the world, the meaning is that the organs are also all-pervading.
He states the conception of the Buddhists:
"of the self alone, which is solitary.
The self is the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse-consciousness); its activity consists of the six *pravṛttivijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses).
The five sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, are produced anew;
[the author] states the view of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika): "And it is the mind alone," and so on.

The "place of enjoyment" (bhogasthāna) is the body, which is the locus of experience; that is to say, it is a new body. He states the Digambara conception: "the soul itself, having leapt up," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), he includes the conceptual constructions of the Lokāyatikas;

for they are proponents of the self as being identical with the body, and they assert that the self is reduced to ashes and that there is no going anywhere for anyone. 3.1.1.2. He raises an objection:
"Is it not the case that [the answer] has already been stated by the two examples cited?"—
to this, he provides the reply in the sūtra:
"But because [the elements] consist of three constituents, and because of their predominance."
The effect of fire is the digestion of food that has been eaten and drunk;
that of water is moisture, perspiration, and so forth;
and that of earth is odor and the like.

But for one who, observing the presence of smell, sweat, digestion, vital breath, and space within the body, perceives it as consisting of the five elements and is not satisfied with the view that it consists of only three [elements]— namely fire, water, and earth— the author says in response:
"And again, it consists of three."

Because it consists of three elements (tridhātu), as it is sustained by the three constituents (dhātu)—wind, bile, and phlegm—it is not possible for that body to be produced solely from water, setting aside the other primary elements (bhūta). If so, why is there a restriction to the mention of water? To this, he says:
"Therefore, it is due to the predominance [of water].

Excluding the earth element, because the effect—the body—consists predominantly of liquid substances such as blood when compared to fire and the other elements, and because its two causes—the material cause (upādāna) and the instrumental cause (nimitta)—also consist predominantly of liquids, there is the statement that "water is man-like" (puruṣavacastva); this is not, however, for the purpose of excluding the other elements. //2// 3.1.1.3.

And because of the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). It is understood that the vital breaths have a substratum within the living body; it is observed that when the living body moves, the vital breaths, following it, also move.
Therefore, as the sixfold sheaths depart from the body, they depart when something [else] departs.
And it is understood that this subtle body, consisting of the elements and the sense organs, is that which is to be directed by them;

for it is not observed that these [mental states] have the mere sense organs as their substrate, such that their movement would be possible if they were based solely on those [organs]. "If it be argued that this is not so because of the scriptural mention of the movement of fire and other elements, we say no, because that is figurative. (Sūtra 3.1.1.4)

Even though it has been clearly stated that the soul departs together with the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the doubt regarding its movement toward fire and other elements is raised for the purpose of addressing an apparent contradiction in the scripture.
For in this context, the movement of body hair and head hair toward plants and trees must first be accepted as figurative due to its contradiction with observed reality.

And so, by the principle of "that which falls between two [established cases]," it is likewise appropriate that their [the vital breaths'] movement is also figurative, owing to the same scriptural contradiction.

And devotion has been stated to be the cessation of [worldly] assistance. (4) 3.1.1.5. If it is argued that [the soul] is not mentioned in the first [oblation], we say no; for it is those very waters which are appropriate [to be the soul]. When the manner in which the waters come to be called "man" at the fifth oblation is questioned, it is both impossible and illogical to claim that waterless faith (*śraddhā*) is the cause of the oblation in the first oblation.

For it is not possible to extract or offer as an oblation faith— characterized by clarity of intellect— in the same way that heart and other organs are extracted and offered after being cut from animals and the like;
nor is such a deviation from the general rule that an effect conforms to its cause tenable.
Therefore, this word "faith" (*śraddhā*) is used for water by way of figurative attribution (*bhakti*).
For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Water, indeed, is the self" (*āpo vā ātmā*).
If it is argued that [the souls do not ascend] because they are not mentioned [in the text], we say no; for those who perform sacrifices and other works are understood [to be implied].
The meaning of this has already been stated.
