In the context of the Agnihotra, there are six questions concerning the six topics of departure, the path, the foundation, satisfaction, return, and the rising toward the world—namely, fire, fuel, smoke, flame, embers, and sparks.
The collection of these six is called the "six questions" (ṣaṭpraśnī).
The definition of that [doubt] is the response. (6) He raises a doubt in order to introduce another sūtra:
"Make King Soma swell, make him diminish"—thus they consume them there.
By means of the repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāreṇa*), they consume the worlds consisting of Soma just as [they consume] Soma through its swelling and diminishing; this is the meaning.
To this, he recites the following:
Or [the term "food"] is figurative because of the lack of selfhood; for the scripture shows this.

Indeed, the qualified person (adhikārī) is the agent who enjoys the fruits produced by ritual action, not one who is himself the object of enjoyment. Therefore, for those who have attained residence in the same world as the moon (candrasālokya), since they would be objects of begging from the gods and others, the word "food" (anna) [cannot apply literally], because it would contradict the scriptural injunction regarding the nature of the means required by the agent for the realization of the sacrifice, namely, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."

Since they are indeed enjoyers, the term "devouring" (bhakṣaṇa) must be understood in a figurative sense merely by virtue of their subsisting on the gods, and not in its primary sense consisting of chewing and swallowing;
with this very point in mind, he states that another scriptural passage accords with this meaning:
"For thus [scripture] shows."

The Śruti states that those who do not know the Self become objects of enjoyment for the gods like cattle, solely because they lack self-knowledge, and not because they are fit to be chewed [as food].

For just as oxen and the like, though they consume their own fodder, are objects of enjoyment for their masters because they assist them by pulling plows and so forth, even so, those performers of sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* who do not know the supreme reality become objects of enjoyment for the gods in this world through offerings of curd, milk, cakes, and the like, and in the next world through the service of attendants; such is the meaning of the Śruti.
Alternatively, there is another explanation for the phrase "because of not knowing the Self; for thus it shows":
one who knows the Self is one who knows the five-fire-vidyā (pañcāgnividyā); one who does not know the Self is "anātmavit."

For it is said, "The gods devour him who does not know the knowledge of the five fires," which is a censure intended to praise the knowledge of the five fires, since that alone is the subject under discussion.
By this, the purpose of the figurative expression (*upacāra*) has been stated. He now states the impossibility [of the literal sense] which serves as the ground for the figurative expression:
For thus the scripture shows that [the self] is an enjoyer: "He,
having experienced the splendor in the world of Soma..."
The remainder has its meaning not obscure. 3.1.2.8.

"Upon the exhaustion of [the results of] what was done, one possessing residual karma (anuśaya) returns by the same way and not by that way, having dwelt there as long as the [results of] his actions endure. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5) [This is the scriptural basis.]
Because of the connection [of the text],
as it is heard: "Whatever one does here" and "having reached the end of whatever karma has been performed here."
Furthermore, because death (*prāyaṇa*) manifests all karma through a single impulse,
it is certainly not logical that there should be a restriction of manifestation when the cause of manifestation is common [to all].
And since manifestation is the act of making [karma] ready to yield its fruit, therefore, every single karma has had its fruit experienced.
And action is opposed to its own fruit;
therefore, based on both scripture and logical reasoning, the descent occurs solely from conduct—that is, from behavior—and not from [ritual] action.
Furthermore, conduct and ritual action are well-known to be distinct according to scripture.
"As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become";
thus, by stating "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct," [the scripture] teaches that conduct alone is the cause of the womb, and not *karman*.

Or, let both *karman* and character (*śīla*) be the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) without distinction; nevertheless, even if this person is himself a performer of sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*),...

Even though he is free from latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) because his enjoyments have been exhausted, nevertheless, due to the force of the latent dispositions residing in his father and others, he will descend from the world of the moon and experience the fruits of their ripening—namely, birth, lifespan, and enjoyments.

For it is recorded in tradition that one person may partake of the fruit of the good or evil deeds of another who is related to them, as in the passage: "If a wife drinks liquor, half her body falls [upon her husband]," and so forth.
Likewise, there are scriptural declarations regarding the fruits of the *śrāddha* rites or the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice accruing to the father, son, and others.

Therefore, because of the introductory statement "as far as the completion [of their work]" (Chāndogya Up. 5.10.5) and in accordance with another scriptural passage stating "whatever he does here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.6), the quality of having "pleasant conduct" must be understood figuratively as residing in another related person—the performer of sacrifices and works of public utility (iṣṭāpūrta).

Thus, it might be concluded that those who have descended are indeed devoid of residual karma (niranuśaya), having already experienced their enjoyment; to this, it is replied: even when that aggregate of karma by which the fruit was enjoyed has passed away, they descend from the lunar orb still possessing residual karma (sānuśaya).
Why? Because of perception and recollection. Scripture perceived through direct perception is denoted by the word "seen" (dṛṣṭa), and tradition (smṛti) has also been presented.
Alternatively, by the word "seen" (dṛṣṭa), enjoyment in its various forms is expressed.

This is the intended meaning: the qualifiers "those of foul conduct" and "those of beautiful conduct" refer to those who have descended [from the world of Brahmā]. And when the primary sense is possible, it is not logical to resort to a figurative sense based merely on a connection [to that primary sense].
Nor is it correct to argue that the primary meaning [of the text] is impossible due to contradiction with the commencement [of the ritual] and contradiction with other scriptural passages;
for the words "as long as" (*yāvat*) and "whatever" (*yatkiñcit*) are applicable even in reference to those works of merit, such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, whose fruits have already been exhausted.

Indeed, the injunction "one should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives" does not prescribe the offering at times such as eating or walking about throughout one's entire life, nor even at midday and so forth, but rather in reference to the evening and morning times.

If it is argued that this is so because the injunctions for morning and evening times have the force of [establishing] a time, and since time cannot be an object of prescription (*anupādeya*), it enters as a causal condition (*nimitta*) even though it is not a subsidiary element (*aṅga*), we say: no.
For here too, such an interpretation is possible in accordance with the primary meaning of the passage beginning with "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*).
In that case, should the initial statement now be restricted in accordance with the concluding summary?
No, it is said in reply:
for even in accordance with the concluding summary, it is not possible for that [initial statement] to function without being restricted.

For it is not the case that all the *saṃpātas*—or rather, the *saṃpātas* of as many persons as there may be—are brought to exhaustion by the experience [of results] there by the performer of sacrifices and other rites;
for if the *karmāśayas* residing in other persons were exhausted by his experience, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, since those *karmāśayas* that have long been experienced and are no longer present are removed by the experience on the lunar orb.
Thus, the Śruti itself, contracting [its scope], even consents to a limitation that results from the requirement of systematic consistency (upasaṃhāra).
By this, the passage "whatever one does here" is also explained.

Furthermore, the performer of iṣṭāpūrta did not merely perform that much in this life, but also, by drawing water with the godohana vessel, he accumulated a new unseen merit (apūrva) resulting in cattle.

Thus, for one who has accumulated merit and demerit through the activities of speech, mind, and body day and night—destined to be experienced here or in the hereafter—it is not possible for that which is to be experienced in the world of mortals and so forth to instead be experienced in the world of the Moon.
Furthermore, unless there is an expiation, such as the knowledge of the Self, it is impossible for the *anuśaya* (residual karma) to be destroyed while its own fruit remains unexhausted.
Therefore, it is logical that this person, possessing that *anuśaya*, returns [to earth] by means of that very *anuśaya*.

Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya will state later that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) does not pertain to a single birth alone. Others, however, considering the fear of a total reversal [of the world] upon the exhaustion of all karma to be groundless, have described the section (*adhikaraṇa*) differently; thus he says: "First, some say... and so forth.
In this context, "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) refers to the remnant of karma that has already yielded its fruit.

Regarding this, the following is investigated: do those who have returned here [to this world] do so because of a residue of their performed sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) whose fruits have already been given; or rather, having exhausted those [karmas] entirely through experience, do they return here due to karma not yet experienced?

In this regard, since sacrifices and other such acts have been eradicated along with their roots through experience, it follows that those who return do so entirely free from residual karma (*niranuśaya*), due to the force of unexhausted karma. To this, it is replied: they return precisely *with* residual karma (*sānuśaya*).
Why? Because of observed analogy.

Just as when honey or ghee contained in a vessel has been washed away, the residue of that which adhered to the vessel—the remaining honey or ghee—cannot be washed away; so too, by analogy with that, this case is understood.
This is how it should be understood:
even when remaining near the lunar disc, one is not able to stay there by means of a mere remnant alone.
It is just as a servant, surrounded by a multitude of elephants, cavalry, and infantry, while serving a great king, might—due to the power of time—be left with nothing but his parasol and sandals.

"It is observed that [certain practices] ought not to be followed, and worldly tradition (smṛti) is rooted in that observation; thus, by virtue of both observation and tradition, they return with their latent tendencies (sānuśaya).
To this, he offers the following refutation:
"And this is not so."
Where the particle *eva* ought to have been used, the particle *iva* has been employed as a mere sweetener (*guḍajihvikā*).
The meaning is that when an object is accessible solely through verbal testimony, there is no occasion for inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*).
The remainder of the text has its meaning self-evident.
He restates the reason for the prima facie view: "As for what was said regarding 'death' (prāyaṇa). He then refutes it:

"That too [is] because of the existence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)" means that it is contradicted by scriptural passages such as "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct," which are intended to establish the existence of latent dispositions.
Furthermore, etc. [refers to the following].
For in this life, pleasure and pain are seen to be experienced in alternation;
if, however, through a single stroke at the time of death, the karmas that have pleasure and pain as their fruits were manifested simultaneously,
then their fruits would indeed be experienced all at once.
Therefore, based on the observation of the sequence of experiences, one must conclude that the stronger [karma] overcomes the weaker.
This should be understood to apply likewise to actions whose fruits consist of the experience of causes belonging to opposing classes of birth.
Furthermore, it is impossible for an action to be manifested and yet not yield its fruit.

For the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of actions consists in their being oriented toward the production of results. Furthermore, if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) were the manifestor [of those actions], then since beings born in the realms of heaven, hell, or as animals lack the capacity for action (*adhikāra*) regarding actions in that particular birth, there would be no production of new actions; this is because the previously performed actions, which have been accumulated in succession, are manifested at the time of death (*prāyaṇa*).
Because their [karma] is exhausted through the enjoyment of its fruit, they would have no remaining karma and thus would not transmigrate;
yet, due to the absence of self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), they would not be liberated—alas, what a wretched and afflicted state!
Furthermore, for the most part, only that which inheres in oneself (*svasamaveta*) manifests as *apūrva*, not that which inheres in another (*parasamaveta*).
"By means of that karma pertaining to their fathers and so forth, they shall subsist"—the remainder is easy to understand. 3.1.2.9.
"If it be argued [that the caste is determined] by conduct (*caraṇa*), [we reply] that Kārṣṇājini holds it is for the purpose of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*)."
By this, he uncovers and refutes the hidden seed of the prima facie argument—that those who descend [to lower realms] are indeed free from latent tendencies (*niranuśaya*).
For it is said: "Absence of anger toward all beings in action, thought, and speech, as well as benevolence and knowledge—this, the wise know, is virtue (*śīla*)."

According to the Smṛti, "conduct" (śīla) or "practice" (ācāra) is distinct from "residual karma" (anuśaya); nevertheless, the teacher Kārṣṇājini held that conduct serves as an indicator of residual karma because it is subordinate to it.
Thus, since the phrases "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct" indicate residual karma, it is established that those who descend are indeed accompanied by residual karma.
[Objection: "It is purposeless [to mention conduct], if this is argued. [Reply: No, because it is dependent upon that [residual karma]. (Sūtra 3.1.2.10)

For the Smṛti text, "The Vedas do not protect one who is devoid of right conduct," by using the word "Veda" as an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the meaning of the Veda, states that right conduct is subsidiary to the performance of the Vedic meaning; it does not mean that right conduct is an independent means to a result. Therefore, because it assists in the performance of the Vedic meaning, there is no pointlessness for right conduct, which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (kratvartha).
By this, it has been stated that conduct (ācāra) serves the purpose of the sacrifice, just like the fuel-sticks (samidh) and other such items.

Now, he says— “Even if conduct serves the purpose of the person”— to show that there is no fault even if it serves the purpose of the person or acts as a refinement of the person (puruṣasaṃskāra), just like bathing (snāna) and other such acts.
Thus, it has been stated that by the word *caraṇa*, which denotes conduct (*ācāra*), all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are indicated.

However, Bādari maintains that the word *caraṇa* refers to action (*karman*) in its primary sense alone—namely, good and evil deeds—as it is said: "But Bādari [says] they are indeed good and evil deeds. (BS 3.1.2.11).
The maxim of the Brahmin and the wandering mendicant (*brahmaṇaparivrājakanyāya*) and the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*).
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. 11. And it is heard in scripture even regarding those who perform undesirable acts and so forth. 3.1.3.12. *aniṣṭādikāriṇām api ca śrutam*.

Because of the traditional teaching of the Kauṣītakins, "Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon," and because the commencement of a body is impossible without going to the lunar world— given the fixed rule regarding the number of oblations in the passage "at the fifth oblation"—

for it is heard without distinction in scripture that those very waters, offered as an oblation into the fire of the woman, become "human speech" through the sequence of transformations into heaven, soma, rain, food, and semen.
Nor is this intended to refer to human beings, because it is heard that those of evil conduct go to their own source even as non-humans;
furthermore, for the purpose of going and returning, only the two paths of the gods (*devayāna*) and the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) are traditionally taught.
Because no other path is heard of;

because it is understood merely as a "station" from the statement, "Be born and die—this is the third station," and it is not perceived as a path; because even for those who have descended from the world of the moon, that state [of being a station] is possible;

and because, even for those devoid of enjoyment there, it is possible to go to the world of the moon for the sake of falling under Yama's power at Saṃyamana and other places—just as one going to a village passes by the roots of trees—due to the incompleteness [of their merit] and the absence of any other route.
Since the statement "not by either path" is intended to demonstrate that [the path] is not fully completed, and does not have the purpose of negating both paths, [an objection is raised]:
if it follows that even those who perform undesirable acts and so forth go to the world of the moon, it is replied: It is true that what is understood as a "place" (sthāna) is not itself a "path";
nevertheless, at the occasion of the reply to the question, "Do you know how that path is not fully completed?"...
Having first negated the two paths, one who declares a third state should explain its opposite for the sake of completion.
If, however, one were to return by that very same path and occupy a station like the continuous succession of birth and death, this would not constitute a third state.
For those who perform sacrifices and other meritorious deeds, upon descending from the lunar orb, do not reach a third state when they enter a pleasant or contemptible womb.
For what reason?
Because of descending by way of the path of the fathers.
Therefore, if even small creatures were to descend by this very same path, [they would likewise attain that state].
This third place cannot be a continuation of the stream of birth and death for them;

therefore, we understand that those who perform undesirable acts (aniṣṭādikārin), having reached the world of Yama along with the realm of Saṃyamaṇa and the seven regions of torment due to being subject to Yama's power, do not descend from the lunar orb.
Consequently, the phrase "whosoever they may be" refers specifically to those who perform desirable acts (iṣṭādikārin) and does not apply to all beings.
Furthermore, the phrase "at the fifth oblation" is intended to enjoin its own specific meaning and does not also intend to prohibit any oblations other than the fifth,

as that would result in a syntactical split (vākya-bheda). Moreover, since the Sūtra "But having experienced [the results] in the realm of Yama" identifies the realm of Yama as the point of departure for the descent, it follows naturally that the prohibition against the lunar orb being the point of departure is established.
And thus, this is indeed a *siddhānta-sūtra* (concluding aphorism);
if it were a *pūrvapakṣa-sūtra* (provisional position), it would have to be interpreted with some difficulty by supplying another doubt.
*Jīvaja* means born from a living being; *jarāyuja* means viviparous.
The attainment of one's own nature [occurs] because of logical possibility.

Although identity is not clearly understood from the passage "having returned as before, to space; from space, to air," nevertheless, because identity is more clearly understood from such statements as "having become air," the phrase "to space as before" also remains established in the sense of identity alone.
Nor is it impossible for one thing to become another,
given the traditional accounts of the transformation of Nandikeśvara’s human body into the form of a divine body, and the transformation of the divine body of Nahuṣa into that of an animal.
Therefore, one should not resort to a figurative interpretation by abandoning the primary meaning.
And the term "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is employed in the sense of a secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), because indication is possible within a quality.
As they have said: "The status of being secondary (*gauṇatā*) is indeed desired for a function [of a word] due to its connection with the qualities being indicated.
This being the position reached, we reply: it is the attainment of similarity (*sābhāvyāpatti*).
Those things whose nature (*bhāva*) is the same are "of like nature" (*sabhāva*); their state is "likeness of nature" (*sābhāvya*), which is to say, similarity (*sārūpya*) or resemblance (*sādṛśya*).
Why?
Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*).
He explains this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"For the primary existence of one thing as another is not logically possible.
This is reasonable: that the body of a deity might transform into the state of a python; however, [the opposite is not].
Because at the time of the god's body, the body of a python does not exist.
If, however, the god and the python's body were to exist simultaneously, the body of the god could not be made into the body of a python even by a hundred craftsmen.
For curd and milk cannot, at the same moment, be transformed into each other's nature.
Likewise here as well, because the subtle body and space exist simultaneously, they cannot be identical with one another.
This same reasoning should be applied to the wind and the other elements as well.
Thus, their existence [in those elements] must be explained as figurative, based on similarity to them.
[Objection: "Surely, let conjunction with space alone be indicated by the state of being space; what is the use of similarity? To this he says:
"And because of its all-pervasiveness, [the soul] is [connected] with space. (3.1.5.23) "[Not after a very long time], because of a specific mark. (3.1.5.24)
The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the term "durniṣprapataram" expresses a difficult exit, but not a delay.
The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, holds that since one cannot experience suffering in the subtle body without the gross body, "durniṣprapataram" indicates a delay. 3.1.6.24.
"Because of the mention [of the soul] as being presided over by another, as before."

It is heard in scripture that after attaining a similarity to space and contact with wind, smoke, and so forth, those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) are now born as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: do the rice, barley, and other stationary things become the locus of experience for those possessing latent dispositions, or do they merely undergo contact while these beings are presided over by other conscious subjects (*kṣetrajña*)?

In such usages as "a human is born" or "a god is born," since the root *jan* is well-known to mean "assuming a body," here too the primary meaning of "birth" is simply the assumption of a body such as that of rice and so forth;

thus, it is logical that those with residual karma (*anuśayin*) are indeed the rice and other plants themselves. Nor can it be argued—on the grounds that no specific karma is mentioned, as in the cases of "those of pleasant conduct" or "those of foul conduct"—that in the absence of such karma, rice and the like cannot become bodies, and therefore they merely come into contact with the conscious entities (*kṣetrajña*) who have already entered them.
Now, [the opponent argues]:

"It is reasonable that because the performers of sacrifices and other rites are mentioned in connection with those very rites, in the absence of such rites, rice and other grains—being presided over by other conscious beings (kṣetrajña)—would have no state of being a body; rather, they would merely come into contact [with the performers]. [To this we reply: This is not so.

Since the performers of sacrifices and other rites are mentioned in connection with those very rites, and since sacrifices and the like are tainted by the fault of violence (hiṃsā) and thus have a blameworthy fruit, it is logical that after the enjoyment of the lunar world, there may also be the fruit of suffering to be experienced in a stationary body.
Nor is it correct to argue that the general rule, "One should not harm any living beings," is sublated by the specific rule concerning the slaughter of the animal for Agni and Soma,

on the grounds that the general rule is weaker because it approaches the particular case through the medium of harming in general and thus operates more slowly than a rule that directly touches the particular case and therefore functions more quickly;
for it is not the case that what is strong necessarily sublates what is weak, but rather that this occurs when there is a conflict.
And there is no contradiction here, because they operate within different spheres of application.

For the injunction "One should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," being recited within the context of a ritual (*kratuprakaraṇa*), establishes its purpose as serving the ritual; it does not, however, remove the fact that it is a cause of harm to the person, which is brought about by the prohibition.
Therefore, let there be no contradiction: while the prohibition establishes that [the act] is a cause of harm to the person, the injunction establishes its purpose for the sacrifice.
As they say: "If someone standing in the midst of a sacrifice were to eat *kalañja* and such things, there is no deficiency in the sacrifice, because it has been accomplished exactly as prescribed."

Therefore, since "birth" (janman) is used in its primary sense, it follows that those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) are born with bodies made of rice and other grains; this being the position reached, the following is stated:

This would indeed be so if, as in the cases of "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct," a specific karma of those possessing residual karma were declared in relation to rice and the like; but this is not the case.
Furthermore, it is not possible for the ritual action (*iṣṭādi-karma*) to be the cause that produces the fruit of suffering to be experienced in the bodies of stationary beings (*sthāvara*).

Because that [pleasure] is, by its very nature, the sole cause of happiness; and because animal sacrifice performed for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) cannot possibly result in suffering—despite being included among those [acts]—since there is the prohibition "one shall not kill," which prohibits killing even when it serves the purpose of the ritual. For the prohibition "one shall not kill" applies only to acts intended for the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

For instance, since the negation "one shall not kill" is defined in dependence upon that which is to be negated, the negation is understood to serve the same purpose as that which is to be negated. Furthermore, this [prohibition] is not recited within the context of any specific ritual procedure— unlike such injunctions as "one shall not speak untruth" or "one does not perform those two [acts] at the animal sacrifice"— by virtue of which the prohibition of speaking untruth might be for the sake of the ritual,
and thus the prohibition itself would also be for the sake of the ritual.
Since the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are prohibited in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the prohibition itself must also serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*).

For if this were the case, it would be understood that even other subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) contribute to the sacrificial benefit (*kratūpakāra*) accomplished by the *ājyabhāgas*.

Therefore, [the prohibition] "one should not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*), which is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) and is imbued with a mandatory force (*vidhi*), pertains to the human activity [of killing].

Due to the contradiction between the injunctive suffix and the root-meaning, the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*)—namely, the act of injury—is abandoned, and only the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) remains as the object to be accomplished.
This is because the person, although not explicitly denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), is presented through the expression of the agent's activity.
Since that [human purpose] is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*), the injunction applies to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) by way of restating it.
Therefore, since the human purpose (puruṣārtha) is what must be negated, the negation itself—whose determination is dependent upon that purpose—also becomes a human purpose.
Thus, the resulting meaning is this: "One should not perform that killing which serves a human purpose.
For even in the case of a negation regarding that which serves the purpose of a ritual (kratvartha), it is not assumed that the act of violence (hiṃsā) provides assistance to the ritual.
Furthermore, when the fact that a person is the agent is directly perceived as the opposing factor, there is no basis for postulating [an unseen agency].
Nor can independence and dependence coexist in a single locus through the principle of "separateness of conjunction" (saṃyoga-pṛthaktva), as is the case with the eating of *svādi* and *ratādi*.

Therefore, the prohibition regarding the human goal does not extend to the ritual purpose; thus, sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* have pure happiness as their fruit, and do not have suffering to be experienced in a stationary body as their fruit either.
Because there is verbal designation [of them] even in the absence of the activity of karma, as in the case of space and so forth;
for those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*), there is merely a connection with rice and other such things, but not the state of being a body.
This very meaning is indicated by the statement of the general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*).
Moreover, regarding the primary sense of "the birth of those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) as rice and so forth":

it is indeed heard in scripture that those possessing latent dispositions, having attained the state of rice and so forth, are consumed by persons and subsequently attain the state of being semen-producers.
This would not be possible for those possessing latent dispositions if they were to possess bodies consisting of rice and so forth.

For if the state of having rice and so forth as a body were intended, then when the rice and other grains are cut and husked by threshing, the bodies of the rice etc. would perish; consequently, the *anuśayins* (those with residual karma) would depart [from that state].

How then could there be for the *anuśayins* the state of becoming those who emit semen (*retaḥsigbhāva*)? However, if it is merely a matter of association (*saṃsarga*), then even when the associated rice and other grains perish, the associated *anuśayins* do not depart; thus, the state of becoming those who emit semen is logically established.
The remainder has been explained. //24// 3.1.6.25. //25// 3.1.6.26.
"Then, the connection with the progenitor of semen":
for a child who is born immediately does not become a progenitor of semen; rather, it is one who has been born for a long time and has reached full maturity.
Therefore, from this as well, it is understood that there is merely a conjunction [of the soul with a body].

(Sūtra 26) Now, does it follow then that for all those possessing latent dispositions (*anuśayin*), there is only a mere conjunction, and thus in cases such as "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) and so forth, the same state would apply? No; he says:
"The body [arises] from the womb. (Sūtra 27)
This is easy to understand. //27//
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Thus ends the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, titled "The Determination of Dispassion through the Contemplation of Going and Returning.
**Third Chapter, Second Quarter:** 1.1. In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says. (3.2.1)
Now, however, the different states of that very *jīva* are elaborated for the purpose of establishing its self-luminosity:
Is the creation in the dream state as real as in the waking state, or is it composed of *māyā*?

Although both creations belonging to the waking and dream states are equally illusory (*māyāmaya*) because they are indeterminable (*anirvācya*) and distinct from Brahman, nevertheless, the waking creation persists until the direct realization of one's identity with Brahman.
However, it ceases through the direct realization of the self-nature of Brahman.
Thus, the meaning of the inquiry is whether this creation is like a dream-creation, or whether it ceases every single day.
"Of the two" refers to the states of abiding in this world and the next world. "Intermediate" (*saṃdhyam*) means that which arises at the junction (*saṃdhau*).

It is not of this world because it produces the direct perception of forms and so forth without the operation of the eyes and other senses belonging to this world; nor is it of the next world because the operation of the sense faculties and so forth belonging to the next world has not yet arisen, being something that will occur in the future.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of form and so forth for one who sees a dream;
therefore, because this [state] lies between the two worlds, the creation must indeed be real in its nature prior to the direct realization of Brahman as the Self.
This is the intended meaning: for here, all false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*) are cited as examples, yet their reality is asserted.
However, dream-cognition has been cited for its relevance to the present topic:
it is logical that an object which a cognition makes known exists exactly as it is,
because that state of being has ascended into the cognition.

If it is argued that because non-reality (*atathātva*) is not perceived, its status as an object of cognition is untenable due to its contradiction with reality (*tathābhāva*), and therefore non-reality is established by a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*); we say no, because the subverting nature of such a cognition is unestablished.
For two cognitions are contradictory only when they present opposing objects within the same domain.
Furthermore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is established through the determination of relative strength and weakness;
however, there is no identity of object here, since the arrangement is justified by the difference in time.
For just as milk, when observed, becomes curd after some time, so too silver, when observed, would become mother-of-pearl after some time;
or else, that object must possess various forms.
If one's eye is affected by exhaustion from intense heat, it perceives that object as having the form of silver; however, for one whose eye is assisted by mere light alone,
it perceives that very same object as having the form of mother-of-pearl.
In the same way, a blue-lotus flower that is both blue and red is perceived as blue when manifested by the sun's rays during the day, but as red when manifested by the light of a lamp at night.

Likewise, one does not perceive existing objects such as chariots while awake due to the absence of sleep, yet perceives them while asleep; thus, there is no contradiction, whether due to a difference in causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) or a difference in time.
Nor can there be a determination of the relative strength or weakness of the preceding and succeeding [texts],
because both are equal in that they operate within their own respective domains, and thus there is no reason for a decisive preference. Therefore, non-contradiction must necessarily be established.
Thus, this is established:
the conditions that are the subject of dispute are correct.
Because it is a cognition, like the cognition of pillars and so forth during the waking state;
the Śruti also demonstrates this point, saying: "Then he creates chariots, horses yoked to chariots, and paths."

Nor should the scriptural statement "There are no chariots there, no yoke-animals, and no roads" be interpreted as having a figurative meaning due to contradiction with the text "He creates. For the statement "He creates" is more authoritative, owing to its agreement with many other scriptural passages and its corroboration by other means of valid knowledge; thus, the statement "there are no chariots" must be explained as being figurative, meaning that chariots fit for perception in the waking state do not exist there, but it does not mean that chariots themselves do not exist at all.
For this very reason, the scriptural mention of an agent from another recension has been cited.
Furthermore, because its creation has the Supreme Intellect (prājña) as its agent, it possesses ultimate reality, just like the creation of ether and the other elements.
Nor is it correct to argue that it does not have the Supreme Intellect as its agent simply because the individual soul (jīva) is its agent.
Because it is the Wise One (*prājña*) alone who is the subject under discussion in the phrase "other than dharma, other than adharma";
and because even if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the agent, the soul is essentially the Wise One due to its non-difference from the Wise One;
furthermore, some dream-cognitions are seen to correspond with waking cognitions.

For example, in a dream, a Brahmin youth wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, said to Priyavrata: "Priyavrata, on the fifth day at dawn, the king will honor you by granting you land consisting mostly of fertile soil. While awake, having experienced such honor for himself, he considers that dream-cognition to be true.
Therefore, the creation during the intermediate state (saṃdhyā) is real from the perspective of ultimate truth.
This being the position reached, it is said:
"But it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety. (Sūtra 3.2.3).
This is the intended meaning here:
first of all, it is not possible for mother-of-pearl to be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of silver, in the same way that curd is a transformation of milk;
for never are silver vessels, even those kept for a long time in the house of a lord, seen to undergo the state of being mother-of-pearl.
It is not the case that at the time of another person's experience of silver, someone else with unimpaired senses does not experience and recognize its state as mother-of-pearl;
nor is it the case that the object possesses both forms.

Rather, due to a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), the nature of water is experienced by one at one time, while the nature of rays of light is experienced at another; this is the correct view.

In the ultimate sense, if this were water, it would perform the causal function (arthakriyā) consisting of the cessation of thirst—which is what is accomplished by water—and even that which is accomplished by a mirage, namely the manifestation of form.
However, no one’s thirst-born parching is ever quenched by mirages.
Nor is it logical to claim that water itself is of two kinds: that which quenches parching and that which does not.
The nature of water (*toyatva*) is pervaded by the capacity for that causal efficiency; therefore, that which does not perform it even in the slightest degree would not be water at all.

Furthermore, a twofold division of this [water] is accepted in order to account for the validity of the cognition "this is water," yet even if such a division were accepted, it could not be established.

For instance, one who perceives water in a mirage and thinks, "This is water produced by an incapacity [to perform its function]," would not run toward it out of thirst, just as one does when perceiving actual rays of light.
Now, [the opponent] runs toward [the object], considering it incapable [of being otherwise].
But what offense has been committed by the universal error of perceiving water in mirages, that one should bypass it and postulate another error?

Nor is there, as in the case of the cognitions of milk and curd, or of a teacher, a maternal uncle, and a Brahmin, a simultaneous apprehension of both the water and the mirage in a single cognition; for from our own experience, there appears between these two mutually contradictory [cognitions] the relationship of the sublated and the sublater.
In that case as well, the previously arisen cognition of silver is the sublated, while the subsequent cognition of mother-of-pearl is the sublater; for negation is preceded by prior attainment.

Since there was no means of attainment prior to the cognition of silver, it is impossible to negate the mother-of-pearl when it has not been attained. However, the mother-of-pearl cognition is capable of subverting the silver that was attained by the previous cognition.
And this nature of being a sublation is determined through one's own experience.
As they have said: "Because it is yet to come, the later does not sublate the earlier; for the earlier arises, and the earlier, in turn, never arises without having sublated the later.

Furthermore, the cognition appearing as present silver is not sublated by a subsequent cognition that takes as its object the mother-of-pearl existing at its own time, because the former does not take its future state as its object.
It is logical [to say] that there is no contradiction because of the difference in time.

Let it be that perception does not know its future state; however, the inference following upon it perceives stability—just like the cause for the existence of a benefit—as long as there is no occurrence of a cognition of destruction.

When there is no occurrence of a cognition of destruction, one thinks: "This silver is stable, because it possesses the nature of silver (rajatatva), like silver previously experienced and now re-identified."
And thus, a perception whose object is silver would, in reality, have as its object a silver that is indeed stable;
and since that silver would consequently pervade the time of the future cognition of the mother-of-pearl, it is sublated by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl due to this contradiction.
As it has been said: "For when silver is being perceived, it is perceived as something long-enduring;
thus, it pervades the time of the future cognition of mother-of-pearl."
Thus it is said.
Some explain that [the self] is apprehended by direct perception as something long-enduring;
that is incorrect.
If fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in the state of persisting for a long time, it is not within the scope of perception, because power (*śakti*) is beyond the senses.
If, on the other hand, it consists in pervading a subsequent period of time, that too is untenable.
Because there is no conjunction with a sense faculty that will exist at a later time, the all-pervasiveness delimited by that [conjunction] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Furthermore, unlike the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no mental impression (*saṃskāra*) here by which one might grasp [the object] even when it is not present.

Therefore, it should be understood that due to the force of extreme habituation, immediately after perception, it is grasped as "long-lasting" through a perception that arises more rapidly and includes an inference in its state of perishing.
For this very reason, not discerning this extremely subtle temporal interval, the Buddhists say:
"The object of perception is twofold: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*).
The apprehended is a single moment, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and [the determined is the universal]."
The object-moment is one, subtle, and that which is to be determined by conceptualization is the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
By this, the cognition of a dream is explained as being false.
As for what was stated regarding a true dream-vision, even there, because there is a lack of correspondence with what was related by the narrator, the Brāhmaṇāyana, [it is not true].
The conversation reported by Priyavrata is merely a coincidence, like "the crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya); it cannot serve as a valid means of knowledge for dream-cognition.

For such [cognitions] are frequently seen to be inconsistent, and the Commentator, while explaining that dreams are not fully manifest, has demonstrated this inconsistency by stating: "He slept during the night."
For even at the time of night, there is day in other regions such as Ketumāla and others beyond Bhārata; thus it is said, "in the region of Bhārata. (3) 3.2.1.4.
"And the scripture is indicative, and those who know it declare so;
that perception is indicative, and it exists by its own nature. (4)
The visible object is unreal; for this very reason, the emission of the final element and so forth, which are to be accomplished by the nature of seeing a woman, persist during the waking state,
whereas those things accomplished by a woman, such as garlands, ointments, and tooth-marks, do not persist.
"And by us, even in a dream, it is not the activity of the Knower (prājña).

The sense is that the inference of ultimate reality based on its being the activity of the Knower does not find a footing, as it is contradicted by perceptual cognition which serves as a subverting proof (bādhaka-pratyaya).
Thus, there is a third state of sovereignty (aiśvarya) intermediate between bondage and liberation. //4// 3.2.1.5.
"But it is concealed by the supreme meditation; for from that come its bondage and its opposite;

or else, because of the connection with the body, even that [is concealed]"—these two *sūtras* have been explained by us in the first *sūtra*. The commentary (*bhāṣya*) on these two is self-explanatory. //5// 3.2.1.6. // 6 // 3.2.2.7.
"The absence [of that state] is in the channels (nāḍīs), in the heart (purītat), and in the Self (ātman), because of scriptural statements regarding them.
For here, the channels, the pericardium, and the supreme Self are heard in scripture as the locations for the individual soul (jīva) during the state of deep sleep.
In this regard, is there an option (vikalpa) among these locations, or rather a combination (samuccaya)?
What follows from this if it is so? This is what follows:

when either the channels (nāḍīs) or the pericardium (purītad) are the place of deep sleep, then even upon the cessation of erroneous apprehension, there is no attainment of the state of the supreme Self (paramātman) by the individual soul (jīva).

Even upon the cessation of ignorance, another cause must be required for the individual soul (jīva) to attain the state of the supreme self (paramātman), and that cause is action alone, not the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna); for the latter is useful only for the mere cessation of erroneous cognition, and since the cessation of erroneous cognition is possible even during deep sleep without the knowledge of reality,
liberation (apavarga) results from action alone, not from knowledge.
As they have said: "Janaka and others, however, attained perfection through action alone.

Therefore, the Supreme Self alone is the locus of deep sleep by way of the channels (*nāḍī*) and the *purītat*; consequently, since the cessation of contrary cognition occurs therein, there is a partial utility for the state of the Supreme Self.
For by that [cessation], this individual soul (*jīva*) merely becomes established in that state.

Due to the absence of knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), because ignorance (avidyā) has not been eradicated along with its very root, the individual soul (jīva) undergoes emergence characterized by the states of waking and dreaming.
Therefore, this inquiry is purposeful.
What, then, was the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)?
There is an option (vikalpa) regarding the locus of the soul in deep sleep among the three locations—the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Just as a single king might sometimes hide in one palace and sometimes in another, so too the single soul sometimes resides in the channels, sometimes in the pericardium, and sometimes in Brahman.

Just as rice and barley, which are heard in scripture as independent alternatives serving as the material for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) used as a means for the sacrifice, are options for a single purpose; [so it is here].

Thus, by virtue of the mention of the seventh case-ending, or by virtue of the mention of "abode," the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth— each having the sense of being a single place of rest— are eligible for optionality, as they are independent of one another. Even where there is a scriptural hearing of the combination of two bases, namely the channels and Brahman— "having descended through the channels, he lies in the pericardium" (purītat)— and where the word "prāṇa" refers to Brahman— as in "then in this prāṇa, which is Brahman, that individual soul becomes one"— there too, the two are independent bases.
However, this is the distinction:

sometimes the channels alone are the support; sometimes, for one moving through the channels, the pericardium alone is the support; and thus it is established that for one moving by those very channels, sometimes Brahman alone is the support. Therefore, in their capacity as supports, the channels, the pericardium, and the Supreme Self are independent of one another.

Thus, it follows that there is an option between these, as in the case of rice and barley, or the Bṛhat and Rathantara chants. To this prima facie view, we reply: the individual soul approaches these—the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth—for the sake of deep sleep by way of combination alone, not by way of option. This is the intended meaning: the status of being optional for things prescribed as permanent is only postulated when no other alternative is possible.
As they have said: "In this way, although it possesses eight defects, since an option (vikalpa) between the sentences regarding rice and barley has been resorted to, no other course is found.

For rice and barley are prescribed as the respective materials for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)—which serves as the means for accomplishing the ritual at hand—without depending on one another; and each of these two is capable of producing the sacrificial cake individually.

In that case, if the sacrificial cake were produced from a mixture [of both], both scriptural injunctions—which enjoin rice and barley respectively as independent of one another—would be sublated. Furthermore, the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) cannot authorize their combination; for that injunction, proceeding by taking into account the subsidiaries exactly as they have been prescribed, is not able to alter them.
Furthermore, if there were a mixing [of the rites], there would be a change in their nature.
And it is not proper for the principal act to be repeated merely in accordance with the subsidiaries, as in the case of the injunction "one should perform both [pressings] at the Gosava sacrifice.
For no repetition of the principal is heard of here; and to perform it in accordance with the subsidiaries would be improper.
Nor is it correct to argue that, just as there is a repetition of the principal Soma sacrifice in accordance with its constituent parts—the cups for Indra-Vāyu and others—so too should it be here;
for in the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma," there is the prescription of a previously unknown sacrifice (*apūrvayāga*).
And in that context, regarding the sacrificial substance of Soma measured at ten handfuls, it is stated: "He presses the Soma."

And by considering another scriptural statement, "He pours soma over [the vessels]," it is enjoined that there are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the separate preparation of portions— by way of the liquid— to serve as the means for the sacrifice, intended for Indra, Vāyu, and others, within the one-span-high vessels; however, Indra, Vāyu, and the other deities are not enjoined with reference to the Soma sacrifice itself.
On account of which there would be an option between them based on their having a single purpose characterized by the accomplishment of the sacrifice;
however, not even a single vessel one span high is sufficient for the taking of ten handfuls of Soma juice, whereby the takings could be optionally chosen as being equal in purpose.
Nor is it logical that one should take only as much as fills a single upward-pointing vessel and discard the remainder;
for this would entail the consequence that taking ten handfuls would serve no visible purpose.
That [taking ten handfuls] would have a visible purpose only if all of it were utilized in the sacrifice.
And when a visible [explanation] is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is not logical. Therefore,

since the entire Soma juice is fit for refinement as a remnant of the sacrifice, and since it is impossible to refine the whole by means of a single drawing (graha), when one part is refined by one drawing, another part must be refined by a subsequent drawing.
Thus, due to the difference in their functions, the various *grahaṇas* (extractions) should be combined.
For this very reason, we observe their combination in the text: "The Adhvaryu priest extracts ten *grahas* at the morning pressing.
And since there is a combination, a sequential order is also logically established.
"The tenth [cup] is drawn for the Aśvins, but it is offered as the third";
likewise, "He draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.
Since these are to be combined, the meaning is that as much as is drawn for a particular deity, so much must be offered to that deity; thus, the sacrifice must be performed repeatedly.

If, however, they were to combine even those things that have been separated and offer them while intending a single deity, then both the acts of separation and the designations of deities would become purposeless with respect to the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
And it has already been stated that when a visible purpose is possible, it is not logical to postulate an unseen one.
Therefore, because a combination [of both materials] is necessarily required there, the repetition of the primary element is adopted even for the sake of following the subordinate quality.

Here, however, since there is no authority for assuming such a repetition, and since any material whatsoever may indifferently serve as the source-substance (*prakṛtidravya*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the individual scriptural injunctions regarding *vrīhi* rice and *yava* barley— each being independent of the other— serve as restrictive rules for a single purpose and thus deserve to be treated as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*).

However, it is not possible for the channels (*nāḍī*), the *puriṭat*, and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—which are mutually independent—to have a single common abode such that an option (*vikalpa*) between them would arise.
For a single referent does not follow merely from the mention of a single grammatical case-ending, since we observe the use of a single case-ending even for things that are to be combined, as in:
"He sleeps on a couch; he sleeps in a palace."
Therefore, since the mention of a single case-ending is inconclusive, another means of determination must be stated;
and that has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
"Even where the channels appear as if independent..."

By the passage beginning with "it makes [the soul] hear as the locus of sleep," the meaning is that a self-reliant scriptural statement must be interpreted in accordance with a dependent scriptural statement. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure.
Now, one might object: "If Brahman alone is the place of dissolution, let that much alone be stated; what is the use of introducing the channels (nāḍīs)? To this, he says:
"Moreover, here...
The word "moreover" (api ca) is used [to introduce a further argument].

This refers to a conjunction and not an alternative; the meaning is that the previous argument, when combined with this present one, establishes the point. The purpose of mentioning the channels here is for the sake of praising those channels which are employed in the instruction on the path.

When the sense organs are pervaded by bile (*pitta*), one does not perceive external objects; because of that, there is an absence of pleasure and pain, and consequently, an absence of contact with the afflictions (*pāpmā*) which are their causes—this is the praise of the channels (*nāḍī*).
But when the light is Brahman, it is self-evident.
Moreover:

The meaning is this: the statement that "the vessels or the pericardium are merely the support for the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva)" was made while provisionally accepting that the soul is something contained within a container;
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthatas), the soul does not possess the status of being contained.

For instance, the channels (nāḍīs) or the pericardium (purītat) are the substratum of the instruments which are the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the individual soul (jīva); however, the soul itself, being non-different from Brahman, is established in its own glory.
Nor is Brahman the substratum of the soul, because of their identity (tādātmya).
It is only when difference is conceptually constructed that the status of Brahman as the substratum of the soul is spoken of.

And thus, because the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) do not manifest during the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), the soul’s very nature as Brahman—that is, its having Brahman as its substratum—is what constitutes its support; it does not have the channels (nāḍīs) or the heart (purītat) as its support.

However, for the sake of initiating the state of deep sleep, the soul has the channels and the heart as its support only insofar as they are the substrata of its limiting adjuncts. Since these two cases have different meanings, there is no option (vikalpa) between them. Furthermore, [the soul] never [lacks a support], as in the case of the soul.

The meaning is that the soul's nature as Brahman, which is its general rule (*utsarga*), cannot be altered during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—provided there is no exception (*apavāda*) in the form of the waking or dreaming states. Furthermore, even those who maintain that there is an option regarding the location [of the soul] must admit that the state of deep sleep is characterized by the cessation of specific cognition;
and this is not possible in locations such as the channels (*nāḍīs*), which are distinct from the Supreme Self, unless there is identity with the Self.
For if this living self were situated there [in the eye], while maintaining the conceit of being distinct from the Self, it would necessarily possess specific cognition;
for thus says the Śruti: "Where, indeed, there is as it were another, there one might see another. But such is not the case when the eye is situated in the Self.
For the Śruti says: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see, or by what should one know?
Therefore, he states that even for one who abides in the Self, the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth are not the door: "Moreover, even if one were to admit an alternative state [of the soul]."
Here, an objection is raised: "But surely even that which has difference as its object... [The word] *bheda* means that which is divided (*bhidyate*).
The meaning is: "even when the object is being divided. He refutes this, saying:
"Certainly, it would be so."
To begin with, the individual soul (jīva) possesses no inherent limitation, because it is omnipresent by virtue of being identical in nature with Brahman.
However, regarding limitation based on adjuncts (upādhi), the soul would know only that which is in proximity to its adjunct, and not everything.
For Devadatta, who does not know Mount Sumeru due to its distance, does not fail to perceive what is nearby simply because of that lack of proximity.

Therefore, by stating that deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—in which all specific cognitions have subsided—is not like the state of a cow or other animals where [the senses] are equally predominant, he also refutes the alternative view:
"Nor do we [hold] here...

Since the entire mass of the Veda has been established as serving the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), it is not proper for even a single syllable of it to be something that does not serve a human purpose.

Furthermore, there is no purpose in establishing that during the state of deep sleep the individual soul (jīva) resides in the channels (nāḍīs) and so forth by way of its own nature; rather, there is a purpose in establishing its becoming Brahman. Therefore, the sense is that there is neither a combination (samuccaya) as co-equal primary elements, nor an option (vikalpa). The rest has been explained according to its definitive meaning (nītārtha). //7// 3.2.2.8. // 8 // 3.2.3.9.
"But that very [Self] [is the one who transmigrates], on account of the recollection of actions, the scriptural statement, and injunctions.

Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*) and others, this new section is commenced with the intention of expressing a distinction based on the delimitation by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
The claim that "it is that very same [Self]" is difficult to establish.
The mention of "he," or "another," or "the Lord" (Īśvara) is merely a formal possibility;
for it is impossible for one whose nature is pure and liberated to have an emergence produced by ignorance.
For this very reason, he is not mentioned at the time of the critical inquiry.

Furthermore, regarding an action enjoined for a single person that is to be completed over two days or more, since there is a memory (*smṛti*) of that which was performed on the previous day, the prefix *anu* is used to indicate recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
For this very reason, it is said, "I am that same [person]. And again: "He runs back according to the rule, according to his source."
*Ayana* means going; *āya* means coming. *Nyāya* is going according to rule.
The individual soul (*jīva*), according to its own rule, moves toward the waking state from the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*)—the state of perfect serenity—returning to its source (*pratiyoni*).
For one who was a tiger in the womb of a tiger, upon returning from deep sleep to the waking state, becomes that very tiger again and not another species.
This is what was said:
"In this place there is neither a tiger nor a lion";
and then, "if one who was sleeping there were to wake up."
For that living being who is asleep rises up within another body, and one situated in that other body rises up within the body belonging to the sleeping living being;
thus, there is no cessation of worldly activity in the other body—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "living being" (jīva) that is distinct from the Supreme Self.
Just as that which is called "pot-space" is not other than the supreme space,
yet appears as if it were other and persists as long as the pot exists; and it is not difficult to distinguish, because its limiting adjunct, the pot, is easily separated.

Thus, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is conceptually constructed through the limiting adjuncts of the distinctions imposed by the substrate of beginningless and indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*), does not in reality differ from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Due to the emergence and suppression of its limiting adjuncts, it appears as if emerged and as if suppressed;
consequently, even in states such as deep sleep, it appears as if suppressed, while in states such as waking, it appears as if emerged.

And since that adjunct consisting of ignorance and its latent impressions (vāsanā) flows on as cause and effect without beginning, it is easily distinguishable; therefore, the individual soul (jīva) conditioned by it is also easily distinguished. The state of swoon (mūrchā) is a partial attainment [of death], because it remains as the only alternative remaining [after waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. It differs from the states of waking and dreaming due to the absence of specific cognition, and it differs from the state of death because of the subsequent revival.

Therefore, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) itself is fainting (*mūrchā*), because there is no difference in the absence of specific cognition. However, prolonged lack of breath, trembling, and so forth are merely internal subdivisions of deep sleep.
For example, someone who has risen from sleep says: "I slept happily; my limbs are light and my mind is serene."
Furthermore, someone might say, "I slept as if in a state of suffering; my limbs are heavy and my mind wanders without stability. Yet, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is not differentiated by this much.
Likewise, even when there is another modification [of consciousness], fainting (*mūrchā*) is not distinguished from deep sleep.
Therefore, it follows that this is not the fifth state, because it lacks common worldly recognition.

To this objection, it is replied: although there is a similarity between delusion (*moha*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*) due to the cessation of specific cognition (*viśeṣavijñāna*), there is nevertheless no identity between them.
For dream and waking are not identical merely by virtue of the similarity in the presence of specific cognition.

As for the distinction between those two states based on the presence or absence of the activity of the external senses, there is also a distinction between deep sleep (*suṣupta*) and delusion (*moha*) due to a difference in their purpose, a difference in their cause, and a difference in their defining characteristics.
For deep sleep is a union with Brahman for the sake of dispelling fatigue,
whereas delusion is a union with Brahman for the sake of abandoning the body.
Although death does not occur even when delusion (*moha*) is present, yet death does not occur when delusion is absent; thus, delusion is for the purpose of death.

Since delusion has causes such as the striking of a pestle and the like, whereas deep sleep (*suṣupta*) has causes such as fatigue and the like, and since delusion is characterized by features such as the closing of the eyes while deep sleep is characterized by a serene countenance and so forth—despite the internal difference between deep sleep and non-sleep—there is oneness due to the lack of difference in their causes, purposes, and characteristics.
Therefore, although there is a merging with Brahman in both the states of deep sleep and delusion, the merging in deep sleep is not the same as that in delusion; thus, "half-merging" is stated.
This "halved" state arises from the combination of similarity and difference.
When this is not another distinct state, then, because of the distinction [from the other], one must resort to further effort for its dissolution.
"But since there is no difference [between the two], there is no need for effort; this is the purpose of the inquiry.
(10) 3.2.5.11. "For the Supreme Being does not possess both characteristics even from the standpoint of location, because it is so everywhere.
He states the intermediate connection:

Regarding the phrase "by which Brahman [it exists] in deep sleep and so forth": although it was established in the sūtra *tadananyatvam ārambhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ* that Brahman is indeed devoid of phenomenal manifestation (*niṣprapañca*), nevertheless, because many scriptural passages containing indications of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) are observed, doubt arises once again; therefore, this [present] undertaking is for the purpose of removing that doubt.
And since the knowledge of that [Brahman] is the means to liberation (*apavarga*), this inquiry is purposeful.
In this regard, because both sets of characteristics are heard in scripture, it follows that Brahman possesses a dual nature.

Even so, since there is a contradiction between having attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) and being without attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*), such that they cannot both be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), one must be inherent by its own nature (*svataḥ*) while the other is due to external conditions (*parataḥ*).
Nor is that which depends on something else non-ultimate;
for it is not the case that the invalidity of the eyes and other sense organs— which are inherently valid— is non-ultimate,
because that would entail the consequence that the effect characterized by erroneous cognition would never arise.

Therefore, since the authority of the scriptures possesses both characteristics, it follows that Brahman has a dual nature in the ultimate sense; to this, it is replied: even by way of its location—that is, by way of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—it is impossible for the supreme Brahman to possess the character of both, for one [nature] is ultimate and the other is superimposed. For if the form produced by limiting adjuncts were ultimate, there would have to be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman.
And that [possibility] has already been refuted.

Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), we see that—just as with a crystal gem which is naturally transparent and white—the limited form consisting of the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) of being infused with lac-dye, such as "having all fragrances" and so forth, is superposed upon Brahman; for the purpose of the Śrutis is to establish its qualitylessness (*nirviśeṣatā*).

Even regarding the state of having distinctions, since scriptural passages such as "And that which is this light consisting of fire in this earth" are intent upon establishing the oneness of Brahman, and because unity and multiplicity cannot coexist in a single entity, the presentation of multiplicity culminates merely as subordinate to unity; furthermore,

since multiplicity is already established by other means of knowledge and is thus merely reiterative (*anuvāda*), while unity is not previously known and can therefore be properly understood as the object of injunction, [the texts] proceed by censuring the perception of difference.

Furthermore, because numerous direct scriptural passages establish non-difference, certain scriptural texts concerning Brahman as possessing form are understood to have meditation (*upāsanā*) as their primary purpose— even though they appear to convey something else— provided there is no sublation [of that meaning],
just as, for example, the case of the embodied forms of the deities.
Furthermore, there are hundreds of scriptural passages (śruti) here that, by directly negating duality, are intent upon establishing non-duality;
and as for those few passages that express duality, their purpose is the dissolution of that very duality.
Therefore, in ultimate reality, Brahman is indeed without distinctions, of a single form, and has the singular essence of pure consciousness.

And it is established that specific qualities such as being "all-scented" (*sarvagandhatva*) or "dwarf-like" (*vāmanitva*), and so forth, are superimposed by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The remainder [of the commentary] has its meaning self-evident. Regarding this, some propose two separate topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).

Is Brahman characterized by both existence (*sat*) and manifestation (*prakāśa*), or is Brahman characterized by existence alone, or by manifestation alone? Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is taken up:
"And like light, because it is not purposeless. By the word "and" (*ca*), "existence" (*sat*) is also included.
Because it is not purposeless;
he establishes the conclusion regarding the word "Being" (sat) applied to Brahman: and he says that it denotes that alone.
It is mere luminosity.
For that which is called "existence" (sattva) is not other than the nature of luminosity;
rather, just as [qualities such as] being all-pervasive or having fragrance, existence is itself the nature of luminosity. Thus, the meaning is that Brahman does not possess both natures.
Having introduced this very point, it has been refuted by him:

if existence (*sattā*) and manifestation (*prakāśa*) were one, they could not possess the characteristics of both; if they were distinct, it would be rejected by the principle that "it is not so even from the standpoint of location" (*na sthānato 'pi*). Therefore, it does not necessitate a separate section of inquiry (*adhikaraṇa*).
But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is indeed no difference, just as in the case of light and its intensity.

Furthermore, if the dissolution of all [meditations] were equally intended for that purpose, then the statement providing the reason for the definitive conclusion—namely, "For that [Brahman] is indeed formless, because it is the principal subject"—would have no scope.
For this statement would find its scope only if some [passages] described form with the aim of meditation, while others were devoted to establishing the formless Brahman.

The meaning is that if all [the texts] were intended for the purpose of dissolving [all distinctions] and thus aimed at establishing the formless Brahman, the aforementioned reason for selection (*vinigamana-hetu*) would not exist.

The statement "because a single injunction (*niyoga*) is perceived, as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices" refers to the *adhikāra* (the qualified person's obligation);
however, due to the difference in their respective adjuncts (*anubandha*), the injunctions in these two cases are distinct from one another.
What is this dissolution of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)?
Is it the dissolution of a real phenomenal proliferation, like [the disappearance of] clarified butter through contact with fire;
or is it the dissolution of a superimposed [proliferation], like the state of being a snake upon a rope through the thorough knowledge of the reality of the rope?
First of all, the phenomenal world consisting of earth and so forth, which is real and common to all, cannot be eradicated by a mere individual.
Moreover, if the phenomenal world were uprooted along with its very roots by Prahlāda, Śuka, and other such preeminent men, the world would become a void;
furthermore, that which is real cannot be eradicated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
It has been stated that the knowledge of Reality (*tattvajñāna*) is opposed to the superimposed form [of the world].

However, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which consists of superimposed forms, can be eradicated by those very sentences intended to make known the reality of Brahman, which bring about the realization of the reality of Brahman; therefore, there is no need for an injunction here. For even by a hundred injunctions, one who is prompted with "Exert yourself toward the knowledge of the Self" or "Perform the dissolution of the phenomenal world" is not able to effect the dissolution of the phenomenal world without the realization of Reality.
Nor is it the case that the realization of the reality of Brahman—the meaning of the Vedāntas—does not occur for one without an injunction to know the Self;

for there exists the fundamental injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), which, by virtue of its intended meaning, establishes the entire mass of the Vedas as being directed toward the realization of their fruitful purpose.
Otherwise, even the injunctive passages concerning ritual action (*karma*) would themselves require further injunctions.
Furthermore, we have established in the *Tattvasamīkṣā* that there is no injunction regarding reflection (*cintā*) or direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*);
this point has been explained in detail precisely therein.

Therefore, these [passages] such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*), which resemble injunctions, are not actually injunctions, just like the [injunction] "One should offer oblations of wild-sesame gruel" (*jartilayavāgvā juhuyāt*).
This has been stated:
even words such as "that which is to be seen" (draṣṭavya) are primarily intended to direct the mind toward reality, not primarily intended as injunctions for the realization of reality.
Furthermore, the reality of Brahman is said to be free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca); therefore, no person capable of being enjoined can exist therein.
For the individual soul (*jīva*) would indeed be the one to be enjoined;

yet, if it abides on the side of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), what is there to be enjoined, since it has been annihilated? Or, if it abides on the side of Brahman, even so, it remains one who cannot be enjoined.
Because Brahman is not subject to injunction;
and if it is argued that although [the self] is non-different from Brahman, it is as if different due to ignorance and is therefore subject to injunction— that is incorrect.
Because ignorance has been dispelled by the scripture which makes known the ultimate state of Brahman,
there is no injunction [of action] even due to the absence of one who is to be enjoined.
Thus it has been said:
The term "jīva" belongs exclusively to the side of phenomenal appearance (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, since knowledge does not arise from that [text] alone even if it were intended as a source of knowledge, one must admit that its purpose is the exposition of reality (*tattva*).
In that case, it is better to accept that its purpose is indeed the exposition of reality, because this is necessarily to be admitted and is established for both disputants.
And he says that this has been accomplished by the method of knowing reality:
"even for one who is facing toward the object of knowledge.
And he says that it is neither possible nor logical [otherwise]: "nor is that possible, nor is it reasonable."

Nor by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
