Furthermore, since the Vedic tradition culminates solely in the injunction (*niyoga*), that which you have accepted through an examination of the scripture—that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self, which is not subject to injunction—is without authority because it contradicts the scripture.

Alternatively, if this scripture both establishes that the individual soul has Brahman as its self, which is not subject to injunction, and yet enjoins the individual soul, then it would be both purposeless and contradictory in meaning; thus he says:
Regarding the word "atha":

In sentences concerning the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites, it is appropriate for the individual soul (*jīva*)—though in reality not subject to injunction—to possess the status of an agent subject to injunction (*niyojyatā*), because the state of being such an agent is superimposed upon it.

For that scriptural sentence does not itself enjoin its status as an agent subject to injunction; rather, having relied upon a status as an agent subject to injunction established by worldly means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*), it prescribes the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
The sense is that this is difficult to reconcile, as it both removes the state of being one who is to be enjoined and simultaneously enjoins [the person].
Regarding the phrase "and in the case of being intent upon injunction":

the meaning is that, upon examining the preceding and following passages, the Upanishads (Vedāntas) are heard to be established in reality (tattva), not heard to be established in injunction (niyoga).

Furthermore, if the sentence were restricted to the sense of an injunction (*niyoga*), then—just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual—the knowledge of the Self would result in liberation, which has bliss as its fruit, only through an intermediate operation consisting of an unseen potency (*apūrva*), similar to how the fruit of heaven is attained.
And in that case, it would follow that liberation is impermanent and subject to degrees of excellence, like heaven; thus he says:
"Like the fruit of karma.
Furthermore, regarding the statements concerning Brahman:

for in the teachings that present [Brahman] both with and without phenomenal expansion (saprapañca and niṣprapañca), the unity of a single injunction is not established due to the difference in the objects to be accomplished (sādhya) and their respective adjuncts (anubandha).

In the case of the sentences concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *prayāja* offerings, although there is a difference in the auxiliary elements (*anubandha*), there is nonetheless non-difference because there is no difference in the objective portion of the qualification (*adhikārāṃśa*) to be accomplished. [The Sūtra] states: "For [the text] denies that the extent is limited to what has been mentioned in the archetype; thereafter it speaks of more. It declares the subject matter of this section: "There are indeed two forms of Brahman... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.1).

There are only two forms of Brahman; for Brahman, which in the ultimate sense is formless, there are only two forms superimposed upon it, by means of which it is itself made to appear as having form. He shows these two:
"the formed and the formless."
This is a restrictive determination through accumulation.

Here, the three elements—earth, water, and fire—are the form of Brahman that is "mūrtam," meaning having solidified parts, with parts interpenetrating one another; that is to say, it is "kaṭhinam" (solid). There are further qualifiers for that very same [form]: "martyam," meaning subject to death.
"Established" means non-pervasive;
that is to say, delimited. "Existent" means being distinguished from others; that is to say, possessing unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*).
Odor, moisture, and heat are the specific, non-common properties that serve as the causes for their mutual differentiation.
Of this very form of Brahman—consisting of fire, water, and earth, and characterized by these four qualities—this is the essence, the core: that which is this sun who shines.
Now, the formless consists of air and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); for that is not solid, thus it is formless, and it is immortal, having the nature of being deathless.
For a material object, being struck by another material object, perishes through the disintegration of its parts; however, such a state is not possible for that which is immaterial.
"This" (etad) means that which goes, moves, and pervades;
"this-ness" (etattvam) means that which is eternally beyond perception.
Of this formless, immortal, and eternal [Being], that which is His essence is this Person who is situated within that solar orb.
He is the instrumental self, called Hiraṇyagarbha and Prāṇa; for He is indeed its essence, its core, and its constant transcendence—this is with respect to the divine realm (*adhidaivata*).

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): that which is other than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the internal space (*antarākāśa*) is this formed [world]—the triad of elements that constitutes the body. This is mortal, this is stable, and this is existent; of this [formed world], [He is the essence].
Of this embodied, mortal, stationary, and existent [element], the eye is its essence—for the eye is indeed the essence of the existent.

Now, as for the unembodied: the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and that space within the self (*antarātman*), which is immortal and which is the "fugitive" (*tyat*); of this unembodied, immortal, and fugitive [element], that person who is in the right eye is its essence—for he is indeed the essence of the fugitive.
For it is understood from scripture that the right eye is the locus of Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the Liṅga in the form of the instrument (karaṇa).

Thus, the distinction between the conditioned forms of Brahman—the manifest and the unmanifest, pertaining respectively to the internal self and the divine—expressed by the words *sat* and *tyat*, has been explained in terms of their relationship as cause and effect.
Now, the form of that Puruṣa, the Liṅga which consists of the instruments, must be described.

This has been stated: the manifold form of the subtle body (*liṅga*), which consists of consciousness and is composed of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the manifest and the unmanifest, has thus been described in its entirety along with its impressions as the "truth-form" (*satyarūpa*). Now, having explained that, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of determining the essential nature of that which was called the "Truth of Truth"—Brahman.

Since the form of truth has been explained without remainder, it must now be stated what remains: the essential nature of that which is the "Truth of Truth," following immediately upon that [explanation] and based on the reason for stating it. Thus he says:
Now, therefore, follows the instruction—the declaration of the True Reality that is the Supreme Self. He declares it as:
"Not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
This section is intended for the purpose of explaining the meaning of this [instruction].
The meaning is: "Is it not the case that only this much is to be taught, and nothing else exists?

Here, by the particle *iti*, that which is proximate is referred to and negated by the negative particle *nañ*. And what is proximate is the two-fold form—consisting of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) along with their latent impressions—as well as Brahman, which serves as the delimiting factor for those two.

In this regard, the following is investigated: Is both the two-fold form along with its latent impressions (*savāsana*) and Brahman itself entirely negated; or rather, is it that Brahman alone remains, while the two-fold form along with its latent impressions is negated?
Although the true nature of Brahman has been established in various sections of the Vedānta, and the cognition of its non-existence has been censured;

Although its existence has been determined by the statement, "It is to be perceived as 'it exists'," that Brahman—whose nature is both being and consciousness—is nevertheless a universal (*sāmānya*) by virtue of being common to all forms, whether with or without latent impressions (*savāsanā*), and whether manifest or unmanifest.

These [forms], such as the manifest and the unmanifest, are its particulars (*viśeṣa*). Now, when each of those particulars is negated, the universal cannot remain, because a universal devoid of particulars is impossible.
As they have said: "A universal cannot exist without particulars, like the horn of a hare.
Therefore, even when those particulars are negated, because that universal Brahman does not persist, this is a negation of everything.
For this very reason, by the negation "Not this, not this," and by the statement "There is nothing else beyond this," the Śruti declares that the reality is indeed the negation of all.
The statement "He is to be apprehended as 'He exists'" is to be understood as an injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), and not as asserting that existence alone is His true nature (*tattva*).
Furthermore, the deprecation of the knowledge of non-existence is intended for the sake of praising Him.
Furthermore, any other exposition of the nature of Brahman found elsewhere is also for the purpose of negation, just like the exposition of the formed and formless aspects.

And although the negation is not explicitly present there, it is connected by virtue of its logical fitness, as they say: "Whatever has a connection with something, that [connection] belongs to it even if it is situated at a distance."
Therefore, the first position is that there is a prohibition of everything without distinction.
Alternatively, because the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of earth and so forth is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (pramāṇa),
whereas Brahman is beyond the reach of speech and mind and thus devoid of all means of valid cognition;

Regarding the doubt as to which [of the two] is being negated, the middle position is as follows: since the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would entail the contradiction of all perception and other means of valid cognition, whereas the negation of Brahman does not entail such contradiction, it is Brahman alone that is connected with the negation because of its suitability, while the phenomenal world is not, due to the opposite being the case; furthermore, the repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended to indicate the absolute non-existence of that [phenomenal world].
Therein, he refutes the first position: "First of all, the negation of both is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of nihilism (śūnyavāda).

This is the underlying intention: for these limiting adjuncts (upādhis), such as earth and so forth, are imagined through ignorance (avidyā), and are not like specific qualities such as redness or whiteness belonging to the universal "horseness."
Furthermore, the removal of an adjunct does not entail the non-existence or non-apprehension of that which is conditioned by it.
For when adjuncts such as a mirror, a gem, or a sword are removed, there is neither the non-existence nor the non-apprehension of the face.
Therefore, even when the adjunct is negated, there is no cognition of the conditioned object as being like the horn of a hare.
It is not correct to say that because there is no distinction in proximity, everything must be subject to negation;
for a negation is not possible without depending upon some positive entity (bhāva). Indeed, something is negated only in relation to something else.
For a negation without a substratum cannot be apprehended.
This has been stated:

when nothing else remains, if another is attempted to be negated, because that [remaining thing] cannot be negated, it follows that it alone must be the ultimate reality (paramārtha), and thus the negation is untenable.
He refutes the middle position: "Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable.

It is logical that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is acquired through innate ignorance (*naisargikāvidyā*), should be negated, because negation must be preceded by prior apprehension (*prāptipūrvakatvāt*).
But Brahman is neither established through ignorance nor through other means of valid cognition;
therefore, that which is apprehended by verbal testimony must be negated.

And thus, since that word which makes [Brahman] known is intent upon it, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman; how then could even its negation be supported by a means of valid cognition?

Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) based on the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning exclusion (*paryudāsa*), because such an option is impossible in the case of a reality whose nature is already established.
Furthermore, that which is beyond the reach of speech and mind cannot be grasped by the intellect.
And how can that which is impossible be negated?
It is logical, however, that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), established by beginningless ignorance, is first referred to and then negated with respect to Brahman.
Having this inconsistency in mind, it was said: "Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable."
He states another reason: "I shall tell you Brahman. This is because it would contradict the initial statement;
for, by examining the beginning, the middle reference, and the conclusion, it was established in the first chapter that all Vedānta texts have Brahman as their sole purport.
Furthermore, in the absence of such expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), a connection with these [negations] cannot be established by means of a prohibition situated at a distance.
Regarding the claim that because Brahman transcends speech and mind, there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding its negation, he says:
"Even the transcendence of speech and mind... [and so forth].
The Vedāntas establish Brahman with great effort,
and it has been stated above that this establishment is not a negation, because such a negation would be untenable.
But now it has been stated that [the description] is purposeless, according to the maxim: "For by washing away the mud...

Therefore, because Brahman is brought into proximity with the mind through the words of the Vedanta, its being beyond speech and mind is not literal; rather, this is merely the commencement of a method of exposition.
Just as objects such as cows are directly pointed out and perceived by being grasped by the horns, Brahman is not so [perceived].
As they have said: "And the determination [of Brahman] occurs by means of the dissolution of the manifold of difference.
Now, one might ask: if there is a negation of what is under discussion, why is Brahman itself not also negated? To this he says:
"For that which is under discussion and that which has been elaborated..."

The meaning is that "the primary" refers to the material cause (*pradhāna*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and not Brahman; for Brahman, being expressed by a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), functions as a qualifier of the phenomenal world and is thus not the primary subject. Therefore, the phrase "it speaks of something other than that" means that by the negation "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), it speaks of something else that is more [substantial]. As for the explanation of the passage "not indeed from this": when it is interpreted as "there is nothing else superior to this Brahman which has been designated as 'not this, not this' and so forth," then it means that beyond the negation of the phenomenal world, it speaks of Brahman itself.
This must be explained:
when, however, by the pronoun "not this" the negation of Brahman’s instruction is referred to, even then it is not to be understood as a mere negation of the phenomenal world;
rather, by that negation, Brahman in its positive form is indicated.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"And thereafter he speaks further.
This is because he speaks even after the negation.

Now, regarding the name of Brahman, namely "the Truth of truth," the Śruti explains it thus: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth. This refers to the subtle body (liṅga), which is compared to saffron-dyed cloth and so forth. That [subtle body] is indeed truth in relation to other things, but the Supreme Truth of even that is Brahman.

Thus, since the opponent asserts that which is beyond negation, it follows that Brahman is not merely the negation of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), but rather has a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*).
In this way, in the previous explanation, it was interpreted as "he states the etymological derivation";
however, in this [second] case, it should be explained as "he states 'the Truth of truth'."
"But because of the designation of both, like a snake and its coils.
By this, there is non-difference in the form of the snake.

However, it has been stated that there is difference in the form of the earring and so forth; therefore, because the objects [of cognition] are distinct, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference. Alternatively, there is no contradiction because they are always perceived as having a single object. For what do we consider to be "contradictory" if it is not something that is perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Furthermore, based on the authority of scripture (*āgama*), even difference and non-difference, though having a single locus, do not bring about contradiction when they are cognized, just like the light and the heat of the sun. Thus, both difference and non-difference are established through the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa*). //27//

He states the non-contradiction between difference and non-difference by means of another method: "Or, like light and its substratum, because it is of the nature of fire" (VS 3.2.6.29). Having thus presented the opponent's view, he states his own position:
"Or, as before" (VS 3.2.6.30).
This is the underlying intention: one who holds the view that there is non-difference in a thing by virtue of its being a substance (*vastutva*),
but difference by virtue of its being an earring (*kuṇḍalatva*),
must be questioned as follows:
Are the states of being a bracelet and being a ring distinct from the object, or are they non-distinct?

If they are distinct, then it must be said that the states of being a bracelet and being a ring are distinct [from each other], but the object does not possess both distinction and non-distinction from them.
For it is not possible for something to be either different or non-different from what is other than difference and non-difference, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if the states of being a bracelet and being a ring do not differ from the object itself, then in that case, what distinction of objects could there be between difference and non-difference? For they are non-different [from each other] by virtue of their non-otherness with respect to the object.

Nor is there a lack of contradiction between difference and non-difference simply because they are always experienced within a single object; for if even things whose intrinsic natures are contradictory were not contradictory, where indeed could contradiction be established?

Furthermore, that which is always experienced yet cannot withstand critical inquiry cannot be real, as this would lead to the absurd conclusion that the identification of the body with the self—which is also always experienced—is likewise real.
This has been elaborated by us in the first sūtra, and thus it is not elaborated here.
Therefore, the distinction of the state of being a living soul (jīva) for the one Self is merely the play of beginningless ignorance (avidyā) and is not real.
Consequently, upon the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), liberation (apavarga) is established.
If this [bondage] were real, its cessation would not be possible through knowledge;
nor is there any means for liberation other than the knowledge of reality.
As the Śruti says: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey."
The remainder has its meaning unobscured. //29// 3.2.6.30. // 30 // 3.2.7.31.
*Paramataḥ setūnmānasambandhabhedavyapadeśebhyaḥ* (On account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference).

Although it has been determined that there is no reality apart from Brahman because of the abundance of scriptural texts, nevertheless, this section is commenced for the purpose of resolving the apparent contradiction with those scriptural passages concerning the "bridge" and so forth.
"Jāṅgala" refers to dry land.

"Prakāśavat," "anantavat," "jyotiṣmat," and "āyatanavat"—these are the four feet of Brahman. Half of those four feet are eight, which are the hooves. Since these eight belong to this Brahman, Brahman is said to have eight hooves (aṣṭaśapha).
That which has sixteen parts (*kalā*) is called "sixteen-parted" (*ṣoḍaśakala*).

These are as follows: east, west, south, and north—these four are like parts or digits (*kalā*). This is the first foot, named "The Radiant" (*prakāśavān*). Because one becomes preeminently radiant through meditation upon this, it is called the "Radiant Foot."

Now, there are four other parts: earth, intermediate space, heaven, and the ocean; this is the second foot, named "The Endless" (*anantavān*). When this foot is meditated upon with the quality of endlessness, it brings about endlessness for the meditator; thus, it is the "Endless" foot. Now, fire, sun, moon, and lightning are four other parts; that is the third foot, named "The Luminous" (*jyotiṣmān*). Because one becomes luminous through meditation on it, it is the "Luminous" foot.
Now, the four parts—namely, the sense of smell, sight, hearing, and speech—constitute the fourth foot, called "possessing a locus" (*āyatanavān*).
For these, beginning with the sense of smell, serve as the means for experience by depending upon the mind as their locus; thus, this foot is named "possessing a locus.
In this way, Brahman has been revealed by the Śruti as having four feet, eight hooves, and sixteen parts.
Therefore, there exists something else beyond that Brahman.
This might be argued:
"If it exists, then let its extent be stated definitively as being just this much."
Therefore he says: "It exists immeasurably.
This means that it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not merely to this extent.

And the designation of difference is threefold: by way of locus, by way of extension, and by way of limit. (31) But [the term "bridge"] is due to commonality; for the quality of supporting the world and its boundaries is the commonality with a bridge. (3.2.7.32) Sāmānyāt tu. The capacity to sustain the universe and its limits constitutes the similarity to a bridge.

For just as threads sustain a cloth precisely because they are its material cause, so too Brahman sustains the world because it is its supporting cause. Moreover, Brahman is the sustainer of the world's boundaries;
otherwise, the ocean—turbulent with garlands of exceedingly swift, massive, and powerful waves—would swallow the entire circle of the earth.
Or the submarine fire, with its mass of flickering flames, might reduce the world to ashes;
or a violent wind might suddenly shatter the cosmic egg.
And so says the Śruti: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows," and so forth. (32) 3.2.7.33.
The mind has the intellect as its purpose, like feet.
Of the mind—which is a representative image (*pratīka*) of Brahman upon which the nature of Brahman has been superimposed—speech, smell, sight, and hearing are the four feet.

For the mind moves through the spheres of the speakable, the smellable, the visible, and the audible by means of speech and the other organs; thus, because it serves as the common medium for movement, the mind is the "feet" of Brahman with respect to the internal self (*adhyātman*).
Of the ether, which is the representative symbol (*pratīka*) of Brahman, there are four feet: fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters.
For these are perceived as being attached to the pervasive sky, like the feet of a cow; thus it is called a "foot.
Having thus explained this Vedic illustration—that [Brahman] is "like that which has feet"—he states this worldly illustration as well:

Alternatively, "like the feet" means "just as in that case. Here too, the meaning is that it is for the sake of the conventional usage of meditation (*ādhyāna*) for those of dull intellect. //33// 3.2.7.34.
"Because of the difference in location, as in the case of light and so forth.

Due to the connection with specific locations in the form of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi), the specific cognition that arises during the waking and dreaming states ceases and is suppressed when those adjuncts are withdrawn, which constitutes the state of deep sleep.
Likewise, the threefold designation of distinctions regarding Brahman is also dependent upon the differences among its limiting adjuncts.

Just as the rays of the sun, entering through the openings of a palace lattice, appear divided due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of those lattice-openings, yet upon the removal of that [condition] they become one with the solar orb and thus connect with it—so it is here as well. 3.2.7.35.
This might be so.

Why is this relation here explained as being somehow a state of oneness (*ekībhāva*) rather than a primary [identity] itself? He answers this with the following sūtra: "And because it is logical" (*upapatteśca*). For the phrase "he has gone to his own self" (*svam apītaḥ*) expresses a relation of identity with one's own nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

The meaning is that if intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is touched upon by this relation-ness, then, being intrinsic, it is not distinct from identity (*tādātmya*), as has been established in the *Tarkapāda*.
Likewise, difference (*bheda*)—whether threefold or otherwise—is also intrinsic; such is the meaning. 3.2.7.36.
"Likewise, because of the negation of another... [is the sūtra].

This has been explained by means of an easily understood commentary. 3.2.7.37. *By this [sūtra], omnipresence [is established] on account of the words "extent" (*āyāma*) and so forth.* Even though the non-duality of Brahman is established, the state of being omnipresent—the all-pervasiveness and the fact that everything possesses the nature of Brahman as its own form—is not yet proven; therefore, he says:

By this refutation of the "bridge" and other [theories], by the refutation of the arguments of others, by the recourse to the negation of other [views], and by the presentation of its own proof, the all-pervasiveness of the Self is also established.

Since non-duality is established, this entire manifestation of the world-appearance, being indeterminable, has Brahman as its substratum; thus, because everything is connected to Brahman, it is established that Brahman is all-pervading. 3.2.8.38.
*Phalamata upapatteḥ* (The fruit [arises] from That, because it is logical). This section begins the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
It might be argued:
"From where does Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and free, derive its status as the Lord (Īśvara), and from where its being the cause of fruits? To this, he says:
"Of that very Brahman, in its empirical [state]..."
This is not considered with reference to its ultimate (pāramārthika) nature, but rather its conventional (sāṃvyavahārika) nature;
and this has been established by us while explaining the statement, "Brahman is built up through austerity.
The desired fruit is heaven.
As they say: "That happiness which is not intermingled with suffering, nor immediately swallowed by it, and which is brought about by desire—that is the locus of the term 'heaven'.
Unwanted [suffering] is that which is to be experienced in places such as the Avīci hell.
The mixed [world] is that which is to be enjoyed by human beings.
Regarding that, it is first established that the fruit must arise from the Lord, who is propitiated by actions.
Now, as to why the fruit does not arise from action alone, he says:
Regarding action (*karman*), which perishes moment by moment— that is, it is directly perceived to perish— the opponent objects:
"This may be so regarding action."

It might be argued that "the karma perishes. The meaning is that even though the fruit has been acquired, it is not experienced either because the [agent] is unfit to enjoy it or because of an obstruction by another karma. He refutes this:
Even that is not entirely pure;
for the qualified aspirants do not desire, "May heaven obtain itself," but rather, "May it become an object of enjoyment for us."
Therefore, since a result is of such a nature as is desired by these [beings], the result is indeed that which is to be experienced;
and since such a [result] does not exist immediately after the action, how can it be a result?
Even so, it is a result by its very nature.
Furthermore, since heaven and hell consist of the most intense pleasure and pain, there must necessarily be an experience—another name for which is "enjoyment"—with respect to them.
Therefore, it is determined that if things capable of being experienced are not being experienced, they do not exist, like the horn of a hare. [The opponent] objects:

Now, it might be argued: "Let there not be the production of the fruit immediately after the action; rather, the fruit will arise from the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is not the direct effect of the action. He refutes this, saying:
"That also is not so."
It has been established through both perception and scripture that whatever is insentient functions only when presided over by a sentient being;
therefore, even the *apūrva* (unseen force), being insentient, must function only when presided over by a sentient being and not otherwise—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he states that the *apūrva* is not even an object of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).
"Because its existence is declared in scripture. (3.2.8.39) And because it is heard [in the Vedas].

"It is indeed heard thus.
Now, an objection is raised: do not such scriptural injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" enjoin the sacrifice as a means toward the result?
For instance, even if sacrifices and the like are themselves the action (*kriyā*) and there is no *bhāvanā* distinct from them, nevertheless, [the result] is not understood from their own words.

Since [the actions] are understood as having a nature to be accomplished (*sādhya*) that exists in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, they do not require another thing to be accomplished; therefore, they cannot be connected with heaven as a further object to be accomplished.

Even if there were an existence other than those [actions], nevertheless, even that expectation of a verbal expression (*bhāṣya*) would refer only to what is brought forward by its own word and established previously.

One must not abandon the meaning of the verbal root [to assume it is the object of cultivation], nor can one accept that "heaven" and so forth— though mentioned in a separate word as a qualification of the person— are the objects of cultivation (*bhāvya*). Furthermore, it is impossible for two things to be related as goals (*sādhya*) within a single sentence,
as that would result in the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*).

Not only verbally but also in reality, it is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone that is directly the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through human effort and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and not heaven (*svarga*) and the like, because the latter are not pervaded by that [effort].

Since heaven and the like are denoted by nouns (*nāmapada*) and thus exist in a state of being already established (*siddharūpa*), they are connected as subordinate factors (*guṇa*)—as means (*sādhana*)—to the object to be accomplished expressed by the verb (*ākhyātavācya*), which is the meaning of the root, according to the maxim: "That which is already established (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being (*bhavya*).
Accordingly, there is a Sūtra of the Great Sage (Jaimini): "When substances are connected with an action, their connection is as subordinate factors."

And thus, since ritual acts such as sacrifice are not desired by a person because they are of the nature of suffering, and since heaven and the like—which are desired—are not their results, sacrifices and the rest do not benefit the person; and since a person has no mastery over those things that do not benefit him, he cannot be an *adhikārī* (eligible agent) with respect to them. Therefore, in order to avoid the futility [of the Veda] demonstrated by this lack of eligibility (*adhikārābhāva*), [the author proceeds as follows].

The entire Veda has as its ultimate purpose the knowledge of Brahman—which consists of eternal bliss and is entirely free from the association of all suffering—by means of dissolving the manifold world of duality (*bhedaprapañca*). For instance, throughout the Veda, the dissolution of some particular distinction is perceived in various places;
for example, in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," there is the dissolution of the identification with the body as the self.
In this context, at first glance, an eligible candidate (*adhikārī*) is understood—one who is distinct from the body and capable of enjoying fruits in the hereafter.

Since eligibility has been refuted by the aforementioned sequence, that [self] which appears despite being non-existent and incapable of withstanding inquiry remains merely as a means; thus, by this sentence, which is intent upon that [ultimate goal], the dissolution of the identification with the body is effected.

Even in the case of the injunction, "One desiring cattle should perform the *praṇayana* with a milking vessel," there is a sublation of the distinction between different qualified persons (*adhikāribheda*), because at first glance one understands that this applies to those already qualified for the primary rite.

Furthermore, prohibitory statements directly prohibit engagement through their negation of activity; and injunctive statements such as, "One desiring a village should sacrifice with the *Sāṃgrahaṇī*," do not aim to counteract the performance of the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* and other rites themselves, but rather serve to prohibit those well-known worldly means by prescribing alternative methods.

Just as one might say, "Eat poison" or "Do not eat in this person's house," so too the status of a treatise as a treatise is established by its prohibition of activity impelled by passion and the like. For if it were to permit activity based on passion by means of teaching methods, it would result in the undesirable consequence of it not being a true treatise, due to its furthering that passion.
But by negating that [connection], the scripture bestows focused attention upon Brahman and thus becomes a true scripture (*śāstra*).

Therefore, since the connection between action and its fruit lacks scriptural authority, the production of diverse fruits arises from the Lord alone—without dependence on karma—aided by beginningless and manifold ignorance (*avidyā*).

How then is there an injunction (*vidhi*)? What is it here? Since an injunction consists merely in the act of impelling, and since that is possible even without a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), [there is no need for one].
Wishing to dispel the doubt that "not every instigator depends upon an authorized agent, since instigators such as the wind do not depend on one," he says:
"And in that case, because the Vedic injunction enters into the state of being the object [of performance], it is understood that the sacrifice is the producer of heaven."
Otherwise, the sacrifice would result in being something that is not performed at all.
This is the intended meaning: for an injunction (*vidhi*) is indeed an instruction (*upadeśa*), as it has been stated, "The knowledge of that [Dharma] is instruction."
Furthermore, instruction regarding an action that serves the purpose of one who is to be enjoined is well known in both worldly usage and in the treatises.
For example: "One desiring health should eat when [the previous meal] has been digested," or "This is a good path; may you go by this."
However, unlike [the case of] ignorance and so forth, the purpose of an instigator is not [the motive] there, because it is intention (*abhiprāya*) that functions as the motivator,

and that [intention] is impossible in what is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). Furthermore, we have established in the *Nyāyakaṇikā* that this instruction has as its object an operation that serves the purpose of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), namely, an operation that accords with what is required by the performer.
And thus, in injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," sacrifices and the like are understood as the means for attaining what is desired by the one desiring heaven and so forth;
otherwise, they would not follow the person who is to accomplish the result.
As it has been stated by the Seer (the Ṛṣi): "But [the Veda] is not a means of accomplishment [for itself], because its purpose is that [other end]."

If [the words] such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) had as their sole purpose a mere instigation devoid of being a means required by the performer, then sacrifices and the like would be ineffective actions;
the meaning is that they would not find an achiever.

Furthermore, even though these [results] are directly to be brought about (*bhāvya*) by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), they cannot be the objects of the productive activity when its scope is delimited by an injunction that prescribes them as means required by the agent.
By this [definition], those things which do not provide benefit to persons would not be objects of [human] endeavor;
for suffering, being of the nature of pain, is not a locus for the accumulation of volitional action (*cetanā*),
whereas heaven and the like are so because they are preceded by cultivation and are underlain by desire.
And because [the sacrifice] consists of joy (*prīti*):

even for those things denoted by names and words—which serve as qualifiers of the person—their status as an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) is perceived, characterized by being the objective of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, since the state of being an end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by the fruit is defined by its being the object to be brought about by the productive activity engaged for the sake of the fruit, and this is characterized by the state of being accomplished through sacrifices and the like, there is no possibility of their coexistence within a single sentence due to a lack of equal primacy.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the fact that being merely "to be cultivated through meditative realization" (bhāvanābhāvyatva) constitutes being "to be accomplished by means of sacrifice" (yāgādisādhyatva), even in the case of an instrument;
otherwise, that [status] would be eliminated everywhere,
since axes and the like would likewise lack such a status in relation to acts of cutting and so forth.

It is established that even though the fruit (phala) is not directly pervaded by the cultivation (bhāvanā), because it stands as the object of that [cultivation] and is thus omnipresent, the person desiring heaven (svargakāma) possesses the qualification (adhikāra) for sacrifices and the like which are the means to attain heaven. Furthermore, injunctions regarding sacrifices such as the Sāṃgrahaṇī—which concern objects not otherwise obtained—cannot function as exclusions (parisaṃkhyā) or as restrictive rules (niyama).
Moreover, in the absence of such qualification, it is impossible to establish either the dissolution of the body and the self, or the dissolution of the distinctions among qualified persons.
If it appears [merely] at first glance, its intent is directed toward that appearance alone and not toward the actual meaning;
for when a sentence can be understood as having a purpose directed toward a meaning that is naturally perceived, it is not appropriate to assume an incidental intent toward something else.
Nor does this entail a contradiction with the scriptures.

For even regarding the means to heaven and so forth, its status as a treatise (*śāstra*) is established; for being a treatise consists precisely in teaching what is beneficial for persons. Since it teaches what is beneficial for both persons with passion and those free from passion, it is universal in its audience, and thus there is no contradiction with reality.
Therefore, it is established that sacrifice is the producer of heaven because it attains the status of being the object of an injunction;
or rather, it is a certain intermediate state of the action—
that is, the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of the action.

This is what is meant: for that which is heard in scripture as the instrument (*sādhana*) of action with respect to its fruit must be the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of that very [action] in order to bring it to completion.
And it is not logical to say that an operation exists only when there is an agent possessing that operation, and not when there is none.
Even though the [subsidiary] apūrvas of the Āgneya and other rites do not exist [as independent entities], they serve as intermediate operations when the supreme apūrva is to be produced.

Furthermore, even though the act of drinking oil does not exist [as a separate entity], it serves as an intermediate operation when nourishment is to be brought about by it, because the various transformations of the oil in the interim are its intermediate operations.
Therefore, it is logical that the apūrva, which is the effect of the ritual action, serves as an intermediate operation when the fruit is to be produced by the ritual action.
Furthermore, when something is postulated because the production of an effect would otherwise be inexplicable, then it is either the prior state of the effect itself,
or [the prior state] of a cause that is not diverse.
The ellipsis is "if [the world arises] from Īśvara alone.

The intention is that if the production of the two-fold effects were due to auspicious and inauspicious *karma*s, then it would follow as a logical consequence that [Īśvara] possesses passion and other such afflictions. 3.2.8.41.
But Bādarāyaṇa [holds the former view], because of the mention of a cause.
For conceptualization is logical only when it follows what is observed, and not otherwise;
indeed, clay lumps, staffs, and so forth have never been seen to be capable of producing jars and the like without being presided over by a potter or similar agent.
Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] due to instances such as lightning or wind, which are not preceded by effort.
For even those [examples] cannot serve as instances of deviation (vyabhicāra), since they too are merely the objects of conceptual construction.

Therefore, whether it be action (*karman*) or the unseen potency (*apūrva*), that which is insentient cannot independently proceed toward its own effect without being presided over by a conscious agent. Nor is mere sentience alone sufficient for this purpose, if it is devoid of the specific knowledge regarding the nature, general application, and particular deployment of the action;
otherwise, one might falsely suggest that the goal is already established simply through the presiding of the *kṣetrajña* (the embodied soul) who lacks such knowledge.
Therefore, just as it has been thoroughly established through thousands of observations of the production of various temples, watchtowers, gate-towers, archways, and so forth—

that insentient things initiate activity only through the superintendence of a conscious being— so too, the sentience of the deity, which is well-known from the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas and remains uncontradicted, cannot be denied; this was also clearly determined in the Devatādhikaraṇa.

It is also well-established that when a worldly Īśvara is propitiated with devotions filled with intense faith—consisting of giving, service, prostration, joining of palms, and praise—he, being pleased, bestows upon the worshipper a fruit corresponding to his own nature; and conversely, through hostile acts, he brings harm to the adversary.

Therefore, in this context, it is contrary to what is observed [in the world] to claim that either mere karma or the *apūrva* (unseen force), being insentient and not presided over by consciousness, produces a fruit.

Just as it is postulated that a destroyed action does not produce a fruit because that would contradict what is observed, so too is it here. Likewise, the view that a sacrifice consisting of the worship of a deity produces a fruit without propitiating the deity is also contradicted by observation;
for a service consisting of the worship of a king does not lead to a result without propitiating the king.
Therefore, for the sake of conforming to what is observed, the propitiation of the deity is produced even by means of sacrifices and the like.
And thus, since the production of the enduring fruit is logically accounted for through the favor of the deity alone, there is no need for an *apūrva* (unseen potency).
Likewise, it is well known from the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* that even by inauspicious action, there occurs an offense against the deity.
From that [state of being a deity], there would follow the production of undesirable results for those who abide [there].
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that a deity who produces results corresponding to the deeds of those who perform good or evil acts is subject to hatred or partiality.
For a king, when favoring one who acts rightly or punishing one who acts wickedly, does not thereby become hateful or attached; likewise, so it is with the transcendent Lord (Īśvara).

Just as when the supreme *apūrva* is to be accomplished, there is a utility for the *utpattyapūrvas* and the subsidiary *apūrvas*, so too, in the propitiation of the Principal [Deity], there is a utility for the propitiations of the subsidiaries and the propitiations of the [subsidiary] origins; it is like the propitiation of a king’s ministers and their attendants being useful for the propitiation of the sovereign himself. Thus, everything is the same except for the difference in attachment.

Therefore, the fruit results from the propitiation of the deity in a manner that does not contradict perceived reality (*dṛṣṭa*), and not from an unseen potency (*apūrva*) or from the mere act itself; for the scriptural and traditional designations of the cause have already been explained.

As for those who, believing that the operation of the intermediate agent (*antaryāmī*) in the production of the fruit is eternal and common to all, criticize the section belonging to the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)—this concludes the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāmatī* commentary on the division of [the *Vivaraṇa*].
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, titled "The Purification of the Meanings of the Words *tat* and *tvam*.
Now begins the third quarter of the third chapter: 3.3.1.
All Vedānta texts convey the same cognition, because there is no difference in the injunctions and other such factors.
He states the connection with what precedes:

"The Brahman that is to be known has been explained. Considering that the knowledge whose object is the reality of Brahman devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) [is what was explained], he raises an objection:
Now, it might be argued that Brahman is indeed an object of cognition (*vijñeya*).

For if Brahman possessed parts, then cognitions directed toward Brahman as qualified by those parts would differ according to the difference in their objects; thus, parts of Brahman have been refuted by the [text] beginning with "prior, posterior," and so forth.
Furthermore, it has been stated that Brahman does not possess a manifold nature (*nānā-svabhāva*), because cognitions do not become differentiated on account of a difference in intrinsic nature.
"Of a single flavor" means it is not hard. But surely, even a single thing is seen to have multiple forms in the world.

Just as Somaśarman, though being one person, appears in many forms—as teacher, maternal uncle, father, son, brother, husband, son-in-law, and the best of the twice-born—it is therefore said: "And because of having a single form.
It has been stated that while many cognitions can occur within a single object-field (*gocara*), they do not possess multiple forms (*anekākāra*).
"Of manifold forms":
form (*rūpa*) means aspect (*ākāra*). He explains:
It is said: "With attributes" (saguṇā).

The meaning is that meditations (upāsanās) directed toward Brahman as qualified by various attributes, as well as those directed toward the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth—which yield results such as visible rewards, invisible rewards, or liberation—differ from one another due to the difference in their objects.
Therefore, he states that the doubt (vimarśa) is justified.
Regarding these, there is this reflection.
He takes up the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "In that regard" (tatra).
Regarding the phrase "firstly, of the name":
there is the text, "Now this is the Jyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee.

In that regard, a doubt arises: does the statement "one should sacrifice" enjoin a quality characterized by a thousand-fold sacrificial fee as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma which is proximate in context?
Or is it the injunction of another ritual action qualified by these attributes? What, then, is the prima facie view?

Since the Jyotiṣṭoma has already been introduced, the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is a reference to that; furthermore, having recited the nominal stem "jyotis" alone and then drawing in [the word] "etena" (by this), the status of a name for the ritual action is established through its grammatical coreferentiality with the action.
Furthermore, since the name is dependent upon the ritual action as its subject (*anuvādya*), it is established in the same manner;

because the word *jyotis* is seen to have a derivative application (*yoga*) to the Jyotiṣṭoma in the passage "In every spring, [one should sacrifice] with the Jyotis"; because it is well-known in the world that a part of a name can indicate the whole name, just as the word *Bhīma* indicates Bhīmasena;
and because the word *atha*, meaning "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), would be untenable if there were no connection [to a preceding context].

Furthermore, since it is simpler to enjoin a mere accessory than to enjoin another action qualified by that accessory, and since the sacrificial fee of one hundred and twelve [cows]—not being enjoined in the original injunction—is equally enjoined [with the new accessory], its optionality with the fee of one thousand cows is established;

therefore, this is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of enjoining the accessory characterized as a fee of one thousand for the very Jyotiṣṭoma under discussion, and not a separate ritual action. This is the prima facie conclusion (pūrvapakṣa).
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: This would be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the former [rite] only if it were the same context (*prakaraṇa*).

However, that context is interrupted. For even though it occurs in proximity, when another name is perceived whose meaning is unconnected with the preceding, "it is improper for there to be multiple meanings" (*anyāyaścānekārthatvam*).

According to this principle, it is established in common worldly experience that, because a general rule (*utsarga*) by its very nature has another purpose, it sets aside the previous cognition and gives rise to a new cognition.
For instance, when one says, "Give a cow to Devadatta, and a horse to Deva," people in the world do not conclude from the word "Deva" that Devadatta is the recipient of the horse.

And likewise, later on, when the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is heard, because it is separated by words whose meanings are unrelated to it, it does not evoke the cognition of that [previously known] ritual action; thus, being incapable of merely enjoining a quality (*guṇavidhi*) therein, it enjoins a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Nor is it appropriate for the word *jyotis* to be applied figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to the Jyotiṣṭoma on the grounds of an impossibility in one instance, provided that no such impossibility exists;
for just because the word *gaṅgā* is used figuratively in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," it does not follow that it is also used figuratively in the expression "the fish in the Gaṅgā."

Moreover, even when a distinction has first been indicated by another name, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *yaji* (the root "to sacrifice") brings about merely the status of being a name for a ritual action; it is not, however, capable of removing the cognition of difference produced by that other name. Thus, the word *atha* (now) serves the purpose of introducing a new topic and indicates a different context (*prakaraṇāntaratā*). And the word *eṣaḥ* (this) refers back to that which is being introduced. Therefore, this is the distinction [of the ritual] due to the difference in names.
"Let it be that there is a difference of action due to a difference in names; but what does this have to do with the subject at hand? To this he says:
"And here [it is] as in the case of those prescribed in other Vedāntas.
Just as the designations such as *Kāṭhaka* and so forth are applied to the texts, so too are they used by common people for the knowledge [contained therein].
Furthermore, there is no distinction on account of which the designation would be primary with respect to consciousness and secondary with respect to the text;
for the act of composition is the identical basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) for both the text and the knowledge.
Therefore, the designation is expressive of the knowledge as well.

And so, if even a different name heard in proximity to the Jyotiṣṭoma—which serves as its counterpart—is a differentiator of the ritual action, then what need is there to mention the case of a rite belonging to another recensional branch (śākhā), which is most remote and designated by a different name that does not serve as its counterpart?

Likewise, a difference in form (rūpabheda) is well known as an indicator of a difference in ritual action, as in such cases as "The curdled milk (āmikṣā) belongs to the Viśvedevas; the whey (vājina) belongs to the Vājins."
This is handed down in the tradition: "One pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas.
For here, a sacrifice is enjoined as inferred from the relationship between the substance and the deity. Immediately following that, this is handed down: "The whey (*vājina*) for the Vājins."

In this regard, the following doubt arises: is the *vājina* (the whey) enjoined as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) in the very same preceding ritual action, or is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*), qualified by a different substance and deity, enjoined as something new (*apūrva*)? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?

Since enjoining a distinct ritual action qualified by a different substance and deity would entail the fault of excessive injunction (*vidhigaurava*), and since it would also entail the fault of postulating a distinct ritual action and a distinct transcendental result (*apūrvāntara*), there is no injunction of a distinct ritual action; rather, [the *vājina* is enjoined] in the very same preceding [action].
The injunction regarding the substance *vājina* pertains to the ritual action itself.

Nor is it correct to argue that, because the quality of *āmikṣā* is enjoined as part of the original production (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), the *vājina* finds no room there and thus points toward a different ritual action;

for both sentences function simultaneously, and since *āmikṣā* and *vājina* are enjoined equally at the time of the production [of the rite], the *āmikṣā* is not "already enjoined" [to the exclusion of the other].

How then could the *vājina* not enter into the ritual act already occupied by this [āmikṣā]? Furthermore, in the case of the term *vaiśvadevī*, there is no Vedic (direct) connection between the Viśvedevas and the *āmikṣā* that would make it stronger than the connection with the *vājina*, which is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*), because both are equally understood through syntactical connection, as both involve the cognition of one word depending on another.
Indeed, when "vaiśvadevī" is uttered, we do not determine that it refers to *āmikṣā* independently of the word "*āmikṣā*" itself.

Or, even if its status as being directly stated by the Veda (*śrautatva*) were granted, nevertheless, the word "vājibhyaḥ"—derived through the etymology "those who possess *vāja*, i.e., food, which is *āmikṣā*"—indicates the Viśvedevas who are connected to that [food].
Even though the word "vājin" is distinct from the word "viśvadeva,"...

The deity-hood belongs to that very word by which the injunction is made during the *uddeśa* (mention), and not to another word; otherwise, since the meaning would be one and the same, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the words *sūrya* and *āditya*, as well as the things denoted by *sūrya* and *āditya*, being deities for a single sacrifice.

Nevertheless, because the word *vājinn* is recorded in the grammatical tradition (*smaraṇa*) as having the sense of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and because the sense of a pronoun refers to what is proximate (*saṃnihita*), and because the Viśvedevas are brought into proximity by the word *viśve devāḥ*, these [Vājins] are to be presented by the word *vājipada* preceded precisely by that [word *viśve devāḥ*], and are not independent like the words *sūrya* and *āditya*.

And thus, for the purpose of indicating that [deity], the word *vājī* indicates the very same deity as qualified by the *viśvedevas*; therefore, there is no difference in the deity due to a different word. Consequently, the *vājina* being enjoined for the *viśvedevas* by depending upon the connection with the *āmikṣā* is not sublated by the *āmikṣā*, but rather is combined with it; thus, it is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), but rather a single action endowed with two substances through the two sentences.

The objection that "the ritual action is thus enjoined" is answered as follows: This would indeed be so if the word *vaiśvadevī* did not denote curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) through the force of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). However, since it is recorded in the grammatical tradition that the secondary suffix denotes the meaning of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*)—namely, "its"—and since a pronoun refers to a proximate qualificandum, the function of the secondary suffix applies precisely there; it does not apply to the Viśvedevas themselves, nor to their relationship.
Nor does it refer to anything merely related to that [deity].

If this were so, why would we not understand *āmikṣā* from the word *vaiśvadevī* alone, and why would we require the word *āmikṣā*? We do not understand it because the denotative power of the word ending in the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is incomplete; we require the word *āmikṣā* in order to complete that denotation.
For a word whose denotation is complete is capable of producing a cognition of its meaning;

however, this [word *tad*], which denotes a specific object already present, requires that presence and thus depends upon the word *āmikṣā*, which brings about that presence. Therefore, how could there be the consequence of a cognition of *āmikṣā* independent of the word *āmikṣā*, or how could there be independence with respect to it?

Therefore, even though there is a dependence on other words, that word which expresses its meaning while depending on another word is stronger and more directly expressed (*śrauta*) because it is understood from a primary word that possesses authoritative status.

However, that which is understood through the comprehension of the meanings of words already expressed by words whose denotative function has been completed—being understood through the sentence (*vākya*) at a subsequent stage—is weaker. Consequently, because the quality characterized as *āmikṣā* is apprehended through the direct expression (*śruti*) of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the substance *vājina* is not connected with the previously mentioned ritual action.

The word *vājī*, being etymologically derived (*yaugika*) and dependent in its application, somehow distinguishes itself from the preceding [word *viśvadeva*] as a relative term; it will indicate the deity denoted by the word *vaiśvadeva*, which is understood to have become a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) with respect to the substance *āmikṣā* [from the word *vaiśvadevī*].
For a pronoun has as its scope that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Furthermore, that which is the primary subject is said to be the topic under discussion, not the subordinate element;

and when there is a basis in authoritative scripture, the assumption of a distinct injunction must indeed be accepted, because the scope of an authoritative means of knowledge concerns the true nature of reality.

Therefore, just as in this case [of the *vaiśvānara* passage] there is a distinction of rites due to qualities that cannot belong to the preceding rite, so too here the knowledge of the six fires (*ṣaḍagnividyā*) is distinct from the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*).
Thus, in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the distinction between knowledge (*vidyā*) is established by the presence or absence [of certain elements].
Likewise, a specific feature of the dharma (*dharmaviśeṣa*) also serves as an indicator of a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*).
For instance, while the Taittirīyas, who study the *Kārīrī* passages, practice eating on the ground, others do not.
Likewise, some who study the *Agni* [section] bring water-jars for their teacher, while others do not;
similarly, some who study the *Aśvamedha* bring fodder for the horse, while others do not;
and still others do so.
However, some practice an entirely different dharma;
and it is not logical that those very same rituals should both desire and not desire the benefit produced by the ground, the sacrificial fee, and so forth.
Therefore, it is understood that the rituals in those various branches are distinct.
To the question, "Let that be so; what is relevant to the present context?", he says:
"And it exists here.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "it does not exist for other followers of different Vedic branches."
Likewise, there are also cases such as tautology and so forth.
For instance, in the injunctions "He offers the *samidh* oblations" and others, the word *yajati* ("he offers") is repeated five times.
In that case, is there a single efficient force (*bhāvanā*) regarding the action, or are there indeed five?

What, then, is the prima facie position? Since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is stated to be distinct in the section concerning "different words" (*śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*) due to the difference in the adjuncts that are the meanings of the verbal roots,

and since a distinction in the meaning of the root cannot be established without a distinction in the root itself, [the *bhāvanā* is distinct] by virtue of the sentence "He offers the *samits*" (*samidho yajati*), which occurs first.
The cultivation of action (*karmabhāvanā*) as enjoined is restated by subsequent sentences;
nor is it a non-restatement due to a lack of purpose, because it is not permissible to question the purpose of that which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since the postulation of multiple *apūrvas* would follow from a difference in the cultivation of action, it is concluded that a single action possesses a single intermediate operation consisting of a single *apūrva*.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "For the sentences concerning the *samidh* and so forth are independent of one another.
Although all of them are equally entitled to primacy, since simultaneous study is impossible, they are studied sequentially;
however, this sequence is not the one that determines their application (*prayojaka*).
For it is when things are mutually dependent that they constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), and only then would there be a motive [for an injunction].
Consequently, since there is no "firstness" (priority), there is no such thing as "attainment" (*prāpta*); thus, what could be the restatement (*anuvāda*) of what?

For a mere reversal of order lacks the capacity to set aside the status of an injunction (*vidhi*) characterized by the impelling of what has not been previously established as a rule (*autsargika-apravṛtta-pravartana*).

For when there is the hearing of a quality (*guṇa*) in the injunction of an action qualified by that quality, there arises a requirement for a reference back to the action (*karmānuvāda*)—out of fear of the complexity of an injunction (*vidhigaurava*) and for the sake of the simplicity of enjoining the quality alone. In this situation, the assistance provided is by way of "revival" (*viparivṛtti*). For example, in the sentence "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), which is intent on enjoining curd, there is a requirement for revival; thus, there is a reference back to the oblation (*homa*) enjoined by "He performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), which is present [in the mind] through revival. And in this case, there is no differentiation of the action based on the quality.
Because words such as *samit* and others, being names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*), lack the character of expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*),

and because no specific distinction is perceived, it cannot be determined— which [sentence] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a ritual enjoined by another statement and which is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Furthermore, that which is called "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) is not first understood as having a connection with an injunction, as is the case with [names] such as *jyotis*.
For an action being enjoined by means of a previously interrupted cognition would have to exclude it from its prior designation;

however, since *samit* and the others are understood from the very beginning as being in grammatical apposition with the action, they acquire the status of names for that action by virtue of that fact.

Thus, when the verb is a restatement (*anuvāda*), these terms are restatements, and when it is an injunction (*vidhi*), they are injunctions; they do not possess independent authority over anything else.

Therefore, since this repetition is intended for the injunction of an action not otherwise obtained by its own inherent force, it differentiates the meditative realization (*bhāvanā*) by differentiating the factors constitutive of that realization within the action; in the same manner, repetition will differentiate the knowledges (*vidyā*) enjoined in one recensional branch from those enjoined in other recensional branches.
And because of incapacity:

for a single person is not able to combine the meditations that consist of the cognitions found in all the Vedāntas, due to the impossibility of studying all the Vedāntas; for if one were to combine the meaning of what has not been studied, it would result in the futility of the injunction to study.
However, this fault does not apply if the meditations differ in each branch (śākhā).
And because of the difference in their conclusions:
for some reciters of the Vedic branches, the conclusion occurs with the statement of the all-pervasiveness of the syllable *oṃ*; for others, it occurs elsewhere.
Therefore, there is a distinction between the meditations.
Furthermore, a distinction is established from the observation of other purposes;
for instance, in the passage, "One who has not observed the vow does not study this," the absence of study by one who has not observed the vow indicates the absence of meditation.
In some cases, meditation (*upāsanā*) is understood from the observation of study (*adhyayana*) even for one who has not observed the vows;
therefore, there is a difference between [the two types of] meditation.
To this, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

"If [the meditations] are recognized as identical in all Vedānta texts, because there is no distinction regarding their beginningless [nature]," he explains that: "recognized as identical in all Vedānta texts" means they are the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in all Vedānta texts.
The cognitions in each respective Vedānta must be those very same ones;
the meaning is that whatever [cognitions] exist in one Vedānta, those same ones exist in other Vedāntas as well,
because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), conjunction, form, and name are included. And here, "impulsion" (codanā) refers to human effort;
for that is the activity of the person.
In that case, this [injunction] indeed operates within the context of an action such as *homa* (oblation) whose verbal root-meaning is uninterrupted.

The human effort that delimits that act—namely, the renunciation (*tyāga*) directed toward a deity, or acts such as pouring water (*āsecanādi*)—is precisely the same in other recensions (*śākhāntara*) as it is here.
Likewise, here too, the human effort directed toward the knowledge of the pre-eminence and excellence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is exactly the same as it is in other recensions.
In this way, the connection with the fruit— characterized by being the eldest and most excellent— is that very same [connection];
the form is also that very same [form],
just as the form consisting of the substance and deity in one recensional branch (śākhā) of a sacrifice is the very same in other branches as well.

In the same way, regarding the *vedana* [instruction] as well, that which constitutes the subject matter—namely, the state of being the eldest and the most excellent among the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in one place—is present in other branches as well. (1) "Some distinction" (3.3.1.2):

It is logical that there is no difference even when the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*), having been produced, is subsequently connected with the offering on eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*) and so forth.

Since that [quality] which has arisen is recognized everywhere, whereas here the difference in quality pertains only to the state of being produced in the fires, how is it that this does not cause a distinction, as in the case of the *vaiśvadevī* [offering]?
Having this specific point in mind, the author of the Sūtras raises an objection:
"If it be argued that there is no [distinction] because of the difference [of fires]. (Sūtra 2.1.23).
The refutation consists in a portion of the Sūtra: "Not even in one [text].
For the Vājasaneyins, too, only five fires consisting of the sacrificial piling (sāṃpādika) are enjoined, just as they are for the Chāndogyas.
The sixth fire, however, is restated for the sake of establishing a correspondence and is not prescribed as a new injunction;
whereas in the *vaiśvadevī* origin-rite, a quality is indeed prescribed—let there thus be a distinction.
Alternatively, even among the Chāndogyas, the sixth fire is certainly recited.

Alternatively, let there be the injunction of six fires for the Vājasaneyins, and let it not exist for the Chāndogyas; nevertheless, because the number five is not enjoined, that number does not possess the status of being "enjoined at origin" (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). Rather, once the fires have been produced, the number—enjoined by accumulation—is restated (*anūdyate*) in order to delimit the fires that are [merely] mentally constructed (*sāṃpādika*).

Therefore, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of those [elements] whose origination has already occurred, and because a number that is not being recognized cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvāda*), and because an additional element being enjoined can only result in an option—as in the case of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup—there is no difference in knowledge (*jñānabheda*) between different recensions (*śākhā*). Since it is not established that [the knowledge] is taught as something newly originated (*utpattiśiṣṭatva*), the dialogues with the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and so forth are also non-different due to recognition across those various recensions. //2// 3.3.1.3.

"Because of the nature of the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya), because of the qualification for the Samācāra [section], and because of the rule regarding the Sava sacrifices, that restriction applies.

For those by whom the knowledge is to be known through the means of the Ātharvaṇa texts, it bestows its fruit only when taught by the text acquired through the prior study of which the Śirovrata was performed, and not otherwise. However, for others such as the followers of the Chāndogya, it is understood from the connection with the study of the Ātharvaṇa texts that the very same knowledge yields its fruit only for those who have performed the Śirovrata.
Furthermore, that connection [of the knowledge] with the Vedic vow is understood from the traditional text: "One who has not performed the vow does not study this.

Even though there is a connection with the knowledge in the statement, "One should impart this very Brahma-knowledge to them," the use of the pronoun "this" (etām), which refers back to what is under discussion, does not contradict its connection with the study; thus, it is the knowledge prescribed in the Āraṇyaka that is being spoken of.

All the oblations, beginning with the seven *saurya* offerings and ending with the *śataudana*, are performed by the followers of the Atharvaveda in a single Atharvan fire, not in the three sacred fires (*tretā*). Furthermore, it demonstrates the unity of knowledge (*vidyaikatva*): because the Vedas repeatedly show the unity of knowledge, even in cases where the Veda does not explicitly state the unity of the various meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahma-vidyā*), their unity is established through the observation of their being generally grouped together and their being treated as such.
For instance, having seen that something is written in a preeminent [text], the thought arises: "This must be preeminent.
As for the claim that there is a distinction between meditations (upāsanā) based on designations such as the *Kāṭhaka* and so forth, that is incorrect;
for these designations are human in origin, arising from the connection of those branches with the teachings of Kaṭha and others, but they do not apply to the meditations themselves.
For these [Upaniṣads] were not proclaimed by Kaṭha and others, nor is their practice distinguished from the practices of others;

and while it might be possible— on the grounds that they were proclaimed by Kaṭha— to apply the name to the texts, and then, through some secondary figurative sense (lakṣaṇā), to apply it to the meditations (upāsanā) associated with them, it is not possible to assume that these [meditations] are themselves designated as "Kaṭha[-proclaimed]."
Furthermore, the difference or non-difference of those [recensions] cannot be the cause for the difference or non-difference of the cognitions [they produce];
otherwise, it would follow that there is no unity among the cognitions of various single branches simply because those recensions themselves are not different.

Moreover, since these designations such as "Kaṭha" and so forth—which are based on the oral teachings of persons like Kaṭha—did not exist prior to those persons, it would result in the untenable conclusion that the difference in cognition caused by them did not exist then, yet exists now.
Therefore, the distinction is not established by name (*samākhyā*).
Repetition (*abhyāsa*) also is not a differentiator here.
It is logical that the repetition of the verb *yajati* occurring within a single recensional branch (*śākhā*) serves as the differentiator for the *samidh* and other offerings.

For in that case, the two general characteristics of an injunction—the making known of what was previously unknown (*ajñātajñāpana*) and the impelling of one who has not yet acted (*apravṛttapravartana*)—would be contradicted; however, in the case of different recensional branches (*śākhā*), because the students are distinct persons, there is no contradiction of the general nature of an injunction even though the text is one and the same.
Furthermore, incapacity is not a cause for division, as the rule of study applies to one's own branch alone, according to the injunction: "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied."
Furthermore, one will acquire and synthesize meanings found in other recensions from others who are learned in those [recensions].
Moreover, the completion of a whole is designated when even a single part related to it is completed;

for example, they designate the completion of the Jyotiṣṭoma during the performance of the Adhvaryu's ritual by saying, "The Jyotiṣṭoma is finished. Therefore, even a difference in completion is not a proof for a difference in meditation.

Thus, since there is no sublation [of this conclusion] and because there is no difference in their injunctions and so forth, it is established that the ritual acts prescribed in all the Vedānta texts are one and the same. Having raised a certain objection regarding a specific point, the author of the Sūtras states the following matter— which was already established in the earlier system (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā)— for the sake of establishing the meaning of what is to be discussed hereafter.
The Sūtra is intended to demonstrate the purpose of this deliberation:
"And [the details] are to be combined when the object is the same, as in the case of supplementary injunctions.

Here, the following objection is raised: "Granted that there is one single cognition based on all the Śākhās, nevertheless, the details mentioned in other Śākhās need not be combined with that cognition mentioned in another Śākhā."
For the benefit [of the sacrifice] is accomplished by just that much of the collection of subsidiary parts as is prescribed for a single action on a single branch, since nothing more is required;
and if more were required, even more would be prescribed there,
yet it is not so prescribed.

Therefore, just as an occasional (*naimittika*) rite—though prescribed with all its constituent parts (*aṅga*)—is nonetheless assisted by the benefit produced by only those parts that can be performed when one lacks the capacity for the rest; so too here, it will be the same because other parts have simply not been prescribed. This being the position reached, it is said in reply: since the unity of the ritual action (*karman*) is established in all cases, a limitation of the benefit (*upakāra*) is not tenable according to the principle of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice.
