For it is not logical that the very same ritual act should both require and not require its seven constituent parts (*saptāṅga*).

However, in the case of a contingent rite (*naimittika*) which must necessarily be performed in accordance with its specific occasion (*nimitta*), a limitation of the auxiliary benefits (*upakāra*) is postulated because it is impossible for all constituent parts to be assembled at all times.

Since the *ājyabhāga* offerings are prescribed within the aggregate of archetypal auxiliary benefits obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*), there would likewise be a limitation of the auxiliary benefits in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.

In this case, however, the injunction in another recension prescribes only a few auxiliary elements; it does not exclude the others. Nor is there an injunction of only those specific parts when the entire aggregate of their assistance has already been obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), as is the case with the *ājyabhāga* offerings. Therefore, since the general rule is that all auxiliary elements are connected to the ritual acts in their true nature, it is not proper to set this aside unless there is a powerful sublationary reason. //5// 3.3.3.6.
If it be argued that there is a difference [in their nature] based on the word, we say no, because there is no distinction.
From Prajāpati, two kinds—two types—were born: the gods and the asuras.
Of these, the gods were indeed fewer, while the asuras were more numerous.
The gods are those endowed with a sattvic intellect born of the scriptures;
for they "shine" (divyanti), thus they are called gods.

The asuras, however, are those whose minds are not fashioned by scriptural reasoning, who are dominated by tamasic tendencies, and who "delight" (ramante) in various sense-objects by means of their vital breaths (asu) that are unrefined and devoid of the senses; therefore, they are called asuras, and for this very reason, they are considered superior [in power].
Since these gods possess knowledge of reality, they are indeed superior;
for the knowledge of reality arises from a prior state of ignorance.
Thus, there may occasionally be an emergence of the sāttvika mode and a suppression of the tāmasa mode within Prāṇa Prajāpati.
Sometimes there is the emergence of tamasic activity and the suppression of sattvic activities;
this is what constitutes rivalry.
Those gods said:

"Come, let us overcome the Asuras by means of the *udgītha* in this sacrificial rite of exorcism; let us conquer the Asuras through the ritual of the *udgātṛ*, characterized by the Sāman-chant portion known as the *udgītha*. Having thus spoken, the text—beginning with the passage "They said to Speech"—condemns speech, breath, sight, hearing, and mind for being pierced by the evil of the Asuras. Then, it [addresses] this one in the mouth—the principal breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) located within the cavity of the mouth, presided over by the deity of breath.

The gods said to the deities, "Sing the Udgītha for us. Having agreed, saying "So be it," Prāṇa sang the Udgītha for them. The Asuras knew, "By means of this Prāṇa as the Udgātṛ, the gods will surpass us.

They rushed toward him and pierced him with evil (pāpman). Just as a stone, having been struck or reached, falls to pieces like a clod of earth, even so the Asuras, falling apart, perished, scattering in all directions.
He states this very point in brief: "In the Vājasaneyaka.
Likewise, he states that this has also been said in the Chāndogya:
Likewise, it is so even in the Chāndogya;
having thus shown the subject matter, he reflects:
"In that regard, there is a doubt."
He takes up the prima facie view— that there is oneness of knowledge—
and then he challenges that prima facie view:

"Is it not improper?"—the meaning is that in one place prāṇa is spoken of as the *udgātṛ* (the chanter), while in another it is spoken of as the *udgāna* (the chanting); thus, there is a clear distinction between the agent and the action.
He provides the resolution:
This is not a fault;
because of the recognition of many more forms, that which is not recognized must be understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā),
not only in another recensional branch (śākhāntara).

He states that this [meditation] is seen even in a single branch, and yet there is no difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) therein: "And also among the Vājasaneyins. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, for the sake of favoring the recognition of many more identical forms, the syllable *om* should also be understood by indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the *udgītha* itself, through its being a constituent part of the *udgītha*. //6// 3.3.3.7.
Or rather, [the two are distinct] because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" (parovarīyas) and so forth.

Even though there is a great deal of mutual recognition [of the same subject], because of the difference in the opening statements and because the concluding portion must be interpreted in accordance with that opening,

and because in a single sentence the same udgītha is mentioned again and again, and because of the use of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka— [the two are distinct].
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that there is a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*) because of the absence of authoritative evidence [to the contrary].
Having introduced the *oṃkāra* as the object of meditation, there follows an explanatory exposition (*upavyākhyāna*) of its qualities, such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*).

For it is said of the *oṃkāra*: among the elements, earth, herbs, man, speech, the *Ṛgveda*, and the *Sāmaveda*, each subsequent one is declared to be the flavor (*rasa*) and the essence (*sāra*) of the preceding one.
Among all of these, the *oṃkāra* is declared in the *Chāndogya* to be the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*).
Nor is there a difference in the intended meaning [of the Upanishads],
for while in one place the *udgītha* and the *udgātṛ* are intended as objects of meditation, in another it is the *oṃkāra*, which is a part thereof, that is so intended.

For it is so stated in the passage concerning prosperity (*abhyudaya*): "Verily, he who, when the moon rises before his sacrificial oblation has been set out, is deprived of offspring and cattle and causes his rival to prosper—he should divide the rice grains into three parts; those which are of medium size, he should offer to Agni..."

"One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Dātṛ; those [grains] which are the largest, for them a pap to Indra Pradātṛ; those which are the smallest, for them a pap cooked in boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this enjoined as a separate sacrifice due to the lapse of time, or is it a removal of the deities from those very rites under discussion when the lapse of time serves as the occasion?

This, then, is the subject matter here: on the new moon day itself, for the sake of the Darśa sacrifice, there is the preparation of the altar, the act of bringing forward the fire, and the purificatory rites for the sacrificer such as the observance of vows;
furthermore, there is the milking for the purpose of the curd.
And on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), the commencement of the Darśa ritual takes place—this is the actual sequence of performance.

However, in the case of a sacrificer who, due to some cause of confusion, has begun the ritual performance on the fourteenth day itself under the impression that it is the new moon day (amāvāsyā), and the moon rises while he is engaged in it—for him this is heard in the scripture: "He whose sacrificial offering has been set out...

By that sacrificer, having completed the qualified obligation based on the occasion (*nimittādhikāra*) even though the moon has risen on what was thought to be the new moon day, he should perform the rites such as the removal of the altar (*vedyuddharaṇa*) on that very day, and then commence the Darśa sacrifice on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).

In this regard, concerning the arising of the moon: is this an independent ritual (*karmāntara*) enjoined subsequent to the *darśa* sacrifice, or is another deity prescribed within that very same *darśa* rite by means of the removal of the previous deities?
In this matter, because only the portions of the oblation are mentioned and because of the capacity of the injunction for the *caru*, it is an independent ritual.
For if it were heard [in the scripture] that "one should divide the oblations from the previous deities," then those very same oblations would [be offered] to another deity.

The injunctions [regarding the portions] do not require one to understand a different ritual action; rather, it is the very same ritual action under discussion that should have its original oblation-material (havis) removed from its former deity and joined with another deity.

In this case, however, because the division of the oblation itself is heard in the text—stating "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts" according to the sequence of middle-sized and so forth—the removal [of the original deity] has not occurred.

Regarding the phrase "the previous deity in the oblation" (*haviṣi pūrvadevatā*): when the oblation is already occupied by a previous deity, another deity being heard of [in the text] that finds no room [therein] would lead to the understanding of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Furthermore, if the previous ritual action were already established, one would have to enjoin both the connection of curd and rice with deities such as Indra and others.
Furthermore, since "loveliness" (*carutva*) has not been enjoined here, that too would have to be enjoined;
and if that were the case, the sentence would be split (*vākyabheda*) due to the injunction of multiple qualities regarding an action already established.

However, it is possible to enjoin a new action (*karmāntara*)—an unprecedented one—characterized by multiple qualities with a single effort; therefore, a distinct action is indeed enjoined on account of the occasion (*nimitta*).
It being argued that the *darśa* sacrifice is omitted due to the lapse of the proper time, it is replied: it is not a separate ritual act.
This is because, after the division of the oblation from its previous deity, another deity is prescribed for the occasion;
furthermore, the purpose of the *caru* is already established by the context.

This would be so if this sentence were intended to enjoin the threefold division of the rice grains themselves, as in "one should divide the rice grains into three parts. However, rather than that, it merely restates the threefold nature of the rice grains—which is already established by another sentence—and enjoins only the act of dividing them. Consequently, since the connection of the oblation with the deities remains unimpeded in that very same ritual action, as before, when the sentences [of the *paryagnikaraṇa*] have been removed...
They are capable of enjoining a connection with another deity;

and thus, because there is recognition of the original context through the medium of the substance, even when there is a connection with another deity, it is not possible to assume a different ritual act.
Consequently, even though the [original] rite is completed, those very same acts must be performed again for the sake of fulfilling the qualification for the occasional (naimittika) duty.
Nor is there an injunction for both the *caru* and the locative case-meaning in the phrase "the *caru* in curd" (*dadhani carum*), because both of those are already established by the context.
For in the original rite, the pounding of rice, the spreading [of the dough], the baking of the *puroḍāśa*, and so forth, as well as the curd and milk, are already established;
therein, when the occasion of the *abhyudaya* arises, the sentence "one should divide the rice-grains joined with curd and joined with milk" [applies].
Having performed the removal of the previous deities, a connection with other deities is established by means of such statements as "those which are intermediate.
Now, the preparation of a *puroḍāśa* cake is not possible with a small quantity of rice grains mixed with abundant curd and milk;

thus, upon the cessation of the *puroḍāśa*, its purpose—the act of spreading [the flour]—also ceases. However, the cooking does not cease, because there is no prohibition against it; and so that which follows from the sense of the matter is enjoined.
Or let there be the postulation of multiple sentences;
for this too is logical by virtue of the force of understanding the context of the subject matter under discussion.
Therefore, it is established that this is indeed the same ritual action, and not a different one.

In the sentence concerning the desire for cattle (*paśukāma*), however, there is an injunction for a new ritual action (*apūrvakarmavidhi*), even though it shares a similar form with sentences regarding prosperity (*abhyudayavākya*). [The text says:

"He who desires cattle, having performed the New Moon sacrifice, should drive away the calves; those that are the largest, he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Samanamat; those that are of middle size, he should offer as a cooked rice-oblation (*caru*) in boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa; those that are the smallest, [he should offer] to Indra..."

"Having performed the sacrifice on the new moon day, one desiring cattle should offer a caru-oblation to Pradātṛ. For here, since the injunction for the Paśukāmeṣṭi occurs after the phrase "having performed the sacrifice on the new moon day" has concluded, it is not logical to regard this as an injunction for a different sacrifice due to the non-continuation of the previous ritual;
rather, it is like the case of the *parovarīyastva* [meditation].

Just as, despite the similarity in the meditation on the *udgītha*, the meditation on the *udgītha* characterized by qualities such as being golden and having a sun-stone for eyes is distinct from the meditation on the *udgītha* characterized by the quality of being "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*), so it is here as well.

Thus, because it is higher than the high (*para*) and more excellent than the excellent (*vara*), the *udgītha* becomes the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyān*), which is the nature of the Supreme Self;
for this very reason, it is infinite (*ananta*).

In order to cultivate the vision of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) upon the *udgītha*, [the text] points to the Supreme Self by means of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) in the passage: "For ether is indeed greater than these elements. (Sūtra 3.3.8). If it is argued that identity is established by the identity of name (*saṃjñā*), that has already been answered: "But even that exists" (Sūtra 3.3.9).
When a difference is more clearly perceived, the identity of name is not a proof of non-difference, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, upon examining the literal words of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the cognition of difference is both internal and independent;
whereas the identity of name, being external to the revelation and being of human origin, is both external and dependent.
Therefore, it is weak and not capable of establishing identity. //8// 3.3.4.9.
"And because of pervasion, [the definition] is consistent.
Regarding the phrase "what is called superimposition": superimposition is a figurative cognition.

Just as, while the cognition and the application of the designation "boy" have not yet ceased in the case of a boy, there occurs the cognition and the application of the designation "lion," such that one says, "The boy is a lion";
so too, there is the cognition of Vāsudeva in an image and the cognition of Brahman in a name, as well as the cognition and the application of the designation "Udgītha" in the syllable *oṃ*.
Furthermore, the [doctrines of] sublation (*apavāda*), oneness (*ekatva*), and qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) have been explained.
Moreover, the employment of two words for a single meaning is observed,
as in "the *āmikṣā* belongs to Viśvedevas" and "consciousness is bliss."
And in the commentary, the simultaneous use of synonyms is also illustrated, as in "sindhura," "karī," "pika," and "kokila.
Having reflected upon the alternative characterized by indecisiveness, he adopts the position:
"there, one or another [of these]."
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "This is said—'And because of pervasion' (*vyāpteśca*)".

Since the syllable *oṃ* occurs at the beginning and the end of every *anuvāka* and every *ṛc*, it pervades all the Vedas. Therefore, for what purpose is this *oṃkāra* endowed with those respective qualities such as being the source (*āpya*) and so forth? To that [he replies]:

In response to the inquiry as to what is qualified as the object of meditation for the sake of attaining results such as the fulfillment of desires, it is specified by the word "Udgītha. Since it is impossible for a whole to possess the status of its own parts, the word "Udgītha"—which denotes a specific division of the *Sāman* chant composed of parts such as the syllable *Oṃ*—indicates by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the syllable *Oṃ*, which is a part related to that whole; however, it is not the case that the whole Udgītha is indicated by the syllable *Oṃ*.
This is because it will be explained later that [the syllable] Oṃ itself is qualified by those respective qualities and qualified by those respective fruits.
Furthermore, a word denoting a whole is seen to be used figuratively for a part, as in "the village is burnt" or "the cloth is burnt" when only a portion of them has been consumed.
However, in the case of superimposition (adhyāsa), there would be both figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) and the postulation of a fruit.
For instance, this meditation on the *udgītha* as the *praṇava*—which possesses qualities such as "attainment" (*āpti*) and so forth—is distinct from other meditations on the *praṇava*.
Furthermore, no fruit is heard of here as it is in those other meditations beginning with "attainment";
therefore, [a fruit] must be inferred.
This fault does not apply to the passage which is intent upon the meditation on the *praṇava* as connected with the *udgītha*.
Moreover, the secondary function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is stronger than the secondary function of metaphorical transfer (*gauṇī*), because of its parsimony (*lāghava*).
For in the case of indication, the word’s primary intent is directed toward that which is indicated, since that very [indicated object] is included within the meaning of the sentence.

Just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the bank—which is being indicated—is included within the sentence-meaning by virtue of its status as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); however, in the case of "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), the word "ox" does not have that [the Vāhīka] as its primary referent through an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of things like dung and urine associated with an ox. Rather, it has as its referent the Vāhīka who is determined to belong to that same class and is endowed with those qualities. Thus, the secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) is weaker; this is what was stated [by the author]: "But even in the case of indication... and so forth.
The secondary function (gauṇī vṛtti) is also described as a type of indication (lakṣaṇā) because it is a part of indication;
for even though the word *vaiśvadevī* applies to the *āmikṣā*, there is nevertheless a much clearer difference in meaning.
For the word *āmikṣā* applies to the *āmikṣā* by virtue of its form.
The term *vaiśvadevī*, however, refers to that very same [offering] as qualified by the Viśvedevas.
Thus, even though both terms have the same referent in Brahman, the difference in their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is much more evident.
Furthermore, the explanation of both is necessary because they possess well-known meanings and because they have distinct meanings.
The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. [Sūtra 10:
"Because of the non-difference of all [the Upanishads] elsewhere.

Since the word *evam* (thus) has the function of referring back to a specific mode of presentation present in the context, and since that which is presented by the word *sākṣāt* (directly) is proximate, while that which resides in another recensional branch (*śākhā*) is remote due to its sequential distance; [the former is intended].

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because of the absence of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), in the Kauṣītaki dialogue on the Prāṇa, the Prāṇa is not to be meditated upon with attributes such as being the "most excellent" (*vasiṣṭha*); rather, it is to be meditated upon merely as the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and the "best" (*śreṣṭha*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: while it is true that the particle *evaṃ* (thus) refers to what is proximate, "proximity" does not consist merely in what is expressed by the words themselves.
Rather, that which is obtained as an inseparable concomitant of the meaning denoted by the relative pronoun *yat* is also indeed proximate in the intellect; it is truly proximate.

Just as in the case of the statement, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood," the sacrifice (*kratu*) is brought to mind by the *juhū*, which is invariably connected with the sacrifice; therefore, because the object of meditation and its fruit are recognized, and because the specific mode—which is invariably connected with that [object]—is present in the intellect even if not explicitly stated here, it is logical that there is a reference by means of the word "thus" (*evam*), which refers back to what is under discussion. This is established by the passage in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.
To that extent, it can be grasped by means of the syllable *om*;
nevertheless, with the intention of saying "even granting this, we shall speak," the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt) stated:
"Even so, [the answer is] in that very same cognition found in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa."

"Abandonment of what is heard" (śrutahāniḥ) means that there would be the abandonment of the Vedic text as it stands alone, and the postulation of something else not heard that is accompanied by other [elements]. The rest is self-evident. //10// 3.3.6.11.
Bliss and the other qualities belong to the primary [Brahman].

This section is intended for the sake of discernment, by way of explaining the actual qualities of Brahman, in order to distinguish them from the injunctions for meditation that treat those qualities as subordinate.
This is just as in the case of the one Brahman.
The qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (saṃyadvāma) and so forth, as well as the qualities such as having "true desires" (satyakāma) and so forth, should not be conflated.
Likewise, the qualities such as bliss and consciousness (ānanda-vijñāna) and so forth should not be conflated with qualities such as omnipresence and eternity mentioned in other passages.
Or, if there were such a conflation, then the quality of being the conductor of blessings and the rest would likewise be conflated with the qualities of having true desires and the rest.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the existence of Brahman as the substratum (*dharmin*).

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that non-determination and determination are established respectively through the nature of the thing itself and through the necessity of performance for the two [respectively]: the real object (*vastu*) and the injunction (*vidheya*).
For the property of a real object (*vastudharma*) persists as long as the object itself exists.

It cannot be said that because something is not mentioned in one place, it does not exist when it has been mentioned elsewhere. However, that which is to be enjoined depends upon human effort; and human effort, being directed toward Brahman as qualified by whatever attributes are prescribed in a given context, remains restricted to those very attributes. It is not capable of bringing forward even an unenjoined attribute, because such effort is dependent on injunction, and injunctions are fixed to their respective limits.

Therefore, bliss, consciousness, and so forth, which are described as being the very self of the reality of Brahman, are obtained wherever Brahman is heard of, even if they are not explicitly mentioned there.

Furthermore, it is established that attributes such as "the gathering of all desirable things" (*saṃyadvāma*), which are objects for the injunctions regarding the effort of meditation, abide according to the specific injunction and not according to the actual state of things.
As for attributes such as having joy as its head (*priyaśirastva*) and so on, the logical principle has been demonstrated by superimposing upon them the status of being objects of meditation.
However, for that [state], the Saṃyadvāma and others have been described.
*Moda* is mere delight; *pramoda* is intense delight. These two are mutual dependencies characterized by increase and decrease. (11) 3.3.6.12. (12) 3.3.6.13. (13) 3.3.7.14.

Because there is no purpose for meditation [on everything]. Regarding the statement, "The objects are indeed superior to the senses," is it intended here to establish the superiority of all things, beginning with the objects?
Or rather, is it that the other [qualities] are presented as being "supreme" (para) for the sake of establishing that very supremacy in the person?

In that case, since the scriptural texts are heard presenting each one—such as *artha* and so forth—as supreme individually, and since it is possible for each to be supreme as it is heard, it is not logical to determine that they all have a single supremacy by overriding their respective stated supremacies.
Nor is it impossible on the grounds of a lack of purpose.

This is because the purpose of meditating upon each of these is precisely to designate them as "the beyond" (*para*), and because there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that such respective meditations possess a specific purpose.
For instance, the *Smṛti* states: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten *manvantaras*."
Those consisting of the elements (bhautika) are a full hundred, while those consisting of the ego-sense (ābhimānika) are a thousand.
Ten thousand Buddhists remain free from the fever of suffering;
a full hundred thousand remain as those who contemplate the Unmanifest.
But having attained the Person devoid of qualities, no calculation of time exists.

Thus, since a division of sentences must be accepted by one who follows authoritative means of knowledge, it might be argued that these sentences—"the objects are higher than the senses," and so on—are intended to establish that each of those [categories], beginning with the objects, is higher [than the preceding]. To this, the following is stated: the entire textual sequence beginning with "the objects are indeed higher than the senses" is devoted to the exposition of the true nature of reality.
It is understood that [the text] is not primarily concerned with the injunction for meditation,
because such an injunction is not heard there. Therefore,
in this context, since the fact that the cognition [of Brahman] possesses an immediate purpose is observed, all [passages] have that cognition as their primary aim.
And it is observed that for one who knows the supreme state of Viṣṇu, there is the cessation of ignorance, which is the cause of the entire cycle of worldly existence and all misfortunes;
for it is seen in various places that the arising of the knowledge of reality is characterized by the cessation of error.
However, no visible purpose is observed for the cognition that takes objects and the like as its primary focus.
Moreover, when a visible [purpose] is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is not logical;
and when it is possible for [a text] to have as its primary aim the supreme human goal, it is not appropriate for it to have a merely intermediate human goal.
Therefore, because it possesses a visible purpose, [it cannot be taken as teaching liberation].
It is understood that this section is intended for the purpose of establishing the supremacy of the Puruṣa.
Furthermore, he states— “Moreover, by means of the negation of another”— that this alone is its meaning because of the [scriptural] emphasis.
But surely, there is no injunction for meditation here; so how can it be said "for the sake of meditation"? To this he says:
"And because of the word 'Self'. (Sūtra 3.3.7.15) "For the sake of meditation" [is stated]. And because of the word "Self. (Sūtra 3.3.7.16)

The meaning is as follows: since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—and especially scripture (*āgama*)—have as their essential nature the communication of meanings not previously attained, and since the Self (*ātman*), which is denoted by the word "Person" (*puruṣa*), is determined by the Veda itself to be difficult to comprehend, and because [the Self] is in fact difficult to comprehend while objects such as wealth are easy to understand, the statement that [scripture] has "wealth and so forth as its purpose" actually signifies that it has the [Self] as its ultimate purpose; this is the "excellent intention" (*āśayātiśaya*) of the Veda.
That is to say, it is because that is its purport.
Furthermore, this is also the case because it expresses what is required by another scriptural passage (*śruti*).
However, if the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) were intended as the primary object, the scripture would not state what is required; thus he says:
Moreover, "he reaches the end of the journey" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).

3.3.8.16. The grasping of the Self [is meant] as in other cases, because of what follows. For in both Śruti and Smṛti, the creation of the world is found to be presided over by the Supreme Lord and to have the Supreme Lord Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent.

Thus, here, by not mentioning the creation of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the initial creation of the world— which is observed to be the work of an intermediate Lord— and the determination of the oneness of the Self prior to its arising, lead us to understand [this creation] as being connected to an intermediate Lord;
for the creation of the Supreme Lord consists of the gross elements such as ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, whereas this [present case] is the reverse of that.
For indeed, that very same single entity possesses both the nature of fire and the power of seeing in relation to its various modifications;
moreover, in this preceding section of the Aitareya [Āraṇyaka], the creation of the worlds is stated to have Prajāpati as its agent,
and it is understood from that context as well that this is precisely so.
Furthermore, worldly transactions such as "He brought a cow from them," which are mentioned in the Śruti, are well-known in reference to specific individual selves and the Supreme Self;
from this also, it is understood that the intermediate Lord (Avāntareśvara) alone is intended.

Since the use of the word "Self" (ātman) is observed here as well, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached that this is a reference to the lower self (aparātmā). To this, it is replied: here there is a comprehension of the Supreme Self, just as in other scriptural accounts of creation, such as "From this Self... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1].
In passages such as "From that, space was produced," and so forth;
therefore, because of the subsequent hearing of creation preceded by reflection in the words "He thought," and because of the determination [of the subject] as "the Self" (ātman), this is intended:
first of all, prior to creation, the state of being solitary, the status of being the Self, and the quality of being the creator belong primarily to the Supreme Lord here.
Therefore, since there is no inconsistency [in the text], it is not appropriate to explain it otherwise.
Nor is the failure to mention the creation of the gross elements (mahābhūtas) a ground for inconsistency in the mention of the creation of the world;

for just as in the actual creation of the universe from Brahman—which begins with space—it is not contradictory to find mentions of a creation beginning with fire, as seen in the passage: "From this Self, space was produced."
Just as it must be supplied there with the words "having created space and air," so too here it must be understood that [the text] says "having created the great elements.

Since knowledge is based on all the Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya*), one should exert effort to perceive what is not explicitly stated for the sake of establishing the validity of the Śruti; one should not, however, allow laxity regarding the creation of the great elements and so forth when it is already stated in the Śruti. Furthermore, the mass of the Vedas, which is to be acquired under the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) and which expresses a purposeful meaning brought about by the injunction for study, is all the more approved insofar as it attains an abundance of purpose.
And just as this [knowledge] serves as a means to the supreme human goal when it has Brahman as its object, it does not do so when it has anything else as its object.
This is what was stated:
"As for this pursuit of specific activities..."
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the creation of the world is not the activity of Hiraṇyagarbha, but rather that of the Supreme Self who has entered into him. Therefore,
because the passage begins with "The Self alone was this [in the beginning]," because there is a reference to Him in the middle by means of His activity of seeing,

and because at the end the various classes of beings along with the gross elements are mentioned and concluded as being established in Brahman, it is certain that this text refers exclusively to Brahman.
However, where there is a scriptural mention of the "person-like" (puruṣavidha) and so forth, that must have another purpose, as there is no other alternative; thus all is clear.
Another alternative [interpretation]:
Is there a single meaning for this entire composition which begins with "Being" (sat) and also begins with the "Self" (ātman), or is there a difference in meaning?

In this context, since the word "Being" (sat) applies without distinction to both the Self and the non-Self, it does not have the Self as its referent; rather, its referent is the universal Being (sattāsāmānya) that pervades all things. Thus, due to the difference in the opening statement, there is a difference in meaning.
Furthermore, the conclusion, "That is the Self, That thou art," must be explained—in accordance with the opening statement—as having the sense of becoming one (saṃpatti);
for that universal Being is to be realized as the Supreme Self.

And because the knowledge of that [one thing] entails the knowledge of all things—since *sattā* (Being), as the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*), pervades the entire expansion of all entities—this being the position reached, it is said in response: There is indeed the apprehension of the Self even for the Chāndogyas, just as for the Vājasaneyins, because of the instruction of identity in the subsequent passage, "The Self is That, Thou art That" (*tattvamasi*). Let it be granted, then, that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), being indeterminable as either existent or non-existent, lacks existence; however, since existence is determinable only as the reality of the Self-substance (*ātmadhātu*), therefore, the Self alone [is real].
He says [in response], having accepted [the objection]:

Since the word "sat" (being) denotes the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) and applies to each individual instance, and since the word "sat" applies both to the Self and to other things, there arises a doubt. Consequently, in accordance with the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*), it is established that "It is Being alone" (*sadeva*) as the Self itself.

For the description of the conclusion must follow the introductory statement (*upakrama*) whose meaning is definitive; the conclusion is not to be described in a way that contradicts an introductory statement of doubtful meaning.
Furthermore, the fruit must be conceived as occurring upon attainment;
nor is the knowledge of particulars possible when only the universal is known.
Indeed, when a tree is known through its general form, its particulars—such as being a *śiṃśapā* and so forth—are not thereby known.

Thus, since everything such as the restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) would be untenable if [the Self] were not for the sake of the Self, it is established that the *Chāndogya* indeed teaches the Self for its own sake.

In this regard, in the preceding prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the meditation on Hiraṇyagarbha was established, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the contemplation of Brahman. 3.3.9.18.
"Because of the mention of what is to be accomplished, it is something not previously known."
He states the subject matter:
"The Chāndogyas and the Vājasaneyins.
*Ana* means breathing; *prāṇa* means breath. Thus, they are those who make that breath *anagna*, or non-naked.
Regarding "the contemplation of non-nakedness":
*manana* means thinking, which is knowledge; that which extends to its culmination is called *cintana*. He states a doubt:
"Why is that? [The opponent asks.

Having initially taken up the position of enjoining both [the mantra and the action] based merely on the sound of the words, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) resorts to the middle position:
"Or rather, it is indeed an injunction."
If this is so, one might ask what the purpose of proclaiming "nudeness" (anagnatā) is; to this he says:
"But for the sake of praising that very [practice].

This is the underlying intention: although there is a Smṛti rule for sipping water (ācamana) for the sake of purification, nevertheless, because it is not enjoined within the context of the meditation on the vital breaths (prāṇopāsana), it is not established as an ancillary part of that meditation; therefore, its injunction here becomes meaningful.

Just as the prohibition against speaking untruth, which is recorded in the Smṛti, becomes meaningful as an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma when it is recited within the context of that sacrifice—namely, "one should not speak untruth"—the author states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "This being the case... (evam prāpte).
He objects:
"But surely this is a scriptural text. He replies:
"No," [he says].
The meaning is that the relationship of root and derivative exists between two things that have the same referent, not between those that have different referents.
He refutes the seed of the prima facie argument residing in the [opponent's] intention:
And this is not a scriptural injunction (*śruti*).
It is appropriate that there be no tautology between the two prohibitions of speaking untruth—one pertaining to the ritual (*kratvartha*) and the other to the person’s welfare (*puruṣārtha*).

However, in this case, the scribed (*smārta*) rule for sipping water (*ācamana*), which is prescribed as an auxiliary to all rites and also as an auxiliary to the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇopāsana*), would be redundant and thus purposeless because of its overlap with the more extensive scribed rule for sipping water.
Nor is there any redundancy with this [text] regarding that which is based on Smṛti, because the former is universal while the latter has a restricted scope.
Having thus rejected the middle position, he rejects the first position:
"And for this very reason, there is no injunction of both."
He states another argument:
"And in the case of prescribing both. He concludes:
Therefore, [the meaning] is already established;
and this is not a doctrine concerning non-nakedness.
The meaning is that praise is not possible in the absence of something to be praised.

Furthermore, that which has not been obtained through another means of knowledge (*māna*) should be praised as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). However, the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding nakedness has not been obtained from elsewhere such that it could serve as a praise;
nor has the act of sipping water (*ācamana*) been obtained from elsewhere such that, being an injunction, it could be praised. Thus he says:
"And for oneself, there is the resolve regarding nakedness.

Furthermore, it is appropriate that a single action has only a single purpose; however, when no other recourse is possible due to the force of a stronger authority, one may postulate multiple purposes for it.
But in the case of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*), since a different action is being enjoined, this fault does not apply; thus he says:
And this being the case, it cannot be said that "this refers to a single instance of sipping water.
Furthermore, because of its association with the injunction for seeing, it is logical that it is indeed an injunction for seeing, not an injunction for sipping water; thus he says:
"Moreover, whatever this may be..."

For just as the perception of food is enjoined in the case of food that is impossible for anyone from a dog down to a fly to eat, so too here, because it is impossible for water to serve as a garment, only a perception [of it as such] is enjoined; this is understood from the association with the injunction for the perception of food.

Furthermore, although the lack of verbal expression (*aśabdatva*) is equal for both perception and eating, nevertheless, perception is observed to be directly performed by the word because it is inseparable from the verbal object of perception.
Eating, however, must be supplied [by implication] merely through its suitability; this is the distinction.

Furthermore, in the case of the *Chāndogyas* and the *Vājasaneyins*, regarding the sipping of water (*ācamana*), the expression "they sip" (*ācāmanti*) is generally a statement in the present tense. Even where there is an injunctive suffix, they consider the injunctive force to be unintended, as in the passage "one should offer oblations of wild sesame gruel" (*jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt*). [The opponent] says that because the meaning is already established by other means, it is indeed an injunction, like "he offers the *samidh* oblation" (*samidho yajati*), etc.—this is expressed in the words "and also, 'they sip'. The remainder has a self-evident meaning. //18// 3.3.10.19.
It is the same because there is no difference.

Here, the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position follows the logic of the section on repetition (*abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa*): since two injunctions for knowledge contained within the same branch do not exhibit any distinguishing feature, there is no certainty as to which is the original injunction and which is the restatement (*anuvāda*). This is because [the latter] would lack the nature of making known what was unknown (*ajñāta-jñāpana*) or impelling one toward what has not yet been undertaken (*apravṛtta-pravartana*).
And since the status of being an injunction is established by its own inherent force, there is a difference in meditation in both cases.

Nor can it be argued that in one case there is a restatement for the sake of enjoining other qualities, while in the other there is not, because other qualities are observed to be enjoined in both places as well; thus, there would be no basis for distinction (*vinigamanā-hetu*), and it would follow that identical qualities are not mentioned [in both].

Therefore, just as in the case of "He offers the *samidh* oblation" and so forth, a difference in meditation results from repetition (*abhyāsa*). To this, it is replied: "There is a single ritual action, because of recognition through identity."
Nor is there a lack of perceived distinction in this regard.

Among those [actions], that action for which many qualities (guṇas) are prescribed is the primary injunction; elsewhere, however, it is a prescription of only a few qualities by way of reference (anuvāda) to that [primary action].

For example, where there is a multitude of umbrellas, chowries, banners, elephants, archers, swordsmen, staff-bearers, bowmen, dagger-men, and infantry, it is understood that "the King is there," but not in a place possessing only a few elephants, horses, and infantry.
Therefore, O Minister, it is the same here as well.

Furthermore, the mention of qualities prescribed in one place in another context is not purposeless, because its aim is to strengthen recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Or rather, let this be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*); for it is not necessary that all restatements must have a specific purpose in every instance.

Because even a mere restatement (anuvāda) of that [meditation] is found here and there, it is established that the meditation in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is indeed the same, due to the inclusion of its qualities. 3.3.11.20.
"In the same way, elsewhere too, on account of the connection."
If, because of recognition as being essentially the same even within a single recension (*śākhā*), there were a commingling of the meditations and the duties prescribed therein,
then it would follow that because the Truth (*satya*) is one and the same, there would also be a commingling of the two Upaniṣads residing in the two spheres [the sun and the heart].
Furthermore, the word "of that" (*tasya*) refers back to what has been previously mentioned, and thus indicates a distinction.

Since "Truth" (satya) is the primary subject under discussion, whereas "with reference to the deities" (adhidaiva) is subordinate as a mere qualification and thus not the primary topic, it follows that—as in the previous case—there is a commingling of attributes because of the non-difference from the primary Truth.
To this, it is replied:
"Not so, on account of the distinction."

It is true that where the connection of attributes with the mere essential form (*svarūpa*) is heard, there it is so, because the essential form is recognized and because the attributes are connected with that alone. However, where the principal entity is understood as possessing qualifications (*saviśeṣaṇa*), the connection of the attributes is with that very entity as qualified, not with it devoid of qualifications, nor with it accompanied by other qualifications.
For when it is said, "Bring the man with the staff," one does not bring a man without a staff who happens to possess a water-pot.
Therefore, the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the True has been stated with reference to the divine; it cannot belong to that same [True] with reference to the self (adhyātma).
Just as following behind is prescribed for a teacher who is walking, but not for one who is standing, so there is no confusion between the two secret doctrines, but rather a fixed distinction.

This has been stated as "because its own nature does not depart" (sūtra 3.3.11). Furthermore, it shows [the same] through the principle of extended application (*atideśa*): for if it were the absolute reality (*tattva*), there would be no extended application. (sūtra 3.3.12) 23.
Furthermore, from this [text], there is the accumulation and pervasion of heaven:
"The heroic powers were accumulated with Brahman as the eldest; O Agni, Brahman stretched out the eldest heaven.
Brahman was born as the first among beings; who, then, is able to rival Brahman?"
"Those whose eldest is Brahman" are the *brahmajyeṣṭhāḥ*; [the word] *jajñe* means "was born.

Although in those various meditations on Śāṇḍilya and others, a distinction of substrata (*āyatana-bheda*) appears—since the qualities such as the "collection" (*saṃbhṛti*) and so forth have the internal organ (*adhyātmika*) as their substratum, while [others] have the celestial (*ādhidaivika*) as their substratum—nevertheless, because of the recognition of the celestial manifestation through the textual sequence beginning with "Greater than heaven," [these qualities are to be included] among those [meditations] such as the sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśakalā*).

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because the meditations on the Self (*vidyā-svāyatana*) are heard [in various places] and ultimately possess the same nature by having Brahman as their support, there can be a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of them as identical; therefore, there should be a combination (*upasaṃhāra*) of qualities such as being "consisting of truth" (*satya-saṃkalpa*) and so forth from the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others with those in the meditation on the sixteen parts (*ṣoḍaśakalā-vidyā*) and the like.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is this: through the recognition of mutual similarity in the hearing of common qualities, one meditation incorporates even those qualities not previously heard in it.

However, in this case, there is no hearing of qualities such as "supporting" (*saṃbhṛti*) and so forth belonging to the knowledge of Brahman, as there is in the hearing of qualities within the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others.

As for whatever superhuman power (*vibhūti*) pertaining to the divine sphere is heard in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, because it is dependent on that specific context, only that much will be accepted; one cannot, by this much alone, carry over qualities such as "supporting," since it has been stated that there is an absence of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding those [qualities] therein.
However, Brahman, as the substratum, is incapable of being recognized [as identical], because that would lead to the over-extension of identity to many things. This has been stated:
However, the "Accumulation" (saṃbhṛti) and other qualities are the objects of passages such as that concerning Śāṇḍilya.

Therefore, it is established that because there is no recognition [of these qualities] in those contexts, the "Accumulation" and the "Pervasion of Heaven" (dyuvyāpti)—that is, this pair of Accumulation and Pervasion—are not to be combined with the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others. //23//
If it is argued that [the Puruṣa-vidyā] is not so because the others are not mentioned therein, [we reply:
the status of being a "sacrifice of the person" (puruṣayajña) is common to both;
nor is there any impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the expression "of the sacrifice of the knower" (viduṣo yajñasya).

Because the word "self" (ātman) denotes one's own nature (*svarūpa*)— as in the phrase "the self of the sacrifice"— and because the sacrificer is the very nature of the sacrifice, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "the wise one" (*viduṣaḥ*) is possible due to his being a conscious being.

Therefore, since there is no distinction in both being human sacrifices and since they share common features such as death serving as the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), it follows that once a single meditation (*vidyā*) is determined, the attributes of both must be combined in both cases.

This being the case, it is said in reply: the manner in which the Tāṇḍins and Paiṅgins effect the identification of the person with the sacrifice, as well as the division of the threefold lifespan into the three *savanas*, and the identification of hunger and so forth with the *dīkṣā* and other rites—none of this applies to the Taittirīyas. For them, there is no such accomplishment of the sacrifice within the person.
In the statement "the self is the sacrificer," this word "self" does not denote one's essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For the sacrificer cannot be the very essence of the sacrifice,
since there can be no identity between the agent and the object of the action.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for consciousness and unconsciousness to be one and the same, and because sacrificial acts are unconscious while the sacrificer is conscious,
it is only for the conscious Self that both the state of being a sacrificer and the state of being a knower are possible.

And thus the meaning is as follows: for a person who knows in this way, the sacrificer is the self by virtue of being related to that sacrifice which belongs to him; in this manner, both the sacrificer’s status as the self and the sacrifice’s relation to the knower would be primary.

Otherwise, if the word "self" (ātman) were to denote its own essential nature, then both the phrases "of the knower's sacrifice" and "the sacrificer is the nature of the sacrifice" would be merely figurative.
Moreover, since there is a possible interpretation [of the passage], it is not appropriate [to take it literally].

Therefore, the status of the person as a sacrifice does not exist in the Taittirīya [text]; thus, there is no similarity on that account. Furthermore, the preparation of the wife, the sacrificer, the Vedas, and the sacred knowledge (vidyā) does not exist for the Taittirīyas as it does for the Tāṇḍins or the Paiṅgins; indeed, their realization of the *savana* [sacrificial sessions] is entirely different.

Therefore, when there is a significant difference [between two texts], it is not appropriate to claim the identity of a knowledge (*vidyā*) based on a mere similarity, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since there is the scriptural restatement "of that very one who knows thus" (*tasyaivaṃ viduṣaḥ*), if multiple matters were enjoined, the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result; such is the meaning.
Moreover, this knowledge of the human sacrifice (*puruṣayajñavidyā*) of the Paiṅgis and the Tāṇḍins is perceived as independent, being connected with different fruits.

For the Taittirīyas, however, there is dependence [on another means], because of the scriptural statement "of one who knows thus," because of the reference to what was previously mentioned, and because of the hearing of that [liberation] as its fruit.
And it is not fitting that independence and dependence should be identical; thus he says: "Moreover, the knowledge of the Self together with renunciation.
He concludes: "Therefore... (3.3.14.25).
Because there is a difference in meaning regarding piercing and other such rites,
he shows the subject of the inquiry with the words:
"Of the Atharvaṇikas."
At the beginning of various Upaniṣads, such as those of the Atharvaṇikas, specific mantras and rituals such as the Pravargya are recited.
Regarding this, he states a doubt: "What are these? [i.e., what is their status?]
He takes up the prima facie view:
"These [mantras] belong to the meditations (vidyās) themselves," because all the meditations are recorded along with their fruits, and the mantras are mentioned in their proximity.

Furthermore, the ritual actions (karmāṇi) that have been traditionally handed down are understood to be subordinate members (aṅga) of knowledge (vidyā), according to the principle that "that which is mentioned in proximity to what possesses a fruit is subordinate to it," since they lack their own independent fruit.
[The opponent] objects: "But surely, of these... [etc.]

For here there exist no means of proof—such as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), or name (*samākhyā*)—that serve to apply [the mantras].

Indeed, it is not the case that, as the *samid* and other [mantras] are recited after beginning with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, so too are mantras or ritual acts recited after beginning with some particular knowledge (*vidyā*).
Nor, in the absence of a general connection, can there be a sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) based merely on the proximity of related items.

Furthermore, knowledge that has been heard and is complete in its constituent parts does not stand in need of these [subsidiary rites], such that their mere proximity—given that a general connection has already been established through the context—could lead to a specific connection. He provides the answer:
"Certainly, even though they are not perceived... [etc.].
Let there not be a longing for those sciences that bear fruit in this very life and possess all their constituent parts in full.

However, for mantras—whose status as means to human ends is established by the injunction for their private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*)—and for rites such as the *pravargya*, whose status as means to human ends is established by their own specific injunctions, there arises a connection based on mutual expectancy due to their proximity to that which is desired and sought by the person; this is like the maxim of the "red-clad" (the dyer). Furthermore, since the meditations (*vidyās*) possess fruits, the mantras and rites, being themselves fruitless, exist for the sake of those meditations.

Nor can heaven be postulated as the fruit for the Pravargya and other such rites, as it is for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; for [the former] descend to that status by virtue of being in proximity to those [rites] that possess fruits.
We shall infer this on the strength of their proximity.

Indeed, when this [sentence] is heard in proximity to a knowledge (*vidyā*) that has already ceased its expectancy, it arouses expectancy even in that [knowledge], because that which lacks expectancy is incapable of being syntactically connected with what possesses expectancy.
And having aroused it, it attains the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).
Furthermore, since it is impossible for something incapable of action to be a benefactor, it conceives of its own capacity to assist the subject matter of the context (*prakaraṇin*).

And even if there is capacity, that which is not enjoined by direct Vedic statement (śruti) cannot attain the status of being an auxiliary to that [rite]; thus, through this sequence, proximity (saṃnidhi) implies a direct statement by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). He raises an objection: "But surely, of these mantras... [and so on].

For it has been stated in the section beginning with "But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct" (*aviśiṣṭastu vākyārthaḥ*) that the utility of mantras consists in their illuminating the matters connected with the ritual performance (*prayoga*).
Yet, we do not perceive any matter related to [the state of] knowledge (*vidyā*) within the mantras.

And although the *pravargya* rite is not heard of as being enjoined in reference to anything specific, nevertheless, through syntactical connection (*vākya-saṃyoga*) and connection with the sacrifice (*kratu-saṃyoga*), it attains a relationship with the sacrifice.

"Before the Upasads, they proceed with the Pravargya. Because the Upasads have an inseparable connection with the sacrifice—just like the *juhū* ladle—even though there are Upasads in the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma as well, they are there only inferential; whereas in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, they are directly enjoined. Therefore, by virtue of its rapid application, it is understood through the sentence that [the Pravargya] is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Furthermore, since the *pravargya* is prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is obtained in its modifications (*vikṛti*) as well by means of the extended injunction (*codaka*), just like the *upasads*.
Or rather, according to the principle that "it should be enjoined in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself because of the avoidance of tautology," its injunction together with the *upasads* is appropriate;
this is what he states:
"And how [is it] from the Pravargya?"—
the sense is that syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) because of the remoteness of the meaning. He provides the resolution:
This is not a fault.
First, regarding "capacity" (sāmarthya):

for instance, in the mantra "I offer you, acceptable to Agni" (*agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), the two words "to Agni" (*agnaye*) and "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*) reveal meanings that are inherent to the ritual action (*karmasamavetārtha*).

However, just as in the case of the remaining words they are explained somehow or other by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with that [central word], so too here, since the word *hṛdaya* has a meaning directly applicable (*samaveta*) to the act of meditation (*upāsanā*), the other words connected in a single syntactical unit with it must be interpreted somehow through figurative (*gauṇī*) or indicative (*lakṣaṇā*) functions; thus, the mantras do not have meanings that are not directly applicable.

And he says— "And [the application of] mantras is seen in meditations"— to show that it is not the case that the application of mantras is never seen in meditations such that one would have to postulate an entirely unseen result.
Although proximity (saṃnidhi), being weaker, is sublated by syntactical connection (vākya) which is stronger, this is so only when there is a contradiction.
There is no contradiction here;
for even though the Pravargya rite has been enjoined by a direct statement (*vākya*) in relation to the Jyotiṣṭoma, its application to the Vidyā is also possible through proximity (*saṃnidhi*).

Just as the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice—which, by the injunction "one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," has spiritual luster as its fruit—is also enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Vājapeya: "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, [he should sacrifice] with the Bṛhaspatisava."
"One should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

For here, the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is understood from the suffix *ktvā*, because that suffix is prescribed when there is a connection between verbal roots (*dhātu*). And how could there be an identical agent if there were a connection with a different meaning of a verbal root?
If there were only a single application (prayoga), then agency would indeed consist in being engaged in that application; and how could that [agency] be one when the applications are distinct?

Therefore, because they have the same agent, the *vājapeya* and the *bṛhaspatisava* constitute a single performance; this is also due to their connection with different root-meanings. Furthermore, since there can be no connection or single performance without a relationship of primary and subordinate, and because it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *vājapeya*, the *vājapeya* is the primary rite and the *bṛhaspatisava* is its subsidiary (*aṅga*).

Nor does there arise the contingency of a relationship of subsidiary and principal (*aṅgapradhānabhāva*) in the case of the statement, "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma.
For this injunction is not recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of either the Darśapūrṇamāsa or the Soma sacrifice.

Thus, since both possess their own independent entitlements (*sādhikāratā*) and no distinction is perceived between them regarding the status of subsidiary and principal, there is an absence of a decisive criterion for such a relationship. Consequently, the commonality of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is taken figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) with the intention of referring merely to the substratum [of the action], and thus there is no fault.

Even if, however, it were studied as part of a specific context (ārabhyādhīta) in some particular recension, stating "having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," it would still be logical that what is studied outside of a specific context (anārabhyādhīta) is precisely what is recognized within the context-study.

This being so, since both are understood to have separate qualifications for performance, their status as equally primary (samapradhānatva) remains unrenounced; otherwise, by way of a subordinate-superordinate relationship, that status would be abandoned.
Therefore, it is established that this conjunction has time as its object.
He introduces the final conclusion: "Thus, the prima facie position having been reached..."

The mantra "hṛdayaṃ pravidhya" (pierce the heart), by its very own natural force, is perceived as expressing a meaning associated with malevolent rites (*ābhicārika-karman*) through all its constituent words. Therefore, this indicative mark (*liṅga*), characterized by its power of denotation, is stronger than both syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), which are respectively more powerful than order (*krama*); how much more so, then, than order itself?

Therefore, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the context (*saṃnidhi*) is set aside, and it is established that [the mantra] is merely a subsidiary part of the magical rite (*abhicārika-karma*). Furthermore, although in the meditations (*upāsanā*) the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*) alone has a meaning inherent to the ritual act,
nevertheless all the other words therein lack such an inherent meaning.

In the case of a rite of exorcism (*ābhicārika*), however, since the purpose of all [the words] is present together, what would be the use of the meaning being inherent in a single word? Nor is it logical that one should establish a mantra within the *upāsanā*s (meditative practices) merely because they are accepted due to proximity. For even in an act of exorcism, the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*)—which has an inherent meaning and is part of a single syntactical unit with other words—is connected to the rite of exorcism by means of the authority of the sentence (*vākya-pramāṇa*).

Since it is impossible to displace [the mantra] by virtue of its proximity (*saṃnidhi*), in the same way, once it is established that even mantras such as "O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice" (*deva savitaḥ prasuva yajñam*)— which possess the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the impulse toward sacrifice— are auxiliary to the sacrifice,
what will the secondary proximity to knowledge (*vidyā-saṃnidhi*) accomplish?
The same applies to others, such as the *Śvetāśvatara* and so forth, some by virtue of their indicative mark (*liṅga*) and some by virtue of direct statement (*śruti*).
"For some [it is established] by another means of proof" or "by the context.
But why is proximity (saṃnidhi) set aside by indicative power (liṅga) and the rest? To this he says:
"For proximity is weak."
The meaning established in the first [chapter on] Tantra is now being recalled.

In that context, however, there is an inquiry as to which is stronger when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), characterized by their having the same object.

An example here is as follows: there is a verse addressed to Indra (*aindrī ṛk*), beginning with "Never art thou a deceiver, O Indra," which is a direct statement (*śruti*) enjoining its application: "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the *aindrī* [verse]."
For here, application to Indra appears to be indicated by the mark (*liṅga*) characterized by semantic capacity.

Furthermore, from the direct statement (*śruti*), specifically from the accusative case in "the *gārhapatya* fire," the status of the *gārhapatya* as the primary beneficiary (*śeṣin*) is understood; and from the instrumental case in "the *aindrī* [verse]," the status of the *aindrī* verse as the subordinate element (*śeṣa*) is understood.

This is so even though, based on the accusative case in "the *gārhapatya* fire," it would also be possible for the *gārhapatya* to be the beneficiary with respect to a verse addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*).
Even though there is no contradiction because the instrumental case-ending in "aindryā" (with the Aindrī verse) permits its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) toward Indra,
nevertheless, when it is connected with another word, it is the sentence (*vākya*) itself that is contradicted by the indicative power (*liṅga*), not the direct statement (*śruti*).
And in that case, the relative strength and weakness are reversed.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the two Vedic statements differ in form and function.

For the second and third case endings, being kāraka-case suffixes, convey the status of the nominal stem's meaning as either an object (*karman*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the action; thus, they are the means of application (*viniyojika*).

Indeed, application consists in the fact that, with respect to the action, the object possesses the status of the primary element (*śeṣitva*) and the instrument possesses the status of the subordinate element (*śeṣatva*).

When the relationship of subordinate and principal with respect to an action is understood from the mere direct statement (*śruti*) without depending on other words, it is "based on direct statement" (*śrauta*).
This application (*viniyoga*), which is generally apprehended through direct statement, is established in its specific form by the power of other words.
This very relationship, characterized by the distinction between qualifier and qualified, is the domain of syntactical connection (*vākya*).

The relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*), however, is based on direct Vedic statement (*śrauta*). Therefore, in view of the qualification obtained through syntactical connection (*vākya*), the directly stated relationship of subordinate and principal is contradicted by indicative power (*liṅga*). Thus, when there is a conflict between direct statement and indicative power, should the accusative case-ending in the direct statement—"of the Gārhapatya"—be interpreted in the sense of the locative case, in accordance with the indicative power, as "in the vicinity of the Gārhapatya"?
"One should worship Indra with the verse addressed to Indra," [says one]. Or rather, let the indicative mark (*liṅga*) be explained in accordance with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
For the Gārhapatya fire is capable of performing its own appropriate function; and Indra [is indicated] because the root *ind* signifies sovereignty.

What, then, is the prima facie conclusion? That the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stronger than the direct statement (*śruti*). Indeed, that which is incapable in a certain respect cannot be applied there even by a thousand direct statements, just as one cannot say, "one should sprinkle with fire" or "one should burn with water."
Therefore, having prioritized semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), one must apply [the mantra] through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
And that capacity of this *ṛc* is perceived with respect to Indra both from other means of knowledge and from the word itself.
For instance, one who knows the words and their meanings clearly understands Indra from the *ṛc* beginning with "kadācana."
And because of the word "aindryā" [in the mantra],
the application of the *aindrī* mantra to the Gārhapatya fire is like the application of fire— which is naturally for burning wood— to the burning of water.
Nor is it correct to say that one should resort to a secondary (jaghanyā) mode of operation to assume an inherent capacity (sāmarthya) merely out of deference to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

Since the capacity [of the word] exists prior [to the application], the scriptural text (śruti) is established only in accordance with that capacity. Therefore, when it is argued that the Aindrī verse must be used for the worship of Indra alone in the vicinity of the Gārhapatya fire, the following is stated: "The scriptural text does not exercise its directive function by placing the knowledge of the indicative mark (liṅga) at the forefront; rather, the indicative mark is the director by placing the knowledge of the scriptural text at the forefront."

For if the cognizer were to determine the application of the *śruti* only after having understood the capacity (*sāmarthya*), then the *śruti* would be weak with respect to the application because it would depend upon the knowledge of the indicative power (*liṅga*).
But this is not the case;
the *śruti* requires the capacity for the sake of application, but it does not require the cognition of that capacity.

Once the application (*viniyoga*) has been understood from that [direct statement], however, it is not possible for one who lacks capacity; therefore, in order to effect that application, capacity is postulated. That capacity exists prior to the application by direct statement, but it is not apprehended prior [to that application].

Since the application (*viniyoga*) is established [by other means], its subsequent cognition arises through the impossibility of it being otherwise; thus, the cognition of capacity (*sāmarthya*), which follows the application by direct statement (*śruti*), must be established in accordance with that [application].
However, indicative power (*liṅga*) is not itself an applicator, but rather applies by postulating a direct statement that performs the application.
For instance, from indicative power alone, one does not naturally perceive that "Indra is to be worshipped by this [mantra]."

However, because of the force of the mention of Indra in this context, although one might infer an application based on the general purpose of the passage falling within that context— which would otherwise be inexplicable—

the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) itself is more appropriate to be inferred than the application whose meaning must be constructed; for the application to be inferred is further removed from the literal sense than the direct Vedic statement.
For it is not possible for the Śākyas to establish through reasoning what has been heard [in scripture] if it is illogical;

nor do people justify the statement "there are three Brahmans here: Kaṭha and Kauṇḍinya" by means of Māṭhara presented by another means of knowledge, nor do they fail to ridicule those who would so justify it.
But they accept that [the words] "māṭhara" and so forth are being made audible;
therefore, the impossibility of the arising of the meaning from what is heard must be established by means of another meaning that is itself heard.

It is established in common worldly experience that [an application] does not occur merely by means of a different object brought forward by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is not appropriate to subject what is established in the world to injunctions or challenges, because that would contradict the world, which serves as the means for knowing the meaning of words.
Therefore, an injunctive scriptural statement (*śruti*) must be inferred.

And thus, while the operation of inferring an applicatory *śruti* from the *liṅga* has only just begun, the application to the *gārhapatya* fire is already established by the directly perceived *śruti*; consequently, the context (*prakaraṇa*) has its expectancy satisfied. Therefore, due to what deficiency would the *liṅga* proceed to construct an applicatory *śruti*?
Because the application of the collection of mantras has been established by the direct scriptural statement (*viniyoga-śruti*) itself;
as they have said: "As long as that which is to be known is unknown or doubtful, it is sought to be known; but once it has been known, the desire for knowledge of the knowers is stilled."

Therefore, it is established that when the capacity of a mantra must be interpreted in accordance with a well-known Vedic application (*viniyoga*), it should be guided even by a secondary sense (*jaghanyā vṛttiḥ*) without abandoning its primary sense (*prathamā vṛttiḥ*). Here, the conflict between indicative power (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) is as follows: "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well with a stream of clarified butter. Sit upon it, O immortal one, and take thy stand, O essence of rice, being well-disposed. In this [mantra], the word *tasmin* (upon it) indicates through its indicative power (*liṅga*) that the entire mantra is intended for the preparation of the seat (*sādane*). However, the syntactical connection (*vākya*)—formed by the two parts, "I prepare a pleasant seat... and "Sit upon it..."—indicates that the first part is for the preparation of the seat and the second part is for the act of sitting (*āsādane*). Since the two are in conflict, the question arises as to which prevails. Because the relationship of the whole to its parts is more intimate than that of two independent sentences, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than the syntactical connection (*vākya*). Thus, the mantra is applied to the preparation of the seat. Furthermore, because the word *tasmin* is not connected to the preceding clause, the mantra is split; the portion ending with *kalpayāmi* is used for the preparation of the seat, while the remainder is used for the act of sitting. This is the view of Bādari. Alternatively, the word *tasmin* may be connected to the preceding clause, and the entire mantra may be used for the preparation of the seat. This is the view of Jaimini. However, since the preparation of the seat is already accomplished by the first part alone, the subsequent portion would be redundant. Therefore, the mantra is divided according to the indicative power (*liṅga*), and both parts are applied to the preparation of the seat. This is the view of Ātreya. Or rather, the mantra should be used for the act of sitting, because the purpose of the mantra is to bring to mind the object of the ritual action (*karmasamavetārtha-prakāśana*). Since the act of sitting is directly connected to the ritual action, whereas the preparation of the seat is not, the mantra is applied to the act of sitting. This is the view of Tautātita. However, the act of sitting is already indicated by the word *sīda* ("sit") itself; therefore, the mantra is applied to the preparation of the seat. This is the view of Āśmarathya. Is this entire mantra to be employed both for the preparation of the seat and for the placing of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), or is it that the portion ending with "I prepare" is for the spreading [of the grass], while the portion beginning with "on that, sit" is for the placing of the cake? If the syntactical unity (vākya) is more authoritative, then the entire mantra applies to both; for the portion beginning with "on that, sit" enters into a single syntactical unity with the preceding part because it depends upon the phrase "I prepare so that it may be well-seated" (suśevaṃ kalpayāmi). Specifically, it means: "On that which I prepare, let it sit."
Now, if the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful, then [the mantra] is to be applied to the making of the seat and the illuminating thereof, for it is capable of that;
and to the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), with the words "may he sit upon it," for it is capable of that.
What, then, is the prima facie view?
Since syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*), the entire mantra is applied in both cases.

For here, when syntactic unity is established through the co-occurrence of words such that they possess mutual expectancy upon being divided, one must subsequently postulate the capacity to denote [the meaning] in accordance with that unity.

This is just as in the mantra "devasya tvā," where because the two words "agnaye" and "nirvapāmi" have meanings connected to the ritual act, the other words are subordinate to them through syntactic unity, and thus their capacity for that purpose is postulated there.
Thus, since the capacity (*sāmarthya*) has been postulated in accordance with the requirement to maintain the understood unity of the sentence, it cannot be set aside;
rather, it follows that the mantra must be employed by means of an applicatory direct statement (*viniyojikā śruti*).
