This being the position reached, it is said in reply: this would indeed be so if the determination of capacity were preceded by the comprehension of the unity of the sentence.

However, for words whose capacities have been determined and which are recited in close conjunction, the determination of their status as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) occurs by virtue of their capacity and the unity of purpose.
As many words as are capable of conveying a single principal meaning and are mutually expectant when separated constitute one sentence.
And in mantras, the object to be performed, being manifested, is the principal element.
Since the preparation of the seat (*sadanakaraṇa*) and the placing of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśāsādana*) are both to be performed as primary acts,

the mantra ending with "I prepare" (*kalpayāmi*) is capable of manifesting the preparation of the seat, while the portion beginning with "sit upon that" (*tasmin sīda*) is capable of manifesting the placing of the sacrificial cake.

Consequently, before the capacity [of the whole] can be inferred on the basis of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the perceived capacity of each individual part brings into existence the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) that assigns each part to its respective meaning.

And thus, when by the Vedic text itself each individual part has been assigned to a single purpose, and the recitation within the context is thereby established, the indicative power (*liṅga*)—which is merely inferred from the sentence (*vākya*)—cannot postulate another, further Vedic text as its applicator. Consequently, even the notion of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) that had arisen becomes a mere semblance, being sublated by the indicative power. However, where there is no conflicting indicative power, the syntactic unity of one, two, or three words whose meanings are connected implies the capacity of the remaining words as well; thus, the sentence functions as an applicator.
Just as in this very case with [the mantras] beginning with "syonam te," it is established that indicative power (liṅga) is stronger than syntactical connection (vākya).
An example of the conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).
Here, *vākya* (syntactical connection) consists of words that, by virtue of their mutual dependence, culminate in a single specific meaning;
whereas *prakaraṇa* (context) is the relationship of those words, having already attained the status of a sentence, with another sentence due to the requirement of a further purpose.

The elders declare that *prakaraṇa* (context) is the statement of that which is to be performed—the cultivation of the fruit—once the meaning of the verbal root has been attained and there arises a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
For example: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
This statement is indeed the *prakaraṇa*.

Thus, when this [injunction] has concluded its application to a certain extent through its own set of words, there arises an expectation for another effect characterized by the assistance of the instruments (*karaṇa*); it is then that there occurs a connection with other sentences such as "He offers the *samits*" and so forth.

For the productive operations (*bhāvanā*) of the *samits* and others, being established by their own injunctions, require a beneficial result to be produced for the person; since they do not obtain any other fruit—whether by the principle of the *viśvajit* sacrifice, by textual ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*), or from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—they are unable to bring the productive operation of the New and Full Moon sacrifices to completion.

Therefore, when there is a requirement for that [principal act], these sentences—which fall into place depending on their own functions—attain the function characterized by the assistance to the instrument required by it; they thus complete the principal act and bring it to fulfillment.
This is a conjunction of the two, like the case of the lost horse and the burnt chariot.
Thus, this is the example of the conflict between *vākya* and *prakaraṇa*, both of which are defined by indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), namely the *sūktavāka* recitation.
For in that [text], the deities of the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) and the deities of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) are recited together.

Since they cannot form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with one another, by virtue of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), the word *indrāgnī* must be displaced from the full moon sacrifice and applied to the new moon sacrifice, because it is there that it is relevant to the context. Now, a doubt arises: should that which is understood as being in syntactical connection with the word *indrāgnī*—namely, "you two have grown strong, you have made [it] greater"—be displaced alone, or should it be displaced along with the word *indrāgnī* itself?

In this regard, if the context (*prakaraṇa*) is more powerful, then the remnant (*śeṣa*), even though its deity has been removed, should be employed; but if the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more powerful, then the word for the deity should be employed in that very place [where it was originally]. What, then, is the prima facie view? That the remnant should be employed even with its deity removed, because it is context alone that establishes the relationship between the subsidiary and the primary. For an injunction that possesses a result brings about the status of being a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the primary sacrifice.
Because, by depending upon that [sentence], the *śruti* and other means of proof bring about a specific connection.
Therefore, it follows that when there is a conflict with the *prakaraṇa*—which is characterized by the statement of the primary *bhāvanā*—the sentence that depends upon it must be set aside.

This being the position reached, it is replied: this would indeed be so if the *prakaraṇa* were to effect the application without regard for the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the form of the thing to be applied.

Moreover, for the sake of application (*viniyoga*), and with reference to that [direct statement], otherwise there would be no displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the mantra for the consecration of Pūṣan and so forth, nor of the twelve-fold *upasads*.
Upon examining their forms, that which is understood more quickly is stronger, while that which is remote is weak.

In that regard, if that form is applied elsewhere by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), or syntactical connection (*vākya*), then it displaces the context (*prakaraṇa*) and is elevated [to that other place].
By the remaining [means], however, the requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*) is fulfilled.

Now, if there is no direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or other such means that operate more rapidly regarding its own [application], then the context becomes the means of application (*viniyojaka*),
as in the case of the *samidh* and other [oblations].
Therefore, it is stated here that syntactical connection (*vākya*) operates more rapidly than context (*prakaraṇa*).
For in the case of context, there is observed merely a mutual requirement between sentences that are complete in their own respective meanings;
whereas in the case of syntactical connection, there is a direct relationship between the words themselves.
Furthermore, while the syntactical unity of the sentence and the context is being inferred, the capacity for denotation is already established by the sentence;

while the capacity is being established by the sentence in one case, it is already established by the capacity in the other; while the application is being effected here by direct assertion (*śruti*), and while the expectancy has been severed and the inference of *śruti* is thus frustrated, that which was previously inferred in the interim by the context is [set aside].
Because of the superior force of the statement "they dissolve," it is established that there is indeed a displacement of those deities who are subordinate to them.
An example of contradiction between order and context:
In the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Rājasūya sacrifice, the narrative of Śunaḥśepa and other elements are recorded in close proximity (*saṃnidhi*) to the principal rite of the Abhiṣecanīya.
Is that [narrative] an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the entire Rājasūya, or of the Abhiṣecanīya alone?
If the sequence (krama) is more powerful, then it applies to the entire Rājasūya; if, however, the order (prakaraṇa) is more powerful, then it applies to the Abhiṣecanīya alone.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
For mere expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) alone is not the cause of syntactic connection (*saṃbandha*).

If it were, then in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*) and "Look at the favor" (*prasādaṃ paśya*), since the word *gām*—which requires only an action—could potentially be connected with *paśya* as well, there would follow the undesirable consequence of an absence of any determining factor (*vinigamanābhāva*).
Therefore, proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is the cause of connection.
And thus, by this very [word] *ānaya* ("bring"), the connection with *gām* ("cow") is determined.
Furthermore, mere proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is not the cause of connection;

otherwise, in the sentence "The king's son comes, let the man be removed," there would be no definitive determination because the word *rājñaḥ* ("of the king") is equally proximate to both the words *putra* ("son") and *puruṣa* ("man").
Therefore, expectancy must be stated as the cause of ascertainment.

In this case, since the word "son" (putra) inherently gives rise to an expectancy because it denotes a related entity, when another word denoting a related entity—which itself possesses an expectancy—occurs in its proximity, that expectancy is fulfilled by that very word; whereas the word "person" (puruṣa), which expresses merely the form of a person and is independent [of such a relation], [does not fulfill it].
There is no connection; rather, it is because of the phrase "let it be removed by another," which requires something to be removed.
Even though proximity exists, there is no connection due to the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
Thus goes the popular saying: "The heated [iron] is joined with the heated [iron]."
Thus, even if something is required, it is not connected as long as it is not brought into proximity;

likewise, even if something is proximate, it is not connected as long as it is not required. Since both [proximity and requirement] possess equal force with respect to the connection, and since a combination of order (*krama*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) is impossible, there is an application by way of option (*vikalpa*) between the Rājasūya and the Abhiṣecanīya.
It follows, therefore, that [the *śaunaḥśepa* episode and others] belong to the entire sacrifice.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: In the *rājasūya*, the requirement for the manner-of-performance (*kathaṃbhāva*) persists from the *pavitra* rite up to the *kṣatrasya dhṛti*. And thus: "When the manner-of-performance remains unfulfilled, whatever is recited for the sake of the primary [sacrifice]..."

According to the maxim, "An action whose fruit is not known [is subordinate] to the context," the *Śaunaḥśepa* narrative and other such elements are subordinate to the *Rājasūya*. However, while the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice—being already free of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the constituent elements mentioned in its own sentence—must have its expectancy aroused by the fact of its being recited in proximity (*saṃnidhi*), meanwhile the *Rājasūya*, which already possesses established expectancy, is assumed to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with it.

Furthermore, while the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is being inferred through that syntactical unity with the *Abhiṣecanīya*, the *Rājasūya*—possessing an already established indicative mark—instantiates the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) that effects the application (*viniyoga*).

While a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is being inferred from an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that has itself been inferred from a syntactical connection (*vākya*), if the application (*viniyoga*) is already established by the already-inferred direct statement,
then the intermediate [application] inferred from proximity (*saṃnidhāna*)— which exists only because the reading within the context (*prakaraṇa*) would otherwise be inexplicable— is dissolved;
for it lacks the force of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, because the *rājasūya*, as the primary context (*prakaraṇin*), is present through the proximity of the mental cognition [of it], its immediate vicinity cannot be otherwise conceived.
Therefore, when there is a conflict with the context, the sequence is indeed sublated; nor can there be an option, because of its weakness. This is established.

An example of the conflict between *samākhyā* (name/designation) and *krama* (order): In the section (*kāṇḍa*) named "Pauroḍāśika" and in the sequence of the Sānnāyya ritual, the mantra for the purpose of purification, "śundhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe," is recited.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is it to be employed for the purification of the *puroḍāśa* vessels because *samākhyā* is stronger, or is it for the purification of the Sānnāyya vessels because *krama* is stronger?

What, then, is the conclusion? That the name (*samākhyā*) is more powerful; for by the term *pauroḍāśika*, those things related to the *puroḍāśa* cake are denoted, and the section proceeding with reference to them is called the *Pauroḍāśika*.

Therefore, while a connection would have to be established through the sequence [of texts] via a succession of inferences from context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, it is already established by the name.

Since it is established by direct audition (śruti) itself, [the connection] is immediate; therefore, due to the remoteness of the meaning, the name (samākhyā) is stronger in its sequence, and thus it follows that the mantra should be employed for the cleansing of the *puroḍāśa* vessels, not for the cleansing of the *sānnāyya* vessels.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "Sequence is stronger than name because of the remoteness of the meaning."
For instance, the name (*samākhyā*) does not directly denote the relationship; rather, it denotes the section (*kāṇḍa*) as qualified by the *puroḍāśa*.
Since that qualification would otherwise be inexplicable, the relationship of the section is inferred, but not directly of the Vedic mantra.
And by means of that [section], the inference of the mantra belonging within it also follows.
Moreover, this relationship—the status of the subordinate and the principal—is not understood through direct statement (śruti) alone;
rather, it is merely a general connection.
Therefore, its similarity to direct statement is far removed, and thus it is not appropriate for it to compete with it in the order of precedence.

Moreover, since its purpose (*idamarthya*) is established by the general context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it cannot be connected to the primary sacrifice alone as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), as is the case with the legend of Śunaḥśepa and others.
This is because a mantra serves as an integral auxiliary (*sāmavāyikāṅga*) by reminding one of the elements actually present during the performance.
Thus, there is no contradiction in this mantra being an auxiliary of the context, provided it illuminates some element belonging to the performance of the primary sacrifice.

When there is a requirement for a specific application, the sequence of the ritual acts (*sānnāṭyakrama*) is capable of postulating an application with respect to the ritual act through the means of inference based on context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; however, the name (*samākhyāna*) is not,
because it is weak.

For instance: when a designation (*samākhyā*) exists as the basis for a relationship, it brings about proximity (*saṃnidhi*) for the sake of establishing that relationship; meanwhile, while expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is being inferred through a proximity perceived directly in the Veda, and while expectancy is being inferred through a proximity already established, in the meantime, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is established elsewhere through the already established expectancy; and while syntactic unity is being established elsewhere, the capacity for assistance (*upakārasāmarthya*) is established; and while the capacity for assistance is being established here through syntactic unity, in the meantime, an explicit injunctive text (*śruti*) is produced by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) to effect the application elsewhere.

As long as there is a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) enjoining [a rite] by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) here, so long will there be an injunction elsewhere by means of a scriptural statement already established;

since the recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*) is justified by that much alone, everything constructed through conventional designation (*samākhyā*) becomes rootless—like a crop being harvested from a field whose seeds have been destroyed.
It should be understood that the section is designated as *pauroḍāśika* (pertaining to the cake-offering) because of the abundance of mantras denoting the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

"A disparity among the indicatory marks (liṅga) and the other means of proof is perceived with respect to the meaning of the scriptural statement, based on their operation across one, two, three, four, or five intervening factors."
Thus, the remoteness of meaning has been stated.
And in that regard: "The direct Vedic statement (śruti) is always sublated; the designation (samākhyā) is always sublated.
But for those in between, there is both sublation and sublation-by, depending on their relative position."

Thus has the distinction been stated by the elders. Although we fear prolixity, out of compassion for those unacquainted with the first Tantra, we have fallen into a detailed exposition; therefore, we shall now desist.

Consequently, just as in the case of the request for permission (*anujñāpanā*) and the granting of permission (*anujñā*), whose sequence is well-known, the two mantras "upahūta" and "upahūyasva" are handed down in the Vedic recension, they are obtained as constituent parts (*aṅga*) in that very same way due to the similarity of the context.

The mantra "upahūta" (you are invited), by its indicative power (*liṅga*), is a mantra for granting permission, not for requesting permission; and the mantra "upahūyasva" (be invited), by its indicative power, is a mantra for requesting permission, not for granting it.
Therefore, in this case, the sequence is set aside by the indicative power, and a contrary relationship of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) is established.

For while it would take time for the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be generated through position (*sthāna*) and a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) to be inferred, the application (*viniyoga*) is already accomplished by the indicative power through the inference of a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Thus, there is a sublation of the sequence whose indicative scriptural statement has not yet been inferred.

Therefore, here too, in the application [of the mantra], there is a sublation of the sequence of knowledge—which is separated by four [steps]—by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) which is separated by only one.
Although this point has already been established in the first *tantra*, that establishment was for the sake of resolving a contradiction; however, here there is no contradiction.
For the connection with the rite of sorcery (*abhicārika-karman*) indicated by the *liṅga* is not contradicted by the sequence produced by the connection with the knowledge (*vidyā*).
Nor is there here a contradiction characterized by the application of what has already been applied, for that would entail such a consequence even in the case of the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice.
If it is argued that this is a contradiction of cognition and not a contradiction of reality, that is equally true even when [the mantra] is applied to knowledge (*vidyā*).
Therefore, since there is no contradiction, there is a further objection that the piercing-mantra (*vedhā-mantra*) is an auxiliary to meditation (*upāsanā*).
To this it is replied: "It is not said that there is a sublation of the order (krama) by way of a contradiction with the indicative mark (liṅga);
rather, once [the application] has been determined by the indicative mark, the order is incapable of being postulated.

For while [an item] is not yet assigned through direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), syntactic connection (vākya), or context (prakaraṇa)—on account of its occurrence in the [respective] section—it is subsequently assigned by means of the order, which possesses the authority of postulating context, syntactic connection, indicative mark, and direct statement."
For at that time, if [the mantra] were already employed [elsewhere], it would follow that its recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*) is purposeless.

However, once the recitation within the context has been established by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, the presumption (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted; therefore, the order (*krama*) cannot produce its own appropriate means of valid cognition, as there is an absence of a cognizable object (*pramiti*).

As for the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice, however, the suffix *ktvā* itself—prescribed under the rule governing the connection of verbal roots (*dhātusaṃbandha*)—establishes the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*).

There is a disparity [between the two cases], because even when a rite has already been enjoined by the principle of "separateness from conjunction" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), it cannot be obstructed by another scriptural statement (*śruti*) from its own authoritative force.
This is what was stated:
"But in the Vājapeya, there is a clearly distinct application for the Bṛhaspatisava."
Moreover, this Pravargya rite is one and the same.

By way of removing the doubt regarding its equality with the Bṛhaspatisava due to their equal strength, there is a combination (samuccaya) [of the two], and not a separate mention because they are mutually dependent. He explains the textual proximity (saṃnidhipāṭha):
"Because of the mention of the forest and so forth" (Sūtra 25).

"But in the case of abandonment (hāni), because the word for 'taking up' (upāyana) is supplementary, it is like the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns, and the singing; that has been stated. Where both abandonment and taking up are heard, there is no dispute regarding their conjunction. Even where only the taking up is heard, abandonment is implied as an inseparable concomitant; thus, there is a conjunction.
However, where only the abandonment (*hāna*) of good and evil deeds is heard in scripture, and their acquisition (*upāyana*) is not heard,
there arises the doubt as to whether that acquisition— that is, the taking over— should be combined [with the abandonment] or not. Here,
the author adopts the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
Regarding the term "non-occurrence" (*asaṃnipāta*):
it might be argued that just as a detail heard in one recensional branch (*śākhā*) is incorporated into that very same meditation when it is not heard in another branch, [so too should it be here].
Thus, because he intends to incorporate the act of bringing [the fuel] as heard in another recensional text (śākhā), he says:
"And because it pertains to a different knowledge.
For if there were identity [of the meditation], then the connection of ritual acts taught in one place would be appropriate even in another.
But here, there is no unity among the meditations (*upāsanā*), because they are distinct as being either with attributes (*saguṇa*) or without attributes (*nirguṇa*).

Now, one might object: "Just as the scripture presents the 'taking away' (*hāna*) according to what is heard regarding the 'attaining' (*upāyana*), so too should the 'taking away' imply the 'attaining'"; to this, he says:
Moreover, [the text says] "having the self as its agent.
For an acquisition does not occur without the departure [of ownership] from the former owner; thus, the establishment of departure is necessarily entailed by the acquisition.
Furthermore, departure is observed even in the absence of acquisition by another, as for instance, the removal of sin through expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

This statement regarding the difference in agents is for the purpose of strengthening the argument; it is not, however, a necessary determinant, because it is inconclusive due to the possibility of [the soul] taking up [the organs] otherwise.
He introduces the established conclusion (siddhānta):
"In this case, when [this state] has been reached... [as follows].
This is its meaning: for that which is enjoined in one ritual action is not transferred to another ritual action, due to the absence of any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

However, that which is not enjoined, but is mentioned as an established fact for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), cannot be abandoned when there is no sublation, because it is perceived through the word itself according to the principle of the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇanyāya*). Thus, when there is an expectation as to what happens to the shaken-off good and evil deeds in the case of a qualityless knowledge (*vidyā*)—like the hair of a horse and so forth—it is not possible for them to be dissolved by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), in the same way [as other impurities].
Because the analogies of the horse’s hair and Rāhu are untenable;
for there is never any dissolution of the horse’s hair or the mouth of Rāhu,
but rather their separation from the horse and the moon.
Furthermore, when [the soul] has perished, it is impossible for there to be the meaning of "shaking off" (vidhūnana) or "releasing" (pramocana).

Therefore, since there is a requirement for an explanatory passage (arthavāda), even a distinction established by the proximity of words is capable of bringing "appropriation" (upāyana) to mind and fulfilling that requirement.
Thus, even knowledge devoid of attributes (nirguṇā vidyā) is to be praised by means of both "casting off" and "appropriation."
The excellence of the praise, however, is the purpose (prayojana) and not the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa);
for even in the absence of excellence, the praise remains logically consistent.
Furthermore, it is never observed that one explanatory passage (arthavāda) depends upon another explanatory passage.
And he says that it is not the case that they do not complete [the number],
stating "and it is well-known";
for this statement regarding the acquisition [of the fires] is for the purpose of praising knowledge (vidyā).
Even though the good and evil deeds of one person may yield fruit for another—

just as the *śrāddha* rite performed by a son brings satisfaction to the father, as the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice of a father benefits the son, and as a wife’s drinking of liquor leads to the husband’s rebirth in hell— [the principle remains that the agent is not exempt from responsibility].
Nevertheless, there is a doubt based on the intention that even the good and evil deeds of another cannot directly belong to someone else.
The resolution is that this is a praise [of the scripture] by way of the attainment of the result.
Furthermore, the statement "when there is the desire to include the qualities" does not intend to imply a literal transfer of good and evil deeds in their essential nature.

Anticipating the objection, "Is this not an untimely discussion regarding the meaning of praise within the section concerning the combination of the qualities of knowledge? the author dispels it while concluding:
"Therefore, by way of the incidental discussion on the combination of qualities.
That is to say, in connection with the combination of the qualities of knowledge (*vidyā*), the combination of the qualities of praise has been investigated.

And the purpose is that one should practice kindness toward the *upāsaka*, not [merely] toward oneself; thus, because it covers [the desire], it is called *ācchādana* (covering), and from that covering comes the word *ācchabda*.
And just as there is "singing along without distinction":
when the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) sing along, it is a singing along by the priests without distinction.
According to the Bhāllavins, however, specifically, the Adhvaryu does not join in the singing.
Therefore, it is understood that this statement of the Bhāllavins—"the officiating priests (ṛtvij) sing along"—is supplementary to that [general rule].
What is meant is this: the officiating priests, with the exception of the Adhvaryu, sing along.
But why is it explained in this way? One might ask: "Why not let these be independent sentences? To this he says:
"Because it is established by another Vedic text."

Out of fear of the contingency of eight defects arising from conceptual construction, even the venerable Jaimini accepts that one sentence may be a supplement to another sentence; thus he says: "This has been stated in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*: 'But rather, it should be a supplement to the sentence, because there would otherwise be an option [of alternatives], and [the supplement] should be a part of the injunctions. He recites this very sūtra by way of its meaning: *api tu vākyaśeṣaḥ syādanyāyyatvādvikalpasya vidhīnāmekadeśaḥ syāt* // 1.2.43 //

Rather, because it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), there should be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the other; for if it were a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*), and that [option] would lead to undesirable consequences—this is the remainder of the argument. Thus, indeed, it is heard in scripture: "This seventeen-fold Prajāpati is attached to every sacrifice," and then, "Therefore, he does not perform the *yeyajāmaha* at the *anuyāja*s."
In this context, without reference to any specific sacrifice, the performance of the *yeyajāmaha* formula has been taught among sacrifices;
and having taught that, it is further recorded in the tradition: "not in the *anuyāja*s.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is there an option between the injunction and the prohibition, or is it a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), such that the *yeyajāmaha* is to be performed in all [sacrifices] except the *anuyāja*s?

Let there not be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding that which has been obtained through worldly means when it is prohibited by a scriptural injunction. For [worldly experience] merely demonstrates its immediate attractiveness; it does not negate its defectiveness in the long run, because it remains indifferent toward that [future consequence].

The prohibitive scripture, however, without contradicting the immediate beauty [of the act], restrains a person intent on engaging in it and makes him understand that its fruit is suffering in the future.

As it has been said: "That which results in suffering must not be done. Therefore, it is able to restrain a person who, though impelled by natural impulse, fears suffering in the future; thus, the scriptural prohibition is stronger than natural impulse, and for that reason, [the latter] does not [prevail].
It is subject to alternative interpretation (*vikalpa*).
However, scriptural injunctions and prohibitions, being of equal force, are treated as optional alternatives, like the taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.
For in that case, because an injunction is observed, it is inferred that there is a greater degree of benefit for the principal rite.
Furthermore, from the observation of prohibitions, it is understood that the result is achieved even when there is a deficiency [in the ritual].
Thus it is said: "If it is argued that it is like [the attainment of] the object [by implication], no; for both are defined by the verbal expression.

Nor should it be said that the performance of the *yeyajāmaha* formula in all sacrifices approaches the specific sacrifice of the *anuyāja* through the medium of the general category of "sacrifice" (*yajati*).

In that case, because the prohibition pertaining to the *anuyāja* offerings operates swiftly—since it is understood that "that [which is otherwise enjoined] is prohibited"—the specific prohibition is stronger than the general rule. This is because, in injunctions such as "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," the latter depends upon the former injunction for the attainment of its own application (the giving of buttermilk). However, here, since the prohibition presupposes something already established, and since the *yeyajāmaha* has not been obtained from any other source, the prohibition must first establish its own application by means of negating that [otherwise required] element.
Therefore, that injunction must be taken into account.

Nor is it correct to argue that, because of this dependence, the injunction is simply stronger than the prohibition— such that there is no option due to their unequal status, but rather the prohibition is merely set aside— for if that were so, the scriptural text containing the prohibition would be the utterance of one who is negligent.
Nor is it the case that what has been stated is equivalent to traditional doctrine;
nor can it be considered a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), like the statement "he does not do those two on the sacrificial animal," because its meaning is not inconsistent with the context.
For it is logically consistent that the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgau) do not exist in the animal sacrifice; however, there is no such absence of the *yeyajāmahe* formula here,
because the *yeyajāmahe* is prescribed for all [sacrificial] acts of offering (*yajati*).
And because those [offerings] exist among the *anuyāja*s,
it cannot be a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) in the sense of "in the non-*anuyāja*s," since, according to the opinion of Kātyāyana, this would entail a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Therefore, it follows that there is an option (*vikalpa*) because [the act] is both enjoined and prohibited.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "An option has been stated regarding the two [alternatives] of taking up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup;
for in that case, no other course is possible."

Therefore, even though it is not corrupted by any fault, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is resorted to on the grounds that [the injunction] possesses authority even as an alternative option, lest it become something merely uttered by a learned person. However, since a solution is possible here through *paryudāsa* (exclusion), it is improper to resort to a conceptual construction involving another alternative.

For in that case, the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be as follows: "In sacrifices other than the *anuyāja*s—that is, in those sacrifices which exclude the *anuyāja*s—the *yeyajāmaha* should be performed."
What follows from this being so?

This is what results: the sentence "not in the *anuyāja*s," which is incomplete and expectancy-laden, is connected with a portion of the preceding sentence—"he performs the *ye-yajāmahe*"; thus, it means that [the *ye-yajāmahe*] is performed in all [sacrifices] except for the *anuyāja*s.
By this it is stated that [the rule] does not apply to the *anuyāja* offerings;

and thus, because the word *yaji* serves as a qualifier, this is simply a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) regarding what is not an *anuyāja*, and since there is no prohibition, there can be no option (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, it is impossible for Kātyāyana—who maintains that compounds are always obligatory (*nityasamāsa*)—to be an unreliable speaker when he contradicts Pāṇini, who is more highly proficient in grammar.
For he teaches the compound within the section on *vibhāṣā* (optionality).
Therefore, it is established that the injunction for the *yeyajāmaha* formula applies to those [offerings] excluding the *anuyāja*s.
He states another interpretation:
Or rather, "in these [fires]" means as follows:
for just as the attribution of good and evil deeds—which are formless—to those [fires] is not straightforward, since trembling conforms to having a physical form;
so too, the transfer of what belongs to one person to another is untenable for the very same reason of being formless.

Therefore, where only "shaking" (*vidhūnana*) is heard, it is better that by the act of shaking one should signify merely the cessation from the commencement of its own effect, and not a moving away from there to another location, as that would entail the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Thus, when the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is reached that "shaking" means the cessation from the commencement of one's own effect, it is replied: Wherever there is a scriptural mention of "taking up" (*upāyana*), there "shaking" must necessarily be explained as "abandoning.
And since in some instances "shaking" occurs in the sense of abandoning, it ought to occur in that same sense elsewhere as well.
For it would not be so if "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*) were understood here in its primary sense;
but that is not the case,
because even there, what is observed is the displacement from one's own activity.
Furthermore, a conceptual complexity that is supported by authoritative evidence does not incur the stigma of being like "the smell of iron" (i.e., it is not a mere gratuitous assumption).
Moreover, since verbal roots have multiple meanings, even if [the root *dhū*] is taken in its sense of "abandoning," it will still primarily mean "shaking off";
for we observe in common usage that the word is frequently employed even in the sense of "abandoning."
Because there is no decisive reason [to the contrary],
and because the author of the *Gaṇapāṭha* is seen there to provide explanations of meaning even by way of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*),
it is therefore logical that here [in this case] the meaning is indeed "loss" (*dhāna*). 26 // 3.3.16.27.
"Because in the state beyond [death] there is nothing to be crossed over; for thus it is understood by others.
Now, one might object: according to the order of the text, the crossing over of good and evil deeds is understood to occur halfway;
however, by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), it is understood to occur even earlier.

Likewise, according to the Śruti of the Śāṭhyāyanins and the Tāṇḍins, both the word and its meaning are stronger than the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama), as in the case of the passage: "He offers the Agnihotra; he cooks the gruel."
Therefore, because there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), this [objection] is not to be undertaken.
To this it is replied: This is not merely a matter of the order of recitation; rather, scripture (śruti) itself states, "He shakes off his good and evil deeds."

The word "tat" (that) is a pronoun; in the sense of "therefore," it refers to what is proximate and thereby expresses its status as the cause. And that which is proximate is what has been mentioned immediately prior:
the arrival at the river Virajā situated on the half-way point. Thus, the abandonment of good and evil deeds occurs precisely at the half-way point.
Nor is there a contradiction with another scriptural passage;
for even though the shaking off of evil occurs at the halfway point, it is logical that this takes place prior to reaching the world of Brahman.
In this way, there is likewise no contradiction with the Śāṭhyāyanins.
For in that context, neither "living" nor "of one who lives" is heard.
Thus, the relinquishing of good and evil deeds occurs precisely on the half-way path.
And so, it is not from the Paryaṅka-vidyā that their destruction occurs; this is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: for one who possesses knowledge whose impurities have been shaken off by the power of *vidyā*, there is attainment of Brahman while proceeding by the northern path; and it is not possible for one whose impurities are undestroyed to travel the northern path, just as one cannot perform the Agnihotra before the cooking of the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*).

This is because scripture declares that *vidyā*, when accompanied by the practice of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), is the means for attaining Brahman seated upon the couch via the northern path.
Furthermore, that [attainment] is impossible for one whose evil has not been destroyed.
It is knowledge itself of such a nature that destroys the stain and, having destroyed the stain, leads one to the higher path; how then could there be stains on the way?
Therefore, the sequence of meaning must be followed by overriding the sequence of the text.

But is it not the case that it has been stated here that it is not merely the order of recitation [that determines the reference], because the use of the pronoun "that" (tad) refers back to what is proximate?
That is incorrect.
In this case, nothing other than the mere proximity of the intellect (*buddhi*) is required;

and since that [proximity] belongs to the knowledge (*vidyā*) as well—just as it does to what immediately precedes it due to the context of knowledge—the scriptural statement is the same in both instances.
Of the two remaining factors, the meaning and the textual order, the meaning is more powerful.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the *Tāṇḍya* and other scriptural passages in the prima facie view;
for the text, "Shaking off [evil] like a horse its hairs," speaks of the activity of an independent person,
and one who has passed away possesses no independence.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with that.
3.3.16.28. *Chandata ubhayāvirodhāt* (By choice, because there is no contradiction between both).
This sūtra applies to certain words.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Just as it is the fruit of knowledge that one who has departed reaches Brahman by the northern path, so too might the abandonment of good and evil deeds occur for that very person midway along the path. To these words of doubt, this sūtra provides the answer, which it explains as follows:
And as for the phrase "of one who has departed from the body":

even the fruit of knowledge, which is the attainment of Brahman, cannot belong to anyone other than such a person, because of the grounds for doubt. As they say: "One does not go there without having been born [in that state]."

Since the destruction of good and evil deeds is possible even while one possesses a human body, it is established that the destruction of good and evil deeds occurs for one who is still alive; for it is impossible for knowledge—when it is a potent cause accompanied by restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth—to effect the destruction of karma [only after death]. "At will" (chandataḥ) means according to one's own desire (svacchandataḥ), that is to say, by one's own choice (svecchayā).
The performance according to one's own will belongs to knowledge accompanied by restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth;
this would pertain to that person while he is alive, not when he is dead. And the relinquishment of good and evil deeds preceded by that [knowledge] would occur only for one who is alive.
Because that which is capable cannot be delayed;

thus, when the effect arises immediately after the cause, the relationship of cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika) is established, and the consistency between the *Tāṇḍi* and *Śāṭhyāyani* Śrutis is maintained. Otherwise, due to the lack of independence [between them], it would have been stated that there is no such consistency.
By this, the contradiction between both [the Śruti and the Smṛti] has been explained.
As for those who have explained the Sūtra as a response to the doubt— namely, "How do the good and evil deeds of one who knows pass over to another?"—
it is because there is no contradiction between the Śruti and the Smṛti, which state that it occurs "by will" (chandataḥ) and "by resolve" (saṃkalpataḥ).
However, in this matter, which is to be understood through scripture (*āgama*), independent reasoning (*yukti*) is not to be introduced.

Since it is possible for those [scriptural passages] to enter into the body of the formal discussion (*adhikaraṇa*), it would be entirely inappropriate to describe them as having a different meaning. 3.3.17.28. "The movement has purpose in both ways; otherwise, there would be contradiction."

Just as a means of attainment (*upāyana*) heard in one place is supplied even where only loss (*hāni*) is mentioned, so too, since the path of the gods (*devayānaḥ panthāḥ*) is heard in proximity to that very [loss], it is fitting that the path of the gods should be supplied even where only the loss of good and evil deeds (*sukṛtaduṣkṛta*) is mentioned.
Nor is there a contradiction with the statement, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," because for one who is stainless,

the attainment of supreme equality is possible upon reaching the world of Brahman by way of the path of the gods. Therefore, it follows that the path of the gods is connected merely to the [attainment of] the state of being stainless.

To this it is replied: "The wise man, shaking off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality. For this [text] declares that for the wise man who has shaken off merit and demerit through knowledge (*vidyā*), there is the attainment of security (*kṣema*). Insecurity, which is based on delusion, must be removed by knowledge characterized by the cognition of reality (*yāthātmyajñāna*). This [attainment of security] does not depend upon a particular location.
Indeed, the knowledge of the true nature of the rope, once arisen for the sake of dispelling the delusion that it is a snake, never requires a particular location.
This is because the very production of knowledge consists in the cessation of ignorance, which is its own opposite.
Furthermore, the attainment of the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) is not required for the production of such knowledge.
For one whose being is purified by the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, knowledge arises even in this very life through hearing and other means.

If it is argued that there is still a need to wait until the fall of the body for the sake of exhausting the karma that has already begun its effects (*ārabdhakāryakarman*), we reply: there is no purpose here for the path of the gods (*devayāna*), because such a view contradicts both scripture and perception; therefore, it is not to be relied upon.
However, as stated in the second Sūtra, there is indeed a purpose for the *paryaṅka-vidyā*.
But as for those who raise the objection, "If even merit (*puṇya*) ceases [upon reaching the world of Brahmā], for what purpose then is there a journey? they introduce the Sūtra [to answer this]:
"The purposefulness of the journey exists in both ways, through the cessation of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*) and through the cessation of meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*).
For if merit were to persist, then even for one who has gone to the world of Brahmā, there would be a return here for the sake of experiencing the fruits of that merit.
Furthermore, by establishing this [view], there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the non-return of one who has gone.
Therefore, they have raised a doubt that should not have been raised at all—that the merit of good deeds (*sukṛta*) is subject to exhaustion just like the demerit of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*).
For when the destination is projected by knowledge (*vidyā*), what room is there for such a doubt as: "If his merit is exhausted, why does he go?"
This state is not based on merit, but rather on knowledge;
therefore, the description given by the elders alone is correct. (Sūtra 3.3.17.30–31) (Sūtra 3.3.18.31):
There is no restriction regarding all [meditations], as there is no contradiction with scripture and inference.

For the *prakaraṇa* (context) is the regulator of ritual elements (*dharma*). If it were not respected, then the ritual elements of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *jyotiṣṭoma*, and so forth would become intermingled.

Furthermore, there would be no transfer (*prāpti*) of those elements into their modifications (*vikṛti*), such as the *saurya* sacrifice and others, or into the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and so forth, by means of the *codaka* (extended injunction).
Because it is entirely based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*).
Furthermore, a *darvihoma* that is neither a primary archetype (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*) is not devoid of ritual properties (*adharman*);
nor is it possible to perform any ritual action endowed with every single ritual property.

This being the case, it is not true that direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of application are themselves the applicators; for even they function as applicators only when a general connection has already been established by context (*prakaraṇa*).

Even in cases where application is understood through direct statement and the rest without recourse to context, context must necessarily be postulated there as well in order to sustain those [direct statements].

Therefore, context must necessarily be accepted both for the sake of application and for its restriction; otherwise, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of direct statement and the others would follow.

Therefore, the path of the gods (devayāna) or the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) is prescribed only in those meditations (*upāsanā*) where it is specifically mentioned, and not in other meditations, because it is not mentioned there. Nor can it be argued that the attainment of that path applies to all meditations based on the general statement, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity" (*śraddhā-tapas*), for it is heard in scripture that the attainment of that path belongs only to those for whom faith and austerity are the supreme goal.
But this is not the case for those devoted to knowledge (*vidyā*).

Moreover, if it were so, since the instruction on the path is contained within one knowledge, it would follow that the instruction on the path should be performed in only one place and not in other knowledges;
yet it is heard [to be so] in other knowledges as well.

Therefore, it follows that not all forms of meditation lead to the path. This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "And those who in the forest meditate with faith and austerity"—this does not state that mere faith and austerity lead to the path; rather, it refers to those who, through knowledge (*vidyā*), ascend by that [path], and not to non-knowing ascetics alone.

By prohibiting the attainment of that [world] through austerity (*tapas*) and faith (*śraddhā*) alone, and by stating that faith and austerity combined with knowledge (*vidyā*) are the means for attaining it, [the text] shows that even those who possess other forms of knowledge share the same path as those who know the five-fire-vidyā (*pañcāgni-vidyā*).
Likewise, elsewhere in the section concerning the five-fire-vidyā, it is stated: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, worship faith as the Truth (*satya*)."
Because the word "truth" (satya) applies to Brahman alone independently [of anything else],
for that alone is the truth, whereas everything else is in some sense only relative truth due to its falsity;
furthermore, because those who know the five fires are included precisely by virtue of possessing this knowledge.
Furthermore, because of the association with knowledge (*vidyā*), it is logical that this [instruction] is intended for those solely devoted to other forms of knowledge;
for it is heard that those who have fallen away from the two paths go to a downward state.
And even there, by virtue of suitability, the path connected here is specifically the path of the gods (*devayāna*).

This is what is meant: the context (*prakaraṇa*) might be the determining factor if there were no scriptural (*śrauta*) or traditional (*smārta*) statement establishing non-restriction; however, such a statement does exist, and it possesses greater authority than the context. Therefore, the path of the gods (*devayāna*) applies to other meditations with qualities (*saguṇa-vidyā*) as well. Furthermore, the purpose of the repeated instruction regarding the path has been explained by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakṛt*). [The souls of those who hold offices] remain [in their positions] as long as their office lasts: *yāvad-adhikāram-avasthitir-adhikārikāṇām*.
Having reflected upon the knowledge of the qualified (saguṇa), one reflects upon the knowledge of the unqualified (nirguṇa).
Liberation cannot be the fruit of the knowledge of the unqualified alone;
for in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas, it is heard that even among the learned, such as Apāntaratamas and others, there occurred both the assumption and the abandonment of various bodies.

That [activity] is not tenable as having liberation as its fruit, because for one who has already attained liberation, such activity is impossible; or, even if it were possible, it would lack the defining characteristics of that state.
For non-return (apunāvṛtti) is indeed its defining characteristic;
therefore, even though knowledge exists, liberation does not result because that [non-return] is not established.
As for the fruits of knowledge, those various manifestations are its results.

It is held that the scriptural statement regarding non-return (*apunarāvṛtti*) is for the purpose of praising that [state]. Nor is it correct to argue that— just as the scripture, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged," implies that the knower awaits the fall of the body— the case of Vasiṣṭha and others likewise implies an awaiting of the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma.
For if it were the case that they must wait for that karma by which the bodies of Vasiṣṭha and others were initiated,

then they would not take up another body; nor does it coherently follow from a straightforward interpretation that "they remain for so long" [referring to the period until the end of their current bodies].
Because it is impossible to delay [the result] when a capable cause is present,
this too must be understood as being for the sake of praising knowledge (*vidyā*).
Therefore, liberation (*apavarga*) is not the fruit of knowledge.
Thus, the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) is advanced by way of challenging liberation;
and here, while it may appear that [the path] is a cause of liberation only occasionally,
the true nature of the prima facie position is rather its being no cause at all.

The established conclusion, however, is this: impelled by the Lord, who is gratified by their performance of knowledge and ritual actions, these [liberated ones], having completed their office, attain the supreme state.
In the case of knowledge devoid of qualities (nirguṇa-vidyā), it is not appropriate to explain the liberation (apavarga) mentioned [in the texts] as being merely figurative praise;

for, upon a thorough examination of the preceding and following passages, the intention of the majority of the Śrutis is determined to lie in this very [liberation]. And it is not proper to interpret otherwise that which constitutes the primary intention.
For it has been said: "There is no meaning of words other than knowledge.

Nor is it correct to argue that the knowledge of Brahman is not the cause of liberation because there is no liberation for those such as Apāntaratamas and others, despite their possessing the knowledge of Brahman, due to their succession of various bodies;
for even when a cause exists, the non-arising of the effect occurs if there is an obstruction, which does not detract from the causal status of the cause.

For it is not the case that gravity, being obstructed by its connection with the stalk and the fruit, did not produce falling; rather, when the obstruction is removed, it produces it, yet it is not the cause of that [falling]. Nor is it the case that water, obstructed by a dam, does not flow toward lower ground; rather, upon the breaking of the dam, it flows toward the lowlands.

In the same way here as well, although the knowledge of Brahman—being obstructed by the station of authority ordained by the Lord, which was secured through the performance of rites and the pursuit of knowledge—has not granted liberation, nevertheless, upon its completion and the removal of that obstruction, [it grants liberation].
He will give [the answer]:

for just as one who has realized Brahman in his final body remains even while awaiting the exhaustion of karma whose fruition has already begun, and then attains liberation upon that exhaustion, so too a wise person such as Vasiṣṭha, though possessing knowledge and action characterized by the fruit of an already commenced mandate, [remains] until the exhaustion of that [karma].

Awaiting the succession of the [final] eon, and performing the successive taking up and discarding of various bodies, he dwells as if still in saṃsāra through a manifestation characterized by non-effort (anābhoga), even though he is liberated.
This is what was stated:
For indeed, it is only their store of karma (*karmāśaya*) that has been set in motion by well-performed deeds for the purpose of yielding the fruit of their respective offices;

however, excluding those karmas whose ripening has already begun (*prārabdhavipāka*), all others have been exhausted through knowledge alone and have been transcended. Furthermore, these [beings] are not "rememberers of former births" (*jātismara*).

For one who, being dependent on another, is cast off from the body and led to another body, remembers what was experienced in a previous birth—that person possesses birth and is called "one who remembers former births" (*jātismara*).
One who moves from one body to another by his own will, as if from one house to another, is not designated as "one who remembers former births.
Having set aside [this objection], that is, having resolved the dispute.
He states the negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"For if, when the commenced fruition of karma has been exhausted and the operation of good deeds [is spent], there were another karma whose fruition had not yet commenced..."

It might be argued: "Even when afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) have been removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), it is not necessarily the case that the entire latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is removed. This is because the deposit of karma—accumulated through the mutual succession of births and deaths since beginningless time, and possessing an indefinite time of fruition—is incalculable.
To this, [the author] replies: "And when the burning away of afflictions such as ignorance has occurred... [as follows].
For it cannot be said that, when the cause of destruction is equal, there is destruction for one and not for another.
[Objection: In that case, would karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest not perish?
And if so, there would be no maintenance of the body for the wise ones such as Vasiṣṭha and others; to this he says:
Regarding the phrase "but of action whose fruit has already begun":

based on the authority of the scripture stating "for him there is delay only so long," it is understood that only action whose fruit is yet to come is exhausted, not that whose fruit has already begun.

Furthermore, since the knowledge of the reality of the Self does not exist in all sages of the various stages of life (*adhikāra*), this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not universally applicable; thus he says:
"And in other types of knowledge" means:
is it then that there is no liberation at all for them? No, he says:
"Later, when their sovereignty perishes."
"Disgusted" means detached.
"Regressing" means dissolution.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that [the results] have fruits pertaining to the next world, there might even be doubt among those of dull intellect concerning things that do not enter the path of experience in heaven and so forth, but are to be understood solely through scripture.
And just as there is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating, "For who knows whether that exists in the other world or not?",

he says, "And because its fruit is directly perceived," meaning that since liberation is established by experience as the fruit of the knowledge of non-duality (advaita), there is not even a trace of doubt.

For the direct realization of the reality of non-duality (advaitatattva-sākṣātkāra), by utterly destroying the phenomenal world (prapañca) superimposed by ignorance (avidyā), pacifies the intense suffering inherent in the limbs of saṃsāra for the person; this is clear both from restatement (anuvāda) and from the strength of logical reasoning, and scripture has been shown [to attest] to it. Furthermore, that is established through the experience of Vāmadeva and others.
Now, one might ask: how does the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) illuminate experience itself? To this he says:
"For [it is not possible] for 'That thou art'...
The meaning is that it is impossible for a statement in the present tense to have a future sense, nor is the insertion of the word "dead" (mṛta) feasible. //32// 3.3.20.33.
"But there is an inclusion of those cognitions regarding the syllable, because of the commonality and the existence of that [syllable], as in the case of the Aupasadā offerings; this has been stated.

This means that there is an inclusion—that is, a subsumption—of all prohibitive cognitions concerning the auxiliary elements (aṅga) that occur in all the Vedas, because of the commonality of the prohibition and because of the recognition of the identity of that syllable (the Akṣara).

Regarding the statement "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal," although this meaning is established with respect to positive attributes by virtue of their being independent, and is likewise established with respect to negative attributes,
nevertheless, this [present discussion] should be understood as an elaboration of that very point. An illustration:
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the son of Jamadagni, it is not deficient":
although another example has already been provided here in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, nevertheless, since the same logic applies, this too can be cited as an example; thus, a different example is shown.
In that regard, the example from the *Śābara-bhāṣya* is the *Ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), which is enjoined by the Yajurveda: "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire."

As an ancillary part of that [Agnicayana], it is prescribed in the Yajurveda itself: "He who, knowing thus, sings the Vāravantīya; he who, knowing thus, sings the Yajñāyajñīya; he who, knowing thus, sings the Vāmadevya.

These Sāmans, moreover, originate in the Sāmaveda. In this regard, a doubt arises: should these be performed with the *uccaiḥ* (loud) accent, which belongs to the [Sāmaveda] where they originate? Or [with the accent belonging to the Yajurveda] at the time of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*)?

Now, those [mantras] which are not specifically assigned [to a particular ritual act] should be employed with the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) tone belonging to that context, according to the Vedic revelation: "The *sāman* is loud; the *yajus* is low-voiced. What, then, is the prima facie view? Since the subsidiaries are enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpattivihita*) itself as being means required [for the primary], and since that [originative injunction] comes first, it follows that the loud tone (*uccaiḥsvara*) based upon it should apply. To this, it is replied: "In the case of a conflict between a subordinate and a principal [element], the principal prevails, because the former exists for the sake of the latter."
Connection with the Veda.
This is the meaning: the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is subordinate, whereas the applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*) is primary.

Therefore, when there is a conflict or contradiction between these two, [the rule] is determined by considering the originative injunction for the quality of loudness (*uccaiṣṭva*), and by considering the applicatory injunction...

This contradiction regarding the state of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is a case of transgression. In that transgression, the connection of the *vāravantīya* and other such [hymns] with the Veda must be understood through their being enjoined by the primary—that is, the principal element—characterized by the form of being employed, and not by the subordinate quality of being produced. Why? Because the state of being employed is primary while the state of being produced is secondary; that is to say, the state of being produced exists for the sake of that which is being employed.
This is what is meant: although the fourfold nature exists even in the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), since there is no distinction in its character as an injunction,
and because the fourfold nature is invariably concomitant with that alone,
nevertheless, the purport (*aidaṃparya*) of the sentences differs.

Among the four forms of a single injunction—namely, origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), entitlement (*adhikāra*), and performance (*prayoga*)—only one particular form is indicated by a specific sentence, provided that it has not been obtained from elsewhere.

In this regard, although the *Sāman* chants are enjoined in the *Sāmaveda*, those sentences are concerned solely with their origin, because their application is already established by sentences belonging to the *Yajurveda*.
Thus, since the desired purpose is not attained through the origin-sentences alone, and since that purpose is understood from the application-sentences, the origin-sentences serve that very purpose.

In this context, when things "come to be," one must grasp that very accent which, by means of the specific sentence in which it is employed, comes into contact with the accomplishment [of the action], and not merely that which contacts the phonetic form alone.
The example provided by the author of the Bhāṣya is likewise to be interpreted in this same manner.

When it is established that mantras originating from the Udgātṛveda are to be employed by the Udgātṛ, since they are also applied to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) offered by the Adhvaryu, they must be used by the Adhvaryu alone in accordance with the primary action, and not by the Udgātṛ;
he applies this principle to the present case with the words:
"so it is here as well. (3.3.20.34)
"Because of this much agreement.
Even though the matter has already been established in the passage, "The two selves have entered the cave," it is here further elaborated:
in one place, both the enjoyer and the non-enjoyer are objects of knowledge.
It is [the case] that the difference in knowledge arises from the difference in the objects of knowledge, specifically because it pertains only to the two enjoyers.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to interpret the phrase "the two drinking" as being figurative— referring to one who drinks and one who does not drink— in the manner of the expression "he places bricks in the form of creation," since it is improper to resort to such a secondary sense when the primary meaning is possible.
Nor can that [secondary] sense be resorted to on the basis of a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa).

For a determination based on a supplementary statement occurs only when there is doubt; however, in this case, there is no possibility of a conflict between the primary and the secondary senses, as they lack equal force.

Furthermore, because the context is sublated by a sentence that possesses greater force than it, it follows that there is a difference in knowledge (vidyā) due to the difference in what is to be known. To this, it is replied: In the passages "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) and "The two drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), the number two is perceived at the time of its origination; therefore, the general rule—that the term "the two drinking" refers to two drinkers—is to be set aside [by the specific context].

And that [middle portion] must be explained figuratively according to the "umbrella-bearer" maxim (*chatrinyāya*), rather than as applying to both [the beginning and the end], in accordance with what is introduced at the outset and what is concluded at the end;
for the middle is to be understood in conformity with that by which one begins and that with which one concludes.

Just as in a textual sequence where there is an introduction proclaiming the defect of redundancy (*jāmitva*) and a conclusion providing its remedy, the intervening [verses]—though they do not explicitly mention that defect—are nevertheless understood to refer to it.

Just as the passages beginning with "Viṣṇu, whose form is a portion, is to be sacrificed to for the sake of avoiding redundancy" (ajāmitva) are led to be mere explanatory statements (arthavāda) rather than being intended as injunctions, because they do not obtain the status of separate injunctions— since syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) is indeed superior to a split in the sentence (vākyabheda)—

so too here, in accordance with that principle, the word "the two drinking" (pibantau) must be understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) as referring to the group consisting of both the one who drinks and the one who does not drink.
Thus, there is a distinction between the knowledges because of the difference in the objects to be known.

Furthermore, in all three of these Vedānta texts, even across the three sections, it is understood through a thorough consideration of what precedes and follows that it is indeed the knowledge of the Supreme Self (paramātma-vidyā) alone that is being taught.
If this is so, then how can there be the mention of the individual soul (jīva)? To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "with the intention of expressing identity":

it is not the individual soul (*jīva*) that is being propounded here; rather, this [soul] is restated merely to demonstrate the non-difference of the individual soul from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Furthermore, since the knowledge of the Supreme Self has non-difference as its object, there is no occasion for an inquiry into difference and non-difference.
Therefore, it is established that there is only one single knowledge here.
[Sūtra 3.3.22] "Because of the inclusion of the aggregate of elements within itself.

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a difference or not between the two knowledges introduced by the questions of Kauṣītaki Kahola Cākrāyaṇa and Uṣasta—which are recorded in the *Naitarantaryā*—we maintain that there is indeed a difference.

Why? Although non-difference is perceived between the question and the answer in both cases, nevertheless, because that same single [instruction] is heard again without distinction, and because there would otherwise follow the contingency of meaninglessness—as in the case of the repetition of the *yajati* sacrifice—difference is established.

Nor is it correct to argue that just as there is no difference when the same thing is taught nine times by the Tāṇḍins in the passage "That is the Self, O Śvetaketu, That art thou," so too here there should be non-difference.
"May the Blessed One explain further to me," for it is heard there that identity is appropriate;
but here it is not so.

Therefore, although the non-difference of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is understood here, nevertheless, since in one place there is meditation on that very same [Self] characterized by the transcendence of hunger and so forth, while in another place there is meditation on it characterized by the absence of body and organs, a difference in the meditations (*vidyābheda*) results.
To this, the following reply is given:

This [passage] does not aim at enjoining meditations, but rather is observed through an examination of the questions and answers to be aimed at establishing the true nature of the reality (*vastusvarūpa*).

What follows from this? This is what follows: since a positive injunction (*vidhi*) has the purpose of bringing about what has not yet been attained, it is untenable when [the object] is already attained.

However, the actual nature of a thing (*vastu-svarūpa*), even when stated again and again, does not incur any fault; for authoritative persons (*āpta*) may indeed say what is beneficial (*pathya*) even a hundred times.
In particular, the Veda is even more highly esteemed than one's parents;
yet there is no absolute tautology here,
because in one case it refers to the transcendence of hunger and other such needs, while in the other it refers to the dissolution of cause and effect.

Therefore, there is one single knowledge because of recognition. Against that partial proponent of the prima facie view who thinks that the Self is presented as distinct by both [these] knowledges, the contradiction with its being the innermost of all has been shown. (35) 3.3.22.36.
"If it be argued that otherwise difference would be untenable, we say no, as in the case of other instructions. (36)
However, the intention regarding the reality of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been shown. The rest is easy to understand. 3.3.23.37.
"There is an exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [them] like the others."
It is not that one contemplates both forms in both cases because the superior assumes an inferior form;
rather, it is the contemplation of the non-difference of the superior form within the inferior soul.
For in this way, it follows that the inferior becomes superior.
This being the case, it is said in reply: because there is an injunction regarding the form of one while restating the other, the contemplation of both is enjoined in both cases.
Otherwise, however, only this much would be stated: "He who is I, he is that";
thus, having restated the individual soul (jīvātman), its state as the Lord (īśvaratva) would be enjoined.
But it is not that the Lord possesses the nature of the individual soul (jīvātman) in the sense of "I am he who is that," as in the case of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
Therefore, both forms are taught for the purpose of meditation in both instances.

Now, it was argued that in this way the superior would result in being inferior; so, when Brahman with attributes (saguṇa) is meditated upon, does the reality of Brahman, which is in fact devoid of attributes (nirguṇa), thereby become inferior? If it is replied that such meditation is merely enjoined for the sake of a certain fruit and does not actually bring about inferiority for it—then here too, the instruction regarding the mutual exchange of thoughts is taught merely for the sake of a fruit, and the superior does not thereby become inferior.
However, we do not disregard the firm identity [of the two] that is taught as a secondary corollary (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*).

Just as the teaching of qualities such as "having true desires" establishes the Lord who possesses those qualities, it is thus established that there is instruction regarding the dual nature in both places. //37// 3.3.24.38.
"For those very same [qualities], such as truthfulness, etc. //38//

That indeed was this very thing; it was truth alone. He who knows this great, first-born being as "Brahman is Truth" wins these worlds; he has already won them—he who thus knows this great, first-born being as "Brahman is Truth," for Brahman is indeed truth.
In this context, the meditation on the previously mentioned Brahman called "the Heart" as "Truth" is enjoined.
The word "that" (tat) refers back to that Brahman called "the Heart," while the phrase "this very same" (etad eva) refers to the alternative mode of meditation about to be described.
In the beginning, that alone existed; it became manifest.
To the question "What was that?", he says: "Truth alone.
That which is manifest (*sat*) and corporeal, and that which is unmanifest (*tyat*) and incorporeal, is "Truth" (*sattya*).
He states the fruit for one who worships that [first-born Yakṣa] with the words, "He who knows this...
He who knows the first-born Yakṣa as worthy of worship—how does he know it? To this he says: "As the Brahman that is Truth."
He conquers these worlds.

Furthermore, the word *inu*—meaning "conquered" or "brought under control"—functions in the sense of the word *ittham* ("thus"). It refers to the enemy present in the mind as something to be conquered, using the pronoun *asau* ("that one").

That which is non-existent would perish. He concludes the point already stated with the words, "He who knows it thus. To the question, "Why does one who knows thus conquer? he replies: "Because Brahman is indeed Truth."
Therefore, the meaning is that the production of the fruit from its worship is also real.
Regarding the phrase "that which is real (satyam)," what is this?
Here too, by the two occurrences of the word *tat*, the two forms and modes are referred to.
To the question, "Upon what object of focus (ālambana) is that [Self] to be meditated upon? the answer is given by the passage beginning with "That Āditya who is this...
and ending with "...he who knows thus slays evil and leaves it behind.
*Upaniṣad* refers to a secret name (*nāma-rahasya*).
Its etymological derivation is: "it destroys evil" (hanti pāpmānam) and "it abandons [evil]" (jahāti).
This is a form derived either from the root *han* (to strike/kill) or *hā* (to abandon).
Thus, by providing this etymology, he declares the fruit to be the destruction of sin.
The author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) states this very subject in the words: "He who indeed [knows] this," referring to the meditation on the syllables of its name.
And thus says the Śruti: "This is that syllable, the Truth. 'Sa' is one syllable, 'ti' is one syllable, 'yam' is one syllable.

The first and last syllables are Truth, while that which is in the middle is untruth. This untruth is enclosed on both sides by Truth and thus becomes Truth itself; untruth does not harm one who knows this."

The suffix *t* with the indicatory letter *ī* (*tīt*) is for the purpose of pronunciation; it should be understood as the letter *t* without an indicatory letter. For here, the first and last syllables are "truth," because they are devoid of the form of death.
In the middle, in the center, is falsehood; for death is indeed falsehood, due to the similarity between the letter *mṛ* (in *mṛtyu*, "death") and the letter *ta* (in *anṛta*, "falsehood").
This very falsehood, which is of the nature of death, is enclosed on both sides by truth.
It is included within the two forms of truth;
therefore, that abundance of truths is merely the multiplicity of truths and does nothing else. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure.
This is the worship of the name of the knowledge of Truth (*satyavidyā*) as "the imperishable" (*akṣaya*).

Although this [meditation] is understood from the text as being identical due to the pull-forward (*anukarṣa*) of the subject "that which is Truth," nevertheless, there is a distinction because of the difference in results,

just as there is between the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices when performed for obligatory purposes versus those performed for optional desires— such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "as long as one lives."
