Regarding the two scriptural injunctions, "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," although there is no difference in their subordinate elements (anubandha), the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that they are distinct; to this, it is replied:
This is indeed one single instruction, because it is recognized as non-different through the reference to what has been previously mentioned in the phrase "That is the truth" (tatsatyam).
Furthermore, there is no difference in the result.

Its *upaniṣad* is "Aharaham. This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to praise another limb of that very [meditation] which is a secret worship by name; it is not an injunction regarding a fruit.

If, however, because there is no mention of a qualification (*adhikāra*) in the injunction for the knowledge, one were to assume such a qualification and thereby postulate a fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage, then—just as in the case of the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice—one would have to assume a combined qualification since no specific distinction is perceived. Consequently, it is established that there is only one single meditation endowed with all the fruits mentioned in the explanatory passages.
He introduces the interpretation of others with the words "But some [say]":

even the Vājasaneyaka has as its subject the eye and the sun, and even the Chāndogya does; thus, because there is no difference in the object of meditation, there is non-difference [between the two texts].

And thus, regarding the point that there is a synthesis of the "Truth" (satya) and other qualities mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka, the sūtra "saiva hi satyādayaḥ" was explained; he now refutes this, saying:
"That is not correct," because this [meditation] based on the udgītha is connected with the ritual action of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

"Even though the connection [of the attributes] is the same, there is a distinction due to the distinction of the objects to be established; thus, because of the difference between the two knowledges (*vidyā*), there is no synthesis. (Sūtra 3.3.25) "Desire and so forth [are to be combined] elsewhere and there as well, on account of the abode and other such factors.

(Sūtra 3.3.39) Although there is a distinction between the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka versions of the knowledge [of the Self] by virtue of being with and without qualities (*saguṇa* and *nirguṇa*) respectively, [the attributes such as desire are to be combined].

For instance, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—"Now, those who depart from here having realized the Self and these true desires"—the objects of desire (kāmāḥ) are heard to be objects of knowledge just like the Self.

In the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad], however, the supreme Brahman devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) alone is taught in the passage, "Speak for the sake of liberation. Nevertheless, there is a mutual combination of qualities between the two.

In the case of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman, the inclusion of qualities associated with the knowledge of the qualified Brahman (saguṇavidyā) is possible solely for the purpose of praising Brahman.

And although in the case of the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇā*), it is not possible to include qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) for the sake of meditation— since these are not enjoined as things to be meditated upon in the knowledge of the unqualified (*nirguṇā*) Brahman, whereby they might be connected here as objects of meditation— but rather their attainment occurs as being inseparable from qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāma*), therefore the term "inclusion" (*upasaṃhāra*) is used.

Thus established is this summary of the meaning of the section: since it is heard that in one case there is the support of space (*ākāśādhāratva*) and in the other the identity with space (*ākāśatādātmya*), even though there is a great deal of similarity, there is no mutual inclusion of qualities between the two meditations (*vidyā*) when they are distinct; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: because the Self (*ātman*) is taught in both places, there is complete similarity. By the word "space" (*ākāśa*), the Self is denoted in one instance, and in the other, that very same Self is denoted as the support of the small space (*daharākāśa*). Therefore, due to this complete similarity, [the qualities] apply to Brahman in both cases.
The collection of all qualities [is thus established].

Even though there is a distinction between the meditations (vidyās) based on whether they possess qualities or are devoid of qualities, the systematic arrangement regarding the collection of qualities has been demonstrated.
Therefore, everything is clear. 3.3.26.40.
The omission of the *ādāra* offering:

In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, there is the rule that the worshipper must eat before his guests. Although this reflection does not directly concern the object of meditation itself, it is nonetheless connected because of its relation to the first meal, which is linked to that [meditation]. Thus, there is a thematic consistency (*saṃgati*).
He shows the subject of the inquiry by citing the Vaiśvānara-vidyā in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
he states the doubt that motivates the inquiry as follows:
"What is meant by 'the omission of food'?

Here, the author raises an objection to the doubt on the grounds that there is no prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) [to counter it]: "Because it is heard [in scripture] that this is connected with the arrival of the rice-balls (bhakta), as in the phrase 'that which is the rice-ball'."
This has indeed been stated in the very first tantra by the rule: "The action regarding the foot is not the motivator for the leading, because the leading is for the sake of another.

For example, the grasping of the dust from the seventh footprint of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) being led for the purpose of purchasing *soma* is not the motivator; rather, it is the leading of the one-year-old cow that is the motivator.
Why is that?

Because the carrying [of the Soma] is prompted by its purchase, and because the seizing of the dust at the seventh step depends upon that [purchase], so too here, since the Prāṇāhuti is connected with the arrival of the rice intended for eating, it has no causal efficiency toward the rice in the absence of eating; thus, there is no prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). This means that this section (adhikaraṇa) is not a *pūrvapakṣa* [in the usual sense].
Having thus cast aside the prima facie argument, he provides the resolution:
This being the case,
he first says that [the suffix] should not be elided;
the word "first" (tāvat) is used for the purpose of setting aside the doubt regarding the final conclusion (siddhānta).
He asks: "Why? The answer: "Out of respect."
He elucidates that very point with the words "For thus":
the Jābālas indeed cause [this] to be heard: "One should eat before the guests."
And the statement "one should eat" is primarily concerned with the Prāṇāgnihotra;

for from the scriptural passage, "Just as hungry children wait upon their mother, so do all beings wait upon the Agnihotra," it is heard that the Agnihotra exists as something to be subsisted upon by its guests, which are the beings. Therefore, by virtue of being part of the same context, here too [the rule] "before the guests... [applies].
The phrase "he should eat" indicates that the primary focus is on the oblation to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*).

This being the case, by first censuring the priority of feeding guests with the words, "Just as if one were to offer the Agnihotra for another without having offered it oneself," the text establishes the priority of the master's meal— that is, the master's *prāṇāgnihotra*— and thereby shows its importance.
[Objection: But surely this scriptural statement regarding hospitality refers only to the case of eating when the host is present, not even to the case of not eating; therefore, [the author] says:

"For that [hospitality] which cannot tolerate the omission of priority—how much less could it tolerate the omission of the *agnihotra*, which possesses that priority? This is the thought: such indeed is the regard for the *prāṇāgnihotra* as a subject of dharma that the scripture does not tolerate even the omission of its attribute of priority; so what need is there to mention its tolerating the omission of the subject itself? This is the meaning.
Having restated the objection of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it:
"But surely they are for the purpose of eating.
For just as the *agnihotra* belonging to the *kauṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice is distinct from the obligatory (*naiyamika*) *agnihotra* due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

Since the Prāṇāgnihotra lacks other constituent elements (dharma) such as specific materials or deities, it requires them; therefore, by virtue of its similarity to the goal and its identity of name with the obligatory Agnihotra, the properties of that [obligatory rite] are extended to it, whereby other material and ritual elements are obtained.

Thus, when the milk and other substances belonging to the obligatory Agnihotra would otherwise apply to the Prāṇāgnihotra, the fact that the material consists of the rice-gruel (bhakta) obtained from the meal is specifically enjoined.
Nor does this much establish that eating is the motivator (prayojaka) [of the Prāṇāgnihotra].
This has already been stated: how it is that because the time for eating has passed, the Prāṇāgnihotra is not motivated by eating.

Nor is there a lack of motivation on the grounds that it uses only a portion of a substance, as in the case of "he cuts off a portion for Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half"; for even that which employs a portion of a substance can still be a motivator.

Just as in the injunction, "They cause the wives to perform the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings with the tail," the tail serves as the motivator (*prayojaka*) for those Patnīsaṃyājas which have a portion of the tail as their substance;
for that indeed is called a non-motivator (*aprayojaka*) whose meaning cannot be understood without the mention of its motivator.
For example, it is not possible to understand "the northern half" without the mention of the cake (*puroḍāśa*) which is its motivator.
But it is possible to obtain the cooked food just as one obtains the tail (jāghanī).

Therefore, just as the tail is obtained even without the animal itself— either by living off the meat provided by another or by taking pieces of meat from a butcher like a shaven-headed man or others—
so too can the cooked food be obtained.
Therefore, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that there is no lapse of the Prāṇāgnihotra when the [regular] meal is omitted.
As for the mention of "water," however, it is the author of the Bhāṣya’s way of employing a substitute to indicate its essential necessity. 3.3.26.41.
*Upasthite 'tastadvacanāt* (Because of the scriptural statement regarding that which is present).
For the statement "that which is fit for oblation" (taddhomīyam) enjoins whatever substance is proximate for the purpose of the oblation;

since the pronoun *tat* cannot complete its denotation without the apprehension of something proximate, it must be fulfilled by referring to that which is proximate— namely, "whatever cooked food arrives first"— in order for its own expression to reach completion.

And since that food is present for the purpose of eating, one cannot employ it [as the sacrificial substance], nor water, nor any other substance, just as in the case of the rule "one cuts off from the latter half for the Sviṣṭakṛt.

Furthermore, the determination of the specific parts of the tail (jāghanī) does not depend on the Agniṣomīya animal, because that tail is seen even when it exists independently in the slaughterhouse; therefore, there is this distinction between this [tail] and the [animal's] tail.
As for what was said—that the injunction of the food-substance serves to set aside the substances obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal transfer)—that is incorrect.
That is incorrect.

Because the name "Agnihotra" occurring in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) possesses that [injunctive] nature, whereas the [name] occurring in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is justified as being merely laudatory by taking up some established similarity; therefore, it cannot enjoin that very nature. Thus he says: "And here there is no acquisition of the properties of the original Agnihotra."

Moreover, if it were admitted that the *dharma*s [of the model sacrifice] are obtained for the *agnihotra* through the force of the *codaka* (extended application), then a great deal of what has been obtained would be sublated. And a resort to sublation is not logically tenable when it is possible to avoid it. Indeed, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* oblation, sublation of what has been obtained is accepted only as a last resort; thus he says: "if the obtaining of those *dharma*s is admitted."
It reinforces the absence of an injunction [for extension] with the words:
"And for this very reason, here too.
Since, by the sequence of reasoning already stated, there is no extension (atideśa), for that very reason the members of the Agnihotra are merely preparatory (sāṃpādika).
However, if that [state] were actually attained, its character as something "produced" (sāṃpādika) would not be tenable.
For it is said that in the case of a beloved woman, her breasts, face, and so forth—which do not actually exist [as such]—are produced in the form of a ruddy goose, a lotus, and so on;
but in the case of a river, the ruddy geese and other creatures themselves are not produced as ruddy geese and so forth.
For this reason as well, we understand that there is no extension by *codaka* (general transfer).
As for the observation of respect (*ādara*), that is intended to establish the priority [of the *bali* offering] in the case of eating.
The sense is that while the substratum (*dharmin*) [the *bali*] is not lost in the alternative where the properties (*dharma*) are not omitted, its permanence is not established merely by that much.
[Objection: But since the host’s meal has been prescribed as occurring after the feeding of guests, how can this [prescription] be set aside? To this he says:
"There is no overburdening of a scriptural statement. The meaning is that there is no overburdening of a specific rule when it serves to set aside a general rule. //41// 3.3.27.42.
There is no restriction regarding the determination of that [result], because it is seen separately; for there is no obstruction to the result.

Just as in the case of the statement, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," which is studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), which—through its connection with the *juhū*—is grasped by the injunction of the performance of the sacrifice as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and thus independent of a separate fruit, and which is understood through the indicative present tense (*siddhavartamānāpadeśa*).
It does not accept [the fruit] as its own result in the manner of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice.

Thus, the meditation connected with the *udgītha*, which has an inseparable connection with ritual action and is subsumed under the injunction for the performance of the rite, is not capable of being assumed to have the fruit characterized by the attainment of all desires— as understood from a statement describing an established present state—
because it exists for the sake of another (the ritual).
And likewise, because it is of ultimate significance;

and thus there is a Sūtra of the Great Sage (Pāramarṣa): "In the case of substances, purificatory rites, and actions, since they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).

This being the case, when the prima facie view is reached that—just as there is a rule regarding the *parṇa*-leaf [for the ladle] in a sacrifice—there is likewise a rule regarding meditation (*upāsanā*), it is replied: It is appropriate that the mention of a fruit in the case of the *parṇa*-leaf is merely an explanatory eulogy.
For the state of being made of parṇa-wood cannot, like a sacrifice or similar acts, undergo a connection with a fruit,
because it is not of the nature of an activity;
and only an activity possesses a fruit.
As they have said: "Because a result is seen for that which has an origin.

Nor is there, as in the case of the desire for one's own pleasure, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) connected to the ritual under discussion (*prakṛta-kratu*) that could serve as a substratum; for the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood (*parṇatā*) is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).

Therefore, it is only through syntactical connection (*vākya*), by way of its relation to the *juhū* ladle, that the ritual must be made known as the substratum for the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood.
Furthermore, a sentence cannot be intended to convey something other than its primary purpose; therefore, the specific purport of that sentence must necessarily be relied upon.

And thus, being intent upon that [purport], it is not capable of establishing a connection between the leafiness and the result, for that would entail the fallacy of splitting the sentence (vākyabheda).

Since meditations (*upāsanā*) are by their very nature activities, it is logically consistent that they are connected to a fruit independently; thus, there is no contradiction in enjoining them for a fruit while taking the *udgītha* and other elements as their substrates, because this constitutes a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*).
Indeed, when meditation having the *udgītha* as its means is enjoined for the sake of a fruit, it does not entail a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

[Objection: But surely meditation is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *udgītha*, which is a constituent part of the ritual action, because of the accusative case-ending in "the *udgītha*" (*udgītham*), just like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth.
And thus, just as in the case of collyrium and the like, the mention of a fruit in regard to the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Not so;
for it has been stated above that here the meditation is not on the *udgītha* itself, but rather on the syllable *oṃ*, which is a constituent part of it.
The syllable *oṃ* is not a constituent part of the ritual action (*karma-aṅga*), but rather a constituent part of the *udgītha*, which itself is a part of the action.
Furthermore, that which is useless cannot be desired [as a goal].

Therefore, as in the case of "he offers the flour-grains" (*saktūn juhoti*), there is a connection [of the text] to the effect arising from the meditation (*upāsana*) which has the syllable *oṃ* as its means, by means of a modification of the application (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*).

Therefore, it should be understood that just as the *godohana* vessel and other such items, although dependent on a ritual (*kratu*), are non-permanent because they are connected with specific results, so too are the meditations (*upāsanā*) on the *udgītha* and other elements.
The rest has been explained in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*).
Nor is this mention of a result merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
If it were merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), its function would be entirely beyond perception; this is not the case when it is intended to convey a result.
However, there is no direct cognition of a result simply because of a statement in the present tense.
For this very reason, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, one does not postulate a result based on an explanatory statement or a statement in the present tense.

But if this [injunction] has as its purpose the fruit [of the action], it is not possible to assert that the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are without fruit because they exist for the sake of another.
[This is] stated "just like the offering" (3.3.28).

Through an examination of the meaning of those respective scriptural passages, once the non-difference in nature between Vāyu and Prāṇa is established, the meditation upon them is also non-different, since their definition is dependent upon that [non-difference]. Nor is there a difference [between them] due to the difference in qualities belonging to the internal (adhyātma) and the celestial (adhidaiva) spheres.
For there is no difference in the possessor of qualities (guṇavat) due to a difference in the qualities themselves.

Indeed, the Agnihotra sacrifice that has already been established by the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra" does not become different because of differences in qualities such as rice-grains and so forth.
For it is only a difference in quality connected with an action at the time of its origination that serves to differentiate the action.
Just as in the case of two rites connected with curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) and whey (*vājina*),
there is no connection with a rite that has already arisen;
likewise, in the instructions concerning the internal (*adhyātma*) and the divine (*adhidaiva*), there is no connection with a meditation (*upāsanā*) that has already arisen.

Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the unity of the knowledge (*vidyā*) is determined by considering the beginning and the conclusion, there is only a single performance of the practice at one time.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: It is true that the knowledge is one; nevertheless, due to the difference in qualities (*guṇa*), there is a difference in the performance of the practice.

Just as there is a difference in the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice even though it is a single rite, owing to the difference in the qualities of the times of evening and morning, so too here, although the meditation (*upāsana*) is one, a difference in the performance is established due to the difference in the qualities pertaining to the internal self (*adhyātma*) and the divine realm (*adhidaiva*). Thus it is proven.
For this instruction on the division between the internal (ādhyātma) and the divine (adhidaiva) is for the purpose of meditation;
it is a separate teaching intended for meditation, just as the rice-grains and other materials are taught separately for the sake of the Agnihotra sacrifice.

"By this, the instruction regarding the vow [is given]" means by this non-difference of reality. And the particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding vows such as those concerning speech and so forth.
[Objection: But here, in the phrase "to this deity," only a deity in general is heard, not Vāyu; so how can it be said that it teaches the attainment of Vāyu?

To this he says: "In the word 'deity,' [it refers to] Vāyu. For Vāyu indeed encompasses fire and the others; thus, with respect to fire and the others, Vāyu is the unlimited (anavacchinna), while fire and the others are limited by him. Therefore, by virtue of the quality of being the "absorber" (saṃvarga), Vāyu is the unlimited deity.
Regarding the phrase "presenting [the offerings] to all":

since there is no difference in the hearing [of the injunction] by those assembled together, and because the deity Indra is non-different [in each case], there might arise a suspicion that the three *puroḍāśas* (sacrificial cakes) are to be offered simultaneously.

However, because the distinction of qualities—namely *rāja*, *adhirāja*, and *svarāja*—is already present in the original prescriptive statement (*utpattivākya*), and because the reversal of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses is enjoined, the deities remain distinct according to their respective positions; consequently, the offerings themselves must be made separately.
For if the offering were simultaneous, the prescription of a transposition would be untenable;
it is only when the offering occurs sequentially that a rule for transposition is meaningful,
because such a sequence is precisely what is intended to be expressed.
The rest is easy to understand. //43// 3.3.29.44.
*Liṅgabhūyastvāt taddhi balīyastadapi* (Because of the abundance of indicative marks; for that is more powerful).

Here, having raised an objection against the introductory statement (*upakrama*) from the perspective of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In this regard, although there are many indicative marks (*liṅga*) suggesting the independence of the mind-altars (*manaścit*) and so forth, nevertheless, they do not establish independence by themselves;
rather, they merely reinforce the independence already established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And in this case, there is no such *pramāṇa* that establishes independence.
Nor is this a mark characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*) by which it might independently bring about [the application];
for that capacity would belong either to the expression or to the meaning.
Likewise, in the case of the *pūṣānumantraṇa* mantra, [its application] is restricted to the consecration of Pūṣan.
Or, for example, in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal," the number one has the capacity to delimit the object to be numbered;
yet this [mention of the number] is not a *liṅga* (indicative mark) characterized by the observation of another purpose in that way,
because, being for the sake of praise, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunctive statement and is therefore subordinate to the injunction.

Therefore, in the absence of a contradiction characterized by functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) leads one to understand that the "mind-altar" (*manaścit*) and so forth are subordinate to ritual action. Nor does the restrictive scriptural statement, "These indeed are built up by knowledge" (*vidyācita eva*), preclude their entry into the ritual;
for if there were a conflict with scripture, the context would not prevail.
Because the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended to exclude external means of accomplishment,

the sentence— "By knowledge alone these [fires] become built for one who knows thus"— which establishes a connection with the person, cannot set aside the context (*prakaraṇa*). Indeed, this is merely an observation of something else for another purpose.
And it has already been stated that this [meditation] does not lead [to the result] independently.

Therefore, even this [meditation on the fires] is not sufficient to contradict the context; these fires, though merely figurative (*sāṃpādika*), enter into the ritual action by virtue of the context, just like the mental [cups].
For in the *Dvādaśāha* sacrifice, it is heard: "With this vessel, the ocean, the sap-filled one, I take for you the cup for Prajāpati, the mind-cup."
In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the *mānasa* (mental) [sacrifice] a part of the entire twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), or is it a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the tenth day falling within its midst?

On this point, because the *mānasa* is designated as distinct from the twelve-day rite in the passage, "The twelve-day rite is speech; the *mānasa* is mind," there is a distinction between them, just as there is a distinction between speech and mind. Furthermore, [it is said]: "The meters of the twelve-day rite have been drained of their essence; they are replenished by the *mānasa* alone. This refers to the twelve-day rite.

Because it is praised as being distinct, and because the relationship between the object of praise and the act of praising is logically possible only when there is a difference, the *mānasa* day is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *dvādaśāha*.

Furthermore, since the days [of the *dvādaśāha*] end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and because the text states, "Having performed the *patnīsaṃyājas*, they proceed to the *mānasa*," the *mānasa* is heard of as occurring after the *patnīsaṃyājas*.

Even in the case of the thirteenth day, since the number twelve is maintained by separating [the *mānasa*], there is no contradiction with the name *dvādaśāha* even by resorting to the weakest [etymological] interpretation.

To this, it is replied: For if the state of there being thirteen days were established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the term "twelve-day rite" (*dvādaśāha*) could be explained through a secondary or figurative application (*jaghanyā vṛtti*).
However, no such other means of valid cognition exists.
Furthermore, a difference in designation does not warrant the assumption that the days are distinct entities.
For that [relationship] is possible even through the distinction between part and whole;
and for this very reason, the relationship between the praised and the praiser is also established,
as in the case of Devadatta with his long hair.

Although the conclusion at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is the general rule, nevertheless, because of a specific statement regarding the tenth day, the mental acts—such as the drawing, placing, and offering of the cups—will take place after the *patnīsaṃyāja*.
For what indeed would a scriptural injunction not cause one to do?
From the statement, "This mental act is indeed the release of the tenth day," it is understood that the mental act is an integral part of the tenth day.

Since *visarga* (conclusion) is the property of that which has an end and is not independent, and because on the tenth day it is stated that "they proceed for the mental [offering]" (*mānasāya pramarpanti*), thereby indicating the tenth day as the substratum, it is established that the mental offering is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that [day] and not a separate day. Thus,
the author of the Dharmamīmāṃsā Sūtras has stated here that the mental offering is an auxiliary of the tenth day belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
The venerable commentator [Śaṅkara] states that even the tenth day is a constituent part of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*);
he says this on the strength of another scriptural passage:
"Just as there is the *Avivākya* [rite] on the tenth day of the ten-night rite."
"Avivākya" is the name of the tenth day.
Furthermore, because of the extended application (atideśa),
there is no similarity whatsoever between the fires consisting of meditation (sāṃpādikāgni) and the fire built with bricks, except for their entry into the ritual action.
Therefore, since it has been argued that [the meditation] is not independent, the following is stated:
"But it is indeed knowledge, because of the definitive determination.

Let it be that other scriptural passages containing injunctions or indications of purpose do not serve to enjoin what is not already established; however, in these cases where there is no explicit mention of an injunction or a statement of purpose, an injunction must be inferred according to the principle: "But the statements are injunctive, because they convey something new. (JS 1.2.18).
And thus, whatever meaning is understood from these [passages], it becomes exactly in accordance with that;
for from these, there is understood the continuity of the *manascit* and other [fires], their definitive nature, their connection with a specific fruit, and their relation to the person (*puruṣa*).
Nor does this [fire-altar] depend on the ritual as its purpose—like the *godohana* vessel and so forth—such that the human purpose would be subject to dependence upon the ritual action.
Nor is the restrictive determination "only that which is piled by knowledge" intended for the purpose of excluding external means;
for it is established by its very nature that knowledge does not depend upon external things.
Therefore, by process of elimination, the restriction is intended to exclude the suspicion that [knowledge] might enter into action like the mental cups (mānasagraha).
And since such a meaning is possible,
the scriptural mention of a particle (*nipāta*) should not be strained by treating it as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*).

Therefore, it is established that scripture (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) set aside the context (*prakaraṇa*) and convey the independence of the mental fire-altars (*manaścid-ādi*) and so forth.
This should be understood in the same way on account of the connection, extension, direct scriptural statement, and so forth;
these are indeed clear in the Bhāṣya itself.

As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—that if they were auxiliary parts of the sacrifice, there would be an option between the previously mentioned brick-altar and the mental altars (manaścita) and others—[that is refuted].
He refutes [the opponent's view] by showing that it would entail an effect similar to that [of ritual action]: "And there is no connection with action while [knowledge] is actually present.

Furthermore, since the predominance of knowledge is observed in the preceding and following sections, that which falls between them is also characterized as having knowledge as its primary focus due to its similarity to them, rather than being a subordinate part of ritual action; thus he states in the Sūtra:
"And because of the subsequent word, it has that nature; however, due to abundance, there is a connection [with ritual]."
The commentary on this is clear:
there is the Rājasūya sacrifice, [established by the injunction] "A king desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. With reference to that, they prescribe a sacrifice named Aveṣṭi.

"A cake on eight potsherds for Agni, gold as the sacrificial fee," and so forth—this is taught with reference to that [archetypal sacrifice]. It is further stated: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed a cake for Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should offer the oblation and then pour clarified butter over it; if a Vaiśya, [he should place] a cake for the Viśvedevas; if a Rājanya, [he should place] one for Indra. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others intended as a condition (*nimitta*) for those who are already established [in the sacrifice], or is this sacrifice being enjoined specifically for the Brāhmaṇas and others?

In this regard, if the meaning of the word "king" (*rājan*) is one who performs the duties of protecting the subjects, removing thorns [from the state], and so forth—that is, if the king is the performer of the kingdom (*rājya*)—then, according to the injunction "the king shall sacrifice with the Rājasūya," the eligibility for the Rājasūya belongs to the performer of the kingdom. Therefore, since Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas alike can be performers of the kingdom, it is established that all of them are eligible for the Rājasūya; thus, [passages] such as "if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" [are intended as restrictive rules].

The Vedic texts have indicative meanings. Now, if "rājya" (sovereignty) is the activity of a king (*rājan*), such that that activity is called "rājya" due to its connection with the king as its agent, then, when the question arises as to who the king is, since there is no established consensus among the Āryas, one must rely on the usage of the Andhras— just as one relies on the usage of Mlecchas to determine the meaning of words such as *pika*, *nema*, and *tāmarasa*.

The well-known application of the word "king" (*rājan*) to the Kṣatriya caste is the cause for that restriction; thus, since only a Kṣatriya is a king, there is no application [of the term] to Brāhmaṇas or Vaiśyas.

Consequently, by setting aside the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Rājasūya, distinct rites performed by Brāhmaṇas and others are obtained as independent acts, and therefore they are not contingent (*naimittika*) upon the status of being a king.
In this regard, what is first established?
That [the titles] are based on specific causes (*naimittika*).
There is no dispute among the Aryans and the Andhras that one who performs the acts of sovereignty is a "king" (*rājan*).

For instance, among Brāhmaṇas and others who perform the protection of subjects and who bear the insignia of the golden staff, the parasol, and the white chowries, the Āryas and the Andhras are seen using the term "rāja" (king) without dispute. Therefore, even when there is a conflict between non-disagreement and disagreement, the usage of the Āryas is stronger than that of the Andhras—just as in the case of the *yava* (barley) and *varāha* (boar)—because the usage of the Āryas is more authoritative. However, when there is a contradiction with the more authoritative usage of the Āryas, the usage of Pāṇini, which is rooted in that [Vedic authority], is disregarded; for it is said: "In case of conflict, however, [the Veda] is independent."

On the grounds that it would be sublated by the maxim "it might be so," or because it must somehow be interpreted as being intended merely for the sake of grammatical derivation—like the cases of the snake and the mongoose—the Śruti texts [mentioning the cause] serve to indicate the occasion (*nimitta*), since the status of the King as the agent of the sacrifice is already established by the rule *rajñaḥ kartā rājā*.
And thus, it follows that the word *yadi* (if) would also be used in its primary sense. This was the position reached.
This being the case, it is said: "In terms of form, there is no distinction between the usage of the Āryas and the Mlecchas;
however, a distinction is shown therein by means of the Vedic supplementary passages."

Thus, regarding the doubt as to whether the word *rājan* here is used in the sense of the agent due to its connection with the action (*karma-yoga*), or in the sense of the object (*karman*) due to its connection with the agent (*kartṛ-prayoga*),

the decision is made by the traditional authority (*smṛti*) of the venerable Pāṇini, who is more learned than others, just like the supplementary Vedic passages (*vākya-śeṣa*). The usage among the Andhras is beginningless,
whereas the usage among the Āryas has a beginning, like the words *go*, *gāvī*, and so forth.
Furthermore, a well-known usage that possesses a beginning cannot set aside the tradition of Pāṇini to establish a popular usage that has no beginning;
for if the usage of words such as *gāvī* were [considered] beginningless, it would follow that even the usage of words such as *go* would possess a beginning.
Therefore, since the popular usage of the Andhras—authorized by the tradition of Pāṇini—is more authoritative, the word *rājan* is used in its primary sense (*mukhya*) to denote the Kṣatriya caste.

Therefore, since the word *rājan* would be used figuratively for one who performs that [act] or for one born of that [caste], the context of the *Rājasūya*—which pertains specifically to the Kṣatriya—is set aside by the presence of the vowel *ā* (in *rājā*), resulting in the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *Āveṣṭi* sacrifice.
Furthermore, the word "if" (*yadi*) follows the logical connection [of the existing rule]; it cannot alter that [connection] when an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) is present.
For this very reason, they say: "If there were a total abandonment of the word 'if,' there would be the assumption of a desired supplement (*rucy-adhyāhāra*)."
And this [discussion] is a reflection based on the premise that there is no separate qualification for the Rājasūya such as "one should cause one desiring food to sacrifice with this [offering]";

for if that were the case, since a person of the three higher castes desiring food would already be eligible under this qualification, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and others would necessarily have to serve the purpose of indicating a specific occasion (nimitta), which is difficult to avoid. //47// 3.3.29.48. //48//
Because [the self] exists in the body as one;
he states the intended meaning of the locus with the word "here" (iha).
He states the purpose of providing this justification with the words "bondage and liberation.
He states that if there were no justification, there would be an absence of the possibility for bondage and liberation:
"Indeed, it is not non-existent" [is the response].
He raises the objection of redundancy with what was stated in the preceding Tantra by saying "But surely...
[nanu].
He refutes [the objection] by stating: "It was said by the author of the Bhāṣya.

It was not stated there by the author of the Sūtras such that it would be redundant; rather, it was brought down from this very point to that place for the sake of its utility in defining the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus, it is merely an extraction of the meaning found right here.
Since the author of the Sūtras will state this here, for that very reason the venerable Upavarṣa has performed an extraction from the [section on] subtraction.
He states that this inquiry is a supplement to both the preceding and the subsequent systems with the words:
"And here... (iha ca).

He states the connection with the preceding section: "Moreover" (api ca). Now, one might ask: "Let the proofs for the existence of the Self be stated here; what is the purpose of this objection? To this he replies: "For [an explanation] preceded by an objection... (ākṣepapūrvikā hi).
He states the objection:
"In this regard, some hold the view that the self is nothing more than the body.
Although consciousness is not observed in earth, water, fire, and air—either collectively or individually—nevertheless, it may exist when they have transformed into the form of the body.
For it is not the case that because yeast and other ingredients, whether combined or separate, are not seen to intoxicate, they fail to intoxicate when transformed into the form of wine.

Likewise, in the experience "I am," it is the body itself that manifests in the form of being fair-complexioned and so forth; it is not something distinct from the body that serves as its substrate, like curd in a bowl.
For this very reason, there is the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "I, who am stout, am going," between the "I" (*ahaṃ*) and attributes like "stoutness.
Sweetness and other qualities, which are never coreferential with curd, do not experience coreferentiality with a bowl, as in "the bowl is white and sweet.
Furthermore, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), being imperceptible, cannot be established by means of inference and the like.
Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition that is non-perceptual.
For it has been said: "Because the powers of beings differ due to the distinctions of place, time, and other factors, the establishment of those powers through inference is extremely difficult."

And if this is the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose existence is necessarily concomitant with what is to be proven through perception, then what need is there to mention the case of verbal testimony, which has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya to have its cause in the presumption (*arthāpatti*) of an entirely imperceptible object, or of analogy (*upamāna*), which likewise concerns such objects?
Gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is an activity directed toward the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful.
And since that [breath] is observed to be dependent upon the body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of inhalation and exhalation and so forth, is indeed a property of the body.

Furthermore, although desire, effort, and the like are internal, they nonetheless have their locus within the body alone; for no substratum other than the body is perceived for them, and they exist only when the body exists.
Otherwise, one would fall into the error of abandoning what is observed and postulating what is unobserved.

Since there is no evidence for a self distinct from the body, and since [the qualities of the self] are possible in the body, it follows that the body alone is the self possessing desire and so forth; to this, it is replied: "Distinction [of the self from the body exists], because [the qualities of the self] do not exist when that [body] is absent, unlike perception. One who asserts that perception is not a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) must be asked: "On what basis have you determined the invalidity of inference and the other means of knowledge?"
For perception, which grasps only the form of the mark (liṅga) and so forth, is not capable of determining the invalidity of these [cognitions].
Indeed, unlike the cognition of smoke, a cognition of invalidity cannot arise for these [cognitions] from the contact of the sense organ with its object;
rather, it arises through the observation of deviation due to differences in place, time, state, and form, or through imaginative construction.
Furthermore, such an extensive operation is not possible for perception.
As they have said: "This [perception] is not capable of performing so many operations, because it arises by the power of a proximate object and is non-discursive.
Therefore, even if one does not wish it, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be admitted in this case.
Furthermore, discerning persons, setting aside those who have already adopted [a position], instruct those who have not yet adopted one or who are in doubt.
And this state of theirs is not within the range of your direct perception;
for these states are certainly not objects of perception like whiteness and so forth, but are rather to be inferred from signs such as speech and behavior.
Nor is inference a valid means of knowledge by which these [entities] are established.
For one who, without knowing the specific nature of men, intends to instruct some random person, cannot be said to possess discernment, as his words would not be worthy of attention.
Furthermore, even animals, seeking to obtain what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful, proceed upon ground dark with tender grass.
And they avoid ground strewn with withered grass and thorns;
however, the nihilist is even more of a beast than a beast, for he does not know the means for achieving what is desired or avoiding what is undesired.
Indeed, perception has no power over this domain of activity and cessation which falls within the scope of inference.
Furthermore, one would not employ speech for the purpose of communicating with others, because the object of a word is not perceptible.
Let it be that there is no [rebirth] for the nihilist; even in this very life, he is presented with a great hell in the form of muteness and the absence of engagement or withdrawal from activity.
And the wise have exerted themselves in refuting this point.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*), although its object is entirely beyond the senses, arises from a matter that cannot otherwise be accounted for.
Furthermore, analogy (*upamāna*) has been established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the definition of the instruments of knowledge through its connection with multiple commonalities.

Therefore, let this [discussion of other means of knowledge] stand aside for now; rather, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) itself, which is directly perceived, takes as its objective support something distinct from the body.

It has been stated that, like a yogi or a tiger, even when there is the conceit of assuming another body during the state of dreaming, that which is the locus of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) is recognized [as being the same]. As for the application of the Sūtra: "But the Self is not non-different from the body; rather, it is different from the body.
Why? Because its existence and non-existence are not contingent upon the existence and non-existence of that [body]."

If consciousness and the like were qualities of the body, then they would have to be specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of it; they could not be general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*) like number, dimension, or conjunction. Furthermore, those which are the specific qualities of the elements are observed to exist as long as the element exists, such as color and so forth. For it is impossible that there should be an element that is devoid of color and the rest.
Therefore, because of its dissimilarity to color and other specific qualities of the elements, consciousness is not a quality of the body.
By this, the claim that desire and so forth are specific qualities of the body is refuted.
Although vital breath, movement, and the like are indeed attributes of the body, they do not arise from the body alone.
Because [these qualities] would follow even in the state of death;
therefore, he for whom these bodily attributes exist by way of superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the self (*ātman*) distinct from the body.
If it were admitted that unseen causes (*adṛṣṭa*) are the cause, it would be untenable for them to have the body as their substratum; thus, the self alone must be admitted [as the substratum].
He states another point of dissimilarity:
"And [the qualities] of the body.
For the qualities of the body, such as color and so forth, are observed to be perceptible both to oneself and to others.
Desire and the like, however, are directly perceived by oneself; thus, they differ from the properties of the body.
For this reason as well, they are properties belonging to something distinct from the body.
In that regard, even if consciousness were a specific quality of the elements, it would nevertheless persist as long as the elements exist.
Nor is there a deviation [from the rule] by means of the power of intoxication,

because capacity (sāmarthya) is a general quality. Furthermore, just as the power of intoxication exists in every part of liquor in a certain measure, so too consciousness would exist in the body and in its parts as well, in a certain measure.
Furthermore, just as many [beings] could not be conscious within a single body—

since it is impossible for many conscious entities to conform to one another's intentions— just as many birds bound by a single snare, though capable and facing in various directions of movement, do not venture even a hand’s breadth beyond their place; so too [is the case here].
In this way, the body as well is not capable of performing any action;
furthermore, the relationship of property and its possessor cannot be determined merely through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Let it not be that every property of space [is present] because it is concomitant with all things;
rather, [it is established] through both positive and negative concomitance.
And in this case, the negative concomitance is doubtful.
And thus, he states that the proving power belongs to the mere positive concomitance (anvaya) alone:
"Moreover, for as long as...

[and so on]. Desiring to state another refutation, [he says]: "The difference consisting of color and so forth is not something other than the four elements; likewise, consciousness is merely a specific transformation of the elements, and not something other than the elements."
The meaning is that [if it were so], there would be a contradiction of the proposition (pratijñā) that "earth, water, fire, and air are the principles" (tattvas).

This is what is being said: the transformation of the world consists only of the four elements; there is no other principle whose transformation constitutes form and so forth, or any other kind of transformation.
Although the status [of the senses] as attributes of the body has already been refuted by the arguments stated here, he says the following with the desire to state further arguments:
If you say, "But now," [we reply]:
the elemental properties such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, being insentient (*jaḍa*), are observed only as objects (*viṣaya*) and not as subjects (*viṣayin*).
Nor should it be argued that some objects might also possess the status of being subjects.

Because it is contradictory for [an action] to operate upon itself; nor does this undesirable consequence apply to cognition, since that non-inert [cognition] is admitted to be self-luminous. And this has already been established previously.
He applies the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "as in the case of apprehension" (upalabdhivat): "Just as this [apprehension]...
From the very same means of valid cognition that apprehends apprehension, the distinctness of the body is also understood.

Therefore, because its distinction from insentient elemental properties is ascertained through the self-luminous cognition itself, let it be that perception is independent of the elements due to this distinction; nevertheless, there is still a lack of proof for the Self. To this, he says:
"And the Self is not merely the nature of perception."
For one who understands [the truth], no difference in apprehension is experienced; therefore, it must be admitted that this [apparent difference] arises from a difference in objects.

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no manifestation of objects as distinct from their apprehension, and we have also established in the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā* that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that can grasp a difference between objects.
This being the case, since both the object and its distinctions are extremely difficult to establish, the talk of a distinction in apprehension based on a distinction in objects is cast far aside.
Therefore, even the status of being an apprehender belonging to apprehension is not real;
rather, it is constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding this, he states that even in the state of ignorance there is non-difference between the perceiver and the perceived: "And [the thought] 'I saw this'.
The meaning of this is that permanence results not only from ontological non-difference, but from non-reality as well.
"And because [phenomena] such as memory are possible.
For if there were plurality [of selves], it would not be possible for one person to have a memory of what was perceived by another; this is the meaning.
He restates a point that has already been refuted, in order to provide another refutation:
Regarding the phrase "as for what was said":
against one who thinks that perception is a property of the body because it arises from the activity of the body, this refutation is offered:
"and it does not belong to the body exclusively."
He concludes the subject under discussion:
"Therefore, it is irreproachable. (Sūtra 54).
3.3.31.55. But those [rites] connected with the auxiliary parts are not [restricted] to the various branches, for they pertain to each Veda.
Because of differences in accents and other factors, the *udgītha* and other chants differ according to each Veda;
however, the meditative reflections (*pratyaya*) connected to them are enjoined differently in each recensional branch (*śākhā*).

In this regard, a doubt arises: are the meditative reflections enjoined in a particular Veda intended only for those *udgītha* and other chants prescribed in that same Veda, or are they intended for the *udgītha* and other chants prescribed even in other Vedas?

What, then, is the prima facie position? By hearing the word "udgītha" in the passage, "One should meditate on the syllable 'Om' as the udgītha," the general category of udgītha is understood. Since that general category cannot exist without specific qualifications, and since the requirement for such qualifications is satisfied by the very specific details prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā) due to their proximity, there is no need to look for another udgītha from a different branch.
And there is no such injury to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) by way of proximity;
for if one were to set aside a meaning directly presented by the *śruti*, then one would indeed injure the *śruti*, but this is not the case.

This is because the general and specific meanings expressed and indicated by the *śruti* regarding the *udgītha* are not sublated, since those found in one's own recensional branch (*sva-śākhā*) are accepted even when those belonging to other branches are not.

As they have said: "Having grasped both the genus and the individual as indicated by the Vedic text, if we were to abandon [the specific color] black and so forth, what Vedic injunction would be violated therein?"

This being the position reached, it is replied as follows: The meditative cognitions (*pratyaya*) connected with the *udgītha* and other such elements should follow along with each Veda across various recensions (*śākhā*), rather than being restricted to each individual recension.

This is because there is no distinction in the general scriptural mention of "the *udgītha*" and so forth. What is meant is this: in cases such as "Bring the white cloth," although the word "cloth" applies without distinction, the mention of "white" sets aside [the cloth's unspecified color] by virtue of its proximity.
Thus [it is said],
because the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words is for the purpose of conveying a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*),
since that [conveying] would otherwise be impossible.

Furthermore, since words do not convey a qualified meaning without first causing the recollection of their own individual meanings, the recollection of those individual meanings—being prompted by the qualified meaning—is not capable of setting aside its own prompter.

Nor is it logical that the recollection of the individual meanings should cease for want of a prompter; for even a Vedic revelation (śruti), though operating without distinction, is restricted to a single specific instance.
However, in this case, the revelation regarding the *udgītha* conveys a qualified meaning without such restriction.
There is no authority whatsoever for such a restriction;
nor can mere proximity override [the general rule].
Furthermore, the confinement of a scriptural statement—which, by virtue of its commonality of form, applies to all specific instances—to a single instance is indeed a contradiction.
Therefore, all meditative realizations have the *udgītha* as their object.
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and so forth.
For us, the conviction that something is contradictory arises only when it is not perceived by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is observed that in the case of mantras and other elements belonging to one Vedic branch, there is a connection with ritual acts belonging to another branch;
since this is likewise seen here, there is no contradiction.
And this has been demonstrated by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) in an easy-to-understand manner. //56// 3.3.32.57.
"The greater importance belongs to the whole, like the sacrifice; for thus [the scripture] shows.

Regarding the Vaiśvānara-vidyā in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the question arises whether there is meditation on the parts individually or only on the whole. In that context, because of the scriptural injunctions for individual meditation—such as "The heaven alone, O venerable King," he said—and because the attainment of results is recorded for each part, and because the attainment of results is also heard of for the meditation on the whole, meditation is of both kinds.

Nor can it be argued that, as in the Vaiśvānara sacrifice— where statements such as "when it consists of eight potsherds" and so forth are merely explanatory (arthavāda) despite the mention of individual results, whereas only the injunction "one should offer the Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds" possesses actual fruitfulness— the same logic should apply here as well.

For in that case, there is the scriptural statement of an injunction: "one should offer [the oblation] on twelve potsherds," whereas in passages such as "it becomes [offered] on eight potsherds," there is a statement in the present tense. Nor can an injunction be inferred from these statements under the principle "but because of novelty" (*vacanāni tv apūrvatvāt*).
For even praise is possible through a statement made by way of partial dissociation;

however, in this case, since there is no distinction between the description as it applies to the whole and to the parts, and because no specific distinction is perceived, there is a difference in that one would have to assume injunctions and results for both cases.
Furthermore, a deprecation is possible at the beginning of the meditation on the whole even with respect to the meditation on the parts.

An objection is raised that there are two kinds of meditation, just as in the statement, "The dark horse carries the oblation. To this it is replied: the greater authority belongs to the meditation on the whole, not to the meditation on the parts.
Although the use of the present tense is common to both cases, nevertheless, by considering the preceding and following context, it is understood that the intent is the meditation on the whole;
for the meaning of a sentence is that toward which it is directed.
For instance, Prācīnaśāla and others, desiring to attain perfection in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, approached Aśvapati Kaikeya;
they each presented their respective partial meditations,
and thereupon Kaikeya, after censuring those various meditations, rejected them and concluded by teaching the meditation on the whole.

And thus, for the sake of achieving syntactical unity and avoiding a split in the sentence, the entire context is seen to have as its purport meditation on the whole. Therefore, the mention of many fruits is for the purpose of praising the principal [meditation].
It is thus established that only the complete means of attainment possesses fruitfulness.
Having set forth the explanation of a certain partial teacher, he refutes it with the words:
"But some here... (kecittvatra).
Since it is improper to resort to a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) when a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is possible, such an interpretation of the Sūtra is not correct;
this is the meaning. //57// 3.3.33.58.
*Nānāśabdādibhedāt* (Because of the difference in words and so forth).
Having established the non-difference of the meditations (*vidyā*) discussed below and having completed that group of investigations,

we must now investigate whether there is non-difference or difference among all the meditations whose objects are the Lord (*īśvara*), and likewise among those whose objects are the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

Now, it may be objected: just as in the case of the unprecedented *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*), although there is no difference in its essential nature, a distinction arises because it is defined by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and since that [meaning]—such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth—is diverse, the *bhāvanā* is perceived as distinct due to the diversity of the adjuncts (*anubandha*) consisting of the meanings of the roots such as sacrifice which constitute the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Likewise, even though the objects of knowledge (*vedya*)—the Lord—are non-different in their essence, there is a distinction among the meditations (*vidyā*) due to the diversity of the limiting adjuncts (*upadhāna*) consisting of qualities such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpatva*). Thus, there is no room for a doubt regarding non-distinction.

It is said: It is logical that there is a difference between the various *apūrva-bhāvanās* (unprecedented creative energies) in the form of ritual effects due to the difference in their respective connections (*anubandha*).

However, in this case, because Brahman is of an eternally established nature (*siddharūpa*), and because its attributes—such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*) and so forth—which have Him as their substratum, are likewise eternally established, there is no difference whatsoever among the meditations (*vidyās*) regarding them.

For instance, a young Kṣatriya who has been described in one place as "broad-chested, with eyes like the cakora bird, and possessing the qualities of a hero" is not [regarded as different] when he is mentioned elsewhere.

Just as one described as having the face of a lion and the shoulders of a bull does not lose those qualities simply because he is also described as having eyes like those of a cakora bird, an object certainly does not change with each description;
for it remains in that very same state everywhere.
Or, if it were not in that same state, it would no longer be that very object.
"For an object is not conceptualized.
Therefore, it follows that there is a distinction between the meditations (*vidyās*) because of the distinction in their objects.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "This would indeed be so if the sentences concerning meditation were established in the nature of the object itself; however, they enjoin the cultivation of meditation directed toward that object."
And that [meditation] takes the form of an action (*kārya*).

Although the cultivation of meditation (*upāsanā-bhāvanā*) is defined in dependence upon meditation, meditation is defined in dependence upon the object of meditation (*upāsya*), and the object of meditation—such as the Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth—is of a fixed nature;
nevertheless, its becoming the object of meditation occurs for someone, at some time, and in some particular form, and thus it remains indeed indeterminate.

Just as a single female body, being perceived by one person as food, by another as a mistress, by another as a daughter, by another as a mother, and by another as someone to be disregarded, is dependent upon the will of the individuals concerned;
so too here, these meditations (upāsanās) do not transcend their status as things to be performed according to the will of the person.
Nor are these meditations differentiated merely because of the differences in their qualities, since they are meditations upon those very qualities.

Furthermore, it is not the case that, as in the instance of the Agnihotra, an injunction for meditation is first established and then qualities such as "having true resolve" (satyasaṃkalpatva) are enjoined as attributes— like curds or rice— in which case there would be a single scriptural unit; rather,
because at the very time of their origination the meditations are understood as being distinguished by those respective qualities,
the Veda is equal with respect to all of them, since no distinction [between them] is perceived therein.
Furthermore, it is not possible to practice the combination of all qualities prescribed in every single branch (śākhā); therefore, [the meditation] is distinct.
Nor is it the case that "those who possess the same qualities, such as Satyakāma and others," [are identical];
for indeed, certain qualities are common to some meditations (vidyās), and thus, if they were part of a single meditation, they would have to be repeated.
Because it has been stated in one place.

However, there is no tautology when the meditations (vidyās) differ; for what is stated in one meditation is not stated in another. Therefore, those qualities must be mentioned for the sake of attributing them to other meditations as well, since those not mentioned would otherwise not be obtained. 3.3.34.59. There is an option (vikalpa), because the fruit is indistinguishable.

In the case of the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other such rites, although they have distinct qualifications for performance, their combination is observed to be governed by restrictive rules because they are obligatory (nitya). However, meditations (upāsanās) are not obligatory, as they are performed for the sake of specific desires (kāmya); therefore, there is no rule regarding their combination.

Consequently, unlike the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices which have the same result and thus involve an obligatory option (niyamavān vikalpa), there is no such rule here; for one who seeks the fullness of results, a combination (samuccaya) of these meditations is also possible—this is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).

Since these meditations (*upāsanā*) are accomplished by the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the object of meditation, if the direct realization of the object is achieved through one meditation, the fruit is obtained from that alone; thus, there is no need for another meditation. Furthermore, since the attainment of the fruit depends solely on that [realization], and because it remains impossible to produce a superior degree of realization even by means of a thousand methods, and because the practice of another meditation would disrupt the one-pointedness of the mind (*cittaikāgratā*), resulting in the failure to complete any particular meditation—therefore, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that here there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) governed by a restrictive rule (*niyama*). 3.3.35.60.

But the optional meditations may be combined according to one's desire, or not, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason. Regarding those meditations which, even without the direct realization of the object of meditation, serve as means to a desired end through unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) alone—just like the optional New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa)—it is appropriate that their optionality or combination depends on the person's will.
As for the subsidiaries (aṅga), their status is according to their respective bases.

Regarding the sūtra *tannirdhāraṇāniyamaḥ* (JS 3.3.42), since the mention of fruits in connection with meditations (*upāsanā*) is considered a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)—according to the logic of the *parṇamayī* [sacrificial ladle]—there arises the doubt that these meditations, being subordinate to the sacrifice, must necessarily be combined. Anticipating this, it is refuted that there is a rule of combination, because when they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), they are not grasped by a single injunction of performance (*ekaprayogavacana*).
Thus, the necessity of combining them is rejected.

But here, even though these [meditations] serve the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*), one objects by raising a challenge to the previously stated point: why is there not a single injunction for their performance?
For although these meditations are performed for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya*), they cannot be independent;
for if they were, then—since they would not depend on the elements of the sacrifice—their performance would follow as a consequence even outside the performance of the sacrifice itself.
And yet they are not employed; for what reason?
Because those [subsidiary acts] which depend on the primary rites (*kratvartha*) are enjoined specifically with reference to their respective fruits.

Thus, since the subsidiaries are dependent on the substrates (*āśraya*), and because the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) necessitates the combination of the substrates, it is logical that there must also be a necessity of combining the subsidiaries; otherwise, their status as being dependent on those substrates would be untenable.

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) belongs to one who considers that the injunctive statement (*prayoga-vacana*) regarding the meditations (*upāsanā*) necessarily implies the existence of a desire for their respective fruits, because in the absence of such desire, there would be no rule for their combined performance.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that the injunctive statement must conform to the specific items as they have been prescribed and indicated; it cannot alter the inherent nature of those items.
However, it remains consistent with that [principle].

In this regard, since those rites for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) are prescribed as if they were obligatory (*nitya*), their status as such cannot be otherwise; therefore, one must necessarily perform them in combination. But as for the meditations (*upāsanā*) connected to specific desires (*kāma*), because desires are non-obligatory (*anitya*), they cannot be restricted by way of mandatory combination.

For desires are not enjoined such that they could be combined [with other injunctions]; rather, they are merely referred to (uddiśyante). And a reference follows the authority of another means of knowledge; it does not alter the object of reference in contradiction to that [other means]. For if it were so, the reference itself would be untenable.

Therefore, because desires are impermanent, the meditations (*upāsanā*) bound to them are also impermanent. This is due to the contradiction between the permanent and the impermanent. Even though their substrata (*āśraya*) are permanent, this very fact constitutes the dependence of the dependent (*āśrita*) upon its substratum: namely, that the dependent exists only when the substratum exists, and not when it does not. It does not mean, however, that there is activity [of the dependent] there and no non-activity. Thus it has been said: "For even those things which are dependent on a substratum... "The human goal [arises] from this [knowledge], according to the word [of scripture]; thus Bādarāyaṇa [holds].

Having established that the Upaniṣads are devoted to the knowledge of the Self—which is the means for attaining the human goal known as liberation (apavarga)—and that meditative practices (upāsanā) are the means for their respective human goals, the preceding series of investigations has been completed.

Now, however, we shall investigate whether the knowledge of the true nature of the Self according to the Upaniṣads is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being a means to liberation (*apavarga*), or whether it is a ritual purpose (*kratvartha*) by virtue of establishing the agent required for the performance of a sacrifice.

And when it is a ritual purpose, then only that much is required by the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice: namely, agency and the state of being the enjoyer of results in the hereafter; yet this is not possible if [the self] were impermanent, because of the consequence that what has been done would perish (*kṛta-vipraṇāśa*) and what has not been done would accrue (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Therefore, [the self] must also be eternal.
Only that much is intended to be expressed in the Upaniṣads;
anything other than this would not be the meaning of the Upaniṣads, as it is either unnecessary or contrary [to their purpose],
such as [the qualities of] purity and so forth.

Although it has been established in various places through extensive treatises that the Upanishads are intent upon demonstrating the Brahman-nature of the individual soul (jīva) by way of restating its existence, nevertheless, here— in order to dispel certain seeds of doubt regarding the prima facie arguments—
that very point is made immovable according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar. Thus, there is a purpose for this inquiry.
In this regard, although the knowledge of the Self is not taught in connection with any specific ritual— unlike the act of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth—

and although the mere agent is not invariably connected to a ritual since the mere agent is seen even in worldly actions, whereby [the knowledge of the Self] might, like the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, connect itself to a ritual through its connection to the agent despite being taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*);

Although by the very statement [of the Veda] it is understood to be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), nevertheless, that kind of self which is taught by the Vedāntas as the agent who partakes in the enjoyment of fruits such as heaven in the hereafter—
distinct from the body and so forth— has no utility in worldly actions. This is because those actions,
which have fruits pertaining to this world (*aihika*), are possible even with an agent of whatever sort, provided he is not distinct from the body.

However, since Vedic rituals that yield results in the hereafter are impossible without him, this person described in the Upaniṣads must indeed be connected with them; because he is invariably present, the knowledge of him—by means of the very sentence that reminds one of those rituals, like the ladle (juhū) and so forth—attains the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice, just as the quality of being made of parṇa-wood does.
Thus, the mention of the fruit is merely an explanatory praise (arthavāda).

As it has been said: "In the case of substances, purificatory rites, and actions, because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). For it is one who is purified by the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads—who possesses such knowledge and faith—that is fit to enjoy the fruits in the next world; thus, through knowledge, he becomes an auxiliary factor in the performance of the sacrifice, and not otherwise, just as rice grains that have been sprinkled with water become an auxiliary factor in the sacrifice.

Furthermore, since it is the transmigrating self alone—indicated by terms such as "dear"—that is declared to be the object to be seen, attributes such as "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) are merely qualifications intended for its glorification;
they do not signify that the Upaniṣads have that [liberation] as their primary purpose.

Therefore, knowledge of the self serves only the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*), by way of purifying the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāra*), and not for the sake of the person’s ultimate goal (*puruṣārtha*).
And to support this point, the conduct and other practices of those who know Brahman, as understood from the Śruti, have been cited;
for it is not only from the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that knowledge of the Self serves the purpose of the ritual,
but also from the use of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*).

But this [statement] does not concern the present Udgītha-vidyā, because of the comprehension of pervasion through the use of the pronoun "that which" (*yat*) together with the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*);
just as in the case: "Whatever region possesses smoke, that possesses fire.
Furthermore, the statement regarding "commencing together" (*samanvārambha*) demonstrates the cooperation of knowledge and action at the commencement of the fruit.

And although that [knowledge] might indeed exist as having equal primacy—like the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya—nevertheless, by the reasoning already stated, it must be understood as being merely a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of ritual action.

Since the performance of ritual action is prescribed for one who possesses knowledge of the meaning of the Veda, and since the Upaniṣads are also part of the meaning of the Veda, their knowledge too is a subordinate member of ritual action.
