rather, it has been stated repeatedly in various places that those [passages] aim to establish that the soul (jīva), referred to in such a manner, is in essence the pure, awakened, and indifferent Brahman.
For the natural function of a word is to convey a meaning not already known, rather than merely restating what is established by other means of valid cognition.

And thus, since the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads is opposed to the performance of ritual acts, there is no connection whatsoever with the sacrifice; how much less, then, could there be its invariable concomitance with it, and consequently its status as a subsidiary part of the sacrifice? Therefore, the scriptural mention of liberation as the fruit is not merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), but rather has the fruit itself as its primary purport.

For this very reason, when there is a desire to teach the supreme Self to that very self which was introduced as a transmigrating soul indicated by [the mention of] "beloved ones" and so forth, the absolute non-difference of that [transmigrating] self from the supreme Self is taught. Just as the absolute non-difference of a superimposed snake from the nature of the rope is established by the statement, "That which is this snake is the rope," so too has it been shown that knowledge is a subordinate part of ritual action; likewise, the view regarding its being a subordinate part of action has been stated.

And by the method of elimination, he will state that "one who is established in Brahman" refers to the wandering mendicant.

Thus, since there is no contradiction, we shall either accept the existence of other stages of life based on this corroborative reference (*parāmarśa*) as if they were established facts, or we shall postulate their establishment in another scriptural tradition.

Regarding the phrase "yadāpi" (even when):

This is the intended meaning:

"One who is firmly established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*).

In this context, the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) are denoted by their own specific terms, while the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) are presented by the word "austerity" (*tapas*), since austerity is their predominant characteristic.

For even a monk, by virtue of the rule of eating only eight mouthfuls and possessing the purity of meditative concentration, becomes one for whom austerity is primary, just like a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
Nor is it impossible for a householder or others who perform ritual actions (*karmin*) to be established in Brahman;
if "being a performer of action" (*karmitā*) refers simply to the yoga of action, that exists in the monk as well through his body, speech, and mind.

Because it would contradict the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, by combining the two stages of life through austerity (*tapas*), the number three is established;
thus, even though all three stages of life are not established in Brahman, they partake of the worlds of merit, whereas he who is established in Brahman among these attains immortality.
Nor is there a contradiction in the fact that those who possess the state of sharing in the world of merit are the very same ones who possess immortality;

for just as Devadatta and Yajñadatta were once of dull intellect, but now Yajñadatta has become sharp-witted through the study of the scriptures, so too here, those who do not abide in Brahman share in the world of merit, while those who do abide in Brahman share in immortality— thus, due to the difference in their respective states, there is no contradiction.
And thus, the word *brahmasaṃstha* will be an etymological compound (*yaugika*) referring to the subject under discussion.

Just as in the case of the injunction "He worships the Āgnīdhra altar with an Āgneyī [verse]," it is the very same *Āgneyī* verse mentioned in the context that is understood, even though it has already been employed elsewhere;

But it is not so indicated; for when there is an application by way of being something to be enjoined, since there is a requirement for the referent of the word *āgneyī* (pertaining to Agni), and because there is no evidence for deviating from the context,
the scripture is sufficiently established by that much alone, and thus there is no possibility of including even those [verses] outside the context.
Nor does the lack of specific application [of the term] imply a lack of applicability;
for if that were so, it would follow that all mantras—since they are applied elsewhere—would likewise fail to apply in other contexts.

Similarly here as well, only the stages of life (āśramas) under discussion, which are present in the mind, are referred to, and not the unmentioned wandering mendicant (parivrāj) alone; such is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
He begins the final conclusion:

It is proper that the conclusion should correspond exactly to how one began;

For when a general rule is possible, it is not logical to resort to an exception.

Nor do purity, contentment, tranquility (*śama*), and the like belong to the category of austerity, because it is unestablished that among the elders (*vṛddha*) these are commonly known as "austerity" (*tapas*).

For this very reason, the elders describe purity and the other [observances] as distinct forms of austerity, stating: "Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas).

For being established in that [state] (tatsaṃsthatā), by excluding its own inherent nature, precludes contradiction and so forth; thus, it applies directly only to that which is established in that state, and not elsewhere.
"But tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth belong to it" means that one's own limb is not a mediator.
The author states that the Śruti demonstrates *brahmasaṃsthatva* (being established in Brahman) as the unique duty of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*):

"Indeed, these other austerities, renunciation (nyāsa) alone surpasses.
What is meant by this is that renunciation, characterized by the abandonment of all desires for the sake of Brahman, is itself Brahman.
Thus, such a state of being established in Brahman, characterized by renunciation, belongs exclusively to the mendicant and not to the others who belong to the [other] stages of life.

The meaning is that wandering as a mendicant (*parivrājya*) is prescribed as an auxiliary to that maturation of the knowledge of Brahmana—which is produced by the sacred word (*śabda*) and consists of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*)—which is the means to liberation; it is not, however, intended for one who is ineligible [for such knowledge]. 21.
"If it be argued that it is mere praise because of the mention [of the stages], we say no, because of its being a new injunction (*apūrvatva*)."

If there is no injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) in proximity here, then even though it is situated in another location, that [Udgītha]— being brought to mind by the Udgītha through its connection with that injunction despite the lack of immediate syntactic relation—

For there is no restrictive reason why syntactic unity must occur only between words that are uttered in close proximity.

This is because it is accepted that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), even those obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) by way of connection (*anuṣaṅga*), provided they are not directly juxtaposed with an injunction (*vidhi*).

Even if a direct juxtaposition with an injunction were heard—such as "one should meditate on the *udgītha*" or "one should meditate on the *sāman*"—nevertheless, that [explanatory passage] serves as a praise (*stuti*) of that very injunction; it does not aim at providing the object of meditation, since the object of meditation is already provided by the statement itself: "The syllable 'Om' is the *udgītha*."
To this it is replied: First of all, there is no possibility of syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) with a distant injunctive sentence enjoining an action.

It is by way of syntactic unity with an injunction that the Arthavādas serve the purpose of praise (stuti), based on the co-occurrence of words already perceived, according to the analogy of the "red-clad" (raktapaṭa) [who is identified by his garment].
However, there is no logical inconsistency whatsoever in the injunction itself without such praise.
As they have said: "But there is that [entity], which serves as the rebuttal when there is a discrepancy.

For this very reason, since there is no need for an injunction (*vidhi*)—which consists essentially in instigation—it is inconsistent to claim that the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the *arthavāda* is obtained through syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*), extension (*atideśa*), and so forth. Indeed, once the means desired by the agent has been understood, there is no utility whatsoever for the cognition of excellence.
Therefore, the injunction regarding ritual action situated at a distance would be purposeless;

for it cannot form a single syntactical unit with that [injunction]. However, since there is a doubt as to whether the proximate injunction of meditation (*upāsanā*) is to be utilized by providing its object or by way of praise, it is more appropriate that it serves a purpose by providing the object, rather than through praise, because the latter is an external factor (*bahiraṅga*).
For that [meditation] has no other recourse;
therefore, it is established that they are for the purpose of worship (*upāsanā*).
"One should do," "it should be done," "it ought to be done," "it may be," and "it shall be"—these are the five forms.
This shall be the fixed characteristic of injunctions throughout all the Vedas.

Indeed, injunction (*vidhi*) is that which is conducive to what is desired by the agent through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), while prohibition (*niṣedha*) is that which is conducive to what is harmful to the agent.
As they have said: "That which has happiness as its fruit is to be performed; that which has suffering as its fruit is not to be performed. And this has been established by us in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*.
Action (*kriyā*) is cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the words expressing it are *karoti* and so forth;
as they say, "the roots *kam*, *bhū*, and *as* express action in general. For this very reason, he has cited *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* as examples.

When a general statement is made, its specific instances—such as "one should cook" and so forth—are also understood; thus, in that context, the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) has an implied agent in the form "one should do," while in "it should be done" (*kriyeta*), the *bhāvanā* has an implied object.
However, in "it must be done" (*kartavyam*), the *bhāvanā* is subordinate to the substance which serves as the object.

In this way, examples of a productive urge (bhāvanā) impelled by an injunction (*vidhi*) whose object is the meaning of a single verbal root should be cited, such as: "One should be a staff-bearer," "One must become a staff-bearer," or "One should have been a staff-bearer.

Furthermore, this verb *bhavati* is used in the sense of coming into being; for example, people employ it in such expressions as "the jar comes into being from the potter's activity" or "the sprout comes into being from the seed."
And people do not employ the expression "the sprout exists from the seed";
therefore, [the statement] refers to existence (*sattā*), not to birth (*janman*).
If it is argued that [these stories] have the purpose of mere entertainment (*pāriplava*), we say no, because they are specified [as having a specific purpose].

Although the narratives known as *upaniṣads* are heard in proximity to [specific] forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), nevertheless, because the weaker factor of proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is set aside by the universal scriptural injunction (*sarva-śruti*)—"All narratives [are to be recited] during the *pāriplava* [rite]"—which intends them for that purpose without exception, these narratives serve only the *pāriplava*. Now, just as in the case of the injunction "One should recite all the *dāśatayī* hymns," even though there is a general application, the specific application of each individual hymn to its respective ritual action is not contradicted; so too here, although there is the application to the *pāriplava*, they may also be subordinate members of the knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*) due to their proximity.
Or rather, it should be said that [the stories] will come to pass;

for while in the *Daśatayīs* the individual applications (*prātisvikaviniyoga*) and the collective application (*samudāyaviniyoga*) possess equal force, here, however, because of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is more powerful.

Therefore, when it is argued that these narratives (*ākhyāna*) are intended solely for the *pāriplava* recitation, the following is stated: there is no application of these narratives to the *pāriplava*.

However, beginning with the injunction "one should recite the Pāriplava," those [stories] which are recorded there, such as "Manu Vaivasvata was the king" and so forth, are the ones specifically enjoined for that purpose;

for they alone are distinguished by the term "Pāriplava. Otherwise, since the requirement would already be fulfilled by the statement "all narratives [are used] in the Pāriplava," the injunction "one should recite the Pāriplava" would be redundant.
However, [the word "all"] is meaningful when it functions as a qualifier of a specific enumeration.
Therefore, by virtue of following those specific qualifiers, the word "all" (sarva) is dependent upon them and does not denote "without remainder" (aśeṣa).
Just as in the expression "All Brāhmaṇas are to be fed," the word "all" is dependent upon the invited guests.

Thus, it is established that the proximity of the Upaniṣadic narratives to knowledge establishes their syntactic unity with knowledge without opposition; they do not, like the passage "He wept" (so 'rodīt), form a syntactic unity with an injunction. Furthermore, this is because of the ease of comprehension, for even children are instructed by means of a narrative, as is well known from the illustrative stories in the grammatical treatises.
For this very reason, there is no dependence on the kindling of the sacred fires and other such ritual acts.
If knowledge were for the sake of the sacrifice, then the sacrifice would be required for its own purpose as an instrument for that sacrifice;
in its absence, for whose benefit would the knowledge serve?

But when it is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), then the sacrifice is not required by it for its own purpose, because of the capacity of that [knowledge] which is independent [of the sacrifice].
By the mention of "kindling the fires" and so forth, the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*) are indicated; thus he says:
"The duties of the stages of life, such as kindling the fires and the like, are not to be required for the accomplishment of the goal of knowledge.
This means they are not to be required for the accomplishment of its own [knowledge's] purpose, but not for its own [intrinsic] establishment.
And this [point] will be explained further below;
with the intention of explaining that, the purpose of the preceding section has been stated.
Regarding what was said as "with the intention of explaining the additional," he states that additional point:
"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse.

There might be the suspicion that, just as the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) are not required for the attainment of one's own goal [liberation], they should likewise not be required for the arising [of knowledge]. Nor is there any contradiction with such texts as "they desire to know by means of sacrifice" (yajñena vividiṣanti).
This is not an injunction, but rather a statement of an existing fact;
and that is also consistent with being a praise.
Furthermore, there are four modes of realization regarding Brahman.

First, there is that which arises from merely hearing the sentences of the Upaniṣads, which they indeed call "hearing" (śravaṇa). Second, there is that which arises from those very same Upaniṣadic sentences when accompanied by inquiry (mīmāṃsā), which they call "reflection" (manana).
The third is the contemplation consisting of a continuous stream, which they call *nididhyāsana*.
The fourth is the state characterized by direct realization; for liberation (*kaivalya*) is its inevitable consequence.

In that regard, first of all, the first two stages of realization are indeed possible for a person who has understood the words and their meanings, and who knows the logical principles governing the application of sentences; thus, there is no dependence on ritual action (*karman*) therein.
And since those very two give rise to the third stage of realization, which consists of reflection (*cintāmayī*), there is likewise no dependence on ritual action there either.

Furthermore, when that [reflection] is cultivated with diligence, continuity, and over a long period of time, it certainly brings about the fourth stage of realization, which is characterized by direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*); therefore, even in this case, there is no dependence on ritual action.
And since liberation is inseparable from that [knowledge], it too has no dependence on action.

Thus, neither in terms of its means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nor its object (*prameya*), nor its origination (*utpatti*), nor its result (*kārya*), does knowledge depend on action; this is the seed of doubt.

When this position has been reached, it is said in reply: there is indeed a dependence on action for the origination of knowledge, by way of producing the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), according to the Vedic scripture: "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*).
Nor is this merely a statement of praise because it expresses a present state, for its meaning is something not previously established (*apūrva*).

Just as the injunction that "one whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood [obtains merit]" is an injunction regarding the *parṇa*-nature of the ladle due to its being *apūrva*, and not a mere statement of a present fact—
since a restatement (*anuvāda*) would otherwise be untenable.

Therefore, for the arising [of knowledge], ritual actions are required by means of knowledge, just like tranquility and the other qualities. Even there, because of their connection with the very nature of knowledge— as seen in the term "one who knows thus" (evaṃvid)— tranquility and the rest are internal factors in the production of knowledge,
whereas ritual actions are external factors due to their connection with the desire to know (vividiṣā).
For instance: from the performance of the obligatory duties prescribed for one’s stage of life (*āśrama*), dharma arises; from that, evil (*pāpman*) dissolves.

For that [evil], while cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—which in reality is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self—exists, defiles the essence of the mind (*cittasattva*) through the delusion characterized by permanence, purity, happiness, and self, because such delusions are bound to unrighteousness (*adharma*). Therefore, when evil is destroyed and the obstruction to perception and reasoning is removed, one can unimpededly determine, by means of both perception and reasoning, the true nature of cyclic existence as being impermanent, impure, and painful.
Then, a dispassion characterized by the perception of dissatisfaction arises toward this [world]. Thereupon, the desire to abandon it occurs to him.

He then seeks the means for its abandonment; and while seeking, having heard from the scriptures and the words of teachers that the knowledge of the reality of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) is the means, he desires to know it. Thus, through the gateway of the removal of the desire to know [the world], there is the arising of the knowledge of the self.
The application of action is for the sake of inquiry; indeed, one who desires to know, being disciplined, is capable of performing hearing and reflection with one-pointed concentration.
Thereupon, in him, the knowledge free from doubt arises through the sentence "That thou art."
Furthermore, for one who has ascertained without doubt the meaning of the sentence "That thou art," there is no further qualification for ritual action;
by virtue of which action could be of use either in the process of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or in its result, which is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

By this, it should be understood that the utility of actions toward liberation (*apavarga*), which is the result of direct realization in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is utterly refuted.

Therefore, the claim that just as self-restraint (*śama*), tranquility (*dama*), and so forth continue for as long as one lives, so too must the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) continue, is an unexamined assertion. It has already been stated that the knower (*vidvas*) has no qualification (*anadhikāra*) for those [duties].

However, in the case of actions with visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*), even in the absence of formal qualification—provided there is no prohibition—an inclination arising from one's own nature (*svārasikī pravṛtti*) is indeed possible for one who is not attached [to worldly results].
For in that case, where the fruit is to be attained through the comprehension of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), there is no requirement for an injunction;
therefore, the statement, "If worldly action is performed without delusion, let Vedic action be likewise for you," is mere idle chatter.

However, as for tranquility, self-control, and so forth, which are undertaken for the production of knowledge, their continued persistence—even if not required—occurs due to their inherent nature in the subsequent states.

This has already been established by us in the first Sūtra and is not being restated here. Therefore, it is proven that the utility of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is by way of generating the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), and not as a direct effect of knowledge itself. The remainder [of the commentary] has its meaning self-evident. //26// 3.4.6.27. // 27 // 3.4.7.28.
"And there is permission to eat all food in case of danger to life, for that is seen [in scripture].

In the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is heard regarding all the sense organs: 'Indeed, having overcome all these, speech and the rest, the principal breath said: "What shall be my food? They replied. This, indeed, is the subject of investigation. All these—speech and the others—having been surpassed, the principal breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) said: "What will be my food?"; they said: [so-and-so].
Namely, that which is food in the world for everyone from dogs and birds down to all living beings—that is your food.

Having thus enjoined the contemplation that everything is the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through this sequence of text, the Śruti says: "Indeed, for one who knows this, there is nothing whatsoever that is not food.
This means that for one who knows that everything is the food of the *prāṇa*, nothing at all remains non-food.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this permission to eat all food enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to this knowledge, like tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities, or is it mentioned merely for the sake of praise?

Although a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) is not perceived here because of the use of the present tense in the phrase "it happens" (*bhavati*), nevertheless—just as in the case of "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood," where despite the use of the present tense, the injunction that it must be made of *palāśa*-wood is understood through the application of the fifth mood (*liṅ*)—so too here, since a specific direction toward action is obtained, [an injunction is inferred].
It is the performance of the injunction;
for in a eulogy, the mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not possess the same purposefulness as it does in an injunction.
Furthermore, the general scripture concerning what may and may not be eaten is set aside by this specific scripture.

An objection is raised: just as a general treatise on the distinction between those who may and may not be approached for sexual union is superseded by a specific treatise that forms part of the Vāmadeva-vidyā and prescribes the avoidance of all women, so too should this [text] be understood. To this, it is replied: "Because of incapacity, because it must be assumed, and because of contradiction with other scriptures, there is a commendation of the meditation that 'all this is food for the vital breath'."
It is not possible for a human being to consume, either simultaneously or successively, the food that constitutes the diet of a dog;
for even a single item from the food of elephants, young camels, and so forth—such as *śamī* pods, *karīra* shoots, thorns, or pieces of wood—is impossible to eat.
Furthermore, in this case, there is no clearer perception of an injunction (*vidhi*) than there is of an indicative mark (*liṅ*).
Nor should an injunction be inferred, because there is no novelty [of the matter];
for that is established even by way of praise (stuti).
Furthermore, when another course is possible, it is not proper to restrict the scope of a scripture that has already functioned in a general manner.

Therefore, it is appropriate to regard the statement "therefore everything is food for the prāṇa" as a praise intended to enjoin the constant reflection [upon this truth]. Furthermore, the capacity [to perform an act] is useful only when it produces a specific inclination toward action, not when the injunction is impossible to carry out.
And the phrase "in case of danger to life" (prāṇātyaye) is intended as a restriction, meaning that the status of everything being food applies only in cases of life-threatening danger.

In this regard, because of the illustrative narrative (upākhyāna) and because the rule is more clearly remembered, and because it is prescribed for both the learned and the unlearned— with the exception of liquor—
it does not apply elsewhere; "ibhyena" means by an elephant-driver.
"Partially eaten" means half-consumed. For that Cākrāyaṇa, while eating the remains of boiled grain left over by elephant-keepers, was addressed by an elephant-keeper:
"Why do you not drink the water as well, like my leftover boiled grain?"
Being addressed thus, he declined that water on account of the fault of it being from leftover food,
and he stated the reason for this:
"I did not eat these kulmāṣas with the thought, 'I shall live,' nor shall I live [on them]."

"Kāma means 'water for drinking'": this refers to my independence regarding water for drinking—meaning that I may obtain it as I desire from rivers, wells, ponds, cisterns, and so forth—provided it is not the case that my life would perish due to a lack of even leftover water; in that situation, there is no fault in consuming what is left over. When the Kuru country was ravaged by hailstorms, a certain sage, emaciated by hunger and devoid of shame, ate half-eaten grains provided by a wealthy man (*ibhya*). [28] 3.4.7.29 [29] 3.4.7.30 [30] 3.4.7.31 [31] 3.4.8.32 [32]
And because they are prescribed, even the duties belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are [to be performed].

For the duties of the stages of life are obligatory, since they must necessarily be performed as means for attaining the eternal [goal], based on the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives. Furthermore, although the term "desiring to know" (*vividiṣanti*) indicates a connection with knowledge (*vidyā*), knowledge itself lacks the necessity of being invariably present; thus, it follows that [the desire for knowledge] is non-obligatory.
Furthermore, the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal is impossible for a single entity,
because there is a contradiction between that which necessarily exists and that which does not necessarily exist within one and the same thing.
Nor can this real contradiction be removed by means of splitting the sentence.
Therefore, it follows that there is indeed no definitive determination (anadhyavasāya) in this case.
By this, the principle "the separateness of conjunction [is established] when one thing has both [qualities]" is refuted.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "This contradiction would exist if [the object] were already established, but not at all when it is yet to be proven."
In this case, where the acquisition of its own nature depends upon an injunction, its continued existence is held to be according to that injunction.
For an established entity is sublated by its connection with contradictory properties;
however, that which has the nature of a goal to be accomplished (sādhya) is not so sublated, as in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, where there is both its taking and its non-taking.
For those two [alternatives] indeed oscillate between options because they are dependent upon an injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, once [the nature of the rite] is established, no further conceptual doubt arises.

Thus, in this context, there is only one rite called the Agnihotra; being enjoined by the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), it has the purpose of destroying the accumulated sins that must necessarily be expiated, and it is therefore mandatory.

Yet, because it serves as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), and since knowledge occurs only occasionally and is not mandatory, even though the rite enters into the domain of non-mandatory performance according to the maxim, "Whether optional or occasional, it enters into the modified sacrifice," it nevertheless—by virtue of its occasional status—[remains distinct].
It does not make the eternal non-eternal;

therefore, because that [non-eternality] is established by that [means], it is proven through the principle of "separateness of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*) that there is no contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal regarding a single effect. Furthermore, the coexistence of actions pertains not to the effect of knowledge, but rather to its production.
"What is the meaning of the statement that ritual actions are auxiliaries to knowledge?
This is the meaning: when rituals exist, it is knowledge alone that operates toward its own effect;
just as in the expression, "The she-ass carries the load together with her ten sons," even though the ten sons are present, it is the she-ass alone that is the carrier of the load.
"Because it does not have the characteristic of being an injunction (avidhilakṣaṇatvāt).
For that which is enjoined is connected with the subsidiaries of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, but that which is not enjoined is not.
This is because the status of being a subsidiary is preceded by being grasped by the "grasper" (grāhaka), and the injunction is the grasper.
Furthermore, because that [realization] is not possible in the case of what is not enjoined,
and because it has been stated in the first sūtra that an injunction is impossible for all four forms of practice with respect to Brahman;
and it has also been stated that the passages "it is to be seen" and "it is to be meditated upon," though having the form of an injunction, are not actually injunctions.

It has been established above that the causal relationship regarding its origination occurs through the production of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by means of the purification of the inner being (*sattva-śuddhi*).

Furthermore, liberation (*apavarga*), which is the fruit of knowledge, is not something to be produced (*asādhya*), for it is characterized as abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-avasthāna*).
And the essential nature of Brahman is not something to be produced, because it is eternal.
The remainder has its meaning not hidden. // 32 // 3.4.8.33. // 33 // 3.4.8.34.
"In every way, it is those same [meditations], because of the dual characteristic.

Just as in the case of "They offer the Agnihotra for a month," where a difference in action arises from the change of context (*prakaraṇāntara*), so too here, by means of the Vedic study (*vedānuvacana*)...

Regarding the statement, "Brahmins desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice," since this is heard apart from the context of the ritual (*kratuprakaraṇa*), and because the cognition of that [context] is excluded by the fact of being in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this is a different action (*karmāntara*).
To this, it is replied: even though there is a different context, it is indeed that same action;

there is merely a difference in connection (*saṃyogabheda*) based on scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*smṛti*). Just as in the cases, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" and "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives," it is the very same Agnihotra connected with both [results].
A different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is not directly a differentiator.

Rather, an injunction (*vidhi*), whose inherent nature is to make known what was previously unknown, would abandon its natural function when there is identity of context due to the force of a very clear recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
However, when recognition is obstructed by a different context, it abandons its natural function and differentiates the ritual action (*karman*).

But here, by enjoining sacrifices and the like— which already exist as established forms— for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), one cannot produce a new form for them, as is the case with [the injunction] "he does not sacrifice" (*na juhoti*) and so forth.
Nor is it correct to say that even there, in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra*, the injunction regarding the month is not the production of a new *agnihotra*,
because the injunction is heard directly concerning the *homa* itself.
Furthermore, because time is not something to be acquired and is not subject to injunction,
the general rule is that an action is enjoined with respect to time, not time with respect to an action; however, in this case,
the scriptural injunction pertains to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), not to sacrifice and the like.
But since those [details] are merely restated as already established, the distinctness of connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*) is established through their being part of a single ritual action.
Having stated the traditional authority (*smṛti*), the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśana*) was stated. (34) 3.4.8.35. (35) 3.4.9.36.
"And also because that is seen in between. (36)

If it is argued that since the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*) are auxiliaries to knowledge, then alas, those who do not belong to a stage of life—such as widowers and others—would have no qualification for knowledge due to the absence of these auxiliary duties of the stages of life, we reply: they are not entirely devoid of action. For Raikva, Vidhura, Vācaknavī, and others, even though they did not belong to a formal stage of life, possessed actions such as recitation (*japa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and the propitiation of deities.

And since it has been stated that the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*) possess the status of auxiliary factors (*sahakāritva*) by way of being indicative marks (*upalakṣaṇatva*), there is no lack of qualification for them regarding knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, [this applies] even when [the duties] were performed in another birth;
indeed, there is no dependence on ritual action (*karman*) for the effect that is knowledge.
Moreover, [this occurs] at the time of arising;
and by means of the offering of the desire to know (vividiṣā), they bring about knowledge through ritual actions.
For those foremost among men who have already produced the desire to know—such as Vidhūra, Saṃvarta, and others—there is no further need for ritual actions.

And although in this life only one who has generated the desire to know (*vividisā*) through the performance of duties belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) is qualified for knowledge—and not anyone else—therefore those without a stage of life, such as widowers and the like, lack qualification;
and thus [knowledge] has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthā*).
The cessation of ignorance (*avidyā-nivṛtti*) is the visible purpose of knowledge.
The meaning is that this [knowledge], being established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), does not depend on a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

"Negation" means obstruction; the meaning is the absence of that [obstruction]. //36// 3.4.9.37 // 37 // 3.4.9.38 // 38 // 3.4.10.39. One should remain a non-ascetic (anāśramin) while in good health;

however, if by fate one becomes a non-ascetic due to separation from a wife and so forth, there would be eligibility for knowledge (*vidyā*). This is understood from the greater authority of the scriptural and traditional texts, such as "They desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*), and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the Śruti: "By that [path] goes the doer of meritorious deeds."

This section is intended to remove the doubt of the dull-witted that, like the ascent, there might sometimes be a descent for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Regarding previous dharmas such as sacrifices and oblations:
out of attachment, one might think, "May I be a householder surrounded by a wife and so forth.

Nor can it be argued that even for one holding an office (an adhikārika), there is a possibility of expiation based on the inference of a fall; for such a thing is impossible. This is because of the traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding the absence of expiation for a *naiṣṭhika* (one who has taken lifelong vows): "I see no expiation for him. Furthermore, the sacrifice of a donkey to Nirṛti is prescribed as an expiation for an *upakurvāṇaka* (a student who has completed his studies), not for a *naiṣṭhika*.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that, like a man whose head has been severed, there is no remedy whatsoever.

As for the application of the Sūtra: that expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) which was determined in the first section (*kāṇḍa*), which deals with qualifications, under the rule "And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow [is prescribed], because the time for the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived," does not apply to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).

Why? Because, according to the Smṛti rule "one who has ascended to the state of a lifelong student [falls from grace]," a fall is inferred from scriptural testimony (*śruti*); therefore, that expiation is inappropriate for him. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.11.42)
Some maintain that this applies even when preceded by the word *upa*. Regarding the state [of celibacy], it is like food; thus it has been said.

First of all, the Śruti directly teaches an expiation without distinction for both the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*) and the temporary (*upakurvāṇa*) celibate student, provided the application of the term is not restricted.
As for the Smṛti statement, "I see no expiation," it refers to a different case.
Moreover, in that case as well, the prohibition of penance is not understood in the sense that "penance should not be performed directly";
rather, [the phrase] "I do not see" implies its non-perception, and thus it must be inferred.
And having inferred that the Smṛti is for the purpose of prohibition, the corresponding Śruti must then be inferred.
Scriptural injunction (*śruti*), however, having a general scope, moves swiftly toward a specific case.
The absence of a prescribed expiation in the Smṛti is intended to indicate the gravity of the effort required [to avoid such contact].
This is what is meant: even by those who have performed purification, no counting [of these individuals] should be performed.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: even for a *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibate), the emission of semen (*avakīrṇitva*)—even if preceded by [sexual intercourse]—is not a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). The particle *api* has the sense of *eva* (only/just). Therefore, some maintain that there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for it. Since there is no distinction between the conflicting views of the teachers, there would be parity [between the two positions].
Alternatively, that which is well-known within the scriptures (*śāstra*) should be accepted, because it is rooted in the scriptures.

And this [point] is established because the existence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is well-known; thus, its basis in the scriptures (*śāstramūlatva*) is proven. The rest is easy to understand. 3.4.12.43.
If there is expiation for those who have taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*) and others, should one then interact with them after they have performed the purification, or not?

In this regard, since non-intercourse [with such persons] is caused by a fault, it might be argued that they are indeed fit for intercourse because that fault is removed by expiation (*prāyaścitta*), or because if it were not removed, the performance of expiation would be useless. To this, it is replied: "But they are excluded from both [worlds], according to Smṛti and custom. The sin (*enah*) produced by the performance of forbidden acts brings about impurity in both worlds; however, in both cases, that impurity is removed by expiations which effect the destruction of that sin.

In some cases, however, only the impurity pertaining to the next world is removed by means of expiations that effect the destruction of sin; yet the impurity pertaining to this world, which has been produced by that very sin, cannot be removed—as in the case of those who have killed women, children, and so forth.
As they say: "One should not even drink water with them, though they may be pure according to dharma."
And likewise: "The sin that has been committed unintentionally is removed by expiatory rites"—this applies even to that which was committed intentionally.
However, one who kills a child and so forth, even though his purification has been accomplished, becomes unfit for social intercourse in this world due to the scriptural injunction;
and the scriptural injunction is: "Those who kill children," and so forth.
Therefore, everything is clear. 43.
3.4.13.44. "Because the fruit is heard as belonging to the master, so says Ātreya.

In the first section (*kāṇḍa*), which deals with the characteristics of the subordinate (*śeṣa*), in the passage beginning with *tathākāmaḥ*, once the connection of the ritual action with the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is established, what [is the purpose of the mention of] desire?

Having raised the doubt as to whether [the fruit] belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) or to the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), it was established that even in the case of ritual acts belonging to the officiating priest, the desire for the fruit of the subordinate qualities (*guṇaphala*) belongs to the sacrificer alone.

However, this is not a redundant repetition, because we are now investigating whether meditations (*upāsanā*) of this kind, which are connected with the constituent parts of the rite, belong to the sacrificer or to the officiating priest.

In this regard, since the fruits [of meditation] are heard in the case of lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), those who lack the qualification [for ritual action] cannot possess them; and while the patron (*yajamāna*)—who enjoys the fruit produced by the ritual—is qualified for it, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are not, as such a result is impossible for them. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement—which stands in the place of a royal decree—in some instances there is a declaration of fruit for the priests; however, in the absence of such a statement, the meditation belongs to the patron, as it bears fruit for him, given that the fruit is declared for him in passages such as, "Baka Dālbhya knew him. Thus, meditation belongs to the patron.

Since the meditation has been established as having the sacrificer as its subject, and because there is no capacity for it to override the rules of logic [regarding the officiating priest], it follows that the act of meditation belongs to the sacrificer alone; to this, it is replied:
"Āuḍulomi holds that it belongs to the officiating priest (*ārlijyam*), for he is hired for that purpose.
From the introductory narrative, it is understood that the meditation belongs to the *udgātṛ* priest.
Therefore, since there exists a powerful subverting argument (*bādhaka*), the narrative must be explained otherwise.

Furthermore, it is not impossible for the fruit of a meditation performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) to accrue to the patron (*yajamāna*); for he is hired by them, and thus it is logical that the fruit should go to him. Consequently, it is not proper to alter the narrative merely out of a fondness for [literal] consistency; this is the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*). //45// 3.4.13.46. // 46 // 3.4.14.47.

"Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship through certainty, should abide in childlike simplicity; and having become disillusioned with both childlike simplicity and scholarship, he then becomes a sage; and having become disillusioned with both non-sagehood and sagehood, he then becomes a true Brahmin.
For wherever an injunctive suffix is heard, that is what is to be enjoined.
And while that [instruction] is heard in the passage "one should remain as a child," it is not heard in the case of silence (*mauna*).
Therefore, just as the phrase "then [the state] of Brahman" is not something to be enjoined because no injunction is heard there, so too is silence.
Nor is it to be enjoined on the grounds of being something previously unknown (*apūrva*).
Therefore, since silence (*mauna*) is established by the very injunction of "the Brahmin should attain wisdom" (*pāṇḍitya*), wisdom itself is silence.
Alternatively, this word *muni* denotes a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), as seen in the passage: "The householder's stage, the teacher’s family, silence, and forest-dwelling.
This [text] is a restatement of that [silence] which has been prescribed elsewhere.
Therefore, it is logical that childhood alone is enjoined here, while "munitude" (mauna), being already established, is restated for the purpose of praise.
This would indeed be so if the word *muni* were a synonym for the learned (*paṇḍita*);
however, learning (*pāṇḍitya*) consists merely of knowledge, whereas *munitude* is the attainment of an excellence of knowledge, as is well known.
However, its application is restricted to the specific stages of life (āśrama) because of the proximity of terms such as "householder" (gārhasthya).

Therefore, since *mauna* (silence/contemplation) is something not previously established, this third stage of *mauna*—consisting of a preeminent knowledge—is enjoined in relation to childhood (*bālya*) and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*). And thus, it is stated that the fact that it is to be realized through direct experience would also be appropriate for an injunction: [The text continues: "But [the sage] says... (referring to the following verse).
"Because of the teaching on the state of being beyond feeling.
To the question, "For whom is this silence prescribed as an auxiliary to knowledge? he says: "For one who possesses that—that is, for the mendicant ascetic (bhikṣu) who possesses knowledge."
He asks:
"How so?
The meaning is that possession of knowledge is perceived, but not the state of being a renunciant (saṃnyāsin).
Because of the monk's authority over that; he shows this: because of the monk's authority over that.
Regarding the phrase "having known the Self," he raises an objection in order to connect it with the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
He refutes this, saying "by the side" (pakṣeṇa); by this,
it is not intended that "one who possesses knowledge" refers to a preeminent degree of knowledge.
Rather, he is one who has engaged in practice for the arising of knowledge, but not yet one in whom excellence of knowledge has arisen.
Thus, the meaning is that in his case, [the possibility of error] exists because of the occasional perception of difference.
"Vidhyādi" means that which is primarily characterized by injunction (vidhi), that is to say, the principal [factor].

For this very reason, the concluding portion [of the ritual] begins with the *samit* (fuel-sticks) and so forth; for that is the injunction (*vidhi*), and it occurs after the primary injunction. The meaning is that, since no injunction is explicitly heard there, an injunction must be inferred because of its novelty (*apūrvatva*). Now, one might object: "If this stage of life (*āśrama*) has childhood as its primary characteristic, why does [the text] conclude it with the householder's stage (*gārhasthya*)? Thus he raises the objection:
Thus, [the objection that] it is distinguished by childhood and so forth is raised;
he recites the answer: "But because of the totality [of the stages], there is a concluding summary by means of the householder."

The meaning is that in the *Chāndogya*, because householdership involves many efforts and many duties, and because it includes certain duties belonging to other stages of life (*āśrama*) such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, there is a mention of them [in the context of the householder] by way of inclusion, but not because the [other stages] are concluded therein.
Thus, by the presentation of these two stages of life, a dull-witted person might occasionally suspect the absence of the others; therefore, to dispel that doubt, the Sūtra states:
"Because the others are also taught, just like the vow of silence (*mauna*)."

The mode of life for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) is likewise manifold; so too is it for those practicing the student's vow (*brahmacārin*). Thus, there is a difference in their modes of life, or rather, the persons who practice them differ.
Therefore, even though there is duality [of classes], the use of the plural number is not contradictory. (Sūtra 3.4.15) 50.
"Not manifesting [itself], because of the connection. (Sūtra 3.4.16)

Regarding the phrase "by childhood" (*bālyena*): since it is well known from the scriptural accounts of the conduct of children that they act, speak, and eat according to their whims, and because this specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) sets aside the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) which enjoins regulations such as purity, it might be argued that the injunction here is for the performance of all the behaviors of a child.

To this, it is replied: Since "childhood" is enjoined as an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā-aṅga*), and because the performance of every single childish behavior would result in a contradiction with the primary purpose, what is intended is that state of being which is conducive to knowledge—namely, the non-maturity of the senses and so forth.

That very [knowledge] is prescribed as having the nature of purity of being (*bhāva-śuddhi*). And thus, since it is possible for this to be established without contradicting other scriptures, there will be no need to resort to the contradiction of other scriptures. 3.4.16.41.
"Even that which pertains to this life [occurs], provided there is no obstruction of what is not yet present, because that is observed."
He states the connection [of the sūtra] with the words: "And because of the dependence on all.
Is knowledge accomplished here in this very life through hearing and so forth, or is there no fixed rule, such that it may be accomplished either here or in the next?

Although ritual acts such as sacrifices have不定 (aniyata) fruits, and since they serve as means for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), it might appear that the arising of knowledge is itself uncertain;

and thus, from the scriptural account of Vāmadeva attaining self-realization while still in the womb, as well as from the Smṛti passage, "One who has attained perfection through many births then reaches the supreme goal," it is understood that [knowledge] pertains to the next world (*āmuṣmikatva*).

Nevertheless, because the objects of knowledge such as sacrifices are not themselves means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatva*), whereas hearing [the scriptures] and so forth are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), these latter alone are the direct means for the attainment of knowledge.

Sacrifices and the like serve as means for the production of knowledge either by effecting the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) or by pacifying the obstacles to the operation of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.
However, hearing and the other [means] produce knowledge independently [of such purification].

Furthermore, when investigators engage in the application of the instruments of valid cognition, they do not desire the production of knowledge even if it occurs after a long time in this life, let alone something pertaining to the next world.
For one who desires to see a jar or the like does not open his eyes for the purpose of seeing that jar at a later time, but rather for its perception at that very moment.
Therefore, the production of knowledge occurs only in this world and is not of indefinite time.
Furthermore, the Śruti and Smṛti texts praise the production of knowledge as pertaining to the next world only by way of figurative eulogy.
Thus, hearing and the other [means] have such a nature that they necessarily yield their fruit, insofar as they produce knowledge even after a lapse of time.

This being the position reached, it is said: since, in this case, when knowledge is to be produced through hearing and the rest, sacrifices and the like are useful either by way of purifying the mind (*sattva*) or by way of pacifying obstacles, for that very reason those sacrifices and so forth—due to their fruit being non-mandatory because of the presence or absence of obstructions from other actions—are not fixed in their result.

It is logical that even hearing and the other [means] have an uncertain result when they depend on those [sacrifices], because they do not produce their result for those whose obstacles have not been removed, or because they fail to produce it in a person whose internal nature (*sattva*) is unpurified. Thus, since those [sacrifices] depend on sacrifices and the like, and since those [sacrifices] have an uncertain result, it is entirely reasonable that hearing and the others also have an uncertain result; in this way, the connection between Śruti and Smṛti is established, and it is not merely a figure of speech.
It will be explained [later].

Furthermore, persons seeking knowledge will desire only that which corresponds to their capacity for the means [of practice]; this is what was meant by the statement: "because intentionality is unrestrained. (51) 3.4.17.52.
Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is determined; because that state is determined.

It is said that, due to the specific intensity of the means for acquiring knowledge—such as hearing the scriptures—which are aided by sacrifices and other rites, a distinction characterized by being either "pertaining to this life" (*aihika*) or "pertaining to the next life" (*āmumika*) is shown regarding the fruit, which is knowledge.

And so, just as there is excellence and deficiency in the fruit of knowledge (namely, knowledge itself) based on the excellence or deficiency of its means, one might suppose that excellence and deficiency could likewise apply to liberation, the fruit of knowledge.

However, no such distinction characterized by being "pertaining to this life" or "pertaining to the next life" is possible in liberation; for when knowledge arises from the full maturation of the meditation on Brahman, liberation is necessarily certain to occur while one is still living, even though the karma whose fruition has already begun (*ārabdhavipāka*) has not yet been exhausted.

Therefore, inferiority and superiority would exist only in the form of liberation itself. Furthermore, since it is observed that for the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) accompanied by attributes, there is an increase or decrease in their fruits corresponding to an increase or decrease in the knowledge itself, it follows that liberation—being the fruit of knowledge—would likewise possess an increase or decrease in its form. To this, it is replied: "In that regard, [there is] no [increase or decrease] in liberation."
In this regard, the scriptural teaching of uniformity and logical consistency support this view;
for that which is to be accomplished becomes qualified by the specific nature of its means of accomplishment.
However, liberation—characterized as the abiding in the eternal nature of Brahman—being itself eternal, cannot be something to be accomplished.

Furthermore, the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and latent dispositions (*āśaya*) along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*) is not something characterized by specific degrees of knowledge or birth, such that liberation would become characterized by specific degrees due to those differences.
Nor does a destruction of the afflictions and so forth that leaves a remainder suffice for liberation.

Furthermore, apart from the distinction between being produced quickly or slowly, no difference in form is perceived even in the case of knowledge (*vidyā*), since scripture declares that it too is of a single nature.
However, in the case of qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*), the excellence or inferiority of its result—its effect—is logical based on the inclusion or exclusion of various specific qualities.
Moreover, in this context, there is no inference based on a general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) regarding the nature of knowledge.
Because it is subject to the fallacy of "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) reasoning, being contradicted by scripture and the arguments arising therefrom;
therefore, since that state of liberation is determined to be uniform, it is logical that there is no distinction in the fruit characterized as liberation. //52//
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* of Śrī Bhagavatpāda, composed by Śrī Vācaspatimiśra.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter, titled "The Investigation into the Internal Means for the Knowledge Devoid of Attributes.
**Chapter Four** (Bhāmatī):
The virtuous need not be entreated here, for they proceed of their own accord; nor can others be compelled.
Those for whom there is an incurable loss of appetite caused by the bile of envy. //1//
I suspect that Indra, now bearing the happiness of his own kingdom without any doubt, will somehow experience distress toward those established in intense austerity;

for these [ascetics], their worldly existence dispelled by the discernment of the meaning of Vedānta made clear merely through the commentary composed by Vācaspatimiśra, are indifferent even to heaven. 2.
"Repetition [is required] because of the repeated instruction.

Since the attainment of the fruit is preceded by the performance of the means, he states the sequence of the two investigations of the objects of knowledge (viṣaya) according to the sequence of those objects themselves—
namely, in the third chapter.

Since the fruit characterized by liberation is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), the acts of seeing, hearing, reflecting, and meditating (*darśana-śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) enjoined for its sake have unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*); therefore, they must be performed according to their specific injunctions, but not repeated beyond that, as there is no authoritative basis (*pramāṇa*) for doing so.

However, regarding cases where the instruction is given only once—such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*)—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the performance should occur only once, just like the *prayāja* offerings and the like. To this, it is replied:

Although liberation has not been previously observed, nevertheless, because it—characterized as the Self abiding in its own nature through the destruction of ignorance along with its latent impressions—is established by scripture; and because the destruction of ignorance by the arising of knowledge is logically established, just as the delusion of a snake is destroyed by the direct perception of the reality of the rope due to ignorance being opposed to the arising of knowledge; and because, through positive and negative concomitance, it is established that the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration alone [leads to this].

Since it is established in the world that the fruit is the direct realization of one's own object, and since there is an inference based on the fact that even the immediate experience in the form "I am the single conscious self entirely free from all suffering" has hearing [the scriptures] and other practices as its means, hearing and the rest serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Moreover, it is not logical for something to have an unseen purpose when its purpose is already seen.

Furthermore, these [means of knowledge], being non-recurrent, are not capable of producing such an experience as the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) characterized by honor, long duration, and continuity.
Nor can a cognition that lacks direct realization here be fit to destroy ignorance which possesses direct realization.

Indeed, for one whose sense organ has been impaired by bile, the direct perception of bitterness in molasses cannot be overturned even by a thousand logical arguments without the direct perception of its sweetness. Even if such a person considers the words of others who possess that knowledge or reflects upon thousands of logical arguments, he will only spit out and discard the molasses. Thus, since meditation (*dhyāna*) and worship (*upāsana*) are understood from common worldly experience to involve internal repetition, it is established that repetition is indeed required. //1//
Having stated the purpose of the section, he raises an objection regarding its having the attributeless Brahman as its object:
"Here he says, 'Let it be so indeed'.
For the repetition of a cognition is meaningful when the experience is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), but not when it is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*).
For the experience of Brahman, which is the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of Brahman, does not transcend Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure.
And since the nature of the eternal Brahman is itself eternal, what purpose would there be here for the repetition of the mental state?
This is what has been stated:
Regarding the phrase "having become one's own self" (ātmabhūtam),
the objector raises a doubt:
"if [the word] is heard only once."
This is the intended meaning: the direct realization of Brahman as the Self does not destroy ignorance, because there is no contradiction between them, as it continues to coexist with that ignorance.
Or, if there were such a contradiction, then since that realization is eternal, ignorance would not even arise; how much less could it continue to coexist with it?
Therefore, for the sake of its cessation, a direct realization of that [nature] must be sought as something adventitious;
and thus, the persistence of the means of cognition becomes purposeful.
The objector stands against this by challenging everything previously stated.
"Nor even through repetition"— for indeed,

the cognition of the meaning of the *jyotiṣṭoma* injunction, even if repeated a hundred times, does not produce direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) as its means of valid knowledge regarding its own object;
for even if such [cognition] were produced, it would be merely intuitive (*prātibha*) due to its observed deviation from reality.
The realization of Brahman as the Self means the direct intuition (sākṣātkāra) of Brahman as the Self.
He raises an objection again: "Not merely the sentence."
The objector refutes this: "Even so, repetition is useless.
If a statement, depending on reasoning, is capable of producing direct realization, then repetition is unnecessary.
Because that [activity], having occurred once and being supported by reasoning, continues until the completion of what is to be done.
Again, he raises an objection: "But it might be argued... (athāpi syāt).
Reasoning and scriptural testimony do not have direct realization as their fruit, because that fruit belongs exclusively to the means of knowledge that is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Since those two, however, apprehend objects beyond the senses, they settle upon mere generalities (*sāmānya*) and do not directly realize the particularity (*viśeṣa*); therefore, repeated practice is cultivated for the sake of realizing that particularity.

For when that practice is pursued with reverence, over a long period, and without interruption, it becomes a firm foundation capable of bringing about the realization of the particularity—just as the mental cultivation of a woman leads to the arousal of passion in a lustful man.
The objector says: "No;
even not once."
Now, this direct realization must either have its source in scripture and reasoning, or its source in mere cultivation.
It cannot be that scripture and reasoning—which result in a cognition that is indirect and merely apparent—can produce the fruit of direct perception characterized by immediate realization.
Indeed, a banyan sprout does not arise from the seed of a *kuṭaja* tree.

And it has been stated that even a cognition arising from the culmination of the intensity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), though appearing as immediate (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*), is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its fallibility.
The objector concludes his own position:
"Therefore, if... [as in the phrase *tasmādyadi*].
The author states another objection to the previous argument: "Nor [is it possible] when [the means] have operated once" (na ca sakṛtpravṛtte).

Indeed, a certain person of pure being (*śuddhasattva*), like Vāmadeva while still in the womb, having heard, reflected, and concentrated for a moment, realizes the identity of the individual self (*jīvātman*) with Brahman.
"Even from that, repetition would be purposeless.

Therefore, since repetition is purposeless because there is neither apprehension nor non-apprehension of that which is partless—unlike the case of the manifest and unmanifest, or like the universal and particular, or like a ruby and so forth—he says:
"Moreover, [it has] many parts... (anekāṃśa).
He provides the solution: "To this it is said—it might be argued that [the scripture] would be purposeless due to repetition.

This is the intended meaning: it is true that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is not the immediate fruit of scripture and reasoning; rather, it is the mind itself, accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the knowledge of the meaning of reasoning and scripture, that becomes established in the direct realization of Brahman.
It stabilizes the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*).

And that [modification] is not invalid as a form of intuitive perception (*prātibha*), like the direct realization of fire derived through inference, because at that time the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire is not beyond immediate perception. However, there is always an immediacy regarding the nature of Brahman as it appears to the individual soul (*jīva*) when conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
for purity, enlightenment, and so forth do not in reality differ from that [Brahman].

Therefore, just as one who has acquired the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the practice of knowing the meaning of the science of music perceives with his own ear, through direct perception, the distinctions among the notes such as *ṣaḍja* and the various melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*), so too does one who has acquired the mental impressions from knowing the meaning of the Vedānta perceive the nature of Brahman in the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
This is the case for one to whom the statement "That thou art" has been uttered even once.
The meaning is: "having heard, reflected, and concentrated for a moment" due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by practice in previous births.
As for the phrase "he who is not able," the meaning is: one who is devoid of the practice of Brahman in previous births.
The point is this: it is not the case that what is perceived can be logically untenable.

Since even in the case of the meaning of a sentence—which appears as something beyond the senses—there exists a gradation of clarity and obscurity, then what need is there to speak of the gradation of clarity in the stream of cognitions that culminates in direct realization? This stream arises following reflection (*manana*), produced by the progressive intensification of the practice of meditative absorption (*ādhyāsanābhyāsa*).
What doubt, then, can there be regarding such a gradation of manifestation?
Thus, it has been stated that even regarding the meaning of a mere sentence, comprehension does not arise instantaneously.

However, the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) possesses word-meanings that are extremely difficult to grasp; therefore, it does not immediately lead to the knowledge of its own overall meaning preceded by the knowledge of the individual word-meanings.
Rather, he says that because the knowledge of the word-meanings is most delayed, the comprehension of the sentence occurs with extreme delay.
Furthermore, regarding this sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), it refers to the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (thou).

It might be argued: the meaning of a sentence consists in the connection between the meanings of its constituent words; therefore, since the determination of that [sentence-meaning] depends upon the cognition of the word-meanings, a sequential apprehension is logical.

However, Brahman—being partless and devoid of any distinct word-meanings with which it could be connected—would, according to whom’s sequence, have a sequential apprehension? It was already stated that it must either be grasped all at once or not grasped at all. To this, he says:
And although the Self to be realized is partless—

yet even though the Self is partless and directly perceived, it appears as if possessed of parts and as if entirely beyond perception through the successive removal of superimpositions such as the body and so forth.
Consequently, its realization as the meaning of a sentence is logically established as a process occurring in stages.

Is this cognition produced by the sentence itself [the means of knowledge] regarding the Self? If so, there would be no direct realization (*sākṣātpratīti*) of the Self, because this [cognition] has its fruit in the future.
To this he says: "But that is merely the prior form of the realization of the Self," meaning the realization characterized by direct perception.

This is what is meant: the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—which follows upon hearing and reflecting on the meaning of the sentence and possesses the three qualifications—is capable of bringing about the direct realization of Brahman; thus, the cognition of the sentence-meaning is the cause of direct realization.
Regarding the phrase "the prior form," he raises an objection:
"It is true that it is so."
For superimposition is sublated by the cognition of reality, but the cognition of reality is not [sublated].

Since the cognition of suffering and so forth arises in everyone at all times with respect to the self, it is correct because it is unsublated; thus, being powerful, it cannot be removed—this is the meaning. [The author] refutes [this]:
No;
for [the self-identification with the body and so forth] is like the conceit of being the body.
Indeed, a thing does not possess ultimate reality merely because it arises for everyone at all times.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the identification of the self with the body would be real; consequently, that too would arise for everyone at all times.
Furthermore, it has been stated in various places that this [identification] is sublated by means of reasoning; likewise, the identification with suffering and so forth is also sublated.
For suffering, grief, and the like cannot belong to a self whose nature is eternally pure and enlightened, since they are subject to arising and passing away.
Nor are phenomena [the nature of that], because it is illogical for things that are absolutely distinct from it to possess it as their nature;

for a cow is not the nature of a horse. Furthermore, the relation itself cannot withstand analysis, whether it be considered as distinct or non-distinct [from the relata], or whether it be considered as a relation or a non-relation.
Moreover, since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, they cannot coexist in a single locus.
Thus, all of this has been established in the second chapter.
This very point has been stated: "Because it is perceived as external to consciousness, just like the body and so forth."
And for this reason as well, he states that suffering and the rest do not have identity [with the Self]—
namely, "and in deep sleep, etc.
This might be so.

Why is the acceptance of repetition (āvṛtti) based solely on the purpose of experience, when by such injunctions as "it is to be seen, it is to be heard," repetition would be prescribed as having a subject matter other than that of the sentence "That thou art"? To this he says:
"Even there, not from the meaning of the sentence 'That thou art'.
In passages such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," a vision (darśana) directed toward the Self is enjoined.

Furthermore, no other vision of the Self is taught in the scriptures apart from that which is the subject of the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), such that what it begins with and what it concludes with would constitute the meaning of the sentence.
Since it begins with "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning" and concludes with "That thou art," that alone is the meaning of the sentence.
Therefore, by attempting to exclude [the primary meaning] from this and enjoin something else, you strike down the principal element with its own subordinate part.
For the bridegroom (*vara*), being the one intended by the action, is the primary recipient (*saṃpradāna*);
thus, they do not obstruct him with the act of marriage, which is a subordinate part of the ritual.

Now, since the sentence has the injunction as its primary focus, it does not have the established fact as its primary focus; rather, the established fact is made known as a subordinate element of that [injunction].

As they say while explaining the Śābara statement beginning with "For the injunction [makes known] what has been, what is being," etc.: "The injunction, while making known the object as something to be accomplished (kārya), makes known what has been and so forth as subordinate to that; and for one thus enjoined, there arises the thought, 'I am authorized in this.

Just as it has been established in the sūtra "But that [Brahman, because of the harmony of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*) that the Vedāntas, which terminate in an existent reality, do not have their purport in an injunction to action.

In this context, on the contrary, it is stated here as a mere supplementary argument that if [the mind] were established in injunction (*vidhi*), it would produce cognitions opposed to liberation, and thus its very nature would be to obstruct liberation. //2//
Nevertheless, people accept [the self] as "the Self" and cause others to grasp it as such.
Even though scriptural passages such as "That thou art" establish that the transmigrating soul possesses the nature of the Supreme Self,
there remains a sense of difference due to the association of contradictory attributes— such as being free from sin versus not being free from sin— which characterize those two respectively.

Because of the definitive conclusions and because of scriptural passages such as "That thou art," which can also be explained as being intended as instructions on symbols— just like "The mind is Brahman" and "The sun is Brahman"— this is indeed an instruction on a symbol.

Nor is it logical to argue that, just as the nature of a rope is enjoined with reference to the object present before one by restating its superimposed character as a snake, so too the state of being the Supreme Self is enjoined with reference to the individual self (jīva) which is of the nature of light;
for it is indeed logical that when an object present before one is perceived in a general form but not grasped in its specific details, there occurs the superimposition of another specific attribute.

In this case, however, since there is no aspect whatsoever of the luminous Self—which is a featureless universal and whose luminosity is not dependent on anything else—that remains ungrasped, what other specific attribute could be superimposed upon which ungrasped specific attribute?

Therefore, because the superimposition of the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) upon Brahman is impossible, it follows that the teaching "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is merely an instruction regarding a symbol (*pratīka*), such as "The living soul is the living soul; Brahman is Brahman.
This being the position reached, it is replied: Śvetaketu’s very Self is to be understood as the Supreme Lord; the Supreme Lord is not distinct from Śvetaketu.
For if there were a difference [between the two], it would result in the status of being secondary (gauṇatva), and it is not proper to accept a secondary sense when a primary one is possible.
Moreover, in the case of an instruction regarding a symbol (pratīka), a single utterance is perceived, as is the censure of the perception of difference;
for in the case of repetition, there is a multiplicity of meaning.
Being figurative does not consist in being extremely remote;
therefore, by examining the preceding and following passages, it is observed that the Śruti aims at the fact that the soul's identity with the Supreme Self is real.
It cannot be argued that the Śruti lacks authority here due to contradiction with other means of knowledge.
Furthermore, the fact that there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth has all been established in the first chapter.

Even though [the Self] is partless, because certain parts—as if it possessed parts—of this [Self], which consists of the manifold phenomenal world superimposed by beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*), its causal factors (*tattva*), and their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*), are not apprehended, there is what appears to be an error; however, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as "error" at all, nor is there anything called "saṃsāra."
However, we consider it logical that all this is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), as it is the locus of every kind of logical inconsistency.
With this intention in mind, it was said:
"If you are thus bound, there is no one who is not awakened."
