Others also say: "If you find satisfaction in non-duality, you are indeed liberated at all times.
This [verse] has a meaning distinct from the previous one. //3//
It is not [to be meditated upon] in a symbol, for that is not so.

For just as Brahman—whose nature is pure and liberated as taught in the scriptures—is to be meditated upon by the individual soul (jīva) precisely as the Self, in such passages as "I am Brahman" and "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," this is for what reason? Because the individual self is real in its form as Brahman, and because of the scriptural teaching that [Brahman] is non-dual.

Just as reflections of Brahman appear on the mirror of the individual soul's ignorance, so too, wherever there is an instruction for the perception of Brahman— such as "the mind is Brahman" or "the sun is Brahman"— in all such cases one should perceive "I am the mind" and so forth, [understanding] that Brahman possesses the status of the primary Self.
And it is logical that the mind and the other faculties possess identity with Brahman by virtue of being its modifications (*vikāra*),
just as jars, bowls, buckets, and the like— which are modifications of clay— possess the nature of clay. Thus,

since such symbolic instructions (*pratīkopadeśa*) are understood in some cases to involve the dissolution (*pravilaya*) of a particular modification, they have as their sole purpose the dissolution of the phenomenal world of duality (*bhedaprapañca*).

The answer is stated: Just as in passages such as "I am Brahman," the identity of the substrate of the ego with Brahman is taught, it is not the case that in passages such as "Mind is Brahman" the status of being the substrate of the ego is attributed to the mind and so forth;
rather, these are to be meditated upon as Brahman.

If it is argued that, since the locus of the *ahaṃkāra* is Brahman, one should meditate upon the mind and other faculties—which are to be meditated upon as Brahman—as being the locus of the *ahaṃkāra*, we say no;
for the word "I" (*aham*) is not heard in such contexts.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate the locus of the *ahaṃkāra* on the grounds of its identity with Brahman, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to meditate upon other modifications of Brahman, such as space (*ākāśa*), within the mind and other faculties—just as one might meditate upon their reflection.

Therefore, whatever has been enjoined as an object of meditation in its specific limited nature must be understood precisely in that limited nature, according to the maxim: "Whatever is stated [in the scripture] is to be accepted exactly as stated. Nothing more should be superimposed, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the purpose of the entire collection of scriptural passages is not the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

For if that were the meaning, the mention of "the mind" (*manas*) as a specific illustrative instance (*pratīka*) would be purposeless; one should have said "the universe" (*viśvam*), just as in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman.

Nor is it appropriate to take the mention of "mind" as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the whole, because when the primary sense of a word is possible, it is improper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, this is because [passages] such as "The sun is Brahman" would otherwise result in meaninglessness;
for it is not the case that the meditator [identifies] the symbols—
the mind and so forth— as the Self, whether through experience or by the authority of scripture.
The meaning is that neither of these two [conditions] exists;
for it would follow that there would be no substitute (pratīka).

Now, one might object: "Just as the limited ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is the locus of the 'I', becomes non-existent through its identity with the unlimited Brahman, so too will it be for the substitutes. To this, he says:
"And because of the destruction of the intrinsic nature of the name and so forth.
For here, the symbols (*pratīka*) are intended to be taught as the primary objects of meditation by virtue of being the locus of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*).
However, in passages such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the locus of the "I-consciousness" is not understood to be the object of meditation.

However, just as the true nature of the rope is made known by means of the description of the serpent, the dissolution of that which is limited and serves as the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is understood.

What follows from this being so? This follows: it is not logical for there to be the destruction of the primary remedial measures (*pratīka*), nor is the performance of the enjoined [meditation] possible upon their destruction.
Furthermore,
it is not because Brahman is the Self [that meditation on Brahman is enjoined].

For the injunctions for meditation do not form a single syntactical unit with the textual passages such as "That thou art," which are intent upon establishing the nature of the individual self (jīvātman) as being Brahman.

The meaning is this: since those [passages] belong to a different context, how could the view of the Self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) be assumed in the instructions regarding the viewing of Brahman (*brahma-dṛṣṭi*) through syntactical unity with them?
For in those cases, the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*), established according to worldly perception as the agent and enjoyer, is not Brahman;
thus, how could the view of the Self be taught in the instructions regarding the viewing of Brahman by identifying that [soul] with Brahman as its Self?
And for this reason, because of the similarity [of the worshiper] with the symbols (*pratīka*).

Although the worshiper, being the individual soul (*jīvātman*), is not a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman, whereas the symbols—such as the mind and so forth—are modifications of Brahman, nevertheless, due to its limited nature, the similarity of the individual soul with the symbols is to be understood. //4//
"The view of Brahman [is to be applied] because of its superiority.

Although grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible in both ways, nevertheless, because Brahman—being the supervisor of all—is the possessor of the fruit by virtue of its capacity to produce the fruit, it is primary; therefore, Brahman alone is to be refined by the views of the sun and so forth, and thus the views of the sun and so forth belong to Brahman itself.

The view of Brahman should not be superimposed upon the sun and other such objects. Furthermore, once the meaning of the scripture has been determined in this manner, the worldly maxim that "the inferior is [superimposed] upon the superior" does not prevail as a refutation; for that maxim is itself set aside due to its contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āgama*). This is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is true that Brahman alone possesses actual primacy everywhere, by virtue of being the presiding witness of all and the giver of the fruit; nevertheless, in accordance with the course of the words, the primacy of the ritual action itself is sometimes inferred.

As in such cases as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta svargakāmaḥ*) and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā sacrifice" (*citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ*),

it has been established that in all these instances, it is the deity propitiated by the sacrifice and other rites who bestows the fruit; nevertheless, because the action is understood from the words themselves to be the instrument (*karaṇa*), its predominance is indicated by its being connected with the fruit.
In some cases, it pertains to a substance (*dravya*), as in "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and so forth.
As it has been said: "In those cases where a substance is intended to be prepared, a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) is understood [as the primary object].
Thus, although in reality it is Brahman alone that bestows the fruit by virtue of being the presiding witness over all, nevertheless, the scripture—

It is declared that when a symbol (*pratīka*) such as the sun is meditated upon with the thought "this is Brahman," Brahman becomes capable of yielding the fruit; or alternatively, that Brahman itself is made the object of meditation by means of the thought "this is the sun" and thereby yields the fruit.
Since the bestowing of fruits is possible for Brahman—the overseer of all—in either case, a doubt regarding the meaning of the scripture is resolved in accordance with common worldly understanding.
This has been stated:
"Once the meaning of the scripture has been determined, it must be so.
Not only is worldly logic the cause for such a determination, but he says that the primary status of words such as "Āditya" as denoting their literal meanings is also a factor.
"And because of its primacy"—this [reasoning] also makes it understood that the word *brahman* possesses this same principle of priority.

For instance: just as words such as *āditya* (sun) function according to their own natural derivation (*svaravṛtti*) in their primary sense, so too will the word *brahman* function in its own primary sense, provided that its own primary meaning is intended here.

If it were so, the use of the word "iti" would be purposeless; therefore, having displaced its own primary meaning, the word "brahma" must be made to refer either to knowledge or to the essential nature [of the Self].
Furthermore, the word "brahma" does not denote objects such as the sun;
rather, this word "iti" refers to the very form [of the cognition], just as in the expression, "The gavaya appeared to me as a cow."

And thus, the meaning is that Āditya and the others are to be understood as Brahman; so he says: "Because of the word 'Brahman' being used in the sense of 'thus' (iti). The remainder has a self-evident meaning. //5// //
"And the notions of Āditya and so forth [are to be superimposed] upon the limbs [of the sacrifice], because that is logical;
or rather, the notions of the *udgītha* and so forth must necessarily be superimposed upon Āditya and so forth.

Even though Āditya and the others exist, since no fruit arises [from them alone], and since it is observed that only an action (*karman*) which possesses the capacity for production yields a fruit, action alone is fruitful.

And likewise, if the rites such as the Udgītha were to be made the objects of cognitions of the sun and so forth, then those forms of the rites would be overwhelmed by the meditations on the sun and so forth.
And in this way, how could a fruit arise from ritual forms that are merely false conceptualizations?

On the other hand, when the sun and so forth are meditated upon through the vision of the *udgītha* and so on, those suns and others—being meditated upon with the cognition of the *udgītha* and so on—are capable of yielding fruit because they are essentially of the nature of ritual action (*karma*).

For this very reason, the application of the terms *ṛc* and *sāman* to the earth and fire is appropriate, since the vision of the *ṛc* is superimposed upon the earth and the vision of the *sāman* upon fire.
Furthermore, if the fire were viewed in the *sāman* and the earth were viewed in the *ṛc*, the opposite would occur;
therefore, he says that this alone is logical: "And thus, this very one... [is the case].
He states another argument for the rebirth: "Moreover, in the worlds...
Indeed, this designation of the substratum is appropriate as an exposition of its being the object [of superimposition] only if the vision of Sāman is superimposed upon the worlds, and not otherwise.
He states the justification for the conclusion of the previous section regarding this very point: "And among those first mentioned... He now proceeds with the established doctrine (siddhānta):

"Only the conceptions of Āditya and so forth"—this means that if the conceptions of the *udgītha* and so forth were merely superimposed upon Āditya and the rest, then, because Āditya and the others are not themselves effects [of ritual action], the application of the conceptions of the *udgītha* and so forth would result in futility.

For nothing is produced by Āditya and the others such that it could become more powerful through knowledge; thus, the utility of the conceptions of Āditya and so forth as a means of refining (*saṃskāraka*) the *udgītha* and other elements is not established.
He objects: "Let it be so in the case of the fruits resulting from the perfection of ritual action (*karma*).

For let it be thus where there is a fruit of action; but where the fruit results from a quality (*guṇa*), since that quality is already established and not something to be produced, there is no such thing as "performing" it. In that case, what is the utility of knowledge (*vidyā*)?
This is the meaning. He refutes [this objection] with the words: "Even in those cases... (teṣv api).
A quality whose nature is already established is not sufficient for the production of an effect or fruit; let it not be that something unrelated to the action at hand produces some random fruit.

Therefore, since the fruit arises from that which is integrated with the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the action at hand, its capacity to produce a more potent result through knowledge is logically established by virtue of its being produced.
"And because the sun and so forth are of the nature of results.

Although there is no distinction between the sun and the *udgītha* insofar as both are modifications (*vikāra*) of Brahman, nevertheless, by virtue of being of the nature of results, the sun and others possess a distinction from the *udgītha* and so forth; this is the meaning.
He further states that the *udgītha* and so forth possess primacy because of their secondary designation:

And furthermore, [the word] "api ca" (moreover) is used because it is established that meditation itself, being an action (*karman*), possesses a fruit. Now, an objection has been raised: since the sun and other objects, which are superimposed (*adhyasta*) as already accomplished entities (*siddharūpa*), overwhelm the nature of actions as things to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpatva*), how can they be fruitful? To this, he says:

"And even for those things seen as the sun and so forth"— this would be so if the nature of the sequence were suppressed by another; however, it is not so here, just as the perception of fire in a boy [is secondary] because the boy-nature is not suppressed by some quality such as intensity, so it is here as well.
This cognition of fire is not like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, by which the nature of the boy would be overwhelmed;
rather, it is figurative (gauṇī).
Likewise, the intention is that this perception of the sun in the Udgītha and so forth is also figurative.
"Thus, the Sāman is superimposed upon this Ṛc"—this is the sense.
Even though the definition [of superimposition] could be established otherwise, there is no assumption of superimposition between the Ṛc and the Sāman as there is between the earth and fire;
rather, by examining the arrangement of the syllables, he says that it is actually the reverse.
"This very Ṛk" [is the meaning].
From the use of the accusative case in the statement, "One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds," it is understood that the Sāmans are the objects of meditation.
In that context, if the meditation on the Sāman were superimposed [upon the worlds], then it would not be the Sāmans that are meditated upon, but rather the worlds, such as the earth and so forth.
Thus, having abandoned the meaning of the accusative case, one might instead imagine the meaning of the instrumental case, as in "with the *sāman*.

The locative case in the word *lokeṣu* is somehow interpreted in the sense of the accusative—just as in the expressions "cows should be penned in the courtyard" (*akāre*) or "flowers [should be placed] on the cloak" (*prāvāre*). Since, according to the reasoning stated, the meaning of the locative must necessarily be imagined in both ways, it is better to follow the meaning of the accusative exactly as it is heard in the text.
The locative case is to be explained as having the sense of the instrumental.

It is thus determined: "One should meditate upon the Sāman, which is fivefold—consisting of the *hiṅkāra*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratīhāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*—with the thought that it is the world, the earth, and so forth.

But surely, where there is an indication of the accusative in both instances, as for example: "One should indeed meditate upon that very sun, which is sevenfold—consisting of the *hiṅkāra*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratīhāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*—as the Sāman"?
To the question, "What is the reason for this specific determination?
he says: "In that case also...

This means that because of the scriptural statement regarding Sāman as the object of meditation—namely, "there also is the meditation on the entire sevenfold Sāman"—the fivefold [Sāman] is likewise "excellent" (sādhu).
And its goodness is its very nature as Dharma; for thus says the Śruti: "The doer of good becomes good.

Since, when prescribing the meditation on Earth upon the mention of the syllable *hiṅkāra*, the expectation would have been "the *hiṅkāra* is Earth," there is this inverted instruction: "Earth is the *hiṅkāra*. //6//
[The meditation] is to be performed while sitting, because of the possibility [of it being so].

For in those cases where the ritual action is enjoined for one who is standing—since it is connected with the constituent parts of the rite—the meditations associated with that action must be performed by one who is standing;
but where [the action] is for one who is sitting, there the meditation also must be performed by one who is sitting.
Nor [is there such a rule] regarding right vision (*samyagdarśana*), because it depends upon the reality (*vastu*) and depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The determination of a reality depends upon the means of valid cognition, and the means of valid cognition does not depend on anything else; thus, even in that case, there is no fixed rule.
As for that which cannot be practiced without great effort, such as ritual counter-measures (*pratīkāra*) and the like—
Or, for example, even in the case of right vision such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*),
this reflection arises:

since there is no restrictive scripture regarding that [vision], when an absence of restriction would otherwise follow, it is established by the supplementary statement "as far as one is able" (*yathā-śakya*) that it belongs only to one who is seated.

Now, in which state is the term *dhyāti* (to meditate) used figuratively? Is it not the case that it does not apply to one who is standing? He says: "And one who is seated is free from exertion. The rest is clear in meaning. // 7 // // 8 // // 9 // //10 //
"Wherever there is one-pointedness, there [is yoga], because there is no distinction.

Since the rule regarding the place has already been established by such scriptural statements as "on even ground, clean, free from pebbles, fire, and sand," someone might raise the objection that rules concerning direction and location—though not explicitly taught here—are implied by the general principle governing the commencement of Vedic rites, just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east.
To favor such a person, the Teacher has stated this out of a spirit of friendship.
Wherever there is one-pointedness of mind, there alone one should apply the cultivation [of meditation], because there is no specific distinction.
For here there is no specific scriptural injunction, as there is in the case of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and others; therefore [it is so]. //11//
"Until the departure, for it is seen even there.
He analyzes the subject matter of the section:
"In that regard, as for those [meditations]... and so forth.
Regarding that realization of Brahman as the Self for which there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*):

a scripture (*śāstra*) indeed makes known the connection between a person to be enjoined and an injunction (*niyoga*) in the form of something to be accomplished; it also establishes that person’s qualification (*adhikāra*), characterized by mastery over that very action.

Since both of these [injunction and qualification] are supersensuous, they constitute the defining characteristic of scripture, because scripture is purposeful only with respect to what cannot be attained through other means of knowledge. However, this is not the case for the realization of Brahman-hood.
Since everything has been seen by one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is nothing here that remains hidden; what, then, can the scripture do in this regard?

One might object: even so, meditations (*upāsana*) have prosperity (*abhyudaya*) as their fruit, and since the relationship characterized by the injunction (*niyoga*) and the person enjoined (*niyojya*), as well as the relationship characterized by ownership (*svāmitva*), are supersensible (*atīndriya*), it would follow that once the purpose of the scripture is accomplished through a single performance [of the meditation], there would remain only the mere repetition (*āvṛtti*) denoted by the term "meditation."

When it is argued that cessation [of transmigratory existence] is attained merely by that much, since the purpose of the scriptures has been accomplished, we reply: according to such scriptural texts as "He becomes possessed of consciousness," where even those actions whose fruits are heaven and the like depend at the time of death upon the consciousness of heaven and so forth,
what need is there to mention the case of meditations (upāsanās) which have supersensuous fruits?

Indeed, those [mental states] will, by means of the very form perceived through the continuous flow of cognition directed toward their respective objects of meditation until the time of death, bring about that cognition at the moment of departure.
What is the need here for the postulation of a result-producing cognition at the time of death? For when a visible means is possible, it is not proper to assume an invisible one.
Therefore, the mental activity proceeds until the time of death.
This has been stated:
"But these are the notions" (pratyayās tv ete).
And thus says the Śruti regarding all objects of the senses: "In whatever manner one departs from this world with a certain resolve, with that very resolve one attains that world after death."
*Kratu* is a specific form of volition (*saṃkalpa*).
And the *smṛtis* have been cited [as sources]. //12//
Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-attachment and destruction of the subsequent and prior parts [of karma], because of the designation thereof.
The third section, concerning the domain of the means [to liberation], is concluded. Now, the investigation regarding the fruit pertaining to this chapter is being expanded upon.

In this regard, first of all, the following is investigated: upon the realization of Brahman—that is, when the knowledge of Brahman has arisen—does the evil karma that results in bondage, which is the opposite result to liberation (mokṣa) that is the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, perish or not? This is the doubt. What, then, is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)?

For that which is enjoined by the scripture for the sake of a fruit, and that which is prohibited for the sake of avoiding misfortune—such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin—possesses an intermediate operation consisting of the *apūrva*. How could that *apūrva* not persist until the experience of pleasure or pain, even when the ritual action has ceased? For in the absence of its cause of destruction, how could it possibly perish?
[This is] because it would entail the consequence of [the world's] being accidental and because it would contradict the scriptures.
If an action whose fruit has not yet been given perishes along with its *apūrva*, then the scripture that teaches the capacity of action alone to produce a fruit would become invalid.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that the knowledge of Brahman, like expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), destroys even those *karmāpūrvas* whose fruits have not yet been given.

This is because even expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are causes for the non-destruction of that [sin]; and since the prescription of such rites is justified merely by the fact that a person burdened with sin (*enasvin*) has become eligible [for them], it is illogical for them to imply the result of destroying previously accumulated evil. For this very reason, the traditional authorities (*smṛti*) declare: "Karma is not exhausted until it has been experienced. If, however, the injunction for expiation—which consists in being a required means—does not find completion merely through the acquisition of a specific person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then, when there is an expectation for what is required, it follows from the scriptural mention of its connection with a fault (*doṣa*) that it has the destruction of that [fault] as its result.
Even so,

there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the power of the knowledge of Brahman to destroy those [impurities] through conjunction with them, because liberation is not like that; for even that [liberation],
like the fruit of heaven and so forth, is logically possible only in dependence upon place, time, and instrumental causes.

On the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra-prāmāṇyāt*), that state will come to pass in which, through experience, the exhaustion of all karma will give birth to the knowledge of Brahman and liberation (*mokṣa*). Or else, by means of yogic powers (*yogarddhi*) in heaven, on earth, or in the intermediate space, the yogi—having fashioned many bodies and sense organs and having experienced the fruits [of his actions]—will, through the power of yoga, exhaust his karmas and become liberated. And since this matter is established by the force of reasoning, such designations as "like a lotus leaf" are intended solely for the purpose of praising the knowledge of Brahman.

When it is argued that [the scripture] must be explained [in this way], it is replied: such an interpretation would indeed be appropriate if there were a contradiction regarding the ritual action (*karman*), but no such contradiction exists.

For a scripture merely makes known the capacity of actions to produce their results; it does not, however, establish the absence of obstruction to those results by some adventitious cause, such as expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and the like. This is because the scripture remains indifferent toward such matters.

If the capacity of a [karmic] result to arise, as taught by the scriptures, is unobstructed by any adventitious action, then that result will indeed be produced, and there is no contradiction with the scriptures.
Furthermore, the traditional rule (smṛti) stating "an unexperienced karma does not perish" refers to actions whose capacity has been obstructed.

Moreover, there is an injunction for the destruction of defects through the higher knowledge (*aparavidyā*), similar to the performance of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*); this applies even to those who have attained lordship (*aiśvarya*), since there is no difference regarding the connection with both [the body and the senses].

Even in the case of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā*), where there is no explicit mention of defects, the capacity for their destruction and non-arising is determined simply by reflecting upon its true nature.

For it is not the case that a living being (*jīva*), whose delusions such as agency and enjoyership have been entirely wiped away by the meditative cultivation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) born from the contemplation of the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), would be unfit for the enjoyment of the fruit [of liberation].

Indeed, fear, trembling, and the like, which are caused by the superimposition of a snake onto a rope, do not persist once the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of the rope has occurred.
However, even though they persist for some time due to the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), they indeed cease.

Confirming this very point, designations such as "like a lotus leaf" and so forth, being consistent with their literal meaning, do not deserve to be explained away in any way as being merely figurative praise.
Now, was it not said that there will exist states of the individual self (*jīvātman*) in which, either through sequential enjoyment or through the power of yoga (*yogarddhi*)...?

Because one might think that a living being, by simultaneously creating various kinds of bodies through its power or by experiencing [results] without succession, would exhaust its karmas and thus become liberated, he says:
"And in this very way, liberation is possible."

For the latencies of karma (*karmāśaya*), which have been active since beginningless time and whose fruition is not fixed as to its timing, cannot be exhausted by enjoyment occurring in a gradual sequence;
for while he is experiencing one, he indeed accumulates further latencies of karma.
Nor is it reasonable that he will exhaust them through enjoyment that is not sequential, while remaining unattached and no longer accumulating other karmas.
Because of the capacity to experience now those [karmas] that were to be experienced sequentially over hundreds of kalpas,
how could karmas with long-term fruits be exhausted all at once?
Therefore, liberation is not possible in any other way.

An objection is raised: "Even though other latent impressions (karmāśaya) with results of pleasure and pain exist, after one has experienced the state of Brahman through the operation of that karma which yields the fruit of liberation, will one not then experience the fruits of other karmas whose ripening has been obtained? To this, he says: "And there is no dependence on place, time, or cause. This means: even if other karmas remain, they cannot obstruct the attainment of liberation because they lack the necessary conditions—namely, the specific place, time, and auxiliary causes required for their own fruition. Furthermore, since the realization of Brahman is itself the ultimate result, no other karma can take precedence over it. Thus, once the state of Brahman is realized, all other karmas are either exhausted or rendered incapable of producing further effects. Therefore, there is no possibility of experiencing the fruits of other karmas after liberation.
Liberation cannot be something that is produced as an effect, for liberation is the very nature of Brahman;
moreover, Brahman is not something that can be created, because it is eternal—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, it is because the fruit of knowledge cannot be something that is beyond direct perception.
Liberation is indeed accepted as the fruit of knowledge;
and the immediate fruit of knowledge is the manifestation of the object of knowledge (jñeya).
That very manifestation, by effecting the destruction of ignorance, conduces to liberation, which is characterized by abiding in the essential nature of the self that is Brahman.
For in this way, knowledge would have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*).

If it were assumed that the fruit of liberation results from knowledge through a succession of unprecedented (*apūrva*) deposits, then knowledge would have a non-evident fruit and thus possess a non-visible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). And the meaning is that when a visible result is possible, the postulation of a non-visible one is not logical.
Therefore, it is established that when Brahman is attained—that is, when the knowledge of Brahman exists and non-duality is realized—there is the destruction of evil deeds. //13//

The same lack of connection applies to the other as well; however, upon the falling away [of the body], there is no such obstruction for unrighteousness (*adharma*). Since unrighteousness is innate and rooted in passion and the like, its obstruction by scriptural knowledge of Brahman is logical.
But as for righteousness (*dharma*) and knowledge, because both are scriptural in nature, [there is no such obstruction].
Because of the contradiction between the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the relationship of the destroyed and the destroyer is not tenable [in their case].
Furthermore, since it is specifically heard in scripture that sin is to be destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman, dharma is not to be destroyed by it;
for it is established by worldly convention that a specific injunction necessarily implies the prohibition of everything else.
Just as when it is said, "Devadatta sees with his right eye," it is understood that he does not see with his left;
and as for the statement, "He indeed crosses over both of these," it applies according to what is possible—
namely, that one crosses over evil deeds through the knowledge of Brahman and good deeds through experience.

Regarding the general statement, "And his works are destroyed," because of the specific hearing of the word "all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*), it must be restricted to the specific sense of "evil works. Thus, when it is argued that through the knowledge of Brahman there is the destruction of evil deeds alone and not of good deeds, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) of the preceding section is extended [to this case]. Indeed, the knowledge of Brahman does not remove evil deeds by means of some unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*); rather, it does so through the very visible means of the dissolution of the enjoyer, the objects of enjoyment, and the act of enjoying. And this same principle applies equally to good deeds as well.
How could even this not destroy [the argument]?

And this being so, the mere similarity of being scriptural is not a cause for non-contradiction; for there is no lack of contradiction between water and fire merely because they share the common property of being perceptible.
Nor is the scripture concerning good deeds purposeless with respect to one who does not know Brahman, since its injunctions are meaningful for such a person.
This being the case, by the scriptural mention of "evil" (pāpman), merit (puṇya) must also be understood to be included;
for in comparison with the knowledge of Brahman, merit has an inferior fruit, since its result is subject to decay and excess.
Liberation is not like this, because it is unsurpassed and eternal.
Furthermore, this word *pāpman* (evil) is seen in the Veda as referring to both merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*).
For example, after enumerating merit and demerit [in the passage], it says: "thereby all evils (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*) are turned away from him.
Therefore, it is established that for both merit and demerit without distinction, there is non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*). //14//
But [the opponent argues that] only those [deeds] whose effects have not yet begun are destroyed, because that is the limit [of the scripture's teaching].

If, through the contemplation of the nature of non-dual knowledge, there is the non-clinging and destruction of both future and past good and evil deeds, then alas, there would be destruction without distinction between those deeds whose effects have begun and those whose effects have not;
for the dissolution of the agent, the object, and so forth is the same in both cases.
Furthermore, since destruction is based upon that [momentary nature],
there can be no persistence [of the entity] due to residual impressions, as in the case of the spinning of a potter’s wheel;
for persistence belongs only to a real entity.

Furthermore, for one who maintains that everything is mere illusion (*māyā*), since merit and demerit are produced as nothing more than illusion, when that illusion ceases, neither merit nor demerit exists, nor do their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) exist as real entities; thus, what could possibly persist?
Nor is it correct to argue that this is just like the case where fear, trembling, and so forth, produced by the delusion of a snake in a rope, continue even after the delusion has ceased.

For even in that case, although the snake is non-existent, the cognition of it remains; and because that cognition and the fear, trembling, etc., it produces, as well as their latent impressions, exist as real entities, they do not cease even when the delusion has ceased.
But in this case, since illusion (*māyā*) does not exist, nor its latent impression (*saṃskāra*), nor its object, what could persist because of its insubstantiality?

There is neither a remainder of impressions nor karma; thus, without distinction, there is the cessation of both those works whose effects have already begun and those whose effects have not yet begun.

Nor is it logical to wait for the body [to fall] on the grounds of the Śruti: "For him, the delay is only so long as he is not released from the body; then he will be merged. For this Śruti does not merely prescribe a difference in the limit [of time].
But "quickness" (kṣipratā) is the other [meaning].

Just as in common usage one says, "This long time of mine has been spent since I bathed and ate," for in that case, bathing and eating are not enjoined as the limits (avadhi), but rather the brevity [of the interval] is being demonstrated. [Otherwise], if both were enjoined...

For it might be argued that the sentence would be split because of the difference in limits and because of the state of being long-lasting; to this, it is replied: although the direct realization of the non-dual reality of Brahman, by its very nature as being opposed to the substrate [of ignorance] manifested by beginningless nescience, is opposed to all karma situated within that [substrate], nevertheless, it immediately destroys the collection of karmas whose fruition has not yet begun, but it does not destroy those whose fruition has already begun—that is, those which have produced a continuous flow of the experience of pleasure and pain extending over the span of a particular birth and lifespan, arranged in a sequence of prior and subsequent moments.
It is the collection of karma;
for that, by virtue of its active manifestation, is stronger than the others which have their functions dormant.

Otherwise, there would not be a long life for the divine sages such as Hiraṇyagarbha, Manu, Uddālaka, and others, whose mental constituents (*buddhisattva*) shine forth on all sides due to their intellects being freed from the veil of the entire web of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Moreover, it is heard in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that these [beings] possess knowledge of reality (tattvajñatā) and lives lasting for great kalpas, kalpas, manvantaras, and so forth. Yet, these are not of small intellect, nor do they wait for the enjoyment of all the fruits belonging to those [long lives], even though they have realized reality. The phrase "for just so long" does not enjoin a long duration; rather, having referred to the long duration established by another scriptural passage, it merely enjoins the limit of the fall of the body. Having this in mind, he says [the following] as a mere matter of propriety:
The Blessed One, the author of the commentary, says:
"First of all, [liberation] does not occur without depending on the latent deposit of karma whose effects have already begun.
And he states that it has never been observed that when one contradictory factor is present, another contradictory factor can persist: "Nor is this ever seen... and so forth.
"Even the realization of the non-agent self"—

for when even in the world the coexistence of two contradictory things is observed for some time, then, by the force of this very principle, it may occur for a long duration as well; it cannot be prevented,
because it is improper to subject what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to the demand for a further causal explanation (*niyoga-paryanuyoga*).
Thus, having established the position of the neutral party, he says to those who consider the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra) to be an authoritative source:
"Moreover, one should not dispute this at all.
Furthermore, the one of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña) is not a seeker (sādhaka), because his prior cognitions do not persist as higher and higher stages of meditation (dhyāna) progress.
But the one whose wisdom is established is unsurpassed;
he is indeed already perfected.
Furthermore, fear, trembling, and so forth, are not effects of knowledge.
Because [the effect] does not arise from mere cognition alone;
for it is the delimitation by the snake that is the cause of his fear, trembling, and so forth,
and since that [delimitation] is non-existent and indefinable, how could there be the production of an effect from a real entity?
Furthermore, even effects such as fear and trembling are not substantially real,
because they too cannot withstand analysis and are therefore indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
And there is no logical inconsistency in the arising of an indeterminable effect from an indeterminable cause.
For as is the Yakṣa, so is the offering; thus everything is clear. //15//
"But the Agnihotra and other such rites are indeed for the sake of that [knowledge], because it is so seen.
If both non-clinging and destruction apply even to merit, then alas, even the obligatory Agnihotra and other rites should not be performed by one desiring to ascend to Yoga,
since those too, like other merits, are destroyed by knowledge.
This is according to the maxim: "Indeed, it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.

Nor can there be no contradiction between knowledge and action on the grounds that they share the single purpose of liberation—as in the statement "they desire to know through sacrifice and giving"—because their simultaneous occurrence is impossible, and thus their having a single purpose cannot be established.

For this Self, belonging to one who knows It and for whom the delusion of the entire phenomenal world—including agency and so forth—has dissolved, neither prior nor subsequent merit produced by action is possible.

Therefore, the statement "they desire to know through sacrifice" is either a description of the present state or a mere praise of sacrifices and other means for the sake of knowledge of Brahman; it cannot be an injunction that prescribes sacrifice as a means to liberation for one seeking liberation.
To this, the following is said:
—True. It is not the case that ritual actions (*karman*) share a single purpose with knowledge (*vidyā*), because they are mutually contradictory and cannot coexist.
However, let it be granted that rituals which are remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) serve as a means to liberation by way of producing knowledge.
Nor is it the case that rituals, being contradictory to knowledge, cannot be causes of knowledge.
This is because effects that are opposed to their own causes are frequently observed.
Thus, it is meaningful to undertake even those karmas that are to be destroyed by their effects, since they serve as the means for the effect characterized by knowledge;
for in the absence of those [karmas], their effect would not arise, and liberation would be impossible.

And thus, regarding the statement "they desire to know through sacrifice," since the optative suffix (*pañcamalakāra*) conveys a new meaning— that knowledge has sacrifice as its means— it will not be explained as having an entirely remote application or as being merely for the purpose of praising knowledge. With this intention, it has been stated:
For just as knowledge itself, being the means of attainment, is figuratively described as the cause of liberation through its channel [of action], so too is action.
Precisely because action does not exist at the time of the arising of knowledge, nor even subsequently, but only prior to knowledge,
it is for this very reason that this statement regarding the identity of their effects refers to a subject matter that has already passed.
He clarifies this very point: "For [it is] not [the case that] the knower of Brahman... //16//
In order to introduce another Sūtra, he asks:
"But what is the subject matter of this? The following Sūtra is the answer to this.
For some, moreover, there is another [view] regarding both:

the statement concerning the destruction [of karma] refers to optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), and the scriptural statement from another recension, "his sons inherit his property," [refers to obligatory rites]. //17//
"For that which is indeed by means of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.11):
for there is sacrifice and so forth conjoined with knowledge, such as "He who, knowing thus,
should sacrifice," and there is also [sacrifice] alone.

In this regard, just as when it is stated, "one should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa," there is the acquisition of a specific distinction—namely, that one should give it to a learned Brāhmaṇa and not to a mere nominal Brāhmaṇa who is ignorant—for what reason? Because of his excellence; likewise, sacrifice and other rites devoid of knowledge are surpassed by those accompanied by knowledge. Therefore, only that [sacrifice accompanied by knowledge] serves as a means to higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) by way of destroying acquired demerit (*upātta-durita-kṣaya*), and not this [other kind].

Consequently, even though the scripture stating "they desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) mentions no specific qualification, it must be applied to sacrifices and the like that are accompanied by knowledge.

To this, it is replied: Since the word "more" (*taratama*) is heard in the scriptural statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful for him," it is understood that even one devoid of knowledge possesses a degree of power;
however, such power is not possible for one who is entirely incapable of action.

Therefore, it is established that even for one who possesses this [lower knowledge], there is some degree of utility for the production of higher knowledge; thus, sacrificial rites and the like, though devoid of [higher] knowledge, must be performed by one seeking higher knowledge. //18//
"But having exhausted the others through experience, he attains [Brahman].
By this sūtra, the author shows that the purpose of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the phrase "those whose effects have not begun" (*anārabdhakārya*) is their cessation through experience.
However, the proof for this has already been provided by drawing it forward from earlier; therefore, it is not repeated here for fear of redundancy. //19//
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakabhagavatpādabhāṣya* composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra.
The Second Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya:
"Speech [is merged] in the mind, because of perception and because of scripture.

Now, one might object that this discussion—beginning with "speech is merged in the mind"—is irrelevant to this section characterized by the investigation of the fruits [of knowledge]; therefore, he says:
Now, regarding the phrase "for the attainment of the fruits in other sciences":

since the departure [of the soul] has as its purpose the path of the gods (*devayānamārga*) for the sake of attaining the fruits of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), the inquiry concerning that [departure] constitutes an inquiry into the fruit by way of a traditional sequence; thus, it is not irrelevant. An objection is raised: "But this sequence of departure is not possible for the knower (*vidvas*), because of the scriptural statement, 'His vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart; they are merged right here. How then can there be an inquiry into this [topic] under the heading of knowledge? To this, he says:
"For the learned and the ignorant are indeed equal"—
thus he states the subject matter with the words "it exists."
He reflects:
"What is here? *viṣaya* means doubt (*saṃśaya*).
He states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
"In that regard, speech alone... This refers to the doubt arising from the conflict between direct scriptural statement (śruti) and figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Having completed the sūtra of the established doctrine, he recites it:
"The function of speech merges into the mind.
He states the purpose for supplying the word "function" (vṛtti) by means of a question.
"How so?"— the meaning is that this is supplied by reflecting upon the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*).

For if one intends to speak of the dissolution of the reality (*tattva*) or of the substratum (*dharmin*), then since there is equality of non-distinction (*avibhāga*) everywhere— in both this world and the next— why would it specify "non-distinction" only for the next world and not for this one as well?
Therefore, it is understood that here the author of the Sūtras intends to express merely the withdrawal of the functions [of the organs] without distinction, as they are not differentiated here.
He states the reason for this established conclusion (siddhānta) by means of a question: "Why? (kasmāt).
Because we observe the withdrawal of the function of speech only when the function of the mind is present,
the non-observation of the withdrawal of speech cannot even be made known by scripture;
moreover, it contradicts the reasoning that originates from scripture.
For scripture, following observed experience, teaches the dissolution of modifications into their material cause (*prakṛti*).
Now, speech (*vāk*) is not the material cause of the mind (*manas*), such that this [speech] would dissolve into it.
Therefore, with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the function and that which possesses the function, the word "speech" (*vāk*) should be explained as referring to its function.
And it is possible for the dissolution of the mental modification (vāgvṛtti) to occur even in the mind, which is not the material cause of speech;
for this is seen in various instances. Thus he says:
"The emergence and suppression of modifications. (1)
And for this very reason, all [the senses] follow [the mind].
Since there is no relation of material cause and effect between the mind and speech, it is not the dissolution of the essence of speech into the mind, but rather the dissolution of its function;

and for this same reason, when the mind still possesses its functions, the functions of all the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, follow into dissolution within the mind, but not the dissolution of their own essential nature.
The separate mention of "speech" (vāk) in this sūtra is with reference to the examples in the preceding sūtra; it does not mean that speech alone is intended here. This is the meaning. //2//
"That mind [merges] into breath, because of the subsequent [scriptural statement].

If the dissolution of an effect occurs into its own material cause, then in the case of the statement "the mind merges into breath," it must be understood that the very nature of the mind itself merges into breath;
for in this way, the designation "mind" will not be an interpretation based on figurative usage.
For the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is indeed possible between breath and mind;

for the scripture states that the mind consists of food (*anna-mayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*), declaring the nature of the mind to be food, and that breath consists of water (*āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ*), declaring the nature of breath to be water.
This is because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between a material cause and its modification.

And thus, since it is established that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the material cause (prakṛti) of the mind (manas), it follows that the mind, which possesses mental modifications (vṛtti), is dissolved into the vital breath; to this, it is replied: True, from the scriptural text "The waters created food," the relationship of material cause and effect is understood between water and food.
However, it does not apply to the vital breath and the mind, which are themselves effects of those two.

If one were to accept a relationship of cause and effect between the two modifications through the channel of the *khayoni* (the source of space), there would be a confusion of categories leading to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, that which is the direct modification of something else dissolves into that very thing; thus, food dissolves into water, but the mind—which is a modification of food—does not dissolve into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a modification of water.

Likewise, in this case as well, it is established that the mental function (*manovṛtti*) dissolves into the vital breath, which is the substrate of the function, but the mind, which possesses the function, does not [dissolve] there. //3//
Therefore, [the breath] rests in the presiding [deity], because of its approaching that [deity] and so forth.

Since the word "heat" (*tejas*) denotes a specific element and is not established as referring to the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), and since the scriptural accounts of the breath's approaching, following, and abiding in the individual soul (*jīvātman*) are also consistent with its merging into heat, the breath indeed has its function completed within heat.

However, since the function [of fire] has entered into the individual soul (jīvātman), it is logical that the vital breath (prāṇa) has its function entered into the individual soul by way of that [fire].

Therefore, when the position is reached that the dissolution of the function of the vital breath occurs in fire itself, it is stated in reply: that aforementioned vital breath abides in the presiding conscious self (vijñānātman) and its function becomes dependent upon that [self].
From what [reasons]? From the reasons consisting of approach (*upagama*), following (*anugama*), and abiding (*avasthāna*).
Regarding that, he states the scriptural passage concerning approach:
"In this very way, this Self... and so forth.
He states the scriptural passage concerning following [the departing soul]: "As he departs...
He states the scriptural passage concerning remaining [in the body]:
"And it becomes endowed with consciousness" (*savijñāno bhavati*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that by which one perceives; it is the aggregate of the sense organs together with the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*). One who abides together with that is "endowed with consciousness. [The opponent] objects:
"Is it not heard in the scripture that fire resides in the nose?
This is an interpolation, an explanation of a meaning not expressed by the words [of the text]. He refutes this:
This is not a fault.
Although it is understood from the passage "the vital breath [merges] into heat" that the function of the vital breath merges into heat,

nevertheless, because the meditations taught in all the Vedic branches are identical, an examination of other scriptural passages leads to the understanding that the merger occurs in the cognitional self (vijñānātman).

Nor is it correct to say that there is a dissolution of fire even there [in the self], because it is understood from scripture that its dissolution occurs in the Supreme Self through the sequence of air and space.

Therefore, by the mention of "fire," the individual soul (jīvātman)—who is the presiding lord over the subtle elements of the five gross elements that constitute the seed of the body accompanying fire—is indicated; thus, the function of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti) also merges into him.
He objects: "But surely this is a scriptural statement.
The meaning is: let the elements associated with fire be indicated by the word "fire," but what does that have to do with the presiding deity (adhyakṣa), since it is not associated with those?
He refutes [this objection]: "That [breath] is the presiding deity (adhyakṣa); thus, [the statement applies] even to the presiding deity.

For when this breath, having reached the presiding deity in the intermediate state, reaches the subtle elements such as fire and the rest precisely through its contact with the presiding deity, then it is appropriate that "the breath is the self."
Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration:
"Even one who [comes] from Srughna," etc. (4).
He asks in order to introduce another Sūtra: "How [is it] in those things accompanied by fire? [The answer is:
"Because they do not indicate [the presence of fire] in a single [instance]."
In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya states the view regarding inference:
"of the effect, which is the body.
The meaning is that just as the gross body is, so too the subtle body to be inferred must likewise consist of the five elements.
He explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "darśayataḥ" (they show): "And they show this meaning.
The dual number is intended either to refer to the question and the answer, or to refer to Śruti and Smṛti.
"The subtle particles (aṇvyo mātrāḥ) are the minute portions of the five elements" (pañcabhūtānām).
He raises an objection regarding a contradiction with another scriptural passage: "But [what about] when speech and the other organs have been withdrawn? etc.
The meaning is that it is understood as having action (*karman*) as its substratum, not as having the primary elements (*bhūta*) as its substratum. He provides the rebuttal: "To this, it is said."
The *grahas* are the sense organs (*indriyas*), and the *atigrahas* are their respective objects.

There is no contradiction in this, for [the senses] are the substratum of actions by way of being their instigators (*prayojakatva*), whereas the elements (*bhūtas*) are the substratum by way of being their material cause (*upādānatva*).

Furthermore, he says that even the term "praise" (*praśaṃsā*) expresses the preeminent status of the substratum of actions as their instigator; for such praise is appropriate only when there exists another, inferior substratum.
And because of the word "praise" (praśaṃsā) in that context. //6//
"And [the path] is common up to the commencement of the journey, and immortality is attained without having burned away [the body].

Here, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) belongs to one who considers that this refers to the possessor of higher knowledge (paravidyā), because of the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of immortality. "Of those who are perplexed" means of men who are doubting.
He objects: "But surely [this occurs] in the context of knowledge (vidyā). He replies:
"Not like sleep and so forth":

in order to describe the state of attaining immortality through higher knowledge alone, other states that share its characteristics as well as those that differ from it are also described in accordance with it;
for by means of both similarity and difference, the understanding of the subject matter intended to be explained becomes much clearer.

However, it is not the case that ignorant persons, being superior to the knower, are enjoined such that they would be explained within the context of knowledge; rather, these are restatements (anuvāda) of things well-known in the world, made for the purpose of establishing knowledge in accordance with them. This being the position reached, it is replied:
And this departure, beginning with "Speech [merges] into Mind" and so forth, is the same for both the knower and the ignorant.
Why? Because it extends up to the commencement of the journey (āsṛtyupakrama).

The "path" (*sṛti*) is the proceeding by way of the path of the gods (*devayāna*), which is the attainment of the world of the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahmaloka*) until the end of the cycle, that is, until the attainment of the world of the effected Brahman. This is the commencement, the beginning, or rather the effort regarding knowledge.
Therefore, this is what is being said: this is not the supreme knowledge (*parā vidyā*), because it relies upon the door of the channels (*nāḍī*).
However, this is lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*).
In it, there is no ultimate burning away of the afflictions (*kleśa*), such that there would be no departure [from the body] therein.

Therefore, by the power of lower knowledge, for the sake of human purpose, one who desires immortality—which is a state of merging with the elements in a relative sense—is subject to this instruction on the commencement of the path characterized by various forms of departure.
The form *upoṣya* is derived from the root *uṣ* meaning "to burn," preceded by the prefix *upa*. //7//
"Until then, because of the designation of transmigratory existence.
Having established that the departure of both the knower and the ignorant consists in their attaining the Supreme Self while a residue of the seed-state remains,
that very point is now being considered.

Is "merging" (saṃpatti) the actual dissolution of the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), such as fire and the rest, into their own causal essence within the self, or is it the remaining in the state of a seed?
If the former position is held,
there is no departure (utkrānti).
Now, as for the subsequent [verse], "Then she [becomes] that":

in that case, there is no dissolution of the reality of the modification into its material cause, as there is not, for example, of speech and the other organs into the mind. And since the Supreme Deity is the material cause of everything that is born, it would follow—given the position that the dissolution of fire and the rest is merely the dissolution of their reality—that this dissolution is absolute. To this, it is replied: "Some enter the womb... [etc.].
For the sake of obtaining a body,
embodied beings follow after the stump [of rebirth] according to their karma and according to their learning.

Thus the Śruti teaches that for one possessed of ignorance there is transmigratory existence (saṃsāra); this [teaching] is not tenable if there is an absolute dissolution of reality. Nor is it correct to say that this is merely the power of the time of death (*prāyaṇa*) with respect to either the knower or the ignorant; for otherwise, [the text would have said] "everyone [attains liberation] at the very moment of death. Thus he says: "Otherwise, indeed, everyone... and so forth.

The scripture of injunctions concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices would be useless, because there is no further rebirth after death due to the absolute dissolution [of all things]. Likewise, the scripture on liberation would be useless, since every living being would attain liberation effortlessly simply by virtue of death. He states that not only would the scriptures be rendered purposeless, but liberation through mere death is also illogical: [He says: "Furthermore, it is unreasonable that liberation occurs merely upon death."
Regarding the phrase "false knowledge" (mithyājñāna):
the meaning is that as long as the cause [of suffering] is not pacified, the pacification of that which possesses it is not possible. //8//

Now, one might ask: why is that fire, accompanied by the other elements, which serves as the substratum for the individual soul (jīva) and moves from this body to another upon departing, not perceived by us?

For it ought to be perceived because it is either large in dimension or composed of multiple substances and possesses color; and why is it not obstructed by other material objects? To dispel this doubt, the following Sūtra is stated:
"And it is subtle because it is perceived as such by its measure.
The word "and" (ca) is displaced in the sequence;
it means that it does not remain [in the body] merely until the end of life.
And that [air] is subtle both by its very nature and by its dimension; for its nature itself is such that it is invisible.

Just as the visual light, though large, has its color and touch unmanifest due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), so too is its subtlety in dimension because it is not perceived—just as motes of dust (trasareṇus) are not perceived except through the rays of the sun entering a lattice window. Thus he explains that its perception occurs through measurement.
For it is said: "Thus, the exit through the channels.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the exit through the eye, or the head, or from other parts of the body is included.
He states the reason for its being unimpeded:
"And because of its transparency.
This too is indeed included within subtlety itself.
For just as a piece of glass or a layer of clouds does not obstruct light, which is transparent by nature.
In this way, the entire collection of things belongs to him. //9//
Therefore, there is no crushing [of the Self] because of this very subtlety, which is characterized by transparency and is synonymous with non-attachment. //10//
And for this very reason, there is this "heat" (ūṣman).
"Reasoning" (upapatti) means logical proof.

This is what is meant: through the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of heat with what is seen and heard, it is established that there exists a certain subtle body distinct from the gross body. //11//
If it be argued that [the Self] is denied [to be the agent], we say no, because of the reference to the embodied self.
He states the purport of the section:
"Because of the qualification, 'having remained here without eating, one attains immortality.'"
He states the subject matter:
"Now, one who is without desire" (*athākāmayamānaḥ*).
Having raised an objection regarding the position of the Siddhāntin, the Pūrvapakṣin refutes it and establishes his own view.
"Therefore, because of the negation concerning the subject matter of higher knowledge" (Brahmasūtra 4.2.12).

For this would be appropriate if the Śruti were to negate the departure from the gross body of the individual self (jīvātman), which is characterized by the subtle body and identified with the vital breath (prāṇa);
however, that is not the case.

For by the pronoun "from that" (tasmāt), which refers to the primary subject, it is the embodied being (dehin)—the subject under discussion regarding worldly prosperity and the supreme good—that is denoted.
Thus, it is understood that from that embodied being the subtle body (the *liṅga-śarīra*) does not depart; rather, it is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) alone who departs together with it.

Furthermore, having traversed the circle of transmigratory existence up to Hiraṇyagarbha through the *brahmanāḍī*, the individual soul (*jīva*), still accompanied by its subtle body (*sa-liṅga*), merges into the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, for the knower, there is no departure even toward the highest deity.
Thus, it follows that the scriptural texts concerning the path and the traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding Śuka, who desired liberation, demonstrate his departure from the solar orb. //12//
This being the case, it is replied:
"For [the departure] is clear for some.
This is not a prohibition against the embodied soul being the material cause of its own departure.
Rather, it concerns the departure from the body.

For instance, in response to Ārtabhāga’s question, having first adopted the position that there is no departure for the transmigrating individual self (*jīvātman*), [the text] itself raises the objection, "In that case, this person would not be dead, because the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) have not departed," and then [proceeds to explain] the dissolution of the vital breaths.

Having made that promise, in order to establish it, he speaks of swelling and inflation as the limits of the departure; by mentioning whose swelling and inflation, he indicates that those [limits] belong to that [entity].
And since "those two" refer to the body, it is understood that the body itself is the point of departure (*apādāna*).
[Objection: "Granted that this may be so for the ignorant transmigrating being, but what follows for the knower? To this he says:
"On account of its similarity to that" (*tatsāmānyāt*). [Objection:
"In that case, since the body was referred to as the primary object by the pronoun *tat*, how can there be an understanding of the body here? To this he says:
"Because of its commonality with that.
Now, one might object: "In that case, since the embodied self (dehin) was referred to by the pronoun as the primary subject, how can there be an understanding of the body here? To this, he says:
"By means of metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra)."
In the reading with the ablative case (*pañcamī*), it should be explained that by the pronoun which refers to the "embodied one" (*dehin*), the body itself is what is being referred to.
However, in the reading with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), there is no such figurative usage; thus he says: "But for those [who read] the genitive."
Moreover, a prohibition applies to that which has already been established, not to that which has not been established.

Since the departure from the body is observed in the case of the ignorant, it follows by analogy that such departure from the body might also apply to the wise; thus, a prohibition is appropriate. However, no departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) with the individual soul (jīva) as their limit has ever been observed anywhere, such that it would need to be prohibited.

Furthermore, he says—“And for the knower of Brahman”—to show that because there is no destination for one whose entire appearance of the phenomenal world has been wiped away by *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) born from the cultivation of non-duality, there is no going.
The construction is: “Even for the gods who seek a place on the path, [there is none] for the knower of Brahman, who is himself placeless.”
He objects: "But is not motion also [a cause]? He replies:
This [attainment] belongs to one who is still embodied, by means of the power of yoga—that is, by the power of the lower knowledge (aparavidyā). //13//
Regarding those [elements], others [hold a different view]; for it has been said:
"This undertaking is intended to remove the doubt arising from the conflict between the scriptural texts concerning their establishment and their dissolution.
Furthermore, those [elements] consist of the eleven organs denoted by the word *prāṇa*, as well as the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
"For one who knows Brahman, [the dissolution occurs] in that very Supreme Self.
He states the doubt that serves as the seed for the subsequent discussion: "But have not the *kalās* already gone [to their source]?"
The number fifteen was stated with the intention of asserting that the nose and the mind are of the same nature.
Here, he states the absence of contradiction by means of the established distinction between the objects of the two scriptural passages: "That indeed... and so forth.

Worldly usage is conventional. This scriptural statement depends upon conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*), not upon ultimate means of valid cognition (*tāttvika-pramāṇa*).
But the other [scriptural passage], beginning with "Thus indeed is he perceived by him," depends upon the realization of the wise and thus depends upon ultimate means of valid cognition.
Therefore, because the objects of the two scriptural passages differ, there is no contradiction between them. //15//
There is no division [of the soul], because of the scriptural statement.
When the cause ceases, that which is caused by it must cease absolutely.
And since division is caused by ignorance, once ignorance has been destroyed root and branch by knowledge, that division cannot remain with any residue.
Nevertheless, this Sūtra [is composed] to remove even the slightest suspicion of "having a remainder" (sāvaśeṣatā) based on the commonality of dissolution. //16//

Then, with its upper opening blazing, the door being revealed by that [light], and by virtue of the power of knowledge (vidyā) as well as through the application of recollection of the path which is a remnant of that [knowledge], he—favored by Him who dwells in the heart—departs by means of the hundred-and-first [vein].
Thus far, the departure of both the knower of the lower knowledge and the ignorant person has been described.
In this regard, does both the knower and the ignorant depart from the head and other locations without distinction, or does the knower depart specifically from the location of the head?

But others say "from other places. Here, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) belongs to one who does not perceive the power of knowledge (*vidyā*). For that [self], which has withdrawn the aggregate of speech and the other organs and desires to rise up, the "abode" (*oka*) or "dwelling place" (*āyatana*) is the heart; its "tip" (*agra*)—
That which is its "blazing" is the illumination of the door and the opening of the exit; the wise man departs from the very place of the head, not from other places such as the eyes and so forth.
Why? Because of the power of knowledge—that is, because of the power of the knowledge of the Heart (Hārdavidyā).
For the instruction on the heart-vidyā is for the sake of attaining the supreme station;

and if one does not depart from the station of the head, there is no attainment of the supreme place. Now, [the author] asks: why is it that even while departing from other stations, one does not attain the supreme world? To this he says:
And because of the practice of recollecting the path that remains after that [attainment].
For the channel leading to the crown of the head is taught as the means for departure, being a remnant of the knowledge of the Heart (Hārdavidyā).

Indeed, by the repeated cultivation of that [path], this individual soul (jīva)—graced by the Brahman well-worshipped within the Heart and recollecting It—attains Its nature and departs through that very channel at the crown of the head, which exceeds the hundred [channels].

For the radiant Brahma-nāḍī has emerged from the heart; having pierced the root of the palate and reached the crown of the head, it becomes one with the rays [of light] and enters the solar orb. For one who practices that [nāḍī], there is an exit through it alone at the time of death. //17//

"Following the rays": whether by night or by day, without distinction, being one who follows the rays, he reaches the solar orb; this is the proposition of the established conclusion (siddhāntapakṣa). //18//
He raises the prima facie objection with a portion of the Sūtra:
"If it be said, 'Not at night'";
and he refutes it with another portion of the Sūtra.
He shows that this connection does not persist as long as the body exists, because it is understood from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, scripture (*śruti*) also demonstrates this point in its entirety:
"From yonder sun the rays extend; they enter into these channels (*nāḍī*); and from these channels they extend forth."
Those rays that have entered into that sun are not spread out [there],
because effects such as heat and so forth are observed;
by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), the moon and water are included.
Indeed, the moonlight consists of the rays of the sun as they become connected with the moon, which is composed of water;
therefore, there is also the movement of solar rays at night.

As for those who say—on account of the independent scriptural statement, "He would reach the sun in as much time as it takes to think"—that when one has died at night, there is no dependence on the rays.
He replies to them:
"And if [it is said] that one is a *preta* at night"—
for students do not study this with such specific qualification.
But as for those who think that even a wise man does not ascend upwards due to the fault of dying at night, [the author] says in response: "But even the wise man...
Knowledge, being enjoined with a connection to a result as if it were obligatory (*nitya*), is not properly understood to have a merely optional (*pākṣika*) result.
Anticipating the view of those who claim that for a learned person who dies at night there is a dependence on the day until reaching the solar orb, he says:
"Even if [he dies] at night. By the connection with the words "as far as... so far," it is heard in scripture that the journey is independent [of time].
Nor can dependence be understood, because it would contradict the syntactic connection [of the words]. //19//
"And therefore, even during the southern course [of the sun].
He says this to refer back to the reason already stated: "And for this very reason, because waiting is not possible."
He states the seed of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) as follows:
"The excellence of dying during the northern course of the sun" (uttarāyaṇamaraṇaprāśastya). He states the refutation (apanoda) as follows:
This refers to the "establishment of excellence.

Therefore, by the force of the reason implied by the word "ataḥ" (therefore), the death of the ignorant person during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*) is praised, whereas for the wise person, there is no distinction between the two times due to the power of their knowledge.

Furthermore, even the fact that the wise Bhīṣma waited for the northern course serves to establish the practice of the ignorant, according to the maxim: "Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do."
Furthermore, the scriptural passage beginning with "From the fortnight of the waxing moon" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5) does not aim at establishing a specific time;
rather, as will be explained later, it establishes the deities who act as guides (ātivāhikīr devatāḥ).
Therefore, there is no contradiction. //20//
He raises an objection in order to introduce another Sūtra: "But [is it not so] at the time when...
The meaning is that here it is *time* itself that is spoken of as the primary factor, and not the *ātivāhikī* deity.
And with respect to yogins, this is recorded in Smṛti; these two [fire and light] belong to Smṛti.

The application of different times belongs to Smṛti in relation to the meditative practice (upāsanā) recorded in Smṛti, due to proximity, but not in relation to that which is recorded in Śruti—this is the meaning.

Here, if there is an injunction regarding different times in Smṛti and an injunction regarding fire, light, and so on in Śruti, then it has been stated that there is no contradiction because of the distinction of objects, since fire and the others function as conducting deities (ātivāhika).

Now, as for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*): even so, in the passage "where time," by means of the designation of time, it is precisely the *ativāhika* deities that are spoken of; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. //21//
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Bhāmatī, a commentary on the Śārīrakabhāṣya, composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra.
The third section of the fourth chapter:
"By the path beginning with light, because that [immortality] is well-known [therein].
Because they reside in different contexts and because they involve different forms of meditation, [the paths are distinct].
The path is independent of one another, due to both speed and determination.

Considering that movement along a crooked path toward a single city implies a faster movement along a straight path, one might suppose there is haste; yet, if there were only one path, in relation to what else could there be haste? Furthermore, the restrictive phrase "by those very rays" would be untenable, as there would be no other path to be excluded; therefore, it is independent of anything else.
