It might be argued that these paths, being means for attaining the single world of Brahman, should be treated as alternatives, like rice and barley; to this, it is replied:
although the path is one, because multiple stages are possible within it, there is no multiplicity [of paths] due to the complexity [involved], as evidenced by the mark of recognition.

For a path consisting of stages leads one to a single destination, such as a city, and not one that is without parts. In this regard, there arises a doubt: do these—the rays, the day, the wind, the sun, and so forth—being stages of the path, constitute a single path; or rather, do they divide the path according to their respective natures? To this, [the answer is]: since it is possible for a division of parts to exist even within a path that is not itself divided, it is not appropriate to postulate a division of the whole (the path) itself.
Because it would entail [the fault of] excessive complexity (*gaurava*),
and because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is established through the recognition of a single part, there is no need to postulate multiple paths.

Furthermore, as for the restrictive expression "by these very rays," it does not serve to exclude other things, because that would contradict other scriptural passages which establish those very [other things].
Therefore, it must be stated that this [particle] determines its independence from others.
Furthermore, a single sentence is not capable of two purposes—namely, establishing a path not previously reached and demonstrating its independence;
thus, it is logical that the particle *eva* merely reiterates the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), which is already established by the force of the injunction itself.
And as for the mention of "speed":

indeed, speed is not conceived with respect to a single destination while taking into account different paths; rather, its occurrence is possible even due to a difference in the destinations themselves.
Just as one says, "Caitra goes quickly from Kaśmīra to Mathurā," so too here, it means that by this means he proceeds quickly to the world of Brahman from some other destination.
"There are many stages on the path in the scriptural texts concerning the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*).

This is the meaning: since the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) to be reached is one, if its attainment were possible by a path with few stages, the teaching of many paths would result in being purposeless; for a conscious being does not act toward that which can be attained through a simpler means.
Therefore, it is logical that the few [elements] should enter into the many, in a manner that does not contradict the majority. //1//
"Vāyu [is reached] after a year, by way of both the general and the specific.
In the absence of direct scriptural statement (śruti) and so forth, the textual order (pāṭha) serves as the regulator for the sequence;
moreover, the causality of Vāyu is heard in scripture only with respect to the mere act of ascending."

"He reaches the wind; for him, the wind parts there as much as the hole of a chariot wheel, and by that he ascends upwards"— thus, the upward ascent is heard to have the wind as its cause, but the reaching of the sun does not have the wind as its cause, because from the statement "he goes to the sun" there is only the perception of going to the sun.

Furthermore, the word "by him" (*tena*), which immediately follows and is syntactically connected to the action of ascending (*ūrdhvīkramaṇa*) already heard, is complete in its requirements and cannot be further connected with the action of the sun's movement. Nor is there any inconsistency in the sun's arrival without the word "by him," such that it would have to be supplied even though it is connected to something else.
In this regard, the reading found within the textual context beginning with "He goes to the world of Agni, he [goes] to the world of Vāyu," etc., serves as the restrictive factor.
Since there is no scriptural statement or other evidence to restrict the sequence to Agni, Vāyu, and Varuṇa based on their established capacities, this being the prima facie view, it is replied:
The word "upward" (ūrdhva) does not denote any particular world;
therefore, its qualification by the sun is appropriate with reference to the distinctions among those worlds.

This would be so if some distinct world were understood from the word "above" (ūrdhva); however, that term merely denotes the upper region and, being incomplete without a specific world, it is established as referring to the Sun, which is the name of a particular world. Thus, since the journey to the world of the Sun is caused by Vāyu, the sequence prescribed by the Śruti is fixed; it is established that the textual order (pāṭha) serves only to indicate the individual items and does not prevail over the sequence because it contradicts the Śruti.

The world of the year (*saṃvatsara-loka*) is not recited by the Vājasaneyins, and the world of the gods (*devaloka*) is not recited by the Chāndogyas; therefore, in order to conform to both traditions, both are included in the recitation. Because of its connection with the months, the year comes first, and the world of the gods follows last. For the month is not connected with the world of the gods, but rather with the year.

Therefore, because of the mutual connection between those two and because the year begins with the month, the sequence of months being established, the world of the gods (*devaloka*) follows after the year.
In that case, for the sake of immediate succession to the sun, one should read "from the world of the gods to Vāyu" instead of "from the year to the sun" in the place of the year and the sun.
The aphorism (*sūtra*), however, stating "from the wind to the worlds" (*vāyupamabdāt*), is indeed expressive here as well.

Nevertheless, this was stated solely with reference to the reading of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, which says, "Beyond a year, they reach Vāyu, who is below Āditya"; this is what he expresses by saying, "But [the text] says 'Vāyu from the year'. //2//
Varuṇa is [the presiding deity] over lightning because of their connection.
On the path beginning with light and ending with lightning, the lord of water (Ap-pati) is beyond lightning;
because of that connection, Indra and the others are likewise considered to be beyond the lord of water.
It has been established that newcomers reside at the end because there is no other place for them; likewise, Indra and others are recited as newcomers after the word *appatiḥ*. (3)
"They are conducting [souls], because of the indicative mark.
The light and so forth are indeed signs, because they resemble the signs on the path;
or rather, they may be the places of enjoyment for the sustainer (the deity), because they are worlds, and thus they are not conducting [souls].
For words such as "light" (*arcis*) have, in common worldly usage, a well-established application to insentient things like fire.

Furthermore, it is not possible for these [entities], being insentient, to possess an independent activity consisting of a regulated process of conveying [the soul], which would require prior intelligence—unlike the case of those [beings] who have you as their authority.
Therefore, because they are denoted by words used in the world, we consider them to be merely the spheres of experience for the supporting individual self (*jīvātman*).
Moreover, from the word *arciṣaḥ* (from the flame), an ablative case is understood;
for the ablative is never seen used for a cause (*hetu*), nor is the ablative ever observed when the cause lacks the quality [of being a source].
In expressions such as "bound because of dullness" (*jāḍyāt*), the ablative case in the sense of a cause (*hetu-pañcamī*) is observed when the words denote qualities (*guṇa-vacana*).
However, the words *arcis* (flame) and so forth do not denote qualities, such that their causality with respect to carrying [the soul] could be stated by means of the ablative.
Furthermore, since the status of being a point of departure (*apādānatva*) exists even for insentient things, they are not "conveyors" (*ativāhika*).

Nor does the fact that the non-human person (*amānava-puruṣa*) is seen to be a carrier with respect to lightning and so forth imply that the light (*arciḥ*) and other stages are also carriers, such that the non-human person would not be heard of as the carrier.
Since he is indeed heard of [as the carrier], we understand from this that the light and other stages do not possess the nature of carriers, just like lightning and the rest.

Therefore, it being argued that the light and other stages are merely places of enjoyment and not conductors (*ativāhika*), the following reply is given: "For those whose organs are withdrawn and who possess a subtle body, in their journey..."
There is no independence, nor are fire and the other elements guides, for they are insentient.
For such a regulated course belongs either to one who is himself discerning, or to one who is not discerning but is directed by a discerning person.

Now, living selves (jīvātman) that have departed—having left behind their gross bodies, possessing subtle bodies, with their aggregate of organs withdrawn—are not themselves discerning like those who are intoxicated or in a swoon; therefore, they could not proceed thus independently if the *arciḥ* and so forth [were merely paths].
Furthermore, whether they be road-signs such as the *śamī* or *kāraskara* trees, or places of enjoyment such as Mount Sumeru or Lake Anavatapta, in either case, because they are insentient,
they lack the independence to lead the eye.
Nor can another sentient leader be postulated beyond these, since sentience is possible for those [entities] mentioned in the scriptures.

Nor is it reasonable to say that the Supreme Lord alone [is the guide] and not others; for, because He is so utterly common to all, the world-protectors, the planetary deities (grahas), and so forth would be rendered ineffective.

Therefore, while the Supreme Lord’s status as the universal supervisor remains established, just as the independence of the world-protectors and others is determined according to their respective functions, so too here, in accordance with scriptural evidence, the meaning of the words is that the light (*arci*) and the others serve specifically as conducting guides (*ativāhika*).
This is correct.
It has been stated that this very point is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) characterized by the bypassing of the person who is not a man (*amānavapuruṣa*).
[The opponent objects: "Because the light (*arciḥ*) and so forth are not fixed."
For a path-marker is indeed fixed because it is non-deviant, whereas that which is unfixed is deviant.
Furthermore, in the word "arciṣaḥ" (from the flame), the ablative case denotes cause (*hetu*) and not point of departure (*apādāna*);
and its status as a quality (*guṇatva*) is due to its being dependent.
Furthermore, a restrictive rule should not be adopted based on Vaiśeṣika technical terminology, as that would contradict common worldly usage.
Moreover, in the phrase "they reach the rays" (te 'rcir abhisaṃbhavanti), only a mere relationship has been stated;
for when a word expresses a general sense and requires a specific qualification, [the context provides it].
By that which is a term of particularity, its corresponding generality is restricted.

Just as when one says, "Bring a Brahmin, he is to be fed," and upon the expectation of a specific [Brahmin], a word such as "Kaṇṭha" occurs in proximity to it, then by that word this [general injunction] is restricted; so it is here as well. // 4 // // 5 //
"By that very [Vaidyuta person], because of the scriptural statement.
Having reached the world of lightning, the non-human person who is the Vaidyuta leads him by himself, and not by Varuṇa or others;
for that is what is heard in scripture—the fact that he alone is the one who carries him.
However, Varuṇa and the others, being engaged in assisting him, are the carriers; thus there is a disparity in their roles, but not in their status as carriers—everything is now clear. //6//

Since the sequence of meaning is more authoritative than the sequence of the text, the sūtras are read according to the sequence of meaning: "Jaimini [holds that the person] beyond [the sun], because of its being primary";
"He leads these to Brahman"—thus there is doubt.

Does [the soul] go to the higher Brahman, or rather to the lower, the effected (kārya) Brahman? Jaimini considered that it goes to the higher Brahman alone by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi), because of the primary nature of the attainment of immortality and because the context concerns the higher [Brahman].

For in the phrase "he leads [them] to Brahman" (*brahma gamayati*), the neuter word *brahman* is primary because it is conventionally established in the sense of the supreme Brahman; thus, as long as this is possible, it is not appropriate to interpret it as referring to the effected (kārya) Brahman by means of attributing qualities (*guṇakalpanā*). Furthermore, the attainment of the fruit of immortality (*amṛtatva*) is not compatible with reaching the effected Brahman.
Because that [individual soul] is subject to death by virtue of being an effect;

furthermore, since in various passages the attainment of Prajāpati’s abode and so forth are spoken of with reference to the Supreme Brahman itself, they cannot possibly concern the lower Brahman, as that would contradict the context.
Nor is it correct to argue that movement toward the Supreme is impossible because it is already all-pervading and thus already attained.
For even when [a destination] has been reached, a motion that results in reaching is observed;

for example, when a monkey moves from the root to the top of a single *nyagrodha* tree and back from the top to the root, there occur continuous conjunctions and disjunctions with that very same *nyagrodha* tree.

Now, it is not correct to say that these [conjunctions and disjunctions] have the parts of the tree as their objects and not the *nyagrodha* tree itself; for if that were the case, the monkey would not be in conjunction with the *nyagrodha* tree at all.

Because a part of a banyan tree is joined with its own parts, and likewise, even for those parts that are currently visible, there is no conjunction with their own parts; by this sequence, [the process] terminates in the atoms which are the ultimate parts.
And since these are beyond the reach of the senses, in what indeed could this wretched conjunction take its place within the path of experience?
Therefore, even against one's will, in accordance with experience, one must accept that the understanding of Brahman as the fruit of attainment is indeed established.
Thus, although that Brahman has already been attained, it will become the object of the understanding for the sake of the fruit of attainment.

Furthermore, the plural number in the expression "in the worlds of Brahman" (brahmalokeṣu) is to be understood merely for the sake of grammatical correctness, even though [Brahman] is a single entity.
And the word *loka* should be understood in the sense of "beholding" or "light," rather than as a specific place characterized by a particular spatial arrangement.
Therefore, by the force of the instruction regarding the journey for the sake of attaining the Supreme Brahman, this is the meaning:

that one who has traveled by way of the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) through the power of knowledge and ritual action, having transcended the *Satyaloka*, reaches the Supreme Brahman—the cause of the world—which is the "world" (*loka*), meaning the light, that is to say, self-luminous.
The subtle body (*liṅga*) dissolves at that very place [Brahmaloka] upon reaching it; for there is no dissolution of the subtle body without such a destination.
Therefore, the Śruti says: "Reaching the Person, they reach their setting in the Person.
With this intention, the teacher Jaimini considered that the non-human being leads [the soul] to the Supreme Brahman.
Bādarī holds that [the soul goes] to the effected [Brahman], because such a movement is logically possible.
Bādarī, the seer of reality, perceived that since the effected Brahman has not been previously attained, the movement serves to reach what was not yet reached;
it leads one to Brahman, but not to the supreme [Brahman], because that is already attained as the very self of the universe.

Prior to the direct realization of the meaning of the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it is indeed logical that the individual soul (*jīvātman*), though in reality unconditioned, yet—due to being delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—conceives itself as if conditioned and, despite being non-different, as if different from the worlds. Thus, it attains through movement those worlds, such as the world of the Archis, which are other than its own nature and not yet attained.

However, for one who possesses the direct realization of the non-dual reality of Brahman, for whom the delusion of the appearance of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has dissolved, there is no destination, no movement, and no mover; what, then, could be consistent with what?

Therefore, the conjunctions and disjunctions of a banyan tree are non-demonstrable [as real entities], because the banyan tree, the monkey, their location, and the conjunctions and disjunctions occurring therein are mutually distinct.

Furthermore, even in that case, there is no "attainment of attainment," because when the prior attainment has been ceased by a disjunction born of action, a subsequent attainment arises precisely as something not previously attained.

Even this is, upon investigation, an expansion of ignorance that cannot be defined in any way; one who is a wise man, having realized the truth of non-duality (*advaita*) through its arising, does not entertain such notions.

If it is argued that even for the wise man of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña) prior to the fall of the body, the persistence of worldly attributes is accepted as a mere appearance, so too for the wise man until the fall of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), there persists the persistence of those attributes; and thus, because he has not yet attained what was unattained, the occurrence of a journey is logical, and upon reaching that destination, liberation occurs through the cessation of the subtle body, on the authority of scripture—[we reply:

no, because the departure [of the vital breaths] is denied for one who possesses the higher knowledge, as in: "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman; from him the vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here."
Just as the simultaneity of knowledge and the attainment of Brahman is heard in such passages as: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "Knowing the bliss of Brahman,

he fears nothing," "When he knows himself as 'I am Brahman,' he becomes all that," and "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness?"— since no sequence [of time] is heard, liberation belongs to one possessed of the higher knowledge.
The intention of the Śruti is clearly indicated by the fact that no other means are required;
and this is logical.

Indeed, when ignorance has been completely uprooted by the direct realization of the identity of the individual self with Brahman—which arises from the constant contemplation "All this is indeed Brahman, I am Brahman"—there remains nothing further to be done.
For one who possesses knowledge, the distinction between the goal to be reached and the traveler has ceased; in its absence, how could such a person proceed upon the path beginning with light?
Nor can the persistence of worldly attributes even in a mere semblance serve as a factor for proceeding there, since such proceeding would be merely accidental.
For one devoid of faith, actions whose results are visible in this world sometimes bear fruit and sometimes do not.

As for the fruits of those [actions] whose purpose is unseen (adṛṣṭārtha), what need is there to speak of them? This was stated in the first sūtra. Furthermore, the instruction regarding the cultivation of the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga) is not intended for an ignorant person seeking to attain the Supreme Brahman; thus, just as in the case of other obligatory rites (nityakarman) and the like, it would follow that his engagement in this [cultivation] would also be possible [only for such a person], yet this is not tenable because it cannot withstand logical analysis.
Is this [meditation on the path] an independent means for attaining the Supreme Brahman, or is it dependent upon that [Supreme Knowledge]?

It cannot be independent, because there is an explicit negation of any other path besides the realization of the Supreme Brahman: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; no other path for traveling exists.
However, if it is dependent upon Supreme Knowledge, does this cultivation of the path provide assistance toward the effect of that Knowledge, or toward the arising of the Knowledge itself?
First of all, [knowledge] cannot coexist with its own effect, because they are mutually contradictory due to having the domains of duality and non-duality respectively.

Nor can it be like sacrifice and so forth, for there is no scriptural statement that it is a direct means for attaining Brahman in the production of knowledge, as in the passage, "He leads these to Brahman.
As for sacrifice and the like, however, their status as auxiliary factors for the production of knowledge arises from their being heard in connection with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

Therefore, in accordance with the many scriptural citations presented and on account of logical consistency, the word *brahman*—whose primary sense is impossible here—must be understood through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the lower Brahman due to its proximity to [the higher] Brahman.
Thus, the use of the plural number in the phrase "in the worlds" is appropriate for the effected world of Brahman (*kāryabrahmaloka*);
for the supreme [Brahman], being partless, it is impossible even by way of such a medium.

If "world-ness" (*lokatva*) were established as residing in a specific configuration on a plane of enjoyment—like that of Ilāvṛtta and other regions—it could by no means be explained through yoga as being manifested [there].
Therefore, it is established that the venerable Bādarāyaṇa was a seer of what is right, whereas Jaimini was not a seer of what is right.

The many prattlings of those who lack authoritative means of knowledge are such that they claim the qualities of an all-pervading substance, as well as consciousness, bliss, and so forth, must themselves be all-pervading.

Arguments such as that the qualities of the Supreme Self possess both difference and non-difference from It, though repeated here for the sake of refutation, have been set aside by us as lacking authoritative basis. As for the construction of the text:

because the travelers (the individual selves) have the nature of the Inner Self (*pratyagātmatva*), [Brahman] is "inner" (*pratyak*) because it moves toward (*añcati*) each and every one; thus, Brahman exists within every object, and the travelers—the individual souls (*jīvātman*)—have That as their very self.

"But elsewhere it is secondary" (gauṇī): for even that which is based on etymology (yaugikī) is indeed secondary (gauṇī) when it depends upon qualities of connection. "Connection with pure limiting adjuncts" (viśuddhopādhisaṃbandham).
Conceptualizations such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth are to be understood as effects.
Although they are impure because they are effects, they are pure because they are causes of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).

"Regressing" (*pratisaṃcara*) refers to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); "practice" (*pratipatti*) refers to the intention toward practice; and "going" (*gati*) refers to movement, since the root *pad* has the sense of going.
*Abhisandhi* means intention (*tātparya*).
It refers to that Brahman whose name or designation is "fame" (*yaśas*).
[The phrase] "by breaking the previous sentence" [is explained as follows]:
The direct statement is more powerful than the context;
and this applies even to Brahman as possessing qualities—
meaning that it is for the purpose of praise.
He objects: "Is it not the case that even for one who has already gone, there is an ultimate state of being 'to-be-gone-to' (gantavyatā) characterized by another location?
The example of the banyan tree and the monkey has been established [as a response].
He refutes this, saying: "No;
because Brahman is devoid of all particularities.

This is the intended meaning: just as the whole of a banyan tree is subject to transformation through qualities born of karma that are characterized by arising and passing away, [so too would it be if Brahman were such].
Let this Supreme Self, which is eternally immutable and in whom the entire manifold of difference has been dispelled, be joined with conjunctions and disjunctions once again;
yet, unlike a banyan tree, He cannot be subject to conjunction and disjunction.
Conjunction and disjunction, however, are possible only for that which is conceptual—the causal world of Brahmā—and not for the Supreme.
He raises an objection: "Because of the scriptural statement that [Brahman] is the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world.
For the state of being the cause of origin and so forth is not possible for one who is unchanging; therefore, [Brahman] must be subject to modification.
And thus, its being an object of going would follow as a real possibility; this is the meaning.
He refutes this:
"No, because of the scriptural texts that negate specific distinctions."
The negation of distinctions possesses the fruit of the human goal (puruṣārtha) by virtue of pacifying all sufferings such as grief;
however, the injunction regarding origination and so forth is fruitless.
Therefore, it is logical that what is taught in proximity to that which possesses a fruit is stated solely for the sake of that [fruit].
And there is the Śruti text: "Seek to know That.

Therefore, by both scripture and reasoning, this sacred tradition is intent upon propounding Brahman as devoid of all distinctions, and not intent upon propounding [the world's] origination and so forth.
Consequently, the movement [of the soul] is not ultimately real.
Moreover, he says that this [notion of] "going" does not withstand scrutiny:
"And in the conceptualization of going...
The two positions regarding parts and modification are based on [the alternatives of] difference and non-difference.
Or [it may mean] "another" in the absolute sense.
Now, why is absolute non-difference not postulated? To this he says:
"Because of absolute identity."
For entities such as jars, being modifications of that [clay], are pervaded by the nature of clay as their inherent essence;
in the absence of that [nature], they do not exist, just as a *śiṃśapā* tree does not exist in the absence of "treeness.
Furthermore, in the two positions regarding modifications and parts, [the cause] exists together with those modifications and parts.
Because Brahman is stable and immovable, movement characterized by saṃsāra—whether as a modification (*vikāra*) or as a part (*avayava*)—is impossible.
For that which is stable by nature cannot become unstable.
Furthermore, the sense is that both identity and difference are impossible for a single entity due to their mutual contradiction.
Now, suppose the individual soul (jīva) were indeed different from Brahman;
thus, even though Brahman does not transmigrate, the transmigration of the soul would be postulated.
Having raised this alternative, he refutes it:
"He is atomic" means "he possesses intermediate magnitude.
This is because it is observed that things of intermediate magnitude, such as jars and the like, are non-eternal. [To this objection, the answer is: No.
Regarding the phrase "primary oneness" (*mukhyaikatva*):
since the contradictory properties of difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same thing, there is a difference in objects due to the difference in cognition and designation.
Because they are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), it is said to be non-different only figuratively; thus, its oneness is not primary—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, in the views that souls are either parts of Brahman, modifications of it, or entirely distinct from it, transmigratory existence would be real; consequently, since their essential nature would be lost upon liberation, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the destruction of the souls.

However, if they are illusory manifestations (vivarta) of Brahman, then Brahman alone is their true nature—just as the original object is the nature of its reflections—and since that [Brahman] is indestructible, there is no destruction of the souls.
Thus he says: "In all these [views]... [sarveṣveteṣu].

He introduces another opinion in order to refute it: "As for what is prattled by some, namely that the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites [are to be performed] even without the knowledge of Brahman."

For just as a fever caused by phlegm does not recur once it has been pacified through the depletion of the accumulated phlegm by means of purgatives and other treatments, provided that one avoids curd and other substances that cause the production of further phlegm;
so too, bondage caused by karma subsides when the accumulated karmas are exhausted through experience.

Since there is no performance of other karmas—which are the causes of bondage—and since an effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause, liberation is established by its own nature through the absence of bondage, just like health.

Furthermore, by performing obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites for the sake of destroying accumulated sins (*upāttadurita*), the transgression caused by sin (*duritanimittapratyavāya*) does not occur. And when no transgression arises, one whose mind is at ease will not engage in prohibited acts.
He refutes this as follows:
That is incorrect,
because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, scripture (*śāstra*) is the authority in this matter, and it teaches self-knowledge alone for one seeking liberation, not the aforementioned conduct.

And no logical proof is effective here, because since saṃsāra is beginningless, the accumulation of karma is also incalculable; and since its time of fruition is indefinite, it is impossible to exhaust it through experience.
Thus he says: "And this cannot even be reasoned about. [The opponent] objects:
"It might be so," [he says]; [to the objection] "it is eternal," he offers this rebuttal:
"Therefore, there is no contradiction" means as follows:

for if obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites were to exhaust even good deeds (*sukṛta*) just as they do evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*), then the injunctions regarding optional (*kāmya*) rites would result in being cast aside like water offered to the dead.
Indeed, there is no one among the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) or the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) who does not perform these obligatory and occasional rites.
Therefore, these [actions] do not contradict merit. He states this as a further elaboration: "And not from the performance of obligatory and occasional rites."
"And when right vision is absent":

for one who possesses right vision and is dispassionate, even while avoiding actions that are prompted by desire or prohibited, he destroys those that may occur through negligence by means of that very right vision.
Furthermore, when knowledge has reached maturity, he simply does not act at all; however, an ignorant person, though even skillful, acts out of negligence.
And even if it were performed, it would not be possible to exhaust [the karma]; this is the distinction.

Furthermore, if the identity of Brahman and the Self is not accepted as being knowable through knowledge—[that is,] if agency and enjoyership, which imply action and experience, are determined to be the very nature of the Self rather than being superimposed upon it, then they cannot be removed.
For an entity cannot be deprived of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because that would entail the destruction of the entity itself.
Nor can enjoyment, which possesses an existent intrinsic nature, be made non-existent;
indeed, even Śakra could not turn blue into non-blue. Thus it has been said:
"Because intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is unavoidable"—

the sense is that while it is impossible to remove an intrinsic nature, it is possible for true knowledge to remove an imputed, indeterminable (anirvacanīya) nature, just as the knowledge of the reality of the rope removes [the error of] a snake.
Not understanding this point, the opponent objects:
It might be argued that the effect consists in being an agent and an enjoyer. To this, he provides the resolution exactly as stated, clarifying the nature of what was not previously illuminated:
And that is not so;

because the relationship between agency, enjoyership, and the connection with their causes is eternal by way of latent capacity (*śakti*), there is the possibility that at some time these [qualities] will manifest, whereby pleasure and pain will be experienced.
Therefore, from such a possibility, how can there be certainty regarding liberation (*kaivalya*)? This is the meaning.
He refutes [the opponent's position] once more, setting it forth again for the sake of strengthening his own argument, and then critiques it:
"Even if there were non-difference from the other," etc. The remainder has a meaning that is not obscure. // 7 // // 8 // // 9 // // 10 // // 11 // // 12 // // 13 // // 14 //
"Badarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord] leads those who do not rely on symbols, because there are defects in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve.
Those whose resolves are not fixed on Brahman go [to other worlds] by means of the knowledge of the five fires; likewise, those who meditate on symbols shall proceed to the world of Brahman.
For there exist meditations on symbols (pratīka), such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and so forth;

those who possess these [meditations] are also entitled to go by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi), just like those who meditate on the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma). This is because, in the sūtra "There is no restriction for all," it is established that going occurs without distinction even in other meditations.
Nor is it the case that for these [practitioners of symbol-meditations], going is impossible as it is for those who know the supreme Brahman.

Nor is it an absolute rule that only those whose resolve (*kratu*) is directed toward Brahman attain the world of Brahman, while those whose resolve is not so directed do not; for even those who do not have such a resolve, provided they know the five fires, attain it.

Furthermore, these [meditations] are indeed "Brahman-resolves," because in every instance—such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman"—there is a pervasive connection with Brahman, and thus the state of having Brahman as one's resolve is possible.
Since a distinction in the fruit is possible even in the attainment of the world of Brahman—

given that it possesses parts and thus admits of degrees of excellence and deficiency— this being the position reached, it is replied: "Because of the progressive increase [of reward] and because they do not possess the nature of those whose meditation is on Brahman itself, the nameless ones shall lead the worshippers of symbols to the world of Brahman."
Let it be that even those who do not perform sacrifices dedicated to Brahman are led to the world of Brahman through the knowledge of the five fires, because of a specific scriptural statement;
for what indeed can a scriptural statement not accomplish? Yet, in this case, such a statement is absent.

Since the general rule of the scripture—“In whatever way one meditates upon Him, that very thing one becomes”—is established, an exception is not appropriate in the absence of a specific statement to the contrary.
Moreover, the worshiper of a symbol (pratīkopāsaka) does not meditate upon Brahman even though there is the accompaniment of the word "Brahman";
rather, he meditates upon a specific particularity such as the Name and so forth as having the form of Brahman.
Thus, this [meditation] is dependent on the Name and so forth, and not dependent on Brahman.
The elders maintain that a "pratīka" is the transference of a cognition whose original substrate is one thing onto another substrate.
Since the cognition whose substrate is Brahman has been transferred onto names and so forth, it is dependent upon the name.
Therefore, the worshiper of that [pratīka] does not have Brahman as his mental resolve (*kratu*), but rather has the name and so forth as his resolve.

Furthermore, even if they were all "sacrifices to Brahman" (*brahmakratu*), no progressive superiority among those who meditate on name and so forth would be possible due to their lack of distinction.
Nor is it the case that the sacrifice to Brahman is a sacrifice whose constituent parts are [the meditations on] its members, such that superiority could be described in relation to those members.
Therefore, excluding those wise ones who take a symbol (*pratīka*) as their support, the non-human being leads all others who take modifications (*vikāra*) as their support to the world of Brahman.

For there is no fault whatsoever in accepting that this twofold state—whereby, if the meaning were twofold, [the Self] leads some who rely on the parts (pratīka) but leads those wise ones who rely on the transformations (vikāra)—is due to the principle that "there is no fixed rule for all [meditations]. Thus, everything is clear. //15//
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Bhāmatī, a commentary on the Bhagavatpāda-bhāṣya, composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra. //3//
The Fourth Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya.
"Manifestation after having become [one with Brahman], on account of the word 'own' (svena).
Since agency belongs to that which was previously non-existent when it comes into being, and not to that which already exists.
Furthermore, because liberation is well-known as being a fruit, it is the emergence of another form;
the production (*niṣpatti*) of something previously non-existent, such as a jar, is its coming into being, but not the production of that which is absolutely existent or non-existent.
Indeed, neither the sky nor a flower in the sky are ever produced.
If liberation were the abiding of the self in its own nature, it could not be accomplished, because that [nature], being as eternally existent as space, lacks prior non-existence.
Nor can the absence of bondage be accomplished for it.
Because that which is of a void nature would, by being an effect, entail the consequence of being non-void;

and because liberation is established as a fruit, it is impossible for that which is not an effect to be a fruit. Thus, when it is argued that if liberation arises through some adventitious form, then its arising "by itself" (svena) is merely a restatement of what has already been obtained, the following is stated in reply: "For when meaningfulness is possible, one does not resort to meaninglessness."
The form of a bond is distinguished as being either existent or non-existent.

For verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about the understanding of what has not been previously apprehended; it is only described as a restatement (*anuvāda*) in some way due to the lack of any other recourse.

However, that which makes known the serene nature of the self—which is devoid of all worldly phenomena and distinguished from that very same [worldly] nature as being unserene—is not properly a restatement, since it brings about the understanding of what was not previously apprehended.
Nor is its production impossible.

For just as in the case of a pot or similar objects, the removal of bondage is established through conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*), since it is well-known in the world;
however, the lack of establishment due to the inability to withstand critical analysis (*vicārāsahatā*) is equal in both cases.
Indeed, it has been stated more than once that what is non-existent cannot arise.

"He becomes blind" indicates the state of dreaming, due to the absence of activity of the external senses. "As it were, he weeps" indicates the waking state, because its nature consists of suffering, grief, and so forth.
"He has gone to utter destruction" refers to deep sleep.
The particle *eva* has the sense of "and" (*ca*) when it does not imply restriction (*anavadhāraṇa*). // 1 // 2 //

The Self [is meant], because of the context. Now, an objection is raised: since the sequence "having reached the light, he manifests in his own form" is heard in the scripture, the attainment of the light must be distinct from the manifestation of one's own form; thus, even if [the self] were material, there would be no contradiction with liberation.
This might be so if it were heard in scripture that [the self], having attained light, would abandon it;

even if such a word were supplied, its statement would be purposeless if it were not abandoned. Furthermore, since it is understood [from the text] "by its own form, which is light itself," and because if that light were a material entity it would be subject to death due to being a modification (vikāra)—and thus liberation would be impossible—this being the position reached, the reply is given: although the primary meaning of the word "light" is established in the material element, [it does not refer here to that].
Nevertheless, by virtue of the context and the sentence, it is appropriate here [to understand this] as referring to the self alone.

For, because of the association with the term "supreme" (*para*) in the expression "the supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*), and because the quality of being "supreme" applies to Brahman alone when it is independent, whereas in the case of other lights it is "supreme" only in relation to something else,
the Self alone is understood here from this sentence;
furthermore, the context has already been stated.
That which, having attained [something], becomes perfected—this is like the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open.
Therefore, it is well said that the liberated one has attained the Light. //3//
Because it is seen as non-different.

Although it has been established in various places that the individual soul (jīvātman) is not distinct from Brahman, [the author] nevertheless says this for the purpose of resolving the designation of the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) in the passage "He moves about there," as well as the designation of the relationship between the attainer and the object to be attained (*sampattṛ-sampattavya-bhāva*). //4//
Jaimini [holds that the final goal] is through the Brahmanic [state], on account of the introductory statements and so forth.
An "introductory statement" (upanyāsa) is the mention of what is already known, such as, "That Self which is free from evil," and so on.
Likewise, an injunction (vidhi) is the making known of what was previously unknown.
"Just as he moves about there, laughing and rejoicing," and "he attains freedom of movement in all worlds"— this is an injunction intended to make known what was previously unknown.
The designation "the All-Knowing One" and "the Lord of All" is a descriptive statement.
This is not a mere enumeration (uddeśa), because there is no other thing to be enjoined; nor is it an injunction (vidhi), because it is not something to be brought about,
as it is designated as already established.
By the force of that etymological explanation, this meaning is understood: "these" refers to the introductory statements and so forth;
"from these causes";
"the Supreme Lord" [is perceived] through forms consisting of existence and non-existence, which are real.
"By means of one's own [meditations], one becomes liberated," so indeed Jaimini has said.

Nor do the attributes such as freedom from sin, which belong to the Self whose nature is consciousness and consists of non-existence (abhāva), nor the attributes such as omniscience, which belong to the Self whose nature is existence (bhāva), destroy non-duality.

For the attributes do not differ from the substratum; otherwise, the relationship between substratum and attribute would cease to exist, like that between a cow and a horse. Thus said the teacher Jaimini. //5//
"Audulomi [maintains] that [the soul is] by means of consciousness alone, because it has that as its essence.
For a single [entity] cannot possess manifold forms; since it is one, it cannot be manifold.
Due to mutual contradiction, the coexistence of difference and non-difference is impossible."
For it is not possible for a single self to possess multiple ultimate properties.
If these [properties] were distinct from the self, the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) would be contradicted by the consequence of duality (*dvaita*).
On the other hand, if they are not distinct, then because they are non-different from the one self, they too could not be mutually distinct.
It would either be like the nature of the self,
or its nature would have to be divided,
because it is non-different from the divided [parts], just like the forms of blue and yellow.

Nor is it tenable to claim that the attributes do not differ from the substratum—the self—but differ among themselves; for, since they are non-different from the substratum due to its non-difference [from them], it would follow that they too are non-different.
Alternatively, if they were different, it would follow that the substratum itself must also be different, as has already been stated.
It has been established in the first Sūtra that difference and non-difference cannot coexist in a single locus because they are mutually contradictory.

Furthermore, although things of the nature of non-existence do not obstruct non-duality, since evil (pāpma) and the like are conceptual (*kālpnika*) and their definition is dependent upon that [non-duality], they too are conceptual; thus, their status as real attributes (*taddharmatā*) does not apply.
By this, qualities such as having true desires, omniscience, and universal lordship are also explained as being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Therefore, Auḍulomi held that for the self which, upon liberation, becomes established as the nature of pure consciousness alone— devoid of all manifoldness (prapañca) and beyond verbal designation— the designations such as "free from evil," "possessing true desires," and so forth, are merely empty of objective referents. This is what was stated:
These qualities, such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth, arise solely from verbal conceptualization (śabdavikalpa); they are not even empirical (sāṃvyavahārika). //6//
"Even so, because of this presentation, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] there is no contradiction due to its prior existence.
This extreme audacity of Auḍulomi is not tolerated;
for even though the teacher Bādarāyaṇa might tolerate that opinion, he does not accept it.
With the words "even so," he accords with the view of Auḍulomi; however, not tolerating [his] arrogance, he says:
"with respect to conventional usage."
This is what is meant: it is true that the Self consists solely of ultimate bliss and pure consciousness;

however, qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpman*) and having true desires (*satyakāmatva*), though not ultimately real because they are dependent on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), are nonetheless established in common worldly experience through conventional means of knowledge (*vyāvahārikapramāṇa*). Therefore, they are not absolutely non-existent, such that the words expressing them would be unreal like the expression "the head of Rāhu. This is the sense. //7//
But it is from mere volition alone, for so the scripture declares.
In the world, volition is seen to accomplish an object without dependence on effort; here, however, that [effort] is determined to be absent due to the lightness [of the process].
For in the world, it is observed that one who desires to accomplish some purpose exerts effort; exerting effort, he strives; and striving, he attains that purpose—such is the sequence seen.
However, the desired object does not present itself immediately after the mere wish.
Therefore, even by means of scripture, which conforms to worldly practice, such a sequence must be accepted for the knower as well.

The restriction, however, that [the departure occurs] "from mere volition" (saṃkalpād eva) is made in view of the worldly weightiness of effort; for due to the power of knowledge, the effort of the knower is lightened. That which is light is, as it were, non-existent.
This might be so.

Just as a woman brought forth by mere mental conception serves as the cause for the emission of the final element among those possessed of lust, so too will fathers and others, though brought forth by his own volition (*saṃkalpa*), be imagined to serve their respective functions; therefore, they are not merely produced by volition alone.

Indeed, there are certain effects that must be accomplished by the actual substance of a thing, such as tooth-marks, jewel necklaces, and the like, which are accomplished by the actual substance of a woman.
However, some effects are to be accomplished through gnosis (*jñāna*), such as the emission of the final element (*caramadhātu-visarga*) and the horripilation (*romaharṣa*) mentioned above.

In that regard, when the father and so forth are brought forth by mere mental intention, let those effects be accomplished by that gnosis alone; however, they ought not to be [physically] accomplished by them.
For the jeweled necklaces and other such things do not become accomplished by the actual woman in the way that horripilation and the like occur for one who is lustful. This is what was stated:

When it is argued that there is "abundant enjoyment," it is replied: The rising of the ancestors and others occurs from [the deceased's] will alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect;
nor is there any sublation here by inference, since that very inference is sublated by scripture.

For scripture, which makes its own object known independently of other means of knowledge, cannot be sublated by another means of knowledge. Inference, however, while requiring as part of its own causal complex— that is, among its constituent factors— the condition that its object not be sublated by another means of knowledge (just as it requires the property of being a predicate of the subject, *pakṣadharmatva*), is sublated by scripture, which contradicts it, through the destruction of that very complex.
For this very reason, the inference regarding the purity of human skull-bones and the like is untenable, as its object is contradicted by scripture.
Therefore, it is correct that for the wise, through the power of their knowledge, the presence of ancestors and others occurs by mere volition alone.
Thus say those who follow the scriptures: "Who indeed, apart from the power of yoga, drinks up the ocean like Agastya, or creates the Daṇḍaka forest like him?"
Therefore, everything is clear. // 8 // // 9 //
Bādari maintains that there is non-existence [of the body], for it is so stated;
because of the qualification "by the mind" which excludes connection with anything else, Bādari’s view is that the separation from the body and senses occurs for the knower.

Jaimini holds that the state of being manifold is either due to a difference of minds arising from the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), or it is merely a figurative praise; for since such [multiplicity] is impossible in the qualityless knowledge of the earth (*bhūmavidyā*), even a non-existent quality may indeed serve as a basis for praise—this is the sense, because of the mention of "alternatives" (*vikalpa*).
For multiplicity is logical only when there is a difference of bodies and senses.
And when the actual meaning is possible, it is not appropriate for there to be mere praise that is devoid of purpose.
For a manifold manifestation that is more distinct does not occur through a mere difference in the mind as it does through a difference in body and sense-faculties.
For this very reason, the Paurāṇikas record that Saubhari, having manifested various bodies, sported simultaneously with the fifty daughters of Māndhātṛ.
And when the actual object exists, a mere figurative praise is not understood to be purposeless.
And its meaningfulness is possible;

for although this [verse] is recited in the context of the earthly knowledge (*bhaumavidyā*) as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), nevertheless, by means of this sovereignty belonging to the state possessing qualities (*saguṇāvasthā*), the very knowledge devoid of qualities is praised prior to that [earthly knowledge].
Moreover, a qualification does not function solely by way of excluding connection with anything else.
Just as Caitra is an archer, so Jaimini maintained that for those possessed of sovereign power, the conjunction of mind, body, and sense organs occurs necessarily. 11.
"Bādarāyaṇa holds that it is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice; for he perceives both scriptural passages—

one concerning the sphere of the mind alone, stating 'by the mind,' and another concerning the distinction of body and senses, stating 'he becomes onefold, he becomes threefold'— and thus Bādarāyaṇa, who maintains there is no fixed rule, does not accept the two preceding restrictive views."
This is because it conforms to two types of scriptural authority (*śruti*).
Furthermore, in such cases, a qualification cannot be understood as merely excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

For, in the case of sensual pleasures, men's delighting with the body together with the mind and the sense organs is already established; thus, there is no doubt regarding the connection with the mind (*manoyoga*), and its exclusion would be redundant.
However, once the connection with the mind is established, its purposefulness is understood through the exclusion of other [connections].
Therefore, it is appropriate here that there is an exclusion of connection with anything else (anyayogavyavaccheda), just as in the expression "he sees with his left eye.
The phrase "like the twelve-day sacrifice" (dvādaśāhavat) [is used].
The twelve-day sacrifice is understood to be a *sattra* when there is an injunction regarding sitting (*āsana*) and the means of subsistence (*upāyi*),
and it is understood to be an *ahīna* when there is an injunction regarding the act of sacrificing (*yajati*).

By the injunction "those desiring prosperity should undertake [it] for twelve days," and by the statement "those who, knowing thus, undertake the sacrificial session (*sattra*)," it is understood that the twelve-day rite is a *sattra* involving many performers.

Likewise, by the injunction "one should cause him who desires offspring to sacrifice with that same twelve-day rite," and because of the fixed number of performers, its status as an *ahīna* (non-*sattra*) is also understood, just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the two-night rite" and so forth.
Now, due to the absence of body and senses, the wise one experiences a subtle enjoyment through the mind alone, like a dream.
Why? Because of logical consistency and because of the scriptural statement, "With the mind, he [sees] these.
If, on the other hand, there were no experience as in deep sleep, this scriptural statement would not be tenable.
Nor is there enjoyment as in the case of one possessing a body, because the appropriation of a body and so forth would be purposeless;
for enjoyment is complete only for one who possesses a body.
The phrase "because it is logical here as well" should be supplied [to complete the argument].
This has been stated in two Sūtras:
"In the absence of a body, [the state] is possible as in the case of the intermediate state (saṃdhyavat);
in its presence, it is like the waking state."
Thus [ends the section]. 12 // 13 // 14 //

"The penetration [of the Lord] is like that of a lamp; for thus it is shown. Although this cognitional self (*vijñānātman*) is in reality non-different from the Supreme Self, it has attained the state of a beginningless individual soul (*jīva*) through the limitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is imagined by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) and is spatially restricted. Being thus restricted, and possessing an internal organ, it enters other bodies—even those created by its own nature—which exist in various locations and are situated in different regions. It does so together with its internal organ, just as a lamp enters various places. For the scripture shows it thus: "Just as the wind enters a single fire, so does He enter all beings" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3). Furthermore, the text "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22) shows that the inner controller is one and the same in all bodies. Therefore, it is established that the Lord, being omnipresent, is the inner controller of all bodies. Thus ends the section on the inner controller. Now begins the section on the size of the soul. Here, the following doubt arises: Is this cognitional self, which is the transmigrating agent, atomic (*aṇu*), or is it of intermediate size (*madhyama-parimāṇa*), or is it all-pervading (*vibhu*)? What is the conclusion? It must be atomic. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching of departing, going, and returning. For the departure of this soul is taught: "When he departs, he departs together with the breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Its going is taught: "He, becoming minute, passes beyond this world" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2). Its returning is taught: "Having come back from that world, he reaches this world" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2). These three—departing, going, and returning—are possible only for an atom, not for something of intermediate size or for the all-pervading. Moreover, because of the scriptural teaching of its being supported by another. For it is taught that this soul is supported by another: "Mounted upon the prāṇa, the self moves about" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be supported by another. Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its having parts. For it is taught that this soul has parts: "The lower one, consisting of mind, having the form of light, is man-sized" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2). And it is impossible for the partless and all-pervading to have parts. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being measured. For it is taught that this soul is measured: "Smaller than a grain of rice, smaller than a grain of barley, smaller than a mustard seed, smaller than a canary seed or the kernel of a canary seed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3). And it is impossible for the partless and all-pervading to be measured. Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its passing out through the skull. For it is taught that this soul passes out through the skull: "He passes out through the skull" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to pass out through the skull. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a part. For it is taught that this soul is a part: "A part of this immortal is what exists as the living being in the midst of the world" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.13). And it is impossible for the partless and all-pervading to be a part. Moreover, because of the scriptural teaching of its entering. For it is taught that this soul enters: "He, having entered within, rules all this from within" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to enter. Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its being minute. For it is taught that this soul is minute: "This person of the size of a thumb is the inner self in the midst of the body" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.12). And it is impossible for the partless and all-pervading to be minute. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a witness. For it is taught that this soul is a witness: "The seer does not see death nor illness nor pain" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a witness. Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its being an agent. For it is taught that this soul is an agent: "Desiring this world, he performs austerity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be an agent. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a knower. For it is taught that this soul is a knower: "The knower of the field knows the field" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.1). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a knower. Moreover, because of the scriptural teaching of its being subject to bondage and liberation. For it is taught that this soul is subject to bondage and liberation: "One who is bound goes to the worlds of action; one who is liberated attains immortality" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.8). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be subject to bondage and liberation. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a transmigrator. For it is taught that this soul is a transmigrator: "He, having departed from here, reaches a good or bad birth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.7). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a transmigrator. Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a hearer, thinker, and knower. For it is taught that this soul is a hearer, thinker, and knower: "It hears, it thinks, it knows" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.9). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a hearer, thinker, and knower. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a perceiver. For it is taught that this soul is a perceiver: "The perceiver of sight, the perceiver of hearing, the perceiver of mind, the perceiver of intellect" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.29). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a perceiver. Moreover, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a doer. For it is taught that this soul is a doer: "The doer of good deeds becomes good" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a doer. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being an enjoyer. For it is taught that this soul is an enjoyer: "The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the mover" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.12). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be an enjoyer. Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a ruler. For it is taught that this soul is a ruler: "He rules all this from within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22). And it is impossible for the all-pervading to be a ruler. Also, because of the scriptural teaching of its being a controller. For it is taught that this soul is a controller: "He who dwells in the eye, yet is within the eye, whom the eye does not know, whose body the eye is, and who controls the eye from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.1
It cannot simultaneously envelop [itself],

nor can it even create another self; for if that which is being created were distinct from the creator, it would not be a self, and if it were a self, there could be no relationship of agent and object, since duality is the basis of such a distinction.

Nor does it create another internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) therein, because that which is being created lacks the status of being its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Indeed, this [individual] is already encompassed by an innate, beginningless internal organ; it cannot now become connected with a presently existing internal organ as its limiting adjunct.
Therefore, just as a wooden machine, when presided over by a conscious operator, follows his will; so too does this [internal organ].

Thus, it being argued that emanated bodies (*nirmāṇa-śarīra*) must also possess sense faculties, the following reply is given: "The state of being a body could never exist without being the locus of experience;
since it has been stated that the state of being a body is threefold, and that [threefold nature] is logically applicable even to the omnipresent [Lord]."

The scriptural passage stating, "He becomes threefold, fivefold, sevenfold, ninefold," and so forth, which describes the manifold state of the knower, is possible only when there is a connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhis) consisting of diverse bodies and sense organs; it does not apply to a difference in the causeless [Self]. For a chariot-driver, who drives after having constructed various different machines, is not designated as being manifold [on account of those machines]. Furthermore, the nature of being a body consists in being the locus of experience, and this is not applicable to machines, which are not loci of experience.
Therefore, he creates other bodies;
nor do those [bodies] function on the side of the body as presided over by him.

Furthermore, for the wise one who is omnipresent and whose ignorance has virtually dissolved—unlike an ordinary person—there is no such mastery over an innate internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) by virtue of which his innate internal organ would enter into a connection with another adventitious internal organ.

Therefore, it is logical that the wise one— the controller of all, the lord of all, whose resolve is true— having fashioned bodies together with their senses and internal organs, and having entered them all at once, dwells liberated in those worlds through each respective sense-organ and internal organ.

The illustration "like a lamp" (pradīpavat) refers to the metaphorical attribution of oneness to individual lamps, despite the fact that there is a distinction between those existing in different wicks due to their distinct individualities.
Similarly, the meaning of the reflection is that the wise one considers the individual soul (jīvātman) to be one even when there is a difference of bodies.
The phrase "following a single mind" means "functioning according to a single intention. //15//
One who is perfected and solitary is called "liberated.
However, the possibility of such a state for him [the individual soul] does not exist because it contradicts the Śruti; thus, he raises an objection against the aforementioned point with the words:
"But how can there be liberation for one who is like water? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).

The form *salilaḥ* is derived from the nominal stem *salila-* by applying the suffix *kvip* in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*) according to the rule *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*, followed by the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class).
What is meant is this: just as water poured into the ocean attains identity with it, so too does the seer [attain identity] with Brahman.
To this, the following Sūtra provides the answer:

"It refers to either deep sleep or union, for it is made manifest [in scripture]. Among these scriptural passages, some refer to deep sleep and others to union (sampatti), because that is the context in which they occur.

The scriptural accounts of lordly power (aiśvarya), however, refer to the state resulting from the ripening of knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā); whereas the intention regarding liberation refers to the persistence of that state [of liberation] even during that [intermediate] condition, just as at twilight, when one perceives the dawn, one uses the designation "day. //16//
[The liberated soul] is excluded from the activity of governing the world, because of the context and because of its non-proximity [to that function].

On account of scriptural texts such as "self-sovereignty" (svārājya) and "acting according to desire" (kāmacāra), it may be unrestrained; yet, even in this state, one who is still a seeker (sādhaka) has his accomplishment dependent upon the Lord regarding his own specific duties.

From such scriptural passages as, "He attains self-sovereignty," "All the gods bring him tribute," and "He becomes one who moves at will in all worlds," it is understood that the sovereignty of the knower—like that of the Supreme Brahman—is independence from others.
Now, one might object: how can this sovereignty, obtained through the meditation on Brahman, be dependent on Brahman rather than being its very nature?
For entities whose birth is dependent upon a cause do not, in their own effects, depend upon their own cause.
But in this case, they are indeed independent;
as it has been said: "A jar depends upon the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth for its birth, but for the act of carrying water, it has no dependence on them."

Nor is it the case that because the attainment of sovereignty by the wise depends upon the Supreme Lord, their sovereignty becomes subordinate to Him— such that the wise, in their own activities, would become dependent on the Supreme Lord just as worldly kings are dependent on a Great King.
Indeed, there is no rule whatsoever that the nature of a thing must be inferior to the nature of that upon which its production depends.
For we observe those who are equal to Him and even those who are superior; thus, a disciple is seen to be either equal to or superior to his teacher.
Furthermore, wicked vassals whose sovereignty depends upon the king are seen to rival the kings or even to conquer them.
Therefore, in this case, although there may indeed be no learned men superior to the Supreme Lord due to His unsurpassed sovereignty, let it be granted that there may be those equal to Him.
And thus, they are not dependent on that [the Lord].

For there is no mutual dependence among things that stand as co-principals. Therefore, being independent, they would proceed even toward the creation of the world through their own activity. To this, it is replied: "Because of their eternity, because of their independence, and also because of the Vedic revelation and its initial context."
And because of the consensus of the learned, the dependence upon the Supreme Lord is established.

For the effect characterized as the creation of the world must belong either to that which has the nature of the cause alone, or to that which has the nature of both cause and effect. In that case, since that which possesses both natures depends upon a root cause for its own production, one must accept that the already established Supreme Lord alone is the cause; thus, let Him alone be the single cause of the world, because He, being eternal, is independent of any cause of His own and possesses an established capacity.
The learned ones, however, possess the capacity for conceptualization regarding the creation of the world;
yet their status as creators of the world is not heard in scripture,
whereas that of the venerable Supreme Lord alone is indeed heard.
For all those scriptural passages proceed with reference to that very [one] alone.

Furthermore, it is never observed that those who are equally principal possess a uniform consensus; thus, when one desires to create, the other would simultaneously desire to dissolve, resulting in creation and dissolution occurring non-sequentially.
Nor would there be any contradiction in both being lords.
However, there is no fault [in our position], because under the sovereignty of that one [Lord], all those who conform to His intention attain unanimity.

In this regard, since those who have acquired their power through causes and whose births are dependent on instruments are unequal due to the perceived distinctions among them, He alone—who possesses eternal sovereignty—is their overlord; thus, the wise are dependent upon Him and are not masters of the Supreme Lord’s activity, namely, creation and dissolution. //17//
Anticipating and refuting the seed of doubt held by the opponent, [the author] states:
"If it be argued that this is because of direct instruction, we say no, because of the mention of those who abide in the spheres of office.

Since sovereignty is dependent upon the Supreme Lord, therefore self-rule consists merely in the powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth, which are inferior to Him, and not in the state of being a creator of insentient matter.
Because of the principle already stated. //18//
And it exists within the modifications; for thus it speaks of its abiding:
"Such is its greatness" refers to the form existing within modification, while "greater than that" refers to the unmodified form.

Likewise, the phrase "one foot of it is all beings" refers to its form as existing within the realm of transformation, while the phrase "its three feet are the immortal in heaven" speaks of its unchanging form. //19//

Furthermore, others point to the Śruti and Smṛti which show that the form of the Blessed Lord is indeed changeless, and those [texts] have been cited. This is what is meant: if you say that when Brahman with attributes (saguṇa) is meditated upon, its attribute of being "unrestricted" (niravagraha) actually exists [in reality], and therefore the one who knows should attain that state of being unrestricted—this is refuted by the following.
Just as when Brahman is meditated upon with its modifications, the modificationless form that exists in reality is not attained— for what reason?
Because the meditator lacks the corresponding resolve—
so too, by meditating on its qualities, the state of being free from all limitations (niravagrahatva) that exists in reality is not attained.
Because in the meditations on the principles (tattva), the person is the agent;

and because for the meditator there is no such agency, since the state of being unrestrained is not within the scope of the injunctions for meditation, and because in meditations there is an absence of human independence due to their dependence on injunctions—or else, if there were independence, it would follow that [the knowledge] would be merely intuitive (prātibha);
and also because of the indicative mark of equality in respect to enjoyment alone.

The creation of the world is not only due to the dependence of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) upon the Lord; it is also because of the indicative mark of the designation [in scripture] which declares equality with that Supreme Lord through mere direct enjoyment.
"They protect" (*avanti*) means they nourish (*prīṇayanti*), that is to say, they cause them to enjoy (*bhojayanti*).
He raises an objection in order to introduce another Sūtra: "But this being so, because [the power] is surpassable" (sātiśayatvāt).
That which exists together with a surpassing excellence (*atiśaya*) belongs to the knower; thus, the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the wise person is surpassable.
And whatever effect possesses excellence, such as worldly sovereignty, by this it has been stated that [the world] is an effect.
And thus, because it is an effect, it follows that it must be finite; however, that is not tenable, because those who know it proceed toward it with the conviction of its infinity. //21//
To this, he recites the following:
"Non-return, on account of the scriptural statement; non-return, on account of the scriptural statement.
Do you seek to prove that the sovereignty of those who have reached the world of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light is limited?

Or is it that the attainment of this world from the world of Brahmā, as if from the world of the Moon, implies that liberation has an end? In the former case, it is a proof of what is already established; in the latter, however, there is a contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti.
And because the gradual liberation of those of such a kind is established [in scripture], he says—
referring to those devoted to the single meditation on the meaning of the sentence "That thou art"— "of those whose darkness has been destroyed by perfect knowledge."
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is darkness (*tamas*).
The direct realization of Brahman free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).
He states that this is not a product characterized by abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpāvasthāna*), such that it would be impermanent:
"Always established" (nityasiddha). //22//

O wise ones, let this work of Vācaspati—which has as its subject matter the collection of Śaṅkara’s commentaries—be respectfully contemplated; for it shatters the host of Asura-like opponents who exceed all ignorance and its adjuncts, and by which the nectar of Brahman is attained from the ocean of the Vedas through the path of right reasoning. What envy can there be toward one's own true interests? (1)
Having crossed the ocean of ignorance for those desiring to attain the true nature of Brahman,
I have fulfilled their heart's desire by acting as the helmsman of the boat of political ethics.
[That which was [composed] by means of the Nyāyakaṇikā, Tattvasamīkṣā, and Tattvabindu, and by means of the treatises on Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta. //3//
I have performed this great merit; its abundant fruit is now offered by me. By means of this, may the Supreme Lord be pleased. //4//
He made his fame inaccessible even in thought to other kings by the mere raising of an eyebrow;
he himself was an expert in the scriptures and possessed a treasury of wealth filled with a flood of gold.
Since other lords of men desire to emulate his deeds but are unable to do so, I have composed this work concerning that illustrious King Nṛga, whose fame is most exalted. (6)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāmatī*, a commentary on the *Bhāṣya* of the venerable Śaṅkara, composed by the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra.
